P2000: A NOx adsorber (lean NOx trap) collects nitrogen oxides while a lean-running engine produces them and turns them into nitrogen during short rich purges. P2000 reports that the trap on bank 1 no longer stores or converts enough NOx; CARB wants this flagged before tailpipe NOx passes a fixed multiple of the standard.
Sooted or drifting oxygen sensors that misjudge trap loading and purges
NOx trap poisoned by sulphur or aged by heat
Engine software that sets the code without a real fault (update available on some models)
Rich purges or desulphation not completed, e.g. because of short trips
Often accompanied by oxygen sensor codes P2A00/P2A01
P2001: P2001 belongs to the second cylinder bank: the NOx storage catalyst fed by bank 2 has lost so much capacity that it no longer holds and reduces the nitrogen oxides of lean running. The code is only possible on V or boxer engines that give each bank its own trap.
Bank 2 NOx trap poisoned by sulphur or thermally aged
Oxygen or NOx sensor on bank 2 reading wrongly
Rich purges on bank 2 repeatedly interrupted
P2002: Diesel Particulate Filter Efficiency Below Threshold (Bank 1)

P2002 means the particulate filter on bank 1 lets too much soot through, typically because the substrate is cracked, partly melted, emptied or bypassed. CARB requires diesel OBD to flag a filter whose filtering performance lets PM emissions exceed the limit.
Filter substrate cracked or melted, often after an uncontrolled regeneration
Faulty differential pressure sensor or leaking sensor hoses on pressure-based systems
Visible soot at the tailpipe in severe cases
P2003: Diesel Particulate Filter Efficiency Below Threshold (Bank 2)

P2003 is set when the particulate filter of bank 2 lets too much soot slip through, which almost always points to a cracked, partly melted, hollowed-out or bypassed core. Separate filters per bank are uncommon, so the code is rare.
Bank 2 filter core cracked or melted after an overheated regeneration
Filter on bank 2 removed, emptied or bypassed
PM sensor or differential pressure measurement on bank 2 giving false values
Visible soot at the tailpipe with a large leak
P2004: Intake Manifold Runner Control Stuck Open (Bank 1)

Intake manifold runner control (IMRC) uses flaps in the intake manifold; petrol engines switch runner length or tumble, diesels close swirl flaps at low load. P2004 means the flaps on bank 1 stay open when the ECM has commanded them closed, judged from the position feedback.
Flap shaft sticking, worn or separated inside the manifold
Runner control valve contaminated or corroded
Vacuum hose or actuator diaphragm leaking
P2005: Intake Manifold Runner Control Stuck Open (Bank 2)

P2005 is the bank 2 version of the stuck-open check, so it only exists on V and boxer engines with a flap set per cylinder bank. The ECM has commanded the flaps on bank 2 closed, but the position feedback says they stayed open.
Cracked or loose vacuum hose to the bank 2 flap actuator
Moisture in the flap potentiometer giving a false position (Audi 4.0 TFSI)
Flap shaft corroded or seized in the open position
Torn diaphragm in the vacuum actuator
Less pulling power at low engine speed
Rpm limit on some Audi V8 engines
P2006: Intake Manifold Runner Control Stuck Closed (Bank 1)
P2006 means the intake manifold runner or swirl flaps on bank 1 stay closed when the ECM has commanded them open. Closed flaps choke the engine at higher load, so this is the case that costs power.
Flaps or shafts seized by deposits or wear
Runner control valve stuck from contamination
Electric actuator or its linkage failed
Loss of power at higher rpm
P2007: Intake Manifold Runner Control Stuck Closed (Bank 2)

P2007 reports that the runner or tumble flaps of bank 2 have not opened although the ECM asked for it. Because closed flaps narrow the intake path, the fault shows up mainly as missing power near the top of the rev range.
Torn diaphragm in the bank 2 vacuum actuator
Flap shaft seized by corrosion or deposits
Grease leaking from an integrated tumble valve actuator (Subaru Impreza/Crosstrek)
Vacuum supply or control valve not working
Slight loss of power at high rpm
P2008: P2008 is the general circuit and open-circuit code for whatever drives the bank 1 flaps: a vacuum solenoid, a motor or a smart swirl actuator.
Spread or corroded terminal in the actuator or valve connector
Broken control or supply wire to the bank 1 actuator
Open winding in the solenoid valve or actuator motor
Faulty output stage in the engine control module
Flaps stay in their rest position, less low-end torque or top-end power
P2009: Intake Manifold Runner Control Circuit Low (Bank 1)

P2009 narrows the bank 1 flap control fault down to a low signal, which in practice means the control line has found a path to ground. GM's 2018 diesel tables flag a resistance to ground below 0.5 Ω in 12 of 15 checks every 100 ms (Type B), and the 2014 Cruze diesel waits until the short has lasted more than 3 s.
Control wire chafed through and touching ground
Internal short in the solenoid or actuator motor
Leaking integrated tumble valve actuator (Subaru Impreza/Crosstrek)
Water or corrosion in the actuator connector
Flaps cannot be switched, uneven running at low speed
P200A: P200A is the functional check of the bank 1 flaps: the circuit is fine, but the flaps do not reach or report the expected positions. GM's 2018 diesels learn both end stops at key-off and fail if the closed stop lies outside 81–92 percent or the raw signal outside 25–40 percent of 5 V, or if a stroke takes over 5 s (coolant at least 60 °C, Type B).
Flap actuator worn, slow or failed
Broken or sticking linkage or flap inside the manifold
Weak battery disturbing the actuator relearn (Kia V6)
Control software that needs an update (FCA 3.0 diesel)
Weaker response at low or high engine speed
P200B: P200B judges whether the flaps of bank 2 move as commanded and settle where they should; it needs a V engine whose second bank has its own flap set or position feedback.
Engine software with an available update (FCA 3.0 EcoDiesel)
Flaps on bank 2 sticking from soot or carbon
Often no noticeable change in driving
P200C: P200C reports that the exhaust at the bank 1 particulate filter has become hotter than the filter may tolerate, typically when a heavily loaded filter burns off during regeneration.
Excess soot load burning off too fast during regeneration
Too much fuel reaching the exhaust (leaking injector, post injection, exhaust brake or injector problems)
Leaking charge-air ducting upsetting combustion and soot model
Faulty exhaust temperature sensor near the filter
Possible power reduction to protect the exhaust system
P200D: P200D is the overheating code for a particulate filter on bank 2 and therefore only appears where the exhaust of the second bank has its own filter and temperature sensors. No manufacturer documents P200D publicly; the published diesel layouts of GM, Ford and Hino run one filter and report its overheating as P200C.
Bank 2 filter overloaded with soot before regeneration
Leaking injector or excess fuel on bank 2 cylinders
Exhaust temperature sensor on bank 2 reading too high
P200E: P200E means the catalyst on bank 1 has run hotter than its design limit. On diesels this is the oxidation catalyst ahead of the particulate filter. GM reads the sensor behind the close-coupled DOC and stores a Type A code above 850 °C in its 2020 table and above 800 °C in 2025, each confirmed over hundreds of samples.
Unburnt fuel reaching the catalyst (leaking injector, post injection, misfire)
Parked regeneration with high soot load running too hot
Exhaust temperature sensor behind the catalyst faulty
Regeneration interrupted, possibly with reduced power
Hot smell or heat from the exhaust area
P200F: P200F flags excessive temperature in the catalyst of bank 2, so it needs an engine whose second bank feeds its own catalyst with its own temperature sensor.
Fuel slipping into the bank 2 exhaust (dribbling injector, misfire)
Bank 2 exhaust temperature sensor reading too high
P2010: Intake Manifold Runner Control Circuit High (Bank 1)

P2010 is the high-side counterpart of P2009 for the bank 1 flap drive: the control line carries voltage it should not, typically because it touches a supply wire or the actuator is shorted internally. GM's 2018 diesels judge a resistance to supply under 0.5 Ω, again 12 of 15 checks and Type B.
Control wire shorted to a battery or ignition feed
Shorted winding in the solenoid or actuator motor
Output stage in the engine control module failed
Flaps stuck in one position, change in low-speed torque
P2011: P2011 covers the electrical drive of the bank 2 flaps, so it appears only on engines with a separate actuator or solenoid per bank.
Open wire or loose connector at the bank 2 solenoid
Open coil in the bank 2 control solenoid
Vacuum-driven coolant pump drawing too much vacuum (Audi 3.0 TFSI)
Bank 2 flaps do not switch, slight loss of torque or power
P2012: Intake Manifold Runner Control Circuit Low (Bank 2)
P2012 means the ECM reads the control circuit of the bank 2 flap actuator too low, usually a short to ground in the wire or inside the actuator.
Integrated tumble valve actuator leaking lubricant (Subaru Impreza/Crosstrek)
Bank 2 control wire shorted to ground
Erratic idle or hesitation on light throttle
P2013: Intake Manifold Runner Control Circuit High (Bank 2)

P2013 points to a control line of the bank 2 flap actuator that sits too high, i.e. a short to battery voltage or an actuator whose winding has shorted so the driver sees supply where it expects a load. No manufacturer documents P2013 publicly.
Bank 2 control wire shorted to a supply wire
Shorted winding in the bank 2 actuator
Engine control module output stage faulty
P2014: Intake Manifold Runner Position Sensor/Switch Circuit (Bank 1)
P2014 is the general electrical code for the flap position feedback on bank 1, used when the control unit sees a broken or shorted circuit without, or before, splitting it into low and high.
Runner position sensor (VW G336) failed internally
Manifold with integrated flap shaft and sensor damaged (VW 2.0T 2008–2011)
Slightly weaker pull or rougher idle while the flaps are parked
P2015: Intake Manifold Runner Position Sensor/Switch Circuit Range/Performance (Bank 1)
P2015 means the position feedback of the intake manifold runner or swirl flaps on bank 1 is electrically present but implausible. How it is judged depends on the design.
Flap linkage sticking or flap separated inside the manifold
Corroded or faulty flap control valve
Actuator electronics or position sensor faulty
Flap adaptation not performed after repair
Rough idle or weaker low-speed torque
P2016: Intake Manifold Runner Position Sensor/Switch Circuit Low (Bank 1)

P2016 says the bank 1 flap position signal sits at the bottom of its range, typically a shorted signal wire or a lost 5 V supply. Ford sets it below 0.24 V after 5 s; the 2014 Touareg 3.0 TDI (CNRB) below 0.15 V.
5 V or actuator supply missing (spread terminal, blown fuse)
Position sensor or smart actuator electronics faulty
Less torque at low revs or flat spot when the runner should switch
P2017: Intake Manifold Runner Position Sensor/Switch Circuit High (Bank 1)

P2017 is the mirror case of P2016: the bank 1 flap feedback is stuck near the supply rail. With a pulled-up input that happens when the signal or sensor ground opens, or when the signal wire touches a voltage source. Ford's limit is 4.7 V for 5 s, Volkswagen uses 4.85 V on the 3.0 TDI and 4.88 V on the 3.0 TSI hybrid of the 2014 Touareg.
Open sensor ground or signal circuit
Signal wire shorted to the 5 V reference or battery voltage
Spread or corroded terminal in the valve or sensor plug
Position sensor or actuator electronics faulty
Flaps parked in default position, slightly changed running at part load
P2018: Intake Manifold Runner Position Sensor/Switch Circuit Intermittent (Bank 1)

P2018 belongs to bank 1 and covers a flap position signal that drops out or jumps for short moments while it otherwise stays within limits, so neither the low nor the high code matures. Few makers publish it.
Loose or fretted pins in the sensor connector
Wire cracked by engine movement or heat near the manifold
Worn resistive track in the position sensor
Warning lamp that comes and goes
Often no noticeable change in driving
P2019: Intake Manifold Runner Position Sensor/Switch Circuit (Bank 2)

P2019 is the bank 2 counterpart of P2014 and only appears on V or boxer engines with separate flap feedback per cylinder row. It reports an electrical fault in the position circuit without stating its direction. Volkswagen's Touareg hybrid of 2014 (CGFA) stores it once the bank 2 signal drops under 0.2 V.
Bank 2 sensor wiring open or shorted
Shared 5 V reference or ground faulty (both banks affected)
Mild loss of low-speed torque if the control unit parks the flaps
P201A: Reductant Injection Valve Circuit Range/Performance (Bank 2 Unit 1)

Engines with two SCR paths give each a DEF dosing valve. P201A concerns the first valve on bank 2: the circuit is not open or shorted, but what the control unit sees while dosing does not fit the command. No manufacturer documents P201A publicly; the pickup and truck SCR systems in the public record use one valve and report this fault as P202E.
Bank 2 dosing valve sticking from urea crystals or deposits
Corroded connector or harness adding resistance to the valve circuit
DEF pressure at the valve outside the expected range
DEF system warning, possibly countdown to speed limitation
P201B: Intake Manifold Runner Control Actuator Supply Voltage Low (Bank 1)
P201B does not concern the control signal but the power feed of an electric flap actuator on bank 1.
Chafed engine harness shorting or interrupting the actuator feed
Blown fuse in the actuator supply
High resistance at the supply pin of the actuator connector
Swirl flaps no longer move, often with other electrical codes
P201C: Intake Manifold Runner Control Actuator Supply Voltage Low (Bank 2)

P201C reports that the electric flap actuator of bank 2 is not getting enough supply voltage. It only makes sense on V engines that give each bank its own powered actuator. No manufacturer documents P201C publicly.
Fuse or relay feeding the bank 2 actuator failed
Damaged supply wire or connector at the bank 2 actuator
Actuator electronics loading the supply down
P201D: Intake Manifold Runner Control Actuator Internal Performance (Bank 1)

P201D is for flap actuators with their own electronics: the bank 1 actuator, or the ECM's check of it, has found a fault inside the unit, such as a failed driver, sensor or self-test, while wiring and supply look normal.
Internal electronics of the smart actuator failed
Actuator overloaded by sticking flaps, internal protection tripped
Swirl control switched off, slightly rougher combustion at low load
P201E: Intake Manifold Runner Control Actuator Internal Performance (Bank 2)

P201E says the electronic flap actuator serving bank 2 has detected or caused an internal malfunction; the wires to it are not the issue. No manufacturer documents P201E publicly, and only engines with a separate smart actuator per bank can set it.
Electronics inside the bank 2 actuator failed
Bank 2 flaps binding and overloading the actuator
Little or no change in drivability
P201F: P201F says reductant pump A keeps running or keeps building pressure although the control unit has switched it off, for example when dosing pauses or after the line has been purged at shutdown. No manufacturer documents P201F publicly.
Pump relay contacts welded or driver stage stuck on
Pump control wire shorted to supply voltage
Internal fault in the pump or dosing control unit
Pump audible after switching off the engine
P2020: Intake Manifold Runner Position Sensor/Switch Circuit Range/Performance (Bank 2)

P2020 flags a bank 2 position signal that is electrically sound but does not fit what the flaps should be doing. On the CGFA hybrid V6 of the 2014 Touareg, Volkswagen triggers it when commanded and measured flap position are more than 40 % apart or the reported value leaves the 0–100 % window.
Bank 2 flap shaft sticking or carbon-fouled
Broken lever or linkage between actuator and shaft
Weak vacuum or leaking actuator diaphragm (vacuum systems)
Sensor shifted or adaptation missing after repair
Reduced pull in the mid range or uneven idle
P2021: Intake Manifold Runner Position Sensor/Switch Circuit Low (Bank 2)

P2021 is the low-signal code for the bank 2 runner position sensor. Ford documents it for vacuum-operated runner control on its V engines in the 2020–2023 summary: the position input below 0.24 V for 5 s, monitored continuously once coolant exceeds 40 °F. In the 2024 edition the same fault is shown as P2019 with failure byte 11.
5 V reference to the bank 2 sensor open
P2022: Intake Manifold Runner Position Sensor/Switch Circuit High (Bank 2)

P2022 sets when the bank 2 flap position input reads close to the supply voltage. Ford's limit is above 4.7 V for 5 s on its V engines with vacuum-operated runners (shown from 2024 as P2019 with failure byte 15); for the Touareg hybrid engine CGFA (2014) Volkswagen gives more than 4.88 V.
Bank 2 sensor ground or signal open
Signal wire touching a 5 V or battery feed
Little or no change in drivability
P2023: Intake Manifold Runner Position Sensor/Switch Circuit Intermittent (Bank 2)

P2023 is meant for a bank 2 flap position signal that briefly drops out or jumps without staying out of range long enough for P2021 or P2022. No manufacturer documents this code publicly; Ford's V-engine summaries stop at low, high and over-travel for bank 2, and Volkswagen's Touareg tables skip it.
Bank 2 sensor plug with loose or corroded contacts
Harness rubbing through near exhaust or valve cover
Worn bank 2 position sensor giving dropouts
Warning lamp appears now and then
Usually no change in how the engine drives
P2024: EVAP Fuel Vapor Temperature Sensor Circuit

The fuel vapor temperature sensor tells the ECM how warm the vapor in the tank and canister is, which matters for leak tests that judge pressure or vacuum as the fuel cools after shutdown. P2024 is the unspecified electrical code for that circuit. On recent Audi models the sensor is built into the leak detection unit J909 at the charcoal canister.
Open or shorted wiring to the temperature sensor or leak detection unit
Misassigned fault entry in the ECM software (Audi 2022–2025)
Leak detection unit with integrated sensor faulty
EVAP readiness not set, possible inspection failure
P2025: EVAP Fuel Vapor Temperature Sensor Performance

P2025 means the vapor temperature reading is electrically valid but does not make sense against other inputs or over time. Audi documents a real-world cause on 2016–2018 A6 and A7 with the 3.0 litre engine: water gets into the tank ventilation path, runs past the leak detection pressure switch (NVLD) into the canister and turns to ice in cold weather.
Water or ice in canister and NVLD switch (Audi A6/A7 3.0)
ECM software setting the code falsely (VW Jetta/Taos 2022)
Temperature sensor drifted or slow to respond
Fuel nozzle shuts off repeatedly when filling the tank
P2026: EVAP Fuel Vapor Temperature Sensor Circuit Low Voltage

P2026 reports a vapor temperature signal stuck near 0 V. With the usual NTC thermistor and pull-up resistor, a low voltage corresponds to an extremely hot reading, so the code nearly always points to a signal wire touching ground or a shorted sensor rather than real heat.
Sensor signal wire shorted to ground
Temperature sensor or leak detection unit shorted internally
Moisture bridging pins at the canister-mounted connector
Implausibly high vapor temperature in live data
P2027: EVAP Fuel Vapor Temperature Sensor Circuit High Voltage

P2027 is the high-voltage counterpart of P2026: the signal sits near the reference, which an NTC sensor would only produce at a temperature far below anything plausible. In practice the sensor circuit is open – a broken wire, an unplugged connector, a corroded pin – or the signal line is shorted to a voltage source.
Open circuit – broken wire or unplugged connector
Signal wire shorted to reference or battery voltage
Vapor temperature shown far below ambient
P2028: EVAP Fuel Vapor Temperature Sensor Circuit Intermittent

P2028 covers a vapor temperature signal that jumps or briefly drops out instead of changing smoothly, as vapor temperature normally does. Public manufacturer documentation for it is lacking: Ford's 2014 list ends with P2027, and the Audi bulletins concern P2024–P2026 only.
Corroded or loose connector at the canister area
Wire chafing against body or tank straps
Moisture inside the leak detection unit with integrated sensor
Warning lamp that switches on and off
P2029: A fuel fired heater burns a small amount of the vehicle's fuel to warm coolant or cabin air, a common add-on on diesels with little waste heat. P2029 is a state code: the controller has taken the heater out of service, usually after repeated failed starts, flame-outs, overheating or an electrical fault.
Lock-out after repeated failed starts or flame-outs (fuel supply, glow plug, combustion air)
Heater shut down after overheating, e.g. low coolant flow
Supply voltage too low or wiring fault to the heater
Little or no auxiliary heat, slow warm-up
Heater does not start when requested
Warning lamp depends on the manufacturer
P202A: DEF freezes at about −11 °C, so the tank carries an electric, often PTC-type heater that thaws enough fluid for dosing after a cold start. P202A covers the control circuit of that heater with the emphasis on an open circuit: when commanded on, practically no current flows.
Loose or burnt connector at the tank, or blown heater fuse
Interrupted wire between control unit and tank
In frost, DEF system warning and inducement countdown
P202B: Reductant Tank Heater Control Circuit Low

P202B belongs to the electric heater in the DEF tank and reports a low reading in its control circuit. Generically that means a signal sitting too low, for example a grounded wire or a drive output pulled down.
Corroded heater connector pins adding resistance
Heater element partly damaged, resistance too high
Control wire chafed through to ground
DEF stays frozen longer after cold starts
P202C: Reductant Tank Heater Control Circuit High
P202C is the high-side fault of the DEF tank heater circuit: the module sees a value above the allowed range, as when the wire touches battery positive or an element that conducts far too well.
DEF control unit calibration (software update on some models)
Heater element with internal short, resistance too low
Heater control wire shorted to battery voltage
Service DEF message, later speed limited
P202D: P202D reports that DEF is escaping somewhere between pump and dosing valve, which the controller typically notices as a pressure that cannot be held. Volvo and Mack use it on their 2014 and later trucks (OBD13 onwards).
Dosing valve weeping or crusted with crystals
Leaking DEF line, fitting or seal
Poor electrical contact faking a pressure loss
White crystalline deposits on DEF lines or dosing valve
Higher DEF consumption, later inducement warnings
P202E: Reductant Injection Valve Circuit Range/Performance (Bank 1 Unit 1)
P202E concerns the first DEF dosing valve on bank 1, which in most SCR systems is the only one. The circuit itself is intact, but the valve does not behave as commanded.
Dosing valve sticking from urea crystals or a clogged tip
Dosing or engine control unit software (updates available on some models)
DEF pressure at the valve outside the expected range
DEF system warning, possibly countdown to speed limitation
P202F: P202F covers the commanded supply stage that feeds the reductant system or, in some layouts, the regeneration hardware, typically a supply pump or its power feed. The circuit is electrically present, but its behaviour does not match the command, for instance current or voltage that drifts outside the window expected for the requested state.
Weak relay or fuse contact in the supply feed
Supply pump drawing excessive current (wear, blockage)
Fault in the dosing or pump control unit
DEF system warning, dosing reduced or stopped
P2030: P2030 is the functional check of a fuel fired heater: it is wired and commanded, but does not ignite, keep its flame or deliver the heat expected. Hino uses the code on 2011–2014 conventional trucks with the J08 engine, where a burner heats the exhaust for particulate filter regeneration.
Fuel starvation at the heater (dosing pump, filter, line)
Worn glow pin or contaminated flame sensor
Combustion air inlet or exhaust of the heater blocked, sooted chamber
Control unit software misjudging the flame (update on some models)
Heater fails to start or goes out
White smoke or fuel smell from the heater exhaust
Burner-assisted filter regeneration does not complete
P2031: Exhaust Gas Temperature Sensor Circuit (Bank 1 Sensor 2)

Exhaust gas temperature sensor 2 on bank 1 usually sits between the oxidation catalyst and the particulate filter, where the ECM uses it to control regeneration temperature. Under the generic circuit title, manufacturers set P2031 for different faults.
Sensor failed or reading off from the model
Water or corrosion in the sensor or harness connector
Wiring open or shorted near the hot exhaust
P2032: Exhaust Gas Temperature Sensor Circuit Low (Bank 1 Sensor 2)
P2032 means the signal of exhaust gas temperature sensor 2 on bank 1 is below its valid range. What that means electrically depends on the sensor type.
Signal wire chafed to ground on the exhaust
DPF regeneration inhibited, soot load rises
P2033: Exhaust Gas Temperature Sensor Circuit High (Bank 1 Sensor 2)

P2033 means the signal of exhaust gas temperature sensor 2 on bank 1 is above its valid range. On the Opel/GM 2.0 CDTi in the Saab 9-5 (2010) the sensor in the particulate filter reads high voltage when cold, so more than 1.6 V for over 1 s means an open circuit, an unplugged connector or a short to voltage; it is Type A.
Sensor element open after heat cycling
DPF regeneration inhibited, soot load rises
P2034: Exhaust Gas Temperature Sensor Circuit (Bank 2 Sensor 2)
P2034 is the general electrical fault of the second exhaust temperature sensor on bank 2, so it only appears where the second bank has its own measuring point downstream.
Sensor lead open or shorted where it runs along the hot exhaust
Sensing element failed after many heat cycles
Water or corrosion in the sensor connector
Sensor ground or supply from the control unit faulty
DEF dosing or particulate filter regeneration restricted
Engine power reduced on some applications
P2035: Exhaust Gas Temperature Sensor Circuit Low (Bank 2 Sensor 2)

P2035 reports that the signal of temperature sensor 2 on bank 2 has dropped below its plausible floor. Whether that is a short or an open depends on the sensor curve: with a thermistor pulled up by the control unit a grounded wire drags the voltage down, whereas some circuits read near zero when the loop is broken. No manufacturer documents P2035 publicly.
Signal wire chafed through to ground on the exhaust or frame
Internal short in the sensing element
Temperature reading on bank 2 implausibly low or at the limit
P2036: Exhaust Gas Temperature Sensor Circuit High (Bank 2 Sensor 2)

P2036 is set when the bank 2, sensor 2 temperature signal climbs above the top of its valid window. On the usual pull-up input that is what an unplugged connector, a broken lead or an element gone open after heat cycling produces, while a short to supply voltage gives the same picture.
Sensing element open after repeated heat cycles
Connector unplugged, loose or with pushed-back terminal
Sensor lead broken near the hot exhaust
Signal wire shorted to supply voltage
Bank 2 temperature shows an implausibly high value
P2037: Reductant Injection Air Pressure Sensor A Circuit

Some heavy-duty SCR systems do not spray DEF on their own pressure alone but blow it into the exhaust with compressed air, supplied by a compressor or an existing air system; Bosch's first Denoxtronic generation was built this way. A pressure sensor checks that this air is present before dosing. P2037 is the general circuit fault of that sensor.
5 V supply or ground of the sensor interrupted or shorted
Damaged harness or corroded connector at the dosing module
Engine or emission warning lamp on
Engine power derate on trucks and machines
P2038: Reductant Injection Air Pressure Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance

P2038 does not mean a broken wire. The air pressure sensor A of an air-assisted DEF injector delivers a valid voltage, yet the value does not fit the operating state: it may show pressure while the air supply valve is closed, too little pressure while it is open, or fail to move when air is switched on and off. No manufacturer documents P2038 publicly.
Leaking or kinked air line between valve and dosing unit
Sensor reading drifted or clogged pressure port
Air supply valve sticking open or closed
Insufficient pressure from the vehicle air system
Rising NOx emissions and possible derate
P2039: Reductant Injection Air Pressure Sensor A Circuit Low

P2039 is stored when the signal of injection air pressure sensor A sits below the lowest voltage a working sensor can deliver. Deutz documents it on its EMR L1 controller as P2039-00 under SPN 4335 and lumps two causes together: a grounded signal and an open circuit, since the input is pulled low when the signal wire is interrupted.
Signal wire open or shorted to ground
5 V reference to the sensor lost
Power derate after a while on machines with inducement
P203A: P203A is the general circuit code for reductant level sensor A, the first or only fill level element inside the DEF tank. Deutz lists it for the EMR L1 main and secondary ECU: the tank level input (J1939 SPN 1761) stores P203A with failure type 13 when the line is interrupted and with types 21 or 22 when the value drops under or climbs over its valid range.
Loose, corroded or DEF-contaminated connector at the tank module
Broken or chafed level sensor wiring between tank and control unit
Failed level sensor or level electronics in the tank unit
Fault in the dosing or engine control unit, sometimes fixed by software
MIL and DEF system warning in the cluster
DEF level gauge missing, frozen or wrong
Countdown to speed limit or no-restart after some distance
P203B: Reductant Level Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance

P203B means the level reading of sensor A is electrically present but cannot be trusted. GM's 6.6L LML and 2014 Cruze diesel set it after 5 s (Type B) when the three discrete level contacts report a combination that is physically impossible, e.g. a higher contact wet while a lower one is dry.
Tank overfilled, so the ultrasonic sensor gets no usable echo
Ice or urea crystals on the sensor after cold soak
Wrong or diluted fluid in the DEF tank
Poor terminal contact at the tank module connector
Level sensor or tank unit defective
MIL, often with a DEF service message
DEF gauge stuck, jumping or showing empty with a full tank
P203C: Reductant Level Sensor A Circuit Low

P203C reports a level sensor A signal stuck at the bottom of its range. On GM's 6.6L LML and the 2014 Cruze diesel this is level contact 1: the tank electronics apply a test pulse, and a reading under 0.17 V for more than 3 s with over 8 V supply counts as a short to ground (LML Type A, Cruze Type B).
Signal wire shorted to ground or chafed at the tank
Level sensor or pump/level module internally faulty
DEF crept into the connector and bridges the terminals
DEF gauge reads empty or not at all
Speed or restart limit after a warning period
P203D: Reductant Level Sensor A Circuit High

P203D is the high-side fault of level sensor A. On the LML Duramax and the 2014 Cruze 2.0D, GM samples level contact 1 1.5 ms after a test pulse: 3.56 to 4.74 V means an open load, above 4.74 V a short to battery, either one for more than 3 s with Type A.
Open circuit, unplugged or loose tank connector
Signal wire shorted to supply or battery voltage
Failed level sensor or tank assembly
MIL with Service Exhaust Fluid System or similar message
DEF gauge missing or showing full permanently
Speed or restart limit if not repaired
P203E: Reductant Level Sensor A Circuit Intermittent/Erratic

P203E stands for a level sensor A signal that keeps dropping out or jumping. FCA explains it best: Ram HD trucks with the 6.7L Cummins (2019–2021) carry an ultrasonic level sensor that needs an air gap above the fluid.
DEF tank overfilled, no air space for the ultrasonic echo
Residual ice or urea crystals covering the sensor
Intermittent contact at the tank connector
Control unit software needing an update
DEF gauge jumps or reads 0 % with fluid in the tank
Warning returns after filling or after a cold night
P203F: P203F is not a sensor fault but the result of the level monitor: the DEF tank holds too little fluid to keep the SCR system working.
DEF tank actually low or empty
Frozen fluid or ice covering the level sensor
Leak at tank, lines or pump unit
Low DEF warnings and range countdown
Speed limit or no restart once the countdown ends
P2040: Reductant Injection Air Pressure Sensor A Circuit High

With P2040 the injection air pressure sensor A reports a voltage above its upper limit, more than a real air pressure could produce. On Deutz's EMR L1 controller this is P2040-00 under SPN 4335, defined as a short circuit to battery.
Signal wire shorted to battery or another powered line
Sensor ground open so the output floats high
Sensor failed with output stuck high
Air pressure value shown at maximum
P2041: Reductant Injection Air Pressure Sensor A Circuit Intermittent
P2041 catches an air pressure sensor A whose signal keeps dropping out or jumping for brief moments, too short or too irregular to be confirmed as a steady low or high fault.
Terminal with lost contact tension at sensor or controller
Wire broken inside the insulation from vibration
P2042: P2042 concerns reductant temperature sensor A, which is a different part from the tank temperature sensor of P205A ff.
Open circuit or loose connector at the pump/supply module
False setting at low battery voltage in frost (Volvo/Mack)
Temperature sensor in the pump unit defective
DEF heating or dosing may be restricted
P2043: Reductant Temperature Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance

P2043 flags a temperature reading from reductant sensor A that is electrically valid but does not fit the other temperatures the system knows. Deutz stores it as P2043-64, a plausibility error of the DEF temperature sensor in the SCR system (SPN 4337), separate from the tank sensor check P205B-64.
Engine control software, fixed by reprogramming (Ford 6.7L)
Temperature sensor drifting or slow to respond
Frozen or partly thawed DEF around the sensor
Contact resistance in the connector shifting the reading
MIL, often without noticeable driving change
DEF heater may run at the wrong time
P2044: Reductant Temperature Sensor A Circuit Low

P2044 is set when the signal of reductant temperature sensor A sits below its valid voltage window. As with other NTC thermistors, a low voltage corresponds to a hot reading, so a signal wire touching ground makes the fluid look extremely hot.
Signal wire chafed through to ground
DEF residue in the connector bridging signal and ground
Scan tool shows an implausibly high DEF temperature
Lines may freeze because heating stays off
P2045: Reductant Temperature Sensor A Circuit High

P2045 covers the opposite end: the voltage of reductant temperature sensor A is higher than any real temperature would produce. With an NTC element this reads as very cold, which is what an interrupted ground, a disconnected plug or a signal wire touching battery voltage cause.
Signal wire shorted to battery or supply voltage
Open sensor ground or unplugged connector
Scan tool shows DEF temperature near the lower limit
Dosing may start late after a cold start
P2046: Reductant Temperature Sensor A Circuit Intermittent

P2046 records short dropouts or jumps in the signal of reductant temperature sensor A. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. Deutz, the clearest user of the P2042 group, lists only an open line, a ground fault, both shorts and a plausibility error for this sensor, but no intermittent entry.
Corrosion from DEF residue in the connector
Harness rubbing through intermittently on the frame
Unsteady DEF temperature in live data
P2047: P2047 covers the electrical path of the first DEF dosing valve on Bank 1, which in nearly every SCR layout is the only one. The controller watches the valve's low-side driver and flags an open load: a broken wire, an unplugged connector or a burnt-out coil.
Loose, corroded or pushed-out terminals at the DEF injector plug
Harness wire broken or chafed through near the exhaust
Open coil inside the DEF injector
Faulty output stage or software in the engine/dosing control module
MIL on, often together with a DEF system warning
Speed limitation countdown after continued driving
P2048: Reductant Injection Valve Circuit Low (Bank 1 Unit 1)

P2048 means the control line of the Bank 1, unit 1 DEF injector is pulled toward ground, typically a chafed wire touching the chassis or an internal short in the coil. GM's LML calibration treats less than about 0.5 ohm between signal and ground for 2 s as a failure (Type A).
Control wire chafed against chassis or exhaust bracket
Shorted winding inside the DEF injector
ECM software setting the code without a fault (Nissan Titan XD reflash)
DEF residue or water bridging the connector pins
DEF dosing suspended, warning in the instrument cluster
Inducement or reduced power after a countdown
P2049: Reductant Injection Valve Circuit High (Bank 1 Unit 1)

P2049 is the opposite electrical case for the Bank 1, unit 1 DEF injector: the low-side control line sees battery voltage, for instance through contact with a powered conductor or water inside the connector.
Control wire shorted to a supply wire in the harness
Moisture or corrosion bridging pins at the injector connector
Internal fault of the DEF injector coil
Defective output stage in the control module
MIL on (on some GM diesels only after the second trip)
Higher NOx because no DEF is injected
P204A: P204A is the general electrical fault of the sensor that measures DEF pressure between pump and injector; in most systems it is built into the pump module.
Open signal or ground wire to the pressure sensor
Sensor supply voltage out of range
Pressure sensor inside the DEF pump unit failed
Power or speed limitation after the countdown
P204B: P204B is a plausibility test: the DEF pressure sensor is electrically fine, but its value disagrees with the system state. GM uses moments when the true pressure is known.
Pressure sensor offset drift inside the pump module
Dosing control unit software misjudging the reading (Hino SB-16-015)
Line not emptied at shutdown, e.g. afterrun interrupted or frozen DEF
MIL on, possibly only after a second trip
P204C: P204C means the DEF pressure sensor output has fallen below its valid range, which points to an open signal wire, a short to ground or a missing 5 V supply. On the 6.6 L LML, GM fails anything under 0.41 V lasting 0.4 s, GM's 2018 diesel table a raw value under 5 % of the supply, and the 2025 DEF controller less than 0.45 V in 6 of 100 samples, each Type A.
Water intrusion in the reductant harness connectors (Ford TSB 19-2315)
Signal wire open or shorted to ground
Missing 5 V reference to the sensor
Failed sensor in the pump/heater assembly
DEF dosing stopped, DEF warning messages
Further reductant codes stored at the same time
P204D: P204D is the high-side counterpart: the pressure signal sits near or above the supply voltage, typically because the signal wire touches 5 V or battery voltage, the sensor ground is open, or the sensor has failed internally.
Open sensor ground or corroded ground terminal
Signal wire shorted to 5 V reference or battery voltage
Internal failure of the pressure sensor in the pump module
MIL on (after two trips on some GM diesels)
P204E: P204E covers a DEF pressure signal that jumps around although it stays inside the electrical limits, as with a loose terminal, a cracked wire or a sensor with an internal contact problem.
Loose or fretted terminal at the pressure sensor connector
Air in the DEF line or uneven pump delivery
Pressure sensor with internal intermittent fault
MIL on, fault may come and go
Accompanying DEF pump or pressure codes
P204F: P204F (Bank 1) is the functional check of the whole DEF delivery path: the parts are electrically intact, yet the system cannot build or hold the pressure needed for dosing.
DEF line clogged by crystals or frozen
Worn DEF pump that cannot reach target pressure
Air leak on the suction side or loose line couplings
Dosing unit faults repaired but SCR memory not reset (Hino)
Control module software needing an update (Ram 3.0 L)
Countdown to speed or power limitation
Code returns after clearing until the cause is fixed
P2050: P2050 reports an open circuit at the first DEF injector of Bank 2, the cylinder bank opposite cylinder 1. The code only makes sense on engines whose two exhaust banks each feed their own SCR branch with a separate valve.
Unplugged or corroded connector at the Bank 2 injector
Broken wire in the harness of the second exhaust branch
Open coil in the Bank 2 DEF injector
Higher NOx from the Bank 2 branch
P2051: Reductant Injection Valve Circuit Low (Bank 2 Unit 1)

P2051 reports a ground fault on the drive wire of the DEF injector assigned to Bank 2, unit 1. Like its siblings P2050 and P2052, it presupposes a twin-bank SCR system with a dedicated valve per exhaust branch, and no manufacturer publishes a calibration or bulletin for it.
Insulation melted or chafed near the Bank 2 exhaust
Shorted coil in the Bank 2 injector
DEF crystals in the connector creating a path to ground
Possible NOx efficiency code for Bank 2 later
P2052: Reductant Injection Valve Circuit High (Bank 2 Unit 1)

P2052 tells that battery potential is present on the switched line of the first Bank 2 injector, for example through a short to a powered wire or moisture bridging connector pins. It belongs to twin-bank SCR layouts in which each cylinder bank owns an injector; publicly, no manufacturer documents this code or its thresholds.
Control line of the Bank 2 injector touching a supply wire
Moisture bridging pins in the Bank 2 injector plug
Faulty output stage for the Bank 2 valve
MIL on, possibly after two trips
P2053: P2053 concerns a second DEF injector on the same exhaust line as Bank 1, unit 1, used where a manufacturer doses at two points, for instance ahead of two separate catalysts.
Disconnected or corroded plug at DEF injector 2
Broken wire between control module and injector 2
Slightly higher NOx, little noticeable otherwise
P2054: Reductant Injection Valve Circuit Low (Bank 1 Unit 2)

P2054 flags a ground short in the switched circuit of the second DEF injector in the Bank 1 line. GM's 2025 diesel table (25OBDG04B) checks DEF metering valve 2 for this with the key on, the engine not cranking and more than 11 V, then sets a Type A code after 30 of 60 samples.
Pinched or chafed wire to injector 2 touching ground
Coil resistance too low due to shorted turns (Ford definition)
Water or DEF in the injector connector
Dosing at the affected valve stopped
P2055: Reductant Injection Valve Circuit High (Bank 1 Unit 2)

P2055 is set when the control line of DEF injector 2 on Bank 1 is shorted to battery positive. In GM's 2025 diesel table (25OBDG04B) the power stage of metering valve 2 reports the short; with more than 11 V and 30 faulty readings out of 60 the ECM stores a Type A fault, just as P2049 does for valve 1.
Control line of injector 2 shorted to battery positive
Coil resistance too high, corroded terminals (Ford definition)
P2056: P2056 refers to the fourth possible DEF injector position: the second valve in the Bank 2 exhaust line. It requires both a twin-bank layout and two dosing points per bank, a combination hardly any production engine uses; no manufacturer publicly documents the code.
Connector of the Bank 2 second injector unplugged or corroded
Broken wire in the Bank 2 dosing harness
P2057: Reductant Injection Valve Circuit Low (Bank 2 Unit 2)

P2057 is the short-to-ground case for the second DEF injector of Bank 2. As with P2056 and P2058, it exists in the code list for engines with two exhaust banks and two dosing points each, yet no manufacturer publishes a calibration or service bulletin for it.
Harness clamped against frame or exhaust bracket
Shorted windings in the injector coil
Valve switched off, NOx conversion reduced
P2058: Reductant Injection Valve Circuit High (Bank 2 Unit 2)

P2058 indicates that the second DEF injector on Bank 2 sees battery voltage on its switched line. Like the other Bank 2, unit 2 codes it is reserved for twin-bank engines with two dosing points per bank, and no manufacturer documents it publicly.
Short to a neighbouring supply wire
Failed output stage in the control module
No dosing at the Bank 2 second valve
P2059: Reductant Injection Air Pump Control Circuit/Open

The air that atomizes DEF in an air-assisted system comes either from a small dedicated compressor or from an existing compressed-air system through a supply valve. P2059 concerns the driver circuit of that pump or valve, above all an open circuit: the output is switched on but no current flows.
Open coil in the air valve or pump motor
Connector unplugged or corroded, wire broken
Fuse or relay in the supply path failed
Shorted valve coil causing overcurrent shutdown
Power derate on trucks and machines
P205A: Reductant Tank Temperature Sensor A Circuit
P205A is the general circuit code for the temperature sensor inside the DEF tank, usually built into the level or heater unit; the separate sensor in the supply path uses P2042 ff.
Open circuit or loose tank connector
Tank temperature sensor in the sender unit defective
Tank heating not working in frost
Speed or restart limit on some models
P205B: Reductant Tank Temperature Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance
P205B is the rationality check of the DEF tank temperature: after a long cold soak every sensor should read about the same, so a tank value far off the rest is flagged.
Tank temperature sensor reading off (offset or gain)
Frozen tank or low fill level distorting the reading
Faulty reference sensor (fuel, exhaust or quality sensor)
MIL, sometimes with an emissions service message
P205C: Reductant Tank Temperature Sensor A Circuit Low

P205C reports the DEF tank temperature signal at the bottom of its range. For voltage-read NTC sensors that means implausibly hot: Ford's 2023 diesels set it below 0.165 V, VW's Touareg below 0.30 V, GM's 2025 DEF controller below 0.3 V (about 75 °C) and GM's 2018 diesel table below 200 Ω, each as short to ground.
Faulty sensor in the heater/sender assembly
DEF in the connector bridging the terminals
Tank temperature in live data stuck at an extreme
Tank heater not working in frost
P205D: Reductant Tank Temperature Sensor A Circuit High

P205D is the top-of-range fault of the tank's temperature sensor. On voltage-read NTC sensors a high signal looks like extreme cold and typically comes from an open circuit, a lost ground or a short to supply: Ford's 2023 diesels set it above 4.3 V, GM's 2025 DEF controller above 4.75 V (about −40 °C, 0.5 s, Type A), and GM's 2018 diesel table above 60,000 Ω…
Open circuit, unplugged connector or broken ground
Sensor in the heater/sender assembly open internally
Signal wire shorted to supply voltage
Tank heater runs although the tank is warm
P205E: Reductant Tank Temperature Sensor A Circuit Intermittent/Erratic

P205E marks a DEF tank temperature that changes faster than any real tank could. GM describes two versions: the 2018 diesel table (1.6L Cruze, 2.8L Colorado) checks whether the signal's time evolution is plausible and fails after 8 out of 10 samples taken every 500 ms, provided no electrical fault of the sensor is present; the 2025 DEF controller flags readi…
Engine control software, fixed by reflash (FCA 6.7L)
Loose or corroded contact at the tank connector
Block heater use causing a fast temperature change
Jumping tank temperature in live data
P205F: P205F is the Bank 2 version of the reductant system performance check, meant for engines in which the second cylinder bank has its own SCR branch with separate pressure supply or valve. It applies when that branch is electrically sound but fails to reach or regulate the pressure or quantity the controller asks for.
Blocked or frozen DEF line to the Bank 2 branch
Bank 2 injector sticking due to DEF crystals
Insufficient pump or metering unit pressure for the second branch
Higher NOx from Bank 2, possible inducement
P2060: Reductant Injection Air Pump Control Circuit Low

P2060 means the control line of the injection air pump or air valve is held at too low a level: when the output tries to switch it on, the voltage collapses because the wire or the load is connected to ground. Deutz defines exactly this on its EMR L1 controller as P2060-00, a high-side short to ground on output SPN 5796, which drives the air pump or valve.
Control wire chafed through to ground
Valve or pump coil shorted to its housing
Water in the connector bridging to ground
Possible blown fuse in the air valve supply
P2061: Reductant Injection Air Pump Control Circuit High

P2061 is the high-side counterpart: the pump or valve output that feeds atomizing air carries voltage when the controller expects it to be off, or the diagnostic sees a level that only a connection to battery positive can explain. Deutz documents it on the EMR L1 controller as P2061-00, short circuit to battery on the high side (SPN 5796).
Control wire shorted to a powered cable in the loom
Output stage in the controller failed
Air valve may run continuously, air system loses pressure
P2062: J2012 keeps this title deliberately broad: the controlled supply that feeds the reductant system or, in some layouts, the regeneration hardware, mostly a supply pump or the relay powering it. P2062 reports an open control circuit, so the commanded stage draws no current. No manufacturer documents P2062 publicly.
Blown fuse or relay not closing in the supply path
Broken wire or unplugged connector at the pump
Engine or emission warning lamp on
Restart countdown or speed limit on some vehicles
P2063: P2063 says the reductant or regeneration supply control circuit reads too low, the classic signature of a grounded control line or of a load drawing far more current than it should, which pulls the driver output down. No manufacturer documents P2063 publicly.
Supply control wire shorted to ground near the tank
Pump motor seized or blocked by DEF crystals
Internal short in the pump winding
Engine or emission warning lamp on
Fuse for the DEF supply blows repeatedly
Dosing suspended, possible speed or restart limitation
P2064: P2064 closes the supply control group that begins with P2062. The line that switches power to the reductant supply, in a few layouts to regeneration hardware, carries a level that only a connection to a positive feed can explain, or the stage stays live while the controller has it switched off. No manufacturer documents P2064 publicly.
Control line chafed through and touching a powered wire
Water or corrosion bridging pins in the supply connector
Faulty output stage in the controlling module
MIL and SCR or DEF warning in the cluster
DEF pump audible after it should have stopped
Countdown toward speed limit or no-restart after repeated faults
P2065: Sensor B is the second fuel level sender, used where one sender cannot cover the whole tank: the passive half of a saddle tank, a secondary tank on dual-tank trucks, or the secondary lever-type sender that Mercedes reads through its fuel pump module.
Loose or corroded connector at the second sender or pump module
Broken wire between sender and the module that reads it
Worn or failed sender card in the tank
Control module software that does not match the tank layout
Fuel gauge reads wrong, stuck or jumps
Low fuel warning comes on with a full tank or not at all
MIL on, evaporative monitor may not complete
P2066: P2066 flags a second fuel level sender whose reading is electrically valid but does not behave like real fuel. Makers test it differently.
Float arm sticking or sender card worn in one spot
Transfer or jet pump not moving fuel between tank halves
Plausibility logic needing a software update (Jeep, Genesis)
Poor contact causing a noisy signal (Ford definition)
Fuel gauge stays put or lags behind real consumption
MIL after refuelling or long drives
Range display and low fuel warning unreliable
P2067: Fuel Level Sensor B Circuit Low

P2067 sets when the input from the second fuel level sender drops below its valid floor, usually a grounded signal wire or a sender resistance near zero. Ford's saddle-tank trucks flag it below 5 ohms (under one A/D count) and allow 30 s for the electrical check.
Sender signal wire shorted to ground or chafed on the tank strap
PCM software for the wrong drivetrain or tank version
Diagnostic logic needing an ECM update (Genesis G80)
MIL on with no change in driving
Fuel gauge too low, empty or dropping suddenly
P2068: Fuel Level Sensor B Circuit High

P2068 is the upper limit fault of the second fuel level sender: its signal sits above anything a working sender can produce, which normally means an open circuit, a lost sender ground or a short to a supply voltage. Ford reports it above 200 ohms, more than 253 A/D counts, using the same 30 s electrical check as for sender A.
Open signal or ground wire, unplugged sender connector
Sender card worn through or wiper lifted off the track
Signal wire shorted to a supply voltage
Low fuel warning or empty gauge with fuel in the tank
Range estimate jumps or is implausible
P2069: Fuel Level Sensor B Circuit Intermittent
P2069 covers brief dropouts on the second fuel level sender: the signal leaves its valid window for moments and comes back, too short for a hard low or high fault.
Worn spot on the sender card at the usual fuel level
Loose or corroded terminal at the tank flange connector
Harness rubbing on a bracket or tank strap
Fuel gauge needle twitches or drops briefly
Low fuel light flickers on and off
P206A: The quality sensor sits in the DEF (AdBlue) tank, usually inside a module that also holds level and temperature elements, and estimates urea concentration, in GM's case by timing ultrasonic echoes. P206A is the general circuit code: the module cannot deliver a usable quality value, without a finer split into range, low or high.
Corroded or loose connector at the tank sensor module
Failed quality sensor or tank sensor module
Damaged signal or supply wiring near the tank
Frozen, aerated or heavily contaminated fluid around the sensor
Countdown to no-restart or speed limit
DEF quality value missing in scan data
P206B: P206B means the quality sensor answers, but its result cannot be used or does not fit what the SCR system does.
Air bubbles on the sensor after filling
Deposits or crystals on the ultrasonic sensor
Internal fault in the quality sensor or tank module
Drifting NOx sensor upsetting the rationality check (Hino logic)
MIL and Service Emission System or DEF message
Fault appears shortly or hours after refilling DEF
P206C: P206C is the low-side fault of the quality sensor, read in two ways. GM treats it as electrical: in its 2018 diesel table the piezo input of the ultrasonic sensor below 0.15 V in 40 of 50 samples sets the code, Type A.
Diluted or wrong fluid in the DEF tank (Ford definition)
Low tank level letting the sensor run dry in curves
Sensor signal shorted to ground or failed sensor element
MIL and DEF quality or emission system warning
Reduced power or speed limit on Ford diesels
Warning that appears after a long curve and then clears
P206D: P206D is the upper limit counterpart of P206C. In GM's 2018 diesel table it is electrical: the piezo input of the ultrasonic quality sensor above 4.5 V in 40 of 50 samples, Type A. Ford's 2023 diesels set it when filtered urea concentration reads 60 % or more for over 900 s, which real DEF never reaches, so either the sensor or a foreign fluid is to blame.
Urea crystals around the sensor after freeze and thaw
Sensor signal open or shorted to voltage, failed sensor
Foreign or over-concentrated fluid in the tank
MIL and DEF or emission system warning
Countdown toward speed limit or no-restart
P206E: Intake Manifold Tuning (IMT) Valve Stuck Open (Bank 2)

Reserved for engines whose second cylinder bank has its own intake manifold tuning valve, the flap that switches plenum volume or runner length for resonance charging. The code says the bank 2 flap was commanded shut but its position feedback still reports it open.
Flap or shaft of the bank 2 tuning valve gummed up by oil vapour and carbon from crankcase ventilation
Bank 2 actuator motor or gear worn, cannot drive the flap into the closed stop
Linkage between actuator and flap shaft detached or broken
End positions not relearned after actuator or manifold replacement
Check engine light after two drives (manufacturer-dependent)
Noticeably less pulling power in one rpm range
P206F: Intake Manifold Tuning (IMT) Valve Stuck Closed (Bank 2)

Here the bank 2 tuning valve ignores an open request: the engine computer asks it to swing to the open end stop, yet the feedback still shows the closed position. The code only makes sense on a V-engine with a separately switched flap per bank, and no manufacturer publishes it; GM and Ford describe a single valve and use P2071 for the stuck-closed case.
Bank 2 flap seized in its closed position by deposits or a dry shaft bearing
Bank 2 actuator internally defective, no longer produces the opening torque
On vacuum-operated designs a leaking hose or check valve leaves the actuator without vacuum
Broken flap seal or foreign object blocking the flap travel
Engine feels flat at high rpm
P2070: Intake Manifold Tuning (IMT) Valve Stuck Open (Bank 1)

The tuning valve switches the manifold geometry for resonance charging; with a position sensor fitted, the engine computer can see whether the flap obeys. P2070 is logged when it was told to close and stays open.
Flap shaft sticking from oily carbon deposits fed by crankcase ventilation
Actuator motor or gear worn, flap stops short of the closed position
Actuator unclipped from the shaft or broken coupling
Learn routine of the end stops aborted, e.g. after repairs or low battery voltage
Check engine light after the second faulty drive (GM Type B)
Weaker pulling power in the speed range the closed flap is meant for
P2071: Intake Manifold Tuning (IMT) Valve Stuck Closed (Bank 1)

Counterpart to P2070: the bank 1 tuning valve receives an open command, but the position feedback keeps showing it shut. In GM's 2006 and 2007 tables the check simply compares commanded and actual flap position under load between 1000 and 3600 rpm, Type B.
Flap seized shut by deposits or corroded shaft bushings
Actuator defective, no longer turns the flap against its return spring
Weak supply to the actuator from a corroded connector or relay contact
Lack of power at high engine speed
Check engine light (GM Type B, Ford without MIL)
P2072: Throttle Actuator Control System - Ice Blockage (Bank 1)

Not related to the tuning valve: P2072 belongs to the electronic throttle system. If the throttle plate cannot move freely in frost, the controller assumes ice and runs repeated open and close strokes to break it loose; the code records that event.
Water from the crankcase ventilation condensing and freezing at the throttle plate
Frequent short trips in frost leave water in the engine oil and breather
Heater of the breather line or throttle body (where fitted) not working
Water entering the air intake through a loose duct or wet air filter
Wrench or engine light after a cold start in frost
Limited engine speed or reduced power
Engine may not start in deep frost
P2073: Manifold Absolute Pressure/Mass Air Flow - Throttle Position Correlation at Idle
The engine computer compares the measured air mass, or the manifold pressure, with what the throttle opening and engine speed predict. P2073 means the two disagree in the idle range.
Unmetered air entering after the air flow sensor (loose clamp, cracked hose, leaking gasket)
Air flow sensor element contaminated or drifted, adaptation runs out of range
Deposits at the throttle plate distorting the idle air path
P2074: Manifold Absolute Pressure/Mass Air Flow - Throttle Position Correlation at Higher Load

Same plausibility idea as P2073, but evaluated above idle, where the measured air mass or manifold pressure must match what throttle opening and rpm predict under load. Ford's diesels learn an airflow adaptation in a load cell; outside roughly +/-20 % (6.7L chassis and 3.0L), or if no stable value is learned within 20 learning events, P2074 is stored.
Clogged air filter shifting the learned airflow value (Ford 6.7L)
Leak in charge air pipes or intercooler on turbo engines
Calibration issue fixed by software update (Ford 6.7L, Hyundai 2.5L)
Air flow sensor reading drifted at high flow rates
Reduced power or limited performance mode (Hyundai)
P2075: Intake Manifold Tuning (IMT) Valve Position Sensor/Switch Circuit (Bank 1)

General circuit fault of the bank 1 tuning valve position feedback, which may be a potentiometer, a Hall sensor or a simple end-position switch. The code is meant for systems that do not split the fault into low, high or intermittent.
Corroded or loose connector at the actuator with integrated position sensor
Signal, reference or ground wire chafed or broken near the hot manifold
Position sensor inside the actuator failed
Flap position monitoring and stuck-valve tests no longer run
P2076: Intake Manifold Tuning (IMT) Valve Position Sensor/Switch Circuit Range/Performance (Bank 1)
The sensor signal is electrically within its limits, but it does not behave plausibly.
Flap binding so that the actuator cannot complete its learn sweep
Worn potentiometer track giving jumpy readings
Digital (SENT) position message corrupted by wiring or actuator electronics
Check engine light after two trips (GM Type B)
Slight power loss in parts of the rev range
P2077: Intake Manifold Tuning (IMT) Valve Position Sensor/Switch Circuit Low (Bank 1)
The feedback signal of the bank 1 tuning valve has dropped below its plausible lower edge, typically because the signal is shorted to ground or the line is open with a pull-down.
Signal wire shorted to ground or chafed against the engine
5 V reference to the sensor interrupted
Actuator with integrated sensor defective (FCA 3.5L, check duty cycle first)
Check engine light (GM Type B; Ford without MIL)
P2078: Intake Manifold Tuning (IMT) Valve Position Sensor/Switch Circuit High (Bank 1)
Opposite of P2077: the bank 1 valve feedback sits above its upper plausible limit. Typical triggers are a short to battery or 5 V on the signal line, or an open sensor ground.
Sensor ground open, e.g. pushed-back pin in the connector
Signal wire shorted to 5 V reference or battery voltage
Electronics of the actuator unit defective
Check engine light (GM Type B; Ford without MIL)
Possibly less power in one rpm band
P2079: Intake Manifold Tuning (IMT) Valve Position Sensor/Switch Circuit Intermittent (Bank 1)
Intended for brief dropouts or jumps in the bank 1 valve feedback that come and go rather than sticking at one limit. No manufacturer documents this meaning publicly.
Loose or fretted terminals in the sensor connector
Wire broken inside the insulation, contact lost with engine movement
Dead spot on the sensor track
Fault often not present during workshop test
P207A: Intake Manifold Tuning (IMT) Valve Position Sensor/Switch Circuit (Bank 2)

Unspecified circuit failure of the position feedback on the bank 2 tuning valve. It presupposes a second, separately sensed valve, which in practice means a V-engine with one switchable flap per bank.
Poorly accessible bank 2 connector not latched or corroded
Harness chafed between manifold and bulkhead
Position sensor of the bank 2 actuator failed
Mostly no change in driving behaviour
P207B: Intake Manifold Tuning (IMT) Valve Position Sensor/Switch Circuit Range/Performance (Bank 2)

On bank 2, the valve feedback is electrically valid yet does not match what the flap should be doing, for instance it changes too slowly, sticks at an intermediate value or disagrees with the commanded state. No manufacturer documents P207B.
Bank 2 flap binding, movement profile does not match the command
Coupling between sensor shaft and flap slipping
Sensor characteristic drifted with age and heat
P207C: Intake Manifold Tuning (IMT) Valve Position Sensor/Switch Circuit Low (Bank 2)

Low signal on the position feedback of the bank 2 tuning valve: the controller sees a value below the window it accepts. Typical electrical causes are the signal shorted to ground or a missing 5 V supply. No manufacturer publishes P207C.
Bank 2 signal wire shorted to ground
Shared 5 V reference pulled down or open
Internal short in the bank 2 sensor
Other 5 V sensor codes at the same time
P207D: Intake Manifold Tuning (IMT) Valve Position Sensor/Switch Circuit High (Bank 2)
The bank 2 valve position signal reads above the highest value the controller accepts. Electrically that points at a broken sensor ground or a short from the signal to a supply voltage.
Sensor ground open at a heat-damaged connector
Signal wire shorted to 5 V or battery voltage
No driveability change in most cases
P207E: Intake Manifold Tuning (IMT) Valve Position Sensor/Switch Circuit Intermittent (Bank 2)

Bank 2 version of the intermittent feedback fault: the valve position signal drops out or jumps for short moments, but returns to normal between events. No manufacturer documents P207E, and even its bank 1 twin P2079 has no published OEM use with this meaning.
Moisture or corrosion in the bank 2 sensor connector
Solder joint or wire breaking open intermittently under heat
Harness not clipped, contact lost under vibration
Fault not reproducible in the workshop
P207F: P207F is the verdict that the tank holds something other than proper DEF, which CARB explicitly requires the OBD system to detect.
Water, coolant or other fluid in the DEF tank
Old DEF degraded by heat or long storage
NOx sensor reading wrong, faking poor conversion
Partly blocked dosing valve delivering too little fluid
Exhaust fluid quality warning in the cluster
MIL and countdown to speed limit or no-restart
Message persists until a quality test or relearn is passed
P2080: Exhaust Gas Temperature Sensor Circuit Range/Performance (Bank 1 Sensor 1)
P2080 means the first exhaust temperature sensor on bank 1 passes its wiring checks, yet its reading does not fit the engine state. Each maker tests this differently.
Sensor element drifted or slow after many heat cycles
Sensor loose, bent or not reaching into the exhaust stream
ECM calibration flags a good sensor (software update released, e.g. Nissan)
Exhaust leak upstream of the sensor cools the reading
Particulate filter regeneration blocked or aborted on diesels
Often no noticeable change in driving
P2081: Exhaust Gas Temperature Sensor Circuit Intermittent (Bank 1 Sensor 1)

P2081 is set when the signal of exhaust temperature sensor 1 on bank 1 jumps between consecutive readings faster than real exhaust gas can change. GM documents two versions. A diesel in table 18OBDG04 flags a change of more than 10 ohms between two samples taken 100 ms apart and needs 20 such failures out of 40.
Loose or corroded pin in the sensor connector
Sensor lead chafed or embrittled by exhaust heat, breaking contact on vibration
Cracked sensing element giving unstable resistance
Engine warning lamp on, sometimes only after the second trip
Exhaust temperature value jumping in live data
Regeneration or turbo protection strategy interrupted
P2082: Exhaust Gas Temperature Sensor Circuit Range/Performance (Bank 2 Sensor 1)

P2082 is the plausibility fault of the first exhaust temperature sensor on bank 2, the cylinder bank without cylinder 1. It only exists where both banks carry separate sensors ahead of the merge point, which in practice means V-type petrol engines with turbo or catalyst protection.
ECM calibration error on affected Nissan/Infiniti models (reprogramming)
Exhaust leak on bank 2 ahead of the sensor
P2083: Exhaust Gas Temperature Sensor Circuit Intermittent (Bank 2 Sensor 1)

P2083 reports an unsteady signal from exhaust temperature sensor 1 on bank 2: the value changes by more than the exhaust can physically manage between two readings, or briefly drops out. Only one maker documents it publicly.
Intermittent contact in the bank 2 sensor connector
Lead damaged by turbocharger or exhaust heat
Bank 2 exhaust temperature flickering in live data
P2084: Exhaust Gas Temperature Sensor Circuit Range/Performance (Bank 1 Sensor 2)

P2084 applies the plausibility check to the second exhaust temperature sensor on bank 1, on diesels usually the one behind the oxidation catalyst or ahead of the particulate filter or SCR stage. GM runs the same tests here as for sensor 1: a heat balance on the 6.6 L Duramax (15OBDG09) and a cold-soak rise check on the 3.0 L LZO (25OBDG04B), both Type B.
Sensor 2 reads low or responds slowly due to ageing or soot
Sensor connectors swapped with another exhaust temperature sensor after repair
Oxidation catalyst not producing the expected heat, so the reading looks implausible
Particulate filter regeneration or DEF dosing restricted
Reduced engine power on some diesels
P2085: Exhaust Gas Temperature Sensor Circuit Intermittent (Bank 1 Sensor 2)
P2085 marks the signal of exhaust temperature sensor 2 on bank 1 as erratic. GM monitors it with the same logic as sensor 1 but on separate counters.
Water or road salt in the underbody sensor connector
Lead rubbing on the exhaust or a bracket, intermittent break
Internal fault in the sensor causing unstable resistance
Engine warning lamp on after repeated occurrence
Erratic sensor 2 value in live data
P2086: Exhaust Gas Temperature Sensor Circuit Range/Performance (Bank 2 Sensor 2)

P2086 would report an implausible reading from the second exhaust temperature sensor on bank 2. Snap-on's code list confirms the wording. No manufacturer document available to us uses the code: GM, Ford and VW keep all diesel sensors on bank 1, Nissan's per-bank petrol layouts stop at sensor 1, and Ford's 2014 petrol list jumps from P2085 to P2088.
Bank 2 downstream sensor aged or sooted, reading off
Sensor loose or not reaching into the gas stream
Leak in the bank 2 exhaust ahead of the sensor
Catalyst or filter protection functions limited
P2087: Exhaust Gas Temperature Sensor Circuit Intermittent (Bank 2 Sensor 2)

P2087 is reserved for a bank 2 sensor 2 exhaust temperature signal that is erratic or drops out. No manufacturer publishes it; we checked GM, Ford, VW, Deutz and the NHTSA bulletin index without a hit, and Ford's 2014 petrol list leaves it out.
Intermittent contact in the bank 2 sensor 2 connector
Lead chafing on the second exhaust pipe
Unstable exhaust temperature value for bank 2 sensor 2
P2088: "A" Camshaft Position Actuator Control Circuit Low (Bank 1)

P2088 concerns the control line of the oil control valve that moves the intake cam phaser (actuator A) on bank 1. On GM engines the ECM feeds the solenoid through a high-side driver; while the output is switched on, a voltage that falls below the controller window means the line has a path to ground (equivalent to less than 0.5 ohms).
Control wire chafed through to ground, e.g. GM jumper harness at connector X154
Oil control valve coil shorted internally
Engine oil wicked into the valve connector
Damaged output driver in the ECM
Less pull and higher consumption with cam timing fixed
P2089: "A" Camshaft Position Actuator Control Circuit High (Bank 1)

P2089 is the opposite fault on the intake phaser valve (actuator A) of bank 1: the control line carries voltage although the ECM has switched the output off. With GM's high-side driver that means a short to a supply, again judged against a 0.5 ohm equivalent.
Control wire shorted to a 12 V feed inside the harness
Pinched or chafed jumper harness at the front cover (GM X154)
Engine warning lamp on, on some GM engines in the first trip
Intake cam timing no longer adjusted, sluggish response
P208A: P208A reports an open or otherwise faulty drive circuit of the main DEF pump, the one that builds dosing pressure. Ford's 2023 diesels flag it when pump voltage sits between 2.6 and 3.4 V or the pump controller supply falls under 6 V, tested with the driver off and confirmed after 8 s.
Unplugged, corroded or broken pump connector or wire
Pump controller or ECU software (Volvo/Mack, JLR, GM 23-NA-008)
Low supply to the pump controller from fuse, relay or ground
Pump motor winding open, pump unit failed
MIL and DEF dosing malfunction message
Fault often logged at cold start
P208B: Reductant Pump A Control Performance/Stuck Off
P208B is the functional check of DEF pump A: the circuit is intact, yet the pump ignores its command or stays off.
Air trapped in the tank filter or suction side after service
Leaking DEF line or connection between pump and dosing valve
MIL with DEF system message, often with P20E8
White urea crust on lines or fittings
Countdown to no-restart or reduced power
P208C: Reductant Pump A Control Circuit Low

P208C sets when the drive of DEF pump A is pulled low, either by a ground fault or by current far beyond normal. Ford's 2023 diesels look for pump current over 5 A or pump controller current over 15 A with the driver off, the same 8 s window as for the open fault P208A.
Pump drive wire shorted to ground near the tank
Seized or crystallised pump drawing excessive current
Software error in the controlling module (JLR Velar)
MIL and DEF dosing malfunction warning
P208D: Reductant Pump A Control Circuit High

P208D means the drive of DEF pump A reads high, typically a wire touching battery positive, so the controller has lost authority over the pump. Unlike the open and low faults, Ford checks this one with the driver switched on: on 2023 diesels pump voltage over 16 V or pump controller current above 5 A sets it, confirmed in only 2 s.
Pump drive wire shorted to a battery feed
Moisture or corrosion in the pump connector
Internal fault in pump or pump controller
Countdown to speed limit or no-restart
P208E: Reductant Injection Valve Stuck Closed (Bank 1 Unit 1)

P208E says the first DEF dosing valve does not open although it is energised correctly. Valve movement shows in the coil current: when the armature lifts, the trace kinks. Ford's 2023 diesels judge every stroke and need 50 failures; the test pauses while P2047 to P2049 report a circuit fault.
Urea crystals blocking the dosing valve nozzle
Valve needle seized from deposits or heat
Contaminated fluid or debris from a dirty pump filter
P208F: Reductant Injection Valve Stuck Closed (Bank 2 Unit 1)

P208F is the Bank 2 version of P208E: the first dosing valve on the second exhaust branch fails to open although its drive circuit is in order. It only applies to engines with two separate SCR branches, each with its own dosing valve, which is rare; most diesel cars and trucks run one valve on Bank 1. No manufacturer documents P208F publicly.
Urea crystals blocking the Bank 2 dosing valve
Valve needle stuck from deposits or overheating
Restricted supply line to the second valve
MIL and DEF or SCR warning
Higher NOx on one exhaust branch
Possible derate or countdown to no-restart
P2090: "B" Camshaft Position Actuator Control Circuit Low (Bank 1)

P2090 refers to actuator B, on engines with twin phasers the exhaust camshaft valve, on bank 1. What Low means depends on how the ECM drives the solenoid. GM's usual high-side output flags a ground short while the valve is energised; the 3.6 L LFX V6 (19OBDG03B) sets P2090 after 20 of 25 samples as Type A, the 2018 hybrid table 18OBDG02 as Type B.
Exhaust valve control wire shorted to ground or engine block
Shorted coil in the exhaust oil control valve
Engine warning lamp on, immediately on some GM V6 engines
Slightly higher consumption and emissions at part load
P2091: "B" Camshaft Position Actuator Control Circuit High (Bank 1)

P2091 says the control circuit of actuator B on bank 1, normally the exhaust phaser valve, sits too high. GM's high-side version on the 3.6 L LFX checks for a short to supply while the output is off and, like P2090, treats it as Type A after 20 of 25 samples; 18OBDG02 uses Type B.
Exhaust valve control wire touching a supply wire
Incorrect splice or pin swap after earlier wiring repair
Failed output stage in the ECM
Exhaust cam stays at default angle, slightly reduced performance
P2092: "A" Camshaft Position Actuator Control Circuit Low (Bank 2)
P2092 is the Low fault of the intake phaser valve (actuator A) on bank 2, which exists only on V and boxer engines with a separate valve per bank. Bank 2 is the side without cylinder 1.
Bank 2 intake valve wire shorted to ground on the cylinder head
Shorted coil in the bank 2 intake oil control valve
Engine warning lamp on, immediately on GM LFX
Uneven running between banks, weaker torque
P2093: "A" Camshaft Position Actuator Control Circuit High (Bank 2)

P2093 reports too high a level on the control line of the bank 2 intake phaser valve (actuator A). Table 23OBDG07 shows why High and Low are not tied to one wiring fault: that GM controller switches the valve on the ground side, so it checks for voltage with the driver switched on and calls it a short to power after 1 s, with the lamp after two trips.
Bank 2 intake valve wire shorted to an ignition or injector feed
Fault in a shared engine harness connector
Bank 2 intake timing fixed, reduced low-speed torque
P2094: "B" Camshaft Position Actuator Control Circuit Low (Bank 2)

P2094 belongs to the fourth phaser valve of a twin-phaser V engine: actuator B, the exhaust camshaft, on bank 2. It is therefore absent on single-cam pushrod V8s and on inline engines. On GM's 3.6 L LFX the high-side output is checked for a ground short while on and treated as Type A after 20 out of 25 samples of 250 ms (19OBDG03B).
Bank 2 exhaust valve wire shorted to ground
Shorted coil in the bank 2 exhaust oil control valve
Insulation damaged by heat near the exhaust manifold
Slight loss of efficiency, higher part-load emissions
P2095: "B" Camshaft Position Actuator Control Circuit High (Bank 2)

P2095 closes the series: the bank 2 exhaust phaser valve (actuator B) shows a high level on its control line. For the 3.6 L LFX, GM table 19OBDG03B describes a high-side driver that finds a short to supply with the output off and sets a Type A code after 20 failures in 25 samples.
Bank 2 exhaust valve wire shorted to a supply wire
Bridged pins in the valve or engine harness connector
Exhaust cam on bank 2 fixed, minor drop in performance
P2096: Post Catalyst Fuel Trim System Too Lean (Bank 1)

Petrol engines run a slow outer control loop on the oxygen sensor behind the catalyst that shifts the mixture target of the front sensor. P2096 means this post-catalyst trim on bank 1 has hit its limit in the lean direction. The name describes the correction, not the engine: the rear sensor keeps reporting rich exhaust, so the loop keeps taking fuel away.
Rear oxygen sensor skewed rich, for example a contaminated reference air duct
Front sensor reading lean, so the engine actually runs rich
Calibration issue fixed by an ECM update
New catalyst not yet broken in
Usually no noticeable change in driveability
P2097: Post Catalyst Fuel Trim System Too Rich (Bank 1)
