P2097 is the opposite limit of the post-catalyst trim on bank 1: the rear oxygen sensor keeps reporting lean exhaust, so the outer loop keeps adding fuel until it reaches its rich limit.
Exhaust leak ahead of the rear oxygen sensor drawing in air
Rear oxygen sensor skewed lean or aged
Calibration issue fixed by an ECM update
P2098: Post Catalyst Fuel Trim System Too Lean (Bank 2)

P2098 is the bank 2 version of P2096 on V and flat engines with a catalyst and rear oxygen sensor per bank. The post-catalyst trim of bank 2 has reached its lean-side limit because the rear sensor of that bank keeps reporting rich exhaust.
Bank 2 rear oxygen sensor skewed rich
Usually no noticeable change in driveability
P2099: Post Catalyst Fuel Trim System Too Rich (Bank 2)
P2099 is the bank 2 counterpart of P2097: the rear oxygen sensor of bank 2 keeps reporting lean exhaust, so the post-catalyst trim of that bank adds fuel until it reaches its rich-side limit.
Exhaust leak ahead of the bank 2 rear sensor
Bank 2 rear oxygen sensor skewed lean or aged
P209A: Reductant Injection Air Pressure Sensor B Circuit

Air-assisted DEF dosing, as in Bosch's first Denoxtronic generation of 2004, mixes the fluid with compressed air before it reaches the exhaust, and a pressure sensor confirms that this air is there. A second sensor B can sit in another air branch or serve as a cross-check for sensor A.
Corroded or loose connector at sensor B, often from DEF residue or road spray
Reference voltage or ground of the sensor interrupted or out of range
Internal electronic failure of pressure sensor B
Input stage in the dosing control unit defective
Malfunction indicator lamp or SCR warning on
DEF dosing suspended, higher NOx output
Engine power derate or inducement countdown on trucks
P209B: Reductant Injection Air Pressure Sensor B Circuit Range/Performance
Here the wiring of air pressure sensor B is intact and the voltage lies inside its valid band, yet the reported pressure makes no sense for the moment.
Sensor B drifting or responding sluggishly
Leak in the atomizing air line between valve and dosing module
Sensing port blocked by urea crystals or dirt
Air supply valve sticking, so the expected pressure change does not occur
Check engine or SCR warning lamp
Dosing reduced or stopped, possible NOx efficiency codes later
No noticeable change in driving until an inducement starts
P209C: Reductant Injection Air Pressure Sensor B Circuit Low

P209C means the signal of the second air pressure sensor in an air-assisted DEF system has dropped below the lowest voltage a working sensor can deliver. With common three-wire pressure sensors this points to a signal wire shorted to ground, a lost 5 V reference or a sensor failed internally; with some input circuits an open signal line also reads low.
Signal wire chafed through and touching ground
5 V sensor supply missing, for example pulled down by another sensor on the same rail
Live data shows pressure at or below zero regardless of air supply
P209D: Reductant Injection Air Pressure Sensor B Circuit High

With P209D the second air pressure sensor reports a voltage above the top of its usable range, close to the supply or battery level. A real air pressure that high is not possible in the system, so the controller treats the value as an electrical fault.
Sensor ground open at the connector or splice
Signal wire shorted to the 5 V reference or battery voltage
Sensor B output stage failed high
Displayed air pressure stays at an impossibly high value
Inducement countdown on heavy vehicles if not repaired
P209E: Reductant Injection Air Pressure Sensor A/B Correlation

When an air-assisted DEF system carries two air pressure sensors, the controller can compare them under conditions where both should read alike, for instance with the air supply shut and the lines vented to ambient, or at a steady dosing point.
One of the two sensors drifted; compare both against a reference gauge
Restriction or crystal build-up in only one air branch
Leak in the air path between the two measuring points
Replacement sensor with a different pressure range fitted
SCR or engine warning lamp on
Live data shows clearly different values for sensors A and B at rest
P209F: Reductant Tank Heater Control Circuit Performance

DEF freezes at about minus 11 °C, so the tank is heated electrically or by engine coolant. P209F is not about a broken wire, which P202A to P202C report, but about the heating not behaving as expected: the tank does not warm up in the allowed time, or the heater or its valve runs too hot.
Control unit software detecting a fault that is not there (FCA bulletins 18-091-16, 08-076-26)
Heater element partly degraded or poorly coupled to the fluid
Coolant heating valve sticking on coolant-heated tanks
Tank temperature sensor reading wrong, so heating looks ineffective
MIL and DEF system message, mostly in cold weather
Frozen DEF not thawed in time, dosing delayed after cold start
Speed limitation if the fault persists
P20A0: Reductant Purge Control Valve A Circuit/Open

After the engine stops, many airless DEF systems suck the fluid out of the line and injector back into the tank so that nothing freezes there. In Bosch's Denoxtronic 2.2 this is done by a 4/2-way valve in the supply module that reverses the flow. P20A0 concerns the drive circuit of this valve, chiefly an interruption.
Coil of the purge or reversing valve open
Connector at the supply module loose or corroded by DEF
Output stage in the engine or dosing control unit defective
MIL on (GM Type A, first trip)
DEF system or emission service message
Risk of frozen DEF line or injector in winter
P20A1: Reductant Purge Control Valve A Performance
P20A1 judges the valve by its effect rather than its wiring. When the purge valve switches the pump into reverse, the pressure in the DEF line must drop.
Reversing valve in the supply module not shifting, often from crystallized DEF
Dosing control unit software detecting falsely (Hino SB-16-015)
Return or suction path blocked so pressure cannot drop
DEF pressure sensor reading wrong during the test
MIL on after shutdown and restart
DEF warning message, possibly with other pump codes
Line not emptied, frost damage possible
P20A2: Reductant Purge Control Valve A Circuit Low

The purge valve that reverses the DEF flow at shutdown is usually switched on the ground side. P20A2 reports that its control line is pulled too low, typically a short to ground somewhere between the driver and the coil, which would switch the valve on unintentionally or keep the driver from sensing it.
Control wire chafed against the frame or tank bracket
Moisture or DEF in the valve connector creating a leakage path
Valve coil shorted to its housing
MIL on at once (GM Type A)
Service emission or DEF system message
P20A3: Reductant Purge Control Valve A Circuit High

P20A3 is the high-side fault of the purge valve circuit: the line carries voltage or current where it should not. GM detects it on the 6.6 L Duramax while the low-side driver is switched on; an impedance of less than 0.5 Ω to controller power lasting 3 s triggers it as a Type A fault.
Valve coil with shorted windings drawing excessive current
Control wire shorted to a battery-fed conductor
Damaged or DEF-contaminated connector bridging pins
MIL on in the first trip (GM Type A)
DEF warning and possibly further pump codes
In frost, risk of DEF freezing in the line
P20A4: Reductant Purge Control Valve A Stuck Open

Stuck open means the purge valve stays in, or leaks into, its emptying position while the system is supposed to dose. Part of the pump output then flows back toward the tank, so working pressure builds slowly, collapses after the pump stops or needs a high pump duty to hold.
Worn or contaminated valve seat leaking internally in the supply module
Urea crystals holding the valve in the purge position
Valve energized permanently by a driver or wiring fault
Warning lamp on, often with low DEF pressure codes
Higher NOx, possibly SCR efficiency codes
P20A5: Reductant Purge Control Valve A Stuck Closed

Stuck closed is the failure in which the purge valve does not switch to the reverse position when the system wants to empty the line. For the CNRB engine of the 2014 Touareg, Volkswagen bases P20A5 on the pressure difference between the start of the pressure reduction and the current value.
Control module software (Ford 6.7 L, reprogram the glow dosing module)
Valve jammed in the delivery position by crystallized DEF
Return line to the tank kinked or blocked
DEF pressure sensor frozen at one value
MIL on, often found after a shutdown cycle
No change in driveability (Ford software case)
Frost damage to line or injector if a real valve fault persists
P20A6: Reductant Injection Air Pressure Control Valve Circuit/Open

In an air-assisted DEF system the compressed air must reach the mixing point at a defined pressure, whether it comes from the vehicle's brake air supply or from a separate compressor. A solenoid valve sets or switches this air pressure.
Solenoid coil of the air pressure control valve open
Connector unplugged or wire broken near the valve
Fuse or supply feed for the valve missing
SCR warning lamp or MIL on
Dosing stops for lack of atomizing air
P20A7: Reductant Injection Air Pressure Control Valve Performance

With P20A7 the air pressure control valve is electrically fine, but the air pressure it should produce does not appear. The check relies on the air pressure sensor: after the valve is opened or its duty changed, the measured value must reach the target band within a set time.
Valve worn or contaminated with oil, water or urea deposits from the air supply
Insufficient supply pressure from the vehicle air system or compressor
Leaking air line or fitting downstream of the valve
SCR warning, often together with air pressure codes
Poor atomization, possible deposits in the exhaust pipe
Rising NOx and later efficiency faults
P20A8: Reductant Injection Air Pressure Control Valve Circuit Low

P20A8 says the air pressure control valve's drive circuit sits at too low a level, which normally means a short to ground. Depending on whether the valve is switched on the high or the low side, this either stops the valve from opening at all or energizes it without command. In both cases the controller loses control of the atomizing air.
Harness chafed through to ground along the frame
Solenoid coil shorted to the valve body
Water in the connector creating a path to ground
Blown fuse possible on high-side switched valves
P20A9: Reductant Injection Air Pressure Control Valve Circuit High

If the control line of the air pressure control valve shows battery voltage or excessive current where it should not, P20A9 is stored. A wire touching a positive feed, a coil with shorted turns or a bridged connector can cause it.
Coil with shorted turns causing overcurrent
Control wire shorted to a positive feed in the harness
Output stage in the dosing control unit defective
Air pressure uncontrolled, often too high or permanently on
P20AA: Reductant Injection Air Pressure Control Valve Stuck Open

P20AA describes a mechanical condition: the air pressure control valve lets air through even when it is commanded closed or to a lower setting. The air pressure sensor then shows pressure in phases where it should have fallen, for example after shutdown or during dosing pauses.
Debris, water or oil from the air system on the valve seat
Valve held open electrically by a wiring or driver fault
Air pressure remains present with the valve commanded closed
Audible air flow at the dosing module, compressor runs more often
P20AB: Reductant Injection Air Pressure Control Valve Stuck Closed

The opposite of P20AA: the air pressure control valve does not open although the controller commands it, so no atomizing air reaches the DEF dosing point. The air pressure sensor stays near ambient during dosing requests.
Valve seized by corrosion or deposits
No supply pressure, for example low air reservoir or closed protection valve
Air line frozen with condensate or kinked
Air pressure stays at zero when dosing is requested
Power derate or inducement on trucks
P20AC: Reductant Metering Unit Temperature Sensor Circuit

P20AC is the general circuit code for the temperature sensor built into the reductant metering unit, meaning the DEF supply or dosing module that pressurises the fluid. The control unit typically relies on this value to judge whether the module has thawed and may start pumping.
Corroded or loose connector at the DEF supply/metering module
Damaged sensor wiring between module and control unit
Temperature sensor inside the metering unit failed (usually replaced with the module)
Input fault in the dosing or engine control unit
Malfunction indicator or DEF/SCR warning lamp on
Dosing delayed or stopped in cold weather
Inducement countdown with speed or restart limit
P20AD: Reductant Metering Unit Temperature Sensor Circuit Range/Performance

P20AD covers a metering unit temperature reading that is electrically valid but does not make sense. A typical check compares it after a long cold soak with other temperatures that ought to agree, or watches whether it climbs once the module heater or warm coolant has had time to act.
Temperature sensor in the metering unit drifted (reads plausible but wrong)
Comparison sensor (DEF tank or coolant temperature) itself faulty
Contact resistance in the connector shifting the signal
Module heating or coolant heating not working, so the expected rise never comes
Warning lamp after a cold start or longer drive
DEF dosing starts late or not at all in winter
Live data shows module temperature out of line with tank and coolant
P20AE: Reductant Metering Unit Temperature Sensor Circuit Low

P20AE is stored when the signal of the metering unit temperature sensor falls below its valid band. If the sensor is an NTC thermistor, the common design, though no maker confirms it publicly for this part, a low voltage stands for a very high indicated temperature.
Signal wire shorted to ground (chafing near tank or frame)
Water or DEF residue bridging the connector pins
Sensor element in the metering unit shorted
Warning lamp on immediately after key-on
Module temperature shown far too hot in live data
DEF dosing suspended, inducement countdown possible
P20AF: Reductant Metering Unit Temperature Sensor Circuit High

P20AF means the metering unit temperature signal has risen above its permitted band. For an NTC thermistor, the likely design though not publicly confirmed for this part, that looks like an extremely cold module. Electrically it is usually an open signal or ground wire, a terminal backed out of the connector or a short to a voltage source.
Open signal or ground wire to the temperature sensor
DEF intrusion and corrosion in the pump connector or harness
Signal wire shorted to a supply voltage
Sensor element in the metering unit open
Module temperature shown far below ambient in live data
DEF warning and delayed or missing dosing
Further SCR codes if the harness is corroded
P20B0: Reductant Metering Unit Temperature Sensor Circuit Intermittent/Erratic

P20B0 flags a metering unit temperature signal that jumps or drops out for brief moments instead of failing steadily. Housing, pump and fluid store a lot of heat, so the real temperature cannot change in leaps; the software treats such steps as a signal defect.
Loose or spread terminal in the module connector
Harness chafing intermittently against frame or tank bracket
Moisture entering the connector during wet or freezing conditions
Warning lamp that comes and goes
Temperature value jumping in live data
Fault often not reproducible in the workshop
P20B1: Reductant Heater Coolant Control Valve Circuit/Open

Many heavy-duty SCR systems thaw the DEF tank and supply module with engine coolant, and an electrically switched valve decides when that warm coolant may circulate; Bosch offers its larger supply modules with either electric or cooling-water heating. P20B1 is set when the control unit finds the drive circuit of this valve open or otherwise defective.
Valve connector unplugged, loose or corroded
Open solenoid coil in the coolant valve
Broken wire between control unit and valve
Malfunction indicator and SCR warning on
DEF thaws slowly or not at all in cold weather
Valve does not click during an actuator test
P20B2: Reductant Heater Coolant Control Valve Performance/Stuck Open

P20B2 is a functional fault of the coolant valve that heats the reductant system: the circuit is intact, but temperatures do not follow the commanded valve position, most often because coolant keeps flowing while the valve should be shut.
Wrong DEF tank or pump temperature input misleading the valve check
Coolant valve mechanically stuck open (deposits, debris)
Valve test blocked by other stored SCR faults, valve wrongly condemned
Malfunction indicator with no other SCR fault stored
DEF tank temperature runs unusually high
Possible engine power restriction if left unrepaired
P20B3: Reductant Heater Coolant Control Valve Circuit Low

P20B3 reports a low reading on the control line of the coolant valve that feeds the DEF heating, the classic picture of a control wire shorted to ground or a solenoid with shorted turns. Depending on how the output stage is wired, the valve then stays permanently energised or never responds, so the DEF can get too warm in summer or remain frozen in winter.
Valve control wire shorted to ground
Valve solenoid with shorted turns (low resistance)
Coolant or DEF inside the valve connector
Malfunction indicator and SCR warning on
DEF tank overheats or does not thaw, depending on valve position
P20B4: Reductant Heater Coolant Control Valve Circuit High

P20B4 is the opposite electrical case to P20B3: the drive circuit of the reductant heater coolant valve reads too high, which points to a short to battery voltage on the control line or, with certain driver designs, an interrupted ground return.
Valve control wire shorted to battery voltage
Open ground return of the valve circuit
Output stage in the control unit defective
Malfunction indicator and SCR warning on
Valve cannot be actuated in an output test
P20B5: Reductant Metering Unit Heater Control Circuit/Open

P20B5 concerns the electric heater inside the reductant metering unit, the element that keeps the pump module from freezing. The control unit sets it when this heater circuit is open or otherwise broken.
Heater element in the metering unit burnt out (usually module replacement)
Broken heater supply or ground wire
Corroded heater terminals at the module connector
Warning lamp mainly in cold weather
DEF dosing starts late after a cold start
P20B6: Reductant Metering Unit Heater Control Circuit Performance

P20B6 is the functional check of the metering unit heater circuit: wiring and driver pass the electrical tests, yet the heating falls short of what the control unit expects, for instance the module temperature barely rises during a commanded heating phase or the current drifts away from its target.
Aged heater element with reduced output
Metering unit temperature sensor reporting a wrong value
Low supply voltage to the heater (weak battery, poor ground)
Warning lamp after cold starts only
Long delay before DEF dosing begins in frost
P20B7: Reductant Metering Unit Heater Control Circuit Low

P20B7 means the metering unit heater circuit reads low. Volkswagen gives this a concrete meaning for the 2014 Touareg CNRB: the control unit checks heater conductance at the start of heating and flags P20B7 below 0.33 siemens, so the element shows more than about 3 ohms; further stages at 0.18 and 0.04 siemens follow.
Heater element resistance too high (aged or partly damaged)
Contact resistance at the heater terminals
Heater wire partly broken (few strands left)
Warning lamp at the start of a cold-weather heating phase
P20B8: Reductant Metering Unit Heater Control Circuit High

P20B8 marks the upper limit of the metering unit heater circuit. The 2014 Touareg CNRB table from Volkswagen sets it when the conductance measured at heating start exceeds 0.74 siemens, meaning the element is below about 1.35 ohms, with additional limits at 0.96 and 0.52 siemens.
Heater element internally shorted (too low resistance)
Heater wires chafed and touching each other
DEF or water bridging the heater terminals
Warning lamp as soon as heating is requested
Heater switched off, DEF stays frozen longer
P20B9: P20B9 flags an open or broken control circuit for reductant heater A, one of the electric elements that keep diesel exhaust fluid liquid in winter. Which element carries the letter A differs by maker: GM's 2025 DEF tables call it heater 1, the tank heater; Ford links the code to the pump/heater assembly in the tank, Deutz to the suction line heater.
Water or DEF residue inside the heater or tank harness connectors (Ford TSB 21-2336)
Heater A element burnt out, so resistance is far above specification
Broken supply or return wire between control module and heater
Heater output stage in the DEF or engine control module defective
Check engine light, often first noticed in cold weather
DEF dosing starts late or not at all after a cold start
DEF system warning followed by a countdown to a speed limit
P20BA: Reductant Heater A Control Circuit Performance
P20BA is the plausibility test for heater A: the circuit is intact, yet the current, resistance or power the element takes does not match the command.
Aged heater element whose resistance has drifted out of the allowed window
Corroded or loose heater terminals adding resistance under load
Control software setting the code without a defect (FCA 18-028-14 reflash)
DEF pump unable to build pressure because of swapped or blocked lines (Volvo/Mack KC-4)
Malfunction indicator lamp with DEF system message
DEF tank stays cold or frozen in winter although the engine is warm
Possible speed limitation after the inducement countdown
P20BB: Reductant Heater A Control Circuit Low
A low reading on the heater A control circuit usually means the output or its wire is grounded, or the element pulls far more current than it should.
Heater A wire chafed through and touching ground
Internal short in the heater element, drawing excessive current
DEF control module calibration setting the code falsely (GM 22-NA-112)
Moisture bridging heater pins to ground in the connector
Malfunction indicator lamp, possibly with a blown heater fuse
Message that speed will be reduced if the system is not serviced
No DEF heating, so dosing is delayed in frost
P20BC: Reductant Heater A Control Circuit High
P20BC means the heater A control circuit reads high: the wire or output has picked up battery voltage, so the element may run when it should be off or cannot be switched at all.
Heater A control wire shorted to a battery-voltage circuit
DEF control unit software fault (FCA 08-076-26 for 2025 Cummins Ram)
Heater output stage or relay stuck switched on
Check engine light and DEF system warning
Heater may stay energized, risking overheating or a drained battery
Reduced power or speed limit once the inducement starts
P20BD: Heater B's control circuit is open. In GM's tables heater 2 is the DEF line heater; the 2025 version detects the open state with the output off and sets a Type A code after two seconds, while the 2018 version relies on an open status reported by the DEF control module with battery voltage above 11 V.
Heating wire in the pressure line broken (line assembly replacement)
Corroded or unplugged line heater connector
Harness to the line heater damaged along the frame rail
Warning lamp, especially after cold nights
DEF pressure builds slowly or not at all in frost
Inducement countdown with eventual speed limit
P20BE: Reductant Heater B Control Circuit Performance

P20BE judges whether heater B, in most designs the heated pressure line, behaves as expected once the wiring itself checks out. GM's 2025 DEF tables flag line heater resistance below 2.80 or above 7.50 ohms, or a power error above 16.5 W, after 8 s (Type A); the 2018 tables accept a voltage-to-current ratio only between 1.51 and 3.57 ohms.
Pressure line heating wire degraded, resistance outside the window
High-resistance joint at the line heater connector
Engine control software setting the code erroneously (FCA 18-028-14)
Low heater supply voltage distorting the current measurement
Malfunction indicator lamp after a heating phase
Ice in the pressure line on cold starts, dosing late
Possible NOx efficiency codes as a consequence
P20BF: Reductant Heater B Control Circuit Low

For heater B the code stands for a grounded control circuit or an overcurrent. Ford, where B is the pressure line heater, sets it when circuit 2 draws more than 15 A with the power stage on; the glow plug module can report such a short within 250 ms.
Line heater wire chafed on the frame and grounded
Water in the line heater connector creating a path to ground
Internal short in the heated pressure line
Check engine light, sometimes with a blown fuse
DEF pressure fault codes in cold weather
Speed limitation if the fault persists
P20C0: Reductant Heater B Control Circuit High

P20C0 reports that heater B's control circuit is high, typically a wire touching a battery feed or a driver that will not switch off. On Ford diesels B is the pressure line heater: with the power stage off, a current below 3 A while the output still carries over 5 V triggers it, and the glow plug module flags the condition in 250 ms.
Line heater control wire shorted to a positive feed
Heater output stage in the DEF, engine or glow plug module stuck on
Bridged pins in a shared connector next to a supply terminal
Malfunction indicator lamp and DEF warning
Line heater may stay on with the engine off, draining the battery
Frozen pressure line once the module disables the heater
P20C1: Heater C's control circuit is interrupted. Where the third element sits again depends on the maker: GM's 2025 DEF tables make heater 3 a second tank heater and test it like the others (output off, 2 s, Type A); Deutz assigns C to the return line heater; FCA's EcoDiesel has a heater 3 of its own.
Heating circuit in the line or tank module open (resistance check at the connector)
Unplugged or corroded heater C connector
Glow plug control module fault where it drives the DEF heaters (GM LML)
Warning lamp mainly after cold soaks
DEF dosing delayed after a cold start
SCR warning and countdown if the fault persists
P20C2: Reductant Heater C Control Circuit Performance

P20C2 says heater C is connected but does not take the power the control unit expects. In GM's 2025 tables heater 3, the second tank heater, must measure between 1.50 and 2.60 ohms and stay within 29 W of its command; otherwise Type A after 8 s.
Heater supply below 5 V because of a weak relay, fuse or feed wire (Ford)
Engine control software setting the code falsely (FCA 18-028-14, 18-019-15)
Heater C element resistance outside its window
Check engine light after a heating cycle
DEF thaws slowly in cold weather
Further heater codes if the common supply is weak
P20C3: Reductant Heater C Control Circuit Low

A low C circuit points to heater C being grounded somewhere or drawing excessive current. GM's 2025 DEF module treats heater 3, its second tank heater, exactly like heaters 1 and 2: a low-band voltage with the output off, or drain voltage and current limits with it on, Type A once 2 s have elapsed.
Outdated DEF control module calibration on 2020–2022 GM diesel pickups (22-NA-112)
Heater C wire grounded through chafing
Shorted heater C element drawing overcurrent
Malfunction indicator lamp, possibly with no real fault present
Driver message that speed will be reduced without service
Unheated tank or line section in frost
P20C4: Reductant Heater C Control Circuit High

P20C4 marks heater C's control circuit as high, meaning it sees battery voltage where none belongs. GM's 2025 tables test heater 3, a second tank heater, with the output switched off against a raised voltage window and set a Type A fault after 2 s of persistence.
Heater C control wire in contact with a battery feed
Heater driver in the DEF or glow plug module stuck on
DEF crystals or moisture bridging pins in the heater connector
Check engine light and SCR warning
Battery drained overnight if the heater stays powered
Inducement and speed limit if left unrepaired
P20C5: P20C5 covers an open control circuit in reductant heater D, the fourth heating element that only a few SCR layouts carry. Deutz is the one maker found that publishes the code: in its EMR5/MD1 fault list D is the downstream line heater, and P20C5 maps to SPN 520471 with FMI 5, an open or too little current.
Heating wire in the downstream DEF line burnt out or broken
Loose or corroded heater D connector
Wire break in the harness to heater D
Dosing delayed while the downstream line thaws
P20C6: Reductant Heater D Control Circuit Performance

P20C6 is the functional check of heater D. FCA documents it for the 3.0 L EcoDiesel under the name Reductant Heater 4 Control Circuit Performance: bulletin 18-068-20 reflashed 2017 Ram 1500 engine computers that showed it, and a 2021 STAR case for 2020–2021 Ram 1500, Wrangler and Gladiator notes that it turns up mostly in severe cold, often without a defect.…
False detection in extreme cold with a still-frozen tank (FCA STAR S2118000006)
Leaking or blocked DEF supply line to the injector
DEF pump unable to build pressure or injector delivering the wrong quantity
Malfunction indicator lamp, mostly after very cold nights
DEF system message, sometimes alongside pressure codes
Often no noticeable change in how the vehicle drives
P20C7: Reductant Heater D Control Circuit Low

P20C7 reports that heater D's control circuit is grounded or overloaded with current. Only Deutz publishes the code: for its downstream line heater (SPN 520471) it maps to FMI 4, a voltage that is too low or a short to a low source. No vehicle maker documents thresholds for heater D.
Heater D wire chafed through to ground
Water in the heater D connector
Internal short inside the heated downstream line
Warning lamp, possibly with a blown fuse
Unheated downstream line and delayed dosing in frost
P20C8: Reductant Heater D Control Circuit High

Diesel exhaust fluid freezes at about -11 °C, so SCR systems carry several electric heating elements in the tank, pump and lines; which one a maker calls heater D varies. P20C8 reports that the control circuit of heater D reads high, meaning the output or its wiring has contact with battery voltage and the element can no longer be switched as commanded.
Chafed harness letting the heater D control wire touch a battery-voltage feed
Moisture or DEF residue in the heater connector bridging pins
Internal short inside heater D or its integrated pump or line assembly
Faulty heater output stage in the engine or DEF control module
Check engine light and DEF or emission system warning
DEF dosing unavailable in cold weather, NOx warning or later speed limitation
Blown fuses and further unrelated codes when a chafed harness is the cause
P20C9: Reductant Control Module Requested MIL Illumination

P20C9 is a forwarding code. Some diesel trucks use a separate DEF or SCR control module with its own fault memory; when that module detects an emission-relevant fault it asks the engine module to switch on the check engine lamp, and the engine module records P20C9.
Emission-relevant SCR fault stored in the DEF control module (heater, pump, pressure, sensor)
Failed upstream NOx sensor reported by the DEF module
Outdated or mismatched software between engine and DEF control module
Check engine light with only P20C9 visible on a generic scan tool
DEF or SCR warning lamp, depending on the underlying fault
Possible power derate if the underlying SCR fault triggers inducement
P20CA: Air-assisted dosing, used mainly on older heavy and medium-duty diesels, mixes diesel exhaust fluid with compressed air from the vehicle's air system and blows the mixture through a nozzle into the exhaust. Airless pump systems in passenger cars and most current light trucks, such as Bosch Denoxtronic 2.2, have no air branch and cannot set this code.
Leaking air hose or fitting between air supply and dosing unit
Worn seal on the air shut-off or pressure control valve
Leak in the vehicle's compressed-air supply feeding the doser
Cracked or poorly sealed dosing unit housing on the air side
Check engine light and SCR warning
Audible hissing near the dosing unit or air lines
Poor DEF atomisation, higher NOx and later engine derate
P20CB: Exhaust Aftertreatment Fuel Injector A Control Circuit/Open

The engine computer checks the drive line of the hydrocarbon doser, a separate valve that sprays diesel into the exhaust ahead of the oxidation catalyst so the particulate filter can be heated for regeneration.
Corroded or loose connector at the doser, which sits under the vehicle in the exhaust area
Heat- or chafe-damaged wire between engine computer and doser
Open solenoid winding inside the doser
Faulty output stage in the engine control module
Particulate filter regeneration does not start or is aborted
Soot load warning and, later, reduced engine power
P20CC: Exhaust Aftertreatment Fuel Injector A Control Performance
Unlike the circuit codes, this one judges what the hydrocarbon doser actually does.
Doser leaking or dribbling fuel into the exhaust while closed
Coked nozzle tip with distorted spray
Exhaust temperature sensor before or after the catalyst reading wrong
Unexpectedly high exhaust temperatures, possibly white smoke or fuel smell
P20CD: Exhaust Aftertreatment Fuel Injector A Control Circuit Low

Here the control line of the hydrocarbon doser has a short to ground. GM's diesel tables 18OBDG04 and 25OBDG04A test the output while the driver is off: if the voltage drops below about 2 V, the line is touching ground.
Control wire chafed through against the frame or exhaust
Water or salt in the doser connector bridging to ground
Internal short in the doser solenoid
Check engine light on after a single trip
Possible fuel smell or smoke from the exhaust
P20CE: Exhaust Aftertreatment Fuel Injector A Control Circuit High

The control line of the hydrocarbon doser is shorted to battery voltage. GM's diesel tables 18OBDG04 and 25OBDG04A detect it while the driver is switched on: current above roughly 8 to 11 A for a set time, or above about 16 to 22 A at once, counts as a short to power.
Control wire touching a powered wire in a damaged harness
Doser solenoid with shorted turns drawing too much current
Faulty output stage in the engine control module
Rising soot load, later reduced power
P20CF: Exhaust Aftertreatment Fuel Injector A Stuck Open

The doser that adds diesel to the exhaust for filter regeneration is judged to stay open, so fuel keeps flowing after the command to close. On Volvo and Mack trucks the nozzle sits right at the turbo outlet and is fed by an AHI module; their troubleshooting guide KC-2157 points first to the fuel supply and then to that module.
Dirt or deposits holding the doser valve off its seat
Upstream shutoff or dosing module letting fuel through
Calibration error, fixed by a software update
White smoke or strong fuel smell from the exhaust
Very high temperatures at catalyst and filter
P20D0: Exhaust Aftertreatment Fuel Injector A Stuck Closed

The exhaust fuel doser is commanded to inject but no fuel gets through, typically because the nozzle tip is plugged. Detection usually relies on line pressure that fails to drop or on too little heat build-up across the oxidation catalyst.
Dosing module or supply valve not passing fuel
Kinked or blocked fuel line to the nozzle
Regenerations fail or are requested constantly
P20D1: Exhaust Aftertreatment Fuel Injector B Control Circuit/Open
Injector B is a second exhaust fuel doser, found only on layouts with two dosing points, for example twin exhaust paths. This code reports a broken control line or open coil on that second unit.
Loose or corroded connector at doser B
Open solenoid winding in doser B
Regeneration incomplete on the affected exhaust path
P20D2: Exhaust Aftertreatment Fuel Injector B Control Performance

With its wiring intact, the second exhaust fuel doser (B) is not delivering what was asked for: too little heat appears across the catalyst during dosing, or heat appears when it should be idle. No manufacturer documents P20D2 publicly.
Partly coked nozzle on doser B
Low or unstable fuel pressure feeding doser B
P20D3: Exhaust Aftertreatment Fuel Injector B Control Circuit Low

The control line of the second exhaust fuel doser (B) is pulled toward ground. No manufacturer documents P20D3 publicly. For injector A, GM's diesel tables detect this by a switched-off output voltage below about 2 V and treat it as Type A with the MIL after one trip (P20CD), because a grounded line can open the valve without command.
Chafed control wire to doser B touching ground
Moisture in the doser B connector
Doser B switched off, regeneration impaired
P20D4: Exhaust Aftertreatment Fuel Injector B Control Circuit High

On the second exhaust fuel doser (B), the control line sits at or near battery voltage, so the driver cannot pull it low to open the valve. No manufacturer documents P20D4 publicly. For injector A, GM's diesel tables flag excess current in the switched-on state as a short to power and rate it Type B (P20CE).
Control wire to doser B shorted to a powered circuit
Shorted turns in the doser B solenoid
Faulty output stage in the control module
P20D5: Exhaust Aftertreatment Fuel Injector B Stuck Open

The second exhaust fuel doser (B) keeps passing fuel after it has been told to shut. No manufacturer documents P20D5 publicly; for the single doser A, Volvo and Mack trace the equivalent code P20CF to the fuel supply or the dosing module, and Ram fixed it on Cummins pickups with software.
Deposits keeping doser B from sealing
Upstream shutoff valve leaking fuel through
Calibration error in the control software
P20D6: Exhaust Aftertreatment Fuel Injector B Stuck Closed

The second exhaust fuel doser (B) fails to deliver fuel even though the control unit commands it open. No manufacturer documents P20D6 publicly. For doser A, Volvo and Mack handle the matching code P20D0 by checking the dosing module and replacing the nozzle, whose tip tends to clog with carbon; the same weak spot applies to B.
Clogged nozzle tip on doser B
No fuel reaching doser B because of a blocked line or closed supply valve
Mechanically seized valve in doser B
Reduced power once the filter is heavily loaded
P20D7: Exhaust Aftertreatment Fuel Supply Control Circuit/Open
Upstream of the exhaust doser sits a valve that releases fuel to it only when a regeneration is wanted, often called the shutoff or fuel cut valve. This code reports an open in its control circuit.
Loose or corroded connector at the dosing module
Broken wire in the dosing module harness
Open coil in the fuel shutoff valve
P20D8: Exhaust Aftertreatment Fuel Supply Control Performance

The supply valve ahead of the exhaust doser is electrically sound, but the pressure it produces in the feed line does not follow its commands. A typical layout, described in a patent assigned to International Engine, measures that line pressure and uses it both to meter the dose and to diagnose the regulating valve.
Low feed pressure from a clogged fuel filter or weak low-pressure pump
P20D9: Exhaust Aftertreatment Fuel Supply Control Circuit Low

For the fuel supply valve feeding the exhaust doser, the control line reads too low, which points to a short to ground. Volvo and Mack store P20D900 and, in AHI troubleshooting guide KC-2157, group it with the other electrical faults of the AHI module: check the module's connector and wiring harness.
Chafed wire in the dosing module harness touching ground
Water in the dosing module connector
Internal short in the supply valve coil
P20DA: Exhaust Aftertreatment Fuel Supply Control Circuit High

For the supply valve ahead of the exhaust doser, the control line reads too high, typically because it touches battery voltage or, on some drivers, an open line pulled up internally. Volvo and Mack log it as P20DA00 and list it in guide KC-2157 among the AHI module electrical faults, with the instruction to check that module's wiring and connector.
Valve control wire shorted to a powered line
Damaged coil in the supply valve
Faulty output stage in the control module
P20DB: Exhaust Aftertreatment Fuel Supply Control Stuck Open

The supply valve that should isolate the exhaust doser from the fuel system stays open after being switched off, so the feed line remains pressurized when no regeneration is running. If the doser itself then leaks, fuel can reach the hot exhaust unasked.
Supply or fuel cut valve sticking open from wear or dirt
Detection or control calibration error, fixed by software
Contaminated fuel leaving deposits in the valve
Fuel smell or smoke if the doser also leaks
Long cranking after fuel system work
P20DC: Exhaust Aftertreatment Fuel Supply Control Stuck Closed

The valve feeding the exhaust doser does not open when a regeneration starts, so the doser receives no fuel. A Hino patent shows how this is recognized: a pressure sensor between the shutoff valve and the dosing valve reads far below a threshold that depends on engine speed.
Clogged fuel filter or water and dirt in the fuel
Internal fault in the dosing module
Regenerations fail, soot load keeps rising
P20DD: Exhaust Aftertreatment Fuel Pressure Sensor Circuit

The pressure sensor in the feed line of the exhaust doser lets the control unit meter fuel and spot a stuck valve or plugged nozzle. This code is the general circuit fault of that sensor; signal too low, too high and unsteady have their own codes (P20DF, P20E0, P20E1).
Internally damaged harness to the dosing module and its sensor
Further codes for the reference voltage or the dosing system
P20DE: Exhaust Aftertreatment Fuel Pressure Sensor Circuit Range/Performance
The doser feed pressure sensor gives a signal inside its electrical limits, yet the value does not fit what the system is doing, for example no pressure rise when the supply valve opens.
Restricted fuel or separator filter from contaminated fuel
Sticking fuel cut or supply valve
Plugged nozzle or leaking fuel/air line
Sometimes further fuel pressure codes such as P0087
P20DF: Exhaust Aftertreatment Fuel Pressure Sensor Circuit Low
The signal of the doser feed pressure sensor sits below its lower limit. Electrically that suggests a grounded signal line or a missing reference voltage.
Real low pressure from a restricted filter or contaminated fuel
Signal wire shorted to ground or reference voltage lost
Outdated detection threshold, fixed by a software update
P20E0: Exhaust Aftertreatment Fuel Pressure Sensor Circuit High

The doser feed pressure sensor reports a signal above its upper electrical limit. On a typical three-wire sensor this happens when the signal line is open and pulled up, shorted to the 5 V reference or to battery voltage, or when the ground is lost.
Signal wire open or shorted to reference or battery voltage
Sensor from a faulty production batch
P20E1: Exhaust Aftertreatment Fuel Pressure Sensor Circuit Intermittent/Erratic

The signal from the pressure sensor in the doser feed line jumps or drops out for short moments, faster than real line pressure could change. Usual reasons are a loose pin, a cracked wire flexing with engine movement, or moisture in the connector. No manufacturer documents P20E1 publicly.
Loose or fretted pins at the sensor connector
Internal fault in the pressure sensor
Check engine light on, possibly coming and going
P20E2: P20E2 flags that bank 1 exhaust temperature sensors 1 and 2 disagree at a moment when both should show nearly the same value. Sensor 1 usually sits ahead of the oxidation catalyst and sensor 2 behind it.
Exhaust temperature sensor 1 or 2 drifted or aged (offset reading)
Corroded or loose connector adding resistance to one sensor signal
Sensors swapped or a non-matching replacement part installed
Engine control software needing an update
Malfunction indicator lamp on, often with no change in driving
Particulate filter regeneration delayed or blocked
Code returns after a long parking period
P20E3: P20E3 reports that exhaust temperature sensors 1 and 3 on bank 1 do not agree. In the usual diesel order, sensor 1 measures before the oxidation catalyst and sensor 3 after the particulate filter, so this pair brackets the whole aftertreatment line. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly.
Sensor 1 or sensor 3 reading offset or responding sluggishly
Water or corrosion in the connector of the rear sensor
Exhaust leak near one sensor letting outside air cool its tip
Temperature values of sensors 1 and 3 differ noticeably on a cold engine
P20E4: P20E4 covers the pair around the particulate filter: sensor 2 at the filter inlet and sensor 3 at its outlet on bank 1 no longer agree.
Filter inlet or outlet temperature sensor aged by heat cycling
Heat-damaged or corroded sensor connector or lead
Heavy soot or ash deposits on a sensor tip slowing its response
Regenerations aborted or happening more often
Filter loading warning in some vehicles
P20E5: P20E5 is the bank 2 counterpart of P20E2: on engines with a separate exhaust and aftertreatment path per cylinder bank, sensors 1 and 2 of the second bank disagree after the system has cooled down. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly; the GM tables that use P20E2 cover single-path diesels.
Contact resistance in a bank 2 sensor connector
Sensor connectors swapped between banks after a repair
Bank 2 sensors show different values on a cold engine
P20E6: Reductant Injection Air Pressure Too Low

This code belongs to air-assisted DEF dosing, where compressed air carries the fluid to the nozzle and breaks it into fine droplets; airless pump systems in cars and most current pickups do not use it. P20E6 means the air pressure in the dosing branch stays below the minimum the control unit needs while dosing is requested.
Insufficient air tank pressure from a leak or weak compressor
Air shut-off or pressure control valve not opening
DEF crystals restricting the air side of the dosing unit
Leaking, kinked or blocked air line to the doser
Check engine light and SCR warning
DEF dosing reduced or stopped, rising NOx emissions
Engine derate after the inducement period
P20E7: Reductant Injection Air Pressure Too High
On air-assisted DEF dosing the control unit regulates the compressed air fed into the mixing chamber so that the nozzle sprays a stable mist.
Air pressure control valve no longer regulating and passing full supply pressure
DEF crystals or deposits restricting the nozzle or mixing path
Air pressure sensor reading too high
Check engine light and SCR warning
Irregular DEF spray, deposits in the exhaust and higher NOx
Engine derate if dosing is shut down
P20E8: Airless DEF systems hold the fluid at a set pressure ahead of the dosing valve with an electric pump, read by a pressure sensor. P20E8 means the measured value stays clearly below that target or cannot be built up at all.
Air in the DEF lines or pump that lost its prime, for example after long storage
Clogged pump inlet, suction tube, filter or tank vent, often from contamination
External leak at a DEF line, connector or the dosing valve
Worn, crystallised or superseded DEF pump unit
Check engine light and DEF system warning message
No DEF dosing, rising NOx and a countdown to speed limitation or no restart
Pump can be heard running longer than usual after key on
P20E9: P20E9 is the overpressure counterpart of P20E8: during closed-loop control the DEF pressure ahead of the dosing valve rises clearly above its target.
Blocked return path, restricted line or dosing valve not opening properly
Debris in the fluid after a damaged filter seal or dirty refilling
Reductant pressure sensor reading too high
Pump control software needing an update
Check engine light and DEF system warning
Dosing shut off, NOx warning and later inducement countdown
P20EA: Reductant Control Module Power Relay De-Energized Performance - Too Early

Many SCR systems supply the reductant control module, and through it pump and heaters, via a power relay. After the key is switched off the relay should stay energised for a short after-run so the pump can empty the lines and the module can save its learned values, and only then drop out on the module's command.
Worn relay contacts or coil interrupting the supply early
Loose fuse, terminal or ground in the relay or module feed
Battery disconnected or voltage collapsing right after shut-off
Reductant control module releasing the relay prematurely
Check engine light, often without noticeable driving symptoms
DEF lines not purged, risk of frozen or crystallised lines in winter
P20EB: Reductant Control Module Power Relay De-Energized Performance - Too Late

Here the opposite of P20EA happens: after the reductant control module has finished its after-run and released the power relay, voltage is still present on the switched side, so the relay opens late or not at all. Typical reasons are welded contacts, a control line shorted to ground that keeps the coil energised, or a module that never ends its shut-down.
Relay control line shorted to ground, keeping the coil energised
Reductant control module or network activity preventing shut-down
Battery drained after the vehicle has been parked
DEF pump or relay audible long after switching off
P20EC: P20EC means the engine computer has registered a temperature in the SCR catalyst of bank 1 above the limit its washcoat can tolerate.
Excess heat release during particulate filter regeneration
Unburnt fuel or oil reaching the exhaust (leaking injector, turbo seal)
SCR temperature sensor reading too high
Regeneration or thermal-management calibration needing an update
Regeneration interrupted or power reduced to protect the aftertreatment
Later loss of NOx conversion (follow-up code P20EE)
P20ED: P20ED applies to systems with two SCR stages in series: a small pre-catalyst mounted close to the engine, often with its own dosing unit, ahead of the main SCR brick. The code says this front stage on bank 1 got hotter than permitted.
Heat from oxidation catalyst or filter regeneration reaching the close-coupled stage
Fuel or oil entering the exhaust upstream of the pre-catalyst
Temperature sensor at the pre-catalyst reading too high
Front SCR dosing stopped or regeneration interrupted
Higher NOx emissions after a cold start
P20EE: SCR NOx Catalyst Efficiency Below Threshold (Bank 1)

P20EE is the main monitor CARB requires for the NOx-reducing catalyst: the share of NOx removed by the SCR catalyst on bank 1, judged by the NOx sensors before and after it, has fallen below what the system needs. Ford's 2023 6.7 L diesel fails it when cumulative efficiency drops under 55 % with the SCR inlet at 200–320 °C.
Diluted or contaminated DEF, or a clogged or leaking dosing valve
Upstream or downstream NOx sensor reading wrong
SCR catalyst aged, overheated or poisoned
Exhaust leak between the two NOx sensors
Calibration needing an update (several manufacturer bulletins)
DEF or exhaust fluid quality warning in the instrument cluster
Speed limitation countdown on some vehicles if the fault persists
P20EF: SCR NOx Pre-Catalyst Efficiency Below Threshold (Bank 1)

P20EF concerns the front stage of an SCR arrangement with two stages on bank 1: the pre-catalyst no longer removes enough NOx. CARB allows catalysts in series to be monitored individually or together; this code is used where the front stage is checked separately, which requires a NOx sensor between the two bricks.
Front DEF dosing valve clogged, crystallised or leaking
NOx sensor before or between the stages reading wrong
Higher NOx at low exhaust temperatures, for example after cold starts
P20F0: P20F0 is the bank 2 version of P20EC: the SCR catalyst in the second exhaust line has been exposed to temperatures above its permitted limit. It presupposes a V engine with one aftertreatment path per bank, which is rare; most diesels merge both banks into one SCR line and use only the bank 1 codes. No manufacturer documents P20F0 publicly.
Leaking injector or misfire on bank 2 sending fuel into the exhaust
Excess heat during particulate filter regeneration on bank 2
Bank 2 SCR temperature sensor reading too high
Reduced power or interrupted regeneration to protect the catalyst
P20F1: P20F1 reports an over-temperature of the SCR pre-catalyst on bank 2, the close-coupled front stage of a two-stage system in the second exhaust line. Both conditions must be met for the code to exist on a vehicle: separate aftertreatment per bank and a split SCR with a front brick near the turbocharger outlet.
Fuel slip from bank 2 cylinders (injector leak, misfire, post-injection fault)
Pre-catalyst temperature sensor on bank 2 reading too high
Regeneration heat reaching the front stage
P20F2: SCR NOx Catalyst Efficiency Below Threshold (Bank 2)

P20F2 is the bank 2 twin of P20EE: the main SCR catalyst of the second exhaust line removes less NOx than required, judged by NOx sensors ahead of and behind it. CARB requires the NOx catalyst to be flagged once its conversion loss would push emissions past the regulatory multiple of the standard.
Poor DEF quality or bank 2 dosing valve fault
Bank 2 SCR catalyst aged or overheated
Exhaust leak between the bank 2 NOx sensors

P20F7 is the bank 2 version of P20F6 and only applies to engines with a second exhaust line that has its own SCR catalyst and dosing valve, typically V engines with separate aftertreatment per bank. P213B: EGR Throttle Control Circuit B Range/Performance

P213B is the functional check of EGR throttle B rather than an electrical one. The module compares the position it commands with the position the flap actually reaches, or judges whether the feedback is plausible; if the gap persists beyond a set time, P213B is logged.

P213C points to a low signal in the drive circuit of EGR throttle B: the output stage sees too little voltage where it expects supply potential, which almost always means a conductor of the flap motor is touching ground. Faulty output stage in the engine control module

Drive wire shorted to battery voltage
Shorted turns in the actuator motor causing overcurrent
Faulty output stage in the engine control module
Reduced power in some operating ranges

P213E records that the engine module stopped the engine on purpose because of a fault on the injection side – rail, high-pressure lines, pressure control or injectors. External leak at rail, high-pressure line or injector seal
Injector stuck open or leaking heavily
Rail pressure control valve or sensor no longer controlling pressure
Engine software misjudging the fault, update available

Fuel smell or visible fuel leak

P213F: Fuel Pump System Fault - Forced Engine Shutdown

P213F is the supply-side twin of P213E: the engine module shut the engine down because the fuel pump system – electric lift pump, its relay or control module, or the engine-driven high-pressure pump – no longer behaves in a way it can accept. No manufacturer documents P213F publicly, so the trigger is not known in detail.
Electric lift pump or its control module failed
Pump relay, fuse or wiring fault
Clogged filter or empty tank starving the pump
No restart or very long cranking
Check engine lamp with fuel pump codes

P2140 checks the second and third pedal tracks, E and F, against each other. As with P2139, no manufacturer explains its own trigger for this code, and FCA's emissions recall T21 for the 2004-2006 Dodge Sprinter just includes it in the list of codes that may follow the ECU reflash.

P2141: EGR Throttle Control Circuit A Low

P2141 flags a low signal in the drive circuit of EGR throttle A, the main diesel regulating flap that lowers intake pressure so exhaust gas can flow back. A wire of the flap motor touching ground, a winding shorted to the housing or a wet connector are the common reasons.

Moisture or corrosion in the flap connector
Actuator motor winding shorted to housing
Faulty output stage in the engine control module

P2142 reports a high signal or overcurrent in the drive circuit of EGR throttle A. Either a motor lead has contact with battery voltage, or the motor draws more current than the output stage allows – from shorted turns or because carbon has jammed the blade.

Shorted turns in the actuator motor
Faulty output stage in the engine control module

P2147 means the common feed of injector group A is pulled toward ground. Software falsely detecting the fault, reprogramming available

P214A reports that the exhaust entering the SCR catalyst was hotter than a calibrated ceiling while no particulate filter regeneration was active. The reading normally comes from the temperature sensor between the filter and the urea mixing section.

SCR inlet temperature sensor reading too high or wrongly placed after repair

Poor contact on the sensor F pins
Pedal held short of its stop
P2169: Exhaust Pressure Regulator Vent Solenoid Control Circuit/Open

The name points to a solenoid that lets an exhaust pressure regulator vent, but the only public, code-exact use found is on Jaguar Land Rover petrol models, where this code family belongs to the active exhaust valve: a solenoid in the tailpipe section switches a flap between quiet and sport sound. P2169 is the open or general fault of its control line.
Vehicle configuration enables an active exhaust valve that is not fitted
Broken wire or loose connector at the exhaust valve solenoid, often from heat or road dirt
Exhaust sound no longer changes with the drive mode
P216A: Fuel Injector Group E Supply Voltage Circuit/Open

Injector group E exists only on engines with at least five cylinders or five separately fed injector groups. GM petrol direct injection uses one group per cylinder, and its 2024 tables (24OBDG07) state it plainly: injector E is cylinder 5. The code covers the high-side feed of that injector.
Injector harness rubbed through at the intake plenum, valve cover bolts or fuel line
High-side driver in the engine control module faulty
Check engine lamp on, often with a cylinder 5 misfire code
P216B: Fuel Injector Group E Supply Voltage Circuit Low

P216B reports the feed of injector group E pulled toward ground. In GM petrol direct injection, group E means the injector of cylinder 5, so the code appears on V6 and V8 engines. GM's 2016 3.6 LGX V6 and 2018 6.2 LT4 V8 tables treat it as the injector 5 high-side line being grounded: while the driver is switched on, 25 A or more flows through it.
High-side wire of injector 5 chafed through to ground, for example on the transmission
Cylinder 5 injector shorted to its housing
Engine control module output stage faulty
P216C: Fuel Injector Group E Supply Voltage Circuit High

P216C is the opposite fault of group E: the feed of the cylinder 5 injector carries voltage when it should not. GM tests it while the high-side driver is switched off; if 1 V or less remains between the signal and the controller supply, the line is treated as shorted to power.
Injector 5 feed chafed against a powered circuit
High-side driver in the engine control module leaking voltage
Moisture or corrosion bridging pins in the injector connector
P216D: Fuel Injector Group F Supply Voltage Circuit/Open
P216D is the general fault of injector group F, which GM petrol direct injection equates with cylinder 6; its 2024 tables (24OBDG07) call it injector F.
Injector harness rubbed through on V6 engines
Water in the bank 2 injector harness connector (Corvette LT6)
Check engine lamp on, cylinder 6 misfire
With the LT6 several bank 2 codes and fuel pressure faults at once
P216E: Fuel Injector Group F Supply Voltage Circuit Low
P216E marks the feed of injector group F, the cylinder 6 injector on GM petrol direct injection, as shorted toward ground. It therefore concerns GM V6 and V8 engines with direct injection.
Cylinder 6 feed wire chafed through to ground
Engine control module output stage faulty
Cylinder 6 misfire and loss of power
P216F: Fuel Injector Group F Supply Voltage Circuit High

P216F is set when the group F supply, on GM petrol direct injection the high-side line of cylinder 6, shows voltage while the driver is off. GM's criterion in its 2016 (16OBDG07A) and 2018 LT4 tables is 1 V or less between the line and the controller supply, which means the wire is practically at battery level.
Cylinder 6 feed shorted to another powered wire
Engine control module driver fault, especially with several high codes
P2170: Exhaust Pressure Regulator Vent Solenoid Control Circuit Low

P2170 reports the control line of the exhaust pressure regulator vent solenoid pulled toward ground. Jaguar Land Rover uses it for the solenoid of the active exhaust valve; its March 2018 shop foreman call lists P2170-11, meaning the line is grounded, on 2018 Discovery Sport and Evoque with active exhaust.
PCM software with an overly sensitive fault strategy, fixed by an update
Exhaust flap stiff, often from a misaligned heat shield or cold weather
Control wire chafed through to ground near the exhaust
Restricted performance message on some models
Exhaust valve heard clicking at start-up
P2171: Exhaust Pressure Regulator Vent Solenoid Control Circuit High

P2171 means the module sees too much voltage on the control line of the exhaust pressure regulator vent solenoid, usually because the line touches battery voltage or the solenoid shorts internally. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly.
Control wire shorted to a battery-fed circuit
Output stage in the engine control module faulty
Exhaust flap stays in one position
P2172: Throttle Actuator Control System - Sudden High Air Flow Detected

P2172 is set when the engine abruptly takes in far more air than the throttle opening can explain, as if a large leak had appeared behind the throttle plate. The controller compares measured airflow (MAF or MAP based) with the flow its throttle model expects and reacts to a quick jump in the difference.
Hose, PCV line or brake booster line slipped off or split
Spread or pushed-out terminals at the MAP sensor connector
Engine software with oversensitive detection (reflash available)
High or hunting idle, hissing noise from the engine bay
P2173: Throttle Actuator Control System - High Air Flow Detected

P2173 reports an air surplus that builds up gradually: across a longer stretch of driving the engine receives more air than the throttle model predicts, which points to a small leak, a cracked vent hose or a plate that no longer seals. FCA calls it High Airflow/Vacuum Leak Detected (Slow Accumulation).
Cracked or loose crankcase ventilation or oil vapour tube
Small leak at an intake gasket or vacuum hose
MAP sensor connector with poor contact
Check engine lamp after some driving
Start/stop system deactivated on some models
P2174: Throttle Actuator Control System - Sudden Low Air Flow Detected

P2174 means the airflow fell abruptly well below what the current throttle opening should deliver. The controller sees a fast negative gap between measured airflow and its throttle-model estimate, as happens when the intake is suddenly blocked, the plate jams or a hose collapses under vacuum. No manufacturer documents P2174 publicly.
Air inlet suddenly blocked by snow, leaves or debris
Throttle plate sticking short of the commanded angle
Airflow or manifold pressure sensor reading too low
Check engine and throttle warning lamps
P2175: Throttle Actuator Control System - Low Air Flow Detected

P2175 tracks an air shortfall that develops slowly: over many operating points the engine receives less air than the throttle position predicts, and the learned correction finally exceeds its limit. A clogged air filter, carbon narrowing the throttle bore, a partly blocked intake or an airflow sensor drifting low are the usual reasons.
Carbon build-up narrowing the throttle bore
Heavily clogged air filter or intake restriction
Idle or airflow adaptation not reset after throttle cleaning
P2176: Throttle Actuator A Control System - Idle Position Not Learned

P2176 says the closed rest position of throttle A could not be learned. At key-on or after shutdown the controller drives the plate onto its lower stop and stores the sensor values; if they stay outside the window after the permitted attempts, the code is set.
Carbon on plate and bore preventing a clean closed position
Ice from a frozen crankcase ventilation holding the plate open
Engine software misjudging the sensor signals (update available)
Idle learn not performed after cleaning or module replacement
Check engine lamp right after start
Reduced engine power after a cold start
P2177: P2177 means bank 1's long-term trim has to add too much fuel once the engine is off idle, at part load and while accelerating. Bosch-type systems learn this as a multiplicative factor that scales with airflow, unlike the additive idle part behind P2187.
Fuel pressure too low under load, for example a weak pump or clogged filter
Air mass sensor reading too low or contaminated
Leak after the air mass sensor, often on the boost side
Calibration error or damaged A/F sensor wiring covered by bulletins
Check engine lamp on after two trips
Hesitation or lack of power when accelerating
P2178: P2178 is the rich-side limit of the bank 1 load adaptation: above idle the long-term trim has to take away more fuel than allowed. GM's Bosch-based V6 engines of 2005 and 2008 set it below a factor of 0.78, the 2023 and 2024 tables below 0.77, each after two trips.
Air mass sensor reading too high
Fuel pressure too high or injectors over-delivering
Calibration error fixed by a software update
Fuel vapour from purge or boiling fuel in the low-pressure system
Check engine lamp on after two trips
P2179: P2179 is the bank 2 version of P2177 on engines with a front oxygen sensor for each cylinder bank: the load-dependent, multiplicative share of bank 2's long-term correction has reached its lean limit. GM's 2005 2.8 and 3.6 V6 and the 2008 3.6 LLT use a factor above 1.23, GM's 2024 tables above 1.27, both over two trips.
Low fuel pressure or air mass sensor fault, usually with P2177 too
Intake leak or front oxygen sensor fault on bank 2
Check engine lamp on after two trips
P217A: Fuel Injector Group G Supply Voltage Circuit/Open
Group G only exists on engines with seven or more injector groups, in practice eight-cylinder engines with direct injection.
Cylinder 7 injector feed shorted to ground or supply in the harness
Check engine lamp on, cylinder 7 misfire
P217B: Fuel Injector Group G Supply Voltage Circuit Low

P217B reports the feed of injector group G as grounded, which on GM's direct-injection V8 engines is the injector of cylinder 7, at the rear of bank 1. GM's 2016 table 16OBDG07A and the 2018 LT4 table of the supercharged 6.2 V8 measure it with the driver switched on: if 25 A or more flows through the high side, the line is grounded somewhere.
Cylinder 7 feed wire grounded at the rear of the engine
Engine control module output stage faulty
P217C: Fuel Injector Group G Supply Voltage Circuit High

P217C means the group G injector supply, cylinder 7 on GM's direct-injection V8 engines, is pulled up to supply voltage. GM tests this while the high-side driver is off: if the line sits within 1 V of the controller supply, the module treats it as shorted to power.
Cylinder 7 feed shorted to a powered wire
P217D: Fuel Injector Group H Supply Voltage Circuit/Open

Group H is the eighth injector group, on GM petrol direct injection the injector of cylinder 8, the last one on bank 2 of a V8. GM's 2023 and 2024 tables call it injector H and use P217D when its high side shows less than 0.5 ohm to ground with the driver off or to the injector supply with the driver on; two events above 9 V store the code in one trip.
Water in the bank 2 injector harness connector, Corvette LT6
Cylinder 8 injector feed shorted in the harness
Check engine lamp on, cylinder 8 misfire
Several bank 2 injector codes at once if the connector is wet
P217E: Fuel Injector Group H Supply Voltage Circuit Low
P217E flags the supply of injector group H as grounded, on GM's direct-injection V8 engines the injector of cylinder 8. GM lists it for the 6.2 LT4 in 2018 and in its 2016 table 16OBDG07A.
Cylinder 8 feed wire chafed to ground
Cylinder 8 injector shorted to its housing
Engine control module output stage faulty
P217F: Fuel Injector Group H Supply Voltage Circuit High
P217F is the last code of the injector group series: the feed of group H, cylinder 8 on GM's direct-injection V8 engines, shows supply voltage although the high-side driver is switched off.
Cylinder 8 feed shorted to a powered wire
Moisture or corrosion in the injector connector
Engine control module output stage faulty
Cylinder 8 misfire, possibly rich running on bank 2
P2180: P2180 closes the series: bank 2's long-term trim must remove too much fuel above idle, so its multiplicative adaptation sits at the rich limit. GM's 2005 2.8 and 3.6 V6 and the 2008 3.6 LLT use a factor below 0.78, GM's 2024 tables below 0.77, both over two trips. VW's 2014 Touareg 3.0 TSI hybrid and 3.6 VR6 set it below -30 % on bank 2.
Injector on bank 2 leaking or over-delivering
Fuel pressure too high or air mass sensor over-reading, usually with P2178
Bank 2 front oxygen sensor reading rich
Check engine lamp on after two trips
P2181: P2181 is the engine computer's verdict that the coolant warms up too slowly or settles below its target, almost always because the thermostat no longer closes. CARB requires the thermostat to be monitored and flags a failure when the warm-up stays more than 11.1 °C under the regulating point.
Thermostat not closing fully because of wear, corrosion or debris on the seat
Engine control software too sensitive, fixed by a reflash on some models (e.g. Kia SA463)
Radiator fan running constantly and overcooling the engine
Low coolant level or air in the system distorting the temperature reading
Check engine light, usually without any change in driving behaviour
Temperature gauge rises slowly or stays below normal
Weak cabin heating in cold weather
Higher fuel consumption on short trips
P2182: P2182 is the general circuit code for the second coolant temperature sensor: the module sees a fault in its wiring or signal but does not sort it into low, high or erratic. Where sensor 2 sits is up to the maker.
Loose, corroded or water-damaged connector at sensor 2
Signal or reference wire to sensor 2 open or damaged
Radiator fan runs continuously as a precaution
P2183: Engine Coolant Temperature Sensor 2 Circuit Range/Performance

P2183 means sensor 2 delivers a voltage inside the valid band, yet the temperature does not fit the other readings. Most makers test this after a long cold soak, when all temperatures should match. The VW Touareg with engine CNRB sets it when the radiator outlet sensor differs by more than 35 K from intake air, ambient or fuel temperature at start-up.
Water ingress or internal corrosion in sensor 2 shifting its reading
Control software misjudging soak time, block heater or cabin heater use
Coolant hoses at the sensor loop swapped or air trapped after service
Aged sensor element drifting out of tolerance
Check engine light, often right after a cold start
Remote start disabled on some trucks
Engine overheat message without real overheating on some hybrids
P2184: Engine Coolant Temperature Sensor 2 Circuit Low

Coolant sensors are NTC thermistors: the hotter they get, the lower their resistance and voltage. P2184 therefore reports a signal from sensor 2 so low that it would mean an impossibly hot engine, typically a signal wire touching ground or a shorted sensor.
Signal wire of sensor 2 chafed through and touching ground
Coolant or water in the connector bridging signal and ground
Check engine light after two drives on GM vehicles
Radiator fans running at full speed
Further codes and warnings if a harness is chafed
P2185: Engine Coolant Temperature Sensor 2 Circuit High

P2185 is the high end of the sensor 2 circuit check. With an NTC thermistor a high signal stands for extreme cold, so the usual reason is an open circuit: a broken wire, an unplugged or corroded connector, or a sensor with an interrupted element; a short to voltage is rarer.
Connector at sensor 2 unplugged, loose or corroded
Signal or ground wire of sensor 2 broken
Signal wire shorted to a voltage source
Fans run permanently as a safety measure
Low coolant or temperature warning without a real cause on some models
P2186: Engine Coolant Temperature Sensor 2 Circuit Intermittent/Erratic

P2186 covers a sensor 2 signal that jumps instead of changing smoothly. Coolant temperature moves slowly because of the mass of the liquid, so a step faster than physics allows points to a loose contact rather than a real change.
Worn or loose pins in the sensor 2 connector
Wire broken inside its insulation or chafed harness making intermittent contact
Sensor 2 with an intermittent internal fault
Check engine light after two drives
Fans switching on and off irregularly
Temperature-related messages that appear and vanish
P2187: P2187 means the long-term fuel trim of bank 1 has to add more fuel than allowed in the idle and low-load range. Many systems, especially Bosch ones, split mixture adaptation into an additive part, which dominates at low airflow, and a multiplicative part for load.
Air leak after the air mass sensor, often at the crankcase ventilation
Damaged front oxygen or A/F sensor wiring
Rough or hunting idle, hissing from the engine bay
P2188: P2188 means the long-term fuel trim of bank 1 has to remove more fuel than allowed in the idle and low-load range, the additive part of the mixture adaptation on Bosch-type systems. GM's 2008 3.6 LLT sets it below -6.0 % at 520 to 1120 rpm and 1.7 to 7.8 g/s, with closed loop and coolant above 60 °C.
Leaking injector or fuel pressure too high
Fuel vapour from the purge valve or oil-diluted crankcase gases
Air mass or manifold pressure reading wrong
P2189: P2189 is the bank 2 version of P2187: on engines with a front oxygen sensor per bank, the long-term trim of bank 2 has to add more fuel than allowed at idle and low load.
Intake gasket or runner leak on the bank 2 side
Shared vacuum leak, usually with P2187 present too
Bank 2 front sensor, its wiring or an injector on that bank
P218A: Throttle Actuator B Control System - Idle Position Not Learned

P218A is the throttle B counterpart of P2176: on engines with a second electronic throttle, usually one per cylinder bank, that second unit failed to learn its closed rest position. GM's 2023 table 23OBDG07 runs the same three-step learn for bank 2 as for bank 1.
Carbon or ice keeping throttle B off its closed stop
Weak motor or gear wear in throttle unit B
Position sensors of throttle B outside the learn window
Supply or signal wiring fault at throttle B
P218B: P218B is a general electrical fault in the second throttle/fuel inhibit line, B. An inhibit line carries a signal with which another unit can tell the engine computer to keep the throttle closed or stop fuelling. No manufacturer documents the B line publicly.
Open or high-resistance inhibit B wire
Corroded or loose pins at the engine or throttle module connector
Fault in the unit that drives the inhibit signal
Check engine lamp on the following drive
P218C: P218C means the inhibit B line is electrically within limits, yet its state or response does not fit what the controller expects: it may signal a lock when none is requested, or fail to react during a function test. No manufacturer documents P218C publicly.
Relay in the inhibit path sticking or switching late
Software versions of the communicating modules do not match
Intermittent contact causing implausible line states
Check engine lamp on the next drive
Occasional power reduction without obvious reason
P218D: P218D reports that the voltage on inhibit line B sits below the lowest permitted value, which normally points to a short to ground, a missing supply from the sending unit or an open line pulled down by the input stage. No manufacturer documents P218D publicly.
Inhibit B wire shorted to ground
Water or corrosion in a connector of the inhibit line
Output stage of the sending module failed
Check engine lamp on the following drive
P218E: P218E says the inhibit B line carries more voltage than the controller allows, typically because it touches a battery-fed wire or the sending unit's output stage is stuck high. No manufacturer documents P218E publicly.
Inhibit B wire shorted to a battery-fed circuit
Voltage fed back through a faulty module after ignition off
Relay contacts welded, keeping the line energised
Check engine lamp on the following drive
P218F: P218F means the SCR system is dosing on paper, but nothing reaches the exhaust: the expected link between dosing commands, pump effort and line pressure is missing. Ford's 2023 diesel summary, which calls the test a reductant delivery check for clogging, runs it while dosing with the pressure error inside 0.5 bar for 5 s.
Dosing valve or its nozzle crystallised and blocked
Leak in the DEF line between pump and dosing valve
Partly frozen line in frost or control software that needs an update
Worn DEF pump that cannot keep up delivery
Check engine light with a DEF or emission system warning
Restart countdown or speed limitation if the fault persists
White crystalline deposits at the dosing valve or line joints
P2190: P2190 is the bank 2 counterpart of P2188: the long-term trim of bank 2 has to remove more fuel than allowed at idle and low load.
Shared cause such as air mass error or purge vapour, usually with P2188 too
P2191: System Too Lean at Higher Load (Bank 1)
P2191 sets once bank 1's long-term trim has run into its enrichment limit in the upper load range, so the engine would be lean there without the correction.
Fuel pump or pressure regulation unable to hold pressure at high demand
Air mass sensor under-reading at high airflow
Charge-air or intake leak behind the air mass sensor (turbo engines)
Hesitation or flat spot under heavy throttle
Loss of power when climbing or towing
High positive long-term fuel trim at high load only
P2192: System Too Rich at Higher Load (Bank 1)
P2192 is the rich-side limit of the bank 1 trim in the upper load zone: the controller has pulled as much fuel as it may and the front sensor still reports excess fuel.
ECM calibration issue covered by a software update (e.g. Kia 1.6 GDI)
Air mass sensor reading too high
Injector leaking or over-delivering at high rail pressure
Fuel smell or dark exhaust under load
P2193: System Too Lean at Higher Load (Bank 2)

P2193 reports for bank 2 what P2191 reports for bank 1: in the upper load zone the long-term trim of that bank sits at its enrichment limit. It only exists on engines with a separate front sensor per bank, such as V6, V8 and boxer engines. The useful question is whether bank 1 shows the same.
Weak fuel supply (pump, filter, pressure regulation), usually with P2191
Intake gasket or runner leak on the bank 2 side
Exhaust leak ahead of the bank 2 front sensor
Bank 2 long-term trim much higher than bank 1 at high load
P2194: System Too Rich at Higher Load (Bank 2)

P2194 means bank 2 has reached the lower limit of its trim in the upper load zone: the ECM is removing as much fuel as permitted, yet that bank still runs rich. Because air mass, fuel pressure and canister purge feed both banks, a rich error caused by them usually brings P2192 along.
Leaking or over-delivering injector on bank 2
Air mass sensor reading high or fuel pressure too high (usually with P2192)
Bank 2 long-term trim strongly negative at high load
P2195: O2 Sensor Signal Biased/Stuck Lean (Bank 1, Sensor 1)
