P2195 means the front oxygen or air-fuel sensor on bank 1 reports a lean mixture that the ECM does not believe, either because it stays lean or because it disagrees with other evidence.
Front oxygen or A/F sensor aged or contaminated
Exhaust leak ahead of the sensor
Sensor signal or reference wiring fault
Possible rough running or higher consumption from wrong fuelling
P2196: O2 Sensor Signal Biased/Stuck Rich (Bank 1, Sensor 1)
P2196 means the front oxygen or air-fuel sensor on bank 1 reports a rich mixture that the ECM does not accept.
Front oxygen or A/F sensor contaminated or aged
Sensor signal shorted or reference circuit fault
P2197: O2 Sensor Signal Biased/Stuck Lean (Bank 2, Sensor 1)
P2197 is the bank 2 version of P2195 on engines with a front sensor per bank: the bank 2 front oxygen or A/F sensor keeps reporting lean in a way the ECM rejects.
Bank 2 front oxygen or A/F sensor aged or contaminated
Exhaust manifold leak on bank 2 ahead of the sensor
Possible rough running or higher consumption
P2198: O2 Sensor Signal Biased/Stuck Rich (Bank 2, Sensor 1)
P2198 is the bank 2 counterpart of P2196: the bank 2 front oxygen or A/F sensor reports rich in a way the ECM does not accept.
Bank 2 front oxygen or A/F sensor contaminated or aged
Sensor signal or reference wiring fault
P2199: P2199 compares two intake air temperature readings that should be close, typically one in the air mass sensor and one further downstream in the intake manifold or a combined pressure and temperature sensor. Each circuit can be fine on its own; the fault is the disagreement.
One temperature sensor drifted or contaminated
Corroded connector or added resistance in one sensor circuit
Calibration issue fixed by a PCM update (e.g. RAM 1500 3.0 EcoDiesel 2020)
Strong heat soak or hot-air leak near one sensor
Scan data shows two clearly different intake temperatures with the engine cold-soaked
P219A: P219A means the ECM sees mixture differences between the cylinders of bank 1 that are large enough to raise emissions, even if the bank average is fine. CARB phased this monitor in from 25 % of 2011 to all 2014 model-year petrol vehicles (13 CCR 1968.2 (e)(6.2.1)(C)).
One injector clogged, leaking or out of flow tolerance
Compression loss through an intake or exhaust valve
Air leak at one intake runner or gasket
ECM logic or sensor signal issue covered by software or wiring bulletins
Slight rough running or misfire codes when one cylinder is far off
P219B: P219B is the bank 2 counterpart for V and boxer engines. Ford's 2012 summary shows one way to find it: the ECM watches the fast ripple of the bank's wide-band sensor over windows of roughly 50 revolutions and sets the code when more than 75 % of them fail, after 300 to 700 s of driving at 1000 to 3000 rpm and 20 to 60 % load.
Leaking or contaminated injector on bank 2
Interference or damage in the bank 2 A/F sensor wiring
Intake runner or gasket leak at one bank 2 cylinder
PCM calibration addressed by a software update
Possible misfire codes on bank 2 cylinders
P219C: P219C names cylinder 1 as the one whose mixture departs from the others. Not every system can do that: CARB lets the stored code point only as far as the monitoring method allows, so many engines just log P219A or P219B.
Cylinder 1 injector clogged, leaking or out of tolerance
Intake runner or injector seal leak at cylinder 1
False detection fixed by ECM reprogramming (e.g. Subaru Crosstrek Hybrid)
Possible P0301 or rough idle if cylinder 1 deviates strongly
P219D: P219D singles out cylinder 2. On engines with two banks, whether cylinder 2 sits on bank 1 or bank 2 depends on the maker's numbering, which decides whether P219A or P219B may appear alongside. Bulletins show three very different outcomes.
Faulty high-pressure injector at cylinder 2 (direct injection)
Charge-air leak upsetting cylinder filling (e.g. RAM 3.0 Hurricane)
Detection logic corrected by software update (e.g. Hyundai Sonata 2.0T)
Reduced power or whistling noise if a charge-air leak is the cause
P219E: P219E points at cylinder 3. Two bulletins show that a mixture code does not always mean a fuel part. Audi stored P219C to P21A1, one code per affected cylinder, on 2010 to 2012 S4, S5 and A6 with the 3.0 TFSI because of an incorrect software setting; the fix was new engine software and, in a later revision, a new crankcase pressure regulating valve.
Exhaust valve leakage at cylinder 3 (e.g. worn guides on Lexus 8AR-FTS)
Cylinder 3 injector delivering the wrong amount
Incorrect ECM software setting (e.g. Audi 3.0 TFSI)
Reduced engine power in severe cases
P219F: P219F singles out cylinder 4, the last cylinder on four-cylinder engines. Infiniti issued a bulletin for 2017 to 2018 QX60 with the direct-injection VQ35DD that stored only P219F without any driveability complaint; the remedy was ECM reprogramming followed by the idle air volume learn.
Oversensitive detection fixed by ECM reprogramming (e.g. Infiniti QX60, Hyundai Sonata)
Fouled spark plug as a consequence of a rich cylinder
Rough running or rattling noise when an injector leaks
No symptom when the cause is software
P21A0: P21A0 can only occur on engines with at least five cylinders. VW's 2014 specification books for the Golf, Jetta, Passat and Beetle with the 2.5 litre inline five list P219C to P21A0, one per cylinder, all judged the same way: the ECM briefly leans one cylinder, measures how much rougher the engine runs and derives an individual fuel correction; a result belo…
Ignition or compression weakness at cylinder 5 affecting the roughness test
Software setting corrected by an update (e.g. Audi 3.0 TFSI)
Possible P0305 or slight vibration at idle
P21A1: P21A1 marks cylinder 6, the last cylinder of an inline six or V6. The clearest example comes from the 2025 RAM 1500 with the 3.0 Hurricane twin-turbo inline six: the charge-air cooler housing had a loose crimp that let boost escape, the cylinders filled unevenly and P21A1 set together with other cylinder codes, accompanied by a whistle and lower boost; the c…
Charge-air cooler or boost leak (turbo engines, e.g. RAM 3.0 Hurricane)
Whistling noise and reduced boost with a charge-air leak
P21A2: P21A2 places a mixture imbalance at cylinder 7, so it only exists on engines with eight or more cylinders. No manufacturer documents this code publicly; the bulletin index of the US safety authority NHTSA contains no bulletin that names it.
Intake runner or injector seal leak at cylinder 7
Possible P0307 if the deviation is large
P21A3: P21A3 blames cylinder 8, on a V8 the last cylinder in the numbering. No manufacturer documentation of this code is publicly available, and no bulletin in the NHTSA index refers to it; the basis is the general CARB requirement for detecting cylinder imbalance, phased in for 2011 to 2014 model years with an emission threshold of 3.0 times the FTP standard (4.0…
Intake leak at the cylinder 8 runner
Possible P0308 with a strong deviation
P21A4: P21A4 is reserved for an imbalance at cylinder 9 and can therefore only appear on engines with ten or more cylinders, a small group of V10 and V12 petrol engines. No manufacturer documents the code publicly and no bulletin in the NHTSA index mentions it.
Possible P0309 with a large deviation
P21A5: P21A5 flags cylinder 10, which on a V10 is the final cylinder and on a V12 sits near the end of its bank. Public manufacturer material for this code does not exist, and the NHTSA bulletin index has no entry for it.
Fault in another cylinder of the same bank shifting the result
P21A6: P21A6 assigns the imbalance to cylinder 11, which exists only on twelve-cylinder engines. No manufacturer has published how it detects this code, and no NHTSA bulletin names it, so it is a placeholder that J2012 provides for large engines. The legal frame is CARB's cylinder imbalance monitor (13 CCR 1968.2 (e)(6.2.1)(C)).
Possible P0311 with a large deviation
P21A7: P21A7 is the last code of the cylinder series that starts with P219C and points to cylinder 12 of a twelve-cylinder engine. There is no public manufacturer description and no NHTSA bulletin for it.
P21A8: P21A8 is the general circuit code for the second reductant level sensor, needed only where a DEF tank reports its fill level through more than one sensing element. GM's 6.6L Duramax (LML/LGH) and the 2014 Cruze diesel read three discrete level sensors, numbered 1 to 3 in GM's tables, which corresponds to A to C.
Damaged or corroded harness or connector at the DEF tank
Level sensor B in the tank assembly failed
DEF system warning message in the cluster
DEF level or range display missing or wrong
P21A9: Reductant Level Sensor B Circuit Range/Performance

P21A9 flags a level sensor B signal that stays inside its electrical limits but does not fit what else the system knows, such as the states of the other level sensors or the fluid consumed. GM's 2018 Cruze diesel (LH7) stores it in the module running the DEF system, under the name Level Sensor 2 Performance.
Frozen or very cold fluid giving an implausible reading
Level sensor B fouled by crystallised urea or degraded
Control module calibration flagging the sensor too early
DEF level shown wrongly or jumping
Fault appears mainly after cold nights
P21AA: Reductant Level Sensor B Circuit Low

P21AA means the second reductant level sensor reads too low a voltage, which GM takes as a short to ground. GM documents it for the 6.6L Duramax LML and the 2014 Cruze 2.0 diesel: the tank level electronics apply a test pulse, and if sensor 2 then shows less than 0.17 V for more than 3 s with over 8 V supply, the ECM receives an error status over CAN.
Sensor 2 signal wire chafed through to ground
Fluid or water in the tank connector
Internal short in level sensor B (tank assembly)
DEF warning message that stays on
DEF range or level display wrong
P21AB: Reductant Level Sensor B Circuit High

P21AB is the high-side counterpart: GM sets it when level sensor 2 shows an open load (between 3.56 and 4.74 V, read 1.5 ms after the test pulse) or a short to battery voltage (above 4.74 V), each for more than 3 s, as Type A on the 6.6L LML and the 2014 Cruze diesel.
Open signal wire or spread terminal at the tank connector
Signal wire shorted to a voltage source
Level sensor B open inside the tank assembly
Check engine light on at once
Several level sensor codes stored together
P21AC: Reductant Level Sensor B Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P21AC reports that the level sensor B signal drops out or jumps for short moments instead of failing steadily. No manufacturer documents criteria for this code publicly.
Loose terminal in the tank connector
Harness flexing or rubbing near the tank mounting
Corrosion from fluid creeping into the connector
DEF warning that comes and goes
Check engine light, sometimes only stored code
P21AD: P21AD covers the electrical circuit of the third reductant level sensor, so it only exists on tanks with at least three level points. GM's 6.6L Duramax and 2014 Cruze diesel are such cases: the tank electronics test sensors 1 to 3 separately and pass each status to the ECM over CAN. GM uses the specific codes P21AF and P21B0 instead of this summary code.
Fault in a supply, ground or connector shared by the level sensors
Level sensor C in the tank assembly failed
DEF range message missing or implausible
P21AE: Reductant Level Sensor C Circuit Range/Performance
P21AE stands for an implausible level sensor C signal whose voltage is still electrically valid. No manufacturer describes a separate check for this code in public material.
Crystallised urea on level sensor C
Partly frozen fluid around the sensor
Level sensor C drifting or degraded
DEF level display does not match the refill amount
P21AF: Reductant Level Sensor C Circuit Low

P21AF is set when level sensor C, called level sensor 3 by GM, reads below 0.17 V right after the tank electronics apply their test pulse, which GM interprets as a short to ground. Supply must be above 8 V and the error must persist for more than 3 s.
Sensor 3 signal wire shorted to ground
Water or fluid bridging contacts in the tank connector
Level sensor C shorted inside the tank assembly
Check engine light after two trips
P21B0: Reductant Level Sensor C Circuit High

P21B0 means GM's level sensor 3 (sensor C) shows an open circuit or a short to battery: either 3.56 to 4.74 V or more than 4.74 V, measured 1.5 ms after a test pulse, for over 3 s. The 6.6L LML and the 2014 Cruze both rate it Type A, lighting the MIL on the first trip.
Tank connector loose, unplugged or with spread terminals
Sensor 3 signal wire open or shorted to voltage
Level sensor C open inside the tank assembly
Check engine light on at once
P203D and P21AB often stored as well
P21B1: Reductant Level Sensor C Circuit Intermittent/Erratic

P21B1 marks level sensor C signals that come and go. Public manufacturer criteria do not exist; GM's diesel tables describe sensor 3 only through the steady faults P21AF and P21B0, each filtered over 3 s.
Harness pinched under a tank strap
DEF warning that appears and clears
P21B2: Excessive Time To Enter Closed Loop NOx Adsorber Control

P21B2 is set when the feedback control of a NOx adsorber (lean NOx trap) has not become active within the time the manufacturer allows once its enable conditions are met. CARB requires this check for vehicles with feedback control of the adsorber or its active injection (13 CCR 1968.2 (f)(8.2.3)(A)(i)).
Fouled or slow oxygen sensor before or after the adsorber
Exhaust not reaching control temperature (short trips, low load)
Exhaust leak ahead of the sensors
Exhaust temperature sensor reporting too low
Regeneration of the NOx trap delayed or skipped
Higher NOx emissions, possible test failure
P21B3: Closed Loop NOx Adsorber Control At Limit - Too High
P21B3 means the NOx adsorber feedback loop has reached its upper adjustment limit and still misses its target, the case CARB describes in 13 CCR 1968.2 (f)(8.2.3)(A)(iii).
NOx adsorber sulphur-loaded or thermally aged
Downstream oxygen sensor responding too slowly
Air leak in the exhaust ahead of the sensors
Too little fuel delivered for the rich phases
Higher fuel consumption from long rich phases
P21B4: P21B4 reports that the NOx adsorber on bank 1 has run hotter than the manufacturer's protection limit.
Too much fuel during regeneration or desulphation
Leaking or dribbling injector on bank 1
Misfire sending unburnt fuel into the exhaust
Exhaust temperature sensor reading too high
Reduced power while the engine protects the catalyst
Strong smell or heat from the exhaust
P21B5: P21B5 is the bank 2 version of the adsorber over-temperature fault and therefore only exists where each cylinder bank feeds its own NOx storage catalyst, which in practice means V engines with two exhaust paths.
Injector on bank 2 delivering too much fuel
Bank 2 exhaust temperature sensor reading too high
Reduced power to protect the catalyst
Uneven exhaust temperatures between the banks
P21B6: After a cold start, petrol direct-injection and diesel engines deliberately move the moment of injection – for example with an extra late pulse – so that more heat reaches the catalyst. CARB 13 CCR 1968.2 (e)(11) wants every element of this strategy checked while it runs and reported apart from warm-engine faults. P21B6 pins such a deviation on cylinder 1.
Injector of cylinder 1 responds late or inconsistently when cold
Corroded or loose connector or harness at injector 1
Injector driver stage in the engine control module faulty
Engine module software with an overly strict cold-start check
Check engine light after one or more cold starts
Slightly rough idle in the first minute after a cold start
No noticeable fault once the engine is warm
P21B7: P21B7 flags cylinder 2 during the cold-start phase only: the injection timing commanded for catalyst heating did not arrive as intended on that cylinder. The heating phase is brief and ends as coolant and catalyst warm up, so the monitor gets one chance per cold start and may need several cold starts before the code is confirmed.
Injector of cylinder 2 worn or coked, opening late at low temperature
Chafed or high-resistance wiring to injector 2
Weak battery lowering injector supply voltage during and after cranking
Check engine light that appears only after cold starts
Uneven running or slight smoke shortly after starting a cold engine
Code may take several cold starts to return after clearing
P21B8: Cylinder 3 is the last cylinder of three-cylinder engines such as Ford's 1.0-litre EcoBoost, a turbo direct-injection unit. There a single cylinder accounts for a third of all combustion events, so a cold-start fault on it tends to be felt more than on larger engines.
Injector of cylinder 3 with deposits or a weak coil
Moisture or corrosion in the plug of injector 3
Engine software update available for the cold-start calibration
Noticeable shaking at cold idle, especially on three-cylinder engines
Check engine light after cold starts
P21B9: Four-cylinder petrol direct injection is the most widespread engine type this code can apply to, and cylinder 4 is its last cylinder.
Deposits on the tip of injector 4 changing its opening behaviour
Harness fault on the injector 4 circuit
Rail pressure barely inside its window during cold start, affecting the last cylinder first
Check engine light, usually without drivability complaints
Slightly longer catalyst warm-up and possibly higher cold-start emissions
Occasional hesitation right after a cold start
P21BA: P21BA can only occur on engines with at least five cylinders – inline fives, V6, V8 and larger. GM's 4.3-litre V6 and 5.3/6.2-litre V8 direct-injection engines use a dual-pulse injection in open loop after a cold start; a GM bulletin explains that the module watches crankshaft speed in this mode and sets P050D (cold start rough idle) if it varies too much.
Injector of cylinder 5 sticking or delivering late when cold
Repair on the wrong injector because of a misread cylinder numbering
Open or high-resistance circuit to injector 5
Check engine light after cold starts
Rough idle during the first seconds after a cold start, possibly together with P050D
P21BB: Cylinder 6 exists on six-cylinder engines and anything larger – inline sixes and V6 units such as Ford's 3.5-litre EcoBoost petrol or the 3.0-litre EcoDiesel in the Ram 1500.
Outdated engine module software (analogous timing codes were cured by reprogramming)
Injector of cylinder 6 worn, coked or with drifting opening delay
Damaged wiring or connector at injector 6
Check engine light after cold starts
On diesels, more white smoke or knocking in the first minutes
Hard start or rough idle when cold
P21BC: From cylinder 7 on, the code is limited to engines with at least seven cylinders – in practice V8, V10, V12 and W12. Common petrol V8 with direct injection are GM's 5.3- and 6.2-litre small blocks, which a GM bulletin describes with dual-pulse injection after a cold start, and Ford's 5.0-litre Coyote, which since 2018 combines port and direct injection.
Direct injector of cylinder 7 slow to open or leaking at low temperature
Chafed or heat-damaged wiring to injector 7
Fault in the high-voltage injector driver of the engine module
Check engine light after cold starts
Rough cold idle, sometimes with P050D or a cylinder 7 misfire code
P21BD: P21BD covers cylinder 8, the last cylinder of a V8. GM's 2025 diesel tables show how close an existing monitor comes to this code: during cold start the module compares requested and scheduled start of injection, with every cylinder from A to H included in the enable checks, and a deviation beyond ±4 in 88 of 176 samples sets the lamp in the first trip.
Injector of cylinder 8 with slow or varying response
Connector or wiring fault at injector 8
Cold-start calibration in the engine module needing an update
Check engine light after cold starts
Rough running or smoke in the first minute after a cold start
P21BE: A ninth cylinder exists only on V10, V12 and W12 engines, so P21BE is limited to a handful of models. Petrol engines in this class with direct injection include the 5.2-litre V10 of Lamborghini and Audi (Huracán, R8, S6 and S8) and the 6.3-litre W12 FSI of the Audi A8, which feeds its injectors from two high-pressure pumps and two rails.
Direct injector of cylinder 9 with deposits or slow response
Low pressure on the rail feeding cylinder 9 (engines with two rails)
Wiring or connector fault at injector 9
Check engine light after cold starts
Slightly uneven idle while the engine is cold
P21BF: Cylinder 10 is the last cylinder of a V10 and exists otherwise only on twelve-cylinder engines. V10 engines are rare: Ford's 6.8-litre truck V10 (firing order 1-6-5-10-2-7-3-8-4-9, in the E-Series until 2019) and the 5.2-litre direct-injection V10 of Lamborghini and Audi.
Injector of cylinder 10 aged or contaminated
Wiring or connector problem at injector 10
Engine module software needing a cold-start calibration update
Check engine light after one or more cold starts
Uneven idle until the engine warms up
P21C0: P21C0 applies only to twelve-cylinder engines (V12 or W12), since passenger-car engines with exactly eleven cylinders do not exist. Examples with direct injection are BMW's N74 twin-turbo V12, found in the BMW 760i and in Rolls-Royce models such as Ghost, Wraith and Dawn, and the 6.3-litre W12 FSI.
Direct injector of cylinder 11 with changed opening behaviour
Heat-damaged wiring or connector at injector 11
Injector driver for cylinder 11 in the engine control module faulty
Check engine light after cold starts
Barely noticeable on the road; a twelve-cylinder engine masks a single cylinder well
P21C1: Cylinder 12 is the last cylinder of V12 and W12 engines. Direct-injection V12 include Ferrari's F140 family (FF, F12berlinetta, 812 Superfast) and BMW's N74; among W engines there is the 6.3-litre W12 FSI. P21C1 reports that during the cold-start heating phase the injection timing of cylinder 12 deviated from its target.
Injector of cylinder 12 with deposits or worn needle
Damaged wiring at the end of the cylinder bank (injector 12)
Cold-start calibration of the engine module out of date
Check engine light after cold starts
Hardly any drivability change, at most a slightly uneven cold idle
P21C2: P21C2 concerns the control line of the relay that supplies current to the DEF heaters. The control module drives the relay coil through an output stage and checks whether the circuit reacts; an open circuit means the coil, its wiring or a connector has lost continuity, so the heaters cannot be energised.
Relay coil burnt open or relay not seated in its socket
Broken control wire between module and relay
Corroded or loose terminals at relay box or module connector
Faulty output stage in the controlling module
DEF system warning, especially at low ambient temperature
Frozen DEF thaws slowly, dosing begins late after a cold start
P21C3: Reductant Heater Relay Control Circuit Low

P21C3 is the low-side fault on the control line of the DEF heater relay: the signal is pulled toward ground, for example by a chafed wire touching the frame or a shorted relay coil, so the relay no longer follows the command.
Control wire chafed through and shorted to ground
Relay coil with internal short or welded contacts
Water or salt in the relay or heater connector
Output stage of the controlling module faulty
DEF heating inactive or running when not commanded
Blown fuse in the heater supply
P21C4: Reductant Heater Relay Control Circuit High

P21C4 means the control side of the DEF heater relay shows voltage when it should be dead. Ford's 2023 diesel summary sets it when the relay stage and all heaters are off and the heater circuit still carries more than 5 V, within at most 5 s; a short to the battery feed or contacts that no longer open are the classic reasons.
Replacement dosing control unit not programmed or with outdated software (FCA)
Control or heater wire shorted to battery voltage
Internal fault in the controlling module
Code appears shortly after a DEF control unit was replaced
Additional communication code such as U11C1 stored
P21C5: P21C5 is a plausibility code: the level sensor A reports valid readings, yet they hardly move when the fluid in the tank should be sloshing. GM spells this out for the ultrasonic sensor in its 2025 diesel tables, where it is sensor 1.
Level sensor calibration in the engine software (update available, e.g. Jaguar)
Ultrasonic level sensor in the tank unit faulty
Crystal deposits or gas bubbles disturbing the echo
Fluid partly frozen or slush around the sensor
Check engine light on after two drives
DEF gauge stays at the same value while fluid is being used
DEF warning messages in the instrument cluster
P21C6: P21C6 applies only to DEF tanks with a second level measurement, labelled B. It is stored when that second reading is electrically fine but stays frozen at one value although the module expects it to change. No manufacturer documents P21C6 publicly.
Second level sensing element in the tank unit faulty
Float or contact held by crystals or debris
Calibration of the level evaluation needs a software update
DEF gauge implausible or not moving
DEF warning in the instrument cluster
P21C7: Reductant Control Module Power Relay/Relays Control Circuit/Open

P21C7 flags a break in the control line of the power relay, or group of relays, that supplies the DEF control module and the loads behind it. Ford's 2023 diesel summary evaluates it inside the same continuous heater relay check as P21C2 to P21C4, so on that design the relay also feeds the heating circuits.
Relay defective or missing from its socket
Open control wire or loose terminal between module and relay
Blown fuse in the relay or module feed
Driver in the controlling module faulty
DEF heating and dosing do not work
SCR warning and countdown to restricted starting or speed
P21C8: Reductant Control Module Power Relay/Relays Control Circuit Low
P21C8 means the control line of the DEF module's power relay, or relays, sits too close to ground. No manufacturer documents P21C8 publicly.
Control wire chafed and shorted to ground
Moisture in relay socket or module connector
Output stage in the controlling module faulty
DEF system without power or permanently powered
Flat battery after the vehicle has been parked
P21C9: Reductant Control Module Power Relay/Relays Control Circuit High

P21C9 is stored when the control line of the DEF module's power relay, or relays, carries more voltage than the driver state allows, typically because the wire touches a battery feed or the driver can no longer pull it down. No manufacturer documents P21C9 publicly.
Control wire shorted to a battery-voltage circuit
Relay contacts welded, switched side stays live
Driver in the controlling module shorted
DEF pump or module audible or active with the engine off
P21CA: Reductant Control Module Supply Voltage Circuit

P21CA is the general code for the supply feed of the DEF control module: the voltage arriving at the module is missing or unusable, without the module assigning it to the low or high case. Volvo and Mack trucks use it, as P21CA00, on the aftertreatment control module that runs the SCR system.
Loose or corroded battery or ground connections of the module
Weak batteries or insufficient charging voltage
Faulty in-line fuse or damaged supply wire
Several sensor communication codes at the same time
P21CB: Reductant Control Module Supply Voltage Low

P21CB says the DEF control module receives too little supply voltage. GM measures it as a difference to system voltage: in the 2018 diesel tables a gap above 3 V between battery voltage and the supply of the SCR power module, seen in 40 of 50 samples taken every 100 ms with the powertrain relay in range and cranking excluded, sets the code; the 2025 tables a…
Voltage drop at fuse, terminal or ground of the module feed
Weak battery or low charging voltage
Damaged or corroded supply wire to the module
Internal voltage measurement of the module faulty
DEF dosing or heating drops out intermittently
Further undervoltage or communication codes from the SCR system
P21CC: Reductant Control Module Supply Voltage High

P21CC is the overvoltage counterpart of P21CB: the DEF control module sees a supply above what its electronics are designed for. Ford's 2023 diesel summary checks the reductant pump controller in a continuous loop and sets P21CC once its supply exceeds 19 V, deciding within 5 s.
Jump start or charging with excessive voltage
Loose battery terminal causing voltage spikes
Battery or charging warning, bulbs unusually bright
P21CD: Reductant Quality Module Supply Voltage Low

The DEF quality module measures the urea concentration in the tank and, on many tanks, shares a housing with the level sensor. P21CD reports that its supply voltage is too low. Ford's 2023 diesel summary sets the code when the quality sensor supply falls below 10 V or rises above 20 V for 15 s, so on Ford the overvoltage case shares this code.
Water and corrosion in the quality module connector (Ford C4851)
Damaged tank harness or supply wire
DEF quality or level warning in the instrument cluster
Communication code for the quality module stored as well
P21CE: P21CE says the DEF quality module as a unit is not working properly: it is supplied and talking to the controller, but its self-test or the plausibility of its output fails, so the controller cannot rely on the concentration it reports.
Contaminated or degraded DEF disturbing the measurement
Crystals or air bubbles on the sensing element
Poor contact at the module connector
DEF system error message in the display
P21CF: P21CF flags an open drive circuit of the second injector on cylinder 1. Which of the two injectors is B depends on the maker: Ford gives the letter to the port injector and keeps A, coded P0201, for direct injection, whereas Mitsubishi calls its direct injectors B and files open circuits under the low code P21DB.
Chafed or broken wire in the port injector harness (on the Bronco Sport near the transmission cover)
Open coil in the cylinder 1 port injector
Loose or corroded plug at the injector
Faulty driver stage in the engine module or separate injector module
Rough idle or misfire on cylinder 1, often with P0301
Further harness codes stored at the same time
P21D0: P21D0 is the open-circuit code for the B injector of cylinder 2. Where that cylinder sits varies: GM's small-block V8 alternates odd and even numbers between the banks, so cylinder 2 opens the right bank, while Ford's V6 and V8 count one bank first and place it next to cylinder 1. Ford defines B as the port injector, the direct injector being A with P0202.
Port injector of cylinder 2 with an open winding
Broken wire or pushed-back terminal in the injector harness
Output stage in the engine or injection module failed
Misfire on cylinder 2, mainly at idle and light load
P21D1: P21D1 concerns the B injector of cylinder 3, which on Ford's 1.5 EcoBoost three-cylinder is the last one in the block. That engine combines port and direct fuel, and Ford names the port injectors B.
Harness damage affecting several injectors at once (Ford Bronco Sport, transmission cover)
Open coil in the cylinder 3 port injector
Rough running or misfire on cylinder 3
With harness damage also transmission codes or no crank
P21D2: P21D2 reports an open in the drive circuit of the B injector on cylinder 4. On four-cylinder engines with dual injection it is the last of the set, for example Ford's 2.0 EcoBoost from 2022 or the 2.3 introduced for the 2024 Mustang, both of which added port injectors to direct injection.
Open winding in the cylinder 4 port injector
Wire broken at a bend or clip near the intake manifold
P21D3: P21D3 can only appear on engines with at least five cylinders and two injectors per cylinder. Documented users are Ford's dual-injection V6 and V8 engines (2.7 and 3.5 EcoBoost of the second generation, 5.0 V8 from 2018) and GM's supercharged LT5 V8. Ford defines B as the port injector; the direct injector of this cylinder is A, coded P0205.
Open coil in the cylinder 5 port injector
Broken wire in the bank harness of the port injectors
Output stage in the engine or injection module failed
Fuel trim of one bank shifted
P21D4: P21D4 is the last B injector code on a six-cylinder engine. Ford's second-generation 2.7 and 3.5 EcoBoost V6 combine port and direct injection, label the port injectors B and test this circuit together with P21CF to P21D3, continuously above 11 V within 5 s; on these engines cylinder 6 is the rear cylinder of the second bank.
Port injector of cylinder 6 open internally
Damaged wire at the rear of the engine, hard to inspect
Connector not fully latched after earlier work on the intake
P21D5: P21D5 belongs to V8 engines with a second injector per cylinder. Two are documented: Ford's 5.0 V8, which gained direct injection alongside its port injectors in 2018, and GM's 2019 LT5, the supercharged Corvette ZR1 engine with primary direct and supplemental port injection.
Open winding in the cylinder 7 port injector
Broken wire or terminal in the port injector harness of that bank
Separate fuel injection control module faulty (GM LT5)
Misfire on cylinder 7, on the LT5 mostly under high load
P21D6: P21D6 is the highest B injector code that any manufacturer documents publicly: both Ford's port injector check (P21CF to P21D6) and GM's LT5 injection module list end here.
Wire damage at the rear of the engine near the firewall
Output of the engine or separate injection module failed
Misfire or lean running on cylinder 8 under load
P21D7: P21D7 would mark an open drive circuit of the second injector on cylinder 9, which presupposes at least nine cylinders. No manufacturer documents this code publicly; the published Ford and GM lists stop at cylinder 8 (P21D6).
Open coil in the second injector of cylinder 9
Broken wire or terminal in the injector harness
Driver stage in the engine control module failed
P21D8: P21D8 covers the second injector of cylinder 10, the last cylinder of a V10. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. A V10 with two injectors per cylinder is on record in the Lamborghini Huracán, whose engine combines direct and multipoint injection, yet which of them its software would call B is unknown.
Second injector of cylinder 10 open internally
Wiring or connector fault at the cylinder 10 injector
Output stage in the engine control module failed
P21D9: P21D9 is reserved for an open circuit of the second injector on cylinder 11 and therefore only makes sense on twelve-cylinder engines with dual injection. No manufacturer documents this code publicly, and no available source names a twelve-cylinder engine that uses it.
Open coil in the second injector of cylinder 11
Damaged injector harness or loose plug
Faulty driver in the engine control module
P21DA: P21DA closes the circuit/open series of the second injectors with cylinder 12. It requires a twelve-cylinder engine with two injectors per cylinder; no manufacturer documents this code publicly and no available source names such an engine using it.
Second injector of cylinder 12 with open coil
Wire or terminal fault in the injector harness
Output stage of the controlling module failed
P21DB: P21DB means the drive circuit of the B injector on cylinder 1 is pulled toward ground. Two makers document it, with opposite meanings of B.
Injector wire chafed through to ground
Injector winding open or shorted to its housing
Engine or injection control module faulty
Reduced torque when several cylinders are affected (Mitsubishi)
P21DC: P21DC is the high-side fault of the cylinder 1 B injector: the line carries voltage where the control unit expects it to be low, typically from a short to supply or between the two injector wires.
Injector control wire shorted to a supply wire
Both injector wires shorted together in the harness
Driver stage of the control module damaged
Torque limited if more cylinders fail (Mitsubishi)
P21DD: Reductant Heater A Current Too Low
P21DD means heater A of the DEF system, which Ford and GM both assign to the tank heater (circuit 1), draws less current than expected while switched on, so it is likely open or barely heating.
Water and corrosion in the pump and heater connector (Ford C3613)
Missing heater supply due to relay, fuse or wiring fault
Heater driver in the control module faulty
DEF stays frozen longer in winter, dosing starts late
DEF warning messages after cold starts
P21DE: P21DE is the low fault of the cylinder 2 B injector circuit. In Mitsubishi's 2022 Eclipse Cross manual, B means the direct injector; the code covers both a break and a grounded wire on the two DI lines of cylinder 2, held for 2 s at 10 to 16.5 V, while the port injector of the same cylinder reports P0264.
Injector line of cylinder 2 touching ground
Fault at the intermediate connector of the injector harness
Possible fuel smell or rich running if an injector stays open
P21DF: P21DF is set when the cylinder 2 B injector circuit shows a short toward supply. Mitsubishi's 2022 Eclipse Cross applies it to the direct high-pressure injector and stores it after a 2 s short with the ignition on and the driver supply above 10 V; troubleshooting first inspects the negative DI wire of cylinder 2 up to the engine module and names the injector…
Negative injector line of cylinder 2 shorted to supply
ECM or injection module driver defective
Less pulling power with multiple faults
P21E0: P21E0 reports a low circuit state on the B injector of cylinder 3. Mitsubishi lists it for the 2022 Eclipse Cross as the direct injector code and does not use the open code P21D1, so an interrupted wire and a short to ground both end up here once they last 2 s.
Cylinder 3 injector wire broken or shorted to ground
Injector of cylinder 3 with open or shorted coil
P21E1: P21E1 is the high fault on the cylinder 3 B injector circuit. In Mitsubishi's 2022 Eclipse Cross that is the direct high-pressure injector, and the module reacts to a short circuit lasting 2 s, checked with 10 to 16.5 V battery voltage. To confirm a repair, the manual points to its OBD drive cycle pattern 1.
Cylinder 3 injector line shorted to supply voltage
Damaged driver in the control module
Torque reduction if several injectors fail (Mitsubishi)
P21E2: P21E2 is the low fault of the B injector on cylinder 4, the last cylinder of an inline four. It is the final direct injector low code in Mitsubishi's 2022 Eclipse Cross list, which uses B for the high-pressure injectors and sets it for an open or a short to ground lasting 2 s.
Cylinder 4 injector wire open or shorted to ground
Intermediate connector fault affecting several cylinders
Noticeably less power with several codes (port injection only)
P21E3: P21E3 marks a high circuit state on the cylinder 4 B injector, normally a short to a supply line. On Mitsubishi's 2022 Eclipse Cross, where B is the direct high-pressure injector, the fault must persist 2 s; it closes the manual's list of direct injector circuit codes for the four cylinders.
Cylinder 4 injector line shorted to a supply wire
Driver stage in the ECM or injection module damaged
Engine runs with reduced torque if further cylinders are affected
P21E4: P21E4 flags a low state on the circuit of the second (B) injector serving cylinder 5. The only public OBD summary that lists it is GM's for the 2019 Corvette ZR1, whose supercharged LT5 V8 pairs direct injectors with port injectors and drives the supplemental ones from a separate fuel injection control module (FICM).
Low-side wire of the cylinder 5 B injector touching ground
Injector winding shorted to its housing
Moisture or corrosion in the injector connector
Driver stage in the injection control module faulty
Rich running or fuel trim pulled back on bank 1
Rough idle or misfire on cylinder 5
P21E5: P21E5 means the cylinder 5 B injector circuit is pulled toward supply voltage. GM documents it for the LT5 V8 of the 2019 Corvette ZR1: the FICM looks at the low side of that injector while its driver is off and treats 0.5 Ohm or less toward power as a short.
Low-side wire of the cylinder 5 B injector shorted to a supply wire
Supply and control wire of the injector bridged in the harness
Injector coil shorted across its terminals
Damaged output stage in the injection control module
Cylinder 5 lean or hesitant at full load
P21E6: P21E6 reports that the B injector circuit of cylinder 6 has found a path to ground. In GM's 2019 tables for the Corvette ZR1 LT5, cylinder 6 is the third position on the right bank, which GM counts as bank 2.
Cylinder 6 B injector harness chafed against engine metal
Internal short to ground inside the injector
Injection control module output stuck low
Rich condition on bank 2, possibly fuel smell
Fouled spark plug or misfire on cylinder 6
P21E7: P21E7 is stored when the B injector of cylinder 6 shows a short toward power. GM's 2019 Corvette ZR1 with the LT5 V8 is the documented user; there the FICM checks the low side only in the driver-off state, flags 0.5 Ohm or less to power, and needs at least 11 V at the powertrain relay with the engine running. The result is a Type A fault after one trip.
Cylinder 6 B injector control wire in contact with a live wire
Shorted turns in the injector coil
Output stage of the injection control module damaged by the short
Lean condition on bank 2 under load
P21E8: P21E8 covers a low, ground-side fault on the cylinder 7 B injector. GM lists it for the 2019 Corvette ZR1, where the LT5 V8 carries a direct and a supplemental injector per cylinder and cylinder 7 is the rearmost cylinder of the left bank (bank 1).
Cylinder 7 B injector wire grounded at the rear of the engine
P21E9: P21E9 indicates that the low side of the cylinder 7 B injector carries supply voltage. On GM's 2019 Corvette ZR1 LT5, the FICM declares this when it sees 0.5 Ohm or less to power with the driver off, provided the engine runs and the powertrain relay delivers 11 V or more; Type A, one trip. The rear left cylinder then gets only its direct injector.
Cylinder 7 B injector control wire shorted to battery voltage
Injector coil with too low resistance
P21EA: P21EA is the ground-short code for the B injector of cylinder 8 and the last low code in GM's 2019 FICM table for the Corvette ZR1 LT5, because the V8 ends there. Cylinder 8 is the rearmost of the right bank (bank 2).
Cylinder 8 B injector wiring chafed through to ground
Water or corrosion in the cylinder 8 injector plug
Hard hot start or misfire on cylinder 8
P21EB: P21EB is set when the cylinder 8 B injector circuit is shorted toward power. It closes GM's run of B-injector codes for the 2019 Corvette ZR1 LT5: the FICM sees the switched-off low side within 0.5 Ohm of supply in 20 of 25 samples and stores a Type A fault, lighting the MIL in the first trip.
Cylinder 8 B injector control wire shorted to a feed wire
Shared harness connector shorted when several injectors are affected
P21EC: P21EC signals a low circuit state, usually a grounded wire or, depending on the maker, also a break, on the B injector of cylinder 9. It can only occur on an engine with at least nine cylinders and two injectors per cylinder. No manufacturer documents it publicly; GM's and Ford's lists stop at cylinder 8.
Cylinder 9 B injector wire shorted to ground
Broken wire, if the maker reports opens under the low code
Injector coil shorted to housing or open
Misfire or rough running on cylinder 9
Mixture deviation on the bank of cylinder 9
P21ED: P21ED is defined for a B injector circuit on cylinder 9 that reads high, meaning the control side is shorted to supply or, on some designs, the two injector wires touch. No manufacturer publishes thresholds or vehicles for it.
Control wire of the cylinder 9 B injector shorted to power
Both injector wires bridged in the harness
Driver stage in the control unit faulty
Cylinder 9 lean in mixed injection operation
P21EE: P21EE is the low-circuit code for the B injector of cylinder 10, the last cylinder of a V10. In practice that points to a ten-cylinder engine with two injectors per cylinder, of which only Lamborghini's Huracán is documented: its V10 pairs a direct injector with a port injector at each cylinder and was presented as the first V10 to combine both.
Damaged or corroded injector connector on cylinder 10
Rough running or misfire on cylinder 10 (P0310)
Fuel trim deviation on the second bank
P21EF: P21EF stands for a high reading on the B injector circuit of cylinder 10. No public manufacturer document covers it, so the exact threshold is unknown; the closest documented model is GM's LT5 V8, where a switched-off low side within 0.5 Ohm of supply counts as a short and sets a Type A fault.
Cylinder 10 B injector control wire touching a live circuit
Short inside a connector shared by several injectors
Output stage overloaded by the short
Cylinder 10 weak or misfiring under load
Lean mixture on the second bank
P21F0: P21F0 is reserved for a low state, typically a wire touching ground, in the B injector circuit of cylinder 11. Setting it requires at least eleven cylinders with two injectors each, so in practice a V12 or W12 with combined port and direct injection.
Cylinder 11 B injector wire shorted to ground
Injector with internal short to ground
Code read on an engine without a cylinder 11 B injector (scan tool or maker-specific use)
P21F1: P21F1 describes a cylinder 11 B injector circuit that sits too high, i.e. its switched side is shorted to supply. The code exists in SAE J2012 for completeness of the cylinder series, but no public manufacturer source uses it, and no twelve-cylinder engine with two injectors per cylinder could be documented.
Control wire of the cylinder 11 B injector shorted to power
P21F2: P21F2 is the generic code for a low circuit state, usually a grounded control wire, at the B injector of cylinder 12. It would need a twelve-cylinder engine with two injectors per cylinder, and none could be documented: the V12s from Lamborghini and Aston Martin inject into the ports only. No manufacturer publishes the code in this sense.
Cylinder 12 B injector wire shorted to ground
Manufacturer-specific use of the number (McLaren Artura high-voltage battery)
Hybrid warning instead, if the code is a McLaren battery fault
P21F3: P21F3 ends the B injector series of SAE J2012: a high signal on the cylinder 12 circuit, caused by a short to supply on the switched side. The series runs from P21CF to P21DA for opens and from P21DB to P21F3 for low/high pairs; the A injector equivalent here is P0295.
Control wire of the cylinder 12 B injector shorted to supply
Driver stage damaged by a lasting short
P21F4: Fuel Control System B Too Lean Off Idle (Bank 1)

P21F4 reports that the second fuel path on bank 1 needs more added fuel than its adaptation may supply once the engine has left idle, in the part-load range. Engines with port and direct injection learn a correction for each path; Ford calls its direct system A and its port system B.
Outdated engine control software (Audi 2.5 TFSI, bulletin 2059429/1)
Port injectors of bank 1 restricted or delivering too little
Pressure in the low-pressure (port) fuel rail too low
Air mass sensor reading too low
Weak performance or hesitation at part load
Often stored together with P2177 or P0087
P21F5: Fuel Control System B Too Rich Off Idle (Bank 1)

P21F5 is the rich limit for the second fuel path of bank 1 in the part-load zone above idle: the learned correction already removes as much fuel as allowed, yet the front sensor still sees surplus fuel.
Outdated engine control software (Audi 2.5 TFSI, bulletin 2059429/1)
Port injector on bank 1 leaking or sticking open
Pressure in the low-pressure rail above specification
Air mass sensor reading too high
P21F6: Fuel Control System B Too Lean Off Idle (Bank 2)

P21F6 is the bank 2 form of P21F4 and only exists on V or flat engines whose cylinder banks each have their own front oxygen sensor and two injection paths. Here the part-load correction of the second path on bank 2 has reached its lean limit. No manufacturer documents this code publicly.
Wiring or connector fault on the bank 2 injector harness
Low pressure in the shared port fuel rail (if bank 1 also lean)
P21F7: Fuel Control System B Too Rich Off Idle (Bank 2)

P21F7 sets when the second fuel path on bank 2 has to remove more fuel above idle than its rich limit permits. It needs an engine with two banks, separate front sensors and dual injection; inline engines such as Audi's 2.5 TFSI only have the bank 1 codes. No manufacturer publishes criteria for P21F7.
Bank 2 front oxygen sensor reading rich
Low-pressure regulation too high (if bank 1 also rich)
P21F8: Fuel Control System B Too Lean at Idle (Bank 1)

P21F8 covers the idle zone: the second fuel path of bank 1 needs more extra fuel at idle than its adaptation allows. Airflow at idle is so small that a fixed amount of unmetered air or a slightly sluggish injector shifts the mixture a lot, which is why makers learn idle separately from part load.
Outdated engine control software (Audi 2.5 TFSI, bulletin 2059429/1)
Unmetered air entering behind the air mass sensor
Port injector on bank 1 delivering too little
Low pressure in the port fuel rail
P21F9: Fuel Control System B Too Rich at Idle (Bank 1)

P21F9 reports that bank 1's second fuel path runs rich at idle even though its correction has already reached the lower limit. No manufacturer documents this code publicly; Audi's 2.5 TFSI bulletin lists only the lean idle code P21F8 and the off-idle pair.
Port injector on bank 1 dripping after closing
Low-pressure fuel regulation holding too much pressure
Fuel vapour entering via crankcase ventilation (fuel-diluted oil)
P21FA: Fuel Control System B Too Lean at Idle (Bank 2)

P21FA is the bank 2 version of the idle lean check for the second fuel path. It applies to engines with two cylinder banks, a front oxygen sensor per bank and dual injection, such as Ford's 5.0 V8, which has combined port and direct injection since 2018.
Intake leak at bank 2 runners or gasket
Partly blocked port injector on bank 2
Bank 2 front oxygen sensor reading lean
P21FB: Fuel Control System B Too Rich at Idle (Bank 2)

P21FB means bank 2's second fuel path is rich at idle while its correction already sits at the rich limit. The code requires an engine with a separate front sensor per bank and two injection paths; no maker documents it publicly.
Port injector on bank 2 leaking or sticking open
Bank 2 front oxygen sensor reading rich
Low-pressure regulation too high or fuel from crankcase ventilation (if both banks rich)
P21FC: Fuel Control System B Too Lean at Higher Load (Bank 1)

P21FC is the lean check of bank 1's second fuel path in the upper load zone, the third cell next to idle (P21F8) and part load (P21F4). Under high load, delivery capacity matters most: a weak lift pump, a clogged filter or a low-pressure rail that sags at high flow show up here first.
Weak in-tank lift pump or clogged fuel filter
Port rail pressure dropping at high flow
Port injectors on bank 1 flowing too little
Charge air leak behind the air mass sensor
Hesitation or power loss at full load
P21FD: Fuel Control System B Too Rich at Higher Load (Bank 1)
P21FD sets when the second fuel path on bank 1 is still rich at higher load although its learned correction has already taken away the permitted maximum. No manufacturer documents the code publicly.
Air mass sensor reading too high at large airflow
Low-pressure regulator holding too much pressure
P21FE: Fuel Control System B Too Lean at Higher Load (Bank 2)

P21FE is the bank 2 counterpart of P21FC: in the upper load zone the second injection path on bank 2 needs more enrichment than its adaptation may supply. It can only appear on two-bank engines with per-bank sensors and dual injection.
Harness or connector fault on bank 2 injectors
Weak shared supply (lift pump, filter, low-pressure sensor) if both banks lean
Loss of pull at full throttle
P21FF: Fuel Control System B Too Rich at Higher Load (Bank 2)
P21FF closes the series: bank 2's second fuel path is rich in the upper load range although its correction already removes the largest reduction allowed. No manufacturer publishes criteria for it.
Port injectors on bank 2 over-delivering at long pulse widths
Excessive pressure in the shared low-pressure rail
Bank 2 front oxygen sensor reading rich
P2200: P2200 is the general electrical fault reported for the front NOx sensor on bank 1, the unit ahead of the SCR catalyst. Such sensors carry their own control unit, which checks the probe wiring and reports the result over CAN.
Internal fault in the NOx probe or its attached control unit
Damaged cable between probe and sensor control unit (heat, chafing)
Moisture or corrosion in the sensor connector
Unstable supply or ground at the sensor control unit
No NOx value in live data from the upstream sensor
SCR or emissions warning, possibly followed by inducement countdown
P2201: Here the upstream NOx sensor on bank 1 is electrically intact, yet its reading is not believable. Manufacturers test this in different ways. VW's 2014 Touareg TDI compares the reading with modelled engine-out NOx (deviation beyond 60 percent), checks a slow fall from 100 to 60 percent (over 4.5 s) and an offset outside +50/-30 ppm.
Aged or poisoned NOx sensing element with offset or slow response
Exhaust leak upstream of the sensor letting in outside air
Fault elsewhere (EGR, fuelling, DEF dosing) that shifts real NOx output
Often stored together with SCR efficiency codes such as P20EE
Increased AdBlue consumption or SCR warning
P2202: P2202 means the raw NOx value sent by the upstream sensor on bank 1 has dropped below the lowest figure a working sensor can report. Since the probe talks over CAN, the check concerns the transmitted value rather than a wire voltage.
NOx sensing element drifted low or internally faulty
Damaged probe lead or connector between element and sensor module
Live data shows a negative NOx value upstream
SCR dosing may switch to a fallback strategy
P2203: P2203 flags a raw NOx value from the upstream sensor on bank 1 that lies above anything the engine can actually emit. The limits differ: GM sets 1,500 or 2,500 ppm on the 6.6L Duramax (LML) and 2,500 ppm on the 3.0L LZ0 (Type B, two trips), VW 1,655 ppm on the 2014 Touareg TDI.
Upstream NOx sensor reading high due to internal failure
ECM software anomaly (GM 3.0L LZ0, bulletins 23-NA-193 and 24-NA-094)
Sensing element contaminated by oil ash or DEF deposits
Implausibly high upstream NOx value in live data
Possible over-dosing of AdBlue or SCR efficiency codes
P2204: P2204 describes an upstream NOx sensor on bank 1 whose signal path works most of the time but keeps dropping out. Smart NOx sensors report the state of their measuring circuit (open wire, short or no error) to the engine computer over CAN; when such fault messages come and go faster than a steady circuit fault would allow, this code fits.
Loose or corroded terminals at the NOx sensor connector
Harness near the exhaust damaged by heat or vibration
Intermittent internal fault in the sensor module
Malfunction indicator lamp on, sometimes going out again
NOx value in live data dropping out briefly
SCR warning that comes and goes
P2205: NOx Sensor Heater Control Circuit/Open (Bank 1 Sensor 1)

The ceramic element of a NOx sensor only measures once its built-in heater has brought it to several hundred degrees. P2205 reports a break on the heater control side of the upstream sensor on bank 1.
Heater element in the NOx probe burnt through
Broken conductor in the lead between probe and sensor module
Malfunction indicator lamp on after one trip
Upstream NOx sensor never becomes ready
P2206: NOx Sensor Heater Control Circuit Low (Bank 1 Sensor 1)

A NOx sensor needs its ceramic element heated to several hundred degrees before it can measure. P2206 means the heater control circuit of the first (upstream) NOx sensor on bank 1 reads low, typically a short to ground or a driver output stuck low. CARB requires diesel OBD to detect heater circuit opens and shorts that conflict with the commanded state.
Internal heater or control-unit fault in the NOx sensor
Heater wiring chafed to ground near the exhaust
Moisture or corrosion in the sensor connector
SCR or emissions warning on the display
P2207: NOx Sensor Heater Control Circuit High (Bank 1 Sensor 1)

P2207 is the high-side counterpart of P2206: the heater control circuit of the upstream NOx sensor on bank 1 shows a voltage that is too high for the commanded state, typically an open heater element or a short to supply voltage. CARB requires the diesel OBD system to flag such circuit faults that contradict the command.
Heater element inside the NOx sensor burnt open
Open circuit or short to voltage in the heater wiring
NOx readiness or SCR efficiency faults may follow
P2208: NOx Sensor Heater Sense Circuit (Bank 1 Sensor 1)

Besides the control line, the NOx sensor heater has a sense or feedback path through which the controller checks how the heater actually responds (current, resistance or element temperature). P2208 marks a general fault in this sense circuit of the upstream sensor on bank 1.
Internal fault in the NOx sensor or its control unit
Damaged wiring between sensor element and sensor control unit
NOx sensor reports no valid value
P2209: NOx Sensor Heater Sense Circuit Range/Performance (Bank 1 Sensor 1)

P2209 is the performance check of the NOx sensor heater: the feedback is electrically present but shows that the element does not reach or hold operating temperature as expected. VW's 2014 TDI specification books (Passat, Touareg) set it when NOx control has not become active more than 180 s after the dew point was passed.
Aged NOx sensor element that heats up too slowly
Low supply voltage or poor ground to the sensor
Prolonged cold or wet exhaust delaying dew-point release
NOx sensor not ready for long periods after start
P220A: NOx Sensor Supply Voltage Circuit (Bank 1 Sensor 1)

A smart NOx sensor draws its own operating power, mostly for the probe heater. P220A means the supply reaching the upstream sensor on bank 1 is outside its window. Ford's 6.7L and 3.0L diesels flag above 16.5 V or below 8.5 V; GM's 3.0L Duramax (LZ0) flags below 9.9 V while the engine runs, Type B after two trips.
Blown fuse, faulty relay or poor ground in the sensor supply
Supply wire chafed, corroded or with high resistance
Supply booster in the glow plug control module (GM 6.6L LML)
Weak battery or charging-system voltage out of range
Upstream NOx sensor shows no value or no communication
Other NOx sensor codes stored at the same time
P220B: NOx Sensor Supply Voltage Circuit (Bank 1 Sensor 2)
P220B concerns the second NOx sensor on bank 1, the one behind the SCR catalyst whose reading proves how well NOx is being converted. Its operating voltage is outside the allowed band.
Fuse, relay or ground fault in the downstream sensor supply
Supply wire to the rear sensor damaged under the vehicle
Downstream NOx sensor shows no value
P220C: NOx Sensor Supply Voltage Circuit (Bank 2 Sensor 1)
P220C is reserved for an engine with a separate exhaust path per cylinder bank, each with its own NOx sensors, and reports that the upstream sensor on bank 2 is not getting a proper supply voltage.
Fuse, relay or ground fault in the bank 2 sensor supply
Supply wiring to the bank 2 upstream sensor damaged
System voltage out of range (battery or alternator)
No NOx value from the bank 2 upstream sensor
P220D: NOx Sensor Supply Voltage Circuit (Bank 2 Sensor 2)

P220D covers the last position in this group: the downstream NOx sensor on bank 2, after that bank's own SCR catalyst, has a supply voltage outside its window. It only exists on engines whose two banks keep separate aftertreatment, which none of the publicly documented diesel applications do; no manufacturer lists the code with thresholds.
Supply fuse, relay or ground fault for the bank 2 rear sensor
Corroded connector exposed to road spray behind the catalyst
Internal fault in the supply stage of the sensor module
SCR efficiency monitor for bank 2 not completed
P220E: NOx Sensor Heater Control Circuit Range/Performance (Bank 1 Sensor 1)

P220E says the heater of the upstream NOx sensor on bank 1 is not behaving as commanded. Ford's 6.7L and 3.0L diesels bundle several checks under it: an open heater found by the sensor hardware, a short to positive (over 5 V on the heater), a short to ground (0 V), and a duty cycle that differs from the expected one by more than 20 percent.
Aged heater element in the upstream NOx probe
Heater wiring or ground with high resistance or shorts
Upstream NOx sensor slow to become ready after start
Often stored with P2201 or P2209
P220F: NOx Sensor Heater Control Circuit Range/Performance (Bank 1 Sensor 2)

P220F is the heater check of the rear NOx sensor on bank 1, the one after the SCR catalyst. Ford's diesel summary (it titles the code as a heater sense circuit fault) flags a heater current under 0.4 A, a short to battery or to ground, or a heater duty cycle more than 20 percent away from the expected value.
Heater of the downstream NOx probe weak or failed
Heater wiring of the rear sensor shorted or with high resistance
Water or salt in the rear sensor connector
P2210: NOx Sensor Heater Sense Circuit Low (Bank 1 Sensor 1)

P2210 means the heater feedback signal of the upstream NOx sensor on bank 1 sits below its permitted range. Typical electrical causes are a short to ground in the sense line or a failed measuring stage in the sensor electronics. GM lists the code as NOx Sensor Heater Feedback Circuit Low for the 2024 Silverado/Sierra 3.0L diesel (LZ0).
Fault in the sensor element or its control unit
No NOx reading in live data
P2211: NOx Sensor Heater Sense Circuit High (Bank 1 Sensor 1)

P2211 flags a heater feedback signal above its permitted range on the upstream NOx sensor of bank 1. An open sense line, a short to supply voltage or an interrupted heater element that the electronics reads as maximum resistance are the usual reasons.
Interrupted heater element in the NOx sensor
Open sense line or short to voltage
P2212: NOx Sensor Heater Sense Circuit Intermittent (Bank 1 Sensor 1)

Besides driving the heater, the upstream NOx sensor on bank 1 has a sense path that reports back how the heater actually responds; GM measures heater resistance on a separate HTemp pin. P2212 means this feedback keeps dropping out or jumping instead of failing for good.
Loose or corroded contact in the NOx sensor connector
Cracked conductor in the probe lead that opens with heat or vibration
Intermittent fault in the sensor module's heater measurement
Malfunction indicator lamp on, possibly intermittent
P2213: P2213 mirrors P2200 for the second cylinder bank: the NOx sensor serving bank 2 ahead of its SCR catalyst reports a general electrical fault. That presumes an engine whose banks feed separate aftertreatment lines.
Internal fault in the bank 2 NOx probe or its sensor control unit
Heat-damaged or chafed lead between probe and sensor control unit
Water or corrosion in the bank 2 sensor connector
No NOx value from the bank 2 sensor in live data
SCR warning, possibly with an inducement countdown
P2214: Under J2012, P2214 is the plausibility fault of the bank 2 NOx sensor: wiring intact, reading not credible. No maker uses it that way in public documents. Hino does use the number differently: on its J08E inline six (Hino 238, 258, 268 and 338 conventional models, 2011 to 2016) P2214 belongs to NOx sensor 2 behind the SCR catalyst.
Aged or poisoned NOx element reading with offset or slow response
Sensor heater cracked by condensation (Hino 2015-2016, SB-15-038/SB-16-002)
Diluted DEF or faulty dosing injector distorting the NOx reading
Exhaust leak upstream of the sensor
Often stored with P2201 or SCR efficiency code P20EE
Higher DEF consumption or SCR warning
P2215: P2215 says the NOx value transmitted for bank 2 falls below the smallest figure a healthy sensor can deliver. Because smart NOx sensors talk over CAN, the limit is a concentration in ppm, not a wire voltage. No manufacturer publishes this bank 2 code; the diesels on record send both banks through one SCR system and use P2202 instead.
NOx element of the bank 2 sensor drifted low
Fault in the measuring electronics of the sensor module
Damaged lead between probe and sensor module
Negative NOx value for bank 2 in live data
DEF dosing switches to a substitute strategy
P2216: P2216 is set when the NOx concentration reported for bank 2 exceeds anything the engine could plausibly emit. It belongs to engines with an SCR line per cylinder bank; none of the documented diesels is built that way, and no manufacturer lists P2216 publicly.
Bank 2 NOx sensor reading too high due to internal failure
Sensing element fouled by oil ash or DEF crystals
Calibration error in the engine or dosing control software
Implausibly high NOx value for bank 2 in live data
P2217: P2217 describes a bank 2 NOx sensor whose measuring path fails only now and then: the reading drops out or the sensor briefly reports an electrical error, then recovers.
Loose or corroded terminals at the bank 2 sensor connector
Lead near the exhaust cracked by heat or vibration
Sporadic fault in the sensor module electronics
Malfunction indicator lamp that comes and goes
Bank 2 NOx value briefly invalid in live data
P2218: A NOx sensor cannot measure until its built-in heater has taken the ceramic cell to several hundred degrees, and the sensor electronics switches that heater itself. P2218 reports a break in the heater control path of the bank 2 sensor, either inside the probe or in the lead to the sensor module. No manufacturer documents the bank 2 version.
Heater element in the bank 2 NOx probe burnt through
Broken conductor between probe and sensor module
Pushed-back or corroded pin in the sensor connector
Malfunction indicator lamp on after one trip
Bank 2 NOx sensor never reports ready
P2219: NOx Sensor Heater Control Circuit Low (Bank 2)

P2219 means the heater control line of the bank 2 NOx sensor is pulled toward ground when it should not be, typically a heater lead chafed against the exhaust or a shorted output stage in the sensor electronics. The control unit then switches the heater off to protect itself.
Heater lead of the bank 2 sensor chafed through to ground
Shorted heater or output stage inside the sensor
Salt water bridging pins in the connector
Malfunction indicator lamp on after two trips
Bank 2 NOx sensor stays cold and delivers no value
P221A: P221A compares the two NOx sensors of bank 1, upstream and downstream of the SCR catalyst. When conditions should make both read alike, the gap between them is too large, so the system cannot tell which value to trust.
One of the two NOx sensors (often the outlet sensor) reading wrongly
Exhaust leak between the two sensors diluting the reading
Faulty DEF dosing distorting the comparison
Often stored with P20EE or other SCR codes
Implausible NOx conversion values in live data
P221B: P221B compares the NOx sensors before and after the SCR catalyst of bank 2. When operating conditions should make them agree, their readings differ by more than the calibration allows, and the controller cannot decide which value is wrong. The code requires a separate SCR line on bank 2, which no publicly documented diesel has; no manufacturer lists P221B.
One of the two bank 2 NOx sensors reading wrongly
Exhaust leak between the two sensors
Dosing that does not stop or leaks, distorting the comparison
Often stored with SCR efficiency codes
Inlet and outlet NOx values for bank 2 disagree in live data
P221C: Reductant Heater B Current Too Low

P221C reports that heater B of the DEF system draws too little current while switched on. GM and Ford both assign B to the heated pressure line that carries DEF to the dosing valve. GM's 2025 Duramax tables flag line heater current under 0.75 A with a PWM command above zero, 40 faulty readings spaced 0.1 s apart, Type A with the MIL after one trip.
Heating element in the DEF pressure line open or burnt
Corroded or loose connector at the heated line
Missing heater supply (fuse, relay or harness)
DEF line may freeze in winter, dosing starts late
DEF system warning, inducement possible if unresolved
P221D: Reductant Heater B Current Too High

P221D is stored when heater B, the electrically heated DEF pressure line at GM and Ford, takes more current or power than its design permits. That usually means a partly shorted element or a lead touching ground, and the controller cuts the heater to save its driver.
Partly shorted heating element in the DEF pressure line
Water in the line heater connector
Malfunction indicator lamp on after one trip (GM)
Line heater switched off, DEF may stay frozen in cold weather
P221E: Reductant Heater C Current Too Low

P221E says DEF heater C pulls too little current while commanded on. Which element is C depends on the system. In GM's 2025 Duramax tables heater 3 is a second tank heater; the code needs a PWM command above zero and trips under 0.75 A after 40 readings taken every 0.1 s, a Type A fault with the MIL after one trip.
Heater C element open or burnt (tank or supply module, by system)
Corroded or wet connector at the tank or pump unit
Slow DEF thawing in cold weather, dosing starts late
P221F: Reductant Heater C Current Too High
P221F flags excessive current through DEF heater C, pointing to a partial short in the element or its lead.
Heater lead chafed to ground at the tank or pump unit
Water or DEF crystals in the heater connector
Malfunction indicator lamp on after one trip (GM)
DEF heating disabled, possible frozen-DEF warnings in winter
P2220: NOx Sensor Heater Control Circuit High (Bank 2)

P2220 is the high-side counterpart of P2219: on the bank 2 NOx sensor, the heater control line carries battery voltage when the heater should be off or regulated, so the element may overheat or the output stage cannot switch. A pinched lead touching a feed wire or a failed driver inside the sensor are the usual causes.
Heater control lead shorted to a supply wire
Failed heater driver inside the bank 2 sensor module
Malfunction indicator lamp on after two trips
Bank 2 NOx reading missing or invalid
P2221: Alongside the heater drive, a NOx sensor has a sense path that tells the electronics how the heater is really behaving, usually by measuring its resistance, which tracks cell temperature. P2221 reports a general fault in that sense circuit on the bank 2 sensor.
Fault in the heater measurement of the bank 2 sensor
Open sense conductor between probe and sensor module
P2222: NOx Sensor Heater Sense Circuit Range/Performance (Bank 2)

With P2222 the heater feedback of the bank 2 NOx sensor is electrically present, yet what it reports does not match the heating command: the cell warms too slowly or settles at the wrong resistance. No manufacturer documents this bank 2 code. Two bank 1 descriptions show the approach.
Aged heater in the bank 2 NOx probe with drifted resistance
Low supply voltage or poor ground at the sensor module
Bank 2 NOx sensor slow to become ready after a cold start
P2223: NOx Sensor Heater Sense Circuit Low (Bank 2)

P2223 indicates that the heater sense line of the bank 2 NOx sensor sits at or near ground potential, so the electronics reads an impossibly low value for heater resistance. A sense conductor rubbed through to the exhaust bracket or a shorted measuring input inside the sensor module are the usual explanations. No manufacturer publishes the bank 2 code.
Sense lead of the bank 2 sensor shorted to ground
Shorted measuring input in the sensor module
Malfunction indicator lamp on after two trips
No valid NOx value from bank 2
P2224: NOx Sensor Heater Sense Circuit High (Bank 2)

P2224 is logged when the heater sense signal of the bank 2 NOx sensor is too high, which the electronics sees as a short to supply voltage or as an interrupted heater reading near infinite resistance. The bank 2 code appears in no public manufacturer document.
Heater element in the bank 2 probe open, read as maximum resistance
Sense lead shorted to a voltage source
Fault in the sensor module input stage
Malfunction indicator lamp on after two trips
P2225: NOx Sensor Heater Sense Circuit Intermittent (Bank 2)

P2225 covers a heater sense circuit on the bank 2 NOx sensor that fails only for moments: the feedback drops out or jumps, then returns to normal, which a steady open or short code would not describe. No manufacturer documents thresholds for P2225 or for its bank 1 twin P2212.
Loose or corroded contact in the bank 2 sensor connector
Cracked sense conductor that opens with heat or vibration
Sporadic fault in the heater measurement of the sensor module
Malfunction indicator lamp that comes and goes
P2226: P2226 is the general circuit code for barometric pressure sensor A, the sensor that tells the engine computer the outside air pressure for air-charge, fuel and boost calculations.
Fault of the barometric sensor built into the engine control module
Damaged wiring or loose connector on an external BARO sensor
5 V reference supply of the sensor pulled down by another faulty sensor
Failure-type suffix (-16, -17, -92, -1F) shown with the code on newer scan tools
P2227: Barometric Pressure Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance

P2227 means the barometric reading is electrically fine but does not fit the other pressure signals. Ford's 2012 summary compares BARO, throttle inlet and manifold pressure after at least 10 s engine-off; the sensor that disagrees with the other two is blamed. While driving at low airflow BARO must stay within 5.5 inHg of throttle inlet pressure.
Ice or sludge in the charge air cooler on turbo engines in severe cold (GM 22-NA-007, 23-NA-002)
BARO sensor reading with an offset or drift
Faulty boost or manifold pressure sensor that skews the comparison
Engine control software that needs an update
Reduced power or hesitation in very cold weather on turbo engines
P0299 or misfire codes stored alongside
P2228: Barometric Pressure Sensor A Circuit Low

P2228 sets when the voltage from barometric pressure sensor A stays below the lowest value a real atmosphere could produce. Ford's gasoline summaries (2012 and 2020-2023) use under 2.0 V, which would mean an altitude above 15,000 ft, for 5 s; on these engines the sensor is mounted on the PCM circuit board.
Signal wire of an external BARO sensor shorted to ground or open
Defective sensor inside the PCM (Ford, Mazda and others), PCM replacement
Low or missing 5 V reference to the sensor
Scan tool shows an implausibly low barometric pressure
P2229: Barometric Pressure Sensor A Circuit High

P2229 reports a barometric sensor A voltage above anything plausible for outside air. Ford's gasoline engines judge more than 4.4 V, an altitude below -1,000 ft, over 5 s; the 2023 diesels use 4.85 V (115 kPa) after 0.5 s. GM's 2018 diesel tables look for contact with a voltage source: over 94.1 % of the 5 V range (115.1 kPa) in 320 of 400 readings, Type B.
Breather filter of a PCM-internal BARO sensor clogged (e.g. engine-bay wax, Mazda 01-008/20)
Signal wire of an external sensor shorted to 5 V or battery voltage
Internal fault of the sensor or the control module
Check engine light, often only after the engine bay has heated up
Scan tool shows barometric pressure far above the real value
P222A: P222A is the general circuit code for a second barometric pressure sensor, B. Only some engines carry one. GM's tables for the 3.0 L twin-turbo V6 (LGW, 2018) and for 2023-2024 twin-throttle engines monitor such a sensor B, but they report its circuit faults with the more specific codes P222C (low) and P222D (high) and do not use P222A.
Damaged wiring or corroded connector at sensor B
Fault in the shared 5 V sensor supply
Usually no noticeable change in how the engine runs
P222B: Barometric Pressure Sensor B Circuit Range/Performance

P222B means sensor B delivers a clean signal whose value is wrong. GM documents two strategies. On the 3.0 L LGW (2018) and a 2016 engine family the ECM estimates outside pressure from boost pressure, airflow and rpm while driving; sensor B fails if it deviates by more than 20 kPa, or 25 kPa once more than 1.24 miles have passed since the last update.
Sensor B reading with offset or stuck at one value
Leak or restriction in the intake path that distorts the comparison
Boost or manifold pressure sensor fault affecting the estimate
Check engine light after two drives
P222C: Barometric Pressure Sensor B Circuit Low

P222C flags a sensor B voltage that has dropped too low, as with a signal wire touching ground. GM's 2018 tables for the 3.0 L LGW set the code below 40 % of the 5 V range, equal to about 50.9 kPa, counted in 320 of 400 readings taken every 12.5 ms; it is a Type B fault with the MIL after two trips.
Signal wire of sensor B shorted to ground
5 V reference to sensor B open or shorted
Scan tool shows a very low reading for the second barometric sensor
P222D: Barometric Pressure Sensor B Circuit High

P222D is stored when sensor B reports an excessive voltage. GM's 2018 tables for the 3.0 L LGW name contact with a supply voltage or a broken line: on that input a broken wire drives the signal up, not down. The limit is 90 % of the 5 V range, about 115 kPa, met in 320 of 400 readings; Type B, MIL after two trips.
Connector of sensor B unplugged or signal wire broken
Signal wire shorted to 5 V or battery voltage
Second barometric reading stuck near the top of its range
P222E: Barometric Pressure Sensor B Circuit Intermittent/Erratic

P222E catches a sensor B signal that jitters. Outside air pressure changes slowly, so GM measures noise directly: every 12.5 ms the difference to the previous reading is taken, and the absolute differences over 80 consecutive readings are added up into a so-called string length.
Loose or corroded terminal at sensor B or the ECM
Electrical interference, for example from a poorly grounded component nearby
Check engine light that may come and go
Second barometric value jumping on the scan tool
P222F: P222F is meant for engines with two barometric sensors whose readings should agree but drift apart, without the software being able to say which of the two is wrong. No maker documents this code publicly.
One of the two barometric sensors has drifted
Supply or ground offset shifting one sensor's signal
Blocked port or breather of one sensor
The two barometric readings differ clearly on the scan tool
P2230: Barometric Pressure Sensor A Circuit Intermittent/Erratic

P2230 flags a barometric pressure (BARO) signal that is electrically present but jumps or drops out for short moments instead of sitting permanently low or high. The engine computer uses BARO for air-charge, fuelling and boost calculations. Ford's 2020-2023 gasoline OBD summary lists P2230 with P2227-P2229 among the BARO faults that inhibit auto start-stop.
Engine harness chafed against an engine component (e.g. vacuum pump pulley, cam cover)
Loose or corroded pin at the BARO sensor or ECM connector
Barometric pressure sensor with an internal contact problem
Check engine light, often coming and going
Other sensor codes stored at the same time if a shared harness is damaged
P2231: O2 Sensor Signal Circuit Shorted to Heater Circuit (Bank 1 Sensor 1)

P2231 means the engine computer sees the heater supply of the upstream oxygen sensor on bank 1 leaking into the sensor's signal path - typically an internal short in the sensor or two neighbouring wires touching in the harness.
Internal short between heater and sensing element in the oxygen sensor
Heater and signal wires melted or chafed together (exhaust heat, routing)
Moisture or contamination bridging pins in the sensor connector
Higher fuel consumption due to open-loop fuelling
Rough idle or hesitation in some cases
