P2232: O2 Sensor Signal Circuit Shorted to Heater Circuit (Bank 1 Sensor 2)

P2232 reports that the heater supply of the oxygen sensor behind the catalyst on bank 1 is bleeding into that sensor's signal line. A switching sensor only produces up to about 1 V, so the ECM watches its signal at the instant the heater is switched off.
Internal leakage between heater and sensing element of the rear oxygen sensor
Signal and heater wires fused or chafed together near the exhaust
Water or corrosion bridging pins in the sensor connector
Check engine light after two drives
Catalyst monitor not completed or catalyst code stored alongside
P2233: O2 Sensor Signal Circuit Shorted to Heater Circuit (Bank 1 Sensor 3)

P2233 is the heater-to-signal short for sensor 3 on bank 1, a third oxygen sensor that some engines fit after a second catalyst or between two catalyst bricks. No manufacturer documents this code publicly.
Internal leakage between heater and sensing element of sensor 3
Sensor 3 wiring melted or chafed along the exhaust or underbody
Corroded underbody connector of the third sensor
Check engine light without noticeable driving change
Emissions inspection failed because of the stored code
P2234: O2 Sensor Signal Circuit Shorted to Heater Circuit (Bank 2 Sensor 1)
P2234 means the heater of the front air-fuel sensor on bank 2 couples into its measuring circuit. On a wide-band sensor the disturbance is small, so the check is finer than on rear sensors.
Front sensor element cracked by thermal shock (water on the hot sensor)
Heater and signal wires of the bank 2 sensor touching in the harness
Moisture in the sensor connector bridging heater and signal pins
Higher fuel consumption when bank 2 runs without lambda control
Other bank 2 front-sensor codes stored at the same time
P2235: O2 Sensor Signal Circuit Shorted to Heater Circuit (Bank 2 Sensor 2)
P2235 concerns the post-catalyst oxygen sensor on bank 2, found on V engines with a catalyst per bank. The ECM sets it when switching off the heater makes the sensor voltage spike.
Internal leakage between heater and sensing element of the bank 2 rear sensor
Sensor wires damaged by heat or chafing near the bank 2 catalyst
Water ingress in the rear sensor connector
Check engine light after two drives
P2236: O2 Sensor Signal Circuit Shorted to Heater Circuit (Bank 2 Sensor 3)

P2236 would be set if the heater of the third oxygen sensor on bank 2 leaked into its signal wire. Such a sensor sits furthest downstream and exists only on engines with two catalyst stages per bank. No manufacturer documents this code publicly, and Jaguar Land Rover's 2015 list for its V6 with sensors 3 on both banks does not use it either.
Internal leakage between heater and sensing element of sensor 3 on bank 2
Long underbody wiring to the rear sensor chafed or heat-damaged
Road salt corrosion in the sensor connector
Check engine light with normal driving behaviour
Readiness for catalyst or oxygen sensor monitor not set
P2237: O2 Sensor Positive Current Control Circuit/Open (Bank 1 Sensor 1)

P2237 points to an open pump-current line (IP or APE) on the front wide-band sensor of bank 1. With that wire broken the output freezes near its stoichiometric value of roughly 1.5 V and lambda stops moving.
Broken pump-current wire or pushed-back pin between sensor and ECM
Pump cell of the wide-band sensor damaged, for example by catalyst-heating strategy or thermal shock
Engine software that sets the code falsely (update available for some models)
Lambda reading stuck at 1.0 in live data
Higher fuel consumption in open-loop fuelling
P2238: O2 Sensor Positive Current Control Circuit Low (Bank 1 Sensor 1)

P2238 is the low-side fault of the pump-current circuit of the front wide-band sensor on bank 1. Saab's 9-5 2.0 turbo (2010) shows a concrete test: on overrun with the injectors shut off, pure air should drive the signal well above its stoichiometric level, and if it stays below 1.7 V for 3 s the code sets as Type B.
Pump-current wire chafed through to ground
Aged or contaminated sensor that no longer reads lean in fuel cut-off
Fault in the sensor interface of the ECM
Check engine light after two drives
Lambda value does not rise during coasting in live data
P2239: O2 Sensor Positive Current Control Circuit High (Bank 1 Sensor 1)

P2239 is the high-side counterpart for the pump-current circuit of the bank 1 front wide-band sensor. On the Saab 9-5 2.0 turbo (2010) it sets when, in closed loop with the mixture deliberately enriched, the signal still sits at 1.48-1.51 V for 1 s, meaning the sensor ignores a change it should report; it is a Type B code.
Pump-current wire shorted to heater supply or battery voltage
Wide-band sensor with internal short or stuck output
Damaged sensor interface in the ECM
Check engine light after two drives
Lambda reading frozen near 1.0 regardless of load
New sensor fails again quickly if the wiring short is not found
P223A: P223A covers the control circuit of a fifth DEF heating element, heater E. Unlike heaters A to D, which each have four codes for open, performance, low and high, heater E gets only this one code, so any electrical fault of its driver or wiring ends up here. No maker documents P223A publicly.
Open or shorted wiring or connector of heater E
Heating element E burnt out or shorted
Faulty output stage in the controlling module
Check engine light and SCR warning
DEF dosing delayed or blocked in freezing weather
P223B: P223B reports a fault in the control circuit of heater F, the sixth heating element of an SCR system. Like its neighbour P223A for heater E, it is a single catch-all code covering open lines and shorts alike.
Damaged wiring or corroded connector of heater F
Heating element F open or shorted
Missing supply from the heater relay or fuse
Check engine light and SCR warning
Reduced power warning after a cold-weather DEF fault
P223C: P223C judges whether the pump current of the bank 1 wide-band sensor makes sense while the engine is coasting with fuel cut off. In that state the sensor sees almost pure air and, as Bosch's LSU 4.9 data show, must drive a clearly positive current.
Aged or poisoned wide-band sensor with wrong pump current in air
Open pump-current, reference-cell or reference-ground wire
Exhaust leak or misfire that distorts the gas at the sensor
Check engine light after two drives
Usually no noticeable change in driving behaviour
P223D: P223D applies the pump-current plausibility test to the front wide-band sensor of bank 2 on V engines.
Worn bank 2 wide-band sensor that no longer pumps correctly in air
Interrupted pump-current or reference circuit of the bank 2 sensor
Sensor heater too weak to keep the element at temperature
Check engine light after two drives
P223E: O2 Sensor Reference Resistance Out Of Range (Bank 1)

P223E checks the internal resistance of the reference (Nernst) cell in the bank 1 wide-band sensor. That resistance falls as the ceramic heats up, so the ECM uses it as a thermometer; Bosch specifies 300 ohms nominal for the LSU 4.9 at operating temperature.
Aged sensor whose reference cell resistance has drifted
Heater not holding the element at temperature (heater, wiring or control)
ECM calibration fault on GM 2.0 turbo LTG (bulletin 16-NA-266)
Check engine light after two consecutive drives
Remote start refuses to start the engine (GM LTG models)
P223F: O2 Sensor Reference Resistance Out Of Range (Bank 2)

P223F is the reference-cell resistance check for the front wide-band sensor of bank 2. GM's 2016 and 2018 tables translate the measured resistance into element temperature and count readings below 700 °C or above 1,000 °C; 64 of 80 samples (2018) or 128 of 160 (2016) at 25 ms set a Type B code.
Bank 2 sensor ceramic aged and high-resistance
Weak heater supply or high resistance in the heater wiring
Sensor overheated by misfire or very high exhaust temperature
Check engine light after two drives
Bank 2 lambda control slow to become active after a cold start
P2240: O2 Sensor Positive Current Control Circuit/Open (Bank 2 Sensor 1)

P2240 is the open pump-current circuit of the front wide-band sensor on bank 2, so it only exists on V engines and boxers. Ford's summaries (2012 and 2020-2023) introduced it to replace P0154; detection works as on bank 1, by lambda failing to react to reference-current pulses or by the NTK interface chip.
Open pump-current wire or loose pin at the bank 2 sensor connector
Bank 2 front sensor damaged by water or thermal shock
PCM calibration that sets the code without a hardware fault (FCA 2025 Hurricane)
Bank 2 lambda value stuck at 1.0 in live data
P2241: O2 Sensor Positive Current Control Circuit Low (Bank 2 Sensor 1)

P2241 reports the pump-current circuit of the bank 2 front wide-band sensor at too low a level, typically a grounded wire or a sensor that cannot pump enough oxygen. No manufacturer publicly documents P2241 with thresholds.
Bank 2 pump-current wire shorted to ground
Aged bank 2 front sensor with weak pump cell
Fault in the ECM sensor interface for bank 2
Higher fuel consumption from open-loop fuelling on bank 2
P2242: O2 Sensor Positive Current Control Circuit High (Bank 2 Sensor 1)

P2242 flags the pump-current circuit of the bank 2 front wide-band sensor as too high, usually a short to the heater feed or battery voltage, or a signal locked at its midpoint although the mixture is being changed. No manufacturer publicly documents P2242 with thresholds.
Bank 2 pump-current wire shorted to heater supply or battery voltage
Internal short in the bank 2 wide-band sensor
Damaged sensor interface in the ECM
Replacement sensor fails again if the short remains
P2243: O2 Sensor Reference Voltage Circuit/Open (Bank 1 Sensor 1)

P2243 flags an open reference voltage line on the front wide-band sensor of bank 1, i.e. the Nernst-cell lead (RE/UN on Bosch sensors, VS on NTK). Ford's OBD summaries set it on Bosch parts when the sensor voltage sits above 4.7 V or below 0.2 V for 10 s; on NTK parts the interface chip reports the break itself.
Broken reference voltage (Nernst cell) wire or pushed-back pin between sensor and ECM
Sensing element cracked or tip broken off, for example by thermal shock
Engine software that sets the code falsely (update available for some models)
Higher fuel consumption from open-loop fuelling on bank 1
Catalyst efficiency code P0420 alongside it if a sensor fragment damaged the converter
P2244: O2 Sensor Reference Voltage Performance (Bank 1 Sensor 1)

P2244 stands for a plausibility fault on the reference voltage side of the bank 1 upstream wide-band sensor: the Nernst-cell signal is electrically intact and within limits, but behaves in a way that does not fit the operating state, for instance offset or too slow. No manufacturer documents P2244 publicly.
Aged or contaminated wide-band sensor (oil ash, silicone, coolant)
High resistance in the reference voltage wire or connector
Exhaust leak ahead of the sensor distorting the reading
P2245: O2 Sensor Reference Voltage Circuit Low (Bank 1 Sensor 1)
P2245 reports that the reference voltage side of the upstream air-fuel sensor on bank 1 reads too low, usually because the wire touches ground or the sensor has shorted internally.
Reference voltage wire shorted to ground (chafed against exhaust or body)
Sensor element damaged internally, for example by water hitting the hot ceramic
Fault in the sensor interface of the ECM
Higher fuel consumption from open-loop fuelling on bank 1
Uneven idle or hesitation in some cases
P2246: O2 Sensor Reference Voltage Circuit High (Bank 1 Sensor 1)

P2246 means the reference voltage line of the bank 1 front wide-band sensor reads too high, typically from a short to battery or heater voltage or a short inside the sensor. No manufacturer publishes a threshold for P2246.
Reference voltage wire shorted to heater supply or battery voltage
Internal short between heater and Nernst cell in the sensor
Fault in the sensor interface of the ECM
Repeat failure of a new sensor if the wiring short remains
P2247: O2 Sensor Reference Voltage Circuit/Open (Bank 2 Sensor 1)

P2247 is the bank 2 version of P2243: the Nernst-cell reference line of the upstream wide-band sensor on the second cylinder bank is open. Ford's summaries trip it on Bosch sensors after 10 s outside 0.2-4.7 V and on NTK sensors via the interface chip, replacing the older P0150.
Broken reference voltage (Nernst cell) wire or loose pin on the bank 2 sensor
Cracked element or broken sensor tip after thermal shock
Engine software that sets the code falsely (update for some models)
Higher fuel consumption from open-loop fuelling on bank 2
Catalyst efficiency code P0430 if a sensor fragment damaged the converter
P2248: O2 Sensor Reference Voltage Performance (Bank 2 Sensor 1)
P2248 is meant for a reference voltage signal on the bank 2 upstream wide-band sensor that is present but implausible, as opposed to an open or shorted line.
Aged or contaminated wide-band sensor on bank 2
High resistance in the reference voltage wire or connector
Exhaust leak ahead of the bank 2 sensor
P2249: O2 Sensor Reference Voltage Circuit Low (Bank 2 Sensor 1)
P2249 indicates that the reference voltage circuit of the front air-fuel sensor on bank 2 is pulled too low, most often by a grounded wire in the harness or a fault inside the sensor.
Reference voltage wire shorted to ground on the bank 2 sensor harness
Internal short in the bank 2 air-fuel sensor
Fault in the sensor interface of the ECM
Higher fuel consumption from open-loop fuelling on bank 2
P224A: P224A concerns the heater of the upstream NOx sensor on bank 1, the one before the SCR catalyst. Its electrical resistance rises with temperature, so the sensor electronics use it to hold the ceramic element at working heat. The code says that resistance is outside its allowed band, pointing to an aged or damaged element or a contact problem.
Heating element of the NOx sensor aged or cracked
Corroded or loose contacts in the sensor connector
Unstable supply voltage to the sensor module
SCR efficiency or NOx plausibility codes may follow
P224B: P224B is the heater resistance fault of the second NOx sensor on bank 1, mounted after the SCR catalyst. This sensor tells the control unit how much NOx is left after dosing, so its readings feed the catalyst efficiency monitor and the closed-loop dosing correction.
Heating element of the downstream NOx sensor aged or damaged
Corrosion in the sensor connector exposed to road spray
Element cracked by water droplets hitting the hot sensor
SCR efficiency monitor delayed or failing
P224C: Alternative Fuel Tank Shutoff Valve A Control Circuit/Open

P224C points to an open or otherwise faulty control circuit of shutoff valve A, the solenoid on a CNG or LPG tank that releases gas only when the engine runs on the alternative fuel. Such valves are normally closed.
Broken wire or unplugged connector at the tank valve
Solenoid coil of the valve open
Supply interrupted by relay or tripped inertia switch
Vehicle will not switch to gas operation or falls back to gasoline
P224D: Alternative Fuel Tank Shutoff Valve A Control Circuit Performance/Stuck Off

P224D means tank shutoff valve A is electrically switched but the system behaves as if it stayed shut. Software can only infer that from a pressure response: once the valve is commanded open, line or rail pressure should climb toward the regulated value, which GM gives as 468-896 kPa for the bi-fuel Impala and Ford as about 724 kPa for its 2003 CNG trucks.
Manual tank valve closed or tank nearly empty
Valve plunger stuck closed, e.g. by contamination
Supply voltage too low to pull the solenoid open
Faulty gas pressure sensor misreporting the response
Engine switches back to gasoline or will not run on gas
Gas fuel gauge shows content although no gas is delivered
P224E: Alternative Fuel Tank Shutoff Valve A Control Circuit Low

P224E sets when the control line of tank shutoff valve A reads too low. The DTC list of CNG upfitter TransEco Energy for its alternative fuel control module (AFCM v1.4) blames the line touching ground or being interrupted, turns on the MIL in both dedicated and bi-fuel setups and lets the system keep operating normally rather than forcing a fallback.
Control wire of the tank valve chafed through to ground
Open circuit, which some modules report under this code
Shorted solenoid coil in the valve
P224F: Alternative Fuel Tank Shutoff Valve A Control Circuit High

P224F reports a control circuit of tank shutoff valve A that reads too high, typically a wire touching battery voltage. In TransEco Energy's AFCM fault list the cause is given as shorted to power, the MIL is lit and the gas system keeps working under the failure mode strategy.
Control wire of the tank valve shorted to battery voltage
Output stage in the alternative fuel control module stuck on
Wiring mistake after a conversion or repair
Tank valve may stay open after switching off
P2250: O2 Sensor Reference Voltage Circuit High (Bank 2 Sensor 1)

P2250 signals that the reference voltage line of the upstream wide-band sensor on bank 2 is too high, as happens with a short to the heater feed or battery voltage, or a breakdown inside the ceramic. No manufacturer documents P2250 publicly, and no bulletin in the NHTSA index names it.
Reference voltage wire of the bank 2 sensor shorted to heater supply or battery voltage
Internal short between heater and Nernst cell
Fault in the sensor interface of the ECM
Repeat failure of a new sensor if the wiring short remains
P2251: O2 Sensor Negative Current Control Circuit/Open (Bank 1 Sensor 1)

P2251 points to an open negative current control line, i.e. the reference or virtual ground (VM on Bosch, COM on NTK) of the bank 1 upstream wide-band sensor. Ford detects it on Bosch parts by a sensor voltage stuck in a narrow band, or by a reference-current pulse that still moves lambda; NTK chips report the break directly.
Broken reference ground wire or pushed-back pin between sensor and ECM
Internal open circuit in the wide-band sensor
Engine software that sets the code falsely (reprogramming for some models)
Higher fuel consumption from open-loop fuelling on bank 1
Possible rough running or failed emissions test
P2252: O2 Sensor Negative Current Control Circuit Low (Bank 1 Sensor 1)
P2252 means the negative current control side of the bank 1 front air-fuel sensor reads too low, typically because that line or the sensor cell is shorted to ground.
Reference ground or sensor-cell wire shorted to ground (chafed against exhaust or body)
Internal short in the air-fuel sensor
Fault in the sensor interface of the ECM
Higher fuel consumption from open-loop fuelling on bank 1
P2253: O2 Sensor Negative Current Control Circuit High (Bank 1 Sensor 1)
P2253 reports that the negative current control side of the bank 1 upstream air-fuel sensor reads too high.
Open sensor-cell wire or connector contact, letting the signal float high
Wire shorted to heater supply or battery voltage
Internal defect in the air-fuel sensor
Higher fuel consumption from open-loop fuelling on bank 1
Repeat failure of a new sensor if a wiring short remains
P2254: O2 Sensor Negative Current Control Circuit/Open (Bank 2 Sensor 1)
P2254 concerns the negative current control line - also called reference ground, virtual ground or COM - of the wide-band air-fuel sensor ahead of the catalyst on bank 2.
Broken reference ground wire or pushed-out pin between sensor and ECM
Internal open circuit in the wide-band sensor
Corroded sensor connector with high contact resistance
Higher fuel consumption from open-loop fuelling on bank 2
Possible rough running or failed emissions test
P2255: O2 Sensor Negative Current Control Circuit Low (Bank 2 Sensor 1)

P2255 reports that the negative current control line (reference ground) of the bank 2 upstream wide-band sensor reads too low, typically a short to ground. No manufacturer publicly documents P2255 with thresholds.
Reference ground wire shorted to ground (chafed against exhaust or body)
Internal fault in the wide-band sensor
Fault in the sensor interface of the ECM
P2256: O2 Sensor Negative Current Control Circuit High (Bank 2 Sensor 1)

P2256 means the negative current control line (reference ground) of the bank 2 upstream wide-band sensor reads too high, typically a short to battery or heater voltage. No manufacturer publicly documents P2256 with thresholds.
Reference ground wire shorted to heater supply or battery voltage
Internal short in the wide-band sensor
Fault in the sensor interface of the ECM
Repeat failure of a new sensor if the wiring short remains
P2257: AIR System Control A Circuit Low

P2257 concerns the control circuit of the secondary air (AIR) pump or its relay, which blows fresh air into the exhaust during cold starts so the catalyst lights off sooner. The code sets when that circuit reads low.
Relay control wire shorted to ground
Secondary air relay with a shorted coil
Water ingress in the relay or pump connector
Secondary air pump silent during cold start
Secondary air flow codes such as P0411 may follow
P2258: AIR System Control A Circuit High

P2258 reports that the line controlling secondary air (AIR) pump A or its relay sits at too high a level, usually because it is shorted to battery voltage or the driver cannot pull it down. The pump only runs briefly after a cold start to heat the catalyst faster, so the fault mainly raises warm-up emissions.
Control wire of the AIR pump relay chafed through and touching a battery-voltage feed
Secondary air relay with shorted coil or welded contacts
Moisture or corrosion in the relay or pump connector bridging terminals
Faulty output stage in the engine control module
MIL on, often without any noticeable change in driving
Secondary air pump silent after a cold start
Higher hydrocarbon emissions during warm-up, possibly a failed emissions test
P2259: AIR System Control B Circuit Low

P2259 is the low-level fault of the second secondary air control circuit, B. A second circuit exists where an engine uses two AIR pumps, two relays or a separately switched air valve; circuit A keeps its own codes P2257/P2258. A low reading usually means the control wire has contact with ground.
Control wire of circuit B chafed against the body or engine and shorted to ground
Relay or air valve B with a shorted winding
Corroded connector at relay B or the air valve
Secondary air pump audible for longer than usual or while warm
Blown fuse of the secondary air pump after a long run
P225A: P225A concerns the front NOx sensor of bank 1, the one ahead of the SCR catalyst. Modern NOx probes come with their own control unit that holds a sensor-specific calibration and reports finished values over CAN; this code means the stored calibration data of that unit cannot be read or fails its check.
Internal memory or checksum fault in the NOx sensor control unit
Replacement sensor with a part number or calibration that does not suit the vehicle
Supply voltage dropout or poor connector contact while the module was storing data
Engine or aftertreatment control unit software that misreads the sensor data
MIL on, usually without any change in how the engine runs
SCR dosing runs without valid feedback, so NOx emissions may rise
Follow-up NOx catalyst efficiency codes possible
P225B: P225B is stored when the control unit of the downstream NOx sensor on bank 1 cannot provide valid calibration data from its memory. That sensor sits behind the SCR catalyst and is what the engine computer uses to judge how well urea dosing reduces NOx, so a sensor without trustworthy calibration leaves the catalyst monitor blind.
Corrupted or unreadable calibration memory in the downstream NOx sensor module
Sensor installed with the wrong part number or an OEM calibration for another application
Moisture or corrosion at the sensor module connector disturbing its supply
MIL on with no driveability complaint
SCR efficiency monitor does not complete or reports P20EE
Possible emissions test failure because readiness stays incomplete
P225C: NOx Sensor Performance - Signal Biased/Stuck High (Bank 1 Sensor 1)

P225C says the upstream NOx sensor of bank 1 reports more NOx than is plausible. Volvo describes its test on US17+OBD19 trucks: during engine motoring with zero fuel the engine makes no NOx, so the inlet sensor must fall below 50 ppm within about 10 s; each failure lights the MIL, which needs three clean drive cycles to go out.
Engine or DEF control unit software that flags the sensor too eagerly
Leak in the charge air path or an EGR valve stuck partly open
Air mass or coolant temperature signal that skews the NOx model
Upstream NOx sensor with a genuine positive offset
MIL on, often without any noticeable driving fault
Code returns after the NOx sensor has been replaced
Higher DEF consumption or SCR efficiency codes in some cases
P225D: NOx Sensor Performance - Signal Biased/Stuck Low (Bank 1 Sensor 1)

P225D is the opposite case to P225C: the upstream NOx sensor of bank 1 reads too little NOx or refuses to rise when the engine should be producing it. Volvo and Mack list P225D among NOx codes where the sensor is very unlikely to be at fault, because the probe is simply measuring fresh air; their guide says not to replace it.
Charge air, intake or exhaust leak that lets the sensor see diluted gas
Sensor ports clogged with soot, for example after fuel contamination
Low-pressure EGR valve partly stuck open
Outdated engine control software that a published flash corrects
Code persists after a new NOx sensor
Possible related intake, EGR or MAF codes
P225E: NOx Sensor Performance - Signal Biased/Stuck High (Bank 1 Sensor 2)

P225E points at the downstream NOx sensor of bank 1, behind the SCR catalyst, reading persistently high. Because that sensor sees what is left after urea dosing, a high value can be a sensor offset or genuine NOx slipping through a weak catalyst, poor DEF or a faulty dosing valve.
Real NOx slip from a weak SCR catalyst, poor DEF quality or a faulty dosing valve
Downstream NOx sensor with a positive offset
Control software that evaluates the sensor incorrectly
MIL on, often together with P20EE
Increased DEF consumption or DEF quality warnings
Power reduction possible if SCR efficiency codes follow
P225F: NOx Sensor Performance - Signal Biased/Stuck Low (Bank 1 Sensor 2)

P225F is set when the downstream NOx sensor of bank 1 reports less NOx than expected or does not move away from a low value. A sensor behind the SCR catalyst that reads too low makes the catalyst look better than it is, so the efficiency monitor can no longer be trusted.
Exhaust leak upstream of the downstream sensor drawing in outside air
Chafed or corroded wiring between sensor module and probe
Downstream NOx sensor with reduced sensitivity
SCR efficiency cannot be confirmed, readiness may stay open
P2260: AIR System Control B Circuit High

P2260 flags secondary air control circuit B sitting at too high a level, as with a short to the supply or a driver output that cannot switch. Circuit B drives the second pump, second relay or a separate air valve, depending on the engine.
Control wire of circuit B shorted to a battery-voltage feed
Relay or air valve B with an open coil, depending on how the driver is diagnosed
Output stage for circuit B in the engine control module defective
Second secondary air pump or valve does not operate after a cold start
Increased cold-start emissions, possibly with a secondary air flow code on one bank
P2261: P2261 means bypass valve A of the turbocharger or supercharger, also called the recirculation valve, does not work mechanically. When the throttle snaps shut it should let charge air flow back to the compressor inlet so the compressor does not surge.
Bypass/recirculation valve sticking closed or with a torn diaphragm
Kinked, collapsed or wrongly routed recirculation or control hose
Electrical fault at the valve solenoid or its connector that prevents opening
Engine control module output reacting wrongly (software or hardware)
Fluttering, chuffing or rattling noise from the turbo when lifting off the throttle
Slightly delayed boost after gear changes
P2262: Turbocharger/Supercharger Boost Pressure A Not Detected - Mechanical

P2262 says boost pressure A does not appear at all although the charging system should be producing it, and the cause appears to be mechanical rather than a sensor fault. The control unit sees the pressure after the compressor stay near ambient or close to manifold pressure.
Intake or charge-air hose disconnected or split, so the compressor cannot build pressure
Wastegate or bypass stuck open, corroded or with a broken linkage
Damaged turbocharger or supercharger (bearing wear, broken drive, wheel damage)
Boost pressure sensor or its hose blocked or detached
Clear loss of power, no turbo or supercharger pull
MIL on, often with a reduced-power mode
Hissing or whistling from the intake if a hose has come off
P2263: P2263 means boost pressure measured in the intake manifold stays too far from the target set by the closed-loop boost control. CARB requires diesel OBD to detect underboost, overboost and slow response of the boost control.
Charge-air hose or cooler duct leaking or pulled off
Restricted exhaust, for example a heavily loaded particulate filter
Hissing or whistling from the charge-air system
P2264: Water in Fuel Sensor A Circuit

P2264 is the general circuit code for water-in-fuel sensor A, the probe in the diesel filter or separator that detects water by its conductivity. GM's 2018 diesel tables explain a neat self-test: after the ignition has been off for more than about 8 h, a healthy sensor briefly signals water during the first 0.3 to 1.8 s after power-up.
Water-in-fuel sensor that no longer performs its power-up self-test
Corroded or loose connector at the filter housing, exposed to road spray
Open or damaged wire between sensor and ECM or tank zone module
Incompatible sensor fitted during a filter change
Service lamp or message on, engine runs normally
No warning if water actually collects in the separator
P2265: Water in Fuel Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance

P2265 means the signal from water-in-fuel sensor A is electrically present but does not behave plausibly, for example a self-test response that comes at the wrong time or a value that sits between the expected dry and wet states. No manufacturer documents P2265 publicly.
Sludge, emulsion or deposits coating the sensor electrodes
Sensor electronics drifting so the output lies between dry and wet
Corroded terminals adding resistance to the signal circuit
Water warning or service lamp that comes and goes
Water warning stays on even after the filter has been drained
P2266: Water in Fuel Sensor A Circuit Low
P2266 is set when the signal line of water-in-fuel sensor A stays below its valid range, typical of a grounded signal wire or of a conductive path that should not be there.
Water intrusion into the sensor connector bridging signal and ground
Sensor with internal resistance outside specification
Signal wire chafed against the frame and shorted to ground
Water-in-fuel lamp on although no water is in the separator
P2267: Water in Fuel Sensor A Circuit High
P2267 reports that the signal of water-in-fuel sensor A sits above its valid range, which usually indicates an open signal or ground path, a disconnected sensor or a short to a voltage source.
Residual contamination on the probes after draining the filter
Unplugged sensor or open signal or ground wire
Signal wire shorted to a supply voltage
Water-in-fuel lamp stays on after draining
P2268: Water in Fuel Sensor A Circuit Intermittent
P2268 is reserved for a water-in-fuel sensor A circuit whose signal drops out or jumps for short moments instead of staying at a fault level. No manufacturer documents P2268 publicly.
Loose or corroded connector at the filter housing losing contact under vibration
Wire chafing intermittently near the frame or filter bracket
Moisture in the plug that changes with temperature and spray
Water warning flickers or appears briefly while driving
Code stored as history with no fault present at the workshop
P2269: Water in Fuel Condition - Sensor A

P2269 is not a wiring fault but a statement about the fuel: sensor A has detected water. On diesels it means the separator is full; Ram's 2025-26 Cummins 6.7L trucks set it with the MIL, and Stellantis traced a persistent case to incomplete draining, fixed by draining and swapping the sensor's signal and ground pins (TSB 14-004-26).
Water separator full and not drained at the service interval
Fuel from the tank or filling station containing water
Residual water after draining or a wet sensor connector faking the alarm
Engine control software needing an update
Water-in-fuel lamp or message, on some vehicles also the MIL
Rough running, power loss or hard starting if water reaches the injection system
Reduced power on some engines to protect the injection system
P226A: Water in Fuel Lamp Control Circuit

P226A concerns the output that switches the water-in-fuel warning lamp, not the sensor. The control unit drives the lamp circuit and checks it electrically; an open lamp, a broken wire or a shorted driver lets it set this code.
Burnt-out warning lamp or corroded lamp socket
Open or shorted wire between control unit and lamp
Faulty lamp driver in the control unit
Water-in-fuel lamp does not light during the bulb check at ignition on
Lamp stays on permanently regardless of the filter state
P226B: Turbocharger/Supercharger A Boost Pressure Too High - Mechanical

P226B reports boost from turbocharger or supercharger A rising too high for a mechanical reason, for instance a wastegate or bypass that will not open or a seized actuator linkage, rather than a sensor or wiring fault. VW's 2014 book for the supercharged Touareg 3.0 TSI sets it when boost passes 250 kPa.
Wastegate flap seized closed by corrosion or carbon
Seized or misadjusted wastegate or VGT actuator linkage
Vacuum or pressure line to a pneumatic actuator leaking or blocked
Sudden power cut or reduced-power mode under load
Unusually strong surge of power just before the cut
P226C: Turbocharger Boost Control A Slow Response
P226C means the boost control actuator of turbocharger A does move, but too slowly, so boost lags behind changes in demand.
Variable vanes or turbine control valve sluggish from soot, varnish or corrosion
Worn electric or pneumatic boost actuator, or a weak control solenoid
Damaged wiring or connector between actuator and control module
Control module software that needs an update (cold-weather false sets)
Hesitant pull from low engine speed, turbo lag
MIL on, sometimes with a torque limit
More smoke on acceleration with diesel engines
P226D: P226D means the bank 1 particulate filter offers so little flow resistance that its core is likely broken, burnt out or removed. CARB requires detection of a destroyed or missing substrate, or a filter replaced by a pipe.
Filter core cracked, melted after an overheated regeneration, or removed
Differential pressure line disconnected, cracked, blocked or routed wrongly
Control software that sets the code without a hardware fault
Incorrect or faulty differential pressure sensor assembly
Visible soot at the tailpipe if the filter core is damaged
Often no driveability change; regeneration behaviour may be affected
P226E: P226E reports a damaged or missing particulate filter core on bank 2, which only exists where each cylinder bank has its own filter.
Bank 2 filter core cracked, melted or removed
Pressure sensing line of bank 2 loose, cracked or blocked
Back pressure sensor reading too low
Usually no noticeable change in driving behaviour
P226F: Turbocharger Boost Control B Slow Response

P226F is the slow-response fault of boost control B, meaning the actuator of a second turbocharger or of the second stage on twin-turbo, bi-turbo or sequential layouts. Which unit the letter B denotes is up to the manufacturer.
Boost actuator of turbocharger B sluggish or worn
Carbon or varnish restricting vanes or flap on turbocharger B
Leaking vacuum line or damaged wiring to actuator B
Delayed boost in the speed range where the second charger takes over
MIL on, possibly with reduced power
P2270: O2 Sensor Signal Biased/Stuck Lean (Bank 1, Sensor 2)

P2270 concerns the oxygen sensor behind the catalyst on bank 1. When the mixture turns rich, this sensor should rise to a high voltage; if it stays low, the ECM treats it as biased or stuck lean and can no longer rely on it for catalyst monitoring or the post-catalyst trim.
Rear oxygen sensor aged, contaminated or slow to reach rich voltage
Exhaust leak ahead of the rear sensor diluting the gas with air
Oil in the sensor connector or a bent terminal
Calibration issue fixed by an ECM update
Catalyst and oxygen sensor readiness not completing
Usually no noticeable change in driveability
P2271: O2 Sensor Signal Biased/Stuck Rich (Bank 1, Sensor 2)

P2271 is the opposite fault of the same bank 1 rear sensor: its voltage refuses to fall when the exhaust should be lean. It is usually checked during a deceleration fuel cut, when almost pure air passes the sensor.
Rear oxygen sensor contaminated by coolant, oil or silicone
Faulty front A/F sensor making the rear sensor look stuck rich
Signal wire chafed against a voltage source
P2272: O2 Sensor Signal Biased/Stuck Lean (Bank 2, Sensor 2)

P2272 applies to V and flat engines with a separate catalyst and rear oxygen sensor on bank 2; that sensor fails to reach a rich reading when the ECM enriches bank 2. GM's 2016 tables (16OBDG05) set it if the voltage is still under 800 mV after 68 g of air during forced enrichment (Type B).
Bank 2 rear oxygen sensor aged or contaminated
Engine oil in the sensor connector, for example from a leaking oil pressure switch
Exhaust leak on bank 2 ahead of the rear sensor
Catalyst monitor for bank 2 not completing
P2273: O2 Sensor Signal Biased/Stuck Rich (Bank 2, Sensor 2)

P2273 means the rear oxygen sensor of bank 2 keeps a high voltage when the exhaust of that bank should be lean. GM's 2016 tables (16OBDG05) check this in fuel cut-off and set the code if the signal is above 100 mV after 9 g of air (Type B); GM's 2024 tables (24OBDG07) compare the lowest voltage during a commanded lean phase with 0.20 V over two trips.
Bank 2 rear oxygen sensor fouled by oil or coolant
Signal wire touching a supply or heater line
Bank 2 front sensor misreading so that the bank actually runs rich
Catalyst monitor for bank 2 not completing
P2274: O2 Sensor Signal Biased/Stuck Lean (Bank 1, Sensor 3)

Sensor 3 exists only where a bank has a third oxygen sensor, usually behind a second catalyst, so that sensor 2 sits between two bricks. P2274 says this last sensor on bank 1 stays lean when it should swing rich.
Third oxygen sensor aged or cracked by thermal shock from water
Exhaust leak ahead of sensor 3 drawing in air
Damaged wiring or connector of sensor 3
P2275: O2 Sensor Signal Biased/Stuck Rich (Bank 1, Sensor 3)
P2275 is the rich-side fault of the third oxygen sensor on bank 1, the last one on systems with two catalysts in series: it keeps a high voltage while the exhaust should be lean.
Third oxygen sensor contaminated or damaged by water
Signal wire of sensor 3 touching a voltage source
P2276: O2 Sensor Signal Biased/Stuck Lean (Bank 2, Sensor 3)

P2276 needs three oxygen sensors on bank 2, so it only occurs on V or flat engines whose second bank carries a front, a mid-catalyst and a post-catalyst sensor. It reports that the post-catalyst sensor of bank 2 does not reach a rich reading.
Bank 2 third oxygen sensor aged or cracked by water
Exhaust leak on bank 2 ahead of sensor 3
Damaged wiring or connector of sensor 3
P2277: O2 Sensor Signal Biased/Stuck Rich (Bank 2, Sensor 3)

P2277 is the rich-side counterpart of P2276: the third, post-catalyst sensor on bank 2 does not drop to a lean reading. On such layouts the check normally runs during a fuel cut, when the second catalyst must fill with oxygen before the sensor can respond, so a slow or fouled element shows up here.
Bank 2 third oxygen sensor contaminated or water-damaged
Signal wire of sensor 3 touching a voltage source
P2278: O2 Sensor Signals Swapped Bank 1 Sensor 3/Bank 2 Sensor 3

P2278 reports that the third oxygen sensors of the two banks are connected the wrong way round, so the ECM reads the bank 1 sensor as if it sat on bank 2 and vice versa. The check changes the exhaust of one bank only, for example by cutting its injectors or feeding air into one exhaust line, and watches which sensor answers.
Sensor 3 connectors of both banks plugged in crosswise after a repair
Harness routed to the wrong side or pins swapped in a connector
Wrong harness, ECM or calibration after a replacement
Catalyst or sensor codes reported for the wrong bank
P2279: P2279 means the ECM has concluded that air enters the engine without being measured or expected, for example because the air mass sensor, manifold pressure and throttle position no longer agree with its air model. Volkswagen and Audi use it widely.
Leaking crankcase breather or PCV pressure-regulating valve
Leak at intake manifold, hoses or seals after the air mass sensor
Whistling at idle, unstable or high idle speed
P227A: P227A is the general circuit fault of barometric pressure sensor C, used when the control unit finds the signal missing or unusable without classifying it as too low or too high.
Loose connector, corroded pins or damaged wiring at sensor C
5 V reference or sensor ground shared with other sensors disturbed
Usually no noticeable change in driving; slight power loss at altitude possible
P227B: Barometric Pressure Sensor C Circuit Range/Performance
P227B means sensor C supplies an electrically sound signal that does not agree with the other pressure readings.
Sensor C drifting or with an offset
Sensor port blocked by dirt, oil or ice, or sensor not seated in its bore
Heavily clogged air filter shifting the pressure ahead of the compressor or throttle
Mostly no driveability change; occasionally reduced boost
P227C: Barometric Pressure Sensor C Circuit Low

P227C flags a voltage from pressure sensor C that is too low. GM's 2018 tables show two variants. On the diesel, where sensor C measures turbocharger inlet pressure and the input has a pull-up, only a short to ground pulls it below 39.4 % of 5 V (about 50.2 kPa); 320 failures in 400 samples make it a Type B fault.
Signal wire of sensor C shorted to ground
Open signal or 5 V supply line on inputs that read an open circuit as low
Replacement control module without the calibration that matches the fitted sensor
MIL on, on some engines immediately
Engine runs on a substitute value, at most slightly less power
P227D: Barometric Pressure Sensor C Circuit High

P227D is the high-voltage counterpart of P227C. On GM's 2018 diesel the sensor C input has a pull-up, so both a short to the supply and a broken signal wire push it above 90.2 % of 5 V (about 115.4 kPa); after 320 failures in 400 samples it is a Type B fault.
Signal wire of sensor C shorted to 5 V or battery voltage
Broken signal wire or sensor ground on inputs with pull-up
Little change in driving; possibly reduced boost or poorer altitude compensation
P227E: Barometric Pressure Sensor C Circuit Intermittent/Erratic

P227E covers a sensor C signal that jumps although every single value is in range. GM measures this as a string length: the absolute difference between each reading and the one taken 12.5 ms earlier is summed over 80 consecutive readings, and a sum above 152 kPa (2018 diesel) or 150 kPa (supercharged LT4) counts as a failure.
Loose or corroded terminals in the sensor C connector
Interference from ignition or actuator wiring routed nearby
Sensor C with an unstable internal element
MIL on, possibly coming and going
Occasional brief hesitation or uneven boost
P227F: Air Flow Restriction/Air Leak Between Air Filter and MAF (Bank 2)

P227F means the passage between the air filter and the mass air flow sensor of bank 2 is restricted or lets air in that has bypassed the filter. By today's wording the code belongs to engines with a separate air path and MAF per bank; P2280 is the bank 1 version.
Air filter clogged with dust or soaked with too much oil
Intake opening blocked by snow, leaves or a collapsed duct
Loose clamp or cracked duct between filter box and MAF on bank 2
Faulty filter restriction or inlet pressure sensor
MIL on, on some trucks with an air filter service message
Reduced power and boost under load
More black smoke on diesel engines
P2280: Air Flow Restriction/Air Leak Between Air Filter and MAF (Bank 1)

P2280 is the bank 1 code for restricted airflow or an air leak between the air filter and the MAF sensor. A blocked filter lowers the pressure ahead of the sensor and limits the air the engine can take in. A leak in this section matters less for fuel metering, since the air still passes the MAF, but it lets unfiltered air and dust reach the engine.
Air filter clogged or soaked with oil
Snow, ice or debris in the air inlet, or a collapsed intake duct
Cracked duct or loose clamp between filter box and MAF
Early software that flags the condition too readily
Less power and slower boost build-up under load
More smoke from diesel engines when accelerating
P2281: Air Leak Between MAF and Throttle Body
P2281 points to air that escapes or enters between the MAF sensor and the throttle body, so the airflow the sensor reports no longer matches what reaches the cylinders.
Loose clamp, split hose or leaking charge air cooler between MAF and throttle
Contaminated or drifting MAF sensor that misreports airflow
Engine software that sets the code without a real leak (update available)
Disconnected crankcase vent or other hose joined to this section
Hissing under boost and less power
Black smoke on diesels or rough idle on petrol engines
P2282: Air Leak Between Throttle Body and Intake Valves
P2282 means air enters the intake behind the throttle, so it reaches the cylinders without passing the throttle.
Brake booster vacuum pipe detached or its check valve stuck open
Crankcase ventilation hose disconnected or cracked
Leaking intake manifold gasket, throttle body seal or vacuum hose
Iced manifold pressure sensor or software miscalculating the leak
MIL on, sometimes with a hissing noise from the engine bay
Harder brake pedal if the brake vacuum line is affected
P2283: P2283 is the general circuit code for the injector control pressure (ICP) sensor. ICP describes the high-pressure engine oil that hydraulically actuated unit injectors (HEUI) use to pressurise fuel, as on Navistar-built Ford Power Stroke diesels; the sensor reports rail pressure so the injection pressure regulator can be closed-loop controlled.
Failed ICP sensor, often with oil inside the connector
Damaged signal, reference or ground wire of the sensor
5-volt reference circuit pulled down by another sensor
Hard or long cranking, especially when hot
P2284: Injector Control Pressure Sensor Circuit Range/Performance

P2284 means the measured injector control pressure does not follow what the PCM commands. Ford's 6.0L Power Stroke summaries (2003 and 2004) run the check continuously every 8 ms with the engine running: a fault is recorded once measured pressure stays more than 3.0 MPa above the target for longer than 7 s, the reverse case being P2290.
ICP sensor reading offset, including a shifted internal O-ring
Injection pressure regulator valve sticking or contaminated
Wrong, aerated or low engine oil disturbing pressure control
Oil wicking into the sensor connector
Engine runs on a substitute pressure value
P2285: Injector Control Pressure Sensor Circuit Low

P2285 is set when the ICP sensor voltage falls almost to zero. Ford's 6.0L Power Stroke summaries for 2003 and 2004 define it precisely: below 0.03 V, checked every 8 ms without entry conditions, decided in under one second.
Signal wire open or shorted to ground
P2286: Injector Control Pressure Sensor Circuit High

P2286 means the ICP sensor voltage has risen to the top of the range. In Ford's 2004 summary for the 6.0L Power Stroke the limit is above 4.83 V, checked every 8 ms and confirmed in less than one second; the 2003 edition already names the code alongside P2285.
Signal wire shorted to the 5-volt reference or another voltage
ICP sensor failed with output stuck high
Reduced power and possibly harsh running
P2287: Injector Control Pressure Sensor Circuit Intermittent

P2287 covers an ICP sensor signal that drops out or jumps for brief moments, too short or too irregular to be judged as a steady low or high fault. No manufacturer documents P2287 publicly; Ford's 6.0L summaries and its 2014 PCM table contain the steady electrical codes P2285 and P2286 but not this one.
Engine oil creeping into the sensor connector
Fretting or loose terminals at sensor or PCM
Harness rubbing on engine parts and shorting briefly
Code returns without a fault visible in the workshop
P2288: P2288 reports that the injector control pressure itself, not just its reading, has climbed above the allowed maximum while the engine runs. Ford's 6.0L Power Stroke summaries put the limit at 27.5 MPa in the 2003 edition and 29.5 MPa in 2004, sustained for more than 3 s.
Injection pressure regulator valve stuck or contaminated
Fault in the regulator drive circuit holding it at high duty
ICP sensor reading higher than the actual pressure
Reduced power with fuel limit active
P2289: Injector Control Pressure Too High - Engine Off

P2289 is a plausibility test carried out with the engine stopped. On a HEUI diesel the high-pressure oil pump is driven by the engine, so once it stops, injector control pressure should drop to almost nothing.
ICP sensor with a positive offset or oil contamination
Partial short between signal and reference voltage
Faulty input stage in the PCM
MIL on, possibly after the engine was switched off
Hard starting if the PCM trusts the false pressure value
P228A: Fuel Pressure Regulator A - Forced Engine Shutdown
P228A is a protective shutdown code: the engine computer has stopped the engine because rail pressure could not be held even with fuel pressure regulator A at full authority.
Fuel supply starved (gelled or waxed diesel, clogged filter, failing in-tank pump)
Fuel metering unit on the high-pressure pump sticking or worn
High-pressure pump no longer reaching the required delivery
Leak in the high-pressure circuit or injector return
Engine stalls while driving or shuts off shortly after starting
Check engine light on, often with P0087
Whining in-tank fuel pump in cold weather
P228B: Fuel Pressure Regulator B - Forced Engine Shutdown
P228B mirrors P228A but concerns fuel pressure regulator B, which in GM's 2018 diesel calibration is the rail pressure regulator valve that spills surplus fuel from the rail.
Rail pressure regulator valve not sealing when closed
Fuel starvation from gelled diesel or a blocked filter
Engine stops on its own and may not restart
Check engine light with low rail pressure codes
Loss of power just before the shutdown
P228C: Fuel Pressure Regulator A Exceeded Control Limits - Pressure Too Low
P228C means rail pressure has stayed below target long enough that regulator A, the path that sets pump delivery, is judged to have used up its correction.
High-pressure pump or its control valve sticking or worn (e.g. after heavy E85 use)
Low-pressure supply too weak or contaminated fuel
Water or corrosion in the injector or pump wiring
Rail pressure sensor reading too low
Check engine light, sometimes clearing after a key cycle
P228D: Fuel Pressure Regulator A Exceeded Control Limits - Pressure Too High
P228D is the opposite of P228C: measured rail pressure stays above the setpoint for too long although regulator A should be cutting delivery.
Pump control or metering valve not reducing delivery
Engine control software needing an update
Rail pressure sensor reading too high
Defective unit or high-pressure pump (truck engines)
Louder injection noise or rough idle
P228E: Fuel Pressure Regulator A Exceeded Learning Limits - Too Low
P228E reports that the self-learned correction of fuel pressure regulator A has reached its lower bound.
Pressure regulator or metering valve worn, characteristic changed
High-pressure pump delivery deviating from its model
Check engine light without noticeable drivability change
Occasional rough running or slower pressure response
P228F: Fuel Pressure Regulator A Exceeded Learning Limits - Too High

P228F is the upper counterpart of P228E: the learned correction for fuel pressure regulator A has run into its maximum. Ford's 2023 diesel summary applies one test to both codes on the 3.0 L and 6.7 L engines, with a limit near a 20 % rail pressure sensor slope error and about 10 s of monitoring at 600 bar or more.
Dirt in the high-pressure system, e.g. via a leaking fuel filter seal
P2290: P2290 belongs to the injector control pressure (ICP) family of hydraulically actuated unit injector (HEUI) diesels such as the Navistar-built Ford 6.0 L Power Stroke, where pressurised engine oil fires the injectors.
Injection pressure regulator (IPR) contaminated or not sealing
Leaking high-pressure oil rail fittings, stand pipes or O-rings
Low, wrong or aerated engine oil
Lack of power and rough running
P2291: Injector Control Pressure Too Low - Engine Cranking

P2291 judges pressure build-up while the starter is turning. On HEUI diesels the injectors only fire once injector control pressure has reached a minimum, so any leak in the pressurised oil circuit shows up as a long crank or a no-start; Wikipedia's Power Stroke article names a contaminated injection pressure regulator and failed high-pressure oil seals as t…
Leak in the high-pressure oil (HEUI) or fuel (common rail) circuit
Injection pressure regulator or rail pressure valve not sealing
High-pressure pump delivering too little at cranking speed
Low cranking speed from a weak battery or starter
Engine cranks long or does not start
Check engine light after the start attempt
P2292: P2292 describes an injector control pressure that jumps around instead of sitting steadily below or above target. No manufacturer documents its detection logic publicly: Ford's 2014 PCM code table lists the code without a MIL marking, and the 6.0 L Power Stroke summaries only describe the steady checks P2284, P2288 and P2290.
Air in the engine oil (foaming, wrong oil, overfill)
ICP sensor or its connector making intermittent contact
High-pressure oil pump starting to fail
Surging or bucking under steady throttle
P2293: P2293 checks whether fuel pressure regulator B really controls rail pressure. In GM's 2018 diesel table regulator B is the rail pressure regulator valve; the code sets when, with that valve in charge, rail pressure rises above a calibrated ceiling of 67 to 217 MPa in 160 of 229 samples at 6.25 ms, Type A.
Rail pressure regulator valve sticking or worn (often replaced with the rail)
Reduced power or stalling in severe cases
P2294: Fuel Pressure Regulator B Control Circuit/Open

P2294 is the open-circuit check of the drive line to fuel pressure regulator B. GM's 2018 diesel ECM tests the low-side driver of the rail pressure regulator valve while the output is switched off: a voltage indicating more than 200 kΩ between signal and ground counts as open, and 44 failures in 88 samples at 6.25 ms set the code as Type B.
Broken wire in the regulator harness
Loose, corroded or pushed-back connector pin
Open coil in the pressure regulator valve
Faulty output driver in the engine control module
P2295: Fuel Pressure Regulator B Control Circuit Low

P2295 stands for the control line of fuel pressure regulator B touching ground. GM's 2018 diesel ECM detects it with its low-side driver switched off: if the measured voltage corresponds to 0.5 Ω or less towards ground, the sample counts as failed, and 44 of 88 samples at 6.25 ms confirm the fault as Type B.
Control wire chafed through to ground
Water or corrosion in the regulator connector
Shorted coil in the pressure regulator valve
Rail pressure too high or unstable, reduced power
P2296: Fuel Pressure Regulator B Control Circuit High

P2296 is set when the control line of fuel pressure regulator B has contact with supply voltage. GM's 2018 diesel ECM checks this with its low-side driver switched on: if the line still shows a voltage equivalent to 0.5 Ω or less towards power, the sample fails, again with 44 of 88 samples and Type B.
Control wire shorted to a voltage supply
Faulty output driver in the engine control module
P2297: O2 Sensor Out of Range During Deceleration (Bank 1 Sensor 1)

P2297 concerns the upstream oxygen sensor of bank 1 and the moment when fuel is cut on deceleration and the sensor should read almost pure air. Diesel calibrations compare the reading in overrun with a modelled value: GM's 6.6L LML faults a gap between measured and calculated value above 0.06 to 0.07, the 3.0L LZ0 a deviation beyond 5 percent (Type B).
Upstream wide-band sensor aged or drifted (wrong reading in air)
Exhaust leak ahead of the sensor drawing in outside air
Air-mass or fuel model error (MAF, injector leakage, EGR) skewing the expected value
Engine software needing an update (GM 3.0L LZ0 2024, bulletin 24-NA-094)
Malfunction indicator lamp on after two trips
Usually no noticeable change in driving behaviour
Possibly stored with P0133 or fuel-quantity codes
P2298: O2 Sensor Out of Range During Deceleration (Bank 2 Sensor 1)

P2298 is the bank 2 version of P2297 and exists only on engines with two cylinder banks, each with its own upstream oxygen sensor. Three GM tables show the two readings of the code. The 2005 3.5L V6 (L66) tests during fuel cut-off with coolant above 69 °C and below 2,200 rpm, faulting a wide-band output above 4.5 V or below 2.9 V, over two drive cycles.
Bank 2 upstream wide-band sensor aged or contaminated
Exhaust leak on bank 2 ahead of the sensor
Damaged sensor lead or connector on bank 2
Malfunction indicator lamp on after two trips
Usually no noticeable change in driving behaviour
Bank 2 fuel trim values may look unusual
P2299: Brake Pedal Position/Accelerator Pedal Position Incompatible
P2299 means the vehicle has seen the brake and the accelerator pressed together in a way it treats as implausible; engine torque is usually cut as a brake-override measure.
Driver resting a foot on the brake while accelerating
Control module software needing an update
Brake light switch or pedal travel sensor misadjusted or sticking
Floor mat or object keeping a pedal partly pressed
Engine power drops while braking and accelerating together
Car does not respond to the accelerator for a moment
P229A: Fuel Pressure Regulator B Exceeded Control Limits - Pressure Too Low

P229A is the low-pressure control-limit check for fuel pressure regulator B. In GM's 2018 diesel table regulator B is the rail pressure regulator valve; while it governs the rail in closed loop, the ECM compares setpoint and measured pressure and flags a deficit beyond about 13 MPa, using the same 640-of-800-sample window and Type B rating as the metering un…
Rail pressure regulator valve leaking internally
Restricted low-pressure supply or clogged filter
P229B: Fuel Pressure Regulator B Exceeded Control Limits - Pressure Too High
P229B flags rail pressure that stays above target while fuel pressure regulator B should be holding it.
Rail pressure regulator valve sticking closed
Rail pressure sensor reading too high
Valve drive signal stuck on (wiring or module)
P229C: Fuel Pressure Regulator B Exceeded Learning Limits - Too Low
P229C means the learned correction for fuel pressure regulator B has reached its lower bound. No manufacturer documents this code publicly.
Rail pressure regulator valve characteristic drifted
Adaptation values not reset after a component replacement
Usually no noticeable change in driving
P229D: Fuel Pressure Regulator B Exceeded Learning Limits - Too High
P229D reports that the learned correction for fuel pressure regulator B has climbed to its upper bound, the opposite of P229C.
Rail pressure regulator valve worn or contaminated
Contaminated fuel reaching the high-pressure side
Occasional unstable rail pressure or rough idle
P229E: P229E is the basic electrical fault of the second NOx sensor on bank 1, the one behind the SCR catalyst that shows how much NOx survives conversion. Its attached control unit checks the probe lines and passes the result to the engine computer over CAN.
Internal failure of the outlet NOx probe or its control unit
Damaged lead between probe and sensor control unit (heat, chafing)
Water or corrosion in the sensor connector
Engine control software needing an update (Nissan Titan XD 2016, NTB16-048)
No valid downstream NOx value in live data
SCR warning; catalyst efficiency check cannot complete
P229F: P229F says the rear NOx sensor on bank 1 is electrically sound but its reading fails a plausibility test. Methods vary. GM's 6.6L LML waits for a burst of engine-out NOx and faults the sensor if its own value moves by less than 3 ppm (Type B); the 3.0L LZ0 watches the stability of the internal pump currents, failing above 0.5 percent unstable time.
Outlet NOx element drifted, slow or poisoned (e.g. sodium from cleaning fluids)
Poor DEF quality or faulty dosing that distorts downstream NOx
Harness or connector fault at the outlet sensor (Volvo/Mack P229F-64)
Engine or dosing software needing an update (several FCA, Hino, Mazda notices)
Often stored together with SCR efficiency code P20EE
Downstream NOx value implausible compared with the upstream sensor
P22A0: P22A0 reports that the rear NOx sensor on bank 1 sends a raw value below the smallest figure a healthy sensor can produce. Because the sensor talks over CAN, the test looks at the transmitted number rather than a wire voltage.
Outlet NOx element drifted low or internally faulty
Damaged lead between probe and sensor module
Malfunction indicator lamp on after two trips
Live data shows a negative downstream NOx value
SCR efficiency monitor does not complete
P22A1: P22A1 flags a raw value from the rear NOx sensor on bank 1 that is higher than anything plausibly left behind the SCR catalyst. GM's 6.6L LML uses 1,500 ppm, or 2,500 ppm in table 14OBDG10; the 3.0L LZ0 and the 2017 small diesels also use 2,500 ppm, Type B after two trips. VW's 2014 Touareg TDI uses 1,655 ppm or a lambda signal above 1.54.
Outlet NOx sensor reading high due to internal damage
DEF quality or dosing problem raising real tailpipe NOx
Implausibly high downstream NOx value in live data
SCR efficiency code P20EE stored alongside
P22A2: P22A2 describes a rear NOx sensor on bank 1 whose measuring circuit reports faults that come and go rather than staying present. Smart NOx sensors pass the state of that circuit (open wire, short or no error) to the engine computer over CAN, so brief, repeated fault reports fit this code. No manufacturer publicly documents a threshold for P22A2.
Loose or corroded terminals at the outlet NOx sensor connector
Harness along the exhaust damaged by heat or vibration
Sporadic internal fault in the sensor module
Malfunction indicator lamp that may go out and return
Downstream NOx value dropping out briefly
Code remains stored after the root fault is fixed
P22A3: NOx Sensor Heater Control Circuit/Open (Bank 1 Sensor 2)

The ceramic element of a NOx sensor measures only after its built-in heater has brought it to several hundred degrees. P22A3 reports a break on the heater control side of the rear sensor on bank 1, behind the SCR catalyst. GM's 6.6L LML sets it when the sensor reports an open heater over CAN longer than 10 s, Type A.
Heater element in the outlet NOx probe burnt through
Broken conductor between probe and sensor module
Malfunction indicator lamp on after one trip
Outlet NOx sensor never reports ready
P22A4: NOx Sensor Heater Control Circuit Low (Bank 1 Sensor 2)

P22A4 means the heater control line of the rear NOx sensor on bank 1 has a short to ground, so the sensor module can no longer drive the heater as commanded. GM documents it on the 3.0L LZ0 as a ground short on the heater control pin, judged once dew point is reached and sensor supply exceeds 9.9 V, 80 failures in 160 samples, Type B after two trips.
Heater element or probe lead shorted to ground inside the sensor
Probe lead insulation chafed against the exhaust or body
Malfunction indicator lamp on after two trips
Outlet NOx sensor stays not ready
P22A5: NOx Sensor Heater Control Circuit High (Bank 1 Sensor 2)

P22A5 is the opposite of P22A4: the heater control line of the rear NOx sensor on bank 1 has a short to supply voltage. The sensor module then cannot switch or regulate the heater, and the element risks running too hot or the module shuts the heater off to protect it.
Heater circuit inside the sensor shorted to supply voltage
Probe lead or connector touching a powered conductor
Malfunction indicator lamp on after two trips
Heater switched off, outlet NOx sensor not ready
P22A6: NOx Sensor Heater Sense Circuit (Bank 1 Sensor 2)

Besides the heater supply, a NOx sensor has a sense line through which its module measures the resistance of the heated element and so infers its temperature. P22A6 reports an electrical fault on that feedback line of the rear sensor on bank 1.
Open heater sense conductor inside the outlet NOx probe or its lead
Water or corrosion in the probe connector
Malfunction indicator lamp on after one trip
Outlet NOx sensor not ready, no downstream value
P22A7: NOx Sensor Heater Sense Circuit Range/Performance (Bank 1 Sensor 2)
P22A7 means the heater feedback of the rear NOx sensor on bank 1 shows a heater that does not reach or hold its target, although no open or short is found.
Aged heater or element in the outlet NOx probe
Water in the NOx sensor connectors (Ford 6.7L 2017-2020, TSB 20-2067)
Harness chafed on the EGR cooler with blown supply fuse (Ford 6.7L 2023)
Weak supply to the sensor module limiting heater power
Outlet NOx sensor becomes ready late or not at all
Often stored with U029E or other NOx sensor codes
P22A8: NOx Sensor Heater Sense Circuit Low (Bank 1 Sensor 2)

P22A8 means the heater sense line of the rear NOx sensor on bank 1 is shorted to ground; the sensor module uses that line to read the element temperature via its resistance. With that line pulled to ground, the module sees a temperature value it cannot trust and cannot regulate the heater properly.
Heater sense conductor shorted to ground inside the probe
Probe lead insulation damaged against exhaust or body
Water bridging pins in the probe connector
Malfunction indicator lamp on after two trips
SCR efficiency check does not run
P22A9: NOx Sensor Heater Sense Circuit High (Bank 1 Sensor 2)

P22A9 is the high-side twin of P22A8: the heater sense line of the rear NOx sensor on bank 1 has a short to supply voltage. The module then reads an element resistance that is far off and loses its temperature feedback, so it cannot hold the probe at working temperature.
Heater sense conductor shorted to supply inside the probe
Probe lead touching another powered conductor
Water bridging pins in the probe connector
Malfunction indicator lamp on after two trips
P22AA: NOx Sensor Heater Sense Circuit Intermittent (Bank 1 Sensor 2)

P22AA covers a heater sense line on the rear NOx sensor of bank 1 that fails only now and then. The module uses this line to read the element temperature and keep the heater on target; if the reading drops out or jumps for short moments, the temperature control briefly loses its reference and the sensor may fall out of its ready state.
Loose or corroded terminal in the probe connector
Lead near the exhaust cracked by heat or vibration
Intermittent internal contact fault in the probe
Malfunction indicator lamp that may come and go
Outlet NOx sensor intermittently not ready
P22AB: O2 Sensor Positive Current Control Circuit/Open (Bank 1 Sensor 2)

P22AB reports a break in the positive current control line of a wide-band probe mounted behind the catalyst or, on diesels, further down the aftertreatment on bank 1. On a Bosch-style five-wire probe this is the pump-current lead (IP/APE) through which the controller moves oxygen into or out of the pump cell.
Corroded, loose or poorly crimped terminal in the sensor or sensor-module connector
Pump-current wire broken or chafed through along the exhaust
Internal open circuit in the downstream wide-band sensor
Downstream oxygen reading frozen or missing in live data
Related catalyst or aftertreatment monitors stay incomplete
P22AC: O2 Sensor Positive Current Control Circuit Low (Bank 1 Sensor 2)

P22AC means the pump-current (positive current) line of the bank 1 downstream wide-band probe reads below its allowed window, usually because the wire touches ground or its insulation has worn through.
Pump-current wire chafed against the body or exhaust and shorted to ground
Internal short in the downstream wide-band sensor
Water or contamination bridging the connector pins
Downstream oxygen value pinned at an extreme in live data
Possible failed emissions inspection because monitors are not ready
P22AD: O2 Sensor Positive Current Control Circuit High (Bank 1 Sensor 2)

P22AD is the high-side fault on the positive current control line of the bank 1 downstream wide-band probe: the pump-current wire is pulled above its expected level, for example by contact with the heater feed or another supply wire. On Saab's 2010 9-5 the pump-current pins measure roughly 2.8 V at the plug, which gives a feel for the normal bias.
Pump-current wire shorted to the heater supply or another positive feed
Internal short between heater and pump cell in the sensor
Faulty sensor interface in the ECM or sensor module
Downstream oxygen reading implausibly high or fixed
Readiness monitors for catalyst or aftertreatment not completed
P22AE: O2 Sensor Reference Voltage Circuit/Open (Bank 1 Sensor 2)

P22AE points to an open reference voltage line of the bank 1 downstream wide-band probe, i.e. the lead of the Nernst (sensing) cell, called RE/UN by Bosch and VS by NTK. Through it the controller reads the cell voltage it regulates the pump current against, so a break leaves the oxygen value meaningless.
Corroded or wrongly plated terminals in the sensor or sensor-module connector
Broken Nernst-cell wire in the harness
Cracked or aged sensing cell with very high internal resistance
Downstream oxygen or lambda value invalid in live data
Other downstream sensor codes may be stored at the same time
P22AF: O2 Sensor Reference Voltage Performance (Bank 1 Sensor 2)

P22AF is a plausibility fault on the Nernst-cell (reference voltage) side of the bank 1 downstream wide-band probe: the wiring is intact, but the cell signal does not behave as the controller expects, for instance it cannot be held at its set point or drifts.
Aged downstream wide-band sensor with raised cell resistance
Soot, oil or coolant deposits on the sensing element
Weak heater or heater control that leaves the element too cold
High-resistance contact in the Nernst-cell circuit
Downstream oxygen reading sluggish or offset compared with the upstream sensor
Catalyst or aftertreatment monitor may report errors as a follow-up
P22B0: O2 Sensor Reference Voltage Circuit Low (Bank 1 Sensor 2)

P22B0 says the reference voltage (Nernst-cell) line of the bank 1 downstream wide-band probe sits below its permitted range. On a Bosch LSU the Nernst cell is a high-impedance source that tolerates at most about 250 microamps, so a chafed wire touching ground drags it down at once. No maker documents this exact code publicly.
Nernst-cell wire shorted to ground through damaged insulation
Internal short in the downstream wide-band sensor
Moisture in the connector creating a leakage path
Downstream oxygen value implausible or unavailable
P22B1: O2 Sensor Reference Voltage Circuit High (Bank 1 Sensor 2)

P22B1 is set when the reference voltage (Nernst-cell) line of the bank 1 downstream wide-band probe reads above its valid range. Because the cell delivers only a few hundred millivolts across about 300 ohms, any contact with the heater feed or another live wire overrides it. A cracked ceramic letting the heater circuit leak into the cell can do the same.
Nernst-cell wire shorted to the heater supply or another live wire
Cracked sensor ceramic leaking heater voltage into the cell
Faulty sensor interface in the ECM or sensor module
Downstream oxygen reading stuck at a limit
P22B2: O2 Sensor Negative Current Control Circuit/Open (Bank 1 Sensor 2)

P22B2 indicates an open negative current control line on the bank 1 downstream wide-band probe. This is the shared return of pump and sensing cell, the virtual ground (VM/IPN on Bosch, COM on NTK), which the controller holds at a mid-level bias of around 2.5 V.
Loose, corroded or pushed-back terminal on the return wire
Return (virtual ground) wire broken in the harness
Internal open circuit in the downstream wide-band sensor
Downstream oxygen reading frozen near a fixed value
P22B3: O2 Sensor Negative Current Control Circuit Low (Bank 1 Sensor 2)
P22B3 reports the negative current control line, i.e. the virtual ground of the bank 1 downstream wide-band probe, as too low.
Return wire shorted to chassis ground through chafed insulation
Internal short inside the wide-band sensor
Faulty bias supply in the ECM or sensor module
Downstream oxygen value implausible or pinned
P22B4: O2 Sensor Negative Current Control Circuit High (Bank 1 Sensor 2)

P22B4 is stored when the negative current control line (virtual ground) of the bank 1 downstream wide-band probe climbs above its intended bias. Because this return sits at a mid-level voltage rather than at chassis ground, a short to the heater feed or battery voltage is the classic trigger, sometimes via moisture or a heat-damaged connector.
Return wire shorted to heater supply or battery voltage
Heat-damaged or wet connector bridging pins
Internal heater-to-cell leakage in the sensor
Downstream oxygen reading erratic or at a limit
P22B5: O2 Sensor Pumping Current Trim Circuit/Open (Bank 1 Sensor 2)

P22B5 flags an open trim line on the bank 1 downstream wide-band probe. Bosch LSU probes carry a trimming resistor in the connector module, wired to pin 5 (RT/IA), that sets each sensor's individual characteristic; the controller reads it to scale the measured pump current. Lose that line and the oxygen value can still move, but with the wrong gain.
Corroded or loose trim-line terminal in the sensor connector
Trim wire broken between sensor connector and ECM or sensor module
Open trimming resistor in the sensor's connector module
Downstream oxygen reading disagrees with the upstream sensor during fuel cut-off
Follow-up aftertreatment or catalyst faults possible
P22B6: O2 Sensor Pumping Current Trim Circuit Low (Bank 1 Sensor 2)
By its name P22B6 is the low fault on the trim line of the bank 1 downstream wide-band probe, i.e. the lead to the calibration resistor in a Bosch-style sensor connector.
Faulty downstream NOx/oxygen sensor delivering an impossible oxygen value
Trim or signal wire shorted to ground in the harness
Negative oxygen percentage shown for the downstream sensor in live data
Possible additional boost or air-flow codes when charge air leaks
P22B7: O2 Sensor Pumping Current Trim Circuit High (Bank 1 Sensor 2)

P22B7 is, going by its title, the high fault on the trim circuit belonging to bank 1's downstream wide-band probe. In GM's diesel tables (2016, 2018 and 2025 group 04) the code is a ceiling test on the oxygen value of the second NOx sensor: the 2016 table flags readings above 24 %, which is more oxygen than fresh air holds, in 100 of 200 samples.
Faulty downstream NOx/oxygen sensor reporting excess oxygen
Chafed engine harness affecting the sensor lines (GM 3.0 LM2)
Trim or signal wire shorted to a voltage source
Downstream oxygen value above 21 % in live data
P22B8: O2 Sensor Positive Current Control Circuit/Open (Bank 2 Sensor 2)

P22B8 is the bank 2 version of an open positive current control line on a downstream wide-band probe: the pump-current wire (IP/APE on Bosch) of the sensor behind the catalyst or aftertreatment on the second cylinder bank has lost continuity. It only exists on engines with two exhaust banks and a wide-band probe after each catalyst, which is rare.
Loose or corroded pump-current terminal in the sensor connector
Pump-current wire broken near the hot exhaust
Internal open circuit in the bank 2 downstream sensor
Bank 2 downstream oxygen value missing or frozen
P22B9: O2 Sensor Positive Current Control Circuit Low (Bank 2 Sensor 2)
P22B9 means the positive current control (pump-current) line of the bank 2 downstream wide-band probe reads below its allowed band, most often because the lead has worn through and touches ground.
Pump-current wire chafed through and shorted to ground
Internal short in the bank 2 downstream sensor
Bank 2 downstream oxygen value at an extreme
P22BA: O2 Sensor Positive Current Control Circuit High (Bank 2 Sensor 2)

P22BA is set when the pump-current (positive current control) wire of the bank 2 downstream wide-band probe is held above its normal bias, typically through contact with the heater supply or a damaged connector letting battery voltage in. No maker documents this code publicly.
Pump-current wire shorted to the heater feed or battery voltage
Faulty sensor interface in the ECM
Bank 2 downstream oxygen value implausibly high
P22BB: O2 Sensor Reference Voltage Circuit/Open (Bank 2 Sensor 2)

P22BB reports an open reference voltage line on the bank 2 downstream wide-band probe, meaning the controller has lost the Nernst-cell signal (RE/UN on Bosch, VS on NTK) it needs to regulate pump current and compute oxygen content. No maker documents this code publicly.
Corroded or loose Nernst-cell terminal in the connector
Reference wire broken in the harness
Cracked sensing cell or internal open in the sensor
P22BC: O2 Sensor Reference Voltage Performance (Bank 2 Sensor 2)

P22BC concerns the plausibility of the Nernst-cell signal of the wide-band probe fitted after the bank 2 catalyst. The leads test fine, yet the cell voltage that the controller uses as its set point drifts, reacts slowly or cannot be held, so the computed oxygen value loses credibility.
Aged downstream wide-band sensor on bank 2 with raised Nernst-cell resistance
Oil, coolant or additive deposits on the sensing element
Heater output too low to keep the cell at working temperature
Contact resistance in the Nernst-cell terminal
Bank 2 downstream oxygen reading lags behind or is offset from the other sensors
Catalyst monitor for bank 2 does not complete
P22BD: O2 Sensor Reference Voltage Circuit Low (Bank 2 Sensor 2)

P22BD reports that the Nernst-cell (reference voltage) lead of the bank 2 post-catalyst wide-band probe sits below its valid window. Bosch allows the cell a load of only about 250 microamps, so a lead whose insulation touches ground, or moisture bridging the plug, pulls the signal down quickly. No maker documents this code publicly.
Nernst-cell lead chafed through and touching ground
Water or corrosion creating a leakage path in the connector
Sensing element cracked by water contact on the hot probe
Bank 2 downstream oxygen value missing or at the lower end in live data
P22BE: O2 Sensor Reference Voltage Circuit High (Bank 2 Sensor 2)
P22BE is stored when the reference voltage lead of the bank 2 downstream wide-band probe carries more voltage than a working Nernst cell can produce.
Nernst-cell lead shorted to the heater supply or another live wire
Cracked ceramic letting heater voltage into the sensing cell
Faulty sensor interface in the engine control module
Bank 2 downstream oxygen reading pinned at the upper limit
Heater codes for the same sensor may appear alongside
