P22BF: O2 Sensor Negative Current Control Circuit/Open (Bank 2 Sensor 2)

P22BF means the negative current control lead of the bank 2 post-catalyst wide-band probe has lost continuity. That lead is the common return of pump and Nernst cell (VM/IPN on Bosch, COM on NTK); without it neither cell has a reference and the signal freezes near its bias. No maker documents this code publicly.
Loose, corroded or pushed-out terminal on the return wire
Return wire broken by heat or vibration near the exhaust
Internal break in the sensor lead or element
Bank 2 downstream oxygen value frozen at a constant reading
Further codes for the same sensor may be stored together
P22C0: O2 Sensor Negative Current Control Circuit Low (Bank 2 Sensor 2)

P22C0 flags the negative current control line (virtual ground) of the bank 2 downstream wide-band probe as too low. The controller deliberately lifts this return above chassis ground, around 2.5 V on Saab's 2010 9-5, which lets the pump cell be driven both ways; once the wire touches ground, that bias and the lean side of the measuring range disappear.
Return wire chafed against body or exhaust bracket, shorted to ground
Internal short from the sensor return to the housing
Faulty bias supply in the engine control module
Bank 2 downstream reading cannot show lean values
Readiness for catalyst and oxygen sensor monitors stays open
P22C1: O2 Sensor Negative Current Control Circuit High (Bank 2 Sensor 2)

P22C1 covers a return line (virtual ground) reading too high on the bank 2 post-catalyst wide-band probe: the line is pushed above the mid-level bias the controller sets, which in practice means contact with the heater supply or battery voltage, often via a melted or wet connector.
Return wire touching the heater feed or another positive supply
Heat-damaged or wet connector bridging the return to a live pin
Internal leakage from heater to sensing cells inside the probe
Bank 2 downstream reading stuck high or implausible
P22C2: O2 Sensor Pumping Current Trim Circuit/Open (Bank 2 Sensor 2)

P22C2 reports an open trim line on the bank 2 downstream wide-band probe. Every probe ships with a calibration resistor in its plug (pin 5, RT/IA on a Bosch LSU) that corrects for spread in its diffusion gap; on Bosch probes it sits in parallel with the controller's sense resistor.
Corroded or loose trim-resistor terminal in the sensor plug
Trim resistor or its lead open inside the sensor connector
Trim wire broken between connector and control module
Bank 2 downstream lambda reads slightly off, most visibly away from lambda 1
P22C3: O2 Sensor Pumping Current Trim Circuit Low (Bank 2 Sensor 2)
P22C3 is the low fault on the trim (label resistor) circuit of the bank 2 post-catalyst wide-band probe.
Trim wire chafed and shorted to ground
High-resistance or corroded trim terminal raising the measured resistance
Defective label resistor in the sensor connector
Code typically appears right after engine start
P22C4: O2 Sensor Pumping Current Trim Circuit High (Bank 2 Sensor 2)

P22C4 is the high fault on the trim circuit of the bank 2 downstream wide-band probe. In Ford's key-on check of NTK label resistors, an estimated resistance that is too low means the line is shorted to power, which sets the trim-high code (P2631 for the bank 2 front probe); the stored resistor rank then stays in use.
Trim wire shorted to the heater supply or another positive feed
Heat- or water-damaged sensor plug bridging the trim pin
Internally shorted label resistor in the sensor connector
Bank 2 downstream lambda slightly off; heater codes may accompany it
P22C5: Turbocharger Compressor Outlet Valve Control Circuit/Open

P22C5 flags an open or broken drive circuit for the turbocharger compressor outlet valve. That valve sits in the charge-air path downstream of a compressor and decides whether this compressor feeds the engine, for example in register or two-stage charging or next to an electric auxiliary compressor.
Valve connector loose, unplugged or corroded
Broken wire in the valve harness, often near hot turbo parts
Open actuator coil inside the compressor outlet valve
Faulty output stage in the engine control module
Reduced power because boost is limited
Weak or delayed pull at the speed where the second boost path should join
P22C6: Turbocharger Compressor Outlet Valve Control Circuit Low

P22C6 is stored when the control line of the compressor outlet valve sits at a voltage that is too low for the current command, which normally points to a short to ground somewhere between the module and the valve.
Control wire chafed through and touching ground
Internal short in the valve actuator coil
Moisture or corrosion bridging pins in the connector
Damaged output stage in the engine control module
Check engine light on soon after starting
Boost limited, engine feels flat under load
Possible blown fuse if the short pulls heavy current
P22C7: Turbocharger Compressor Outlet Valve Control Circuit High

P22C7 means the drive line of the compressor outlet valve reads higher than the module expects, typically because the wire has a short to battery voltage or the coil draws excessive current while the driver is on. Modern output stages notice the overcurrent and switch off to protect themselves, so the valve then stops responding even though nothing is open.
Control wire shorted to a battery-voltage feed
Shorted turns in the valve coil causing overcurrent
Replacement valve with unsuitable coil resistance
Faulty output stage in the engine control module
Valve no longer switches, boost reduced
P22C8: Turbocharger Compressor Outlet Valve Stuck Open

P22C8 is a functional fault: the compressor outlet valve stays open at a moment when the control strategy expects it shut, so pressure or airflow in the boost path does not follow the command. Mercedes-Benz uses it on the M256.8 inline six with its 48-volt electric auxiliary compressor.

Oil film or deposits holding the valve flap open
Actuator or linkage no longer able to close the valve
P22C9: Turbocharger Compressor Outlet Valve Stuck Closed
P22C9 says the compressor outlet valve did not open when commanded, so air from the compressor it controls cannot reach the engine and the expected boost is missing.
Check valve in the charge-air pipe jammed shut (Mercedes M256)
Valve actuator, vacuum or pressure supply unable to open the valve
Valve seized by deposits or corrosion
Noticeable loss of power under load
Boost malfunction, possibly with underboost code
P22CA: Turbocharger Compressor Outlet Switching Valve Control Circuit/Open

P22CA reports an open drive circuit for the compressor outlet switching valve. In two-stage or register boost systems the outlet flap is often moved by vacuum or pressure, and this electrically driven switching valve decides when that actuating medium reaches it; Ford's two-stage patent notes such valves may be worked electrically or by vacuum.
Switching valve connector loose or corroded
Broken wire between module and switching valve
Open coil in the switching solenoid
Faulty output stage in the engine control module
Boost changeover no longer happens, power limited
Hesitation when accelerating through the switching speed
P22CB: Turbocharger Compressor Outlet Switching Valve Control Circuit Low
P22CB is set when the control line of the compressor outlet switching valve shows too little voltage for the present command, most often because the wire or the solenoid has a short to ground.
Control wire chafed and shorted to ground
Internal short in the switching solenoid
Water or corrosion in the solenoid connector
Boost path stuck in one mode, uneven power across the rev range
Reduced power at low or high engine speed
P22CC: Turbocharger Compressor Outlet Switching Valve Control Circuit High
P22CC indicates that the drive line of the compressor outlet switching valve carries more voltage or current than allowed, usually a short to a battery feed or a solenoid with shorted windings.
Control wire shorted to a battery-voltage feed
Shorted windings in the switching solenoid
Faulty output stage in the engine control module
Outlet flap no longer switches, power reduced
Fault returns as soon as the valve is commanded
P22CD: Turbocharger Compressor Outlet Switching Valve Stuck Open

P22CD is a plausibility fault: the engine control module commanded the compressor outlet switching valve shut, yet boost pressure, airflow or a position signal behave as if the switched path were still open.
Switching solenoid mechanically stuck in the open position
Leaking, cracked or swapped control hose to the flap actuator
Outlet flap or its actuator unable to close
Sluggish boost build-up at low engine speed
Hissing or whistling noise from the intake side
P22CE: Turbocharger Compressor Outlet Switching Valve Stuck Closed

P22CE is set when the compressor outlet switching valve was told to open but the boost system shows no sign that the switched path changed over. Nissan documents the code as TC Outlet Switching Valve Stuck Closed for the 2016 Titan XD with the Cummins 5.0 litre V8 diesel and its two-stage turbocharger.
Engine control software reacting wrongly in cold weather (Nissan Titan XD bulletin)
Collapsed, kinked or frozen control hose to the outlet flap actuator
Switching solenoid stuck in the closed position
Insufficient vacuum or pressure supply for the actuator
Check engine light on, mostly in cold weather
Hesitation when accelerating until the engine is warm
Weak pull in the speed range where the second stage should help
P22CF: Turbocharger Turbine Inlet Valve Control Circuit/Open

P22CF points to an open drive circuit of the turbocharger turbine inlet valve, the exhaust-side valve that either lets gas skip the small first-stage turbine of a series two-stage system or isolates a second turbine in a parallel-sequential layout.
Actuator connector loose, heat-damaged or corroded
Broken wire near the exhaust manifold or turbo
Open winding in the turbine valve actuator or its control solenoid
Faulty output stage in the engine control module
Reduced power, boost control in fallback mode
Turbo lag or a missing second-stage push
P22D0: Turbocharger Turbine Inlet Valve Control Circuit Low
P22D0 is logged when the drive circuit of the turbine inlet valve shows a voltage below the expected range, the classic sign of a short to ground in the wire or inside the actuator.
Heat-damaged wire rubbing through to ground
Internal short in the valve actuator or control solenoid
Damaged output stage in the engine control module
Power limited, boost too low or uneven
Code sets right after start without a test drive
P22D1: Turbocharger Turbine Inlet Valve Control Circuit High
P22D1 tells you the drive circuit of the turbine inlet valve reads too high, which usually means a short to battery voltage or an actuator that draws overcurrent.
Actuator wire shorted to a battery-voltage feed
Actuator winding shorted or mechanically jammed, drawing overcurrent
Faulty output stage in the engine control module
Reduced power, boost control in fallback mode
Fault comes back as soon as the valve is driven
P22D2: Turbocharger Turbine Inlet Valve Stuck Open

P22D2 means the turbine inlet valve stays open after the module asked it to close. In a series two-stage system, an open valve lets exhaust skip the small high-pressure turbine, so low-speed boost and response suffer.
Soot or corrosion seizing the valve shaft in the open position
Leaking or detached control line on a vacuum-operated actuator
Actuator or linkage unable to close the valve
Position sensor reporting open although the valve moved
Noticeable turbo lag at low engine speed
P22D3: Turbocharger Turbine Inlet Valve Stuck Closed

P22D3 is stored when the turbine inlet valve does not open on command. In a series two-stage layout all exhaust must then pass the small high-pressure stage even at high load, raising back-pressure and risking overboost or turbo overspeed, so the module caps power. In a parallel-sequential layout the second turbo never comes in.
Engine software setting the code falsely (Jeep Cherokee 2026 bulletin)
Valve seized closed by soot or corrosion
Actuator, linkage or vacuum supply unable to open the valve
Power capped at higher engine speed and load
P22D4: Turbocharger Turbine Inlet Valve Position Sensor Circuit
P22D4 is the general circuit fault of the sensor that reports how far the turbine inlet valve is open.
Loose, heat-damaged or corroded sensor connector
Damaged sensor wiring near the turbo
Failed position sensor, often integrated in the actuator
Reduced power, turbo valve held in a fallback position
P22D5: Turbocharger Turbine Inlet Valve Position Sensor Circuit Range/Performance

P22D5 is a plausibility fault of the turbine inlet valve position signal. The voltage stays inside its electrical limits, yet it does not match what the module expects, for instance the reading lags the commanded position, fails to reach the learned end stops or does not change when the valve is moved.
Valve or linkage sluggish from soot, so position lags the command
Position sensor drifting or misaligned on the actuator
End positions not relearned after actuator replacement
Jerky or delayed changeover between turbo stages
P22D6: Turbocharger Turbine Inlet Valve Position Sensor Circuit Low
P22D6 is set when the position sensor signal of the turbine inlet valve falls below its lowest valid voltage.
5-volt reference open or pulled down by another shorted sensor
Internal failure of the position sensor
Reduced power, valve in fallback position
Other sensor codes on the same reference circuit possible
P22D7: Turbocharger Turbine Inlet Valve Position Sensor Circuit High

P22D7 is logged when the position signal of the turbine inlet valve rises above its highest valid voltage. A reading pinned near the reference level usually comes from an open sensor ground, a signal wire touching the 5-volt reference or battery voltage, or a failed sensor element, not from the valve itself.
Signal wire shorted to the 5-volt reference or battery voltage
Internal failure of the position sensor
Reduced power, valve held in fallback position
P22D8: Turbocharger Turbine Inlet Valve Position Sensor Circuit Intermittent/Erratic

P22D8 covers short dropouts or jumps in the position signal of the turbine inlet valve: the value leaps faster than the valve could physically move, or briefly disappears and returns. Such patterns typically come from a connector with fretting contacts, a wire breaking inside its insulation near the vibrating, hot turbo, or a sensor that fails under heat.
Loose or fretting contacts in the sensor connector
Wire breaking intermittently from heat and vibration
Position sensor dropping out when hot
Check engine light on, sometimes only now and then
Brief loss of power on rough roads
P22D9: Cylinder 1 Alternative Fuel Injector Control Circuit/Open

P22D9 reports a broken control circuit at the gas injector of cylinder 1, the solenoid that meters CNG or LPG into the intake port whenever a bi-fuel or dedicated gas engine runs on the alternative fuel. The driver stage notices the break because no current flows when it switches on, or because the expected off-state voltage on its pin is missing.
Open solenoid winding in the cylinder 1 gas injector
Loose, corroded or unplugged connector at the gas injector
Broken wire or failed splice in the gas system harness
Defective driver stage in the gas or engine control module
Engine changes back to gasoline or refuses to switch to gas
Misfire on cylinder 1 in gas mode (dedicated engines)
P22DA: Cylinder 1 Alternative Fuel Injector Control Circuit Low

P22DA means the cylinder 1 gas injector control wire reads too low. TransEco Energy's DTC list for its CNG control module (AFCM v1.4) blames either a grounded wire or an open line, turns on the MIL in bi-fuel installations and reacts the same way it would to the matching gasoline injector fault. Ford's 2014 OBD code list carries P22DA as a MIL code as well.
Control wire of the cylinder 1 gas injector chafed through to ground
Interrupted control wire or connector (logged as Low by some modules)
Water or corrosion in the injector connector
Faulty output stage in the gas control module
Very rough running on cylinder 1 in gas mode, possibly rich misfire
Gas system switches back to gasoline
P22DB: Cylinder 1 Alternative Fuel Injector Control Circuit High

P22DB flags a control circuit of the cylinder 1 gas injector that stays too high. TransEco Energy's AFCM fault list traces it to a short to battery voltage, lights the MIL for bi-fuel use and applies the same fallback as for the gasoline injector fault; Ford's 2014 code list also marks P22DB for the MIL.
Control wire shorted to battery or injector supply voltage
Shorted turns in the cylinder 1 gas injector coil
Output stage of the gas control module damaged
Lean misfire on cylinder 1 in gas mode, often with P0301
P22DC: Cylinder 1 Alternative Fuel Injector Control Circuit Range/Performance

P22DC is meant for a cylinder 1 gas injector whose circuit is electrically intact but whose response looks wrong, such as a current trace that never reaches its peak or does not fall back to the hold level, or a coil whose resistance has drifted.
Cylinder 1 gas injector sticking from oil residue or debris in the gas
Injector coil resistance outside its specification
Weak supply voltage to the injector bank
Injector of the wrong type or impedance installed
Uneven running in gas mode, misfire counts on cylinder 1
Higher gas consumption or switch back to gasoline
P22DD: Cylinder 2 Alternative Fuel Injector Control Circuit/Open

P22DD signals an interruption in the circuit of the cylinder 2 gas injector. On many systems that circuit is not driven by the engine computer: Ford's 2003 bi-fuel CNG trucks used a separate alternative fuel control module holding drivers for both injector sets, with heavier stages for the gas injectors because they draw more current.
Burnt-out or open coil in the cylinder 2 gas injector
Connector at the cylinder 2 injector loose or pulled off
Wire break between gas control module and injector
Failed injector driver in the separate gas control module
Gas mode not available or ends shortly after switching
Misfire on cylinder 2 when running on gas
P22DE: Cylinder 2 Alternative Fuel Injector Control Circuit Low

P22DE stands for a control line of the cylinder 2 gas injector whose voltage is too low. TransEco Energy's AFCM fault table blames a grounded or interrupted wire and turns on the MIL for bi-fuel vehicles; Ford's 2014 OBD code list includes P22DE as a MIL code too.
Cylinder 2 injector control wire grounded on engine or body
Open wire or pin, reported as Low by modules like the TransEco AFCM
Shorted output transistor in the gas control module
Rich misfire or fouled spark plug on cylinder 2 in gas mode
Gas operation interrupted, engine runs on gasoline
P22DF: Cylinder 2 Alternative Fuel Injector Control Circuit High

P22DF indicates that the control circuit of the cylinder 2 gas injector reads high, which TransEco Energy's AFCM table attributes to a short to power; MIL on for bi-fuel use. Ford's 2014 code list likewise flags P22DF for the MIL.
Cylinder 2 control wire touching a live supply wire
Internal short in the cylinder 2 gas injector coil
Driver protection in the control module tripping due to a fault
P22E0: Cylinder 2 Alternative Fuel Injector Control Circuit Range/Performance
P22E0 covers a cylinder 2 gas injector circuit that passes the plain open and short checks yet responds outside its expected window.
Cylinder 2 gas injector opening or closing too slowly
Coil resistance of the injector out of tolerance
Driver stage or supply unable to provide the required current
Uneven idle on gas, cylinder 2 misfire counts
Fuel trim drifts in gas mode
P22E1: Cylinder 3 Alternative Fuel Injector Control Circuit/Open

P22E1 marks an open control circuit at the cylinder 3 gas injector. Circuit continuity checks of this kind run all the time: California's OBD rule defines continuous monitoring as always enabled with at least two samples per second, so a break is caught within moments once the gas system is in use. No maker documents P22E1 openly.
Cylinder 3 injector connector left off or not latched after service
Open coil in the cylinder 3 gas injector
Wire broken where the harness runs along the gas rail
Gas mode switches off soon after changeover
Cylinder 3 misfire on dedicated gas engines
P22E2: Cylinder 3 Alternative Fuel Injector Control Circuit Low

P22E2 is logged when the control circuit of the cylinder 3 gas injector reads low. In TransEco Energy's AFCM table the cause column says shorted to ground or open, the MIL comes on in bi-fuel systems and the reaction copies that for a gasoline injector fault. Ford's 2014 code list lists P22E2 as a MIL code.
Cylinder 3 control wire rubbed through against a bracket or the manifold
Broken wire or terminal in the cylinder 3 injector circuit
Shorted driver output in the gas control module
Cylinder 3 runs rich or misfires in gas mode
Smell of unburnt gas at the exhaust
P22E3: Cylinder 3 Alternative Fuel Injector Control Circuit High

P22E3 tells that the cylinder 3 gas injector circuit is held high. TransEco Energy's AFCM list names a short to power, MIL on for bi-fuel use, and Ford's 2014 code list also ties P22E3 to the MIL. With the line stuck at supply voltage the injector cannot be switched on, so cylinder 3 gets no gas and misfires lean.
Cylinder 3 control wire shorted to a 12 V feed
Shorted turns in the cylinder 3 gas injector
Faulty output of the injector control module
Lean misfire on cylinder 3 in gas mode, often with P0303
Noticeable loss of power on gas
P22E4: Cylinder 3 Alternative Fuel Injector Control Circuit Range/Performance

P22E4 points to a cylinder 3 gas injector whose circuit works but whose electrical behaviour does not match the command. Peak-and-hold gas injectors first draw a high opening current and then a lower holding current; Ford's patent US 8,161,946 treats an injector that stays at peak or ignores commands as degraded and reports this back to the engine computer.
Armature of the cylinder 3 gas injector gummed up by oil or debris
Injector coil aged or overheated, resistance out of range
Weak driver output or poor supply ground
P22E5: Cylinder 4 Alternative Fuel Injector Control Circuit/Open
P22E5 is the open-circuit code for the cylinder 4 gas injector; on four-cylinder gas engines it is the last injector of the set. The driver sees no current when it switches the injector on.
Open coil in the cylinder 4 gas injector
Heat-damaged or brittle connector near the exhaust side
Broken wire in the cylinder 4 injector circuit
Gas mode unavailable, car runs on gasoline only
Cylinder 4 dead on a dedicated gas engine
P22E6: Cylinder 4 Alternative Fuel Injector Control Circuit Low

P22E6 reports a low signal on the cylinder 4 gas injector control wire. TransEco Energy's AFCM table gives short to ground or open as the cause and turns the MIL on in bi-fuel installations, keeping the same failure response as for gasoline; Ford's 2014 code list carries P22E6 with the MIL as well.
Cylinder 4 control wire grounded through damaged insulation
Separated terminal or broken wire in the cylinder 4 circuit
Damaged driver output in the gas control module
Cylinder 4 runs rich or cuts out on gas
Engine stays on or returns to gasoline
P22E7: Cylinder 4 Alternative Fuel Injector Control Circuit High

P22E7 says the control circuit of the cylinder 4 gas injector reads high. TransEco Energy's fault table blames a short to power and lights the MIL for bi-fuel use; Ford's 2014 code list also marks P22E7 as a MIL code. The injector then cannot open and cylinder 4 misfires lean whenever gas is selected.
Cylinder 4 control wire in contact with a 12 V circuit
Cylinder 4 injector coil with internal short
Output stage of the controlling module defective
Cylinder 4 misfire only after the switch to gas
P22E8: Cylinder 4 Alternative Fuel Injector Control Circuit Range/Performance

P22E8 applies when the cylinder 4 gas injector circuit is complete but the measured response lies outside the plausible range, for instance an opening current that rises too slowly or a hold phase that never settles. No vehicle maker documents P22E8 openly; the published lists from TransEco and Ford end at Low/High.
Cylinder 4 injector fouled by oil or liquids, often from a neglected gas filter
Aged injector coil with changed resistance
Low system voltage during cranking or at idle
Rough idle on gas, smooth on gasoline
Gas mode ends after a while
P22E9: Cylinder 5 Alternative Fuel Injector Control Circuit/Open

P22E9 is the open-circuit code for the cylinder 5 gas injector and can only appear on engines with five or more cylinders, such as the V6 of GM's bi-fuel Impala or the 6.0-litre V8 of its bi-fuel Silverado and Sierra. The driver detects the break because current is missing when the injector is commanded on.
Open coil in the cylinder 5 gas injector
Loose connector in the harness branch for this bank
Open driver output in the gas or injector control module
Engine returns to gasoline after switching to gas
Cylinder 5 misfire if gas operation continues
P22EA: Cylinder 5 Alternative Fuel Injector Control Circuit Low
P22EA stands for a low voltage on the cylinder 5 gas injector control wire, a code limited to engines with at least five cylinders.
Cylinder 5 control wire shorted to ground along the gas rail
Interrupted wire or terminal, flagged as Low by some modules
Shorted output stage in the gas control module
Cylinder 5 runs rich or misfires in gas mode
P22EB: Cylinder 5 Alternative Fuel Injector Control Circuit High

P22EB reports that the cylinder 5 gas injector control circuit is too high, which TransEco Energy's AFCM list attributes to a short to power with the MIL on for bi-fuel use; Ford's 2014 code list likewise carries P22EB for the MIL. The injector stays closed, so cylinder 5 burns no gas and misfires lean, usually logged together with P0305.
Cylinder 5 control wire chafed against a supply wire
Overheated cylinder 5 gas injector with shorted turns
Overloaded driver output in the gas control module
Lean misfire on cylinder 5 in gas mode, often with P0305
P22EC: Cylinder 5 Alternative Fuel Injector Control Circuit Range/Performance
P22EC is the plausibility code for the cylinder 5 gas injector circuit on engines with five or more cylinders: wiring and coil pass the basic checks, but the injector does not respond as commanded.
Sticking armature in the cylinder 5 gas injector
Driver or supply not delivering the full opening current
Rough cylinder 5 on gas or return to gasoline
Fuel trim on the affected bank drifts in gas mode
P22ED: Cylinder 6 Alternative Fuel Injector Control Circuit/Open

P22ED marks an open control circuit at the cylinder 6 gas injector, the last injector on six-cylinder engines like the 3.6-litre V6 of GM's 2015 bi-fuel Impala, where the ECM drives the CNG injectors directly. Current is missing when the injector should open, so the module records the break.
Open coil in the cylinder 6 gas injector
Loose or corroded connector at cylinder 6
Broken wire between control module and cylinder 6 injector
Vehicle runs on gasoline although gas is selected
Cylinder 6 misfire on dedicated gas engines
P22EE: Cylinder 6 Alternative Fuel Injector Control Circuit Low

On engines that burn natural gas or propane through their own gas injectors, the control module watches the drive line of each gas valve. This code means the line to the cylinder 6 gas injector sits at a lower voltage than the switching state allows.
Control wire of the cylinder 6 gas injector chafed through to ground
Broken wire or loose plug at the gas injector (counted as Low by this system)
Faulty output stage in the PCM or gas control module
Rough running or misfire on cylinder 6 in gas mode
System switches to gasoline or will not enter gas mode
P22EF: Cylinder 6 Alternative Fuel Injector Control Circuit High
The counterpart to P22EE: the drive line of the cylinder 6 gas injector stays near battery voltage even when the output stage should pull it down.
Control wire of the cylinder 6 gas injector touching a battery-voltage feed
Gas harness spliced or pinned incorrectly during the conversion
Moisture bridging supply and control pins in the injector plug
Output stage in the control module no longer switches
Lean misfire on cylinder 6 in gas mode
P22F0: Cylinder 6 Alternative Fuel Injector Control Circuit Range/Performance

Unlike the pure wiring faults P22EE/P22EF, this code is meant for a cylinder 6 gas injector circuit that is electrically intact but behaves implausibly, for example a current rise or switching response that does not fit the command.
Cylinder 6 gas valve sticking from oil or deposits carried in the gas
Coil resistance drifted out of the expected window
Corroded plug causing a slow current rise
Uneven idle or hesitation in gas mode
Cylinder 6 misfire count rising on gas only
P22F1: Cylinder 7 Alternative Fuel Injector Control Circuit/Open
A general circuit or open-wire code for the gas injector of cylinder 7, which only exists on V8 and larger engines. No manufacturer documents this code publicly.
Plug of the cylinder 7 gas injector loose or left off after service
Broken control or supply wire in the gas harness
Misfire on cylinder 7 in gas mode
Fallback to gasoline on bi-fuel vehicles
P22F2: Cylinder 7 Alternative Fuel Injector Control Circuit Low

Low voltage on the control line of the cylinder 7 gas injector. The code appears in Ford's 2014 code list with MIL and in the installer table of the Altech-Eco/TransEco CNG kits, which on Ford's V8 (F-150 5.0) and V10 (Super Duty 6.8) engines use the PCM to drive gas valves for all cylinders; cylinders 9 and 10 of the V10 get manufacturer codes there.
Cylinder 7 injector control wire grounded on the engine or bracket
Open wire or poor pin contact (reported as Low)
Cylinder 7 misfire or rich running on gas
P22F3: Cylinder 7 Alternative Fuel Injector Control Circuit High

Here the cylinder 7 gas valve drive line is held high, so the output stage cannot switch the valve on. Ford's 2014 list carries P22F3 with MIL; the Altech-Eco/TransEco table for its Ford V8 and V10 CNG systems names a short to power as cause, applies MIL only to bi-fuel trucks and notes that gas module version 1.4 cannot detect this fault itself.
Cylinder 7 control wire shorted to a switched or battery feed
Wiring error at the splice between factory and gas harness
Output stage in the control module open
Lean misfire on cylinder 7 in gas mode
Gas operation dropped in favour of gasoline
P22F4: Cylinder 7 Alternative Fuel Injector Control Circuit Range/Performance

Plausibility code for the cylinder 7 gas injector circuit: wiring passes the open/short checks, yet the electrical response of the valve does not match what the driver expects. No manufacturer documents this code publicly.
Cylinder 7 gas valve slow or sticking from oil residue
Injector coil resistance shifted with heat or age
Weak supply voltage to the gas injector bank
P22F5: Cylinder 8 Alternative Fuel Injector Control Circuit/Open

Open-circuit code for the gas injector of cylinder 8. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. In the two manufacturer-side lists found, the Ford overview from 2014 and TransEco's sheet for gas-converted Ford V8 and V10 trucks, cylinder 8 has only P22F6 and P22F7, and the TransEco table explicitly assigns an open line to P22F6.
Cylinder 8 injector plug corroded or disconnected
Wire fatigued at a flex point of the gas harness
Coil of the cylinder 8 gas valve open
Cylinder 8 misfire whenever the engine runs on gas
Change to gasoline on bi-fuel vehicles
P22F6: Cylinder 8 Alternative Fuel Injector Control Circuit Low

Cylinder 8 is the last cylinder with a generic gas injector code; beyond it the Altech-Eco/TransEco table for the Ford 6.8 V10 switches to manufacturer codes. P22F6 reports a control line for the cylinder 8 valve that is too low.
Cylinder 8 control wire grounded through damaged insulation
Open wire or unplugged injector (reported as Low)
Misfire on cylinder 8 only in gas mode
P22F7: Cylinder 8 Alternative Fuel Injector Control Circuit High

P22F7 means the drive line of the cylinder 8 gas injector cannot be pulled down and stays near supply voltage. Ford lists it with MIL in the 2014 code list; in the conversion data from Altech-Eco/TransEco the cause given is a short to power, keeps the MIL off on dedicated CNG engines and marks the fault as not detectable by gas module version 1.4.
Cylinder 8 control wire pinched against a supply line
Supply and control pins swapped in the gas harness
Damaged output stage in the control module
Cylinder 8 lean misfire in gas mode
P22F8: Cylinder 8 Alternative Fuel Injector Control Circuit Range/Performance

Functional code for the cylinder 8 gas injector circuit, meant for cases where wiring is intact but the valve reacts outside the expected window. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. Both at Ford (2014 list) and at Altech-Eco/TransEco the series stops at P22F6/P22F7 for this cylinder.
Cylinder 8 gas valve opening late or partly due to contamination
Coil degraded by heat at the rear of the engine
Contact resistance in the injector plug
Hesitation under load in gas mode
P22F9: NOx Sensor Performance - Slow Response Low to High (Bank 1 Sensor 1)

P22F9 concerns the NOx sensor ahead of the SCR catalyst on bank 1 and how fast it follows a rise in engine-out NOx. After a load step the control module times the sensor signal and compares it with the curve of its own NOx model.
Front NOx sensor aged or contaminated (oil ash, silicone, cleaning agents), reacting slowly
ECM calibration error, fixed by reprogramming (GM 24-NA-058 for the 2024 L5P)
Exhaust leak ahead of the sensor diluting the gas sample
Soot or deposits covering the protective cap of the sensor
Check engine light on after two drives
Usually no noticeable change in driving
P22FA: NOx Sensor Performance - Slow Response High to Low (Bank 1 Sensor 1)
P22FA mirrors P22F9 for the falling edge: when engine-out NOx drops, mostly as the driver lifts off into overrun, the front NOx sensor on bank 1 takes too long to come down.
Engine software anomaly, cured by reprogramming (GM PI1485, FCA 18-018-15, 18-008-21)
Front NOx sensor aged or contaminated, signal decays slowly
Exhaust leak near the sensor disturbing the measurement
Warning about poor DEF quality on some GM diesels
Usually no change in engine behaviour
P22FB: NOx Sensor Performance - Sensing Element (Bank 1 Sensor 1)

P22FB questions whether the measuring element of the front NOx sensor on bank 1 still reads true. GM's 2025 diesel tables hold its filtered value against modelled engine-out NOx and fail it below minus 36 % or above plus 77 % (version A) or outside minus 51 to plus 100 % (version B), as a Type A fault with the MIL in one trip.
Measuring cell of the front NOx sensor drifted or damaged (Volvo/Mack P22FB-92)
ECM or DEF control unit software, fixed by reprogramming (Isuzu SB22-L-001, GM 23-NA-159, Mazda 01-004-22)
Real engine-out NOx differs from the model, e.g. through an EGR fault (P0402)
Exhaust leak ahead of the sensor
Check engine light on, on GM's 2025 diesels already after one drive
Rough idle or surging if an EGR fault is behind it
P22FC: NOx Sensor Performance - Slow Response Low to High (Bank 1 Sensor 2)

P22FC is reserved for the rear NOx sensor on bank 1, behind the SCR catalyst, when its signal climbs too slowly after NOx at that point increases. No manufacturer documents this code publicly, and the NHTSA bulletin index has no entry for it.
Rear NOx sensor aged or contaminated by urea deposits, oil ash or cleaning agents
Exhaust leak between SCR catalyst and sensor
Calibration of the test itself, check for software updates
P22FD: NOx Sensor Performance - Slow Response High to Low (Bank 1 Sensor 2)

P22FD stands for the falling edge at the rear NOx sensor on bank 1: after a NOx peak downstream of the SCR catalyst, the signal decays more slowly than permitted. No manufacturer documents this code publicly, and no bulletin in the NHTSA index names it.
Rear NOx sensor aged or coated, signal falls too slowly
Urea crystals around the sensor tip after dosing faults
Exhaust leak close to the outlet sensor
SCR efficiency code may appear as well
P22FE: NOx Sensor Performance - Sensing Element (Bank 1 Sensor 2)

P22FE tests the measuring cells of the rear NOx sensor on bank 1. On GM diesels the check runs after the engine is switched off: the sensor alters its internal pump currents so that about 1000 ppm of oxygen sits in the second cavity, and the result is compared with a reference written into its memory at the supplier. Blocked cavities lower NOx sensitivity.
Measuring cavities of the rear NOx sensor clogged or cells drifted
ECM or DEF control unit software (GM PIP5615A, 23-NA-193, Isuzu SB22-L-001)
Contamination by urea residue, oil ash or additive cleaners
Code sets after shutdown, so it often appears at the next start
P22FF: SCR NOx Catalyst Inlet Temperature Too Low
Diesel engines raise exhaust temperature on purpose so the SCR catalyst can reduce NOx; this code reports that the gas entering the SCR stays too cold despite that.
Long idling or light-load operation keeps exhaust cold
Exhaust leak ahead of the SCR cools the gas or skews the reading
Exhaust temperature sensor reading too low while still in range
Engine software with overly strict monitor (update available on some makes)
Reduced NOx conversion, possible further SCR efficiency codes
P2300: Ignition Coil A Primary Control Circuit Low
P2300 reports that the control line to ignition coil A is pulled towards ground. GM, Saab and VW assign coil A to cylinder 1.
Coil A (cylinder 1) with an internal fault pulling the control input to ground
Control wire of coil A chafed through and touching engine ground
Water or corrosion in the coil A connector
Engine module driver or software fault (FCA 2023: PCM reflash)
Misfire and rough running on cylinder 1
Fuel to cylinder 1 cut off by the engine module
P2301: Ignition Coil A Primary Control Circuit High
P2301 is the mirror image of P2300: the control line of coil A, i.e. cylinder 1, carries voltage at a moment when the engine module is trying to pull it low.
Coil A with an internal short feeding supply voltage onto the control input
Control wire of coil A rubbing against a 12 V line in the harness
Broken control line or loose pin (counts as P2301 on Saab Trionic 8)
Faulty output stage in the engine module
Cylinder 1 misfires, engine shakes at idle
Jerking and loss of power under load
P2302: P2302 looks at the high-voltage side of coil A – the secondary winding, the boot and the spark plug of cylinder 1 – rather than at the control line covered by P2300 and P2301. Only a few makers use it.
Worn or fouled spark plug in cylinder 1, gap too wide
Cracked coil boot letting the spark jump to the cylinder head
Secondary winding of coil A breaking down
Ion-sense evaluation in the PCM (FCA 18-069-16: PCM replaced)
Misfire on cylinder 1, often together with P0301
P2303: Ignition Coil B Primary Control Circuit Low
P2303 tells you that the trigger wire of coil B – cylinder 2 in GM, Saab and VW documentation – has found a path to ground.
Coil B (cylinder 2) faulty, pulling the control line low
Insulation damage on the coil B control wire touching ground
PCM software assigning the code to the wrong cylinder (Ford Bronco, FCA 2.0 turbo)
Engine runs on fewer cylinders, less power
P2304: Ignition Coil B Primary Control Circuit High
P2304 means the control line of coil B (cylinder 2) is held at too high a voltage – usually a short to a supply line, sometimes an internal coil fault.
Coil B control wire shorted to a voltage-carrying line
Internal fault in coil B or its built-in driver
Engine module fault (Polaris Slingshot 2026: ECM replaced)
Interrupted control line on systems that report it here (Saab Trionic 8)
P2305: P2305 is about coil B's output side: the secondary winding, the connection to the plug and the spark plug of cylinder 2. Where a maker uses it, the module does not just watch whether the coil was switched, but whether a usable spark happened.
Spark plug of cylinder 2 worn, oily or with the wrong gap
Coil B boot cracked or damp, spark leaking away
Faulty ion-current evaluation in the PCM
Misfire on cylinder 2, sometimes only under load
P2306: Ignition Coil C Primary Control Circuit Low
With P2306 the engine module has seen the output for coil C, cylinder 3 at GM, Saab and VW, dragged down to ground.
Driver electronics inside coil C defective
Coil C control wire grounded through chafing or a pinched harness
Corroded or bent pins at the coil C connector
P2307: Ignition Coil C Primary Control Circuit High

P2307 sets when the coil C control line, cylinder 3 in most layouts, is shorted to a voltage source. On GM's 3.6-litre LLT V6 (2008) the check is a continuity test against voltage that runs below 6,000 rpm with the battery between 9.99 and 18.1 V and needs 4 s at a stretch or 50 s in total.
Coil C control wire touching a battery-voltage line
Coil C with an internal short to its supply
Code filed against the wrong cylinder by PCM software (Ford Bronco SSM 52342)
Broken control wire on systems reporting opens here (Saab Trionic 8)
P2308: P2308 points at the high-voltage path of coil C, normally cylinder 3: winding, boot and plug. The code is uncommon. FCA's 3.6 V6 in the 2015–2016 Caravan and Town & Country calls it coil 3 secondary circuit with insufficient ionization.
Spark plug of cylinder 3 worn or fouled
Boot of coil C leaking high voltage
FCA vans built 27 July–11 September 2015: PCM fault (bulletin 18-069-16)
Misfire on cylinder 3 with P0303 stored
P2309: Ignition Coil D Primary Control Circuit Low
P2309 stands for a grounded control lead to coil D – cylinder 4, which on a four-cylinder engine is the last coil in the row.
PCM software fault setting several coil low codes (FCA 2.0 turbo 2023)
Damaged harness section carrying several coil lines
Poor contact or moisture at the coil D connector
P230A: Cylinder 1 Air-Fuel Ratio Imbalance - Adjustment At Limit During Balance

P230A belongs to a second series of cylinder imbalance codes. P219C reports that cylinder 1 runs a mixture unlike the others; P230A goes a step further and says the balancing function has already moved the fuel correction for cylinder 1 to its end stop without evening it out.
Injector of cylinder 1 delivering too much or too little (deposits, wear)
Air leak at the intake port or injector seal of cylinder 1
Valve of cylinder 1 not sealing (worn seat or guide), low compression
Poor contact at the connector of injector 1
Rough idle, possibly misfire on cylinder 1
Higher fuel consumption or exhaust smell
P230B: Cylinder 2 Air-Fuel Ratio Imbalance - Adjustment At Limit During Balance

P230B singles out cylinder 2: its individual fuel correction has reached the limit during cylinder balancing and the imbalance remains. Audi is one of the few makers whose use of the code is on record.
Injector of cylinder 2 delivering too much or too little (deposits, wear)
Air leak at the intake port or injector seal of cylinder 2
Valve of cylinder 2 not sealing (worn seat or guide), low compression
Calibration error in the cylinder assignment (Audi 2.0 TFSI Gen 3, bulletin 2060348)
Rough idle, possibly misfire on cylinder 2
Higher fuel consumption or exhaust smell
P230C: Cylinder 3 Air-Fuel Ratio Imbalance - Adjustment At Limit During Balance

P230C is the balance-limit code for cylinder 3. On three-cylinder engines this is the last cylinder of the row; on fours and larger engines it sits further inside. The engine control trims the fuel of each cylinder separately to even out mixture differences, and P230C means the trim for cylinder 3 is used up.
Injector of cylinder 3 delivering too much or too little (deposits, wear)
Air leak at the intake port or injector seal of cylinder 3
Valve of cylinder 3 not sealing (worn seat or guide), low compression
Poor contact at the connector of injector 3
Rough idle, possibly misfire on cylinder 3
Higher fuel consumption or exhaust smell
P230D: Cylinder 4 Air-Fuel Ratio Imbalance - Adjustment At Limit During Balance
P230D flags cylinder 4, so the engine needs at least four cylinders. The balancing function has run the individual fuel trim for that cylinder to its limit and the mixture still deviates.
Injector of cylinder 4 delivering too much or too little (deposits, wear)
Air leak at the intake port or injector seal of cylinder 4
Valve of cylinder 4 not sealing (worn seat or guide), low compression
Poor contact at the connector of injector 4
Rough idle, possibly misfire on cylinder 4
Higher fuel consumption or exhaust smell
P230E: Cylinder 5 Air-Fuel Ratio Imbalance - Adjustment At Limit During Balance
P230E concerns cylinder 5 and is genuine only on engines with five or more cylinders, such as inline fives, sixes and V8s. The balancing logic has exhausted the individual fuel trim for cylinder 5.
Injector of cylinder 5 delivering too much or too little (deposits, wear)
Air leak at the intake port or injector seal of cylinder 5
Valve of cylinder 5 not sealing (worn seat or guide), low compression
Calibration error in the cylinder assignment (Audi 2.0 TFSI Gen 3, bulletin 2060348)
Rough idle, possibly misfire on cylinder 5
Higher fuel consumption or exhaust smell
P230F: Cylinder 6 Air-Fuel Ratio Imbalance - Adjustment At Limit During Balance

P230F is the balance-limit code for cylinder 6 and can only appear on engines with six or more cylinders, inline sixes, V6 units and larger. On a V6, cylinder 6 shares its bank and front oxygen sensor with two others, so its individual trim has to be estimated from that bank signal or from crankshaft speed.
Injector of cylinder 6 delivering too much or too little (deposits, wear)
Air leak at the intake port or injector seal of cylinder 6
Valve of cylinder 6 not sealing (worn seat or guide), low compression
Poor contact at the connector of injector 6
Rough idle, possibly misfire on cylinder 6
Higher fuel consumption or exhaust smell
P2310: Ignition Coil D Primary Control Circuit High

P2310 sets when the coil D control line, belonging to cylinder 4, carries voltage while the engine module tries to switch it to ground. Saab's Trionic 8 (9-3, 2003) uses a 2 V limit held for over 1 s and evaluates cylinder 4 together with cylinder 2 for its ion-based combustion signal; the injector of the affected cylinder is shut off.
Coil D control wire shorted to a voltage source
Interrupted line reported as high on Saab Trionic 8
Defective driver in the engine module
P2311: P2311 concerns the secondary side of coil D, usually cylinder 4. The secondary winding has thousands of turns of fine wire and delivers roughly 15–40 kV, so insulation that is merely tired can let the spark escape to ground instead of crossing the plug gap.
Aged insulation in coil D or its boot letting the spark leak to ground
Spark plug of cylinder 4 worn, gap grown
Oil in the plug well softening the boot
Misfire on cylinder 4, worse in damp weather or under load
P2312: Ignition Coil E Primary Control Circuit Low
P2312 is the first code of this series that only engines with five or more cylinders can set: it flags the control lead of coil E, i.e. cylinder 5, as shorted to ground.
Short in the coil supply shared by one bank (Saab LAU: coils 1, 3, 5)
Coil E control wire chafed against ground
Wrong cylinder assignment in PCM software (Ford SSM 52455)
P2313: Ignition Coil E Primary Control Circuit High
P2313 reports that the control line of coil E, cylinder 5, is shorted to positive, and therefore needs an engine with at least five cylinders.
Aftermarket device spliced into the coil wiring (Saab LAU note)
Coil E internally shorted to supply
Coil E control wire touching a 12 V line
PCM cylinder mapping error (Ford Bronco 3.0, TSB 24-2406)
P2314: P2314 reports a fault on the high-voltage side of coil E, which only five-cylinder and larger engines have; it normally fires cylinder 5. The control line may be perfectly sound; what failed is the energy reaching the plug or the combustion that should follow.
Spark plug of cylinder 5 worn or fouled
Coil E secondary winding or boot damaged
PCM fault on FCA vans from the 2015 build window
P2315: Ignition Coil F Primary Control Circuit Low
P2315 indicates that the switching line of coil F – cylinder 6 – is grounded, so six-, eight- and larger engines only.
Fault in the bank 2 coil supply affecting coils 2, 4 and 6 (Saab LAU)
Coil F control wire chafed to ground near the rear of the engine
P2316: Ignition Coil F Primary Control Circuit High

P2316 means the coil F control line, cylinder 6, sits at a voltage it should not have while the module switches it – a short to supply or a fault inside the coil. In VW's 2014 Touareg tables the high threshold is a signal voltage above about 5.1–7.0 V.
Coil F control wire shorted to a supply line
Intermittent contact in the harness near coil F
Misfire on cylinder 6, P0306 may also be stored
P2317: P2317 concerns the high-voltage side of coil F, which serves cylinder 6 on engines with six or more cylinders. With coil-on-plug designs there is no separate lead any more – Ford notes that individual coils did away with plug wires – so a secondary fault lies in the coil, its boot or the plug.
Spark plug of cylinder 6 worn or wrongly gapped
Coil F boot cracked or contaminated
P2318: Ignition Coil G Primary Control Circuit Low

P2318 says the command wire of coil G, cylinder 7, is touching ground, so it only occurs on V8, V10 or V12 engines. GM's 2019 table for the 5.3-litre L84 truck V8 lists it as a Type B code (50 of 63 failed samples, battery above 11 V, MIL after two trips).
Water or corrosion at the coil G connector
Control wire of coil G grounded by heat or chafing damage
PCM cylinder mapping error on Ford 6.8/7.3 (SSM 52455)
V8 runs noticeably rough, power reduced
P2319: Ignition Coil G Primary Control Circuit High

P2319 sets when the coil G control line, belonging to cylinder 7 of a V8 or larger engine, shows a short to voltage. GM's 2019 tables include it for the LT5 Corvette V8 as a Type B code with 50 of 63 failed samples.
Coil G control wire shorted to a supply line
Code assigned to the wrong cylinder by PCM software (Ford SSM 52455)
Cylinder 7 shut off for periods of 30 s (Ford)
Rough running and loss of power
P231A: Cylinder 7 Air-Fuel Ratio Imbalance - Adjustment At Limit During Balance
P231A takes the series to cylinder 7; since P2310 to P2319 are ignition coil codes, the versions for cylinders 7 to 12 start at P231A. Only engines with eight or more cylinders can set it.
Injector of cylinder 7 delivering too much or too little (deposits, wear)
Air leak at the intake port or injector seal of cylinder 7
Valve of cylinder 7 not sealing (worn seat or guide), low compression
Rough idle, possibly misfire on cylinder 7
Higher fuel consumption or exhaust smell
P231B: Cylinder 8 Air-Fuel Ratio Imbalance - Adjustment At Limit During Balance
P231B is the balance-limit code for cylinder 8, the last cylinder of a V8 and an inner one on V10 and V12 engines. The fuel trim for that cylinder has hit its stop while balancing.
Injector of cylinder 8 delivering too much or too little (deposits, wear)
Air leak at the intake port or injector seal of cylinder 8
Valve of cylinder 8 not sealing (worn seat or guide), low compression
Poor contact at the connector of injector 8
Rough idle, possibly misfire on cylinder 8
Higher fuel consumption or exhaust smell
P231C: Cylinder 9 Air-Fuel Ratio Imbalance - Adjustment At Limit During Balance

P231C points to cylinder 9 and therefore exists only on ten- and twelve-cylinder engines, a small group of mostly high-performance and heavy-duty petrol units. The balancing logic has pushed the fuel trim for cylinder 9 to its limit. No manufacturer documents the code publicly and the NHTSA index has no bulletin for it.
Injector of cylinder 9 delivering too much or too little (deposits, wear)
Air leak at the intake port or injector seal of cylinder 9
Valve of cylinder 9 not sealing (worn seat or guide), low compression
Poor contact at the connector of injector 9
Rough idle, possibly misfire on cylinder 9
Higher fuel consumption or exhaust smell
P231D: Cylinder 10 Air-Fuel Ratio Imbalance - Adjustment At Limit During Balance

P231D is the cylinder 10 code of the balance-limit series. On a V10 it marks the last cylinder, on a V12 one of the inner ones; smaller engines cannot set it. The individual fuel correction for cylinder 10 has reached its end stop while the controller tried to equalise the mixture. No maker publishes a description, and no NHTSA bulletin lists it.
Injector of cylinder 10 delivering too much or too little (deposits, wear)
Air leak at the intake port or injector seal of cylinder 10
Valve of cylinder 10 not sealing (worn seat or guide), low compression
Poor contact at the connector of injector 10
Rough idle, possibly misfire on cylinder 10
Higher fuel consumption or exhaust smell
P231E: Cylinder 11 Air-Fuel Ratio Imbalance - Adjustment At Limit During Balance

P231E belongs to cylinder 11 and can only come from twelve-cylinder engines, V12 or W12. The per-cylinder fuel trim for cylinder 11 sits at its limit during balancing. There is no public manufacturer description and no NHTSA bulletin.
Injector of cylinder 11 delivering too much or too little (deposits, wear)
Air leak at the intake port or injector seal of cylinder 11
Valve of cylinder 11 not sealing (worn seat or guide), low compression
Poor contact at the connector of injector 11
Rough idle, possibly misfire on cylinder 11
Higher fuel consumption or exhaust smell
P231F: Cylinder 12 Air-Fuel Ratio Imbalance - Adjustment At Limit During Balance

P231F closes the balance-limit series at cylinder 12, the last cylinder of a twelve-cylinder engine. It says the balancing routine has used up the fuel trim for that cylinder without matching it to the rest. Public manufacturer documentation is missing, and the NHTSA index contains no bulletin naming it.
Injector of cylinder 12 delivering too much or too little (deposits, wear)
Air leak at the intake port or injector seal of cylinder 12
Valve of cylinder 12 not sealing (worn seat or guide), low compression
Poor contact at the connector of injector 12
Rough idle, possibly misfire on cylinder 12
Higher fuel consumption or exhaust smell
P2320: P2320 points at the high-voltage half of coil G, normally the coil on cylinder 7, so only engines with seven or more cylinders can log it. FCA is the maker on record: STAR case S2118000002 from March 2021 for the 2020–2021 Ram 1500 names P2320 as coil 7 secondary circuit with insufficient ionization.
Coil 7 connector not fully seated or latched (FCA)
Spark plug of cylinder 7 worn, fouled or with wrong gap
Coil G secondary winding or boot breaking down
Ion-current evaluation in the PCM faulty
Misfire felt on cylinder 7, often with P0307
Engine shakes at idle or under load
P2321: Ignition Coil H Primary Control Circuit Low
With P2321 the engine module has seen the switching line of coil H pulled to ground; on a V8 coil H is the final one, on a V10 it is number eight.
Water ingress or corrosion in the coil H connector (GM PIP5147)
Coil H control wire chafed through to ground
Coil driver stage in the engine module damaged
Rough idle and weaker pulling power
P2322: Ignition Coil H Primary Control Circuit High

P2322 is the counterpart to P2321: the coil H control line, cylinder 8 on most V8 layouts, reads as if it were tied to voltage. GM monitors it the same way on the 2019 LT5 and L84 engines, as a Type B code, flagged once 50 of 63 samples fail.
Coil H control wire shorted to a voltage-carrying line
PCM assigns the code to the wrong cylinder (Ford SSM 52455/52342)
Output stage in the engine module faulty
One cylinder repeatedly shut off for about 30 s (Ford)
Noticeable vibration and loss of power
P2323: P2323 concerns the spark side of coil H, the coil on cylinder 8. It is the last code of FCA's ion-sensing series: STAR case S2118000002 (2021) for the 2020–2021 Ram 1500 reads it as coil 8 secondary circuit with insufficient ionization, and an older FCA parts review lists it together with the cylinder misfire codes P0301–P0308.
Coil 8 connector loose or not latched (FCA)
Worn or fouled spark plug on cylinder 8
Coil H boot cracked or tracking to the head
Cylinder 8 misfire, frequently stored with P0308
P2324: Ignition Coil I Primary Control Circuit Low
Coil I is the ninth coil, so P2324 only appears on ten- or twelve-cylinder petrol engines.
Coil I control wire grounded on the engine or exhaust side
Moisture or corroded pins at the coil I plug
PCM coil driver for cylinder 9 failed
P2325: Ignition Coil I Primary Control Circuit High

P2325 flags a short to voltage on the trigger line of coil I, the ninth ignition output. Ford is again the only maker that lists it publicly: in its OBD summaries P2325 sits among the codes for a coil driver shorted high, and the 2014 Ford code list shows it as a MIL-lighting code checked with the engine running.
Coil I control wire touching a 12 V feed
PCM driver stage for coil I faulty
Cylinder 9 drops out in roughly 30 s cycles
P2326: P2326 would report a fault in the high-voltage output of coil I – coil, boot or plug of the ninth cylinder. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. FCA's ion-sensing secondary codes, the closest analogue, end at coil 8 (P2323), and Ford, the one maker with public coil I codes, monitors that coil only on its driver side (P2324/P2325).
Spark plug on cylinder 9 worn or bridged
Coil I boot perforated or oil-soaked
P2327: Ignition Coil J Primary Control Circuit Low

P2327 is the highest ground-side coil code Ford publishes: its driver short-circuit-low list in the 2012 and 2020–2023 OBD summaries runs from P2300 up to P2327 and stops there, matching a ten-coil engine such as the 6.8-litre Modular V10. Coil J serves the tenth cylinder in Ford's count.
Coil J (cylinder 10) failed with internal short
Coil J signal wire shorted to ground near the rear of the engine
Corroded or water-filled coil J connector
PCM driver for coil J defective
Higher fuel consumption from cylinder shut-off cycles
P2328: Ignition Coil J Primary Control Circuit High

P2328 marks the end of Ford's published coil list: it is the last entry in the driver short-circuit-high group of the 2012 and 2020–2023 OBD summaries, and the 2014 Ford code list puts it directly before the evaporative codes with a MIL flag.
Coil J control wire shorted to battery voltage
PCM output for coil J damaged
Engine runs rough and pulls weakly
P2329: P2329 covers the secondary side of coil J, meaning the spark path to the plug of cylinder 10. No public manufacturer source assigns it. Ford, whose V10 is the obvious ten-cylinder candidate, lists coil J only on the primary side (P2327/P2328) and in its 2014 code list skips every secondary code of the series.
Carbon tracking on the coil J boot
Jerking under acceleration, worse when damp
P232A: P232A is stored by the engine module when the transmission control module has demanded that the engine be switched off.
Serious transmission fault detected by the TCM (stored there as its own code)
Disturbed CAN communication between TCM and engine module
Low battery voltage or poor supply/ground at the TCM
Mismatched or outdated TCM/engine software after repair or replacement
Engine shuts off while driving or at idle
Engine cranks but does not stay running until the fault is cleared
Transmission warning and further codes in the TCM
P232B: Cylinder 11 Fuel Injector A Offset Learning At Min Limit

Common-rail diesels keep a small-quantity correction for every injector. During overrun fuel cut the module fires one injector alone with a tiny known amount (GM: about 1.5 mm³), judges the torque from crankshaft acceleration and records how much the energizing time has to change at each rail pressure level.
Injector of cylinder 11 leaking or delivering too much at small quantities
Injector correction code not or wrongly entered after replacement
Disturbed crankshaft speed signal falsifying the torque evaluation
Often no noticeable change; possibly louder combustion noise or rough idle
Possibly smoke or higher fuel consumption
P232C: Cylinder 11 Fuel Injector A Offset Learning At Max Limit

P232C is the upper-limit partner of P232B for injector A in cylinder 11. The small-quantity learning has found that this injector needs far more energizing time than the nominal map to produce the expected torque pulse, and the stored correction has hit its maximum at one or more rail pressure levels.
Injector of cylinder 11 coked, worn or sticking (delivers too little)
Injector correction code missing or wrong after replacement
Poor fuel quality or contamination promoting deposits
Rough idle or uneven running at low load
Possibly harder starting or more smoke
P232D: Cylinder 12 Fuel Injector A Offset Learning At Min Limit

The offset-learning codes for injector A of cylinders 1 to 10 sit at P02CC to P02DF; cylinders 11 and 12 were placed separately at P232B to P232E, and P232D is the lower limit for cylinder 12, the last cylinder of a V12.
Injector of cylinder 12 leaking or opening early
Correction code not programmed after fitting a new injector
Crankshaft signal disturbed (tone wheel, sensor, flywheel)
Possibly harsher combustion noise or knocking at idle
P232E: Cylinder 12 Fuel Injector A Offset Learning At Max Limit
P232E closes the row of injector A offset-learning codes: cylinder 12, upper limit.
Injector of cylinder 12 coked or worn (delivers too little)
Injector correction code missing or wrong
High resistance in the injector wiring slowing the opening
P232F: O2 Sensor Out of Range During Deceleration (Bank 1 Sensor 2)
P232F checks the downstream oxygen signal of bank 1 while fuel is cut on deceleration and the exhaust holds almost pure air.
Downstream sensor drifting or aged (on GM diesels the O2 signal of NOx sensor 2)
Exhaust leak near the downstream sensor
Damaged sensor wiring or connector (chafing, corrosion)
Leaking injector or upstream sensor fault distorting the overrun comparison
Usually no change in driving behaviour
MIL only after two trips with the fault (GM Type B)
P2330: Ignition Coil K Primary Control Circuit Low

P2330 belongs to coil K, the eleventh coil, which only twelve-cylinder petrol engines have – V12 units such as those built by BMW, Mercedes-Benz, Lamborghini or Ferrari, or the VW group's W12. No manufacturer documents this code publicly; the published coil lists stop earlier (Ford at J, GM at H).
Coil K control wire damaged and grounded in the bank harness
Coil K driver in the engine module faulty
Slight roughness, often hard to feel on a V12
P2331: Ignition Coil K Primary Control Circuit High

P2331 is the short-to-power version for coil K, cylinder 11 in a straightforward count. No manufacturer documents this code publicly; neither Ford nor GM, whose OBD descriptions explain the primary codes in detail, build engines with eleven or more coils.
Coil K signal wire shorted to a supply wire
Engine module output for coil K defective
P2332: P2332 reserves a code for trouble between coil K and the plug of cylinder 11. No manufacturer documents it publicly: the only published secondary-circuit series, FCA's ion-current codes, covers coils 1 to 8, and twelve-cylinder makers do not release their code lists.
Oil in the plug well of cylinder 11
Spark plug of cylinder 11 worn out
P2333: Ignition Coil L Primary Control Circuit Low

P2333 is the ground-short code for coil L, the twelfth and final coil letter in the SAE scheme. It fits only V12 or W12 engines. There is no public manufacturer documentation for it; the published lists of Ford and GM end at coils J and H.
Coil L control wire chafed to ground
Damaged or corroded coil L connector
Coil L output stage in the engine module failed
P2334: Ignition Coil L Primary Control Circuit High

P2334, the last primary-side coil code of the series, reports a short to voltage on the coil L trigger line. No manufacturer documents this code publicly; it can only occur on engines with twelve individual coils.
Coil L control wire shorted to a voltage source
Engine module output for coil L defective
P2335: P2335 closes the ignition coil block of J2012: a fault on the high-voltage side of coil L, the twelfth coil. No manufacturer documents this code publicly, and none of the reviewed ion-sensing or secondary-monitoring documents reaches past coil 8.
Check engine light on, possibly flashing with heavy misfire
P2336: Cylinder 1 Above Knock/Combustion Vibration Sensor Threshold

The engine module listens to the knock sensors and assigns each vibration burst to the cylinder whose combustion falls into that crank-angle window, so it can retard spark on one cylinder alone. P2336 means the knock intensity attributed to cylinder 1 has exceeded the calibrated threshold.
Engine damage from machining debris or casting sand (Stellantis 2.0L PHEV, bulletin 09-009-26)
Carbon deposits or hot spots in cylinder 1
Fuel with too low octane rating
Cylinder 1 running lean (injector delivering too little)
Knocking or pinging noise from the engine
Less power because spark is retarded
P2337: Cylinder 2 Above Knock/Combustion Vibration Sensor Threshold

P2337 is the cylinder 2 entry of the per-cylinder knock series P2336–P2347. Using crank position, the engine module splits the knock sensor signal into one window per combustion event and compares the vibration level in cylinder 2's window with its threshold; above it the code is stored and spark for that cylinder is pulled back.
Internal damage from debris left in the engine (Stellantis 2.0L PHEV)
Deposits on piston or valves of cylinder 2
Wrong or worn spark plug in cylinder 2
Mechanical noise falling into cylinder 2's knock window
P2338: Cylinder 3 Above Knock/Combustion Vibration Sensor Threshold
P2338 sets when the knock signal assigned to cylinder 3 rises above its threshold.
Carbon build-up or a hot spot in cylinder 3
Injector of cylinder 3 delivering too little (lean, hot combustion)
Engine damage from casting sand or chips (Stellantis 2.0L PHEV)
Knock sensor loose or wrongly torqued, picking up noise
P2339: Cylinder 4 Above Knock/Combustion Vibration Sensor Threshold

P2339 covers cylinder 4. On a four-cylinder engine this is the last cylinder of the series, which is why Stellantis bulletin 09-009-26 lists exactly P2336 to P2339 for the 2.0L turbo PHEV (sales code ECX, Jeep Wrangler 4xe 2024–2025, Grand Cherokee 2023–2025): any of the four codes with the MIL on, often together with a knocking noise, qualifies for an engin…
Machining debris or casting sand damaging the engine (Stellantis bulletin 09-009-26)
Low-octane fuel or high intake temperature
Knocking noise from the engine compartment
P233A: Fuel Pressure Regulator C Control Circuit/Open

Fuel pressure regulator C is a third pressure actuator that only a few high-pressure systems have; which valve carries the letter is up to the manufacturer. GM's 2025 diesel table 25OBDG04B assigns C to a second fuel metering unit valve on the pump, driven by the ECM through a high-side and a low-side switch.
Valve connector loose, corroded or a terminal pushed back
Engine harness wire broken where it rubs on brackets or clamps
Coil of the metering valve interrupted
Output driver in the engine control module faulty
Check engine light on in the first trip
Rail pressure deviates, hesitation or reduced power
P233B: Fuel Pressure Regulator C Control Circuit Low

P233B points to the ground side of fuel pressure regulator C: the line between valve and low-side driver has contact with ground. In GM's 2025 diesel table 25OBDG04B, regulator C is the second fuel metering unit valve, and the ECM checks this line while the driver is switched off.
Insulation of the control wire worn through against engine or bracket
Moisture or corrosion bridging pins in the valve connector
Metering valve winding shorted to its housing
Low-side driver in the engine control module damaged
Rail pressure too high or unstable, rough running
P233C: Fuel Pressure Regulator C Control Circuit High

With P233C the ECM sees the control line of fuel pressure regulator C pulled towards battery voltage. GM's 2025 diesel table 25OBDG04B runs this test while the low-side driver of the second metering unit valve is switched on: if the voltage across the driver stays high, the line evidently has a path to power of less than about 0.5 Ohm.
Control wire chafed against a battery-fed wire in the harness
Damaged valve connector with pins touching
Shorted turns in the metering valve coil
Low-side driver in the engine control module faulty
P233D: Fuel Pressure Regulator B Solenoid Supply Voltage Control Circuit/Open

Where the ECM switches the solenoid of fuel pressure regulator B on both sides, the ground-side line is checked under P2294 to P2296 and the feed from the high-side driver under P233D to P233F. P233D is the open-circuit code for that feed.
Supply wire to the regulator solenoid broken or terminal loose
High-side driver in the engine control module faulty
Rail pressure not controllable, reduced power
P233E: Fuel Pressure Regulator B Solenoid Supply Voltage Control Circuit Low

P233E concerns the feed side of fuel pressure regulator B: the line from the ECM's high-side driver to the solenoid is shorted to ground. GM documents it for its 2025 diesels (table 25OBDG04A); there, regulator B means the rail pressure regulator valve.
Supply wire to the regulator rubbed through to ground
Regulator solenoid shorted internally or to its housing
Water or corrosion in the regulator connector
High-side driver in the engine control module damaged
Check engine light on in the first trip
P233F: Fuel Pressure Regulator B Solenoid Supply Voltage Control Circuit High
P233F is set when the feed line of the fuel pressure regulator B solenoid carries voltage even though the ECM has its high-side driver switched off.
Regulator supply wire touching a battery or ignition feed
Bent or bridged pins in the regulator connector
High-side driver in the engine control module stuck on
Check engine light on in the first trip
Rail pressure too high or unstable
P2340: Cylinder 5 Above Knock/Combustion Vibration Sensor Threshold

P2340 reports knock above threshold for cylinder 5, so it can only occur on engines with at least five cylinders – inline-five, six-cylinder, V8 or larger. The principle matches the rest of the series: the module evaluates the knock sensor signal in the crank-angle window of each combustion and retards spark individually when one cylinder knocks.
Carbon deposits or glowing particles in cylinder 5
Injector of cylinder 5 delivering too little
Wrong heat range or damaged spark plug
P2341: Cylinder 6 Above Knock/Combustion Vibration Sensor Threshold

Cylinder 6 is the last cylinder of inline-six and V6 engines, and P2341 reports that its share of the knock sensor signal has crossed the limit. Modern knock control adjusts ignition timing for every cylinder on its own, so a single cylinder can run retarded while the others keep optimum spark; the code tells which one keeps knocking.
Fuel octane too low for the engine
Deposits in the combustion chamber of cylinder 6
Loose component or valve train noise read as knock
Lean mixture in cylinder 6 from a restricted injector
Knocking at full throttle or uphill
P2342: Cylinder 7 Above Knock/Combustion Vibration Sensor Threshold

P2342 applies only to engines with seven or more cylinders, in practice V8s and larger. It says the vibration picked up by the knock sensor during cylinder 7's combustion window has exceeded the threshold.
Loose bracket, heat shield or valve train noise in cylinder 7's window
Deposits or hot spots in cylinder 7
Knock sensor of that bank loose or wrongly torqued
P2343: Cylinder 8 Above Knock/Combustion Vibration Sensor Threshold

P2343 belongs to cylinder 8, the last cylinder of a V8, and is stored when the knock intensity measured in that cylinder's crank-angle window stays above the calibrated limit. The knock control first answers with spark retard for cylinder 8 alone, and on turbocharged engines it may also lower boost; the code marks that this cylinder keeps knocking.
Wrong plug type or gap in cylinder 8
Cylinder 8 running lean from low injector delivery
Pinging or knocking, mostly under load
Reduced power, possibly less boost on turbo engines
P2344: Cylinder 9 Above Knock/Combustion Vibration Sensor Threshold

A ninth cylinder exists only on V10 and V12 engines, so P2344 is confined to a small group of vehicles: V10s such as Ford's 6.8L Triton in E-Series vans, Super Duty pickups and the Excursion, the Dodge Viper and Ram SRT-10, and performance cars from BMW, Audi and Lamborghini, plus the V12s.
Deposits or hot spots in cylinder 9
Fuel of too low octane for a high-output engine
Wrong or fouled spark plug in cylinder 9
Knocking or pinging under heavy load or towing
P2345: Cylinder 10 Above Knock/Combustion Vibration Sensor Threshold

P2345 is the knock code for cylinder 10, the last cylinder of a V10, so it appears mainly on engines such as Ford's 6.8L Triton truck V10, the Viper V10 used by Dodge, and the V10s of BMW M5/M6, Audi and Lamborghini.
High load, towing or high intake temperature with marginal fuel
Valve train noise interpreted as knock
P2346: Cylinder 11 Above Knock/Combustion Vibration Sensor Threshold

Cylinders 11 and 12 exist only on V12 engines, for example BMW's V12 in the 7 and 8 Series, Mercedes-Benz's M120 and its successors, and the V12s of Ferrari, Lamborghini and Aston Martin. P2346 reports that cylinder 11 has knocked above the threshold that the knock control allows in its crank-angle window.
Deposits or hot spots in cylinder 11
Fuel below the required octane rating
Disturbed crank or knock sensor signal shifting the cylinder assignment
P2347: Cylinder 12 Above Knock/Combustion Vibration Sensor Threshold

P2347 ends the per-cylinder knock series that starts with P2336 for cylinder 1; it is the code for cylinder 12 and thus appears only on V12 engines such as those from BMW, Mercedes-Benz, Ferrari or Lamborghini. The engine module has found that the vibration in cylinder 12's combustion window exceeds the threshold and is holding back that cylinder's spark.
Mechanical noise near the sensor of that bank
P2348: A cylinder pressure sensor, usually built into the glow plug of a diesel, reports the combustion pressure of one cylinder so the ECM can trim injection for it. P2348 is the general circuit code for the sensor of cylinder 9, meant for modules that do not split faults into low and high.
Sensor or glow plug connector of cylinder 9 loose or corroded
Reference, signal or ground wire damaged
Often no noticeable change in driving
P2349: P2349 is the plausibility code for the combustion pressure sensor of cylinder 9: the signal is electrically valid but does not match what the ECM expects for the operating point. CARB requires input sensors to be checked for rationality where feasible, in both directions.
Glow plug seat leaking or plug tightened to wrong torque
Genuinely low compression in cylinder 9 distorting the comparison
P234A: P234A means the signal of the cylinder 9 combustion pressure sensor stays below its permitted minimum.
5 V reference interrupted or shorted to ground
Sensor in the glow plug defective
Check engine light after two trips
Peak pressure reads 0 kPa on the scan tool
P234B: P234B is stored when the cylinder 9 combustion pressure sensor signal sits above its upper limit.
Connector at the cylinder 9 glow plug not plugged in
Sensor ground or signal wire interrupted
Reference or signal wire shorted to voltage
Check engine light after two trips
Peak pressure shows an implausibly high fixed value
P234C: P234C covers a cylinder 9 combustion pressure signal that jumps or briefly drops out instead of staying permanently low or permanently high.
Intermittent contact at the glow plug connector
Harness rubbing on the cylinder head, breaking contact under vibration
Sensor electronics unstable at high temperature
Check engine light, often coming and going
Fault stored but hard to reproduce in the workshop
P234D: Unlike the sensor circuit codes, P234D judges the pressure itself: the value measured or modelled for cylinder 9 stays below what the ECM expects, while the sensor is electrically in order.
Injector of cylinder 9 delivering too little or clogged
Compression loss from valve or piston ring wear
Combustion gas escaping at the glow plug seat
More smoke and higher fuel consumption
P234E: P234E reports that the pressure determined for cylinder 9 exceeds the expected maximum. No manufacturer documents the cylinder-9 code publicly.
Engine software misjudging combustion (update available at some makers)
Injector of cylinder 9 leaking or injecting too much
Warning lamp on, sometimes with misfire codes
Loss of power if the cylinder is shut off
P234F: P234F flags that the pressure signal of cylinder 9 changes too little: the rise and fall the ECM expects across each combustion cycle is missing or very small. For cylinder 9 there is no manufacturer documentation.
Sensing element of the glow plug stuck by carbon

Usually no change in engine behaviour
P2350: P2350 is the opposite of P234F: the cylinder 9 pressure signal swings more than plausible, with peaks or steps that do not fit the engine's operating state. No manufacturer publishes the code for cylinder 9.
Interference or chafing on the sensor signal wire
Sensor electronics in the glow plug failing
Injector of cylinder 9 dribbling after closing
P2351: P2351 does not concern the sensor but the quality of combustion in cylinder 9, as judged from the pressure trace: the energy released per cycle, or its balance against the other cylinders, falls outside the permitted window. No manufacturer documents the code publicly, nor its cylinder-1 analogue P039E.
Injector of cylinder 9 coked, leaking or sticking
Poor fuel quality or water in the fuel
P2352: P2352 is the catch-all code for the electrical circuit of the cylinder 10 combustion pressure sensor, meant for engine computers that make no distinction between low and high. A tenth cylinder exists only on V10 and V12 engines.
Glow plug/sensor connector of cylinder 10 not fully latched or corroded
Harness branch to the rear cylinder of the bank chafed or heat-damaged
Electronics in the pressure-sensing glow plug failed
Combustion noise may become slightly harder
P2353: P2353 means the cylinder 10 pressure sensor delivers a signal that is electrically within limits but not believable for the current operating point – the reading is skewed, not cut off. CARB expects input sensors to be checked for such rationality faults, not just for open or shorted circuits.
Sensor offset drifted with age and heat
Carbon on the heater rod hampers pressure transfer to the diaphragm
Replacement glow plug with calibration for another engine
No noticeable change in engine behaviour
P2354: P2354 reports that the signal of the cylinder 10 pressure sensor stays below its lower limit.
Signal wire shorted to ground, e.g. chafed on the cylinder head
5 V reference interrupted or shorted to ground
Internal fault of the pressure-sensing glow plug
Check engine light after the second faulty trip

P2355: P2355 means the cylinder 10 pressure signal is stuck above its upper limit. Taking the Saab 9-5 diesel with GM's 2.0 engine as the model, the Type B high codes for its four cylinders (P0398 on cylinder 1) wait until the signal has stayed above the threshold for over 2 s with the engine running.
Signal or low reference wire open, connector pulled off
