P2357: P2357 is not about the wiring: the pressure measured or modelled for cylinder 10 itself is below expectation while the sensor circuit tests fine. No manufacturer publishes this code, and the cylinder-1 counterpart P039A is equally undocumented.
Injector of cylinder 10 delivering too little fuel

Combustion gas leaking past the glow plug seal

P2358: P2358 indicates that the pressure determined for cylinder 10 exceeds its upper expectation. No manufacturer documents this cylinder-10 code.

Warning lamp on, sometimes together with misfire codes
Reduced power if the cylinder is switched off
P2359: P2359 means the pressure trace of cylinder 10 changes too little: the build-up through compression and combustion is flatter than the ECM expects. No manufacturer documents this code for cylinder 10.
Heater rod stuck in carbon, pressure no longer reaches the diaphragm
Cylinder 10 builds up hardly any pressure
P235A: P235A is the counterpart to P2359: the cylinder 10 pressure signal swings more than the combustion can explain, with spikes or steps from one cycle to the next. A public manufacturer description of this tenth-cylinder code does not exist.
Interference on a damaged or poorly shielded signal wire
Poor engine ground or corroded ground point
Sensor electronics delivering an unstable signal

P235B: P235B rates how well cylinder 10 burns, derived from its pressure curve – for instance from the energy each working cycle releases or from how it compares with the other nine cylinders of a V10. No manufacturer documents this code, nor the cylinder-1 equivalent P039E.

P235C: P235C stands for a fault in the circuit of the cylinder 11 combustion pressure sensor without saying whether the signal is too low or too high. Sensor electronics in the glow plug failed

P235D: P235D is set when the combustion pressure reported for cylinder 11 is electrically valid yet does not fit the engine's state – for example a compression peak that is clearly off while no fuel is being injected.

P235E: With P235E the signal of the cylinder 11 combustion pressure sensor is too low, typically close to zero.

Signal wire chafed through to ground

Only twelve-cylinder engines have this cylinder, and no maker documents the code; the Saab 9-5 diesel serves as the model with P0398 for cylinder 1, a Type B code that needs more than 2 s over the threshold.

P2360: P2360 records a cylinder 11 combustion pressure signal that is unsteady – brief dropouts or spikes that do not last long enough for a low or high code. Since only twelve-cylinder engines have cylinder 11, and none is documented with pressure sensors, the code has no public manufacturer description.
Fretting corrosion or loose fit at the connector terminals
Sensor electronics in the plug head failing when warm
Check engine light that comes and goes

P2361: P2361 says the combustion pressure of cylinder 11 is too low although the sensor works electrically. No manufacturer documents this code, since no twelve-cylinder engine with combustion pressure sensing is publicly described.
Injector of cylinder 11 with reduced flow or clogged nozzle
Worn piston rings or burnt valve lowering compression
Leak at the glow plug seat

P2362: P2362 is stored when cylinder 11 shows more combustion pressure than the ECM considers plausible. No manufacturer publishes it, because no twelve-cylinder engine with cylinder pressure monitoring is documented.
Injector of cylinder 11 leaking or hanging open
Injection timing too early for this cylinder
Engine control software misjudging the pressure
Loss of power if the cylinder is shut off
P2363: P2363 flags a cylinder 11 pressure signal with too little swing between its low point and the combustion peak. No manufacturer documents this code; cylinder 11 only exists on twelve-cylinder engines, none of which is publicly known with pressure-sensing glow plugs. Saab's 9-5 diesel files the related P039C for cylinder 1 as a Type B signal fault.
Piezo-resistive sensing element has lost sensitivity
Deposits holding the heater rod in place
Engine runs normally in most cases
P2364: P2364 is stored when the pressure signal of cylinder 11 varies too strongly, from cycle to cycle or within one cycle. No maker publishes this code. Saab's 9-5 diesel has the analogous P039D for cylinder 1, a Type B signal fault reacting to 0.2 s outside its window.
Interference coupling into the signal line
Ground connection with changing contact resistance
Moisture in the glow plug connector
P2365: P2365 means the ECM judges combustion in cylinder 11 to be poor, based on the pressure signal rather than on crankshaft speed alone. No manufacturer publishes this code; twelve-cylinder engines with pressure-sensing glow plugs are not documented.
Fouled or leaking injector of cylinder 11
P2366: P2366 is the general circuit code for the combustion pressure sensor of cylinder 12; it does not tell whether the signal sits too low or too high. Twelve is the highest number on a V12 or W12. Whether a maker counts bank by bank or along the crankshaft, number 1 is normally the front cylinder, which places 12 at the opposite end of the engine.
Glow plug connector not fully latched or loose
Damaged wire in the harness branch to the rearmost cylinder
Pressure reading for cylinder 12 missing or fixed in live data
P2367: With P2367 the cylinder 12 pressure signal is electrically within its limits but makes no sense for the operating point. A natural yardstick is the motored cycle: on overrun nothing burns, so the curve has to peak at top dead centre.
Sensor zero point or gain drifted
Combustion gas escaping at the glow plug seat
Glow plug of a different calibration fitted
Implausible peak pressure value for cylinder 12 compared with the others
P2368: P2368 is stored when the voltage coming from the cylinder 12 pressure sensor stays below its lower limit. As the last cylinder of a V12 or W12, it has no publicly documented application, so Saab's 9-5 diesel code P0397 serves as the template.
5 V reference open or shorted to ground
Sensor electronics in the glow plug head failed low
Warning lamp after two trips with the fault
Peak pressure of cylinder 12 stuck near zero
P2369: P2369 means the cylinder 12 pressure input reads above its upper limit. Like the rest of the cylinder-12 family, it is not documented publicly by any maker. On Saab's 9-5 diesel the matching cylinder-1 code P0398 is set after more than 2 s above the threshold and is evaluated once per operating cycle.
Signal shorted to a voltage source
Glow plug sensor electronics outputting a fixed high value
Check engine light after the second trip
Cylinder 12 shows an impossibly high pressure in live data
P236A: P236A covers brief, irregular disturbances of the cylinder 12 pressure signal – faults that come and go without settling into a lasting low or high state. Its model is the Saab 9-5 diesel code P0399, which responds as soon as the signal stays outside its band longer than 0.2 s.
Loose or corroded terminal in the plug connector
Harness rubbing through under engine vibration
Glow plug sensor with intermittent internal fault
Warning lamp that switches on and off over several days
Pressure value of cylinder 12 jumps when the harness is moved
P236B: P236B reports that cylinder 12 builds too little combustion pressure while its sensor circuit itself is in order. No manufacturer documents the code, because no V12 or W12 with cylinder pressure measurement has been made public.
Intake or exhaust valve of cylinder 12 not sealing
Worn piston rings or head gasket leak
Gas leaking past the glow plug seal
Misfire code for cylinder 12 stored as well
P236C: P236C flags combustion pressure in cylinder 12 above its allowed value. A public twelve-cylinder application does not exist.
Injector dripping or delivering too much pilot fuel
EPC or check engine lamp on
Loss of power when the cylinder is switched off
P236D: P236D is stored when the cylinder 12 pressure trace swings too little – the curve stays flatter than compression and combustion ought to make it. No manufacturer documents this code for a twelve-cylinder engine.
Carbon deposits restricting the heater rod
Flat pressure curve for cylinder 12 in live data
P236E: P236E means the pressure signal of cylinder 12 scatters more than the ECM tolerates, either within one cycle or from one cycle to the next. No manufacturer publishes the code; the reference is Saab's P039D for cylinder 1, a Type B fault that needs only 0.2 s outside its window. Two groups of causes are possible.
Injector delivery varying from shot to shot
P236F: P236F is the ECM's verdict that combustion in cylinder 12 falls short, judged from the evaluated pressure curve rather than from a single limit. No manufacturer documents it, as no twelve-cylinder engine with cylinder pressure sensing is public.
Injector of cylinder 12 coked or worn
P2370: Fuel Volume Regulator B Control Circuit/Open

A fuel volume regulator is the solenoid valve at the high-pressure pump that decides how much of the pump's stroke reaches the rail. Regulator B only exists where a second valve or second pump is fitted – the 5.2 litre V10 of Audi and Lamborghini, for instance, has two cam-driven high-pressure pumps for its two rails.
Connector at regulator B loose or corroded
Rail pressure deviation and possible reduced power
P2371: Fuel Volume Regulator B Control Circuit Performance

P2371 is a functional fault of the second fuel volume regulator: the control circuit works electrically, but the valve does not achieve what the ECM asks of it. No manufacturer publishes a definition for regulator B, so the A side helps.
Regulator B valve sticking from dirt or wear
Rail pressure fluctuates or misses its target
P2372: Fuel Volume Regulator B Control Circuit Low

P2372 says the line driving fuel volume regulator B is pulled too low, as a rule by contact with ground. No manufacturer documents this B code publicly; it mirrors P0003 on regulator A. Ford's 2023 diesel detects that condition with the valve switched off: the voltage reported by the driver chip then falls below 2.8 V, where about 5 V would be normal.
Control wire chafed through to ground
Internal short in the regulator coil
Rail pressure too high or too low depending on the affected side
P2373: Fuel Volume Regulator B Control Circuit High

P2373 points to too much voltage or current in the control circuit of fuel volume regulator B, typically from a short to battery voltage or a shorted coil. No manufacturer publishes the B version; P0004 on regulator A is the model. Ford's 2023 diesel sets that code when the energised valve draws more than 3.7 A, while 2.2 A is the normal maximum.
Control wire shorted to battery voltage
Regulator coil with shorted turns drawing excess current
Rail pressure deviation codes stored as well
P2374: Turbocharger/Supercharger Inlet Pressure Sensor B Circuit

P2374 covers any wiring or sensor-side failure of a second pressure sensor mounted upstream of a compressor. Where the letter B belongs is the manufacturer's choice; on parallel twin-turbo V engines, where each turbocharger serves one cylinder bank, a second inlet sensor for the other compressor is the obvious candidate.
Connector or wire of sensor B open, corroded or shorted
Sensor B reports an internal error
P2375: Turbocharger/Supercharger Inlet Pressure Sensor B Circuit Range/Performance

With P2375 the signal of compressor inlet pressure sensor B is electrically valid but implausible – stuck, offset or out of step with the other pressure values. No manufacturer publishes the B code; GM's 2018 table for the supercharged LT4 V8 describes the A counterpart P012B in detail.
Air filter on the side of compressor B clogged
Leaking or collapsed duct ahead of compressor B
Check engine light after two trips
Uneven boost between the two turbochargers
P2376: Turbocharger/Supercharger Inlet Pressure Sensor B Circuit Low

P2376 is set when the output voltage of compressor inlet pressure sensor B drops below its lower limit. No maker documents the B code publicly; GM's A version P012C on the supercharged LT4 gives an idea of the scale. There the threshold is 3 % of the 5 V reference, equal to roughly 6 kPa – a value no intake can reach in reality.
Signal wire of sensor B shorted to ground
5 V reference to sensor B open
Live data show an inlet pressure far below ambient
P2377: Turbocharger/Supercharger Inlet Pressure Sensor B Circuit High

P2377 means sensor B ahead of the compressor delivers a voltage above its upper limit. Publicly no manufacturer defines this B code, so GM's P012D for the supercharged LT4 serves as a reference: it trips above 97 % of the 5 V reference, which equals about 124 kPa at that sensor, again with 320 failed samples out of 400 at 12.5 ms intervals and Type B.
Signal wire shorted to 5 V reference or battery voltage
Sensor ground of sensor B open
Moisture bridging terminals in the connector
Implausibly high inlet pressure in live data
P2378: Turbocharger/Supercharger Inlet Pressure Sensor B Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P2378 records a signal from compressor inlet pressure sensor B that jumps or briefly drops out without staying beyond a limit.
Harness damaged by heat from the turbocharger
Warning lamp that comes and goes
P2379: O2 Sensor Out of Range During Deceleration (Bank 2 Sensor 2)

P2379 covers the oxygen sensor behind the catalyst on bank 2 at the moment the injectors are shut off on a closed throttle: the exhaust is then close to fresh air, and a sensor whose reading stays outside the expected lean window is suspect. No manufacturer documents P2379 publicly.
Bank 2 downstream sensor aged or contaminated, reacting too little to fuel cut
Exhaust leak near the bank 2 rear sensor diluting or distorting the sample
Chafed sensor lead or corroded connector on the bank 2 rear sensor
Leaking injector on bank 2 keeping fuel in the exhaust during overrun
No noticeable change in how the car drives

P237A: O2 Sensor Exhaust Sample Error (Bank 1 Sensor 2)

P237A says the rear oxygen sensor of bank 1 is not getting, or not reporting, a representative sample of exhaust: its reading does not fit the gas that should be flowing past it after the catalyst, typically because outside air enters through a leak or the sensing element is no longer exposed properly. No manufacturer documents P237A publicly.
Leak at a flange, joint or cracked pipe ahead of the bank 1 rear sensor drawing in air
Rear sensor element damaged, coated or loose in its boss
Contaminated or blocked reference air path of the sensor (wiring or connector)
Catalyst monitor not completing or reporting implausible results
Possible ticking exhaust noise from a leak
P237B: O2 Sensor Exhaust Sample Error (Bank 2 Sensor 2)

P237B is the bank 2 version of the sample check on the post-catalyst oxygen sensor and therefore only appears on engines with two exhaust banks, mostly V6 and V8 units with a separate downstream sensor on each side.
Air leak in the bank 2 exhaust between catalyst and rear sensor
Bank 2 rear sensor damaged, poisoned or not seated correctly
Rear sensors of bank 1 and bank 2 swapped at the connectors after a repair
Bank 2 catalyst monitor incomplete or failing
P237C: Exhaust Heat Exchanger Exhaust Bypass Valve A Control Circuit/Open

Some hybrids route the exhaust through a coolant heat exchanger after a cold start to warm the engine and cabin sooner, and flap A sends the gas around it once heat is no longer wanted. P237C is set when the drive circuit of that bypass actuator shows an open or a general circuit fault.
Water inside the heat exchanger assembly or actuator (Ford Maverick SSM 51921)
Bypass valve actuator with open winding or failed electronics
Broken wire or loose connector in the hot area under the vehicle
Engine and cabin may warm up more slowly in cold weather
Further heat exchanger codes such as P2C22 stored alongside
P237D: Exhaust Heat Exchanger Exhaust Bypass Valve A Control Circuit Low

P237D concerns the same drive line as P237C, the one that operates bypass flap A of an exhaust heat recovery unit, but here the module measures a voltage that sits too low – the usual picture of a control wire touching ground or an actuator shorted internally. Moisture in a connector under the car can produce exactly that.

Control wire chafed through against the body or exhaust bracket
Slower heater response after a cold start
P237E: Exhaust Heat Exchanger Exhaust Bypass Valve A Control Circuit High

P237E is logged when the driver for exhaust bypass flap A on a heat recovery unit sees a control voltage above its expected range. The likely story is a short from the control wire to a supply feed or an actuator whose internal driver has failed in a way that pulls the line up. The flap then no longer follows the warm-up strategy.
Heat exchanger bypass actuator with failed internal driver (Ford F-150 SSM 53003)
Control wire shorted to a supply circuit in the harness
Cabin heat may build up later on cold days
P237F: Exhaust Heat Exchanger Exhaust Bypass Valve A Control Performance
P237F is not about wiring of the drive but about the result: the bypass flap A of the exhaust heat recovery unit was commanded, yet the effect the module expects does not appear.
Water, corrosion or torn seal at the exhaust coolant temperature sensor 3/4 connectors (Ford SSM 52543)

Bypass actuator or flap sluggish, sticking or worn
P2380: P2380 is the general circuit code for EGR sensor D. Which sensor carries the letter D is up to the maker.
Internal fault reported by the smart EGR pressure sensor
Corroded or loose connector at the sensor
Unstable supply or ground to the sensor
Possibly slight knock tendency or higher NOx with EGR reduced
P2381: P2381 means the signal of EGR sensor D is stuck at the top of its electrical range.
Open sensor ground or reference return
Chafed engine harness shorting the signal to a supply (GM 21-NA-149)

P2383: P2383 flags an EGR sensor D whose signal is electrically fine but makes no sense. Two published strategies show how differently makers test it.
Sensor hoses swapped, cracked or disconnected (Ford EGRP)
Sensor drifted so that it reads a pressure difference with the engine off (GM)

P2384: P2384 marks an EGR sensor D signal that jumps or drops out for brief moments without staying at a fixed fault level.

P2386: P2386 says the signal of EGR sensor E sits at or above the upper end of its electrical range. P2387: P2387 is stored when the signal of EGR sensor E falls below its valid electrical range. Further low-voltage codes on sensors sharing the same reference
P2388: P2388 covers an EGR sensor E whose signal is electrically valid but does not agree with what the engine controller expects from the operating state. Typical tests compare the reading with a known condition, such as zero pressure difference with the engine off, or with a modelled value from other sensors. No manufacturer documents P2388 publicly.
Sensing hoses blocked, cracked or swapped
Soot deposits at the sensor port
Sensor E reading implausible at engine off
P2389: P2389 points to an EGR sensor E signal that is mostly plausible but now and then jumps, spikes or drops out. Engine controllers detect this by watching the rate of change between consecutive readings rather than absolute limits.
Weak pin tension or unlatched connector
Harness damaged by heat or rubbing near the exhaust
Sensor with an intermittent internal fault
MIL on, sometimes going out again
Fault cannot be reproduced at the workshop
Jumps visible in the sensor E data stream
P238A: Water in Fuel Sensor B Circuit
P238A is the general circuit code for water-in-fuel sensor B, used where a diesel has two water-detecting points, for example a frame-mounted primary filter and a second separator.
Water or corrosion in the sensor B connector at the chassis filter
Damaged harness along the frame rail
No warning for real water in the chassis filter
P238B: Water in Fuel Sensor B Circuit Range/Performance

P238B means water-in-fuel sensor B delivers a signal that is electrically valid but implausible, for instance a value stuck between the clear dry and wet states, or a self-test answer that arrives at the wrong moment. No manufacturer documents P238B publicly.
Dirt film or deposits on the sensor electrodes
Residual water or emulsion around the probe after incomplete draining
Water-in-fuel warning without water being found
P238C: Water in Fuel Sensor B Circuit Low

P238C is set when the signal line of water-in-fuel sensor B stays below its valid range. Because the sensor reads conductivity, anything that bridges its terminals or pulls the signal to ground can cause it: a chafed wire, a wet connector or a sensor body full of water. No manufacturer documents P238C publicly.
Water bridging the terminals in the sensor connector
Signal wire chafed through to ground on the frame
Fault appears after washing or rain
P238D: Water in Fuel Sensor B Circuit High
P238D reports that the signal of water-in-fuel sensor B sits above its valid range, usually from an open circuit, a disconnected sensor or a short to voltage.
Spray water in the connector at the chassis-mounted fuel filter
Corroded terminals on harness or filter housing side
Sensor in the filter housing failed
Water-in-fuel lamp or message on at low mileage
P238E: Water in Fuel Sensor B Circuit Intermittent
P238E is meant for a water-in-fuel sensor B circuit whose signal flickers or drops out for short periods instead of staying at one fault level. No manufacturer documents P238E publicly.
Moisture entering and drying out in the connector
Loose terminals losing contact on rough roads
Broken harness clips letting the wire rub on the frame
Water-in-fuel lamp flickering or coming and going
Fault not present when tested at the workshop
P238F: Water in Fuel Condition - Sensor B
P238F is no wiring fault: it states that water-in-fuel sensor B has detected water, meaning the separator at that point has collected enough to bridge the probe.
Water collected in the chassis filter separator
Fuel contaminated with water from tank or filling station
Separator drained incompletely after an earlier warning
Rough running or power loss if water reaches the injection system
P2390: Diesel Intake Air Flow B Control Circuit/Open

P2390 concerns the drive circuit of the second electronically operated intake throttle that some diesel engines carry; which flap a maker labels A or B is its own choice. With the driver switched off, the engine module checks whether the motor circuit is closed; an open wire, a pulled connector or a burnt motor winding sets this code.
Connector at the B throttle unplugged, loose or with pushed-back terminals
Broken motor lead in the harness between module and throttle
Open motor winding inside the throttle unit
Faulty output stage in the engine control module
MIL on, often without a noticeable change in driving
Particulate filter regeneration delayed or blocked
Engine may shake more when switched off because the flap no longer closes
P2391: Diesel Intake Air Flow B Control Performance

P2391 compares where the B intake throttle should be with where its position sensor says it is. If the gap stays too large under a steady command, the module concludes that the flap is sluggish or obstructed, typically by soot and oil deposits from EGR and crankcase gases, a worn gear stage or a weak motor. No published manufacturer table covers P2391.
Soot and oil deposits making the B flap stiff
Worn plastic gears or shaft bearing in the throttle unit
Weak motor or high resistance in the drive circuit
Position sensor reporting an offset angle
Regeneration of the particulate filter does not complete
Occasionally reduced power or uneven response
P2392: Diesel Intake Air Flow B Control Circuit Low

P2392 is set when the module finds the motor output for the B intake throttle pulled towards ground, for example by a chafed wire touching the engine, water inside the connector or a shorted motor. The output stage protects itself and switches off. No manufacturer documents P2392 publicly.
Motor lead chafed through and touching engine or body ground
Water or corrosion in the throttle connector
Internal short of the throttle motor to its housing
Damaged H-bridge in the engine control module
MIL on, code returns immediately after clearing
Little or no change in driving
P2393: Diesel Intake Air Flow B Control Circuit High

P2393 is the counterpart of P2392: one of the B-throttle motor leads has contact with battery voltage, for example through a pinched harness or a bridged pin in the connector, so the output stage sees an overcurrent as soon as it switches. No manufacturer publishes P2393.
Motor lead pinched against a live wire or terminal
Bridged pins in the connector (moisture, corrosion)
Shorted turns in the throttle motor
Faulty output stage in the engine control module
Possibly blown fuse or further circuit codes on the same supply
P2394: Diesel Intake Air Flow B Control Stuck Open

P2394 means the B intake throttle remains wider open than requested even though the module drives its motor hard towards closing. A flap that cannot throttle fails to create the manifold depression that strong exhaust recirculation and regeneration heating depend on. No manufacturer documents P2394 openly.
Deposits holding the flap in an open position
Broken gear tooth or stripped drive between motor and shaft
Motor too weak to overcome the return spring
Foreign object or broken part blocking the flap
Frequent or failing particulate filter regenerations
P2395: Diesel Intake Air Flow B Control Stuck Closed

P2395 reports a B intake throttle that remains nearer to its closed stop than the module asks for. Of the two stuck faults this is the more serious one, because a flap jammed near its seat starves the engine of air. No manufacturer publishes thresholds for P2395.
Deposits locking the flap near its closed stop
Broken return spring, flap no longer opens when unpowered
Jammed gear train or seized shaft bearing
Ice on the shaft or flap after cold, damp conditions
Marked loss of power, limp mode
Rough running or stalling in severe cases
P2396: Diesel Intake Air Flow B Position Sensor Circuit
P2396 is the general electrical fault of the sensor that reports the angle of the B intake throttle, a potentiometer or, on newer units, a contactless Hall sensor with analogue or SENT output.
Damaged reference, ground or signal wire
Failed position sensor in the throttle unit
Flap switched off, EGR runs with limited control
P2397: Diesel Intake Air Flow B Position Sensor Range/Performance

P2397 covers a B-throttle position signal that stays inside its electrical window but does not make sense, for instance a reading that does not move when the motor is driven, or one that disagrees with the commanded angle. CARB asks for such rationality checks on inputs wherever feasible. No published manufacturer table covers P2397.
Sticking flap that lags behind the command
Worn potentiometer track or drifting sensor
Contact resistance in connector or signal wire
Play between gear and flap shaft
Displayed flap angle does not follow the command
P2398: Diesel Intake Air Flow B Position Sensor Circuit Low

P2398 is logged when the position signal of the B intake throttle falls below its lower limit. Likely reasons are a signal lead shorted to ground, a lost 5 V supply, or a broken signal wire that the module input pulls low; on SENT sensors the transmitted raw value can also leave its range. No manufacturer documents P2398 itself.
Open 5 V reference or open signal wire
Shared 5 V reference pulled down by another faulty sensor
Further 5 V sensor codes at the same time
P2399: Diesel Intake Air Flow B Position Sensor Circuit High

P2399 is the upper-limit counterpart of P2398: the B-throttle position signal reads higher than any real flap angle can produce. That usually points to a lost sensor ground, a signal wire touching the 5 V reference or battery voltage, or water bridging the terminals in the connector. No manufacturer is known to publish P2399.
Signal wire shorted to 5 V reference or battery voltage
Moisture bridging terminals in the connector
P239A: Diesel Intake Air Flow B Position Sensor Circuit Intermittent/Erratic

P239A describes a B-throttle position signal that keeps jumping or dropping out for short moments, too briefly to set the low or high code. Loose terminals, a harness that cracks as the engine rocks, corrosion or a worn potentiometer track are typical; on digital SENT sensors corrupted messages have the same effect.
Loose or corroded terminals in the sensor connector
Wire breaking or rubbing intermittently with engine movement
Worn potentiometer track or faulty SENT sensor electronics
Electrical interference on the signal line
Code stored without a permanent fault on testing
P239B: Diesel Intake Air Flow B Control Motor Current Range/Performance

P239B checks the current the B-throttle motor draws while its H-bridge is switched on. A blocked or very stiff flap, a partly shorted winding or the two motor leads touching each other push the current beyond what the module expects. No manufacturer publishes P239B with values.
Flap blocked or very stiff, motor running at stall current
Short between the two motor leads in harness or connector
Faulty current measurement in the control module
Flap switched off and resting at spring position
Often stored together with P2391 or the stuck codes
P239C: Diesel Intake Air Flow B Control System - High Air Flow Detected

P239C belongs to the air-mass control loop rather than to the throttle alone: with the B intake throttle taking part in that control, the module sees more fresh air than its target and cannot bring the reading down even at the limit of its authority.
EGR valve stuck closed or EGR cooler clogged
B throttle unable to close far enough
No noticeable driving change in most cases
Often stored together with EGR flow codes
P239D: Diesel Intake Air Flow B Control System - Low Air Flow Detected
P239D is the mirror image of P239C: the measured fresh-air mass remains below target although the control loop involving the B intake throttle is already at its limit.
Clogged air filter or restricted charge-air path
Contaminated air-mass meter reading too low
Loss of power, possibly limp mode
P239E: O2 Sensor Out of Range During Deceleration (Bank 1 Sensor 2) - Duplicate Listing of P232F

P239E carries in common code lists exactly the same wording as P232F: a downstream oxygen sensor on bank 1 reading outside its expected window while fuel is cut on deceleration. No manufacturer, OBD summary or service bulletin on record uses P239E, and no source gives it a meaning of its own.
Scan tool code table showing the duplicate number instead of the maker's code
Aged or drifting rear oxygen sensor on bank 1
Exhaust leak ahead of the rear sensor
MIL on without noticeable driving change
Code text in the scan tool contradicts the manufacturer's documentation
P239F: O2 Sensor Out of Range During Deceleration (Bank 2 Sensor 2) - Duplicate Listing of P2379
P239F appears in code lists with the identical title already given to P2379: the post-catalyst oxygen sensor of bank 2 is out of range while the injectors are switched off on a closed throttle.
Scan tool listing the duplicate number for a maker-specific fault
Aged rear oxygen sensor on bank 2
Air leak in the bank 2 exhaust ahead of the sensor
P23A0: O2 Sensor Exhaust Sample Error (Bank 1 Sensor 2) - Duplicate Listing of P237A

P23A0 repeats, word for word, the title of P237A in the usual code lists: the rear oxygen sensor of bank 1 does not see, or does not report, a representative sample of post-catalyst exhaust. No manufacturer uses P23A0 in any published OBD table or service bulletin, and no source defines it differently, so it is a duplicate listing of P237A.
Scan tool code table using the duplicate number
Air leak in the exhaust ahead of the rear sensor on bank 1
Sensor mounted poorly or element contaminated
P23A1: O2 Sensor Exhaust Sample Error (Bank 2 Sensor 2) - Duplicate Listing of P237B

P23A1 is listed with the same title as P237B: the bank 2 oxygen sensor behind the catalyst reports something that cannot be genuine exhaust from that bank. Only engines with two exhaust banks and a downstream sensor on each side could produce it.
Scan tool reporting the duplicate number
Leak in the bank 2 exhaust pipe ahead of the rear sensor
Damaged wiring or connector of the bank 2 rear sensor
Readiness for catalyst monitor stays open
P23A2: Exhaust Heat Exchanger Exhaust Bypass Valve B Control Circuit/Open

P23A2 reports an open or otherwise broken drive circuit for the second exhaust bypass flap, valve B, of an exhaust heat exchanger. Such units route the exhaust through a coolant heat exchanger after a cold start and send it past once engine and cabin are warm; a valve B only exists where the layout needs two flaps. No manufacturer documents P23A2 publicly.
Connector at the valve B actuator loose, corroded or unplugged
Control wire broken near the hot exhaust or at a harness clip
Actuator coil or internal electronics of valve B open
Slower engine and cabin warm-up in cold weather
No change in how the vehicle drives
P23A3: Exhaust Heat Exchanger Exhaust Bypass Valve B Control Circuit Low

With P23A3 the module sees the control line of exhaust bypass valve B sitting lower than its commanded state allows, which usually means that the wire or the driver stage of the actuator has found a path to ground. Water or road salt in a connector under the vehicle is a typical trigger. P23A3 itself appears in no public manufacturer document.
Control wire chafed through and touching body or exhaust ground
Moisture or salt bridging pins in the actuator connector
Internal short in the valve B actuator
Heater output builds up slowly after a cold start
Fault may reappear after rain or washing
P23A4: Exhaust Heat Exchanger Exhaust Bypass Valve B Control Circuit High

P23A4 is stored when the control circuit of exhaust heat exchanger bypass valve B reads higher than expected – a short to a battery feed, a chafed wire touching another supply, or an actuator whose electronics pull the line up. Because the flap no longer obeys, the warm-up strategy has to run without it.
Control wire shorted to a 12 V feed in the harness
Failed electronics inside the valve B actuator
Output stage in the controlling module faulty
Bypass flap does not respond to an actuator test
P23A5: Exhaust Heat Exchanger Exhaust Bypass Valve B Control Performance

Unlike the circuit codes, P23A5 judges the result: the module commanded valve B, the second exhaust bypass at the heat exchanger, but it does not see the response it expects, for example in position feedback or in how the exhaust-side coolant temperatures change. No manufacturer publishes P23A5.
Flap of valve B sluggish from soot or corrosion
Exhaust coolant temperature sensor connector wet or corroded, distorting the plausibility check
Overly strict calibration, fixed by a software update
Cabin heat slow to arrive in winter
P23A6: Exhaust Heat Exchanger Exhaust Bypass Valve B Stuck Open
P23A6 says that bypass valve B of the exhaust heat exchanger stays open while the module wants it closed.
Flap seized in the open position by carbon or corrosion
Linkage between actuator and flap broken or detached
Actuator no longer able to move the flap
Engine and heater take noticeably longer to warm up
Hybrid engine runs more often in cold weather
P23A7: Exhaust Heat Exchanger Exhaust Bypass Valve B Stuck Closed

P23A7 is the opposite of P23A6: the second bypass valve (B) on the exhaust heat exchanger does not open on command and stays closed. Depending on the layout, all exhaust is then forced through the heat exchanger even when the engine is fully warm, which adds heat to the coolant and some back pressure – most relevant under load and in hot weather.
Flap stuck closed by deposits or corrosion
Damaged or water-filled heat exchanger obstructing the flap
Coolant temperature higher than usual under load
Possibly reduced power or a changed exhaust note
P23A8: Exhaust Heat Exchanger Exhaust Bypass Valve B Position Sensor Stop Performance

P23A8 concerns the position feedback of exhaust bypass valve B at its mechanical end stops. Systems with a position sensor learn the readings at the fully open and the fully closed stop and compare later readings with them; if a stop value drifts out of its window, or the flap no longer reaches the stop at all, this code is set.
Deposits or a bent flap keep valve B from reaching its end stop
Position sensor in the actuator drifted or loose
End stops not relearned after a repair
Valve position in live data does not reach the expected end value
P23A9: P23A9 records that the engine was stopped, or kept from running, because the engine module lost contact with a control unit whose messages it needs to operate the engine safely. The title names only the consequence; which data link is meant is defined by each manufacturer, and none publishes P23A9.
Damaged CAN wiring, connector or termination
Partner module without power or ground, or low battery voltage
Failed or wrongly programmed partner module
Software versions of the modules not matching after repair

MIL or other warning lights on
P23AA: P23AA concerns bypass valve A of a turbocharger or supercharger, which opens a path around the compressor to relieve boost when the throttle closes or at part load. The code means the valve no longer follows its command and sits fixed.
Valve or actuator mechanically seized (deposits, wear)
Faulty electric actuator or position sensor of the valve
High resistance in wiring or connector
Fluttering or surging noise when lifting off
MIL on, possibly limited power mode
P23AB: A NOx sensor is a smart part: the probe in the exhaust is wired to a small control unit with its own processor, which runs the heater, evaluates the cell currents and reports over CAN. P23AB means that this electronics in sensor 3 of bank 1 – usually the one behind a second SCR catalyst – reports an internal error or fails its self-checks.
Internal electronics of the sensor 3 control unit defective
Supply voltage dips or poor ground resetting the sensor electronics
Sensor control unit damaged by heat or water ingress
Sensor 3 values missing or frozen in live data
SCR or emissions warning on the display

The sensor's own control unit watches the leads between its electronics and the ceramic probe and tells the engine computer over CAN whether a measuring circuit is open or shorted; the user manual of Drivven's NOx sensor module kit, published by NI, lists these status states for the N…

Corroded or loose terminals at the sensor 3 connectors
Probe or sensor electronics failed internally
No NOx reading from sensor 3 in live data
P23AD: P23AD flags the third NOx sensor on bank 1 as electrically intact but not trustworthy.
Aged or poisoned sensing cell giving unstable pump currents
High contact resistance in the sensor 3 wiring
Exhaust leak near the sensor upsetting the measurement

Sensor 3 NOx value jumps in live data
SCR efficiency monitor may not complete
P23AE: P23AE is set when the third NOx sensor on bank 1 reports a concentration below anything physically possible.
Engine harness chafed, disturbing the sensor 3 supply or signal
Sensor 3 with a negative offset from ageing or damage
Check engine light after two trips
Negative or zero NOx value for sensor 3 in live data
Other harness-related codes stored at the same time

GM's 2025 diesel table 25OBDG04B sets the code when the raw reading of the post-second-catalyst sensor exceeds 2,990 ppm in 120 of 240 samples, provided the air system control is active or DEF dosing is ready; the rating is Type B, so the MIL follows on the second trip.
Wire broken inside the insulation near a connector in the exhaust sensor harness
Sensor 3 failed with a reading stuck high
Short between sensor lines in the harness
Check engine light after two trips

P23B0: P23B0 is meant for a third NOx sensor on bank 1 whose circuit faults come and go instead of staying present, so the status the sensor module reports over CAN keeps toggling between valid and faulty.
Loose or fretting terminal in a sensor 3 connector
Harness rubbing or flexing near the exhaust, breaking contact under vibration
Moisture entering a connector in wet weather
Check engine light that goes out and returns
Sensor 3 value drops out briefly in live data
P23B1: NOx Sensor Heater Control Circuit/Open (Bank 1 Sensor 3)
A NOx sensor only measures once its built-in heater has brought the ceramic element up to temperature. P23B1 reports that the heater control side of the third sensor on bank 1 is open.
Heater element in the sensor 3 probe burnt through
Broken heater conductor between probe and sensor module
Probe connector not fully engaged after a repair
Check engine light after one trip
P23B2: NOx Sensor Heater Control Circuit Low (Bank 1 Sensor 3)
P23B2 points to the heater control line of bank 1's NOx sensor 3 being pulled to ground.
Heater control wire chafed against ground
Internal short in the heater of sensor 3
Water bridging the heater pins in the connector
Check engine light after two trips
Sensor 3 slow or unable to become ready
P23B3: NOx Sensor Heater Control Circuit High (Bank 1 Sensor 3)
If, on NOx sensor 3 of bank 1, the heater control pin sits at supply voltage when the electronics expect it to switch, P23B3 is stored.
Heater control wire shorted to a supply line
Heater driver inside the sensor 3 electronics failed
Check engine light after two trips
Sensor 3 heater status shows an error in live data
P23B4: NOx Sensor Heater Sense Circuit (Bank 1 Sensor 3)

Besides its drive line, the heater of a NOx sensor has a sense connection through which its resistance, and with it the element temperature, is measured. P23B4 reports a fault in that sense path for the third sensor on bank 1.
Heater sense lead broken between probe and module
Backed-out or corroded terminal at the probe connector
Internal break in the sensor 3 probe
Check engine light after one trip
P23B5: NOx Sensor Heater Sense Circuit Range/Performance (Bank 1 Sensor 3)
P23B5 says the heater feedback from NOx sensor 3 (bank 1) is present but implausible: the element does not reach or hold the resistance that matches its target temperature.

Aged heater element whose resistance no longer matches the target
Blown fuse in the NOx sensor supply after a short

Check engine light after one trip

P23B6: NOx Sensor Supply Voltage Circuit (Bank 1 Sensor 3)

P23B6 concerns the power feed of the third NOx sensor on bank 1, the smart probe behind the second SCR catalyst. Its built-in control unit needs a stable supply, and when the voltage it reports leaves the allowed range the engine module stores this code.
Blown fuse in the NOx sensor supply after a short elsewhere in the harness
Supply or ground wire chafed through on the engine or frame (GM 3.0L LM2)
Corroded or loose pins in the sensor 3 connector under the vehicle
Weak battery or charging fault pulling the sensor supply down
Check engine light after two trips
Sensor 3 shows no NOx value in live data
Further NOx sensor or communication codes stored at the same time
P23B7: NOx Sensor Heater Control Circuit Range/Performance (Bank 1 Sensor 3)

P23B7 is set when the heater drive of NOx sensor 3 on bank 1 looks electrically sound but does not behave as the control strategy expects, for instance a heater duty cycle far from what the element should need to reach operating temperature.
Aged heater element that needs far more or less power than expected
High resistance in heater supply or ground contacts
Sensor supply voltage at the lower limit, so the heater cannot keep up
Sensor 3 takes long to become ready or drops out of its active state
P23B8: NOx Sensor Heater Sense Circuit Low (Bank 1 Sensor 3)
Smart NOx sensors report heater temperature through a separate sense connection, which GM calls the HTemp pin. P23B8 means this line on sensor 3 of bank 1 is pulled to ground.
Sense wire chafed through and touching body, frame or exhaust ground
Water or salt bridging the sense pin to ground in the connector
Internal short in the sensor or its control unit
Check engine light after two trips
Sensor 3 does not report valid NOx values
Often stored together with other wiring-related codes
P23B9: NOx Sensor Heater Sense Circuit High (Bank 1 Sensor 3)

P23B9 is the counterpart of P23B8: the temperature feedback wire of NOx sensor 3 on bank 1 carries a voltage that only a short to battery or to another live wire can explain. The sensor then cannot report a trustworthy heater temperature, so it withholds its NOx output.
Sense wire shorted to the heater supply or another battery-fed wire
Harness insulation melted by contact with hot exhaust parts
Internal fault in the sensor or its control unit
Check engine light after two trips
Possibly a blown fuse in the sensor supply
P23BA: NOx Sensor Heater Sense Circuit Intermittent (Bank 1 Sensor 3)

With P23BA, the heater feedback signal from the third NOx sensor of bank 1 keeps vanishing or leaping for a moment and then recovers, rather than staying broken. P23BA itself is not described in any public manufacturer document.
Terminal in the sensor 3 connector with weak contact pressure
Sense lead cracked by vibration or heat and opening only at times
Moisture entering the plug through a damaged seal
Check engine light that comes and goes
Sensor 3 briefly leaves its ready state

P23BB: P23BB says the heater element of NOx sensor 3 on bank 1 has a resistance outside its permitted band. Because the resistance of the ceramic heater climbs with temperature, it doubles as the thermometer of the probe, so an aged or cracked element heats poorly and reports a false temperature as well. No manufacturer publishes P23BB.
Heater element aged by long service at high exhaust temperature
Element cracked by water droplets hitting the hot ceramic
Added resistance from a corroded heater contact
Sensor 3 slow to become ready after a cold start
Implausible NOx readings from the rear sensor
P23BC: Every smart NOx sensor carries its own control unit with a memory holding trim and reference data written for that individual probe at the factory. P23BC means this memory in sensor 3 on bank 1 cannot be read or fails its integrity check, so the engine module can no longer trust the readings. No manufacturer documents P23BC publicly.
Memory inside the sensor control unit corrupted or failed
Voltage dips or spikes on the sensor supply disturbing the memory
Replacement sensor with a calibration that does not match the vehicle
Sensor 3 readings ignored by the engine module
P23BD: NOx Sensor Performance - Signal Biased/Stuck High (Bank 1 Sensor 3)
P23BD means NOx sensor 3 on bank 1, the last probe downstream of the second SCR catalyst, reports more NOx than the operating state allows, or its value no longer comes down from a high level.
Measuring cell drifted upward with age or contamination
Monitor calibration too strict, fixed by an engine software update
Sensor element damaged by thermal shock or poisoning

Sensor 3 reading stays high in overrun
P23BE: NOx Sensor Performance - Signal Biased/Stuck Low (Bank 1 Sensor 3)

P23BE is the low-side mirror of P23BD: NOx sensor 3 on bank 1 shows less NOx than is plausible, or it stays near zero while the engine is clearly producing some. Behind a working SCR system the true value is small anyway, which makes a low-stuck sensor the more dangerous error for monitoring, because it can hide a failing catalyst.
Exhaust leak or air drawn in ahead of sensor 3, diluting the gas
Measuring cell lost sensitivity and reads too low
Sensor not seated correctly so it samples too little exhaust
Sensor 3 reads near zero under load
Possibly an audible exhaust leak at the rear section
P23BF: NOx Sensor Performance - Slow Response Low to High (Bank 1 Sensor 3)

P23BF concerns how quickly NOx sensor 3 on bank 1 follows a rise in NOx. The control module waits for an increasing transient and times the climb of the sensor signal against what a model predicts. No manufacturer publishes P23BF.
Soot, oil ash or urea residue blocking the gas inlet of the sensor
Measuring cells aged beyond their response specification
Element running too cold because the heater is weak
Sensor 3 signal trails the front sensor during acceleration
No change in how the engine runs
P23C0: NOx Sensor Performance - Slow Response High to Low (Bank 1 Sensor 3)

With P23C0 the third NOx sensor on bank 1 is too sluggish when NOx falls, for instance when the driver lifts off and the engine goes into fuel cut-off. The module measures how long the reading takes to come down between two levels. No manufacturer documents P23C0 publicly.

Holes in the protective tube partly blocked by soot or urea crystals
Sensor aged and no longer able to release its reading quickly
Sensor 3 value stays raised for seconds after lifting off
P23C1: NOx Sensor Performance - Sensing Element (Bank 1 Sensor 3)
P23C1 asks whether the measuring cells of NOx sensor 3 on bank 1 have lost sensitivity, for example because deposits clog the internal cavities.
Internal measuring cavities clogged by ash or other deposits
Sensing cells worn out after high mileage
Wiring fault upsetting the sensor supply during the test (GM 3.0L LM2)
Check engine light after one trip
No noticeable change in engine behaviour
