Poor cold starts on high ethanol blends
Engine warning lamp, depending on manufacturer
P23D1: Instead of one heater for the whole rail, some flex-fuel systems give every cylinder its own heating path, either a heated injector or an element at each rail outlet. P23D1 is the open or general circuit fault on the path for cylinder 1, so that cylinder gets unheated ethanol during a cold start.
Burnt-out heater at cylinder 1 (heated injector or rail element)
Broken wire or unplugged heater connector at cylinder 1
Corroded terminals in the cylinder 1 heater connector
Failed channel 1 output in the fuel heater control module
Cylinder 1 misfire right after a cold start on ethanol
Rough idle until the engine warms up
Engine warning lamp, depending on manufacturer
P23D2: Cylinder 1 Fuel Heater Control Circuit High
P23D2 is the high-voltage fault on the cylinder 1 heater circuit; note that in this series the high code comes before the low code (P23D3).
Cylinder 1 heater control wire shorted to a positive feed
Channel 1 switching element stuck on in the heater unit
Damaged connector letting the heater pin touch a supply pin
Cylinder 1 heater stays on, higher current draw
Engine warning lamp, depending on manufacturer
P23D3: Cylinder 1 Fuel Heater Control Circuit Low
P23D3 reports that the control circuit of the cylinder 1 fuel heater is pulled toward ground. It follows the high code P23D2 in the numbering, not the other way round.
Cylinder 1 heater wire chafed to ground on the intake or engine
Heater at cylinder 1 shorted to its housing
Fuel or water in the cylinder 1 heater connector
Shorted channel 1 output in the heater unit
Single-cylinder misfire on cold ethanol starts
Blown fuse in the fuel heater circuit
Engine warning lamp, depending on manufacturer
P23D4: P23D4 is not about wiring at all: the cylinder 1 heater circuit is electrically intact, yet it fails to heat as it should. The heater unit measures what each heat circuit delivers, so a heater that draws too little current, warms too slowly or reaches a lower temperature than its neighbours stands out.
Aged cylinder 1 heater with reduced heating power
High-resistance connection in the cylinder 1 heater circuit
Deposits reducing heat transfer at a heated injector
Low battery voltage during the heating phase
Cylinder 1 runs rough for a while after a cold start on ethanol
Engine warning lamp, depending on manufacturer
P23D5: Cylinder 2 has its own fuel heating path on flex-fuel engines that warm the fuel per cylinder, and P23D5 says this path carries no current although the heater is commanded on, or the control line shows a general fault. To the heater unit the open simply looks like a missing load on channel 2.
Heater at cylinder 2 burnt through (open element)
Cylinder 2 heater plug loose or not latched after intake work
Broken conductor in the cylinder 2 heater lead
Channel 2 output of the heater control unit failed
Cylinder 2 misfires briefly after a cold start on ethanol
Uneven idle in the first minute when cold
Engine warning lamp, depending on manufacturer
P23D6: Cylinder 2 Fuel Heater Control Circuit High

P23D6 flags the control circuit of the cylinder 2 fuel heater as high. A heater driver typically checks the line both with the channel off and with it on; a level that stays near supply voltage in both states points to a control wire touching a positive feed or to a driver that no longer pulls the circuit down.
Cylinder 2 heater control wire touching a positive feed
Switching FET of channel 2 failed in the conducting state
Bent connector pin touching a supply terminal
Heater at cylinder 2 runs on or does not switch
Engine warning lamp, depending on manufacturer
P23D7: Cylinder 2 Fuel Heater Control Circuit Low

For P23D7 the module reads the cylinder 2 heater control line as low, which on these power circuits nearly always means a path to ground: a chafed wire, a heater element shorted to its body, or fuel or water bridging the connector pins.
Cylinder 2 heater wire chafed through to ground
Heating element at cylinder 2 shorted to its housing
Fuel or water bridging pins in the cylinder 2 heater plug
Rough cold start on one cylinder
Engine warning lamp, depending on manufacturer
P23D8: P23D8 concerns how well the cylinder 2 heater works, not its wiring. According to Bosch, the Flexstart heated rail warms pure ethanol fuel at rates of as much as 30 °C a second, so a system of this kind knows roughly how quickly each heating point ought to warm up.
Cylinder 2 heater element with reduced output
Varnish or scale on the heated surface at cylinder 2
Corroded contact dropping voltage under heater load
Cylinder 2 runs rough for about a minute after a cold ethanol start
Engine warning lamp, depending on manufacturer
P23D9: P23D9 is the open-circuit or general circuit fault of the heating path for cylinder 3. The fuel heater control unit drives each heater through a channel of its own; when channel 3 is switched on but no load current appears, the connection to the heater is considered broken.
Terminal pushed out of the cylinder 3 heater connector
Wire broken where the harness flexes near the rail
Failed channel 3 output in the heater unit
Stumble on cylinder 3 after a cold ethanol start
Engine warning lamp, depending on manufacturer
P23DA: Cylinder 3 Fuel Heater Control Circuit High

P23DA tells that the control side of the cylinder 3 heater sits at a high level. The likely pictures are a control wire touching a positive feed, so voltage stays on the line when the channel is off, or an output stage that has failed conducting, so heater 3 runs without command.
Cylinder 3 control wire shorted to a positive feed
Flat battery after the car has stood for some hours
Heater at cylinder 3 warm long after switch-off
Engine warning lamp, depending on manufacturer
P23DB: Cylinder 3 Fuel Heater Control Circuit Low
With P23DB the cylinder 3 heater control circuit is too low, meaning the line or the heater itself has found a path to ground.
Water in the cylinder 3 heater connector
Harness chafed through at a damaged clip near the rail
Heated injector at cylinder 3 shorted internally
Engine warning lamp, depending on manufacturer
P23DC: P23DC is set when the heating at cylinder 3 works electrically but delivers too little effect. Bosch writes that its heater unit follows the heat output of all four circuits and hands a temperature reading to the engine controller, so a channel that warms more weakly than the others can be singled out.
Cylinder 3 heating element below its rated output
High-resistance crimp or plug in the cylinder 3 heater circuit
Misfire on cylinder 3 during warm-up on ethanol
Lean running in the first minutes
Engine warning lamp, depending on manufacturer
P23DD: P23DD reports an open or general fault on the fourth and last heating channel. Bosch builds its heater unit with exactly four heat circuits and its heated rail for either three- or four-cylinder operation, so this code belongs to four-cylinder layouts.
Heater plug at cylinder 4 left loose after intake work
Dead channel 4 in the heater control unit
Uneven running on one cylinder for the first seconds after a cold start
Engine warning lamp, depending on manufacturer
P23DE: Cylinder 4 Fuel Heater Control Circuit High

P23DE means the cylinder 4 heater control circuit is at a high level where the module expects otherwise. Either the line has contact with a voltage source, or the driving stage no longer switches off, so heater 4 may keep running.
Channel 4 driver no longer switching off
Cylinder 4 heater line touching a voltage source
Connectors swapped or mismated after repair
Hard restart when the engine is hot
Engine warning lamp, depending on manufacturer
P23DF: Cylinder 4 Fuel Heater Control Circuit Low
P23DF marks the cylinder 4 heater control circuit as low, which in practice is a short to ground between the control unit and the heater. The channel then stays off until the next start.
Chafed insulation on the cylinder 4 heater lead at the rail end
Heating element at cylinder 4 shorted to its housing
Moisture in the cylinder 4 heater plug
Shorted channel 4 output in the heater unit
Rough cold start on one cylinder
Engine warning lamp, depending on manufacturer
P23E0: P23E0 judges the effect of the cylinder 4 heater rather than its wiring: the circuit is intact, but the heat delivered or the temperature reached falls short of what the conditions call for. One factor specific to resistive heaters is supply voltage.
Aged heater at cylinder 4 with reduced output
Poor contact in the cylinder 4 heater circuit
Weak battery or low system voltage during heating
Rough start in cold weather on high-ethanol fuel
Engine warning lamp, depending on manufacturer
P23E1: P23E1 covers the electrical drive of EGR valve C, a third exhaust gas recirculation actuator next to valves A and B. Which valve carries the letter C is up to the manufacturer; no carmaker documents P23E1 publicly. The code means the module has found the control circuit open or otherwise faulty.
Unplugged or corroded connector at EGR valve C
Open motor winding or solenoid coil in valve C
Broken drive wire between engine module and valve C
Warning lamp with otherwise normal driving
P23E2: P23E2 is raised when the drive circuit of EGR valve C is electrically intact but the valve does not respond to it as expected: commanded and measured position, or drive current and movement, drift apart.
Soot and lacquer making valve C sluggish
Worn gears or linkage in the valve C actuator
Actuator motor of valve C losing torque
Occasional hesitation when EGR is cut
P23E3: P23E3 says the control circuit of EGR valve C reads low. On motor or solenoid driven EGR valves this mostly means one of the drive lines has a short to ground, so the output stage would draw excessive current or sees a level it cannot produce by itself.
Drive wire of valve C shorted to ground
Internal short in the valve C motor or coil
Faulty output stage in the engine module
Warning lamp, little change in driving
P23E4: P23E4 is the high counterpart: the control circuit of EGR valve C carries a level that is too high. Typical are a drive line touching a battery feed, a connector pin bent onto a supply terminal, or an output stage that no longer pulls its side low.
Drive wire of valve C touching a battery feed
Bent pin in the valve C connector
Engine module output stage not pulling low
Valve C moves unexpectedly or not at all
P23E5: P23E5 means EGR valve C stays open although it is commanded closed. The 2018 GM diesel calibration decides the A-side code P042E like this: once the driver is switched off, the return spring should bring the valve to its closed default within 2 s; if the measured position is still above 5 % after that, the code sets at once as Type A, MIL on the first trip.
Carbon deposits holding valve C open
Broken return spring in valve C
Warning lamp on the first trip
P23E6: With P23E6 the module concludes that EGR valve C does not open when commanded and stays at or near its closed stop. The consequence is the reverse of P23E5: the engine runs smoothly, but the exhaust share from this path is missing, combustion temperature and NOx go up, and a petrol engine may knock more readily.
Valve C glued shut by soot
Seized shaft or stripped drive gear
Actuator motor too weak to break the valve free
No change in driving, but higher NOx
P23E7: P23E7 means the module calculates less recirculated exhaust through path C than it expects for the current operating point. The valve may well move correctly; the gas simply does not get through, for example because the passage, cooler or valve seat is choked with soot.
Soot-choked EGR passage or valve seat on path C
Clogged EGR cooler in path C
Air mass or pressure sensor reading off, skewing the calculation
P23E8: P23E8 reports that more exhaust gas passes through the third recirculation path, C, than the module allows for the current operating point – the reverse of P23E7. A valve C that does not seat fully, a leaking bypass or a flow sensor reading too high are the usual explanations.
EGR valve C held partly open by carbon deposits
Worn valve seat or leaking bypass in path C
Air-mass or EGR flow sensor reading off, so flow is overestimated
Engine stalls when coming to a stop
P23E9: Camshaft A Position Signal Output Circuit/Open (Bank 2)

P23E9 concerns a signal the engine control module sends out rather than one it receives: on some engines the ECM passes a conditioned copy of the bank 2 camshaft A position signal on to another module that needs engine phase information.
Broken wire in the output line to the receiving module
Terminal pushed back or corroded in a connector
Receiving module unplugged or without its load resistor
Faulty output driver inside the engine control module
Stored code with no noticeable change in engine running
Fault entries in the module that receives the camshaft signal
Start-stop or shift functions may be restricted
P23EA: Camshaft A Position Signal Output Circuit Low (Bank 2)

P23EA sets when the ECM's output line that relays the bank 2 camshaft A position signal to another control unit is pulled toward ground. The check is blocked during cranking: the module commands the output high and expects the line to rise; if it stays low, the wire is chafed against ground or the receiver has an internal short.
Output wire chafed through to ground on the engine or body
Receiving module with an input shorted to ground
Moisture or dirt bridging terminals in a connector
Output stage in the engine control module failed
Harsher shifts or delayed engagement if the transmission module uses the signal
P23EB: Camshaft A Position Signal Output Circuit High (Bank 2)

P23EB is the opposite fault to P23EA: the bank 2 camshaft A output line, which the ECM drives as a switched low-side signal for another module, stays high when it should be pulled low. Typical reasons are a wire touching a supply circuit, moisture in a connector or a defective driver in the ECM.
Output wire shorted to a battery or 5 V supply wire in the harness
ECM output transistor no longer switching to ground
Related fault codes in the receiving control module
Comfort functions such as start-stop deactivated
P23EC: Camshaft B Position Signal Output Circuit/Open (Bank 1)

P23EC belongs to the camshaft B group – on most layouts the exhaust camshaft – and refers to bank 1, the side with cylinder 1. The ECM rebroadcasts the phase signal of that camshaft on a dedicated output wire, and P23EC reports that this wire, or the driver stage feeding it, shows an open or undefined circuit condition.
Open circuit in the camshaft B output wire
Connector at the ECM or receiver not fully latched
Input stage of the receiving module defective
Stored code, often found during a routine scan
Receiving module runs on substitute values
P23ED: Camshaft B Position Signal Output Circuit Low (Bank 1)

With P23ED the ECM detects that its camshaft B output for bank 1 reads low although it has released the line to go high. Most often a harness section rubbing through to the engine block, a crushed connector pin or a shorted input in the receiving module is to blame.
Harness rubbed through against the engine block
Crushed or bent connector pin touching ground
Shorted input in the receiving module
Downstream module reports missing camshaft signal
Possible fallback behaviour in transmission or hybrid functions
P23EE: Camshaft B Position Signal Output Circuit High (Bank 1)

P23EE flags a camshaft B, bank 1 output line that the ECM cannot pull low: the voltage stays near supply level, pointing to a short to a battery-fed or 5 V wire, a faulty pull-up in the receiving unit or a failed ECM driver transistor.
Output line shorted to a battery or sensor supply wire
Faulty pull-up circuit in the receiving module
Code logged while the engine runs normally
Faults or reduced functions in the module fed by the signal
P23EF: Camshaft B Position Signal Output Circuit/Open (Bank 2)
P23EF covers the last combination of this series: camshaft B, usually the exhaust shaft, on bank 2, the cylinder bank without cylinder 1.
Wire break in the bank 2 camshaft B output line
Terminal backed out of the connector housing
Receiving module disconnected or with failed input
Code stored without warning lamp on many vehicles
Module relying on the signal sets its own fault codes
P23F0: Camshaft B Position Signal Output Circuit Low (Bank 2)

P23F0 is stored when the bank 2 camshaft B output stays at ground potential while the ECM expects it to float high. A low reading can come from insulation damage near the exhaust side, where heat makes harness sleeves brittle, or from a receiving module whose input has failed shorted.
Heat-damaged insulation on the exhaust side grounding the wire
Receiving module input failed short to ground
Defective output stage in the ECM
Harsher shifts or delayed gear changes
P23F1: Camshaft B Position Signal Output Circuit High (Bank 2)

P23F1 means the camshaft B output for bank 2 sits at a high level that the ECM did not command. Its driver switches the line to ground to form the pulses; if the line stays high while switched, current is coming in from elsewhere – typically a short to a supply wire in a shared harness bundle, sometimes water bridging terminals.
Short to a supply wire within a shared harness bundle
Receiving module feeding voltage back into the line
Code present, no change in engine behaviour
Communication or plausibility faults in the receiving module
P23F2: Cylinder 1 Injector B Air-Fuel Ratio Imbalance

P23F2 says that the mixture in cylinder 1 has drifted away from the other cylinders and that the control unit holds the second injector of that cylinder, injector B, responsible. Only engines that feed each cylinder through two injectors can produce it. Toyota first paired a port and a direct injector in each cylinder with D-4S on the 2005 2GR-FSE V6.
Injector B (usually the port injector) of cylinder 1 clogged or dripping
Leaking injector O-ring or intake runner gasket at cylinder 1
Loose connector on injector B of cylinder 1 (often with P21CF)
Slightly rough idle or a misfire count on cylinder 1
P23F3: Cylinder 2 Injector B Air-Fuel Ratio Imbalance

P23F3 points to cylinder 2 and to its injector B, the second of two injectors feeding that cylinder. The smallest engines able to raise it have three cylinders, for example Ford's 1.5 EcoBoost, which pairs port and direct injection and can switch one cylinder off at light load.
Injector B of cylinder 2 delivering too much or too little fuel
Air leak at the intake port or injector seal of cylinder 2
Work done on the wrong cylinder because of the maker's numbering scheme
Chafed wire to injector B of cylinder 2 (check P21D0)
Shaking at idle, most noticeable on small three- or four-cylinder engines
P23F4: Cylinder 3 Injector B Air-Fuel Ratio Imbalance

P23F4 refers to cylinder 3: the control unit has found that this cylinder burns leaner or richer than the others and traces the deviation to injector B. On a three-cylinder engine with port and direct injection, such as the Ford 1.5 EcoBoost, cylinder 3 is the last one; on four- and six-cylinder engines it lies in the middle of the block or bank.
Port injector (injector B) of cylinder 3 dripping or partly blocked
Leaking seal at the intake port of cylinder 3
Low compression or leaking valves on cylinder 3
Possible misfire code P0303 at the same time
Uneven idle when the engine is warm
P23F5: Cylinder 4 Injector B Air-Fuel Ratio Imbalance

P23F5 concerns cylinder 4, the end cylinder of a four-cylinder engine. Many four-cylinder units now carry two injectors per cylinder: Toyota's 8AR-FTS turbo (D-4ST) and its Dynamic Force engines such as the M20A (D-4S), Hyundai's Smartstream G2.5 GDi and T-GDi, and the updated Ford 2.3 EcoBoost of the 2024 Mustang.
Deposits or wear in injector B of cylinder 4
Low-pressure (port) fuel rail problem showing first at cylinder 4 (look for P2BF0/P2BF1)
Air leak at the intake runner of cylinder 4
Fuel trim shifted on the single bank
P23F6: Cylinder 5 Injector B Air-Fuel Ratio Imbalance

P23F6 flags cylinder 5 and is the first code in this row that a four-cylinder engine can never set. Engines with port plus direct injection and at least five cylinders are mostly V6 and V8 units: Ford's second-generation 3.5 EcoBoost V6, first shown in the 2017 Ford GT, Toyota's 2GR-FKS V6 with D-4S, and the V8s named at P23F8.
Port injector of cylinder 5 out of tolerance
Intake manifold gasket leaking near cylinder 5
Intermittent contact in the injector B wiring of cylinder 5 (P21D3)
Fuel trim of the affected bank drifts
P23F7: Cylinder 6 Injector B Air-Fuel Ratio Imbalance

P23F7 belongs to cylinder 6, the highest-numbered cylinder on a V6 or straight six. Toyota's GR V6 family is a typical carrier: the 2GR-FSE in the Lexus IS and GS and the later 2GR-FKS both use D-4S, in which the port injector supplies part of the fuel next to the direct injector, its share depending on load and engine speed.
Port injector of cylinder 6 deviating in the ranges where it carries most of the fuel
Air leak at the intake runner or injector seat of cylinder 6
Injection split calibration needing a software update
Fault comes and goes depending on driving style
Occasional roughness at low or medium load
P23F8: Cylinder 7 Injector B Air-Fuel Ratio Imbalance
P23F8 identifies cylinder 7 and its injector B, so it needs at least seven cylinders, in practice a V8 or V10.
Port injector of cylinder 7 clogged or leaking
Fault in the separate injector B driver module, where fitted (e.g. GM LT5)
Fuel trim of one bank off while the other bank is normal
P23F9: Cylinder 8 Injector B Air-Fuel Ratio Imbalance
P23F9 points to cylinder 8, the highest number on any V8. GM's 2019 tables for the LT5 Corvette show how far a V8 with port and direct injection resolves imbalance in practice: only bank by bank.
Injector B of cylinder 8 with wrong flow rate
Leak at the intake runner or PCV connection near cylinder 8
Front oxygen sensor of the bank giving a distorted signal
Bank-level imbalance code (P219A/P219B) stored as well
P23FA: Cylinder 9 Injector B Air-Fuel Ratio Imbalance

P23FA concerns cylinder 9, which among passenger-car engines fitted with dual injection realistically means a V10. The best-known example is the 5.2 litre V10 of the Lamborghini Huracán, described as the first V10 to combine direct and multi-point injection.
Leak in the intake path of cylinder 9
Valve seat or compression problem on cylinder 9
Little or no effect on the high-revving engine's behaviour
Bank trim of the second cylinder group shifted
P23FB: Cylinder 10 Injector B Air-Fuel Ratio Imbalance

P23FB marks cylinder 10, the highest cylinder number of a V10. Among dual-injection engines, the Huracán's 5.2 litre unit is the documented case; it adds multi-point injection to direct injection. In its firing order cylinder 10 follows directly after cylinder 5.
Port injector of cylinder 10 dirty or worn
Injector seal leaking air at cylinder 10
Heat-damaged wiring to injector B of cylinder 10 (check P21D8)
Bank 2 or misfire code stored alongside
P23FC: Cylinder 11 Injector B Air-Fuel Ratio Imbalance
P23FC is reserved for cylinder 11, so it can only belong to twelve-cylinder engines that add an extra injector in every cylinder. Such a pairing is hard to find in public engine data.
Second injector of cylinder 11 delivering a wrong quantity
Code read from an engine that has no injector B (scan tool or software issue)
Hardly any change in smoothness on a twelve-cylinder engine
P23FD: Cylinder 12 Injector B Air-Fuel Ratio Imbalance
P23FD closes the cylinder series at number 12. It states that the twelfth cylinder runs out of step with the rest and that the cause lies with its injector B.
Second injector of cylinder 12 out of tolerance
Intake leak or valve sealing fault at cylinder 12
Code reported by a tool on an engine without a second injector
Bank or misfire code stored at the same time
P23FE: Bank 1 System B Air-Fuel Ratio Imbalance

P23FE reports a cylinder-to-cylinder imbalance on bank 1 that the control unit attributes to fuel system B, without naming a cylinder. Ford's 2024 OBD summary explains the letter for its dual-injection engines: the port path is Fuel Control System B with its own lean and rich codes (P2BF0/P2BF1 for bank 1), while direct injection forms system A.
Port fuel rail pressure or low-pressure supply wrong on bank 1
Several port injectors on bank 1 fouled by deposits
Intake manifold leak on the bank 1 side
Front oxygen sensor of bank 1 responding poorly
Lean or rich fuel trim on bank 1, possibly P2BF0 or P2BF1
P23FF: Bank 2 System B Air-Fuel Ratio Imbalance

P23FF mirrors P23FE for bank 2 and can only occur on V, W or boxer engines, because inline engines have no second bank. It means the cylinders on the side without cylinder 1 deviate from each other and the fault is assigned to injection system B, which on Ford's PFDI engines is the port path (lean and rich codes P2BF2/P2BF3).
Several port injectors on bank 2 with deposits or wear
Intake manifold gasket leaking on bank 2
Supply problem in the port fuel rail feeding bank 2
Front oxygen sensor or its wiring on bank 2 distorting the signal
Fuel trims of the two banks clearly apart
Possibly P2BF2 or P2BF3 as well
P2400: EVAP System Leak Detection Pump Control Circuit/Open
P2400 is stored when the engine computer finds the drive line of the evaporative leak detection pump open, so the pump cannot be switched for the tank leak test.
Corroded or loose pump connector, broken wire in the drive line
Open winding or internal fault in the leak detection pump
Coolant in the pump's vacuum supply line from a failed coolant pump changeover valve (VW Touareg 3.6)
Faulty output stage in the engine control module
No noticeable change in driving behaviour
P2401: EVAP System Leak Detection Pump Control Circuit Low
P2401 means the control line of the leak detection pump is pulled to ground level, usually by chafed insulation touching the body or by an internal pump fault.
Control wire chafed through and touching ground near the tank or rear wheel arch
Internal short inside the leak detection pump
Water ingress in the pump connector causing a leakage path to ground
Leak test not completed, EVAP readiness missing
P2402: EVAP System Leak Detection Pump Control Circuit High

P2402 points to the opposite fault of P2401: the pump control line sits at supply voltage or the pump draws too much current. GM's Volt tables call it a short to power detected while the driver is on; when it is active the ECM runs an intrusive check, running the pump for 15 s on command, with a Type B code after 20 failed samples out of 25.
Leak detection pump motor seized or drawing excessive current
Control wire shorted to a battery-voltage feed
Control module software that does not clear the fault after repair (Acura TLX Type S recall)
Check engine light that may persist after repair until software is updated
EVAP readiness incomplete, inspection may fail
P2403: EVAP System Leak Detection Pump Sense Circuit/Open

The sense circuit carries the feedback by which the engine computer knows what the leak detection pump is actually doing. P2403 is logged when that feedback is missing as if the line were open. The January 2014 Golf book from VW sets it once the sense signal stays at a low voltage for more than 0.5 s.
Broken feedback wire or backed-out terminal at the pump connector
Water or ice trapped in the pump or its filter (Jaguar XJ)
Failed feedback element inside the pump
More often after winter driving or car washes
P2404: EVAP System Leak Detection Pump Sense Circuit Range/Performance

P2404 is a plausibility code: the pump feedback is electrically present but does not behave as the leak test expects. VW's 2014 Golf data book sets it when the sense signal stays high for more than 30.4 s (12 s on another engine) over 30 checks, or when high signal time during pumping adds up to more than 10 s.
Condensation inside the leak check module (Subaru ELCM, software update available)
Worn or sticking pump that no longer reaches its expected state in time
Coolant or debris in the pump's vacuum or vent line
Check engine light, often returning after clearing
P2405: EVAP System Leak Detection Pump Sense Circuit Low

P2405 is set when the feedback signal of the leak detection pump stays below its permitted window, typically from a short to ground on the sense line or a fault inside the pump. No public source states a voltage threshold for this code.
Internal DMTL pump fault, often after dirt ingress through the dust filter
Corroded connector at the pump mounted near the rear wheel arch
Check engine light, possibly set while the car is parked
P2406: EVAP System Leak Detection Pump Sense Circuit High
P2406 is the mirror image of P2405: the pump feedback reads above its allowed range, as with a short to a voltage source or a sense line that floats high. Thresholds are not published.
Water or ice from road spray in the pump filter (Jaguar XJ)
Sense wire shorted to a voltage feed or open ground at the pump
Pump damaged by contamination entering through the dust filter
Fault often appears after wet or freezing weather
P2407: EVAP System Leak Detection Pump Sense Circuit Intermittent/Erratic

P2407 reports a pump feedback that jumps around instead of staying steady. On current-measuring DMTL pumps VW's 2014 Golf and Touareg books define it precisely: the pump current fluctuates by more than 1 mA during the reference measurement, or it drops by more than 6 mA for at least 3 s while pumping, checked with the engine off and on.
Over-sensitive diagnostic calibration, fixed by ECM software update (Audi, VW 2022-23)
Loose contact or corrosion at the pump connector
Worn pump motor with unstable current draw
Check engine light, sometimes only after the car has been parked
P2408: P2408 is the general circuit code for a sensor or switch that tells the engine computer whether the fuel cap or filler is closed. It is set when that circuit shows a fault not narrowed down to low, high, plausibility or dropout, which are P2410, P2411, P2409 and P2412.
Faulty fuel cap or filler switch
Damaged wiring or connector at the filler neck
Aftermarket cap that does not actuate the switch correctly
Check engine light or fuel cap warning
EVAP leak test may be skipped
P2409: P2409 is the plausibility code of the fuel cap sensor family: the circuit is electrically sound, but the reported cap state does not fit other information. A switch that never changes over a refuelling event, or one that reports closed while the leak test sees a gross leak, would be typical cases. No manufacturer publicly documents P2409.
Cap switch mechanically stuck in one position
Wrong or damaged cap that does not operate the sensor
Misaligned filler door or neck after body repair
Check engine light or fuel cap message although the cap is tight
EVAP test results may be rejected
P240A: EVAP System Leak Detection Pump Heater Control Circuit/Open

Some leak detection pump modules, such as the DMTL units on VW, Jaguar Land Rover and Maserati petrol engines, carry a small heating element that keeps moisture and ice from upsetting the pump and its pressure measurement. P240A is set when the heater's drive circuit appears open.
Burnt-out heating element inside the pump module
Broken heater wire or corroded terminal at the module connector
Missing supply voltage to the heater (fuse, relay)
Further EVAP pump codes in cold or wet conditions
P240B: EVAP System Leak Detection Pump Heater Control Circuit Low

P240B covers a heater control line of the leak detection pump that is held at too low a voltage, which in practice means a short to ground on the wire or inside the module. Per VW's 2014 data books for the Golf and Touareg, the code appears when the heater signal falls below roughly 2.74-3.26 V.
Heater wire shorted to ground near the pump
Internal fault in the DMTL pump module (Land Rover replaces the pump)
Moisture in the connector creating a path to ground
P240C: EVAP System Leak Detection Pump Heater Control Circuit High

P240C flags the heater circuit of the leak detection pump at the high end: VW's 2014 Golf and Touareg books set it when the heater current exceeds about 2.2-4 A, which points to a shorted element or a line touching battery voltage.
Shorted heating element in the pump module, often after water ingress
Heater control wire shorted to battery voltage
Faulty heater output stage in the engine control module
Other DMTL codes after frost or heavy rain

P244C: Exhaust Temperature Too Low For Particulate Filter Regeneration (Bank 1)

During an active regeneration the engine raises exhaust temperature with late injections so the soot in the particulate filter can burn. P244C is stored when bank 1 does not get hot enough or does not stay hot long enough.
Oxidation catalyst aged or face-plugged, so the post-injected fuel does not light off
Regenerations repeatedly cut short by short trips, idling or engine shut-off
Exhaust temperature sensor ahead of catalyst or filter reading too low
Exhaust leak ahead of the catalyst cooling the gas
Malfunction indicator lamp and particulate filter warning on
Regenerations noticeably frequent or never finishing
Reduced power once the filter is heavily loaded
P244D: Exhaust Temperature Too High For Particulate Filter Regeneration (Bank 1)

This is the overheating side of the bank 1 regeneration check. While soot is being burned off, the controller keeps exhaust temperature inside a window; if it climbs past the upper limit, the substrate and the oxidation catalyst risk cracking or melting, so the burn is stopped and P244D is logged.
Too much fuel reaching the exhaust (leaking injector or aftertreatment doser)
Heavily overloaded filter burning off too fast
Exhaust temperature sensor or its wiring giving implausibly high readings
Regeneration aborted, filter warning stays on
Reduced power to protect the aftertreatment
P244E: Exhaust Temperature Too Low For Particulate Filter Regeneration (Bank 2)

P244E only exists on engines that have a separate particulate filter for the second cylinder bank, which is rare. No manufacturer documents this code publicly; it mirrors P244C, so the logic described for bank 1 applies here.
Bank 2 oxidation catalyst no longer converting post-injected fuel
Bank 2 exhaust temperature sensor reading low
Driving pattern too short for a complete regeneration
Exhaust leak on bank 2 ahead of the catalyst
Filter warning, regeneration does not complete
P244F: Exhaust Temperature Too High For Particulate Filter Regeneration (Bank 2)
The bank 2 counterpart of P244D: during a filter burn the second bank's exhaust gets hotter than the substrate tolerates. No manufacturer documents P244F publicly.
Surplus fuel on bank 2 from a leaking injector
Bank 2 exhaust temperature sensor or wiring reading too high
Bank 2 filter heavily overloaded before the burn
P2450: EVAP System Switching Valve Performance/Stuck Open
The switching valve sits in the evaporative system and either seals off part of it during the leak test or redirects flow; P2450 means the valve does not do its job or remains open.
Switching valve sticking open or not sealing
Internal fault of a leak detection pump that houses the valve
Monitor software needing an update (known on some Ford trucks)
Cracked or loose vapor hose at the valve
Malfunction indicator lamp on, usually no noticeable driving change
Possible fuel odor near the tank area
P2451: EVAP System Switching Valve Stuck Closed

P2451 is the reverse fault of P2450: the evaporative system switching valve will not open when commanded, so vapor or test pressure cannot pass where the system expects it. It shows up mainly on vehicles with a sealed, pressurized fuel tank, such as plug-in hybrids.
Tank shutter or switching valve stuck closed
Fuel tank pressure sensor giving wrong values to the monitor
Software or test-sequence issue (fuel door handling on some hybrids)
Fuel door or refueling release slow or not working on sealed-tank hybrids
P2452: Diesel Particulate Filter Pressure Sensor A Circuit

The pressure sensor A of the particulate filter, usually a differential sensor with hoses to the filter inlet and outlet, tells the ECM how loaded the filter is. Despite its generic circuit title, P2452 is in practice an offset check made when no exhaust flows.
Sensor offset drifted or moisture inside the sensor
Sensor hose blocked by soot or condensate
Regeneration too early, too late or inhibited
P2453: Diesel Particulate Filter Pressure Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance
P2453 means the particulate filter pressure signal is electrically fine but does not behave like a real filter pressure. Manufacturers use two kinds of test.
Sensor hose disconnected, split, kinked or blocked
Sensor skewed or stuck, for example from moisture ingress
High resistance in sensor wiring or ECM grounds
DPF warning, regeneration inhibited or too frequent
P2454: Diesel Particulate Filter Pressure Sensor A Circuit Low

The particulate filter pressure sensor is a three-wire part: the ECM feeds it 5 V and ground and reads a signal that rises with the pressure difference across the filter. P2454 means that signal sits below the lowest plausible value.
Signal wire open or shorted to ground, connector unplugged
Internal sensor failure, for example from moisture
5 V reference shorted by another sensor on the same supply
P2455: Diesel Particulate Filter Pressure Sensor A Circuit High
P2455 means the particulate filter pressure sensor signal sits above the highest plausible value, at the top of the 5 V range.
Signal wire shorted to 5 V reference or battery voltage
P2456: Diesel Particulate Filter Pressure Sensor A Circuit Intermittent/Erratic

Here the pressure sensor A signal is within range but jumps in a way no real exhaust flow could cause. GM's 2017 and 2018 diesels compare each raw sample with the one before; a step larger than 20 % repeated over 80 or 160 samples sets the code after two trips, but only if no electrical fault is present.
Loose or corroded sensor connector terminals
Harness chafing or heat damage near the exhaust
Condensate in the sensor or its pressure hoses
Regeneration started at odd times or blocked
P2457: EGR Cooler A Efficiency Below Threshold
The EGR cooler is supposed to bring recirculated exhaust close to coolant temperature; P2457 says cooler A no longer removes enough heat, as CARB requires diesel systems to detect.
Cooler passages fouled with soot and lacquer
Bypass flap stuck in bypass position or bypass module loose
EGR outlet temperature sensor reading too high
Low coolant level or poor coolant flow through the cooler
Monitor software misjudging efficiency (known on some trucks)
Higher NOx, sometimes reduced EGR or power
Coolant loss or white smoke if the cooler is also leaking
P2458: During a regeneration the engine raises exhaust temperature, mostly by late post-injection burned in the oxidation catalyst, until the soot in the particulate filter oxidises. P2458 means a regeneration took longer than the calibrated limit, so the filter was not cleaned in the expected time.
ECM calibration that needs an update (documented by Volkswagen)
Short trips that keep regenerations from finishing
Oxidation catalyst too weak to reach regeneration temperature
DPF warning or MIL, depending on the manufacturer
Cooling fan and raised idle running on after shutdown
P2459: P2459 means the particulate filter is being regenerated more often than the calibration expects. CARB requires diesel OBD to flag regeneration so frequent that emissions would exceed the limit; frequent regeneration also dilutes oil and costs fuel. Ford's 2023 diesels set it when the average distance between completed regenerations falls below about 40 km.
High soot output from the engine (injectors, EGR, air leaks)
Differential pressure reading too high (sensor, blocked or swapped hoses)
Filter loaded with ash or defective from manufacture
Higher fuel consumption and rising oil level
Reduced engine power if the fault persists
P245A: The bypass lets cold-start EGR skip the cooler and is switched back to cooling once the engine is warm. P245A flags the bank 1 control circuit, usually as an open.
Open wire or unplugged connector at the bypass actuator
Actuator motor or solenoid winding open
Control software needing an update (some Ford diesels)
EGR cooler bypass no longer switching; possible P2457 or P24A5 as follow-up
P245B: EGR Cooler Bypass Control Circuit Range/Performance (Bank 1)
P245B is set when the bank 1 bypass is electrically intact but does not reach or hold the commanded position, or when switching it has no visible thermal effect.
Bypass flap or shaft sticking from carbon deposits
Weak vacuum supply or leaking hose on vacuum-operated bypass
Slow EGR temperature sensor after the cooler
Longer warm-up or higher NOx when the bypass stays in one position
P245C: EGR Cooler Bypass Control Circuit Low (Bank 1)
P245C reports that the control line of the bank 1 bypass actuator is pulled toward ground.
Control wire chafed through and touching ground
Water or corrosion bridging connector pins
Bypass stuck in one position, possibly with EGR cooler efficiency code
P245D: EGR Cooler Bypass Control Circuit High (Bank 1)

P245D is the short-to-supply case of the bank 1 bypass circuit. For the Duramax with a DC-motor bypass, GM's 2017 tables watch the current through the H-bridge while it drives the flap: more than 8 A in 160 of 200 samples sets a Type B fault.
Control software reporting a false actuator fault (known on some Ram diesels)
Control wire shorted to a battery or ignition feed
Actuator motor drawing excessive current (low-resistance winding, binding)
Bypass actuator switched off by the controller and left in default position
P245E: Particulate Filter Pressure Sensor B Circuit
Which sensor is B depends on the maker. Ford's 2013 6.7 L Power Stroke has an exhaust pressure sensor ahead of the filter as A and a two-port differential sensor across it as B.
Sensor B offset drifted or moisture inside the sensor
Pressure hose kinked or blocked so pressure is trapped
Wiring or connector fault on the sensor B circuit
Soot load estimate unreliable, regeneration timing affected
P245F: Particulate Filter Pressure Sensor B Circuit Range/Performance
With P245F the controller decides that the sensor B value is electrically fine but makes no physical sense.
Sensor B hose cracked, disconnected or blocked
Condensate in the pressure line falsifying the reading
Sensor B drifted out of calibration
Control software needing an update (some Jeep models)
Filter regeneration triggered too early, too late or blocked
P2460: Particulate Filter Pressure Sensor B Circuit Low
P2460 means the analog output of pressure sensor B has fallen below the lowest voltage a working sensor can deliver.
5 V reference to sensor B missing or shorted
Signal wire chafed and shorted to ground
Sensor B internally failed with output stuck low
Regeneration based on a model only, possibly more frequent
P2461: Particulate Filter Pressure Sensor B Circuit High

When pressure sensor B reports a voltage above its usable range, P2461 is stored. Ford sets the limit at 4.90 V for 2 s on the 2013 6.7 L diesel, where B is the differential sensor across the filter, and at 4.73 V for 5 s on the 2024 gasoline particulate filters.
Condensate in the sensor tubes producing false high readings
Sensor ground open or signal shorted to reference or battery voltage
Sensor B internally failed with output stuck high
Reduced power because the filter appears heavily loaded
P2462: Particulate Filter Pressure Sensor B Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P2462 covers a sensor B signal that drops out or jumps for short moments without staying outside its range long enough for the low or high codes.
Terminal losing contact under engine vibration
Harness rubbing on a bracket or exhaust part
Malfunction indicator lamp on, sometimes only after rough roads or rain
Pressure reading jumping in live data
P2463: Diesel Particulate Filter Restriction - Soot Accumulation (Bank 1)

P2463 means the soot load in the particulate filter has passed the level at which the engine still regenerates it on its own. GM's 2009 Duramax sets it at 70 g or more for 5 minutes, the 2014 Cruze 2.0 diesel at more than 32 g for 30 s, both as Type A codes; GM's 2018 diesels use the pressure-based soot model with 120 failures in 150 samples.
Regenerations not completed because of short trips or long idling
Differential pressure sensor, its hoses or wiring reading too high
Fault that prevents regeneration (fuel doser, temperature sensor)
DPF full or exhaust filter message in the cluster
MIL on and reduced engine power
P2464: Diesel Particulate Filter Differential Pressure Too Low (Bank 2)

P2464 is stored when the pressure drop across the second particulate filter stays smaller than the controller predicts for the current exhaust flow. Only engines that run a separate filter on each bank, typically larger V diesels, can log it.
Pressure sensing hose of the bank 2 filter detached, cracked or leaking
Upstream sensing port or line blocked with soot or condensate
Filter substrate cracked, melted or removed
Visible soot at the tailpipe if the filter is damaged
Regeneration suspended or reduced power on some engines
P2465: Diesel Particulate Filter Differential Pressure Too High (Bank 2)

P2465 means the second particulate filter builds up more back pressure than the controller accepts for the exhaust flow it calculates. The code is only possible where each cylinder bank has its own filter. No maker documents the bank 2 version in a public table; its bank 1 twin P244B gives the logic.
Bank 2 filter heavily loaded with soot or ash
Downstream sensing hose blocked, kinked or swapped
Dented or obstructed exhaust pipe behind the filter
Loss of power, possibly limp mode
P2466: Exhaust Gas Temperature Sensor Circuit (Bank 2 Sensor 3)

P2466 is the general circuit code for the third exhaust temperature probe in the bank 2 exhaust path, so it only appears on engines with two separate aftertreatment lines. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly.
Temperature probe failed internally or open
Connector or wiring near the exhaust damaged by heat
Probe loose or not reaching into the gas stream
Implausible or missing value for this probe in live data
Filter regeneration or DEF dosing suspended
P2467: Exhaust Gas Temperature Sensor Circuit Range/Performance (Bank 2 Sensor 3)
P2467 means the third exhaust temperature probe on bank 2 delivers an electrically valid signal that does not match the operating state. A public threshold for this exact code is not available.
Probe aged, drifting or frozen at one value
Probe loose or pulled out of the gas stream
Coolant entering the exhaust through a leaking EGR cooler (Ford 2.0 L EcoBoost)
Controller software judging the probe too strictly
Temperature value lags or deviates from neighbouring probes
White smoke and coolant loss if the EGR cooler leaks
P2468: Exhaust Gas Temperature Sensor Circuit Low (Bank 2 Sensor 3)

P2468 reports that probe 3 in the bank 2 exhaust line delivers a signal below the lowest value the input can produce with an intact circuit. With the usual resistive probes this nearly always means the signal line or the sensor itself has a ground short. No manufacturer lists this bank 2 code publicly; the neighbouring low codes show the scale.
Signal wire chafed through and touching ground
Connector melted or with water ingress
Probe shows an implausible value at a standstill
P2469: Exhaust Gas Temperature Sensor Circuit High (Bank 2 Sensor 3)

P2469 is logged when bank 2 probe number 3 pushes its input above the permitted ceiling. An unplugged connector, a broken wire or a burnt-out sensing element produces exactly that, as does a signal line shorted to a voltage source.
Connector unplugged or wire broken (open circuit)
Signal line shorted to a voltage source
MIL on, often already in the first trip
Probe shows a maximum or invalid value
P246A: Exhaust Gas Temperature Sensor Circuit Intermittent/Erratic (Bank 2 Sensor 3)

P246A flags a third bank 2 exhaust temperature probe whose reading jumps from sample to sample faster than real gas temperature could, even though every single value stays inside the legal range. The bank 2 code itself is not described by any manufacturer in public material.
Loose or corroded terminal in the probe connector
Harness strands broken by heat and vibration
Cracked sensing element giving unstable contact
MIL on after a repeated fault
Temperature trace jumps in live data
Fault may come and go with bumps or engine heat
P246B: Vehicle Conditions Incorrect for Particulate Filter Regeneration

P246B says the controller wanted to clean the particulate filter but the vehicle did not offer the conditions its strategy needs, for example enough exhaust heat, a long enough run or a functioning air path. It describes a failed or blocked regeneration request rather than a defective part on its own, so the real cause is usually stored beside it.
Another stored fault (e.g. intake throttle, sensors) blocking regeneration
Failed intake air shutoff throttle (Land Rover TDV6)
Short trips or long idling without enough exhaust heat
Regeneration does not start or is aborted repeatedly
Filter warning or rising soot load
MIL on together with the root-cause code on some vehicles
P246C: Particulate Filter Restriction - Forced Limited Power (Bank 1)

P246C is the final stage of the bank 1 filter loading monitor: the filter is judged so clogged that the controller reduces engine output to protect engine and filter. Ford uses it on diesels with an immediate MIL plus wrench light.
Soot overload after repeatedly missed or aborted regenerations
Mostly stationary or low-speed operation without full regenerations
Filter at the end of its life with high ash content
PCM calibration overestimating soot load (Ford bulletins)
MIL and service or wrench light on
P246D: Particulate Filter Pressure Sensor A/B Correlation
P246D compares two pressure readings at the particulate filter that ought to agree under steady conditions. Which sensor is A and which is B is decided by each manufacturer.
Sensing hoses swapped, kinked or leaking
Water or soot in a sensing line
One pressure sensor drifting out of calibration
Regeneration too early, too late or suspended
Pressure values of the two sensors disagree in live data
P246E: Exhaust Gas Temperature Sensor Circuit (Bank 1 Sensor 4)
P246E is the general code for the fourth exhaust temperature probe on bank 1, usually the last one in the aftertreatment line.
Probe aged or failed, reading far from the model
Probe loose or not reaching into the gas stream
Exhaust leak near the probe cooling the reading
Value of the last exhaust probe deviates from expectation
P246F: Exhaust Gas Temperature Sensor Circuit Range/Performance (Bank 1 Sensor 4)

P246F stands for a fourth bank 1 exhaust temperature probe whose signal is electrically fine but physically implausible. Both main users test it after a long soak. Ford's diesels compare it with three other probes after at least 6 h off and allow no more than 50 °C between them, which unmasks a probe stuck at one value.
Probe stuck at one value or drifting
Probe loose or backed out of the exhaust pipe
Probe connectors swapped with a neighbouring sensor
MIL on after the second faulty trip
Probe disagrees with neighbouring temperatures after a cold start
Usually no noticeable change in driveability
P2470: Exhaust Gas Temperature Sensor Circuit Low (Bank 1 Sensor 4)

P2470 means the signal of bank 1 probe number 4 has dropped below its valid floor, which on resistive probes indicates a short to ground. Ford's diesels flag a voltage under 0.10 V with the key on and 9 to 16.25 V supply, checked continuously over about 2 s.
Signal wire chafed through and touching ground
Low battery voltage during diagnosis distorting readings (Ram)
Implausible value for the last exhaust probe
P2471: Exhaust Gas Temperature Sensor Circuit High (Bank 1 Sensor 4)

P2471 is set when the fourth bank 1 exhaust temperature probe drives its input above the upper limit, the picture of an open circuit, an unplugged sensor or a short to voltage. Ford's diesels call more than 2.66 V a fault.
Connector unplugged or wire broken (open circuit)
Signal line shorted to a voltage source
MIL on, on GM possibly in the first trip
Last exhaust probe shows maximum or substitute value
P2472: Exhaust Gas Temperature Sensor Circuit Intermittent/Erratic (Bank 1 Sensor 4)
P2472 reports that the last bank 1 temperature probe (sensor 4) changes its signal too abruptly between two readings, although each reading on its own lies in range.
Loose or corroded terminal in the probe connector
Wire fatigue near the hot exhaust pipe
Cracked sensing element giving unstable contact
MIL on after the second faulty trip
Temperature value flickers in live data
Fault comes and goes, often after rough roads
P2473: Exhaust Gas Temperature Sensor Circuit (Bank 2 Sensor 4)

P2473 covers the wiring of probe number four in the bank 2 exhaust line as a whole, so it only occurs on engines with two separate exhaust paths and a long sensor chain on each. The controller sets it when the probe line delivers a value it cannot assign to a clean low or high fault, for instance an open circuit or a sensor reporting an internal error.
Broken wire or unplugged connector at the bank 2 probe
Fault in the control unit input stage
No usable value for bank 2 probe 4 in live data
P2474: Exhaust Gas Temperature Sensor Circuit Range/Performance (Bank 2 Sensor 4)

P2474 flags a plausibility problem: the electrical signal of bank 2 probe 4 is valid, yet the temperature it reports does not fit what the engine controller expects. Typical tests compare the probe with its neighbours after a long soak, when all should read about ambient, or with a modelled value during driving.
Probe aged and reading off by a constant amount
Exhaust leak upstream of the probe falsifying the reading
Probe 4 of bank 2 differs clearly from the other probes after a cold soak
P2475: Exhaust Gas Temperature Sensor Circuit Low (Bank 2 Sensor 4)

P2475 is stored when the voltage from bank 2 probe 4 falls below the lowest value the probe can produce in normal use. With the resistive PTC probes common on diesels this points to a short between signal and ground, or to a sensor shorted internally.
Signal wire rubbed through against the exhaust or body
Water in the connector bridging the pins
Bank 2 probe 4 shows an implausibly cold or fixed value
P2476: Exhaust Gas Temperature Sensor Circuit High (Bank 2 Sensor 4)

P2476 covers the opposite end of the scale from P2475: the signal of bank 2 probe 4 sits above its usable ceiling. Because the probe forms a voltage divider with a pull-up resistor in the control unit, an interrupted wire, a disconnected plug or a short to a supply voltage all drive the input high.
Open signal or ground wire, often heat-damaged
Connector loose or not locked after service work
Signal wire shorted to a supply voltage
Probe reads maximum or an implausibly hot value
P2477: Exhaust Gas Temperature Sensor Circuit Intermittent/Erratic (Bank 2 Sensor 4)

P2477 targets a signal from bank 2 probe 4 that jumps around, while each individual sample may still be in range. Real exhaust temperature changes only gradually because the probe and pipe have thermal mass, so sudden steps between consecutive readings betray a wiring or contact issue.
Loose or corroded pins in the probe connector
Wire strands breaking near the hot pipe
Cracked probe element with unstable contact
MIL on after the second faulty trip
Value of bank 2 probe 4 jumps in live data
Fault code returns after being cleared
P2478: Exhaust Gas Temperature Out of Range (Bank 1 Sensor 1)

Unlike the circuit codes, P2478 judges the temperature itself at the first exhaust probe of bank 1, usually ahead of the oxidation catalyst. Ford's 2015 diesel summary for the 6.7L and 3.2L engines groups it with the EGT circuit check: the test is high-side only and trips at roughly 1150 °C, because the PTC probe curve leaves no separate low threshold.
Real overheating from excess fuel or a leaking injector
Overly sensitive diagnosis needing a software update (VW Passat 2012)
Probe reading too high due to ageing
Lack of air from a boost leak or turbocharger fault
Power reduced to protect the exhaust parts
Smoke or a hot smell from the exhaust in real overheating
P2479: Exhaust Gas Temperature Out of Range (Bank 1 Sensor 2)

P2479 applies the same temperature-limit idea to the second bank 1 probe. On the 2015 Ford 6.7L layout this is EGT12 at the oxidation catalyst outlet, where the exotherm of a regeneration shows up first, so a runaway burn or excessive post-injection can push the reading towards the limit.
Excessive heat during regeneration, e.g. too much post-injection
Leaking injector adding unburnt fuel to the catalyst
P247A: Exhaust Gas Temperature Out of Range (Bank 1 Sensor 3)
P247A is the out-of-range verdict for the third bank 1 probe, which sits further down the aftertreatment line. It is the best documented code of this series.
Overloaded particulate filter burning off too fast
Regeneration not reaching target temperature (VW low-side check)
Emergency mode with reduced power possible
P247B: Exhaust Gas Temperature Out of Range (Bank 1 Sensor 4)

P247B concerns the last probe in the bank 1 chain. In Ford's 2015 6.7L overview that is EGT14, mounted downstream of the particulate filter, so it sees the heat that leaves the filter during regeneration.
Thermal runaway in the particulate filter
Unburnt fuel reaching the filter from injectors or a dosing valve
Regeneration stopped, filter load warning possible
P247C: Exhaust Gas Temperature Out of Range (Bank 2 Sensor 1)

P247C is the bank 2 counterpart of P2478: the first exhaust probe on the second cylinder bank reports a temperature outside its permitted window, typically next to the turbine outlet or catalyst inlet of that bank. It needs a V engine with separate exhaust paths and its own probe per bank.
Bank 2 running hot from extra fuel or a faulty injector
Air shortage on bank 2 from a boost leak or turbo fault
Reduced power to protect the exhaust
Bank 2 probe reads clearly above bank 1
P247D: Exhaust Gas Temperature Out of Range (Bank 2 Sensor 2)

P247D applies to the second probe on bank 2, by analogy with P2479 normally downstream of that bank's oxidation catalyst, where the heat released by burning fuel during a regeneration is measured. It is set when the reported temperature leaves the plausible window, in practice mostly on the high side.
Too much heat in the bank 2 catalyst during regeneration
Probe reading high even on a cold engine
Bank 2 probe 2 differs from its bank 1 twin
P247E: Exhaust Gas Temperature Out of Range (Bank 2 Sensor 3)

P247E does not question the wiring but the value itself: the third exhaust probe on cylinder bank 2 reports a temperature the engine control unit will not accept, in practice mostly an implausibly hot one. The code only makes sense on a V engine whose two banks keep separate exhaust paths up to the third measuring point.
Uncontrolled soot burn or too much post-injection fuel on bank 2
Probe drifted and reports values too high
Leaking injector or turbo oil leak on bank 2
Warning lamp on, regeneration may be aborted
Reduced power to protect the aftertreatment
P247F: Exhaust Gas Temperature Out of Range (Bank 2 Sensor 4)

P247F flags an unacceptable reading from the fourth exhaust temperature probe of bank 2, the position that on most layouts sits behind the particulate filter. A genuine reading near the limit there means heat is leaving the filter, which points to a runaway regeneration. No manufacturer documents P247F publicly.
Overloaded particulate filter burning off too fast
Probe ageing with readings drifting upwards
Probe swapped with another position after a repair
P2480: Exhaust Gas Temperature Sensor Circuit/Open (Bank 1 Sensor 5)

P2480 is the general circuit or open-circuit fault of a fifth exhaust temperature probe on bank 1. Five probes in one line are rare; GM's small diesels with oxidation catalyst, SCR, second catalyst and filter are among the few layouts that use them.
Broken or chafed lead to probe 5
Corroded or loose connector near the exhaust
Measuring element of the probe burned through
Missing or frozen value for probe 5 in live data
P2481: Exhaust Gas Temperature Sensor Circuit Low (Bank 1 Sensor 5)
P2481 means the signal of the fifth bank 1 exhaust probe has dropped below its lower electrical limit, which on a resistive probe usually indicates a short to ground.
Signal lead chafed through and touching ground
Internal short in the probe after heat damage
Neighbouring probe replaced because positions were confused
Engine warning lamp after two trips
Probe 5 reads implausibly in live data
P2482: Exhaust Gas Temperature Sensor Circuit High (Bank 1 Sensor 5)

With P2482 the fifth bank 1 exhaust probe delivers a signal above its upper electrical limit. On GM diesels this code also covers the open circuit: the 2018 table sets it above 1400 Ω, both as a short to power with the driver off and as an interruption with the driver on, after 10 of 20 samples, Type B. The 2020 table makes it Type A.
Broken lead from heat or vibration
Warning lamp, on GM from 2020 after a single trip
Probe 5 shows a fixed extreme value
P2483: Exhaust Gas Temperature Sensor Circuit Range/Performance (Bank 1 Sensor 5)

P2483 is the plausibility test for the fifth bank 1 exhaust probe: the circuit is electrically fine, but the reading does not behave like a real exhaust temperature. GM's 2025 diesel tables describe the check in detail.
Probe not fully seated in its boss after exhaust work
Probe output stuck or responding too slowly
Heavily sooted probe tip insulating the element
Probe 5 barely changes while the other probes heat up
P2484: Exhaust Gas Temperature Sensor Circuit Intermittent/Erratic (Bank 1 Sensor 5)

P2484 catches a fifth bank 1 exhaust probe whose signal jumps faster than any real exhaust temperature can change. GM's diesel ECMs compare consecutive samples taken every 100 ms. In the 2018 table the resistance difference between two samples is evaluated, and 15 failed samples out of 30 set a Type B code.
Intermittent contact in the probe connector
Harness insulation worn by heat or rubbing
Warning lamp, sometimes going out again
Erratic jumps of probe 5 in live data
P2485: Exhaust Gas Temperature Sensor Circuit/Open (Bank 2 Sensor 5)

P2485 reports a circuit or open-circuit fault at a fifth exhaust temperature probe on bank 2. That requires a V engine with two separate aftertreatment lines carrying five probes each, a layout no public maker document shows. No manufacturer documents P2485.
Interrupted lead between control unit and probe
Connector left unplugged after exhaust work
No valid value for this probe
P2486: Exhaust Gas Temperature Sensor Circuit Low (Bank 2 Sensor 5)

P2486 is set when the signal of the fifth bank 2 exhaust probe sits below its lower electrical limit, typically because the lead or the probe itself shorts to ground. No manufacturer documents P2486 publicly; it presupposes two exhaust banks with five probes each.
Lead insulation damaged and touching ground
P2487: Exhaust Gas Temperature Sensor Circuit High (Bank 2 Sensor 5)

With P2487 the control unit sees the fifth bank 2 exhaust probe above its upper electrical limit, the picture of a short to supply voltage or, on many designs, of an open circuit. There is no public maker document for P2487.
Signal lead shorted to a supply line
Probe shows maximum or no value
P2488: Exhaust Gas Temperature Sensor Circuit Range/Performance (Bank 2 Sensor 5)

P2488 is the rationality check for the fifth bank 2 exhaust probe: the signal is electrically valid but does not follow the operating state. No manufacturer documents P2488; a second bank with five probes is unknown in public maker material.
Probe not reaching into the gas flow
Exhaust leak cooling the measuring point
P2489: Exhaust Gas Temperature Sensor Circuit Intermittent/Erratic (Bank 2 Sensor 5)

P2489 points to an unsteady signal from the fifth exhaust probe on bank 2: the value stays within its electrical limits but jumps or drops out briefly. This code is not documented by any manufacturer, as no public layout carries five probes per bank on a twin-bank engine.
P248A: Reductant Heater A Sense Circuit Low
P248A concerns the sense line with which the control unit measures the supply voltage reaching DEF heater A, and reports that voltage as too low.
Corroded heater supply connector at the tank
Worn heater relay contact causing voltage drop
Weak battery or charging fault during heating
Warning lamp or DEF system message
Frozen DEF not thawed in winter, dosing delayed
P248B: Reductant Heater A Sense Circuit High

P248B is the upper counterpart to P248A: the sense signal for the supply of DEF heater A reads higher than permitted, for example when the line shorts to battery voltage, when the supply stays live although the heater is switched off, or when the sense input itself fails. No manufacturer documents P248B in public material.
Sense lead shorted to battery voltage
Faulty sense input in the control module
Possible battery drain if the heater stays powered
P248C: Reductant Heater B Sense Circuit Low
P248C reports too little voltage on the sense circuit of DEF heater B. In GM's diesel tables from 2016 to 2018 heater B is the line heater, i.e. the heated hose from the pump to the dosing valve.
Corroded plug at the heated DEF line
Voltage drop across fuse or relay of the line heater
Damaged supply lead along the frame
P248D: Reductant Heater B Sense Circuit High

P248D means the heater B sense input reads too high, typically the heated line. Possible pictures are a sense wire shorted to battery positive, a supply that remains on after the heater has been switched off, or a faulty input stage. Public maker documentation for P248D does not exist.
Sense wire shorted to battery positive
Defective input stage in the module
P248E: P248E is the bank 2 counterpart of P245A: the engine controller sees no proper load on the output that drives the EGR cooler bypass of the second cylinder bank, most often because the circuit is open. Only engines with a separate EGR path per bank can set it, which in practice means V engines with two coolers.
Unplugged connector or broken wire at the bank 2 bypass actuator
Open motor or solenoid winding in the bank 2 actuator
Faulty output stage in the engine control module
Longer warm-up or higher NOx on one bank because the bypass stays put
P248F: EGR Cooler Bypass Control Circuit Range/Performance (Bank 2)

With P248F the bank 2 bypass circuit is electrically sound, yet the flap does not do what the controller asks: it lags behind the setpoint, stops short of its end position or switching shows no effect on the gas temperature after the cooler. No manufacturer publishes a bank 2 version of this check.
Bypass flap on bank 2 sluggish from soot and carbon
Leaking vacuum line or weak vacuum on pneumatic actuators
Often no noticeable change in driving
P2490: EGR Cooler Bypass Control Circuit Low (Bank 2)

P2490 means the drive line of the bank 2 cooler bypass actuator sits too close to ground potential, typically a grounded wire between controller and actuator. It mirrors P245C on bank 1. No manufacturer documents P2490 publicly.
Drive wire rubbed through and touching engine ground
Water or corrosion in the bank 2 actuator connector
Bypass on bank 2 stuck in one mode, possibly followed by cooler efficiency codes
P2491: EGR Cooler Bypass Control Circuit High (Bank 2)

P2491 reports excess voltage or excess current in the drive circuit feeding the bypass actuator on bank 2, the classic sign of a short to supply or of a winding whose resistance has collapsed. It is the bank 2 sibling of P245D, and no maker publishes its own description of it.
Control wire touching a battery or ignition feed
Actuator winding with too low resistance or seized motor
Controller software reporting a false actuator fault
Bypass flap on bank 2 rests in its default position
P2492: EGR Cooler Bypass Position Sensor Circuit (Bank 1)

The position sensor tells the controller where the bank 1 cooler bypass flap actually is; position-controlled flaps cannot be regulated without it. P2492 is the general circuit code for that sensor, used when the fault cannot be classed as a short to ground or to the supply. No manufacturer documents P2492 publicly.
Damaged sensor wiring near hot exhaust parts
Loose or corroded connector at the bypass valve
5 V sensor supply missing or shared circuit shorted
P2493: EGR Cooler Bypass Position Sensor Range/Performance (Bank 1)

P2493 is a plausibility fault: the bank 1 bypass position signal stays inside its electrical limits, but its value or behaviour does not fit the commanded flap position or the learned end stops. GM names the code in preliminary bulletin PI1449 for the 2015 Silverado and Sierra with the LML Duramax, where it showed up together with P2495, P24C4 and P06A3.
Worn or defective bypass valve with integrated sensor
Deposits shifting the learned end positions
Unstable 5 V reference shared with other sensors
Check engine light on, often with further bypass codes
Bypass position in the live data does not match the command
P2494: EGR Cooler Bypass Position Sensor Circuit Low (Bank 1)

P2494 is set when the raw voltage of the bank 1 bypass position sensor drops toward zero. GM documents it for the Duramax diesel: in the 2017 tables the signal must be below 1 % of the 5 V reference in 200 of 250 samples, checked every 6.25 ms once cranking is over and the powertrain relay supplies more than 11 V.
Open 5 V reference wire to the sensor
Internal sensor fault in the bypass valve
Check engine light after two trips
Bypass control falls back to a default position
P2495: EGR Cooler Bypass Position Sensor Circuit High (Bank 1)

P2495 covers a bank 1 bypass position signal that climbs close to the reference voltage. On GM Duramax diesels the 2017 calibration fails it above 99 % of 5 V in 200 out of 250 samples, with the same enable conditions as the low test, and rates it Type B.
Defective bypass valve with integrated sensor
Fault in the shared 5 V reference circuit
Signal wire touching a voltage source
Check engine light after two trips
Additional sensor supply codes stored at the same time
P2496: EGR Cooler Bypass Position Sensor Circuit Intermittent/Erratic (Bank 1)

P2496 targets a bank 1 bypass position signal that jumps, drops out briefly or changes faster than the flap can physically move, without staying outside the electrical limits long enough for P2494 or P2495. No manufacturer documents P2496 publicly; GM's Duramax tables, which do cover the same analog sensor, only list the low, high and learning checks.
Loose or spread terminal in the sensor connector
Wire breaking inside the insulation from engine movement
Worn contact track inside the sensor
Check engine light that comes and goes
Bypass position value jumps in the live data
P2497: EGR Cooler Bypass Position Sensor Circuit (Bank 2)
P2497 is the generic circuit fault of the position sensor on the bank 2 cooler bypass, so it can only appear on engines whose second bank has its own EGR cooler with feedback-controlled flap.
Damaged wiring to the bank 2 position sensor
Failed position sensor or bypass valve
Bypass on bank 2 no longer regulated
P2498: EGR Cooler Bypass Position Sensor Range/Performance (Bank 2)

With P2498 the bank 2 bypass position signal is electrically valid but not believable, for example because it does not change when the flap is commanded, settles at an unexpected value or no longer matches the end stops learned earlier. There is no public manufacturer description for this bank 2 code.
Worn bank 2 bypass valve with built-in sensor
Flap binding so the sensor reads a position other than commanded
End-stop learn values invalid after a repair
Measured and commanded bypass position differ on bank 2
P2499: EGR Cooler Bypass Position Sensor Circuit Low (Bank 2)

P2499 stands for a bank 2 bypass position voltage that has fallen to the bottom of its range. No manufacturer documents the bank 2 code publicly. For orientation, GM's 2017 Duramax tables fail the bank 1 sensor (P2494) once its output drops under one percent of the supply and need 200 bad results out of 250 before the Type B fault is stored.
5 V sensor supply interrupted or pulled down
Bank 2 bypass position reads near zero
P249A: EGR Cooler Bypass Position Sensor Circuit High (Bank 2)
P249A is logged when the bank 2 bypass position signal sits near the top of the reference voltage. Like its siblings on this bank, it is not described by any manufacturer in public documents.
Lost ground at the bank 2 position sensor
Signal wire in contact with a supply line
Water ingress in the sensor connector
Check engine light after two trips
Bank 2 bypass position shows full scale
P249B: EGR Cooler Bypass Position Sensor Circuit Intermittent/Erratic (Bank 2)

P249B flags short dropouts or implausible jumps in the bank 2 bypass position signal that are too brief to count as a steady low or high fault. Public manufacturer documentation for it does not exist, and even the well documented bank 1 sensor on GM's Duramax only has low, high and learning checks, without an erratic test of its own.
Fretting or loose terminal in the bank 2 sensor plug
Harness brittle from heat near the turbocharger
Check engine light appears now and then
Bank 2 position value flickers in the live data
P249C: Excessive Time To Enter Closed Loop Reductant Injection Control

P249C covers the SCR dosing strategy rather than a part: after start-up the engine controller is expected to switch from fixed, map-based urea dosing to dosing corrected by the NOx sensor signal, and this code means that switch happened too seldom or too late.
Downstream NOx sensor slow to become ready or faulty, so closed loop cannot start
Implausible exhaust gas temperature signal upstream or downstream of the SCR
Mostly short or cold trips keep the SCR below its working temperature
Engine control software calibration requiring an update
Often no noticeable change in driving behaviour
NOx sensor or exhaust temperature codes may be stored as well
P249D: Closed Loop Reductant Injection Control At Limit - Flow Too Low
With P249D the NOx feedback loop of the SCR system has pushed its long-term correction as far as it may go because the delivered amount of DEF appears too small for the measured NOx.
Dosing valve partly blocked by urea crystals or deposits
Weak DEF pump or restricted supply line and filter
Diluted or wrong fluid in the DEF tank
NOx sensor reading too high and misleading the controller
Increased DEF warnings or later speed or power limitation
P249E: Closed Loop Reductant Injection Control At Limit - Flow Too High

P249E is the counterpart to P249D: here the SCR feedback has trimmed the dosing down to the lowest correction it is allowed, because more reductant seems to arrive than the NOx reading calls for. GM's 2014 diesel table flags a long-term adaptation factor below 0.41 (Type B); the 2018 table lists the low-side check as a two-trip Type B fault.
Dosing valve leaking or sticking partly open
Ammonia slip from an aged or overloaded SCR catalyst seen by the NOx sensor
White crystalline deposits at the dosing point
P249F: Excessive Time To Enter Closed Loop Particulate Filter Regeneration Control

During an active filter regeneration the controller is meant to steer the temperature ahead of the particulate filter with feedback from the exhaust temperature sensors, usually by adjusting late fuel injection or a hydrocarbon dosing valve in the exhaust. P249F is stored when the regeneration spent too little of its duration in that feedback mode.
Engine or aftertreatment module software needing an update
Exhaust temperature sensor ahead of the oxidation catalyst or filter reading wrongly
Hydrocarbon dosing valve in the exhaust restricted or slow to respond
Regenerations repeatedly interrupted by short trips or changing load
Regeneration may take longer or repeat more often
P24A0: Closed Loop Particulate Filter Regeneration Control At Limit - Temperature Too Low
P24A0 means the regeneration temperature loop is already giving all the extra heat it may, yet the gas ahead of the particulate filter stays below target.
Hydrocarbon dosing valve or its fuel supply restricted
Oxidation catalyst aged or face-plugged, so the fuel does not burn ahead of the filter
Exhaust temperature sensor reading too low
Exhaust leak ahead of the sensors cooling the gas
Regenerations take long or do not finish
P24A1: Closed Loop Particulate Filter Regeneration Control At Limit - Temperature Too High
Here the regeneration loop has reduced its heat input as far as possible, but the temperature ahead of the filter still runs above target.
Hydrocarbon doser or fuel injector leaking extra fuel into the exhaust
Fuel supply part causing unstable doser pressure (Hino 2020 bubbler filter)
Exhaust temperature sensor reading too high
Heavy soot load burning faster than the controller can follow
P24A2: P24A2 judges the outcome of a regeneration on the bank 1 filter: the event ended, but the estimated soot left in the filter is still above the allowed level. Ford's 2023 diesel summary runs this once per regeneration for up to 40 minutes and compares the soot estimate at the end with a threshold.
Regenerations interrupted by short trips or engine shut-off
Exhaust temperature not reaching target (doser, oxidation catalyst, sensors)
Differential pressure sensor or its hoses giving a wrong soot estimate
Malfunction indicator lamp or filter warning on
More frequent regenerations, higher fuel consumption
Reduced power if soot keeps building
P24A3: P24A3 is the bank 2 entry for a particulate filter whose soot load, estimated from differential pressure, exhaust flow and a soot model, has climbed to the point where it noticeably restricts flow and needs a regeneration. It only appears on engines with two separate filter strands, such as some V engines.
Mostly short trips so passive and active regeneration cannot finish
Excess soot from injectors, EGR or boost problems
Differential pressure sensor or hoses on bank 2 giving a false high reading
Particulate filter or engine warning lamp
P24A4: Particulate Filter Restriction - Soot Accumulation Too High (Bank 1)
P24A4 marks the critical stage for the bank 1 filter: the soot load is so high that a normal regeneration risks overheating and cracking the substrate. Deutz names P24A4-00 a critical soot load.
Earlier soot warnings or failed regenerations not dealt with
Excess soot from injectors, EGR valve or turbocharger faults
Filter saturated with ash at end of service life
Differential pressure measurement reading falsely high
Marked loss of power, limp mode
Malfunction indicator and filter warning lamp on
P24A5: P24A5 means the bank 1 cooler bypass is mechanically stuck, and makers read that in both directions. GM's 2017 Duramax DC-motor flap is judged stuck in bypass if the position is still above 15 % after P245B; the 2018 vacuum version is moved between both modes and fails when the gas temperature after the cooler barely reacts, both Type B.
Bypass flap seized by soot and carbon deposits
Actuator, linkage or vacuum supply no longer moving the flap
Incorrect EGR cooler fitted at the factory
Engine software that sets the fault too readily
Slow warm-up or more soot when the flap is stuck in cooling
Higher NOx and EGR gas temperatures when stuck in bypass
