P24A6: P24A6 is reserved for a mechanically stuck cooler bypass on bank 2. No manufacturer documents it publicly; the Ford and GM diesel summaries that describe the stuck test all apply it to a single bank and use P24A5.
Missing vacuum on a pneumatically switched bypass
Uneven exhaust temperatures between the two banks
P24A7: EGR Cooler Coolant Pump Control Circuit/Open

Some diesel engines feed the EGR cooler with an electric auxiliary coolant pump so the cooler gets flow at low engine speed or after shut-off, independent of the main pump. P24A7 means the engine controller sees an open or otherwise faulty control line to this pump, typically when the driver stage detects no load while switching.
Loose, corroded or unplugged pump connector
Broken control wire in the harness
Open winding or electronics in the pump
EGR may be reduced, NOx output rises
P24A8: EGR Cooler Coolant Pump Performance/Stuck Off

Unlike the circuit codes, P24A8 is about the pump's effect: it is commanded on, the wiring looks fine, yet the controller concludes that it does not deliver, for example because its speed feedback stays low or the expected temperature drop across the EGR cooler is missing.
Air pocket in the auxiliary circuit after service or a leak
Pump motor seized or impeller blocked
Coolant loss or bubbling at the expansion tank
EGR temperature or cooler efficiency codes may follow
P24A9: EGR Cooler Coolant Pump Control Circuit Low

P24A9 reports that the voltage on the control line of the electric EGR cooler coolant pump is lower than the driver stage expects in its current switching state, which usually points to a harness or pump-internal short to ground, or to a chafed wire touching the engine block.
Control wire chafed through and shorted to ground
Insulation melted near exhaust or EGR parts
Internal short in the pump electronics
Pump may run continuously or not at all
P24AA: EGR Cooler Coolant Pump Control Circuit High

With P24AA the controller finds the control line of the EGR cooler coolant pump at a higher voltage than its switching state allows. The classic causes are a short circuit toward battery voltage, for example where the harness rubs against a powered wire, moisture in the connector, or a pump that no longer draws current so the line floats up.
Control wire shorted to a battery voltage feed
Water or corrosion in the pump connector
Pump electronics failed so no current is drawn
Pump may not run when commanded
P24AB: EGR Cooler Coolant Pump Stuck On

P24AB is set when the EGR cooler coolant pump keeps running although the controller has switched it off, seen for instance in continued speed feedback or current draw. Causes include a driver stage or relay that stays closed, a short that bypasses the switching side, or pump electronics that ignore the command.
Relay or controller output stage stuck closed
Short in the harness bypassing the switched side
Pump electronics no longer responding to the command
P24AC: EGR Cooler Coolant Pump Feedback Circuit Low

Electronically commutated coolant pumps often report their state back to the controller on a separate feedback wire, typically as a speed or diagnostic signal. P24AC means that this return line sits below its valid range: shorted to ground, pulled down by a damaged pump, or permanently in an error level the pump uses to signal a dry run or blockage.
Pump signalling an internal fault, dry run or blockage
Corroded feedback pin in the connector
P24AD: EGR Cooler Coolant Pump Feedback Circuit High

P24AD is the high-side counterpart of P24AC: the return signal from the EGR cooler coolant pump stays above its valid band. Since such feedback lines are usually pulled up inside the controller, a broken wire or a disconnected pump often shows as a constantly high level, as can a short to a voltage feed.
Feedback wire broken or pump unplugged, line pulled high
Feedback wire shorted to a voltage feed
Pump electronics no longer pulling the signal down
Often no noticeable effect while driving
P24AE: The resistive particulate matter sensor behind the diesel particulate filter collects soot on interlocking electrodes; a rising current between them shows that particles are leaking through the filter. P24AE covers a fault in that electrode circuit.
Sensor element contaminated or damaged by moisture
Harness or connector to the sensor control unit damaged by heat or water
Fault in the separate sensor control unit
P24AF: P24AF tests whether the particulate matter sensor behaves plausibly while it burns itself clean. During that heated phase the electrodes must show a small but definite current, and the heater must change the signal in an expected way.
Sensor element aged or glazed, no longer responding
Sensor heater weak so the regeneration temperature is not reached
Element cracked by condensate after cold start
P24B0: P24B0 flags an electrode signal of the particulate matter sensor that sits too low, typically an open line or a cracked element that no longer conducts as expected. Ford's 2023 diesel summary watches the electrode supply continuously while the sensor measures and sets the code when it drops below 41.55 V for about 1.6 s.
Sensor element cracked or electrode interrupted
Open electrode line between sensor and sensor control unit
Sensor control unit cannot supply the electrode voltage
Particulate filter monitor does not complete
P24B1: P24B1 reports the electrode side of the particulate matter sensor reading high, which usually points to a short to a voltage source or to a soaked, conductive element. Ford's 2023 diesel summary sets it when electrode current exceeds 41 µA for about 3 s during measurement.
Condensate on the sensor element making it conductive
Electrode line shorted to a voltage source
Internal sensor fault, replacement sensor needed
Particulate filter monitor does not complete
P24B2: P24B2 stands for a PM sensor electrode reading that cuts out or jumps for short moments rather than staying permanently low or high. Such dropouts usually come from a loose pin, a chafed harness near the hot exhaust or moisture in the connector.
Loose or corroded pin in the sensor connector
Harness chafing on hot exhaust parts
Engine control software that needs reprogramming
Malfunction indicator lamp on, sometimes going out again
Particulate filter monitor does not complete
P24B3: Particulate Matter Sensor Heater Control Circuit/Open

P24B3 means the heater inside the particulate matter sensor cannot draw the current it should while it is switched on, typically because the heater line is open. The heater is needed to burn soot off the electrodes.
Heater element burnt out inside the sensor
False detection in the control software
Particulate filter monitor does not complete
P24B4: Particulate Matter Sensor Heater Control Circuit Range/Performance

P24B4 is a plausibility check on the heater of the particulate matter sensor, and makers apply it differently. Ford's 2023 diesel summary looks during measurement, with the heater switched off, and sets the code if heater voltage still exceeds 7 V for 2 s.
Protection tube of the sensor blocked by soot or deposits
Heater element aged and heating too slowly
Extra resistance in the heater harness
Heater output in the sensor control unit not switching off
Malfunction indicator lamp on (not with every manufacturer)
Particulate filter monitor does not complete
P24B5: Particulate Matter Sensor Heater Control Circuit Low
P24B5 points to the heater line of the particulate matter sensor being pulled toward ground, so the heater control sees an implausible current while heating is requested.
Internal heater fault in the sensor
False detection by the control software
Particulate filter monitor does not complete
P24B6: Particulate Matter Sensor Heater Control Circuit High
P24B6 reports the heater of the particulate matter sensor carrying current although it is commanded off, the classic sign of a battery-side short or a stuck driver stage in the sensor control unit.
Heater line shorted to battery voltage
Heater output stage in the sensor control unit stuck on
Sensor element damaged by uncontrolled heating
Particulate filter monitor does not complete
Sensor may fail again quickly if the short is not fixed
P24B7: P24B7 concerns the resistance of the heater element in the particulate matter sensor, which drifts as the platinum track ages. Ford's 2023 diesel summary measures it once per drive right after key-on, with the sensor between -30 and 150 °C, and sets the code if resistance leaves 1.06 to 2.93 Ω at the cold end or 1.81 to 4.12 Ω at the warm end.
Wrong sensor temperature distorting the expected value
P24B8: EVAP System Leak Detection Pump Pressure Sensor Circuit

P24B8 is the general circuit fault of the pressure sensor that sits inside an evaporative leak check module together with the pump and the switching valve. The sensor gets a 5 V reference from the engine computer and reports canister-side pressure during the engine-off leak test.
Open or shorted 5 V reference, ground or signal wire to the leak check module
Corroded or loose connector at the leak check module near the canister
Pressure sensor inside the leak check module failed
Engine control module does not supply the sensor reference
EVAP readiness monitor does not complete
P24B9: EVAP System Leak Detection Pump Pressure Sensor Circuit Range/Performance
P24B9 means the leak check module's pressure sensor delivers a signal that is electrically valid but not believable.
Pressure sensor in the leak check module drifted or noisy
Engine control software needing an update (FCA bulletins)
Moisture or dirt in the module's pressure port
Chafed wiring or loose pin causing signal disturbance
EVAP leak test aborted, readiness not set
Usually no noticeable change in driving
P24BA: EVAP System Leak Detection Pump Pressure Sensor Circuit Low
P24BA reports that the voltage from the leak check module's pressure sensor has fallen below the lowest value a working sensor can produce.
Sensor signal wire shorted to ground
5 V reference open or pulled down by another sensor on the same supply
Pressure sensor inside the leak check module failed
P24BB: EVAP System Leak Detection Pump Pressure Sensor Circuit High

P24BB is stored when the leak check module's pressure signal climbs above the top of its usable range. GM uses 4.85 V, about 97 % of the reference or roughly 120 kPa, again with 640 of 800 samples and Type B; the limit appears unchanged from the 2018 Volt up to GM's 2025 table 25OBDG03A for conventional ELCP systems.
Open sensor ground or signal wire, letting the input float high
Signal wire shorted to the 5 V reference or battery voltage
Pressure sensor inside the leak check module failed
EVAP leak test not run, readiness incomplete
P24BC: EVAP System Leak Detection Pump Pressure Sensor Circuit Intermittent
P24BC is meant for a pressure signal from the leak check module that drops out or jumps briefly, too short to latch the low or high limit. No manufacturer documents P24BC publicly.
Loose or spread terminal in the leak check module connector
Harness chafing near the canister or tank, intermittent short or break
Water or corrosion in the module connector
Sensor in the leak check module failing intermittently
Malfunction indicator lamp on, sometimes going out again
EVAP readiness monitor completes only occasionally
P24BD: EVAP System Leak Detection Pump Switching Valve Control Circuit/Open

P24BD points to the drive circuit of the switching valve inside the leak check module. This small solenoid moves the canister vent path between open air and the reference orifice, so the module can first measure a known leak and then test the real system. The code stands for an open or generally faulty control circuit.
Switching valve coil open inside the leak check module
Open control or supply wire, blown fuse or relay fault
Output driver in the engine control module faulty
EVAP leak test does not run
On some designs fuel door locked or purge disabled
P24BE: EVAP System Leak Detection Pump Switching Valve Control Circuit Low
P24BE says the voltage on the switching valve control line is too low while the valve should be idle.
No supply from the relay to the valve (fuse, relay, wire)
Switching valve coil open inside the module
Control wire between module and ECM shorted to ground
Fuel filler door does not open with the opener switch
Refuelling system service message on the display
P24BF: EVAP System Leak Detection Pump Switching Valve Control Circuit High

P24BF flags too much current in the switching valve circuit while the valve is energised. Mitsubishi's 2023 Outlander PHEV measures coil current through its low-side driver and sets the code when it reaches 2 A or more for 2 s with the valve commanded on.
Switching valve coil shorted inside the module
Control wire shorted to battery voltage
Output driver in the engine control module faulty
P24C0: EVAP System Leak Detection Pump Switching Valve Stuck On

P24C0 is a mechanical fault found during the leak test itself: the switching valve stays in its energised position, or the pump around it does not do its job. Mitsubishi's 2023 Outlander PHEV checks this when the parked car wakes its controller 5 h, 6 h or 8.5 h after shutdown.
Switching valve mechanically stuck inside the leak check module
Leak detection pump stuck on or not running
Open or shorted pump circuit or connector damage
Module pressure sensor frozen at one value
Fuel filler door does not open
P24C1: EVAP System Leak Detection Pump Switching Valve Performance/Stuck Off
P24C1 means the switching valve does not respond when commanded, so the vent path stays where it was.
Switching valve stuck in rest position inside the module
Open or shorted valve circuit so the valve never moves
Dirt or water from the vent line jamming the valve seat
Fuel filler door does not open
P24C2: Exhaust Gas Temperature Measurement System - Multiple Sensor Correlation Bank 1

Diesel exhaust lines often carry three or four temperature probes in a row, ahead of the oxidation catalyst, the particulate filter and the SCR catalyst. P24C2 says that on bank 1 the readings of these probes no longer agree with each other, without pinning the error on one of them.
One exhaust temperature probe has drifted with age and reads too high or too low
Corroded or heat-damaged connector adding resistance to one probe signal
Engine control software with too tight correlation limits (update available on some models)
Probes swapped between mounting positions after a repair
Particulate filter regeneration suppressed or aborted
Often no noticeable change in driving behaviour
P24C3: Exhaust Gas Temperature Measurement System - Multiple Sensor Correlation Bank 2

P24C3 is the bank 2 counterpart of P24C2 and only makes sense on engines whose two cylinder banks feed separate exhaust strings, each with its own set of temperature probes. The controller has found that the probes of the second string disagree among themselves beyond what the operating state allows. No manufacturer documents P24C3 publicly.
One bank 2 temperature probe has drifted and no longer matches the others
Contact resistance in a bank 2 probe connector or harness
Exhaust leak near one probe cooling its tip
Particulate filter regeneration may be inhibited
P24C4: EGR Cooler Bypass Position Sensor Exceeded Learning Limit Bank 1
The bypass flap of the EGR cooler learns its end stops, and P24C4 means the learned values for bank 1 have left the window the software accepts.
Worn bypass valve whose integrated position sensor no longer reaches its learned values
Soot deposits shifting the end stops of the flap
Signal offset from connector corrosion or a weak 5 V reference
Learning repeatedly cut short because the controller is woken right after key-off
Malfunction indicator lamp on after the second trip
Reduced EGR cooling, higher NOx output
P24C5: EGR Cooler Bypass Position Sensor Exceeded Learning Limit Bank 2

P24C5 belongs to engines with a second EGR cooler and bypass flap on bank 2. It reports that the end positions learned by that flap's position sensor fall outside the accepted window, so the controller can no longer trust where the flap really stands.
Worn bank 2 bypass valve or sensor track
Deposits changing the end positions of the bank 2 flap
Signal shift caused by wiring or connector resistance
Higher NOx emissions due to poorly controlled EGR cooling
P24C6: Inside the particulate matter sensor a meander-shaped platinum track measures element temperature, which the sensor needs to control its heater. P24C6 is the general circuit fault of that temperature signal.
Open or shorted temperature line in the harness
Fault in the sensor control unit
Particulate filter monitor does not complete
P24C7: Particulate Matter Sensor Temperature Circuit Range/Performance

P24C7 checks whether the temperature the particulate matter sensor reports fits the exhaust around it. Ford's 2023 diesel summary does an offset test after a cold soak of at least 6 hours, flagging more than 45 °C against the mean of the exhaust temperature sensors, and a dynamic test while driving that fails below -150 or above 60 °C against a model.
Sensor element damaged or temperature track drifted
Extra resistance between sensor and sensor control unit
Faulty exhaust temperature sensor used as reference
Particulate filter monitor does not complete
P24C8: Particulate Matter Sensor Temperature Circuit Low

P24C8 would be set when the temperature signal of the particulate matter sensor sits below its valid range, for example because the meander line is shorted to ground. No manufacturer documents this code publicly; the available summaries fold low and high readings into other codes.
Internal fault of the sensor element
Particulate filter monitor does not complete
P24C9: Particulate Matter Sensor Temperature Circuit High
P24C9 reports the PM sensor temperature reading stuck at the high end, which GM explains as a short toward supply voltage or a broken meander line.
Broken temperature lead near the sensor body
Temperature line shorted to a voltage source
Reference voltage of the temperature circuit too low
Particulate filter monitor does not complete
P24CA: Particulate Matter Sensor Temperature Circuit Intermittent
P24CA is reserved for a PM sensor temperature reading that fails only now and then instead of staying out of range. No manufacturer documents this code publicly.
Cracked joint inside the sensor lead
Malfunction indicator lamp coming and going
Particulate filter monitor does not complete
P24CB: Some SCR diesels have a switch at the DEF filler neck that tells the engine controller when the cap is opened, so a refill can be recognised and the tank level and fluid quality reassessed. P24CB is the general circuit code for this switch: the controller sees a signal that fits neither the open nor the closed state.
Cap microswitch sticking, especially in hot and humid conditions
Corroded connector or chafed wire at the filler neck
Dried DEF crystals around the switch actuator
Malfunction indicator lamp on, often right after refilling DEF
Refill not recognised, DEF warnings may persist
P24CC: Reductant Tank Cap Switch Circuit Range/Performance

P24CC is a plausibility fault: the cap switch at the DEF filler neck delivers an electrically valid signal, but its behaviour does not match what else the controller knows, for instance a switch that still reports an open cap long after refilling, or one that never changes state while the tank level clearly rose.
Switch stuck in one position so it no longer follows the cap
DEF residue hindering the switch plunger
Damaged or non-original filler cap that does not actuate the switch
Malfunction indicator lamp on after a DEF refill
Fill level or refill message not updated
P24CD: Reductant Tank Cap Switch Circuit Low

P24CD means the signal line of the DEF cap switch sits below its valid voltage band. With the usual pull-up input that points to the line being pulled to ground: a short in the harness near the filler neck, a switch with an internal short, or moisture bridging the contacts.
Signal wire chafed through to ground near the filler neck
Moisture or DEF in the switch or connector bridging to ground
Cap state shown permanently wrong, refills not detected
P24CE: Reductant Tank Cap Switch Circuit High

With P24CE the controller sees the DEF cap switch signal above its permitted band. On a pull-up input this typically happens when the line is open, because the input then floats up to the reference, or when it touches a supply wire; a broken switch contact can look the same.
Disconnected plug or broken wire letting the input float high
Signal wire touching a supply line
P24CF: Reductant Tank Cap Switch Circuit Intermittent/Erratic

P24CF is stored when the DEF cap switch signal jumps between states or drops out briefly although nobody touches the cap, typically while driving over rough roads. The controller counts unexpected changes and flags the circuit as unstable even if every single value lies within limits.
Loose or corroded terminal in the switch connector
Switch that sticks only partly and chatters
Harness rubbing on the tank or body
Malfunction indicator lamp, sometimes coming and going
P24D0: Particulate Matter Sensor Supply Voltage Circuit Low
P24D0 concerns the power feed of the particulate matter sensor and its control unit, which sinks when the supply line has excess resistance or a short toward ground.
Corroded fuse, relay contact or ground adding resistance
Fault in the sensor control unit
Particulate filter monitor does not complete
Further particulate sensor codes stored at the same time
P24D1: Before each measurement the particulate matter sensor heats its element to burn off collected soot. P24D1 means that this cleaning phase did not finish properly. Ford's 2023 diesel summary flags the code when the sensor cannot return to measuring after regeneration, judged over 120 s.
Sensor heater degraded, not reaching cleaning temperature
Heavy deposits on the sensor element
Particulate filter monitor does not complete
P24D2: Besides the control output, many DEF heaters have a sense line on which the controller reads back the voltage actually reaching the element. P24D2 marks a general fault on this sense circuit for heater A, such as an open lead or a reading that makes no sense at all, as opposed to the voltage being merely too low (P248A) or too high (P248B).
Broken or disconnected sense wire to heater A
DEF creep or water corroding the heater connector
Faulty measuring input in the SCR or engine control module
DEF warnings in cold weather, dosing delayed after a cold start
P24D3: P24D3 is the same kind of fault for heater B, which GM and Ford assign to the heated DEF line from pump to dosing valve. The read-back line of this heater is broken or delivers nonsense, so the controller cannot tell whether the hose is really powered; the narrower low and high cases are P248C and P248D. No manufacturer documents P24D3 in this sense.
Open sense wire or loose plug at the heated DEF line
Damaged heated line with internal conductor fault
Manufacturer-specific use of the code (FCA uses it for PM sensor supply), software update
DEF dosing faults or warnings at low temperatures
P24D4: EGR Cooler Coolant Pump Feedback Circuit
Where an electric auxiliary pump moves coolant through the EGR cooler, the pump usually reports back to the engine controller on a separate wire, for example with a speed or status signal.
Open feedback wire or loose connector at the pump
Failed pump electronics no longer sending a status signal
Blown fuse or failed relay leaving the pump without power
EGR reduced, possibly higher NOx and changed engine noise
Coolant temperature warnings if the pump really stops
P24D5: EVAP System Pressure Sensor/Switch B Circuit
P24D5 is the general circuit code for a second EVAP pressure sensor, called B to tell it apart from the main sensor A (P0450 range).
Open or shorted reference, ground or signal wire of sensor B
Loose or corroded connector at sensor B
P24D6: EVAP System Pressure Sensor/Switch B Circuit Range/Performance

P24D6 is a plausibility fault of EVAP pressure sensor B. GM's 2023 table 23OBDG03A checks the canister vapour pressure sensor at the start of a cold drive: after more than 3,600 s soak the offset must sit within a window around barometric pressure; a filtered ratio above 0.73 sets the code, Type A.
Wrong sensor version installed (GM HD trucks, narrow-range instead of wide-range)
Sensor offset drifted away from barometric pressure
Kinked hose or blocked port at the sensor
Engine control software needing an update (FCA, Audi)
Other EVAP codes such as a switching valve fault may appear alongside
P24D7: EVAP System Pressure Sensor/Switch B Circuit Low

P24D7 is set when EVAP pressure sensor B sends a voltage below its valid window. GM's 2023 table (23OBDG03A) watches its canister pressure sensor continuously and fails below 0.15 V, 3 % of the reference, with 640 of 800 samples, Type B; the sensor normally works between 0.5 and 4.5 V.
Signal wire of sensor B shorted to ground
P24D8: EVAP System Pressure Sensor/Switch B Circuit High

P24D8 reports EVAP pressure sensor B reading above its valid voltage. In GM's 2023 table 23OBDG03A the canister pressure sensor fails above 4.85 V, 97 % of the reference, counted over 640 of 800 samples and treated as Type B.
Open ground of sensor B, signal floats high
Signal wire shorted to reference or battery voltage
P24D9: EVAP System Pressure Sensor/Switch B Circuit Intermittent

P24D9 covers a sensor B signal that keeps flickering instead of failing outright. Mitsubishi's 2023 Outlander PHEV runs this check once per drive cycle inside the parked leak test, when the controller wakes at its scheduled times and coolant and intake air lie between 4 and 35 °C.
Loose terminal or poor contact at the tank pressure sensor
Harness chafed along the fuel tank
Tank pressure or tank differential pressure sensor unstable
Refuelling system service message on the display
P24DA: Particulate Matter Sensor Exhaust Sample Error Bank 1

P24DA checks that the particulate matter sensor actually samples exhaust gas, which is how the system detects a sensor that has been pulled out, sits in a blocked protection tube or is mounted wrongly.
Sensor removed from the exhaust or installed wrongly
Sensor no longer responding to exhaust flow
Particulate filter monitor does not complete
P24DB: Reductant Purge Control Valve B Circuit/Open

After shut-down an SCR system empties its lines back into the tank so no fluid freezes in them; in Bosch's Denoxtronic 2.2 a 4/2-way valve in the supply module reverses the flow for this. Valve B is a second purge valve, for instance in layouts with two dosing branches. P24DB reports a drive circuit fault of valve B, mostly an interruption.
Broken wire or unplugged connector to purge valve B
Open solenoid winding in valve B
DEF-induced corrosion in the supply module connector
DEF line not purged after shut-off, freezing risk in winter
P24DC: Reductant Purge Control Valve B Performance

P24DC judges purge valve B by its effect, not by its wiring: once the controller switches the valve to purge, the pressure in the DEF line it serves should fall noticeably, and here it did not. No manufacturer documents P24DC publicly.
Valve B mechanically stuck by crystallised DEF
Blocked return path or filter in the supply module
Frozen DEF line or dosing fault after cold nights
P24DD: Reductant Purge Control Valve B Circuit Low
P24DD means the control line of purge valve B shows too little voltage at a moment when it should be high.
Control wire chafed to ground near tank or frame
Valve coil shorted to its housing
Water or DEF in the connector
Valve may remain in purge position, dosing pressure not reached
P24DE: Reductant Purge Control Valve B Circuit High

With P24DE the control line of purge valve B stays at high voltage while the controller is actually pulling it to ground to switch the valve. That points to a short to the battery feed on the wire between valve and controller, or a valve coil with too little resistance, so that the driver protects itself and the valve never shifts.
Control wire touching a supply line
Valve coil with shorted turns and too low resistance
Damaged driver stage in the control module
DEF line not purged, frozen line after frost
P24DF: Reductant Purge Control Valve B Stuck Open

Stuck open means purge valve B remains in, or leaks toward, its emptying position while the system should be dosing. Part of the pump flow then goes back to the tank, so working pressure builds slowly, drops quickly when the pump stops, or needs a high pump duty to hold.
Internal leak or worn seat in purge valve B
DEF crystals preventing the valve from returning to dosing position
Control circuit fault keeping the valve energised
DEF pressure too low, reduced dosing and rising NOx
Warnings about reduced SCR function, possibly later engine power limits
P24E0: Reductant Purge Control Valve B Stuck Closed

Stuck closed means purge valve B does not move into its emptying position when commanded after shut-down, so the line it serves stays filled with fluid under residual pressure. In normal dosing this goes unnoticed; the risk appears in frost, when the trapped DEF freezes in hose, pump or injector and can crack them. No manufacturer documents P24E0 publicly.
Valve B seized by crystallised DEF or corrosion
Weak coil that no longer pulls the valve over
Intermittent open in the control circuit during shut-down
Frozen or burst DEF line or injector after frost
P24E1: An NH3 sensor behind the SCR catalyst measures ammonia that slipped through unused, letting the controller trim dosing and detect overdosing or an aged catalyst. P24E1 is the general circuit code for this sensor: its signal is missing, implausible or erratic. Deutz lists P24E1 for its MD1 engine controller with SPN 4377 and FMI 2, i.e.
NH3 sensor element or its electronics failed from heat and age
Heat-damaged wiring or connector near the exhaust
Software calibration issue, update available on some engines
Less precise DEF dosing, possible ammonia smell or higher NOx
P24E2: P24E2 flags an NH3 sensor whose signal is electrically valid but makes no sense: the ammonia value sticks, drifts or contradicts what the dosing model expects from the SCR catalyst. On heavy trucks the sensor is a smart unit with its own electronics that test probe and circuitry and report over J1939.
Sensing element aged or poisoned by deposits, giving a drifting ammonia value
Urea crystals around the sensor tip after overdosing
Exhaust leak near the sensor diluting the sample
Check engine light after two trips
DEF consumption noticeably higher or lower than usual
Possible ammonia smell at the tailpipe
P24E3: P24E3 means the NH3 sensor signal lies below the lowest value an intact sensor can deliver. Usual culprits are a short to ground between probe and its electronics module, a terminal pushed back in the connector or a defect inside the probe.
Chafed harness between probe and sensor module shorting to ground
Internal fault in the ammonia probe
Corroded or pushed-back terminal at the probe connector
Scan tool shows ammonia reading stuck at minimum
P24E4: P24E4 is set when the NH3 sensor signal climbs above anything a working sensor could report, so the value is rejected as electrically impossible rather than merely implausible. Typical reasons are a short to a supply voltage, a broken line pulled up internally, or failing electronics that output a saturated value.
Signal line shorted to a supply voltage in the harness
Open line between probe and module read as maximum value
Sensor electronics module outputting a saturated value
Ammonia reading pinned at the upper limit
P24E5: P24E5 covers an NH3 sensor signal that jumps or drops out for short moments while staying mostly in range. Vibration, heat cycling of the exhaust and road salt make loose connector pins and cracked insulation near the SCR can the main suspects.
Loose or corroded pins at the sensor or module connector
Harness insulation cracked by exhaust heat and vibration
Sporadic internal fault in the sensor electronics
Warning lamp that comes and goes
Live data shows spikes in the ammonia value
P24E6: Like a NOx sensor, the ammonia sensor only measures once its ceramic element is hot, so it carries an electric heater. P24E6 reports that this heater circuit is open or otherwise electrically faulty: the driver commands heating but sees no current flowing.
Heater element inside the NH3 probe burnt through
Broken wire in the sensor pigtail near the hot exhaust
Heater terminal without contact in the connector
P24E7: P24E7 points to a heater circuit of the NH3 sensor that reads too low: the feedback voltage stays near ground, or the current is far below what the heater should draw. Most often the heater feed is shorted to ground, which can also blow the fuse or switch off the driver to protect it; a heater whose resistance has risen sharply gives a similar picture.
Heater supply line shorted to ground
Heater element with strongly increased resistance
Blown fuse in the heater supply
Ammonia value missing or delayed after start
P24E8: With P24E8 the heater circuit of the NH3 sensor reads too high. Either the line is shorted to a supply voltage so that the heater cannot be switched off, or the driver measures overcurrent because the element has failed with low resistance.
Heater control line shorted to battery voltage
Heater element failed with low resistance, causing overcurrent
Heater driver in the sensor module defective
P24E9: P24E9 is not about a broken wire but about how the heater works: the circuit is intact, yet the NH3 probe does not reach or hold its operating temperature in the expected time, or its temperature control swings. Deutz lists P24E9 for its MD1 engine controller as SPN 4382 with FMI 2, meaning erratic or incorrect heater data.
Aged heater element no longer delivering full power
Condensate on the ceramic cooling it or causing thermal shock
Low supply voltage limiting heater power
Check engine light, often together with an NH3 sensor performance code
Ammonia reading available late or unstable
P24EA: The NH3 sensor is a smart unit: its electronics module needs its own power feed, usually switched battery voltage through a fuse or relay, to run the probe, the heater and the J1939 link.
Fuse or relay in the sensor feed faulty or loose
Damaged or corroded power or ground wire to the sensor module
Supply monitoring in the sensor module defective
Further NH3 sensor or communication codes stored
P24EB: NH3 Sensor Supply Voltage Circuit Low

P24EB reports that the power feed of the NH3 sensor module sags below its lower limit. Below that point the heater cannot bring the probe up to temperature and the electronics may reset, so ammonia readings and sensor messages become unreliable.
Weak or discharged batteries pulling system voltage down
High resistance in the ground path of the sensor module
Corroded fuse or relay contacts causing voltage drop
Warning lamp, often after cold starts
NH3 sensor drops off the data link at times
P24EC: NH3 Sensor Supply Voltage Circuit High

P24EC is stored when the feed voltage measured at the NH3 sensor module exceeds its upper limit. Overvoltage can damage the heater driver and the electronics, so the module may switch off heating and measurement to protect itself.
Overvoltage from jump-starting or a booster charger
Sensor supply line shorted to another higher feed
Other modules may also report high system voltage
P24ED: Every NH3 sensor leaves the factory with individual correction values for offset and gain stored in its own electronics. P24ED means this memory fails its integrity check, for instance a checksum mismatch or unreadable data, so the module cannot convert the raw probe signal into a trustworthy ammonia value.
Calibration data in the sensor module corrupted
Power loss while the module was writing data
No valid ammonia value although wiring tests pass
P24EE: P24EE says the microcontroller inside the NH3 sensor module has failed its own self-test, for example a watchdog reset, a RAM or ROM error or a timing fault. The engine controller only learns this through the status the sensor sends, because the processor is what runs the probe, the heater and the J1939 messages.
Electronics of the NH3 sensor module failed
Unstable supply voltage causing processor resets
Module damaged by heat or water ingress
NH3 sensor data missing or frozen
P24EF: Some control modules drive a discrete wake-up output that switches other units on before or alongside the network. P24EF reports an open circuit on that line.
Broken wake-up wire in the harness
Pin pushed back or corroded in a module connector
Wake-up output of the control module defective
Connected module stays asleep, with related communication codes
P24F0: P24F0 means that a control module drives its wake-up output on, but the line voltage stays down, pointing to a ground short or a load drawing far too much current. In GM's 2016 and 2019 hybrid tables the HPC2 module runs this check whenever the output is commanded on and reports a fault if the control voltage is at or below 5.52 V.
Wake-up line shorted to ground at a chafe point
Moisture in a connector bridging the line to ground
Receiving module loading the wake-up input too heavily
P24F1: With P24F1 the wake-up line carries voltage while its driving module has the output switched off, so a short to a battery feed or a second source keeps it live. GM's HPC2 module in the 2016 and 2019 hybrid tables flags 13.21 V or more in the off state, using the same 480-of-560 sample count at 12.5 ms and Type A, MIL after one trip.
Wake-up line shorted to a battery feed
Signal timing between ignition module and receiving unit, solved by coding
Voltage fed back from another module that stays awake
Check engine light and several warning messages
P24F2: EGR Temperature/Charge Air Cooler Temperature Correlation

P24F2 compares two readings in the intake path of a diesel with cooled exhaust gas recirculation: the gas temperature after the EGR cooler and the air temperature behind the charge air cooler. When conditions say both should be close, for instance after the engine has cooled down, a wide gap shows that one of the two sensors cannot be trusted.
Outdated PCM calibration flagging the correlation without a real fault (Chrysler 3.0 L diesel)
EGR temperature sensor drifting or sooted up
Charge air cooler outlet temperature sensor reading wrong
Corroded connector adding resistance to one sensor signal
Check engine light, often without any noticeable driving fault
EGR operation reduced as a precaution on some calibrations
Implausible EGR or charge air temperatures in live data after a cold soak
P24F3: P24F3 sets the temperature reported from the DEF (reductant) tank against the fuel temperature. After a long soak both liquids rest close to ambient, so a clear mismatch exposes a sensor that reads wrong although each signal may be electrically valid. No manufacturer explains P24F3 in a public service document.
DEF tank temperature sensor (often integrated in the tank or sender module) reading wrong
Local heat source such as an exhaust leak warming one sensor
Contact resistance in a sensor connector
Warning lamp, often after a cold start
DEF tank and fuel temperature far apart in live data after an overnight stop
P24F4: NOx Sensor Delayed Response - High to Low (Bank 1 Sensor 1)

P24F4 concerns the dead time of the upstream NOx sensor on bank 1 when engine-out NOx falls, typically on lift-off into overrun: the reading stays put too long before it starts dropping, even if the later descent is normal.
Soot or oil ash on the diffusion barrier of the front sensor
Aged measuring cells reacting late to falling NOx
Exhaust leak ahead of the sensor distorting the transient
Front NOx value lingers on lift-off
P24F5: NOx Sensor Delayed Response - High to Low (Bank 1 Sensor 2)

P24F5 is the same delay check for NOx sensor 2 on bank 1, which sits behind the SCR catalyst and judges its conversion. If its value lags when NOx at the outlet falls, the efficiency estimate is distorted and the SCR monitor could pass or fail wrongly, so the sensor must react in time.
DEF crystals or ammonia slip attacking the rear sensor element
Aged measuring cells of sensor 2 reacting late
Condensate in the cold tailpipe area affecting the sensor
Possibly an SCR efficiency code alongside
P24F6: Exhaust Aftertreatment Fuel Air Purge Valve Stuck Open

Heavy Volvo and Mack trucks regenerate the particulate filter with an aftertreatment hydrocarbon injector (AHI, the 7th injector) that sprays diesel ahead of the oxidation catalyst; compressed air from the truck supply then blows the line to the nozzle clear.
Oil or water in the purge air from an unsuitable or worn air-dryer cartridge
Debris holding the purge valve in the AHI module open
Damaged AHI nozzle or leaking fuel/air line toward the nozzle
Doser air supply pressure outside the 221 kPa specification
Particulate filter regeneration does not complete
Warning lamp and aftertreatment message on the dash
Rising soot load and more frequent regeneration requests
P24F7: Exhaust Aftertreatment Fuel Air Purge Valve Stuck Closed

P24F7 is the reverse case of P24F6: the purge valve of the aftertreatment fuel/air system will not open when commanded, so no compressed air reaches the dosing line and the 7th injector after a dosing phase.
Purge valve jammed by oil, water or particles from the air system
Air supply to the AHI module restricted or below specification
Coked or kinked line between AHI module and nozzle
Internal fault of the AHI dosing module
Active regeneration aborted or not started
Possible engine derate as soot load climbs
P24F8: Exhaust Aftertreatment Fuel Air Purge Valve Control Circuit

P24F8 is the electrical fault of the fuel/air purge valve: the control unit finds the solenoid drive circuit not working, typically an open wire or a coil that draws no current. Volvo and Mack report it as P24F813, the suffix 13 meaning open circuit.
Broken wire or chafed harness between engine controller and AHI module
Corroded or loose plug at the AHI dosing module
Interrupted coil of the purge valve solenoid
Warning lamp right after the circuit test runs
P24F9: Exhaust Aftertreatment Fuel Air Purge Valve Control Circuit Range/Performance

P24F9 covers a purge valve control circuit that is electrically present but behaves implausibly, for example when measured current or a feedback signal does not follow the commanded state within the expected time. Unlike P24F8, P24FA and P24FB, this variant appears in none of the Volvo/Mack AHI documents, and no manufacturer documents P24F9 publicly.
Purge valve moving slowly because of deposits
Solenoid coil resistance drifting with heat or age
High-resistance contact in the module plug
Warning lamp, sometimes only under heat
P24FA: Exhaust Aftertreatment Fuel Air Purge Valve Control Circuit Low

P24FA reports that voltage on the purge valve control line is lower than the driver stage expects in the current switching state: a short to ground on the wire, a coil with too little resistance or a weak supply.
Control wire chafed through to chassis ground
Purge valve coil with shorted turns
Moisture in the AHI module connector
Warning lamp shortly after key-on or during dosing
P24FB: Exhaust Aftertreatment Fuel Air Purge Valve Control Circuit High

With P24FB the purge valve control line sits higher than allowed, a pattern that points to a short to battery voltage or to a broken low-side path, so the controller cannot pull the line down. In the Volvo/Mack AHI guide P24FB00 is listed right beside P24FA00 among the electrical codes, and the first check is the harness and the plug at the dosing module.
Control wire shorted to a battery-voltage feed in the harness
Interrupted return path between valve and controller
Controller output stage protecting itself against overcurrent
P24FC: Particulate Matter Sensor Heater Control Circuit Driver Current/Temperature Too High

P24FC concerns the output stage that powers the heater of the particulate matter sensor: the driver reports excessive current or an internal temperature past its limit, which suggests a heater with shorted turns or too little resistance, or an overheating sensor electronics unit.
Internal failure of the smart PM sensor (heater or electronics)
Water ingress cracking the ceramic element or shorting the heater
Unusually high exhaust temperature at the sensor, e.g. during repeated regenerations
No soot reading from the PM sensor, DPF monitoring not completed
P24FD: P24FD is intended to flag that the particulate filter in position A is not the expected part or is absent, for example after a filter delete or when an unsuitable replacement has been fitted. No manufacturer documents P24FD publicly.
Particulate filter removed or replaced by a straight pipe
Leaking or blocked pressure lines making a present filter look absent
Visible soot at the tailpipe if the filter is missing
P24FE: P24FE means the controller concludes that the SCR catalyst is missing or not the expected part. Ford runs this test on the 6.7 L diesel (2023 summary) for about 60 s with SCR inlet at 195–340 °C and feedgas NOx of 70–500 ppm, and sets the code when cumulative SCR efficiency falls below 0 %.
SCR catalyst removed or replaced by a non-matching part
Upstream or downstream NOx sensor misreading (Ford sensor 11, Hino NOx sensors)
Controller software detecting removal falsely, fixed by reprogramming
Diluted DEF or faulty DEF injector collapsing NOx conversion
Warning or service lamp (Hino sets the service lamp, MIL stays off)
NOx downstream of the SCR as high as upstream in live data
P24FF: P24FF signals that the diesel exhaust fluid itself has become too hot while the engine runs. The controller reads the DEF temperature sensor in the tank and flags a value above its limit during operation; hot urea solution ages faster and can form deposits.
DEF tank coolant solenoid valve installed against its flow direction (Volvo)
Tank heating valve stuck open so hot coolant keeps flowing
Missing heat shield or exhaust leak warming the tank or lines
DEF temperature sensor reading too high
Warning lamp with SCR or DEF message
DEF tank temperature far above ambient in live data
P2500: P2500 points to the L line, the turn-on wire between engine module and alternator regulator that on many older layouts also runs through the charge warning lamp. The module reads back the voltage on this wire; when it stays below the expected level, for instance because the line is chafed to ground or the regulator holds it down, this code is logged.
L wire chafed through and shorted to ground
Alternator regulator faulty and pulling the L terminal low
Corroded or loose plug at the alternator
Output stage for the L line in the engine module defective
Battery or charge warning lamp on
Hard or no start after some time
P2501: With P2501 the engine module sees too much voltage on the L line to the alternator regulator. The wire is then either touching a battery-fed conductor, or the module cannot pull it down because the regulator side or the lamp path is open, so the line floats up to supply level.
L wire shorted to a battery-fed wire in the harness
Break in the L circuit or plug off at the alternator
Charge lamp does not light during the bulb check or stays on
Charging voltage unusually high or not controlled
P2502: P2502 is the general charging-system code: the engine module compares the voltage the generator actually delivers with what it has requested and finds a mismatch that it does not classify as simply too low or too high. Mazda uses it as a malfunction in the voltage produced by the generator.
Alternator or regulator not reaching the requested voltage
High resistance at ground or B+ connections (Mazda mild hybrid DC-DC converter)
Slipping drive belt or worn tensioner
Battery with internal fault distorting the charging voltage
Charge warning lamp on while driving
P2503: P2503 means the charging output is below target: with the engine running the module expects the generator to lift system voltage, but it stays too low. FCA calls the code Charging System Output Low.
Loose or burnt B+ connection between alternator and fuse box
Failed overrunning pulley or slipping belt
Battery lamp and check engine lamp on
Dim lights, electrical consumers dropping out
Engine stalls or will not start
P2504: P2504 is logged when the charging output overshoots: the measured voltage rises above what the module asked the generator to produce. FCA names it Charging System Output High and publishes several cases. A 2021 Ram 1500 lit the check engine lamp after a repair, with P2504 set and P2503 stored, and the advice was to voltage-drop every circuit involved.
High resistance at B+ fuse array or ground straps distorting the reading
Battery current or voltage sensor delivering wrong values
Check engine lamp, sometimes battery lamp
Very bright lights, bulbs failing early
P2505: P2505 covers the supply inputs of the engine module in general. GM documents it in the 2014 diesel engine table 14OBDG04: the module checks its permanent battery feed, the line that keeps the engine-off timer alive while the ignition is off.
Battery disconnected or permanent-feed fuse removed or blown
Open or corroded permanent supply wire or connector
Supply monitoring inside the module defective
P2506: P2506 is the plausibility variant: the supply reaching the engine module is electrically present but its value or behaviour does not fit the operating state. No passenger-car maker publishes how it detects this.
Resistance in supply fuse, relay contact or connector
Excessive current drawn through the module supply (Deutz)
Internal supply monitoring of the module faulty
Check engine lamp (Ford lists it as MIL code)
Sporadic stalling or restarts of the module possible
P2507: P2507 reports that a supply input of the engine module sits too low. Makers read this differently.
Supply fuse missing, pulled for transport or not fully seated
Weak battery or voltage dips during repeated starts
Corroded supply wire, ground or relay contact
Internal 5 V supply of the module failing (Ford diesel)
Often no symptom, code found during service (Mazda)
P2508: P2508 is set when a supply input of the engine module reads above its permitted range. Ford documents it for the 2023 6.7 L Power Stroke diesel: the module checks its internal 5 V supply rail and flags P2508 once that rail exceeds 5.5 V, with continuous monitoring, roughly 5 s to mature, and the module awake (key on, running or after-run).
Internal 5 V regulator of the engine module defective
Supply or sensor wire shorted to battery voltage
Overvoltage from charging fault or jump start
Other diagnostics such as the DEF quality test suspended
P2509: P2509 records a brief loss of the engine module's supply, a dropout rather than a lasting low or high value. Two Cummins-powered pickups show how easily it appears.
Battery disconnected before the module finished its after-run
Loose battery clamp, ground or supply connector
Module software too sensitive, fixed by reflash (Ram 6.7 L)
MIL on, often without drivability complaint
Code appears right after battery work
P250A: P250A is the general circuit code for the engine oil level sensor, a unit in the sump that today mostly measures by heated element or ultrasound and often reports oil temperature as well. Its use varies.
Sensor harness chafed or pinched (GM X154 jumper harness)
Engine oil overfilled, sensor reading out of range (Mazda CX-9)
Oil level sensor defective or leaking at its seal
Corroded or oily connector at the sump
Oil level warning or message in the cluster
Oil level display missing or wrong
With harness damage, further engine codes and stalling (GM)
P250B: Engine Oil Level Sensor Circuit Range/Performance

P250B fires when the oil level sensor answers electrically but its reading is implausible, for instance a level that jumps, stays frozen while the engine runs, or contradicts the value after a stop. Continuous sensors see a lower level in operation than at rest, so the plausibility logic has to account for running state, temperature and inclination.
Plausibility logic in the engine module too strict, fixed by update (Alfa Romeo)
Sensor element aged or contaminated by sludge
Oil level far outside the calibrated range after a service
Oil level message without real oil loss
Level display jumps or stays fixed
P250C: Engine Oil Level Sensor Circuit Low

P250C means the oil level sensor's signal line is pulled too low, the classic picture of a short to ground or, depending on the input design, a break that lets the line drop. Deutz describes its P250C-00 the same way: level sensor line grounded or interrupted.
Signal wire shorted to ground near the sump
Open circuit or unplugged sensor connector
Warning logic in the engine module, fixed by reflash (Hyundai 2.0 Nu)
No oil level reading in the cluster
P250D: Engine Oil Level Sensor Circuit High

P250D is stored when the oil level sensor line rises above its valid range. The usual explanation is contact with a positive conductor; with pull-up inputs an interrupted line or missing sensor ground can also drive the signal high. Deutz gives the clearest definition: its EMR controller files P250D-00 as the level sensor shorted to battery.
Signal wire shorted to supply voltage
Sensor ground open or signal line interrupted
P250E: Engine Oil Level Sensor Circuit Intermittent/Erratic

P250E flags an oil level signal that drops out or jumps in an unrealistic way while the circuit otherwise looks intact. Typical sources are a loose terminal, a wire that breaks only under engine movement, or a sensor that loses its echo or heating cycle intermittently.
Loose or oily terminal in the sensor connector
Wire breaking intermittently from engine movement
Sensor losing its measuring cycle sporadically
Oil level message appears and disappears
P250F: P250F is not a wiring code: the oil level sensor works, and the measured level is below the minimum.
Oil burned past valve stem seals or piston rings
External oil leak or too little oil after a service
Warning logic triggering with correct level, fixed by update (Hyundai)
Low engine oil message and check engine light
Oil level near or below minimum on the dipstick
P2510: ECM/PCM Power Relay Sense Circuit Range/Performance
P2510 judges whether the main relay of the engine module behaves as commanded, based on what the module senses on the switched supply. GM's 2014 diesel tables describe two checks.
Main relay contacts welded or sticking
Relay dropping out early (weak coil, poor socket contact)
Battery disconnected or supply lost during after-run
Relay driver or EEPROM handling in the module faulty
MIL after two trips (GM type B)
Battery drain if the relay stays closed
Lost adaptations if the relay opens too early
P2511: ECM/PCM Power Relay Sense Circuit Intermittent

P2511 covers short dropouts on the line through which the engine module reads back the output of its main relay. The relay is commanded on, yet the sensed voltage briefly vanishes and returns, typical of a chattering contact, a cracked solder joint in the relay or a loose terminal in the fuse box.
Worn or chattering main relay contact
Loose relay socket or fuse box terminal
Engine may stall briefly or hesitate
P2512: P2512 concerns the wired request line between the event data recorder and the engine module. The recorder, normally part of the airbag control unit, stores a short history of speed, throttle, brake and other pre-crash data when it senses a crash or near-crash, and needs powertrain values for that.
Request wire broken or connector unplugged
Airbag/recorder module missing, replaced or not configured
Engine module configured for a recorder line that is not fitted
Possibly a service or wrench indicator
P2513: Event Data Recorder Request Circuit Low

P2513 is set when the event data recorder request line reads too low at the engine module. A wire rubbed through to body ground, a crushed harness after body work, or water in a floor connector are the obvious suspects; a low line may also be read as a permanent request.
Moisture or corrosion in an under-floor connector
Recorder or engine module input stage faulty
Possibly a service or wrench indicator
P2514: Event Data Recorder Request Circuit High

P2514 tells you the request line between the event data recorder and the engine module sits at too high a level. The recorder, normally housed in the airbag control unit, keeps a short log of speed, pedal and brake data around a collision and fetches engine values through this line.
Request wire chafed against a powered circuit
Missing ground or unplugged connector at the airbag/recorder module
Input stage in engine or recorder module faulty
Code stored with no effect on driving
Possibly a wrench or service indicator instead of the check engine light
P2515: A/C Refrigerant Pressure Sensor B Circuit

P2515 is the general circuit fault of a second refrigerant pressure sensor, called B. Heat pump systems and vehicles with electric compressors often measure pressure at several points in the circuit; which position is B is up to the maker.
Pressure sensor electronics failed (Audi early build sensors)
Connector corroded or wiring to the sensor damaged
Evaluating module (thermal management or engine) faulty
A/C does not cool or cools only intermittently
Further A/C pressure codes such as P0530 stored
P2516: A/C Refrigerant Pressure Sensor B Circuit Range/Performance

P2516 flags a pressure sensor B whose reading is electrically valid but does not behave like real refrigerant pressure. In GM's hybrid OBD tables sensor B is the low-side sensor, evaluated by the hybrid processor that also runs the electric compressor.
Pressure sensor stuck at one value
Compressor runs but hardly changes pressure (very low charge, blockage)
High resistance in signal or ground wire
Check engine light after two drives (GM type B)
P2517: A/C Refrigerant Pressure Sensor B Circuit Low
P2517 means the signal of refrigerant pressure sensor B has dropped below its usable floor.
Signal wire open or shorted to ground
5 V reference missing (wire or shared supply pulled down)
A/C compressor does not switch on
Check engine light after two drives on GM hybrids
P2518: A/C Refrigerant Pressure Sensor B Circuit High

P2518 is stored when pressure sensor B reports a signal close to its supply voltage. GM, which uses B for the low-side sensor in its hybrid tables, sets the limit at 98 % of the reference, about 4.90 V.
Signal wire shorted to 5 V or battery voltage
Moisture or corrosion in the sensor connector
Check engine light after one drive on newer GM hybrids
P2519: P2519 covers the general circuit fault of a wired input through which the climate control asks the engine module for compressor operation. The engine module needs this request early, to raise idle speed, add torque reserve and then energise the compressor clutch relay.
Request wire broken or connector loose
Climate control unit or A/C switch not sending a valid signal
Idle speed does not rise when A/C is selected
P251A: P251A concerns the switch the operator uses to arm the power take-off on a work truck. The control module reads this switch line and only allows PTO mode, often with a raised working idle, when the signal is plausible. This code means the module sees no valid state, typically an interrupted wire or a switch that no longer closes.
Poor PTO or engine-to-frame ground (paint under the eyelet, corrosion, bolt bottoming out)
Broken or unplugged wire between PTO enable switch and module
Worn PTO enable switch that no longer makes contact
Faulty connection made during body or equipment installation
PTO cannot be engaged or drops out intermittently
Working idle speed is not raised when PTO is selected
Stored code with normal driving behaviour
P251B: With P251B the module reads the PTO enable switch input as stuck at a low level, below what either switch position should produce. A wire chafed through to chassis ground, water in a connector or a switch shorted internally are the usual explanations.
Switch signal wire chafed against frame or body
Moisture or corrosion in the switch connector
PTO will not engage, or engages without being selected
P251C: P251C is logged when the PTO enable switch line sits above its valid window, close to supply voltage. That points to a signal wire touching a battery or ignition feed, a reference that has lost its ground, or a pull-up that the switch can no longer pull down.
Switch signal wire shorted to a battery or ignition feed
Missing ground on the switch or module reference
Switch stuck in the applied position
PTO engages or high idle starts without operator request
PTO cannot be switched off normally
P251D: P251D covers the engine shutdown line of a power take-off installation. On trucks with body equipment such as cranes, pumps or aerial devices, a hard-wired signal lets the PTO controller or an equipment stop button tell the engine module to switch the engine off.
Open shutdown wire or loose connector at the body interface
Fault in the body equipment's stop switch or controller output
Shutdown input enabled in calibration but not wired by the upfitter
PTO locked out or equipment will not run
Equipment stop button no longer shuts down the engine
P251E: P251E reports that the PTO engine shutdown input reads too low. Whether low means stop now or all clear depends on the maker's wiring, so the practical effect varies: the module may treat the line as an active stop request and refuse to keep the engine running in PTO mode, or it may simply flag the line as shorted and ignore it.
Shutdown wire chafed through to chassis ground
Corroded connector at the body builder interface
Equipment stop switch shorted to ground
Engine stops or will not stay running while PTO is used
P251F: P251F is the high-side fault of the PTO engine shutdown input: the voltage stays near supply level where the module expects a defined switching state. A shutdown wire touching a powered circuit in the body harness, a missing ground on the equipment controller, or an add-on module that drives the line permanently are typical.
Shutdown wire shorted to a powered circuit in the body harness
Retrofitted control module holding the line high
Engine does not stop when equipment shutdown is triggered
P2520: P2520 is set when the voltage on A/C request input A stays below the band the engine module accepts. Depending on whether the input is active-high or active-low, a grounded wire then reads as a permanent request or as none at all – either way the module distrusts it.
A/C does not switch on, or compressor runs although A/C is off
Idle speed behaves oddly when the A/C is toggled
P2521: With P2521 the engine module sees A/C request input A held above its valid range, typically because the wire touches a supply line, the input has lost its pull-down or the sending control unit drives it permanently high. Two makers list the code by number. Ford includes P2521 in the 2014 BOSS 302S engine module table without a lamp mark.
Request wire shorted to a supply voltage
Climate control unit drives the line permanently high
Code newly reported after an engine software update (Sprinter T21)
A/C compressor runs although A/C is switched off
Raised idle speed without A/C request
P2522: P2522 is the general circuit code for a second wired A/C request input, B. Why an engine module would need two such lines is left to each maker; plausible uses are a separate rear evaporator, a second request stage or a redundant line to cross-check input A.
Input B wire broken or connector loose
Sending climate module or switch faulty
A/C function served by input B unavailable
Idle dips when the compressor engages without notice
P2523: P2523 reports that A/C request input B is pulled below its valid range. On the wire level this usually means a conductor grounded against body metal, a sending module whose output transistor has failed shorted, or a wet connector draining the signal.
Input B wire shorted to ground
Output stage of the sending module shorted
Moisture in a connector of the request line
Compressor not engaging or engaging unasked
P2524: P2524 indicates that A/C request input B reads above the level the engine module treats as valid. A line chafed against battery or ignition feed, an open pull-down inside the module or a control unit that latches its output high are the usual explanations.
Input B wire shorted to battery or ignition voltage
A/C cannot be switched off or on as expected
P2525: P2525 is the general circuit fault of the pressure sensor on a vacuum reservoir. Diesels, and many hybrids and electric drives, lack usable intake vacuum and run a separate pump, often driven from the camshaft or by an electric motor, that fills a reservoir.
Sensor wiring open or connector loose
Shared 5 V reference disturbed by another sensor
Check engine light depending on maker
Reduced boost or EGR function in default mode
P2526: Vacuum Reservoir Pressure Sensor Circuit Range/Performance

P2526 marks a vacuum reservoir pressure reading that stays inside the electrical range but does not fit the situation, for instance no rise in vacuum after the pump has run, or a value frozen while actuators draw on the reservoir.
Leaking vacuum hose, check valve or reservoir
Mechanical or electric vacuum pump delivering too little
Check engine light, often with boost or EGR codes
Weak exhaust brake or reduced power
Hissing noise from a leaking line
P2527: Vacuum Reservoir Pressure Sensor Circuit Low

P2527 means the signal from the vacuum reservoir pressure sensor has fallen below the lowest voltage a working sensor can produce. Whether low volts stand for deep vacuum or for atmospheric pressure depends on the sensor curve, but a reading at the floor is treated as an electrical fault, not as a vacuum value.
5 V reference open or pulled down
Boost or EGR control in default mode, less power
P2528: Vacuum Reservoir Pressure Sensor Circuit High

P2528 is logged when the vacuum reservoir pressure sensor delivers a voltage near or at its supply, beyond anything the sensing element can output. A signal wire touching 5 V or battery voltage, a broken sensor ground, or corrosion bridging pins in the connector are the classic findings.
Signal wire shorted to 5 V or battery voltage
Corrosion bridging pins in the connector
Check engine light depending on maker
Reduced power with actuators in default position
P2529: Vacuum Reservoir Pressure Sensor Circuit Intermittent

P2529 covers a vacuum reservoir pressure signal that drops out or jumps for short moments rather than staying wrong. The engine module notices changes faster than a reservoir could physically empty or fill, or brief excursions to the electrical limits that recover again.
Loose or spread terminal in the sensor connector
Harness chafing or wire breaking under engine movement
Check engine light comes and goes
Occasional brief loss of power or boost
P252A: P252A is the general circuit code for an engine oil quality sensor, a unit in the sump that judges the state of the oil from its physical properties. Hella's PULS+C variant, for example, adds measurements of viscosity, density and permittivity to ultrasonic level sensing, so oil changes can follow real wear instead of a fixed mileage.
Sensor connector loose, unplugged or corroded by oil and moisture
Broken signal, supply or ground wire near the oil pan
Internal electronics of the oil quality sensor failed
Oil condition or service interval display missing or showing a fault
Warning message in the instrument cluster, usually without engine light
P252B: Engine Oil Quality Sensor Circuit Range/Performance

P252B covers an oil quality sensor whose signal is electrically valid but makes no sense in context. Plausibility logic can weigh the reported oil properties against oil temperature, time since the last service or the engine's own oil ageing model; a value that stays frozen while conditions change, or leaps after a top-up without reason, is suspect.
Deposits or sludge on the sensing element distort the measurement
Oil grade or viscosity outside what the sensor calibration expects
Sensor aged or drifting, reading frozen or offset
Plausibility logic in the engine software too strict
Oil condition display shows implausible values or a fault message
Service interval calculated inconsistently after an oil change
P252C: Engine Oil Quality Sensor Circuit Low

P252C is stored when the oil quality sensor's signal sits below the range the engine computer accepts. Typical reasons are a signal wire chafed through to ground, a supply line that has lost its voltage or an internal short in the sensor; depending on the input circuit an open wire can also drag the reading down.
Signal wire chafed against the oil pan or engine block (short to ground)
Sensor supply voltage missing (fuse, supply wire)
Internal short in the oil quality sensor
Oil condition value missing in the cluster or service menu
Service reminder falls back to fixed intervals or shows a fault
P252D: Engine Oil Quality Sensor Circuit High

P252D means the oil quality sensor reports a voltage above its valid window. A short of the signal line to a positive conductor, a broken sensor ground or, with pull-up inputs, an interrupted signal wire can all push the value to the upper stop. Sensor electronics that latch high are a further possibility.
Signal wire shorted to a supply or battery-voltage wire
Sensor ground or signal wire interrupted, connector pin pushed back
Sensor electronics stuck at a high output
Warning or blank oil condition value in the cluster
Oil change reminder appears too early, too late or not at all
P252E: Engine Oil Quality Sensor Circuit Intermittent/Erratic

P252E points to an oil quality signal that briefly drops out or jumps while the circuit is otherwise intact. Typical sources are a terminal that loses contact when the engine shakes, a harness rubbing on the sump or a sensor whose internal measuring cycle is occasionally disturbed.
Loose or corroded terminal in the sensor connector
Harness rubbing on the oil pan with intermittent contact
Sensor electronics failing intermittently with heat or vibration
Oil condition message appears and disappears
Fluctuating oil condition or service interval values
P252F: P252F is not a wiring fault: the level sensor works and reports more oil in the sump than the permitted maximum. Deutz's EMR controller files the condition as P252F-00 under oil level parameter SPN 98 with FMI 15, and Ford's 2014 BOSS 302S code table lists P252F without a lamp entry.
Too much oil added at the last oil change or top-up
Fuel dilution from frequent short trips or diesel particulate filter regeneration
Coolant entering the oil (head gasket, oil cooler)
Oil level warning in the instrument cluster
Dipstick reading above the maximum mark, oil may smell of fuel
Possible rich mixture codes after long drives
P2530: P2530 is the general fault of the hard-wired run signal that tells a powertrain module the ignition switch is in its run position. Modules use this line to wake up, power their outputs and decide when to start their internal shutdown routine; many also cross-check it against the ignition status sent over the network.
Blown fuse or faulty relay in the run feed
Loose terminal at the module or ignition switch
Warning lamps or stored codes in several modules
Engine may stall or not start
P2531: Ignition Switch Run Position Circuit Low

The engine module logs P2531 if the run-position input stays low although the vehicle state says the ignition is on, for example while the engine runs or the network reports run. The supply side is the usual suspect: an open fuse, a relay that does not pull in, a wire grounded on the body or a switch contact that no longer carries current.
Open fuse in the run circuit
Run signal wire shorted to ground
Engine stalls or will not restart
Several warning lamps or communication codes at once
P2532: Ignition Switch Run Position Circuit High

P2532 means voltage is present on the run-position input when it should be absent, typically after key-off or while the network reports the ignition as off. A run feed backfed through another component, a relay with welded contacts or a wire touching a permanent battery feed can cause it.
Voltage backfeed into the run circuit through another component
Run wire touching a permanent battery feed
Battery drained after the vehicle is parked
Modules or fans keep running after key-off
P2533: P2533 is the general fault of the circuit that is live in both the on and the start position of the ignition switch, often called run/crank. Unlike the pure run line it must stay powered while the starter turns, so modules rely on it to remain awake during cranking. Ford lists P2533 in its 2014 BOSS 302S code table with the M marker for the MIL.
Powertrain module software or parameters (Ford Mach-E 2021, reprogramming per TSB 21-2244)
Fuse or relay fault in the run/crank feed
Loose or corroded terminal at the module
Possible no-start or stall during cranking
P2534: Ignition Switch On/Start Position Circuit Low

P2534 is the most widely documented of this group. GM's 2025 tables let the TCM fail it when its run/crank input is false while the ECM reports run/crank active, 99 failures out of 240 samples at 25 ms, Type A; the brake control module (EBCM) sets it when its primary wakeup line reads low for 3 s while the network says run or crank, Type B.
Engine harness chafed at a bracket (GM HD trucks, upper control arm bracket)
Module software needing an update (GM 6L50 TCM, Ram eTorque HCP)
Loose terminal on the wakeup line at TCM or BCM
Transmission or other modules set follow-up codes
P2535: Ignition Switch On/Start Position Circuit High

P2535 means the run/crank input stays active while it should be off. GM's 2025 tables fail it in the TCM after 320 of 400 samples with run/crank true while the ECM reports it inactive, Type A, and in the brake control module (EBCM) when the primary wakeup line stays high for 3 s against the network status, Type B; the 2016 Volt uses more than 6.0 V on the li…
Voltage backfeed from another module (GM K111 fuel pump driver via water-in-fuel sensor circuit)
Run/crank wire touching a battery feed
MIL on, code returns at every key-on after clearing
P2536: P2536 is the general fault of the accessory input, the signal that is live when the key or start button is in the accessory position and that on many vehicles also acts as a wake-up line between body and powertrain modules. The code does not say whether the line is open, low or high, only that its state cannot be used.
Fault in the accessory feed or wake-up output of the body module
Loose or corroded terminal on the accessory line
Worn accessory contact in the ignition switch
Remote start or key-off functions not working
Accessories behave inconsistently in the accessory position
P2537: Ignition Switch Accessory Position Circuit Low

P2537 reports that the accessory or accessory wake-up input sits low where a high level is expected. GM documents it in detail: on the 2016 Volt the ECM fails it when the accessory input is false while the propulsion system has been active for more than 0.5 s; it is a Type B fault over 2 trips, and the 6-speed TCM tables evaluate the same input with no MIL.
Open or high-resistance accessory wake-up circuit between BCM and ECM/TCM
Body control module not driving the wake-up output
Poor terminal contact at ECM or TCM connector
Power liftgate works only with ignition on
Blower may keep running after engine shutdown (diesel)
P2538: Ignition Switch Accessory Position Circuit High

P2538 is set when the accessory input reads high in a state where it should be inactive, for instance once the vehicle is switched off and the body module should have released the line. Backfeed from an aftermarket device, a stuck accessory relay or a wire touching a battery feed are the obvious causes.
Backfeed from aftermarket equipment connected to the accessory line
Accessory wire chafed against a battery feed
Radio or accessories stay on after key-off
P2539: Low Pressure Fuel System Sensor Circuit

P2539 is the general circuit code of the sensor that reports the supply pressure ahead of the high-pressure pump. In VW's 2014 specification books for the Passat, CC and Touareg it is set once the signal exceeds 4.80 V, which the Passat book attributes to a broken line or contact with the positive supply; below 0.2 V VW stores P2541 instead.
Signal or ground wire open, connector not engaged
Signal wire shorted to the 5 V reference or battery voltage
Failed low-pressure fuel sensor or pressure switch
Code logged only in a static self-test without a real fault (Ford Transit 2015)
Hesitation or reduced power under load
P253A: The PTO sense circuit tells the powertrain modules whether the power take-off is really engaged, usually through a pressure or limit switch on the PTO unit.
Open sense wire or disconnected plug at the PTO unit
Failed PTO pressure or limit switch
PTO feedback configured in the module but no PTO fitted
PTO status not shown or PTO functions unavailable
P253B: P253B is not about a broken wire but about a PTO feedback signal that is electrically valid yet does not fit the situation. A module can compare the sense input with the operator request, engine speed or transmission state: PTO reported engaged although nobody selected it, or no engagement feedback although the PTO was commanded long enough ago.
Limit or position switch on the PTO misadjusted
PTO engagement mechanism or clutch sticking
Low air or oil pressure at the PTO engagement and pressure switch
PTO engagement reported wrongly in the cluster or scan tool
P253C: P253C flags a PTO feedback input that reads too low for any valid switch state. Where the sense switch closes to ground on engagement, a grounded wire looks like a permanently engaged PTO; where it pulls up, the same fault hides every engagement.
Sense wire rubbed through to ground near the PTO
Oil or water in the sense switch connector
PTO shown as engaged although it is off, or never shown as engaged
P253D: P253D means the PTO feedback input reads above its valid range. Besides genuine shorts to voltage or an open ground on the sense switch, Ram documents a software cause: bulletin 21-013-15 (replacing 21-005-14) covers 2013–2014 Ram 3500 pickups and 3500, 4500 and 5500 chassis cabs with the 6.7L Cummins and Aisin AS69RC six-speed, where the MIL came on with P2…
Outdated TCM calibration (Ram heavy-duty with Aisin AS69RC, reflash per bulletin)
Sense wire shorted to a voltage source
Open ground or reference at the PTO sense switch
MIL on without a noticeable PTO problem
PTO status wrong in scan data
P253E: P253E is stored when the PTO feedback signal flickers between states faster or more often than a real engagement could explain. Vibration on a frame-mounted or transmission-mounted PTO is the classic trigger: a loose terminal, a cracked wire near a bracket or a bouncing switch contact make the signal chatter.
Loose or spread terminal in the sense switch connector
Wire cracked by vibration near the PTO
Worn sense switch with bouncing contact
PTO-related idle or shift strategy switches on and off
P253F: P253F states that the engine computer considers the oil used up. Depending on the design this verdict comes from an oil quality sensor or, more often, from an oil life model that tallies operating conditions such as load, temperatures and estimated fuel dilution.
Oil change overdue, oil actually aged
Oil life counter not reset after the last oil change
Strong fuel dilution from short trips, cold operation or frequent regenerations
Oil life calculation in the engine software too aggressive (update available)
