Oil change or oil quality warning in the cluster
Remaining oil life shown as zero or dropping unusually fast
P2540: Low Pressure Fuel System Sensor Circuit Range/Performance

P2540 checks whether the low-pressure fuel sensor's reading is credible. The signal stays inside its electrical window, yet the pressure it reports does not fit what the supply side should be delivering.
Weak in-tank or lift pump causing real pressure deviation
Restricted fuel filter or kinked supply line
Hesitation or power loss under load
P2541: Low Pressure Fuel System Sensor Circuit Low

P2541 means the signal of the low-pressure fuel sensor is below its valid range - typically a short to ground on the signal line or a lost 5 V sensor supply. VW's 2014 specification books set it below 0.2 V on the Passat, CC and Touareg (VW labels it short to ground, low input or out of range low), whereas a signal above 4.8 V leads to P2539.
5 V reference supply missing or pulled down by another sensor
P2542: Low Pressure Fuel System Sensor Circuit High

P2542 means the low-pressure fuel sensor reports a voltage above its permitted range. Deutz is explicit: its MD1 controller stores P2542 when the supply pressure sensor signal rises beyond its normal voltage or is shorted toward the high side (SPN 94, FMI 3), and the EMR system describes P2542-00 as a battery short.
Signal wire shorted to the 5 V reference or battery voltage
Sensor ground wire or pin interrupted
Failed low-pressure fuel sensor with high output
Reduced power or stalling if real pressure is low
P2543: Low Pressure Fuel System Sensor Circuit Intermittent

P2543 reports a low-pressure fuel sensor signal with brief interruptions or spikes, although it remains within its electrical range most of the time - a loose pin, a chafed wire or a sensor with an internal contact problem.
Loose or corroded pin at the sensor connector
Chafed signal or supply wire with intermittent contact
P2544: Torque Management Request Input Signal A
P2544 concerns torque requests that another module, usually the transmission control module, sends to the engine module – for example to cut torque during a shift.
Loose or unseated pins at the transmission connector
Data bus disturbance or failing gateway
Transmission module software or internal fault
Check engine light, often with several U-codes
Harsh shifts or reduced engine power
P2545: Torque Management Request Input Signal A Range/Performance

P2545 means torque request A arrives intact but carries values the receiving module cannot accept as plausible – a requested torque outside the expected window, a request that contradicts the operating state, or one that does not follow up as it should. Ford's 2014 BOSS 302S engine module table lists P2545 with M, i.e. with check engine light.
Transmission oil leak or incorrect oil level (JLR 9HP48)
Requesting module sends implausible torque values
Check engine light (Ford) or transmission warning
P2546: Torque Management Request Input Signal A Low

P2546 says that torque request A, the channel over which one module asks another to raise or cut engine torque, reads below its permitted floor. On a hard-wired request this points to a line pulled toward ground; on a data-bus request it means a value pinned at or under the minimum the receiver accepts.
Oil leak or low oil level in the transmission
Wired request line shorted to ground
Transmission warning message or check engine light
Fault often stored together with P2545
P2547: Torque Management Request Input Signal A High

P2547 is logged when torque request A sits above the highest value the receiving module will accept. A wired input would read like a line touching a supply voltage or a lost ground at the sender; a bus message would carry an out-of-scale number. The receiver ignores such a request, since following it could mean an unwanted torque increase.
Request line shorted to a supply voltage
Requesting module sends a value above the scale
Poor ground at the requesting module
Shift-related torque reduction no longer works, firmer shifts
Check engine light depending on make
P2548: Torque Management Request Input Signal B
P2548 is the general fault on a second torque request channel, B, used when a further module besides the transmission may ask the engine for less or more torque.
Data bus disturbance between brake module and engine module
Brake/traction control module sends corrupted messages
Weak battery or poor module power supply
Check engine light after two trips (GM Type B)
Traction or stability control warning lamp
Reduced traction intervention on slippery roads
P2549: Torque Management Request Input Signal B Range/Performance

P2549 covers a torque request on channel B that arrives readable but makes no sense: a requested torque outside the expected band, a request that contradicts the current driving state, or one that changes in a way the sender could not plausibly mean. The wiring or bus link is assumed intact here, which separates it from the general fault P2548.
Requesting module (e.g. brake/traction module) computes implausible values
Software levels of sender and engine module do not match
Faulty input data at the requesting module, such as wheel speed
Check engine light depending on make
Traction control intervenes abruptly or not at all
P254A: P254A covers the first PTO speed selector: the switch or sensor an operator uses to choose one of the preset working speeds for a power take-off. The engine controller expects a defined signal on this line; with P254A it finds no valid state, typically a broken wire, an unplugged connector or a switch contact that never closes.
Broken selector signal or return wire
Selector or upfitter connector disconnected or pushed-out pin
Switch contact that no longer closes
PTO stays at standby speed instead of the selected step
Selected working speed cannot be called up
Stored code without effect on normal driving
P254B: P254B is the rationality fault of PTO speed selector 1. The wiring is intact and the voltage sits inside the electrical limits, yet the reading does not fit any configured position, or it contradicts other information the controller holds, for example two speed requests at once or a value that lingers between steps.
Wrong resistor value in the upfitter's speed coding
Controller configured for a different selector type
PTO does not leave standby speed
Wrong working speed for the selected position
P254C: PTO Speed Selector Sensor/Switch 1 Circuit Low

P254C reports that the signal from PTO speed selector 1 sits below the lowest voltage the controller accepts, which in practice means the signal wire touches ground or the switch is shorted internally. Whether a maker can detect this at all depends on the design.
Selector signal wire chafed through to ground
Internal short in the selector switch
Water in an exterior selector connector
PTO speed stuck at one step
P254D: PTO Speed Selector Sensor/Switch 1 Circuit High

With P254D the controller sees the PTO speed selector 1 input above its upper limit. Causes are a signal wire rubbing against a battery-fed circuit, a broken ground or sensor return that lets the line float to the pull-up voltage, or a selector supply that is too high.
Signal wire shorted to a battery-fed circuit
Open ground or return line letting the input float high
PTO jumps to the highest preset speed
P254E: PTO Speed Selector Sensor/Switch 1 Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P254E is set when the signal from PTO speed selector 1 changes faster or more often than a real switch operation can explain, or briefly drops out and returns.
Loose terminal at the selector or upfitter connector
Corroded splice in the upfitter wiring
Vibration on a body-mounted switch panel
Engine speed surges while the PTO is running
PTO drops briefly to standby speed
P254F: P254F concerns the circuit of the hood switch, which tells the control units whether the engine hood is open. Engines that can start on their own, such as in hybrids or stop/start systems, need this to block an automatic start while someone works under the hood.
Hood switch dirty, corroded or misadjusted
Damaged wiring or connector at the hood latch
Bent hood latch after a front-end repair
Check engine light after two trips (GM Type B)
Auto-stop or hybrid engine start disabled
Hood-open warning while the hood is closed
P2550: Torque Management Request Input Signal B Low

P2550 marks the second torque request input, B, as stuck below its lower limit. A hard-wired line would be pulled to ground by chafed insulation or a fault in the sending stage; in a networked design the sender would be reporting a value that lies under the bottom of the defined range.
Request line chafed through and shorted to ground
Output stage of the requesting module defective
Check engine light depending on make
Traction-related torque reduction no longer applied
P2551: Torque Management Request Input Signal B High

P2551 is the high-side fault of torque request B: the signal sits above the top of its valid window. Typical electrical causes would be a line touching a battery feed, an interrupted reference ground or a sender that drives its output to full scale.
Request line shorted to battery voltage
Open ground or reference at the sender
Requesting module drives its output to full scale
Check engine light depending on make
Traction control warning, engine ignores intervention requests
P2552: P2552 is the general circuit fault of throttle/fuel inhibit A, a line over which the engine module can be told, or can itself command, that throttle opening or fuelling must be blocked. It acts as a safety path next to the normal pedal-to-throttle chain.
Inhibit line open, e.g. broken wire or pushed-out pin
Inhibit relay or its supply defective
Engine module input or output stage faulty
Usually no check engine light (Ford non-MIL)
Possible power limitation or no throttle response
P2553: P2553 means the throttle/fuel inhibit path A is electrically present but does not behave as commanded.
Inhibit relay sticking or contacts worn
Fault in the relay control or feedback wiring
Internal fault in the engine or throttle control unit
Check engine light on the drive after the fault was found
Possible reduced power or throttle limp mode
P2554: P2554 reports that the voltage on throttle/fuel inhibit circuit A is too low. In GM's 2005 L66 parameter sheet the limit is below 0.498 V on the analogue inhibit circuit, read by the powertrain module while it is still processing after the ignition has been switched off. The table lists a warm engine, coolant at 69.5 °C or more, among the enable conditions.
Connected relay or control unit pulls the line down
Check engine light on the following drive
Sluggish throttle response or reduced power
P2555: P2555 indicates excess voltage on throttle/fuel inhibit circuit A. The same 2005 GM document for the L66 V6 uses two limits depending on key state: more than 10 V while the ignition is on, or more than 4.5 V once it is off, with the fault judged after 4 s.
Inhibit circuit shorted to a battery-fed wire
Missing ground on the receiving side
Check engine light on the next trip
Limited throttle opening or reduced power
P2556: P2556 is the general circuit code for the coolant level sensor or switch, normally fitted in the expansion tank. Deutz uses it on its EMR L1 engine control for industrial engines with the sub-code P2556-F0, a ground error, under SPN 111. Mercedes-Benz goes its own way and stores P2556-7B, meaning the sensor reports a fluid level that is too low.
Damaged wiring or ground at the level sensor
Air cushion in the expansion tank (Mercedes EQB)
Real coolant loss, e.g. internal charge air cooler leak
Low coolant warning in the cluster
Coolant level appears correct after opening the cap
P2557: Engine Coolant Level Sensor/Switch Circuit Range/Performance

P2557 means the coolant level signal is electrically present but not believable. The Deutz EMR L1 engine control is the one documented user and fills the code twice under SPN 111: P2557-00 for a sensor value outside the valid range, and P2557-1C when the supply voltage feeding the level sensor is itself out of range.
Sensor supply voltage out of range (Deutz P2557-1C)
Level sensor element contaminated or failing
Air pocket or foam in the expansion tank distorting the reading
Coolant level warning appears and disappears
Engine protection warning on industrial engines
P2558: Engine Coolant Level Sensor/Switch Circuit Low

P2558 reports that the coolant level sensor or switch signal sits too low on the electrical scale. Deutz assigns it on the EMR L1 controller as P2558-14 under SPN 111 and groups two causes together: a grounded line or an interrupted one, which on that input both pull the reading to the bottom.
Broken wire or corroded connector at the expansion tank
Permanent low coolant warning despite a full tank
No warning possible if the level really drops
P2559: Engine Coolant Level Sensor/Switch Circuit High

P2559 is the high-voltage fault in the circuit of the coolant level sensor or switch. In the Deutz EMR L1 code list it appears as P2559-12 under SPN 111 meaning the line is shorted to battery plus; Deutz keeps open circuits under P2558 on that input, so a high reading there really points to contact with a positive feed.
Signal line chafed against a positive feed
Open circuit on pull-up type switch designs
Low coolant warning does not work
Warning lamp or message for the level sensor
P255A: P255A belongs to the second PTO speed selector input, which lets the operator call up a further preset working speed in addition to selector 1. The controller finds no valid state on this line: a wire is broken, a connector is off, or the switch contact never closes.
Broken wire between selector 2 and the module
Upfitter connector for selector 2 not mated
P255B: P255B flags an implausible reading from PTO speed selector 2 although its circuit is electrically intact. Because a second selector normally works together with the first, the check can compare both: requests that cannot coexist, a level that sits between valid positions, or a selection that the configured number of presets does not allow.
Upfitter wiring ties selector 1 and 2 together
Number of programmed presets does not match the switch
Second preset ignored or wrong speed reached
PTO speed control falls back to standby
P255C: PTO Speed Selector Sensor/Switch 2 Circuit Low
P255C means the input of PTO speed selector 2 reads lower than the controller's bottom limit, usually because the signal wire has a short to chassis ground or the switch is shorted inside.
Selector 2 wire shorted to chassis ground
Harness pinched under a body mounting
Engine always runs at the second preset in PTO mode
P255D: PTO Speed Selector Sensor/Switch 2 Circuit High

P255D is stored when PTO speed selector 2 delivers a signal above the permitted maximum. A chafed wire touching a battery-fed circuit, a lost sensor ground, or an upfitter feeding 12 V into an input meant to be switched to ground are the realistic causes.
Selector 2 wire chafed against a battery-fed circuit
Upfitter applies 12 V to a ground-switched input
Lost ground or return line of selector 2
PTO switched off by the controller
P255E: PTO Speed Selector Sensor/Switch 2 Circuit Intermittent/Erratic

P255E concerns short dropouts or rapid changes on the PTO speed selector 2 signal that do not match deliberate operation. Selector 2 is often the remote control on the body, close to pumps, booms or spreaders, so vibration, spray water and cable movement hit it harder than an in-cab switch.
Spray water or moisture in the body-mounted remote switch
Cable to the remote control flexing at a boom or hinge
Loose crimp or terminal in the selector 2 circuit
Engine steps through preset speeds unexpectedly
P255F: P255F flags the A/C request A input as electrically sound but implausible: the request may switch on and off far more often than a real compressor demand would, stay set while the climate control is off, or disagree with what the engine module sees from the compressor side.
Climate control module sends erratic requests
Loose contact on the request line causing chatter
Idle speed fluctuates when the A/C cycles
A/C cooling intermittent or switched off
P2560: P2560 is not an electrical fault but a level finding: the coolant level sensor works, yet it reports less coolant than the minimum. Deutz uses it on the EMR L1 control as P2560-00 under SPN 111 with failure mode 1, meaning the level has fallen under its warning threshold.
External leak at hoses, radiator or water pump
Internal leak, e.g. charge air cooler or head gasket
Air trapped after a coolant service
Visible coolant traces or sweet smell
P2561: A/C Control Module Requested MIL Illumination

P2561 is a messenger code. The climate control module has found an emission-relevant fault in its own area, such as a component that feeds the engine's A/C idle strategy, and asks the engine module to switch on the warning lamp, since only the master controller may drive it.
Emission-relevant fault stored in the climate control module
Failed A/C sensor or actuator behind that fault
Climate control module internal or software fault
A/C may not cool or may be switched off
Further codes stored in the climate control module
P2562: Turbocharger Boost Control Position Sensor A Circuit

P2562 flags a general electrical problem in the circuit of the position sensor that reports where turbocharger boost actuator A stands - the variable vane linkage on many diesels, the electric wastegate actuator on turbo petrol engines.
Open or corroded wiring or connector between position sensor and engine computer
Electronic wastegate actuator rod length out of adjustment
Position sensor inside the actuator failed
Reduced power because boost is limited
P2565 stored at the same time on some engines
P2563: Turbocharger Boost Control Position Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance

P2563 means the position feedback of the turbocharger boost control actuator - variable vanes or wastegate - does not match the commanded position, without an open or short being reported. GM's 2009 Duramax diesel table sets it when vane position differs from target by 15 % or more for 5 s (Type B, warning light after two trips).
Kinked, twisted or leaking vacuum hose to the boost actuator
Leaking actuator diaphragm or sticking vanes
Broken or missing adjustment stud, actuator travel out of tolerance
Noticeable loss of power, limp mode
Underboost code P0299 stored at the same time
P2564: Turbocharger Boost Control Position Sensor A Circuit Low

P2564 is stored when the voltage from the boost actuator position sensor stays below the lowest value a working sensor can deliver, which usually points to a short to ground or a lost reference supply. GM's 2009 Duramax table uses 0.277 V (5.5 %, vanes fully open) held for 1 s once the engine has run 3 s, Type B.
Signal wire chafed through and touching ground near the turbocharger
5 V reference supply to the sensor missing or shorted
Failed position sensor or vane actuator
Noticeable loss of power or limp mode
Other sensors on the same 5 V supply may report faults too
P2565: Turbocharger Boost Control Position Sensor A Circuit High

P2565 means the boost actuator position signal sits above the highest plausible value, typically from an open signal wire, a short to the 5 V reference or battery voltage, or a failed sensor. GM's 2018 diesel ECM table flags it at an analog reading above 95 % in 200 of 250 samples (Type A, warning lamp on the first trip).
Open signal wire or unplugged actuator connector
Signal wire shorted to the 5 V reference or battery voltage
Wastegate actuator rod set to the wrong length (electric wastegate engines)
Failed vane actuator with integrated sensor
Loss of power, sometimes limp mode
Unusual turbocharger noise on some diesels
P2566: Turbocharger Boost Control Position Sensor A Circuit Intermittent
P2566 reports that the signal from the boost control position sensor flickers or drops out briefly instead of being steadily wrong.
Loose or corroded pin at the position sensor connector
Heat-damaged or chafed sensor wiring near the turbocharger
Worn position sensor in the actuator
Intermittent loss of power or limp mode
Check engine light, sometimes going out again
P2567: Direct Ozone Reduction Catalyst Temperature Sensor Circuit

P2567 is the general circuit fault of the sensor fitted to a direct ozone reduction (DOR) radiator - a radiator with a catalytic coating that converts ground-level ozone in the passing air and earns low-emission vehicles an NMOG credit. CARB section (e)(14) requires the OBD system to detect a missing or deteriorated DOR function.
Damaged sensor wiring or connector at the radiator
Replacement radiator without coating or without sensor fitted
No change in driveability or engine cooling
Possible failed emissions inspection because of the stored code
P2568: Direct Ozone Reduction Catalyst Temperature Sensor Circuit Range/Performance

P2568 is the plausibility check of the sensor on a direct ozone reduction (DOR) radiator, whose coating converts ozone in the cooling air. VW's 2014 specification books for the CC and Tiguan set it on a failed ID check or a failed functional check of the temperature sensor.
Aftermarket radiator without ozone coating or without the identification sensor
Identification sensor not bonded after radiator replacement
Check engine light, often after a radiator replacement
No change in driveability or engine cooling
P2569: Direct Ozone Reduction Catalyst Temperature Sensor Circuit Low
P2569 means the radiator-mounted sensor of a DOR system (direct ozone reduction: a radiator coating that breaks down ozone in the incoming air) shows an electrical fault toward ground.
LIN wire to the radiator sensor chafed and shorted to ground
Water or salt corrosion in the radiator sensor connector
Internal short in the radiator sensor
No change in driveability or engine temperature
P256A: Engine Idle Speed Selector Sensor/Switch Circuit/Open

P256A refers to the switch or sensor with which the driver chooses a raised idle speed, for example to run a generator, an inverter or belt-driven equipment while parked, independent of any PTO. The controller sees no valid state on this input, which points to an open wire, a disconnected plug or a switch that no longer makes contact.
Open wire in the idle selector circuit
Selector connector loose or not mated
P256B: Engine Idle Speed Selector Sensor/Switch Range/Performance
P256B means the idle speed selector delivers a value that is electrically valid but makes no sense in context.
Aftermarket idle control wired into the same circuit
Idle or PTO configuration changed without matching hardware
P256C: Engine Idle Speed Selector Sensor/Switch Circuit Low

P256C says the idle speed selector input is pulled below its lowest valid level, typically by a signal wire shorted to ground or a switch with an internal short. Where the selector is a simple ground-switched input, the controller would read such a short as a permanent request, so a dedicated low code presupposes a coded or monitored circuit.
Idle selector wire shorted to ground
Internal short in the idle selector
Code returns after every key cycle
P256D: Engine Idle Speed Selector Sensor/Switch Circuit High

P256D is logged when the idle speed selector signal rises above the highest value the controller treats as valid. Causes include a wire chafed against a battery-fed circuit, an open sensor return that lets the input float high, or an accessory module that drives the line with system voltage. No manufacturer documents P256D publicly.
Selector wire chafed against a battery-fed circuit
Open return line letting the input float high
Accessory module feeding system voltage into the line
P256E: Engine Idle Speed Selector Sensor/Switch Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P256E records an idle speed selector signal that drops out or flickers for short moments, more often than real switch use would cause.
Loose crimp or terminal in the selector circuit
Harness moving with engine vibration at idle
Raised idle drops out and comes back
Engine speed rises and falls at standstill
P256F: P256F is the plausibility fault of a second A/C request input, B. Its wiring checks out, yet the engine module finds the state or timing illogical, for instance a request present while the first input and the climate controller say no cooling is wanted, or one that flickers instead of holding steady.
Climate control logic sends inconsistent B request
Intermittent connection on the B request line
Fault in a second evaporator or compressor stage control
Idle dips or surges with A/C operation
P2570: Direct Ozone Reduction Catalyst Temperature Sensor Circuit High
P2570 is the high-side electrical fault of the sensor fitted to a DOR radiator, the ozone-converting coated radiator found on some low-emission petrol cars.
Sensor not connected or not fitted after radiator replacement
Broken LIN wire or loose terminal
Check engine light, often right after radiator work
P2571: Direct Ozone Reduction Catalyst Temperature Sensor Circuit Intermittent/Erratic

P2571 stands for an unsteady or intermittently lost signal from the temperature sensor of a direct ozone reduction (DOR) catalyst. Unlike P2569 and P2570, which describe a lasting low or high fault, this code covers readings that jump around or vanish for moments.
Loose or corroded terminal at the radiator sensor plug
Sensor no longer firmly bonded to the radiator
Harness damaged by vibration at the radiator mounting
Check engine light that may come and go
No noticeable effect on driving or cooling
P2572: Direct Ozone Reduction Catalyst Deterioration Sensor Circuit
P2572 points to a general fault in the circuit of a sensor meant to judge how much ozone-converting activity is left on a direct ozone reduction (DOR) catalyst, such as a coated radiator.
Damaged wiring or connector at the DOR sensor
Replacement radiator without the sensor fitted
No effect on engine power or cooling
P2573: Direct Ozone Reduction Catalyst Deterioration Sensor Circuit Range/Performance

P2573 means the deterioration sensor watching a DOR (direct ozone reduction) catalyst delivers a signal that is electrically within limits but does not fit the expected behaviour, for example a value that never changes with conditions or contradicts other inputs.
Deterioration sensor drifting or stuck at one value
Non-original radiator with a sensor that does not match
Radiator face heavily fouled, skewing the sensor reading
Check engine light after several drive cycles
No change in how the car drives
P2574: Direct Ozone Reduction Catalyst Deterioration Sensor Circuit Low

P2574 is set when the deterioration sensor circuit of a direct ozone reduction (DOR) catalyst reads below its valid range, the usual signature of a short to ground or a failed sensor pulling the line down. No manufacturer documents P2574 publicly.
Sensor wire shorted to ground at the radiator
Car drives and cools as before
P2575: Direct Ozone Reduction Catalyst Deterioration Sensor Circuit High

P2575 reports a deterioration-sensor signal above the valid range on a direct ozone reduction (DOR) catalyst - typical for an open circuit, a missing ground or a short to a supply voltage. No vehicle maker has published how it uses P2575, and no service bulletin naming it turned up in the NHTSA index.
Connector left off or damaged during radiator work
Signal wire shorted to a supply voltage
No change in power or engine temperature
P2576: Direct Ozone Reduction Catalyst Deterioration Sensor Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P2576 describes a deterioration-sensor signal on a direct ozone reduction (DOR) catalyst that comes and goes or jumps without a physical reason, rather than staying low (P2574) or high (P2575).
Loose or corroded terminal in the sensor connector
Harness chafing at the radiator support
Cracked connector housing letting water in
Check engine light, possibly only now and then
P2577: Direct Ozone Reduction Catalyst Efficiency Below Threshold

P2577 means the OBD system has concluded that the direct ozone reduction (DOR) catalyst - usually a radiator coated with an ozone-destroying catalyst such as BASF's PremAir - no longer converts enough ozone.
Catalytic coating worn, damaged or covered with dirt
Faulty DOR sensor giving a false result
No change in engine cooling or performance
P2578: P2578 is the catch-all electrical fault for speed sensor A, the pickup that counts revolutions of the turbocharger or supercharger shaft, normally by sensing a tone feature on the compressor wheel or its nut.
Loose, corroded or oil-soaked connector at the speed sensor
Harness chafed or heat-damaged near the hot turbocharger housing
Internal failure of speed sensor A
Fault in the engine control module input stage
Reduced power because boost is limited as a precaution
Turbo speed missing or frozen in live data
P2579: Turbocharger/Supercharger Speed Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance
P2579 means speed sensor A delivers a signal, but the shaft speed it reports does not fit the operating state the engine computer expects from boost, airflow and load.
Speed sensor A dropping out intermittently
Engine software that misjudges the speed plausibility (update available on some models)
Intake or boost leak that makes the shaft speed differ from the model
Mechanical turbocharger problem such as bearing drag or wheel damage
Sudden loss of power that returns after lifting off the accelerator
Turbo speed in live data jumping or inconsistent with boost
P257A: P257A is an output fault on the control line of the vacuum reservoir, usually a solenoid or switching valve the engine computer uses to connect, isolate or vent a vacuum storage tank.
Loose or corroded connector at the reservoir control valve
Broken wire in the control or supply line
Open solenoid coil in the control valve
Faulty output stage in the engine control module
Vacuum-driven actuators such as EGR or turbo vanes respond poorly
P257B: P257B points to a vacuum reservoir control circuit whose voltage is too low, which in practice usually means a ground short on the line between the control unit and the reservoir valve, or a driver stage that cannot hold the line at its proper level.
Control wire chafed through and shorted to ground
Shorted coil in the reservoir control valve
Damaged output stage in the engine control module
Follow-up codes for EGR or turbocharger position
P257C: P257C sets when the control line of the vacuum reservoir valve reads too high, typically from a short to battery positive or a fault in the driver stage, so the valve can no longer be switched as commanded.
Control wire shorted to a battery-voltage line
Internal fault in the reservoir control valve
Faulty output stage in the engine control module
Weaker boost or EGR response in some cases
P257D: P257D is the plausibility fault of the engine hood switch. The line is electrically readable, but the value falls into a band the module regards as impossible, or two redundant switches disagree. Hood status matters because stop-start, hybrid and remote-start logic must never crank the engine while someone is working in the bay.
Hood switch or plunger worn, misadjusted or contaminated
Fluid or corrosion in the switch or ECM connector shunting the signal
Second hood switch or latch switch reporting a different state
Replacement switch with wrong resistance coding
Check engine lamp after two drives
Hood ajar message although the hood is closed
Auto stop-start or remote start not available
P257E: P257E says the hood switch signal has dropped below its lowest valid level, which usually means the signal wire touches ground or the switch is shorted inside. GM's 2018 engine table 18OBDG04 sets it for a resistance-coded switch at 325 ohms or less, the 2019 hybrid table 19OBDG01 at 14.6 % of range or less, each with 80 failures in 100 samples and Type B.
Hood switch signal wire chafed to ground near the latch
Hood switch and horn connectors swapped after front-end repair
Switch shorted internally by water or impact damage
Hood ajar indicator on with the hood shut
P257F: P257F is the high-side counterpart of P257E: the hood switch reading rises above the top limit, which points to an open signal line, a pin that has backed out of its connector, or a short to a voltage source.
Open hood switch signal wire or unplugged switch
Loose or pushed-back pins in a front harness connector
Signal line shorted to a voltage source
Hood warning may be shown or may be missing when the hood is really open
P2580: Turbocharger/Supercharger Speed Sensor A Circuit Low

P2580 says the signal from turbocharger or supercharger speed sensor A stays at the low end, so the engine computer sees too little or no usable pulse activity - typically from a short to ground, a weak sensor or a pickup that cannot read the target.
Debris on the tone wheel or an extra O-ring in the sensor bore
Speed sensor A with weak or missing output
Turbo speed reads zero or very low in live data
Possible boost limitation and reduced power
P2581: Turbocharger/Supercharger Speed Sensor A Circuit High

P2581 is set when speed sensor A reports a level above what a healthy circuit can produce, so the engine computer cannot trust it. Typical triggers are a signal wire shorted to the supply or battery voltage, an open signal or ground path that lets the input float high, or a sensor with a shorted output stage.
Signal wire shorted to supply or battery voltage
Open ground or signal wire letting the input float high
Speed sensor A with a shorted output
Implausibly high or fixed turbo speed in live data
P2582: Turbocharger/Supercharger Speed Sensor A Circuit Intermittent

P2582 points to a speed sensor A signal that cuts out or jumps for short moments while being fine in between, so the fault may be gone by the time the vehicle reaches the workshop. Loose terminals, a cracked wire that opens under vibration or heat, and a sensor failing internally when hot are the usual suspects.
Loose or spread terminal in the sensor connector
Wire break that opens only under vibration or heat
Speed sensor A failing when hot
Brief power dips that come and go
Warning lamp that may switch off again
Turbo speed trace with dropouts or spikes
P2583: Cruise Control Front Distance Range Sensor Single Sensor or Center

P2583 points to the front distance sensor of adaptive cruise control – the only radar, or the centre unit where several are fitted. The engine module keeps the code because adaptive cruise acts directly on engine torque.
Snow, ice, dirt or a non-approved grille trim in front of the radar
Radar software needing the manufacturer update
Radar misaligned after a knock or bumper repair
Radar unit or its wiring faulty
Adaptive cruise control switches off or cannot be engaged
Warning to clean the radar sensor
Collision mitigation braking unavailable, warning lamps on
P2584: Fuel Additive Control Module Requested MIL Illumination

P2584 belongs to diesel cars that add a fuel-borne catalyst to the tank so the particulate filter can burn off soot at lower exhaust temperatures. A separate additive module meters the fluid after each refuelling, in proportion to fuel added, and watches its pump, level sensor and its own circuits.
Additive reservoir empty or level sensor faulty
Additive dosing pump or injector failed
Additive module wiring, supply or CAN link faulty
Additive quantity counter not reset after refill or filter change
Loss of power as soot load rises
P2585: Fuel Additive Control Module Warning Lamp Request

P2585 is the softer sibling of P2584. Here the fuel additive module asks for a warning lamp other than the MIL – typically a service or particulate filter indicator – because something needs attention before emissions suffer.
Refill or new additive bag not registered with the scan tool
Level sensor in the additive reservoir faulty
Service or particulate filter warning lamp on
Message about additive level in the instrument cluster
P2586: Turbocharger Boost Control Position Sensor B Circuit

P2586 covers a general electrical fault at position sensor B, which reports where the second boost control actuator stands - the vane mechanism or electric wastegate of a second turbocharger on engines that regulate two of them separately.
Connector or terminal fault at the actuator B position sensor
Harness to actuator B damaged by exhaust heat
Position sensor inside actuator B failed (often replaced as a unit)
Reduced power because boost is capped
No valid position value for actuator B in live data
P2587: Turbocharger Boost Control Position Sensor B Circuit Range/Performance

P2587 is a plausibility fault: position sensor B gives an electrically valid reading, but the reported position of the second boost actuator does not follow the command, or the value lies outside what the mechanism can physically reach. No manufacturer documents P2587 publicly, so the logic is known only from sensor A.
Sticking variable vanes or wastegate linkage on turbo B
Kinked or leaking vacuum line or diaphragm on pneumatic actuators
Actuator rod or adjusting stud out of adjustment or broken
Noticeable loss of power or overboost cut
Commanded and actual position of actuator B diverge in live data
P2588: Turbocharger Boost Control Position Sensor B Circuit Low

P2588 is stored when the voltage from position sensor B of the second boost actuator drops below the lowest value a working sensor can deliver - most often a grounded signal line or a missing 5 V reference. No manufacturer documents P2588 publicly; the thresholds known for sensor A give the order of magnitude.
Signal wire of position sensor B shorted to ground
Lost or shorted 5 V reference supply
Failed position sensor B in actuator B
Further sensor codes if a shared reference is shorted
P2589: Turbocharger Boost Control Position Sensor B Circuit High

P2589 means the signal that position sensor B returns for the second boost actuator sits above its plausible maximum, typically from an open signal or ground wire, a short to the reference or battery voltage, or a sensor with a defective output. No manufacturer documents P2589 publicly.
Open signal or ground wire of position sensor B
Signal wire shorted to reference or battery voltage
Wastegate rod set so the sensor reads at its upper end
Malfunction indicator lamp on, often on the first trip
Position of actuator B stuck near the maximum in live data
P258A: P258A stands for an open or otherwise faulty control circuit A of an electric vacuum pump, which supplies the brake booster on engines that provide too little manifold vacuum, such as hybrids, downsized turbo petrol engines and diesels.
False entry after a long engine crank while the pump is unpowered
Faulty pump relay, blown fuse or poor relay contact
Open wire or loose connector between module, relay and pump
Engine or brake warning lamp on
Harder brake pedal at low speed or after several stops
P258B: Vacuum Pump Control Circuit A Range/Performance

P258B is the range/performance code for control circuit A of the vacuum pump: the pump is commanded, but its monitoring feedback or the vacuum it produces does not fit. Ford's 2018-2019 hybrid OBD summary sets it from the brake module when the monitoring line sits outside 1.3-5.0 V with the relay off, or below 250 mV for 1 s with the relay on.
Worn or failed electric vacuum pump
Leaking hose or check valve that makes the pump run too long
Blown pump fuse, spread terminals or poor ground
Outdated engine software controlling pump duty cycle
Engine, brake or stability warning lamp on
Hard brake pedal, less brake assist
P258C: Vacuum Pump Control Circuit A Low

P258C reports that control circuit A of the electrically driven vacuum pump reads too low, typically because the control or relay line is shorted to ground, the relay coil is faulty, or a blown supply fuse leaves the monitoring line without voltage. Depending on how the circuit is laid out, the pump may then run nonstop or not at all.
Control or relay wire shorted to ground
Faulty pump relay or relay coil
Engine or brake warning lamp on
P258D: Vacuum Pump Control Circuit A High

P258D marks a control circuit A of the vacuum pump whose signal sits above the expected range, most often a short to battery positive on the relay or pump control line, so the control unit can no longer switch the pump as it wants.
Control wire shorted to a battery-voltage line
Faulty output stage in the controlling module
Engine or brake warning lamp on
Vacuum pump runs continuously, even with the engine off in some cases
P258E: P258E is the plausibility check of the power take-off enable switch. The line is not open or shorted – those faults are P251A to P251C – but the state of the switch does not fit the other PTO inputs, for instance an enable request without a valid arming step or contact signals that contradict each other.
PTO switch contacts worn or contaminated, mode signals disagree
Upfitter wiring or load-engage switch interfering with the enable input
Remote enable used without arming sequence or with wrong switch type
PTO module configuration not matching the installed switches
PTO cannot be switched on or switches off unexpectedly
Driver information message about PTO conditions
P258F: P258F concerns the sending side of a torque management link. One controller – for example the engine module talking to a transmission or hybrid controller, or the reverse – transmits torque requests and finds that its own output is faulty, missing or not accepted by the receiver.
CAN wiring or connector fault between the modules
Software levels of sending and receiving module do not match
Low voltage or poor ground at one of the modules
P2590: Turbocharger Boost Control Position Sensor B Circuit Intermittent/Erratic

P2590 is set when the position signal of the second boost actuator flickers, jumps or drops out for short moments instead of being steadily wrong. Unlike its sensor A counterpart P2566, this code is defined as intermittent/erratic, so an unsteady signal without full dropouts falls under it as well. No manufacturer documents P2590 publicly.
Loose terminal or intermittent contact in the sensor B connector
Sensor track worn by vibration, giving a noisy signal
Chafed harness that shorts or opens briefly
Warning lamp that may come and go
Jumping position value for actuator B in live data
P2591: Cruise Control Front Distance Range Sensor Left

P2591 is reserved for the left front distance sensor in cruise systems that combine several radars across the front; a single or centre unit uses P2583 and the right one P2592. No manufacturer documents P2591 publicly.
Bumper cover damaged, replaced or repainted over the left sensor
Left sensor bracket bent, sensor aimed wrongly
Ice, mud or stickers covering the sensor area
Sensor or wiring to the left corner faulty
P2592: Cruise Control Front Distance Range Sensor Right
P2592 marks a fault of the right-hand front distance sensor in multi-radar adaptive cruise layouts; the left unit reports P2591, a single or centre radar P2583. No maker publishes this code.
Right sensor knocked out of alignment by kerb or parking contact
Road salt or water corrosion at the right sensor connector
Sensor not recalibrated after bumper replacement
Warning message for the radar or driver assistance system
P2593: P2593 concerns the second turbocharger speed sensor, found where an engine has two turbochargers, for example one per cylinder bank. It marks an electrical fault on that sensor's circuit that is not further classified; the specific forms are P2595 (low), P2596 (high) and P2597 (intermittent), while P2594 covers a plausibility error.
Connector problem at speed sensor B
Harness to the second turbocharger damaged by heat or chafing
Internal failure of speed sensor B
Power reduced, often only slightly with one turbo affected
No speed value for the second turbo in live data
P2594: Turbocharger Speed Sensor B Circuit Range/Performance
P2594 means the second turbocharger speed sensor produces a signal, but its reported speed does not agree with what the engine computer predicts for that turbo.
Detached divider in the air filter box disturbing the flow to one turbo
Intake or exhaust leak on the bank of the second turbo
Speed sensor B delivering an implausible signal
Fault often appears only under particular load or gradient conditions
Turbo speeds of both banks differ noticeably in live data
P2595: Turbocharger Speed Sensor B Circuit Low

P2595 is logged when the signal of turbocharger speed sensor B stays below the range the engine computer accepts, as with a short to ground or a sensor whose output has collapsed. Bentley names it for the W12 in Continental GT, GTC and Flying Spur from 2018 and later also in the Bentayga, stored in engine control unit 1 or 2.
Speed sensor B with collapsed output
Signal wire of sensor B shorted to ground
Corroded or contaminated connector at sensor B
Speed of the second turbo shown as zero or very low
P2596: Turbocharger Speed Sensor B Circuit High

With P2596 the engine computer sees the line of turbocharger speed sensor B sitting above its valid window - the usual pattern for a signal shorted to supply voltage, an interrupted ground or a defective sensor output.
Signal wire of sensor B shorted to supply or battery voltage
Defective output stage of speed sensor B
Implausibly high speed for the second turbo in live data
P2597: Turbocharger Speed Sensor B Circuit Intermittent

P2597 records short interruptions or jumps in the signal of the second turbocharger speed sensor, between which the circuit works normally. Such faults usually sit in a connector, a wire that breaks contact under engine movement or heat soak, or a sensor that drops out when hot. No manufacturer documents P2597 publicly.
Loose terminal or poor pin contact at sensor B
Wire breaking contact under engine movement or heat soak
Speed sensor B dropping out when hot
Occasional warning lamp, sometimes only after long drives
Dropouts in the speed trace of the second turbo
P2598: Turbocharger Boost Control Position Sensor A Performance - Stuck Low

P2598 means the boost control position of turbocharger A, normally the vane or wastegate position reported by the actuator, appears stuck toward its low end: the measured value no longer follows the command although the signal is electrically valid.
Sooted or seized variable vanes that no longer follow the actuator
Vacuum leak or kinked hose on pneumatically driven actuators
Worn or failed electric vane actuator
One-off entry from unusual operation, e.g. after delivery transport
Lack of power under load, boost limited
P2599: Turbocharger Boost Control Position Sensor A Performance - Stuck High

P2599 is the high-side stuck fault for position sensor A: the turbocharger actuator stays at, or reports, a position beyond where it should be, while the sensor circuit itself works. GM documents it twice.
Vanes or wastegate stuck toward the closed position by soot or corrosion
Weak return spring or binding linkage that keeps the actuator from its rest position
Vacuum control solenoid or hose fault on pneumatic actuators
Defective actuator electronics on smart actuators
Overboost cut-out or noticeable power reduction
Black smoke or rough response under load
P259A: Turbocharger Boost Control Position Sensor B Performance - Stuck Low

P259A applies to engines with a second boost control actuator, for instance a twin-turbo layout or the second stage of a two-stage system, whose position is read by sensor B. The code is stored when that actuator's reported position stays at the low end and stops tracking the command even though the signal is electrically sound.
Sticking vanes, flap or wastegate on charger B
Weak vacuum or electrical supply to actuator B
Worn actuator B or misadjusted linkage
Weak acceleration, notably in the range where charger B works
P259B: Turbocharger Boost Control Position Sensor B Performance - Stuck High

P259B is logged when the boost control actuator watched by position sensor B is found stuck at the high end of its travel, or fails to return to its rest position, while the sensor signal itself is plausible. A sensor B exists mainly on twin-turbo or two-stage engines. No manufacturer publishes P259B.
Mechanism of charger B seized toward the closed or high position
Return spring or linkage of actuator B binding
Vacuum solenoid or hose of actuator B faulty (pneumatic systems)
Power cut-out under full load to prevent overboost
P259C: Excessive Time To Enter Closed Loop Turbocharger A Boost Control

P259C reports that closed-loop boost control of turbocharger A was not reached within the expected time after its enabling conditions were met. Instead of trimming the actuator from boost or position feedback, the controller stays in open-loop or default mode.
Boost pressure or actuator position sensor fault that blocks closed-loop control
Actuator A fault, often with its own stored code
Charge air leak preventing boost from reaching the range where control starts
P259D: Excessive Time To Enter Closed Loop Turbocharger B Boost Control

P259D is the turbocharger B version of the closed-loop timing fault. On engines with two separately regulated chargers, the control unit expects the boost regulation of the second unit to switch to feedback operation within a set time, and here it did not.
Fault on position or pressure sensing for charger B
Actuator B or its control circuit faulty
Leak in the charge air path of charger B
Reduced power, especially at higher load
P259E: Turbocharger A Boost Control Position At Low Limit

P259E means the boost control of turbocharger A has run out of range at the low end: the actuator is at its limit, yet boost stays well under the target. Ford's 2023 diesel OBD summary places it in the underboost monitor.
Leak in charge air pipes, intercooler or clamps
Variable vane actuator or vane mechanism not reaching the commanded position
Exhaust leak upstream of the turbine
Boost pressure sensor reading too low
Clear loss of power under load
Whistling or hissing from the charge air side
P259F: Turbocharger A Boost Control Position At High Limit
P259F is the counterpart of P259E: the regulation of turbocharger A has hit its upper limit, and measured boost runs above the value the engine computer asked for.
Vanes or wastegate stuck toward the closed position
Actuator or its vacuum/electrical control not opening as commanded
Engine control software needing an update
Boost pressure sensor reading too high
Sudden power cut at high load
P25A0: Turbocharger B Boost Control Position At Low Limit

P25A0 says the regulator of turbocharger B has run to its low limit without reaching the boost target, so the second charger delivers too little pressure even with full control authority. It only exists on engines where two chargers are regulated separately. No manufacturer documents P25A0 publicly.
Leak in the charge air path served by charger B
Wastegate or vanes of charger B not closing as commanded
Lower power than usual, uneven pull
P25A1: Turbocharger B Boost Control Position At High Limit

P25A1 is set when the boost control for turbocharger B is pinned at its upper limit and still cannot bring pressure down to the requested value, so the second charger overshoots. Like P25A0 it is limited to engines with two individually controlled chargers, and no manufacturer has published its own criteria for P25A1.
Wastegate or vanes of charger B stuck toward closed
Blocked, leaking or misrouted control line of actuator B
Boost pressure sensor giving wrong values
P25A2: Brake System Control Module A Requested MIL Illumination
P25A2 is a messenger code: the brake system control module has stored an emission-relevant fault of its own and asks the engine module to light the check engine lamp.
Emission-relevant fault stored in the brake control module
Weak battery or low system voltage upsetting the brake module
Brake or related module software needing an update
Lost communication with a partner module such as the front camera
ABS, stability or driver assistance warnings at the same time
Brake pedal may feel soft in some cases
P25A3: P25A3 is a state code, not a wiring fault: the hood is reported open at a moment when the control strategy expects it closed, for example while an automatic restart, a remote start or a hybrid engine pull-up is pending. No manufacturer documents P25A3 publicly.
Hood only on the safety catch, not fully latched
Hood switch or striker misadjusted after body work
Latch-integrated switch sticking in the open position
Hood open warning in the cluster
Auto stop-start and remote start locked out
Engine keeps running at standstill instead of stopping
P25A4: P25A4 is the general circuit fault for the fuel mode select switch – the button on bi-fuel vehicles with which the driver chooses between gasoline and an alternative fuel such as CNG or LPG.
Open wire or unplugged connector at the fuel mode switch
Faulty connection in a bi-fuel conversion harness
Fuel cannot be changed with the switch
Fuel indicator light on the switch dark or flashing
P25A5: P25A5 flags a performance problem with the fuel mode select switch. The circuit is electrically sound, yet the switch behaves in a way that cannot be genuine, such as a momentary button that appears to be held down for minutes or a press that never returns to rest.
Switch button sticking or contaminated by liquid
Panel trim pressing on the switch after installation work
Replacement switch of the wrong type or coding
Fuel mode changes by itself or not at all
P25A6: Fuel Mode Select Switch Circuit Low

P25A6 means the fuel mode select switch signal has fallen below the range the module accepts. On a switch that pulls a reference line towards ground when pressed, this is the signature of a signal wire rubbed through to the body or of moisture bridging the switch contacts; a grounded line could otherwise pass for a button held forever.
Switch signal wire chafed to ground behind the dash
Moisture or spilt liquid bridging the switch contacts
Vehicle remains in one fuel mode
P25A7: Fuel Mode Select Switch Circuit High

P25A7 reports a fuel mode select switch signal above the accepted window. With a pull-up input this mostly means the switch never closes its path – an open signal or return wire, a connector half off, a broken switch – or that the line has contact with a supply voltage, for example where an alternative-fuel conversion tapped into nearby wiring.
Open signal or return wire, connector not seated
Signal wire touching a supply voltage, e.g. after aftermarket wiring
Fuel indicator on the switch may stay dark
P25A8: Fuel Mode Select Switch Circuit Intermittent/Erratic

P25A8 records a fuel mode select switch signal that jumps or drops out briefly instead of staying in a stable state. The module sees transitions it cannot attribute to a real press, often while driving over rough roads, which points to a loose terminal, a cracked solder joint in the switch or a harness rubbing behind the trim.
Loose terminal or poor contact at the switch connector
Cracked solder joint inside the switch
Harness rubbing behind the trim and shorting briefly
P25A9: P25A9 covers the electrical circuit of the piston cooling oil control valve, the solenoid that switches the oil jets spraying the underside of the pistons. Under load the jets protect the pistons; when the engine is cold or lightly loaded they can be shut off to warm up faster and save oil pump work.
Valve connector unplugged, corroded or wire broken
Harness damaged by heat near the engine block
Output driver in the engine control module faulty
Check engine lamp on after two drives
Possible power reduction to protect the pistons
P25AA: Piston Cooling Oil Control Circuit Low

P25AA flags a voltage at the piston cooling oil control valve output that sits too low for the commanded state, typically a short to ground between the module and the valve. This valve decides whether the oil jets under the pistons spray.
Valve control wire chafed through and touching ground
Internal short in the piston cooling valve
Water or oil in the valve connector bridging the pins
Faulty output stage in the engine control module
Check engine lamp after two drives
Possible power limitation to protect the pistons
P25AB: Piston Cooling Oil Control Circuit High
P25AB is the counterpart on the supply side: the control line of the piston cooling oil valve is pulled toward battery voltage.
Control wire pinched against a live supply wire
Valve side of the circuit shorted to its own supply
Faulty output stage in the engine control module
Check engine lamp after two drives
Piston cooling jets no longer switched
P25AC: Piston Cooling Oil Control Circuit Performance/Stuck Off
P25AC is a functional fault rather than a wiring one: the valve is told to let oil reach the piston jets, but the feedback shows no flow.
Valve jammed by swarf or dirt in the oil
Piston cooling pressure switch faulty or unplugged
Low oil level or weak oil pressure feeding the jet circuit
Restricted oil passage to the jets
Check engine lamp after two drives
Engine power reduced under high load
Risk of piston damage if driven hard for long periods
P25AD: Piston Cooling Oil Control Circuit Stuck On
P25AD describes the reverse mechanical failure: the piston cooling valve ought to be shut, yet oil keeps reaching the jets.
Broken return spring in the valve
Piston cooling pressure switch stuck in the pressure position
Check engine lamp after two drives
Slightly lower oil pressure reading at idle
P25AE: Piston Cooling Oil Pressure Too Low

P25AE means the oil pressure reaching the piston cooling jets is below what the engine controller requires, even though the valve circuit itself shows no electrical fault. Volvo and Mack heavy trucks store it as P25AE00.
Oil temperature sensor reading wrong (Volvo/Mack bulletin)
Low oil level or oil starvation under hard load
Worn oil pump or leaking pressure relief valve
Clogged oil filter or piston cooling jets
Low oil pressure warning at the same time
P25AF: Coolant Temperature Control Module Requested MIL Illumination

P25AF is a messenger code. A separate coolant temperature control module, used on some vehicles with electrically managed cooling for engine, battery or power electronics, has stored an emission-relevant fault of its own and asks the engine module to turn on the check engine lamp.
Emission-relevant fault stored in the coolant temperature control module
Faulty coolant valve, pump or sensor handled by that module
Thermal module software needing an update
Possible temperature warnings or reduced heating
P25B0: P25B0 means the main fuel level sender keeps reporting the same level although the engine has clearly been burning fuel. Ford runs this as a continuous check: the module totals the fuel injected, converts it into a share of tank capacity and compares that with how far the sender reading has moved.
Float arm caught on the tank wall, baffle or pump module
Worn spot on the sender resistor track holding the wiper at one value
Float soaked with fuel and sunk to the bottom
Fuel consumption calculation in the PCM not matching the tank
Fuel gauge stays at the same mark over a long distance
Engine runs out of fuel while the gauge still shows fuel
P25B1: P25B1 points at the second fuel level sender, the one found in the passive half of a saddle tank or in an additional tank. Its reading no longer changes in step with the fuel actually burned.
Float of sender B jammed or resistor track worn
Jet pump or its line no longer drawing fuel from the passive tank half
Blocked or kinked transfer line between the tank chambers
Gauge reading too high or barely falling as the tank empties
Engine stalls from fuel starvation with an apparently quarter-full tank
P25B2: Fuel Level Sensor A or B Stuck
P25B2 is the shared variant for tanks with two senders: the module has found that the level information is frozen but does not commit to which of the two senders is responsible.
One of the two senders mechanically stuck
Fuel no longer moved between tank halves by the jet pump
Corroded connector on the tank unit freezing one signal
Gauge stuck or moving far less than fuel used
P25B3: P25B3 says the wastegate of turbocharger A stays further open than the module commands, so exhaust bypasses the turbine and boost falls short.
Missing retaining clip disconnecting actuator rod from the wastegate lever
Electric wastegate actuator failed or rod bent
Wastegate flap or bushing seized in the open position by heat or carbon
Diagnostic calibration needing an update (Toyota GR Corolla)
Clearly reduced power and slow boost build-up
Check engine lamp on, often with an underboost code
Wrench or reduced power warning on some models
P25B4: P25B4 is the reverse of P25B3: the module asked wastegate A to open, yet the valve stays shut or opens far too little. Ford uses the same position comparison for both directions (error over 20 mm for 2.5 s); in 2024 it appears as P0243 with failure type 73. Other makers infer the fault from pressure.
Wastegate flap or spindle seized shut by carbon or corrosion
Actuator or linkage unable to move the valve
False detection by engine software (Porsche Cayenne, Audi RS 5)
Internal turbocharger fault requiring replacement (Ford SSM 50670)
Power reduced because the module limits boost
P25B5: P25B5 concerns wastegate B, which on twin-turbo V engines belongs to the second turbocharger, normally on the other cylinder bank. The valve remains open beyond what the PCM commands, so this turbo delivers too little boost while the A side may work normally.
Wastegate B linkage loose or disconnected
Actuator B failed or its position sensor reading wrong
Flap of wastegate B seized open
Reduced power, especially when accelerating under load
Check engine lamp and/or wrench indicator on
P25B6: With P25B6 the second wastegate refuses to open when commanded, so turbo B cannot be regulated down and may push boost beyond the target; the module then usually caps torque. Ford detects it with the B-side position comparison (over 20 mm for 2.5 s, no P0247 or P2ABE present) and in 2024 files it as P0247 with type 73.
Loose nut on the turbo actuator arm (Ford Bronco TSB 24-2112)
Wastegate B flap or spindle seized shut
Actuator B unable to drive the valve open
Power limited, sometimes after a short boost spike
Check engine lamp on, possibly with P0299 or an overboost code
P25B7: Auxiliary Ignition Switch On/Start Position Circuit

P25B7 covers the hard-wired input from an auxiliary ignition switch that commands the On and Start positions from a second location, for example a rear panel behind the cab, a work platform or a remote station on a chassis-cab truck.
Open wire or loose connector in the harness to the body or remote panel
Worn or corroded contacts in the auxiliary switch
Input stage of the reading module damaged
Engine cannot be started or switched on from the auxiliary position
Normal key or push-button start still works
Stored code, often without other complaints
P25B8: Auxiliary Ignition Switch On/Start Position Circuit Low

P25B8 means the auxiliary On/Start input sits at a low level when the module expects it to be active, or never rises when the remote switch is operated. Typical reasons are a switch contact that no longer closes, a blown fuse feeding the remote panel, a broken wire in the long harness run to the body or a short to ground at a frame connector.
Blown fuse or failed relay feeding the auxiliary switch
Signal wire shorted to ground on the frame or body
Auxiliary switch contact no longer closes
Corroded exterior connector with high resistance
Remote start or on request is ignored
Engine may shut down when the auxiliary position is used to keep it running
P25B9: Auxiliary Ignition Switch On/Start Position Circuit High
With P25B9 the module sees the auxiliary On/Start line at a high level when it ought to be inactive, for example after key-off or with no request from the remote panel.
Signal wire chafed against a battery or ignition feed
Auxiliary switch stuck in the On/Start position
Backfeed through an upfitter relay or accessory
Moisture in an exterior switch box or connector
Battery drains overnight because modules stay awake
Auxiliary start function disabled or behaving erratically
Starter may engage or click unexpectedly
P25BA: P25BA concerns the dash or panel switch with which the driver starts, or on some trucks blocks, a diesel particulate filter regeneration. The engine controller reads the switch as a discrete input and sets this code when the circuit is open or otherwise unusable, so a press no longer reaches it.
Switch connector loose or unplugged behind the dash
Broken signal or reference wire to the switch
Internal open circuit in the regeneration switch
Parked regeneration cannot be started when the cluster asks for it
Filter or regeneration warning lamp stays on longer than usual
P25BB: P25BB reports that the regeneration switch input reads a low level the switch itself cannot produce. Depending on the wiring, this points to a short to ground in the harness, a contact that is permanently closed to ground or a damaged switch module.
Switch signal wire shorted to ground
Switch panel damaged by liquid or impact
Parked regeneration may be unavailable when soot load is high
P25BC: P25BC is the high-voltage counterpart: the regeneration switch line carries a level near supply voltage that no switch position can produce. A wire chafed against a battery or ignition feed, water in a switch connector or a switch whose internal resistor network has failed are plausible causes.
Switch signal wire shorted to battery or ignition voltage
Internal fault in the switch or its resistor network
Regeneration switch ignored by the engine controller
Unexpected regeneration messages in the cluster
P25BD: P25BD protects against engine runaway, where the engine keeps speeding up although the controller injects no fuel, for instance because oil from a failed turbocharger seal or combustible vapour drawn into the intake is being burned. GM documents the monitor in its diesel ECM tables.
Turbocharger seal failure feeding oil into the intake
Oil carry-over from crankcase ventilation, e.g. overfilled or diluted oil
Combustible vapour drawn in from the surroundings
Erroneous engine speed signal or controller fault
Engine revs up uncontrollably and then shuts off
Heavy smoke from the exhaust before shutdown
Possible severe engine damage after the event
P25BE: P25BE concerns the output with which the engine controller tells an alternative fuel system, usually a CNG or LPG installation, to stop gas operation, for example after a fault, with an empty gas tank or while the engine warms up.
Open control wire between engine controller and gas system
Poor splice or connector in a retrofit gas installation
Open coil in a gas disable relay
Output driver in the engine controller defective
Vehicle stays on gasoline or will not switch to gas
Fuel mode indicator flashes or shows a system fault
P25BF: Alternative Fuel Disable Control Circuit High

P25BF flags a voltage on the alternative fuel disable output that is too high for the state the engine controller is commanding. On a low-side driver this usually means a short to battery or ignition voltage, for instance where a gas kit harness has been routed along a hot feed or tapped into the wrong wire.
Control wire shorted to battery or ignition voltage
Retrofit gas kit tapped into the wrong circuit
Faulty input stage in the gas controller backfeeding voltage
Gas operation blocked, vehicle runs on gasoline only
P25C0: Alternative Fuel Disable Control Circuit Low

P25C0 is set when the alternative fuel disable output reads too low, typically a short to ground somewhere between the engine controller and the gas system. With a high-side driver that pin would then be unable to deliver its voltage; with a low-side driver the line would look permanently switched.
Control wire shorted to ground, often where routed along the frame
Chafed insulation on a retrofit gas kit harness
Output stage in the engine controller damaged
Vehicle refuses to switch to gas
Fuel system fault message or flashing fuel indicator
P25C1: P25C1 relates to the incoming side of the alternative fuel disable function: a signal line on which the engine controller reads whether gas operation is blocked, either as feedback from the gas system or as a request from it, for example when a CNG or LPG controller detects low tank pressure or its own fault.
Open signal wire from the gas system
Gas controller without power or ground, so no signal is sent
Corroded underbody connector of the gas system
Gas mode unavailable or drops out while driving
P25C2: Alternative Fuel Disable Signal Circuit High

P25C2 means the alternative fuel disable signal arriving at the engine controller sits above its valid range. Likely explanations are a short to a voltage feed, a missing ground at the gas controller that lets its output float up, or an open line combined with an internal pull-up in the reading module.
Signal wire shorted to a voltage feed
Missing ground at the gas controller letting its output float high
Open signal wire pulled up inside the reading module
P25C3: Alternative Fuel Disable Signal Circuit Low

P25C3 is logged when the alternative fuel disable signal reaching the engine controller is too low to be valid. A short to ground on the way from the gas system, a gas controller that has lost its supply, or a damaged output stage in that controller can each pull the line down.
Damaged output stage in the gas controller
Fuel mode indicator flashes or shows a fault
P25C4: Brake Booster Temperature Sensor A Circuit

P25C4 covers the first temperature sensor of an electromechanical brake booster, in which an electric motor and gear set take the place of the vacuum diaphragm, as in Bosch's iBooster. The booster electronics use this value to protect motor and control unit from overheating during long or repeated braking.
Temperature sensor inside the booster unit defective
Fault in the booster control electronics
Brake system warning in the cluster
Brake pedal may feel harder if assistance is reduced
Stored code, often together with chassis codes
P25C5: Brake Booster Temperature Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance

P25C5 is the plausibility fault for brake booster temperature sensor A: the circuit is electrically intact, but the reported temperature does not fit, for example a value that jumps implausibly, stays frozen while the motor works hard, or disagrees with the second sensor. No manufacturer documents P25C5 publicly.
Sensor drifted out of its characteristic curve
Contact resistance at the booster connector skewing the signal
Measurement error in the booster electronics
Brake warning message, sometimes only after long braking
Brake assistance reduced as a precaution
P25C6: Brake Booster Temperature Sensor A Circuit Low
P25C6 means the signal of brake booster temperature sensor A is too low, which GM describes as the sensor line being shorted to ground.
Sensor signal wire shorted to ground
Internal short in the temperature sensor
Check engine lamp after two trips
P25C7: Brake Booster Temperature Sensor A Circuit High

P25C7 flags a sensor A signal that is too high; GM interprets it as the temperature line shorted to supply. In the EBCM part of table 23OBDG07 for the 2023 Corvette Z06 the voltage must exceed 3.27 V five consecutive times within 0.6 s with the ignition on, and the fault is Type B with two trips to the MIL. Tables 24OBDG07 and 25OBDG03A repeat these values.
Sensor signal shorted to the supply line
Open sensor circuit or missing sensor ground
Check engine lamp after two trips
P25C8: Brake Booster Temperature Sensor A Circuit Intermittent/Erratic

P25C8 is meant for a sensor A signal that drops out briefly or jumps faster than any real temperature in the booster could change, the typical footprint of a loose pin, a cracked solder joint or a wire that breaks under vibration. Each event may be too short for the low or high check to confirm, which is why this separate code exists.
Loose or spread terminal in the booster connector
Cracked solder joint inside the booster electronics
Brake warning that appears and disappears
P25C9: Brake System Control Module B Requested MIL Illumination
P25C9 tells the engine module that a second brake system control module, labelled B, has found an emission-relevant malfunction and wants the check engine lamp switched on.
Fault stored in brake system control module B
Weak battery or low system voltage
Communication fault between module B and its partners
Brake or stability warnings at the same time
P25CA: Intake Camshaft Actuator Park Lock Control Circuit/Open (Bank 1)

Some cam phasers carry a locking pin that holds the rotor in a fixed base or middle position for starting and while oil pressure is still building. Where that pin is released and engaged by its own solenoid, the controller supervises this extra circuit.
Open winding in the intake phaser lock solenoid
Connector off or terminal pushed back after engine work
Broken wire between module and lock solenoid
Intake cam timing held at a default position, less power
P25CB: Intake Camshaft Actuator Park Lock Control Circuit Low (Bank 1)

P25CB points to a control line for the intake phaser lock on bank 1 that reads lower than it should, most often a short to ground on the wire or inside the lock solenoid. Depending on how the driver is wired, the solenoid may then stay energised or never receive current, so the lock pin is either released all the time or cannot be pulled back.
Lock control wire shorted to ground
Internal short in the lock solenoid
Weak battery or voltage dip during cranking
Brief rattle from the timing drive at start
Reduced power with fixed intake timing
P25CC: Intake Camshaft Actuator Park Lock Control Circuit High (Bank 1)
With P25CC the controller sees the intake phaser lock control line on bank 1 sitting higher than expected, typically because it touches a live wire or the solenoid's ground path is shorted to supply.
Lock control wire shorted to a supply voltage
Harness insulation melted near the exhaust or turbo
Faulty output stage in the engine control module
Sluggish response with intake timing fixed
P25CD: Intake Camshaft Actuator Park Lock Control Circuit/Open (Bank 2)

P25CD is the bank 2 version of the open-circuit lock fault and therefore only appears on V or boxer engines whose second cylinder bank has its own intake phaser with a separately switched lock pin. The controller finds the lock solenoid circuit on that bank interrupted or electrically implausible, so it can no longer release or set the pin deliberately.
Open circuit inside the bank 2 lock solenoid
Bank 2 lock solenoid connector unplugged or corroded
Wire break in the harness across the engine
Less power, bank 2 intake timing fixed
P25CE: Intake Camshaft Actuator Park Lock Control Circuit Low (Bank 2)

P25CE stands for a low signal on the lock control line of the bank 2 intake phaser: the wire or the solenoid winding has found a path to ground, or the module's output is stuck pulling low. Because the second bank's harness often runs along the back of the engine or under the intake manifold, chafing at brackets and heat damage are frequent findings.
Bank 2 harness chafed through at a bracket
Shorted winding in the bank 2 lock solenoid
Low system voltage setting lock codes on both banks
P25CF: Intake Camshaft Actuator Park Lock Control Circuit High (Bank 2)

P25CF is logged when the bank 2 intake phaser lock control line stays above its permitted voltage band. Common reasons are contact with a powered wire, moisture bridging connector pins to a supply terminal, or a failed output transistor in the controller.
Bank 2 lock control wire touching a powered circuit
Moisture in the connector bridging to a supply pin
Failed output transistor in the engine control module
Lumpy idle from uneven bank timing
P25D0: Exhaust Camshaft Actuator Park Lock Control Circuit/Open (Bank 1)

P25D0 moves the open-circuit lock fault to the exhaust side: the solenoid that releases the locking pin of the bank 1 exhaust cam phaser can no longer be driven because its circuit is interrupted or reads implausibly. The lock keeps the exhaust cam at a defined position while the engine starts, before the phaser has enough oil pressure to hold itself.
Open winding in the exhaust phaser lock solenoid
Broken wire to the exhaust lock solenoid
P25D1: Exhaust Camshaft Actuator Park Lock Control Circuit Low (Bank 1)

P25D1 indicates that the control signal for the bank 1 exhaust phaser lock is too low, normally a grounded wire or a solenoid winding that leaks to ground. The exhaust side is the hotter one, so insulation that has hardened and cracked near the manifold or turbocharger is a typical finding.
Heat-cracked insulation grounding the lock wire
Engine oil wicked into the connector
Exhaust timing fixed, slightly less power
P25D2: Exhaust Camshaft Actuator Park Lock Control Circuit High (Bank 1)

P25D2 is set when the bank 1 exhaust phaser lock control line carries more voltage than the controller allows in the current switching state, for example because it is shorted to an ignition-fed wire or the solenoid's return is tied to supply.
Lock control wire shorted to an ignition-fed circuit
Solenoid return path shorted to supply
Damaged output stage in the engine control module
P25D3: Exhaust Camshaft Actuator Park Lock Control Circuit/Open (Bank 2)

P25D3 concerns engines with two cylinder banks and a lockable exhaust phaser on each: the lock solenoid circuit of the bank 2 exhaust phaser is open or electrically implausible, so the module loses control over its pin.
Bank 2 exhaust lock connector left loose after timing work
Open winding in the bank 2 exhaust lock solenoid
Open in a supply shared with other phaser solenoids
P25D4: Exhaust Camshaft Actuator Park Lock Control Circuit Low (Bank 2)

P25D4 reports a lock control line for the bank 2 exhaust phaser that is pulled down below its expected level. Grounding through damaged insulation, a solenoid with shorted turns or oil that has crept into the connector are the usual explanations.
Heat sleeve slipped, wire grounded at the manifold
Shorted turns in the bank 2 exhaust lock solenoid
P25D5: Exhaust Camshaft Actuator Park Lock Control Circuit High (Bank 2)

P25D5 closes this series: the bank 2 exhaust phaser's lock control signal sits above its allowed voltage, pointing to a short to battery or ignition voltage, a return path tied to supply, or a defective output in the module.
Bank 2 exhaust lock wire shorted to battery or ignition voltage
Harness fault affecting several actuator lines
Defective output in the engine control module
P25D6: Exhaust Heat Exchanger Exhaust Bypass Valve A Position Sensor Stop Performance

An exhaust heat exchanger moves exhaust heat into the coolant after a cold start; a flap (bypass valve A) decides whether gas flows through it or around it, and a position sensor reports where the flap is. P25D6 targets the end-stop values of that sensor: at the fully open and fully closed stops the reading must sit inside a learned or calibrated window.
Carbon build-up or a bent flap stopping short of its end stop
Worn valve actuator or linkage play
Position sensor shifted on its mount or drifting
End stops not relearned after parts replacement
Check engine lamp on without noticeable driving change
Slower engine warm-up or weaker cabin heat in winter
P25D7: Fuel level sensor C is a third level input, needed only where the fuel is spread over more chambers or tanks than two senders can cover, for instance on trucks with an extra tank. P25D7 is its general circuit code: the module sees an electrical fault on this input but does not classify it as low, high or intermittent.
