Damaged wiring between tank C sender and module, often under the vehicle
Corroded or loose connector at the sender
Gauge or range wrong or replaced by a default value
P25D8: P25D8 says that the third fuel level input delivers an electrically valid signal whose behaviour is not believable: it jumps, drifts or disagrees with the fuel actually used or transferred. A sender frozen at one value has its own code, P25DC, so P25D8 covers the remaining plausibility faults. No manufacturer documents P25D8 publicly.
Worn or dirty resistor track in sender C giving jumps
Transfer pump or line fault so the level in tank C does not change as expected
Damaged or loose float on sender C
Fuel gauge jumps or shows unrealistic values
Check engine lamp on after repeated detection
P25D9: Fuel Level Sensor C Circuit Low

P25D9 reports that the signal of the third fuel level sender has dropped below its lowest valid value. With the usual resistor-type sender this points to very low resistance, typically a signal wire shorted to ground or a sender shorted internally. Whether low means empty or full depends on how the sender is wired, so the gauge may stick at either end.
Signal wire of sender C chafed and shorted to ground
Water in the tank connector bridging signal and ground
Gauge pinned at full or empty
P25DA: Fuel Level Sensor C Circuit High

P25DA is set when the third sender's signal climbs above the top of its valid range. On a resistor sender fed through a pull-up, that almost always means an open path: a broken wire, a disconnected plug, a burnt-out spot on the resistor track or a missing ground return. A short to a voltage source has the same effect.
Broken signal or ground wire to sender C
Tank connector loose or unplugged after work on the tank
Interrupted resistor track inside sender C
Signal wire shorted to a voltage supply
Gauge stuck at one end of the scale
P25DB: Fuel Level Sensor C Circuit Intermittent

P25DB describes short, repeated dropouts in the third fuel level input: the signal leaves its valid range for moments and returns, rather than staying low or high. Typical culprits are a loose pin, a wire that breaks contact only when the vehicle flexes or the tank moves, and a sender whose wiper briefly lifts off the resistor track over rough roads.
Loose or spread terminal in the sender C connector
Wire breaking contact when the frame or tank moves
Sender wiper lifting off a worn resistor track
Fuel gauge flickers or drops briefly to empty
Check engine lamp may come and go
P25DC: P25DC is set when a third fuel level sender, sender C, keeps returning the same reading although the engine has consumed a meaningful amount of fuel. Such a third input exists only on vehicles with extra or divided tanks, for example saddle tanks or auxiliary tanks on trucks. No manufacturer documents P25DC publicly.
Float arm of sender C caught on a baffle, pump bracket or tank wall
Worn spot on the sender C resistor track holding the wiper at one value
Fuel transfer to or from tank C not working, so its level really does not change
Fuel gauge or range display frozen over a long distance
Risk of running out of fuel despite a displayed reserve
P25DD: "A" Camshaft Position - Stuck In Locked Position (Bank 1)

Many modern cam phasers hold their rotor with a spring-loaded pin at a defined angle, often in mid travel, so the engine starts with stable valve timing before oil pressure builds. P25DD means the intake phaser on bank 1 is still latched at that angle although the controller has asked it to unlock and move, so variable timing is lost on that camshaft.
Low oil level or pressure, or oil of the wrong viscosity, unable to push the pin out
Oil control valve for the bank 1 intake phaser sticking or its screen clogged
Lock pin seized in its bore by sludge or wear inside the phaser
Less pulling power, especially in the mid-speed range
P25DE: "A" Camshaft Position - Unable to Achieve Locked Position (Bank 1)

P25DE is the reverse of P25DD: the intake cam phaser on bank 1 should return to its lock angle and let the pin engage, typically as the engine is about to stop or idles before an automatic stop, but the controller never sees the expected locked position.
Debris or wear in the phaser keeping the pin from dropping into its slot
Oil control valve sticking so the lock range of the spool is never reached
Aged or contaminated oil slowing the phaser at hot idle
Short rattle or knock from the timing drive right after starting
Rough start or unsteady idle in the first seconds
P25DF: P25DF belongs to the same block as the lock codes P25DD and P25DE, but it does not describe the latch itself.
Worn or partly clogged oil control valve for the bank 1 intake phaser
Oil overdue, diluted or of the wrong grade
Internal leakage in the phaser letting the angle drift
Uneven idle or slight hesitation when accelerating
P25E0: "A" Camshaft Position - Stuck In Locked Position (Bank 2)

On engines with two cylinder banks, P25E0 is the bank 2 counterpart of P25DD: the intake camshaft actuator stays latched at its locking angle when the module wants it free to advance or retard. Because only one side is affected, the cam angles of the two banks no longer match, and the module may hold both sides in a fallback position.
Insufficient oil pressure at the bank 2 head, low level or clogged feed screen
Bank 2 intake oil control valve sticking
Lock pin mechanically jammed in the phaser
P25E1: "A" Camshaft Position - Unable to Achieve Locked Position (Bank 2)

P25E1 is set when the intake phaser on bank 2 fails to re-engage its lock. The controller commands the phaser toward the locking angle, usually when shutting down or before an idle stop, and then checks whether the measured cam angle settles there; on bank 2 it does not. No manufacturer has published a description of P25E1.
Low oil pressure at hot idle from worn pump, bearings or thin oil
Varnish or debris in the bank 2 intake phaser
Control valve unable to move the spool into its lock range
Brief rattle from the timing drive on start-up
Unsteady running right after a cold or warm start
P25E2: P25E2 points to poor position control of the bank 2 intake camshaft actuator: the measured angle tracks its target less accurately or with more oscillation than the calibration allows, while no clear lock fault is present. It is the bank 2 sibling of P25DF.
Bank 2 intake solenoid valve worn or sluggish
Internal leakage across the phaser vanes
P25E3: "B" Camshaft Position - Stuck In Locked Position (Bank 1)

P25E3 concerns the exhaust side: the bank 1 exhaust phaser, camshaft B, remains held by its lock pin when the controller wants to move it. Exhaust timing then stays at its parking angle, which limits how the module can use valve overlap for internal exhaust gas recirculation and scavenging.
Low or contaminated oil at the exhaust phaser
Bank 1 exhaust oil control valve sticking
Damaged rotor or lock pin inside the exhaust phaser
Slight loss of power, possibly failed emissions test
P25E4: "B" Camshaft Position - Unable to Achieve Locked Position (Bank 1)
P25E4 means the bank 1 exhaust phaser does not reach and engage its locking position when the controller asks for it, for example before shutdown or an automatic engine stop.
Engine control software needing an update (documented for Stellantis Hurricane engines)
Low oil pressure at hot idle so the phaser cannot swing into the lock
Debris in the exhaust phaser or a sticking control valve
Engine fails to restart after an automatic stop, restarts after an ignition cycle
P25E5: P25E5 reports that the exhaust camshaft actuator on bank 1 is controlled less precisely than intended: its angle lags, overshoots or oscillates around the target beyond calibrated limits, without a latch fault.
Worn or dirty control valve for the bank 1 exhaust phaser
Degraded engine oil or a blocked oil filter
Noisy exhaust camshaft position signal making the angle look unstable
P25E6: "B" Camshaft Position - Stuck In Locked Position (Bank 2)

P25E6 tells that on bank 2 the exhaust cam phaser has not left its locked angle despite a command to adjust. The module then has one exhaust camshaft that can no longer be phased, which shifts valve overlap on that bank and can upset idle quality and the emissions balance between the two banks.
Restricted oil feed or clogged screen to the bank 2 cylinder head
Bank 2 exhaust oil control valve stuck
Lock pin seized in the bank 2 exhaust phaser
P25E7: "B" Camshaft Position - Unable to Achieve Locked Position (Bank 2)

With P25E7 the module reports that the bank 2 exhaust phaser could not be brought into its locking position: when the lock is requested, the cam angle does not settle at the parking value or the pin does not hold it there. A start without the pin engaged tends to be rough, and on stop-start engines a smooth restart becomes less certain.
Aged or sludged oil slowing the bank 2 exhaust phaser
Spool of the bank 2 exhaust control valve hanging
Worn lock pin or pin bore so the pin no longer holds
Calibration issue fixed by a control unit update
Hesitant restart after an automatic engine stop
P25E8: P25E8 is the last code of the locked-position block and covers the control quality of the bank 2 exhaust camshaft actuator: the module sees the angle wander from, overshoot or trail its setpoint more than allowed, while lock-related faults are absent.
Wear in the bank 2 exhaust control valve
Wrong oil viscosity or a clogged oil filter
Worn rotor seals inside the exhaust phaser
P25E9: Some engines drive their mechanical supercharger through an electromagnetic clutch, so the blower only turns when extra low-speed torque is wanted. Eaton's TVS blower on the T6 Drive-E four-cylinder from Volvo is built this way, where the turbocharger takes over at higher revs.
Worn friction faces or too large an air gap, so the clutch slips or will not pull in
Clutch coil with an internal fault producing too little magnetic force
Low supply voltage or high resistance at the clutch connector
Accessory drive belt slipping or damaged at the supercharger pulley
Weak acceleration from low engine speed
Normal pull once the turbocharger takes over
P25EA: Here the clutch between pulley and supercharger rotors stays engaged although the engine computer wants the blower uncoupled, for example at idle or steady cruising. The blower then keeps turning, costs drive power and fuel, and its air has to be routed past it.
Engine control software misjudging the clutch state (Audi Q7 3.0 TFSI, bulletin 2048402)
Clutch plates stuck together by wear debris, corrosion or overheating
Clutch coil kept energised by a wiring fault or a stuck driver stage
Higher fuel consumption at part load
Supercharger whine also at idle or cruising
P25EB: P25EB covers the electrical drive of the supercharger clutch when it is neither cleanly shorted nor open, yet the values do not fit the command – for example a coil current that is too small or too large for the applied duty cycle, or a signal that drops out briefly.
Clutch coil whose resistance has changed through heat or partial winding short
Corroded or loose connector at the clutch or engine module
Wire chafed near the hot supercharger housing causing intermittent contact
Jerky or missing supercharger engagement at low revs
P25EC: The engine module measures a voltage on the supercharger clutch control line that is lower than expected for the commanded state. Most often the line has a short to ground.
Control wire shorted to ground, often chafed on brackets or the engine block
Faulty output stage in the engine control module
Supercharger permanently engaged or permanently off, depending on circuit design
Reduced power at low engine speed
P25ED: With P25ED the voltage on the clutch control line sits above the expected level. Common reasons are a wire shorted to battery voltage, or – on a ground-switched coil – an open coil or broken lead, because the line is then pulled up to supply voltage. A short to voltage can overload the driver stage, which protects itself by switching off.
Control wire shorted to battery voltage
Open clutch coil or broken wire on a ground-switched circuit
Output stage in the engine control module damaged
Sluggish pull-away, supercharger does not cut in
P25EE: P25EE covers the second control circuit of an electric brake vacuum pump, the part of the wiring that should carry voltage while the pump is switched on.
Broken wire or loose connector between relay and pump
Hard brake pedal, especially with the engine off or in electric drive
Brake or traction warning lamp in addition to the check engine lamp
P25EF: Vacuum Pump Control Circuit B Range/Performance

P25EF says that the B circuit driving the electric vacuum pump is electrically present but its behaviour does not match the command: the feedback on the switched side looks implausible, or the pump runs without the expected effect on brake vacuum. No manufacturer documents P25EF publicly.
Worn vacuum pump that runs but builds too little vacuum
Leaking vacuum hose or faulty check valve
Corroded terminals causing an unstable feedback voltage
Vacuum pump running longer or more often
P25F0: Vacuum Pump Control Circuit B Low

P25F0 is stored when the pump's B control circuit reads lower than expected, usually because the switched supply or feedback line is shorted to ground or loaded down by a pump motor with an internal short. A short to ground on the supply side often blows the pump fuse, so the pump then stops altogether. No manufacturer documents P25F0 publicly.
Chafed supply or feedback wire shorted to ground
Internal short in the vacuum pump motor
Water ingress in the pump connector
P25F1: Vacuum Pump Control Circuit B High

P25F1 marks a high reading on the vacuum pump's second (B) control circuit: the module sees voltage on the switched side when it should be low, for example because the line is shorted to battery voltage, the relay contacts have welded together or the pump has lost its ground.
Feedback or supply line shorted to battery voltage
Lost ground connection at the pump
Vacuum pump running constantly, even with the vehicle switched off
P25F2: A third boost pressure sensor, C, only makes sense on engines with several charging stages or chargers – for example a supercharger feeding a turbocharger, or a two-stage turbo system – where pressure is measured between the stages as well as ahead of the throttle. Which location carries the letter C is up to the manufacturer.
Loose, corroded or oily connector at boost sensor C
Signal, 5 V reference or ground wire damaged
Reduced power, boost limited to base level
P25F3: Turbocharger/Supercharger Boost Sensor C Circuit Range/Performance
P25F3 means boost sensor C delivers a signal that is electrically valid but does not agree with what the other pressure readings and the engine model suggest.
Charge air leak near the measuring point of sensor C (hose, clamp, seal)
Sensor port fouled by oil from crankcase ventilation or a drifting sensor
Faulty barometric or manifold pressure sensor skewing the comparison
Hissing noise if a charge air leak is present
P25F4: Turbocharger/Supercharger Boost Sensor C Circuit Low

Boost pressure sensors of this kind output a voltage that rises with pressure, so P25F4 – a signal below the lowest valid value – points to the wiring or the sensor rather than to the charge air. Usual reasons are a signal wire shorted to ground, a missing 5 V supply, or an open signal line on an input pulled down by the control unit.
5 V reference open or pulled down by another faulty sensor on the same supply
Scan tool shows a pressure far below ambient for sensor C
P25F5: Turbocharger/Supercharger Boost Sensor C Circuit High

P25F5 reports a signal from boost sensor C above the highest plausible value. Since the voltage climbs with pressure, a reading at the top end usually means an electrical fault: the signal shorted to 5 V or battery voltage, an open sensor ground, or an open signal wire where the input is pulled up.
Sensor ground open or high resistance
Signal wire shorted to 5 V or battery voltage
Check engine lamp on, depending on the manufacturer
P25F6: P25F6 is the overall monitor for a second secondary air injection system, lettered B, on engines with two separately controlled air delivery paths; system A reports through P0410 and P0411. During warm-up after a cold start a pump pushes fresh air into the exhaust, so leftover HC and CO burn off and the catalyst lights off sooner.
Secondary air pump of system B worn, seized or water-damaged
Switching or check valve of system B stuck, often after debris from the pump
Cracked, loose or disconnected air hose or vacuum line
Faulty pump relay, fuse or wiring of system B
MIL on, usually after a cold start
Secondary air readiness monitor not complete, emissions test failed
Unusual whining or no pump noise during the first minute after a cold start
P25F7: AIR System B Incorrect Flow Detected

With P25F7 the engine controller finds that the air delivered by secondary air system B does not match its expectation while the system is switched on after a cold start. Depending on the design, it judges the flow from how the oxygen sensors on that side react, from a pressure sensor in the air line or from pump behaviour.
Air pump of system B delivers too little air
Switching or check valve fouled or stuck partly closed
Air passages to the exhaust restricted by carbon deposits
Leaking air hose so that part of the flow escapes
MIL on after one or two cold starts
Emissions test failed or readiness incomplete
P25F8: Turbocharger/Supercharger Bypass Valve C Control Circuit

Bypass valves in the intake let charge air flow around a compressor: on turbo engines they are the recirculation valves that open on a sudden throttle lift so the compressor does not surge, and on engines with a supercharger they can route air past the blower while it is idling or uncoupled.
Broken wire or loose connector at bypass valve C
Open coil in the valve or its solenoid
Fluttering noise when lifting off the throttle
P25F9: Turbocharger/Supercharger Bypass Valve C Control Circuit Low
P25F9 tells that the control line of bypass valve C reads too low a voltage, normally because it touches ground somewhere or the coil is shorted.
Output stage in the engine control module faulty
Too little boost if the valve stays open
Surging or fluttering on lift-off if it stays shut
P25FA: Turbocharger/Supercharger Bypass Valve C Control Circuit High

With P25FA the control line of bypass valve C carries more voltage than the engine module expects for the commanded state. A wire shorted to battery voltage is the classic reason; on a ground-switched valve an open coil or broken lead also lets the line float up to supply level.
Control wire shorted to battery voltage
Open valve coil on a ground-switched circuit
Damaged output stage in the engine control module
Fluttering or surging noise when lifting off the throttle
P25FB: Turbocharger/Supercharger Bypass Valve C Control Circuit Range/Performance

P25FB is set when the control circuit of bypass valve C is not open or shorted, but its electrical behaviour does not match the command – for instance a current that rises too slowly or settles at the wrong level, or a signal that drops out now and then.
Valve coil resistance changed by heat ageing
Contact resistance or moisture in the valve connector
Sluggish valve armature due to deposits
P25FC: P25FC concerns the valve itself, not its wiring: bypass valve C is electrically in order but does not move as commanded, sticking open, shut or somewhere in between. A valve stuck open lets charge air leak back to the compressor inlet, so boost falls short; one stuck shut cannot relieve pressure when the throttle closes, and the compressor surges audibly.
Oil and soot deposits from crankcase ventilation jamming the valve
Torn diaphragm or broken spring inside the valve
Cracked valve housing or leaking seal
Loud fluttering when lifting off the throttle
P25FD: Turbocharger/Supercharger Bypass Valve C Temperature Too High

This code says bypass valve C has become too hot. Recirculation valves are placed in the charge air path close to the compressor and thus near the hot turbine side, and an electric valve's coil adds its own heat when energised for long periods.
Heat soak from the turbocharger, e.g. after hard driving or with missing heat shields
Valve coil drawing too much current due to an internal fault
Sluggish valve held energised longer than intended
Fluttering on lift-off or reduced boost after hard driving
P25FE: P25FE is the umbrella code for the supercharger disconnect clutch: it says the clutch function has failed without naming whether it is stuck, slipping or electrically faulty.
Worn or seized clutch on the supercharger pulley
Fault in the coil, wiring or connector of the clutch
Engine control software that misjudges the clutch state
Weak response at low engine speed
P25FF: Electrical System Voltage Stabilizer Control Module Performance

P25FF reports that the module which steadies the 12 V supply for sensitive electronics does not work as intended. Such stabilizers mainly appear on cars with automatic engine stop/start: every restart drags the battery voltage down hard, according to a semiconductor maker briefly below 4 V, which would otherwise reset radios, displays and similar loads.
Internal fault in the voltage stabilizer or DC/DC converter module
Aged or wrong-type 12 V battery so the module cannot hold the voltage
Current backfeed or poor supply/ground connection at the module
Radio or display resets when the engine restarts
Warning light depending on the maker
P2600: P2600 means the controller sees an open circuit on the line that drives electric coolant pump A, directly or through its relay. GM's 2023 ECM table tests the auxiliary coolant pump relay output while it is off: more than 200 kOhm for 5 of 6 seconds sets the code as Type B, so the MIL follows after two trips.
Internal open circuit in the electric pump or its electronics
Water or coolant ingress causing poor contact at the pump
Chafed or broken control wire, loose connector or failed relay
Coolant level too low (named by Hyundai as possible trigger)
MIL or hybrid warning lamp on
Rising coolant temperature in hybrid or after-run operation
P2601: Coolant Pump A Control Circuit Performance/Stuck Off
P2601 is set when electric coolant pump A is commanded on, yet its feedback or its effect shows that it is not really working, while the wiring itself tests sound.
Electric pump seized, worn or running too slowly
Control module software misjudging the pump (update available)
Air pocket or low coolant so the pump runs dry
Coolant temperature stays high after shutdown
P2602: Coolant Pump A Control Circuit Low
P2602 reports that the control circuit of electric coolant pump A reads low - typically a ground short, or a matching fault report from the driver stage.
Internal fault in the electric coolant pump or its electronics
Coolant or water ingress into the pump connector
Fault code stored; MIL depends on the maker (GM 2008 LLT table none, GM 2023 ECM table Type B)
No after-run of the pump after a hot shutdown
P2603: Coolant Pump A Control Circuit High

P2603 means the drive line of electric coolant pump A reads high - usually a short to the supply side, or an overcurrent seen by the driver stage. Ford's 2020-2023 gasoline OBD summary assigns pump A to the auxiliary high-temperature loop for cabin heating and sets P2602/P2603 when the smart driver reports a fault within 5 s.
Control wire shorted to battery voltage
Seized or sluggish pump drawing excessive current
Faulty driver stage in the ECM
Fault code stored; MIL depends on the maker (GM 2008 LLT table none, GM 2023 ECM table Type B)
Higher coolant temperature after hot shutdown
P2604: Intake Air Heater A Circuit Range/Performance

P2604 is the functional check of intake air heater A - the grid heater in the intake that warms the charge air of a diesel engine for cold starts. The circuit responds, but current, voltage drop or heating effect do not match the command.
Worn or sticking intake air heater relay
Loose or burnt terminals on the heater supply cable
Degraded or partly open heater grid
White smoke and rough running after a cold start
P2605: P2605 points to an open circuit at intake air heater B, a second heating element in the intake of a diesel engine; the control unit finds no current path through the element, its relay or the cabling. Volvo's EMS code lists keep heaters A, B and C apart.
Loose, corroded or burnt terminal at heater element or relay
White smoke after a cold start
P2606: Intake Air Heater B Circuit Range/Performance
P2606 means heater B in the intake does respond, but the current it draws or the voltage drop across its circuit lies outside the window the engine controller expects.
Extra resistance from corroded contacts, e.g. in the master disconnect switch
Aged heater element with changed resistance
Outdated engine software (update published by the maker)
White smoke until the engine is warm
P2607: Intake Air Heater B Circuit Low

P2607 says the signal from the circuit of intake air heater B stays too low, which normally means a grounded control or feedback line, or a relay output pulled down. No manufacturer documents P2607 publicly.
Control or feedback wire chafed through to ground
Internal short in the preheat relay
Moisture or corrosion in a connector of the heater circuit
White smoke after a cold start
P2608: Intake Air Heater B Circuit High
P2608 is logged when the circuit of intake air heater B reads too high, for instance a short to battery positive on the control line or a relay that stays energized when it should be off.
Preheat relay contacts welded or sticking closed
Control or feedback wire shorted to battery positive
Engine software needing the maker's update
Batteries run down after short trips or standstill
Hard cold starts or white smoke
P2609: P2609 judges the intake air heating as a whole rather than one circuit: the controller compares what the grid heater should achieve with what it measures, for example via the current drawn or the rise in intake air temperature during preheat. Ram has published two service documents for its 6.7 L Cummins pickups. Bulletin 18-012-12 REV.
Worn heater grid or relay (replace as a set)
Overheated or loose supply cable between relay and grid
Engine software with an outdated diagnostic (reflash available)
Intake air temperature sensor reading implausibly
White smoke and rough idle after a cold start
P260A: P260A reports an open circuit in the output a control module uses to engage the power take-off, typically the coil circuit of a PTO relay or engagement solenoid.
Relay coil wiring missing, broken or only one side connected by the upfitter
Open coil in the PTO relay or engagement solenoid
Corroded or loose connector in the chassis wiring
PTO indicator flashes or stays off
P260B: P260B is stored when the PTO control output reads too low, the classic case being a grounded wire leading to the PTO relay coil. GM documents the code as P260B.00, a low voltage on the PTO relay control line, among the faults the PTO module can set on 2008-2014 Silverado and Sierra 3500 HD chassis cabs.
Relay control wire chafed against the frame or body
Shorted coil in the PTO relay or solenoid
Relay wired incorrectly during body installation
P260C: P260C signals that the PTO control output reads too high, usually because the relay control line touches a powered wire or the relay coil draws too much current. GM lists it as P260C.00, a high voltage on the PTO relay control line, in the diagnostic table of the PTO module that GM fitted to Silverado and Sierra 3500 HD chassis cab trucks from 2008 to 2014.
Relay control wire shorted to a powered circuit
Relay or solenoid coil with too low resistance
Faulty splice or add-on wiring from the body installation
PTO will not engage or will not release
P260D: P260D concerns the output that drives the lamp or LED telling the operator that the power take-off is engaged; the module has found a fault in that lamp circuit.
Open or shorted wire to the indicator, often in add-on wiring
Fault in the PTO switch assembly with integrated LED
PTO indicator stays dark or lit regardless of PTO state
P260E: Particulate Filter Regeneration Lamp Control Circuit
Diesel machines often have a separate dashboard lamp that tells the operator a particulate filter regeneration is needed or running. P260E covers the circuit that switches this lamp.
Lamp wire shorted to ground or to supply
Lamp or bulb holder open, or lamp not fitted on this machine
Corroded connector at dashboard or engine controller
Regeneration lamp dark or permanently lit
Missed regeneration requests leading to high soot load
Later power reduction by the engine controller
P260F: Some evaporative leak tests run long after the engine is switched off, so Ford gives them a small dedicated processor that works during the soak. P260F is set when that monitoring processor does not behave as intended.
Internal fault in the EVAP monitoring processor or module
Supply, ground or CAN wiring fault at the monitoring module
EVAP readiness not set, small leak test not completed
P2610: ECM/PCM Internal Engine Off Timer Performance

Several emission monitors need to know how long the engine was off, for example to judge a cold start or an evaporative test after a soak. P2610 reports that the module's engine-off timer gives implausible values.
Engine module software prone to false timer faults (update available)
Battery disconnect, transport fuse removed or supply dropout during soak
Timer message from another module (e.g. cluster) missing on CAN
Internal timer fault in the control module
MIL on, usually without drivability change
Cold-start and EVAP monitors may not run
P2611: A/C Refrigerant Distribution Valve A Control Circuit/Open

A refrigerant distribution valve is an electrically switched valve in the A/C circuit that opens or blocks the refrigerant path to one branch, for example a rear evaporator or a battery chiller. P2611 tells you the engine or powertrain module can no longer drive valve A because its control line or coil is open.
Valve solenoid coil burnt out or internally open
Corroded or loose connector at the valve, often near condensation
Broken control wire between module and valve
Faulty output stage in the controlling module
One A/C zone (e.g. rear) blows warm or cannot be shut off
Reduced battery cooling on hybrids or EVs, possibly limited charging power
Stored code, often without warning lamp
P2612: A/C Refrigerant Distribution Valve A Control Circuit Low
P2612 is stored when the voltage on the drive line of refrigerant distribution valve A stays lower than the module expects, which normally points to a ground fault in the wire or inside the valve.
Brittle or corroded connector at the valve (VW N280 plug near the starter)
Internal short in the valve coil
A/C does not cool or compressor does not engage (VW)
One cooling branch or zone remains inactive
Code stored, usually no other driveability symptom
P2613: A/C Refrigerant Distribution Valve A Control Circuit High

P2613 means the control circuit of refrigerant distribution valve A reads too high: the wire has a short to the supply side, or the driver stage senses excessive current when it switches the valve. No manufacturer documents this code publicly; Ford lists only the open-circuit code P2611, and the VW use of P2612 refers to the compressor regulator valve.
Control wire shorted to a battery-voltage feed
Valve coil with shorted windings drawing too much current
Defective driver in the controlling module
An A/C branch keeps cooling although it should be off
Valve output switched off, so the branch does not work at all
P2614: Camshaft A Position Signal Output Circuit/Open (Bank 1)

Some engine computers pass a copy of the camshaft position signal on to another module, for example an injector driver unit or a valve timing controller. P2614 means that this outgoing line for camshaft A on bank 1 is broken or its pulses never reach the receiver.
Broken wire or loose terminal between sending module and receiving module
Camshaft sensor signal itself missing or out of sync with the crank signal
Receiving module (e.g. injector control module) not reading the signal
Defective output stage in the engine control module
P2615: Camshaft A Position Signal Output Circuit Low (Bank 1)
P2615 points to a camshaft A (bank 1) position output line that the engine module finds pulled to ground.
Output wire chafed through and touching ground
Moisture or corrosion bridging the connector pins to ground
Internally shorted input in the receiving module
Faulty output driver in the engine control module
Stored code, often without warning lamp
Valve timing control in fallback mode
P2616: Camshaft A Position Signal Output Circuit High (Bank 1)
P2616 is the opposite fault to P2615: the outgoing camshaft A position line on bank 1 stays at supply potential although the module has switched its low-side driver on and wants the line low.
Output wire shorted to a battery or ignition feed
Low-side driver in the engine module no longer switching
Back-feed through a damaged or corroded connector
Hard starting or hesitation after start
Cam phasing faults logged by the receiving module
P2617: When an engine module relays the crankshaft position signal to another controller, P2617 says that this forwarded line is open or the pulses go missing at the receiver.
Open wire or pushed-out pin on the crank output line
Crank sensor signal itself missing or out of sync with the cam signal
Receiving module (e.g. injector control module) faulty
Engine cranks but does not start
P2618: Crankshaft Position Signal Output Circuit Low

P2618 reports a crankshaft position output line that is shorted to ground. GM uses it widely, from the 2011–2012 hybrid tables to the 2019 ECM summaries, wherever the engine module provides a crank position output.
Harness pinched or chafed so the output touches ground
Water or corrosion in the output connector
Shorted input stage in the receiving module
Output driver failure in the engine control module
MIL on after two drive cycles
Related faults or substitute mode in the receiving module
P2619: Crankshaft Position Signal Output Circuit High
P2619 is set when the crankshaft position output line is held at supply voltage while the module's low-side driver is switched on and expects it to be pulled down.
Damaged insulation lets the output touch a positive feed
Low-side driver in the engine module failed open
MIL on after two drive cycles
Receiving module reports implausible crank signal
Possible reduced power or start problems
P261A: P261A reports an open circuit in the drive of an auxiliary electric coolant pump labelled B. Ford's gasoline OBD summaries for 2020-2023 and 2024 define pump B as the high-temperature loop pump for component cooling and check it continuously over 5 s with at least 11 V on board.
Pump connector not fully seated or with spread terminals
Auxiliary pump with internal open (electronics or motor)
Broken supply or control wire, or failed relay where fitted
Malfunction indicator lamp on, sometimes only sporadically
No after-run circulation, heat soak after hot shutdown
P261B: Coolant Pump B Control Circuit Performance/Stuck Off

Unlike the wiring codes around it, P261B judges whether coolant pump B actually delivers when commanded. The verdict comes from pump feedback or from its effect on coolant temperatures, so the circuit can test fine while the pump does nothing.
Auxiliary pump motor or electronics failing intermittently
Air pocket after coolant service, pump runs dry
Impeller blocked by debris or deposits
Engine or turbo runs hotter after shutdown, possible boiling noises
Heater or component cooling weak in certain conditions
P261C: Coolant Pump B Control Circuit Low
P261C points to a control line of coolant pump B pulled toward ground. VW's 2014 Touareg data book sets it when the signal voltage drops below 2.8-3.2 V.
Chafed wire to ground near exhaust or engine parts
Internal short in the pump electronics, often after water ingress
Auxiliary pump does not run, no after-run cooling
Rising temperatures at turbo or electronics in heavy use
P261D: Coolant Pump B Control Circuit High

With P261D the module finds the drive of coolant pump B too high, either a short to the supply side or a current above the permitted limit. VW's 2014 Touareg book uses a current test here, roughly 2.2 to 4 A as the threshold.
Stiff or partly seized pump drawing excess current
Control wire shorted to a battery-voltage circuit
Faulty driver stage in the engine module
Pump switched off for protection or running permanently
Possible battery drain if the pump keeps running after shutdown
P261E: Coolant Pump B Control Circuit Stuck On

P261E covers the case where coolant pump B keeps working although the module has commanded it off. That can be an output that stays energised, a relay with welded contacts, or, on switchable mechanical pumps, a shroud or valve that no longer closes, so coolant circulates during warm-up.
Pump relay with welded contacts or output stage stuck on
Switchable pump shroud or vacuum/solenoid valve not closing
Control line shorted to battery voltage
Engine warms up slowly, heater stays cool longer
Pump audible after the engine is switched off
Warning lamp and possibly a thermostat code
P261F: Coolant Pump A Control Circuit Stuck On

P261F means electric coolant pump A reports activity while the module has it switched off. GM's 2025 ECM table 25OBDG04B describes the test: with the pump commanded off or below 299 rpm for 2 s and more than 11 V on board, a feedback speed of 3,100 rpm or more for 8 of 10 seconds sets the code as Type B; the warning lamp follows on the second faulty trip.
Impeller driven by main pump flow at high rpm, fixed by ECM software (GM)
Vacuum leak or contaminated switching valve of a switchable pump (Mercedes OM651)
Pump electronics reporting wrong speed or not switching off
Check engine lamp after two faulty trips
Slower warm-up when the pump really keeps running
P2620: P2620 concerns a line on which the engine module sends a throttle position value out to another unit, for instance a transmission or body controller, as an analogue or pulse-width signal. The code means the module detects that this output circuit is open, so the receiver gets nothing usable.
Open wire or loose pin on the throttle position output line
Corroded connector at the sending or receiving module
Output stage in the engine control module defective
Stored code, warning lamp behaviour depends on the maker
Irregular shift points or idle control in the receiving module
P2621: P2621 flags the throttle position output line as shorted to ground or reading below its permitted voltage band. A receiving module such as a transmission controller would then see a value that looks like a fully closed throttle all the time.
Output wire chafed against body ground
Corrosion bridging the output pin to ground
Shorted input in the receiving module
Stored code in the engine module
Receiver behaves as if the throttle were always closed (late or odd shifts)
P2622: P2622 means the throttle position output line sits too high, typically because it is shorted to a supply wire or the driver in the sending module cannot pull it down. The receiver would read a value resembling wide-open throttle even at idle, which can confuse shift scheduling or torque calculations.
Output wire shorted to a battery or ignition feed
Driver in the sending module unable to pull the line low
Stored code in the engine module
Receiver acts as if at full throttle (harsh or late shifts)
P2623: Engines with hydraulically actuated unit injectors (HEUI) fire their injectors with engine oil pressurised by a high-pressure pump; the injection pressure regulator (IPR) valve sets that oil rail pressure. P2623 says the PCM cannot drive the IPR because its circuit is open.
Loose or corroded IPR connector, broken wire on the high-pressure pump cover
Faulty IPR driver in the PCM
Engine cranks but does not start
P2624: Injector Control Pressure Regulator Circuit Low
P2624 is reserved for a control circuit of the injection pressure regulator that sits too low, typically a ground short on the line switched by the PCM. No manufacturer documents this code publicly.
IPR control wire chafed to ground near the valley or pump cover
Damaged driver stage in the PCM
Rough running, knocking or erratic power
P2625: Injector Control Pressure Regulator Circuit High
With P2625 the module sees the injection pressure regulator circuit at too high a level: the switched line is shorted to battery voltage, or the IPR coil draws more current than the driver allows.
IPR control line shorted to a battery-voltage circuit
IPR coil with reduced resistance causing overcurrent
Faulty IPR driver in the PCM
P2626: O2 Sensor Pumping Current Trim Circuit/Open (Bank 1 Sensor 1)

Wide-band lambda probes such as the Bosch LSU 4.9 carry a calibration resistor in their plug; the engine module uses it to scale the pumping current. P2626 says this trim path at the front probe of bank 1 looks open.
Front wide-band probe defective (trim resistor, pump cell or heater damage)
Trim line broken or pin pushed back in the six-pin probe connector
Moisture or corrosion in the probe connector raising the measured resistance
Engine software requiring an update after probe replacement (some makes)
Fuel control falls back to open loop on bank 1
Slightly higher fuel consumption or rough idle
P2627: O2 Sensor Pumping Current Trim Circuit Low (Bank 1 Sensor 1)

P2627 marks a trim signal below its plausible range at the first wide-band probe of bank 1. On Ford petrol engines with NTK probes the interface chip sets it when the resistor line (RL) is open or touches ground; Bosch-equipped Fords do not use it.
Trim/resistor line open or chafed to ground between probe and engine module
Wide-band probe or NOx sensor internally faulty
Loose or leaking charge-air ducts on diesel engines (GM L5P)
Further oxygen or NOx sensor codes stored at the same time
On diesels possibly boost or aftertreatment codes and reduced power
P2628: O2 Sensor Pumping Current Trim Circuit High (Bank 1 Sensor 1)

With P2628 the trim input of the front wide-band probe on bank 1 lies above its permitted range. Ford's 2020-23 petrol summary reserves it for NTK probes, where the interface chip reports the resistor line shorted to battery voltage.
Trim line shorted to battery or another supply in the harness or plug
Wide-band probe or NOx sensor delivering an implausible value
Exhaust leak ahead of the sensor drawing in outside air
Mixture control without probe feedback, higher consumption
On diesels NOx-related codes and possible SCR warnings
P2629: O2 Sensor Pumping Current Trim Circuit/Open (Bank 2 Sensor 1)

P2629 is the bank 2 counterpart of P2626 and only exists on V or boxer engines with two front wide-band probes. The module finds the trim branch of that probe interrupted. GM's 2023 table 23OBDG07 calculates the parallel resistance between the probe's APE and MES pins and fails values above 240 ohms as an open compensation resistor, two trips.
Bank 2 front probe faulty, including heater damage (Mercedes M278/M157)
Open trim wire or loose terminal at the bank 2 probe connector
Outdated engine software (update called for together with new probes)
Bank 2 fuel control without wide-band feedback
Possibly further bank 2 fuel trim codes
P262A: Fuel Injector - Pilot Injection Not Learned
Common-rail diesels learn how long each injector must be energised to deliver its tiny pilot shot.
Driving pattern rarely offers long overrun phases in high gear (towing, city use)
Injector drift or wear so the test pulse does not give a usable response
Disturbed crankshaft speed or rail pressure signal
Non-original engine calibration interfering with the learning routine
Louder combustion knock, especially at idle and light load
Often no noticeable change in driveability
P262B: Control Module Power Off Timer Performance
P262B concerns the timer that keeps counting inside a control module while the vehicle is shut down, used to measure how long it has been off.
Poor ECM power or ground connection, momentary supply loss
Ignition relay or its control circuit not supplying the module
Diagnostic calibration too sensitive to fast engine cool-down
Internal timer hardware fault in the control module
MIL on after two drive cycles
Possibly other control module codes stored at the same time
P262C: Engine modules supply groups of sensors from separately regulated 5 V outputs, lettered A, B, C and so on; G is the seventh such supply. P262C is the general fault of this output, typically an interruption so that the sensors behind it lose their feed and report signals near zero together.
Broken reference wire or splice feeding the sensors of circuit G
Loose or corroded pin at the engine module or a sensor plug
Internal regulator of the engine module for output G failed
Several sensor codes appearing at the same time
Reduced power or limp mode depending on the affected sensors
P262D: Sensor Reference Voltage G Circuit Low

P262D says the 5 V reference output G of the engine module is being dragged below its lower limit. Usually something on the line conducts to ground: a chafed wire, water in a plug, or one sensor with an internal short loading the whole group. A useful test is to unplug the sensors on circuit G one by one and watch whether the voltage recovers.
Reference wire G chafed to ground or engine metal
One sensor on circuit G with internal short pulling the supply down
Water or corrosion in a connector of the group
Weak internal regulator of the engine module
Several sensors report low or invalid values together
Limp mode, reduced power or starting problems possible
P262E: Sensor Reference Voltage G Circuit High

With P262E the 5 V supply G that the engine module feeds to a sensor group sits above its upper limit. That points to an external voltage source getting onto the line, for example a reference wire rubbed through against a 12 V feed or a sensor signal wire, or to a regulator inside the module that no longer holds its setpoint.
Reference wire G shorted to a 12 V feed or another powered circuit
Sensor on the group feeding voltage back into the reference
Internal regulator of the engine module out of tolerance
Readings of several sensors too high or implausible
Limp mode or reduced power possible
P262F: Sensor Reference Voltage G Circuit Range/Performance

P262F is the plausibility check of reference output G. The voltage is neither shorted nor missing, yet it wanders outside a tighter tolerance band or jumps around, which falsifies every ratiometric sensor on that circuit.
Poor ground connection of the engine module
Loose pin or splice on circuit G opening briefly under vibration
Sensor on the group drawing excessive current
Drifting internal regulator of the engine module
Sporadic implausible values from several sensors
P2630: O2 Sensor Pumping Current Trim Circuit Low (Bank 2 Sensor 1)

P2630 reports a trim input that is too low at the upstream wide-band probe of bank 2, the cylinder bank without cylinder 1. Ford's petrol summaries of 2020-23 set it only with NTK probes, where the sensor interface chip sees the resistor line open or grounded; the same chip check runs for about 10 s before a fault is stored.
Resistor line of the bank 2 probe open or rubbed through to ground
Damaged or heat-affected connector near the exhaust
P2631: O2 Sensor Pumping Current Trim Circuit High (Bank 2 Sensor 1)

P2631 flags a trim value above the valid window for the first wide-band probe on bank 2. Ford assigns it to NTK probe installations: the interface chip notices the resistor line pulled up to battery voltage, as from a chafed wire touching a powered circuit.
Bank 2 resistor line shorted to a powered wire in the harness
Bank 2 front probe with internal short
Non-matching replacement probe or repaired connector without the original resistor
Possibly additional circuit codes from the same harness
P2632: Fuel pump B is a second pump beside the main one: a transfer pump between two tanks, an in-line booster or a second in-tank pump. P2632 reports an open in its control circuit. On the 6.6 L LML Duramax with dual tanks, GM's 2014 table 14OBDG10 drives the transfer pump relay through a low-side driver and sets the code as Type B after 3 s above 200 kOhm.
Failed transfer pump relay, fuse or relay socket
Open wire or corroded connector at the pump or tank
Pump motor or pump driver module open internally
Outdated scan tool cannot command the pump (GM PIT5212B)
Fuel from the second tank is not transferred, gauge drops faster
Possible stalling when the main tank runs dry
P2633: Fuel Pump B Control Circuit Low

P2633 is the ground-short code of the second fuel pump circuit. GM's 2014 LML diesel table checks the ground-switched relay output of the fuel transfer pump while it is off and flags 0.5 ohm or less between signal and ground, held for 3 s, as Type B.
Chafed pump wire grounded against frame or tank strap
Water in the connector under the vehicle
Blown fuse, second pump does not run
Fuel not transferred from the auxiliary tank
P2634: Fuel Pump B Control Circuit High

P2634 indicates that the drive of the second fuel pump reads as shorted to battery voltage or carries too much current. For the 6.6 L LML with dual tanks, GM's 2014 table judges the transfer pump relay output while it is switched on and treats 0.5 ohm or less toward controller power, lasting 3 s, as a Type B fault.
Control wire shorted to a battery-voltage feed
Worn or binding pump drawing excess current
Relay with shorted coil or stuck contacts
Second pump runs constantly or is shut off by the module
Fuel level display between tanks inconsistent
P2635: P2635 judges the main fuel pump by its result rather than its wiring: the module compares the measured fuel pressure with the commanded value and flags a pump that falls short or overshoots.
Worn or leaking in-tank pump module
Clogged filter or blocked pickup, e.g. gelled diesel in cold weather
Low supply voltage or poor ground at the pump or pump control module
Fuel pressure sensor reading wrong without its own code
Hesitation, surging or loss of power under load
Whining noise from the fuel tank
P2636: P2636 is the flow check for fuel pump B, in practice mostly the transfer pump of trucks with two tanks. GM's 2014 table for the 6.6 L LML compares how fast the levels in both tanks fall while the pump runs; if they do not move as expected for 140 s, a Type B fault is stored.
Weak transfer pump not moving enough fuel between tanks
Restricted transfer line or design-related flow limit (GM recall 17067)
Refuelling with engine or ignition on confuses the level-based check
Faulty fuel level sender in one of the tanks
Fuel gauge shows empty although the second tank holds fuel
Engine may stall when the main tank runs dry
P2637: Many automatic transmissions ask the engine to cut torque briefly during an upshift and then check whether the engine actually did so. P2637 is stored by the transmission controller when that feedback for request A shows the engine did not follow.
Engine control module calibration not following the torque reduction request
Transmission calibration not matched to the engine
J1939/CAN data link fault between engine and transmission
P2638: Torque Management Feedback Signal A Range/Performance

P2638 says the torque feedback for request A is present but its value does not fit the situation, for example an engine torque figure that drifts away from what the transmission expects during a shift.
Idle learn not completed after PCM reset or delivery
Outdated transmission software with oversensitive torque monitoring
Engine torque estimate skewed by air leaks or sensor errors
MIL on and gear position indicator flashing
P2639: Torque Management Feedback Signal A Low

P2639 means the torque management feedback signal A stays below its valid range, so the transmission controller cannot read a usable torque confirmation from the engine. No manufacturer explains this exact code publicly.
Engine and transmission software versions not matched
Torque feedback message missing or corrupted on the data bus
Hard-wired feedback line shorted to ground
P263A: P263A means the engine module has found the line that switches the malfunction indicator lamp shorted to ground.
MIL control wire chafed and touching ground
Loss of ignition 1 voltage via main relay or fuse block terminal
Faulty lamp input in the instrument cluster
Code stored even though the lamp cannot report it reliably
P263B: P263B is stored when the MIL control line is stuck at supply voltage while the module has switched its driver on to light the lamp. GM treats an impedance toward power of about 0.5 ohm as the fault and needs 4 failures within 5 samples, each 50 ms apart, provided run/crank voltage is at least 11 V and no remote start is running.
MIL control wire shorted to a positive feed
Ignition 1 supply interrupted at relay or fuse block
Lamp driver in the engine module failed
Engine warning lamp does not light, not even at key-on bulb check
Other emissions codes stored without warning
P263C: Modern diesel glow systems switch each plug through a semiconductor driver inside a glow plug control module (GPCM). P263C reports that such a driver does not behave as commanded.
Output stage inside the glow plug control module failed
Glow plug or plug wire with short, overloading the driver
Poor GPCM power feed or ground causing erratic switching
Check engine light, glow indicator may flash
Hard or long cranking when cold
White smoke and rough running after a cold start
P263D: DEF turns solid at about -11 °C, so SCR systems heat the tank, pump and lines electrically. P263D concerns the power stage that switches these heaters rather than a heater element.
Heater power stage overheating from excessive load current
Partially shorted heater element or wiring drawing too much current
Internal fault of the module that drives the heaters
Check engine light and DEF/SCR warning
DEF not thawing in cold weather, dosing delayed
Countdown to speed or power limitation possible
P263E: Glow Plug Control Module 1 Over Temperature

The first glow plug control module measures its own internal temperature and reports P263E when it runs too hot, since its power semiconductors carry tens of amps during glowing. GM's 6.6 L L5P Duramax tables set it at a module temperature above 123 °C while the plugs are commanded on and coolant is below 60 °C, type B.
Defective glow plugs drawing excess current (e.g. Ram ProMaster plugs without O-ring)
Repeated start attempts or very long glow periods in severe cold
Internal fault or poor heat dissipation of the glow plug module
Check engine light, glow lamp flashing
Glowing cut short, hard cold starts
P263F: Glow Plug Control Module 2 Over Temperature

P263F is reserved for engines with a second glow plug control module, for instance one per cylinder bank on large V engines; it reports that this second unit has exceeded its permitted internal temperature.
High-current or shorted glow plugs on the bank served by module 2
Long or repeated glow phases in severe cold
Internal fault or poor cooling of glow plug module 2
Check engine light, glow lamp flashing
Harder cold start, uneven running until warm
P2640: Torque Management Feedback Signal A High

P2640 is the high-range fault of torque management feedback signal A: the confirmation that the transmission controller receives after asking the engine for a torque change carries a value above the plausible upper limit.
Engine ECM software reports torque values the transmission calibration does not accept
Outdated or wrong transmission controller calibration
Hard-wired feedback line shorted to voltage (where used)
Check transmission lamp or MIL on, depending on calibration
Torque reduction during shifts no longer active
P2641: On Allison automatics, feedback B belongs to Low Range Torque Protection (LRTP): in the low ranges the TCM caps engine torque to spare gears and output shaft and checks that the engine respects the cap. P2641 sets when the engine reports more torque than permitted.
Engine ECM software below the level required for the transmission (Cummins, Mack, Volvo)
Engine broadcasts torque above the low-range limit requested by the TCM
Transmission calibration not matched to the engine
Low Reverse or other low ranges unavailable
Code appears under high load, often without noticeable drivability change
P2642: Torque Management Feedback Signal B Range/Performance

P2642 means feedback signal B arrives and lies inside its valid range, yet its value makes no sense for the current operating state, for example a torque figure that drifts away from what a limited request should produce or that changes implausibly fast. No manufacturer explains P2642 publicly.
Engine and transmission software versions do not match
Idle or torque adaptation not learned after service
Faulty input to the engine torque model (air mass, intake air temperature)
P2643: Torque Management Feedback Signal B Low

With P2643 the transmission controller sees feedback signal B below its lower limit, so it cannot confirm that the engine is holding the torque level it asked for. No manufacturer describes this exact code in public documents.
Torque message missing or sent with a default value on the data link
Bus or signal wiring damaged, short to ground
Low ranges or reverse low not selectable
Harsh shifts because torque reduction is missing
P2644: Torque Management Feedback Signal B High
P2644 reports that torque management feedback B exceeds its upper range limit. No manufacturer publishes a code-specific description.
Engine software sends torque with a scaling the transmission does not expect
Engine calibration older than the level required by the transmission maker
Wired feedback line shorted to voltage
P2645: Engines that switch valve lift or deactivate cylinders through their rocker arms use an actuator, usually an oil control solenoid, to send oil to the locking pins. P2645 means the engine controller sees the drive circuit of actuator A on bank 1 as open: the state it commands and the state it reads back on the line disagree.
Open coil in the rocker arm oil control solenoid
Loose, corroded or oil-soaked solenoid connector
Broken wire in the control or supply line
Faulty output driver in the engine control module
MIL on, often on the first trip
No change to high lift, weak pull at high engine speed
Cylinder deactivation or economy mode no longer engages
P2646: "A" Rocker Arm Actuator System Performance/Stuck Off (Bank 1)
P2646 is a mechanical-hydraulic plausibility fault: actuator A on bank 1 was commanded to switch the rocker arms, yet the engine did not change lift, or responded too weakly.
Low oil level, wrong viscosity or sludged oil
Sticking spool or clogged screen in the oil control solenoid
Seized locking pin in the switching rocker arm
Faulty lift controller or outdated ECM calibration (Toyota Valvematic)
MIL on after a completed test drive
Engine feels flat above mid-range speed
P2647: "A" Rocker Arm Actuator System Stuck On (Bank 1)
Here actuator A on bank 1 is believed to stay engaged: the rocker arms remain locked in the switched mode although the controller has asked for the default lift.
Oil control solenoid leaks oil while switched off
Locking pin jammed in the engaged position
Faulty rocker arm oil pressure switch (Honda VTEC)
P2648: "A" Rocker Arm Actuator Control Circuit Low (Bank 1)
P2648 points to a low-side electrical fault on the control line of rocker arm actuator A, bank 1: the line reads low, typically a short to ground or a solenoid with shorted turns.
Control wire chafed through to ground
Shorted turns in the solenoid winding
Moisture or oil bridging pins in the connector
No switching to the second lift stage
P2649: "A" Rocker Arm Actuator Control Circuit High (Bank 1)

The counterpart to P2648: the control circuit of rocker arm actuator A on bank 1 reads high, which means a short to battery voltage or a driver that cannot pull the line down. In GM's 2015 table 15OBDG05 the check needs the output driver commanded on, ignition in crank or run and supply above 11 V; 100 failures in 120 samples set a Type A fault.
Control wire shorted to a battery or ignition feed
Output driver in the engine controller no longer switches
Open ground side of the solenoid circuit
Lift switching disabled or permanently active
Rough running at idle if the actuator stays energised
P264A: "A" Rocker Arm Actuator Position Sensor Circuit (Bank 1)

Some valve lift systems report back where the rocker arm actuator actually is, rather than relying on oil pressure; continuously variable designs driven by an electric motor, such as Toyota Valvematic, work this way.
Loose or corroded position sensor connector
Damaged signal, supply or ground wire
Lift held at a fixed value, less power
P264B: "A" Rocker Arm Actuator Position Sensor Circuit Range/Performance (Bank 1)

Range/Performance means the bank 1 feedback sensor for actuator A delivers a signal inside its electrical limits that still does not fit what the engine expects, for example a position that lags or overshoots the commanded one, or that fails to move when the actuator is driven.
Sensor loose or misaligned on its mount
MIL on after a drive cycle
P264C: "A" Rocker Arm Actuator Position Sensor Circuit Low (Bank 1)

P264C is set when the signal from the position sensor of rocker arm actuator A, bank 1, sits below its valid window. Typical electrical explanations are a short of the signal wire to ground, a lost 5 V reference, or a sensor that has failed internally.
Weaker pull, lift no longer varied
P264D: "A" Rocker Arm Actuator Position Sensor Circuit High (Bank 1)

With P264D the position signal of actuator A on bank 1 reads above its plausible maximum. An open ground return, a signal line touching the 5 V or battery feed, or water in the connector can push it up. Because a reading at the upper stop looks like an impossible position, the controller rejects it and runs a fixed lift.
Signal wire shorted to 5 V or battery voltage
Water ingress in the sensor connector
Engine runs on a fixed lift setting
P264E: "A" Rocker Arm Actuator Position Sensor Circuit Intermittent/Erratic (Bank 1)

P264E covers a feedback signal from the position sensor of actuator A, bank 1, that drops out or jumps for short moments rather than staying low or high. Loose terminals, a cracked wire flexing with engine movement, or interference on an unshielded line are the usual reasons, and the fault may vanish when the vehicle is parked.
Loose or spread terminal in the sensor connector
Wire cracked inside the insulation by engine movement
Electrical interference on the signal line
MIL on, sometimes clearing by itself
P264F: Engine Serial Number Not Programmed or Incompatible
Some engine controllers store the serial number of the engine they belong to, much like the VIN. P264F is logged when that entry is empty or does not fit.
Engine serial number not written after PCM/ECM replacement
Serial number from another engine or used control module
Stored configuration lost through a memory fault in the module
MIL on after control module replacement
Usually no change in how the engine runs
P2650: Some engines split rocker arm switching into two stages or groups, each fed by its own oil control solenoid; the second one is called actuator B. P2650 is logged when the engine controller finds the drive line of that B solenoid on bank 1 open, so switching the output on or off brings no matching electrical response.
Open winding in the B rocker arm oil control solenoid
Terminal pushed out or corroded in the solenoid B connector
Wire chafed through near the valve cover or harness clips
Failed output stage for solenoid B in the engine control module
Second switching stage never engages, less power or economy in that range
Possibly no other noticeable change in driving
P2651: "B" Rocker Arm Actuator System Performance/Stuck Off (Bank 1)

In the generic definition, P2651 says the B stage of rocker arm switching on bank 1 did not engage when requested, or engaged too weakly to be confirmed. Controllers usually verify the change through an oil pressure switch in the rocker gallery or through a measurable shift in engine behaviour.
Intermittently failing rocker arm oil pressure switch (Honda i-VTEC)
Oil level too low or oil of the wrong grade
Clogged filter screen or sticking spool in solenoid B
Locking pin in the switchable rocker arm seized by deposits
MIL on, sometimes only now and then
Engine lacks pull in the speed range served by stage B
Fault may not return right after clearing
P2652: "B" Rocker Arm Actuator System Stuck On (Bank 1)

P2652 means the controller thinks stage B of the bank 1 rocker switching stays engaged after release was commanded, usually because the confirming oil pressure switch still signals pressure. Honda documents it in two ways.
Rocker arm oil pressure switch B reporting pressure permanently
Solenoid B lets oil through in its closed position
Locking pin stuck in the engaged position
Switch signal line shorted to voltage (Honda four-cylinder meaning)
MIL on, possibly together with P3400 on Honda V6
Rough or uneven running, especially at low load
P2653: "B" Rocker Arm Actuator Control Circuit Low (Bank 1)

P2653 points to a voltage that is too low on the control line of rocker arm solenoid B, bank 1. On a solenoid switched from the supply side, a line rubbing against the engine block or a shorted coil pulls the signal down while the output is active; the controller's driver then reports an overcurrent or a low-voltage state.
Control wire of solenoid B shorted to engine ground
Shorted turns inside the solenoid B coil
Engine oil inside the connector creating a leakage path
MIL on soon after the fault appears
B stage switched off, reduced power or economy
P2654: "B" Rocker Arm Actuator Control Circuit High (Bank 1)
P2654 reports a voltage that is too high on the wire that drives rocker solenoid B, bank 1, typically when the line touches a battery-fed wire or the driver's ground side is bridged.
Solenoid B control wire shorted to a battery-fed circuit
Internal short in solenoid B lowering its resistance
Shorted output transistor in the engine control module
Rough idle or misfire if the B stage stays engaged
Possible blown fuse on the solenoid supply
P2655: P2655 is the bank 2 twin of P2645: on a V or boxer engine with a separate rocker arm actuator per cylinder bank, the drive circuit of actuator A on the side without cylinder 1 is open, so the state the controller sets and the state it sees on the wire differ. No manufacturer documents P2655 publicly.
Broken wire in the harness to the bank 2 solenoid
Terminal pushed out of the connector housing
Open coil in the bank 2 oil control solenoid
P2656: "A" Rocker Arm Actuator System Performance/Stuck Off (Bank 2)

For bank 2, P2656 reports that actuator A was told to switch the rocker arms but the expected change in valve lift did not show up, or it was too small. Since such engines give every bank a separate oil feed and solenoid, a clogged screen or sticking spool on that side alone is enough.
Low, wrong or sludged engine oil
Clogged oil screen or sticking spool at the bank 2 solenoid
Seized locking pin in a bank 2 rocker arm
MIL on after a completed test
Weaker response at higher engine speed
P2657: "A" Rocker Arm Actuator System Stuck On (Bank 2)

P2657 is the stuck-on case for bank 2: actuator A keeps the rocker arms of the second bank in their switched mode after the controller has asked for the base setting. On a cylinder deactivation design that could mean valves stay closed on that side; on a two-step design the high-lift profile stays active at idle.
Bank 2 solenoid passing oil while switched off
Locking pin stuck in the engaged position
Debris in the bank 2 oil passage
P2658: "A" Rocker Arm Actuator Control Circuit Low (Bank 2)

P2658 flags the bank 2 control line of rocker arm actuator A as too low, the classic sign of a short to ground or a coil with damaged windings. The test is purely electrical and runs whenever the controller drives the output, regardless of oil condition.
Bank 2 control wire shorted to ground
Damaged winding in the bank 2 solenoid
Harness insulation damaged by exhaust heat
P2659: "A" Rocker Arm Actuator Control Circuit High (Bank 2)

P2659 covers the bank 2 control circuit of actuator A reading high: the wire is shorted to a voltage source or the controller's driver stage no longer switches it to ground. No manufacturer documents P2659 publicly.
Bank 2 control wire shorted to a voltage source
Controller output stage no longer switching to ground
Neighbouring pins bridged in the connector
Bank 2 lift stays switched or switching is disabled
P265A: "B" Rocker Arm Actuator Position Sensor Circuit (Bank 1)
Lift systems that move the rocker geometry with an electric motor, such as Toyota Valvematic, need a sensor that tells the engine controller the actual adjustment angle.
Loose or corroded connector at the B position sensor
Open 5 V reference or sensor ground wire
Failed position sensor inside the lift controller
Lift held at a fixed value, sluggish response
P265B: "B" Rocker Arm Actuator Position Sensor Circuit Range/Performance (Bank 1)

Toyota documents this code on Valvematic engines, where an electric lift controller turns a shaft that alters rocker geometry and reports its angle back. P265B is set when that feedback stays electrically valid but does not track the target. Bulletin T-SB-0011-14 (2014 Corolla, 2ZR-FAE) pairs it with P2646 and fixes it by reflashing the ECM.
Continuously variable lift controller sticking or worn
Stored learn values no longer match the mechanism
Drifting angle sensor in the controller
MIL on, often together with P2646
Reduced power and slower throttle response
Fault may return after a short rev to 3,500 rpm
P265C: "B" Rocker Arm Actuator Position Sensor Circuit Low (Bank 1)

The angle or position sensor of rocker arm actuator B, bank 1, normally works inside a voltage band that never touches the lower rail. If the reading falls below that band, the engine controller logs P265C, because a value near zero cannot correspond to any real actuator position.
Sensor B signal wire grounded through damaged insulation
Internal fault in position sensor B
Engine runs with fixed lift, less power
P265D: "B" Rocker Arm Actuator Position Sensor Circuit High (Bank 1)

P265D stands for a feedback signal from position sensor B, bank 1, that sits above its valid ceiling. A reading pinned near the supply voltage usually means the signal is no longer pulled toward a real value: the sensor ground has opened, the signal wire touches a reference or battery line, or moisture has bridged pins in the plug.
Open ground wire of position sensor B
Signal wire shorted to the 5 V reference or battery voltage
Moisture bridging pins in the sensor plug
Lift frozen at default, weaker acceleration
P265E: "B" Rocker Arm Actuator Position Sensor Circuit Intermittent/Erratic (Bank 1)

Here the bank 1 position signal for actuator B is neither stuck low nor high; instead it jumps, flickers or briefly vanishes faster than the mechanism could physically move. The engine controller compares successive readings and flags P265E when the rate of change or the number of dropouts exceeds what a motor-driven lift mechanism can produce.
Fretting corrosion on sensor B terminals
Conductor broken inside its insulation, opening under vibration
Interference from ignition or other high-current wiring
MIL on and off over several trips
P265F: Variable A/C Compressor Control Circuit Range/Performance

Variable-displacement A/C compressors change their output through an electric control valve on the back of the compressor housing. On Ford's externally controlled design the PCM drives that valve with a pulse-width signal and aims for an evaporator temperature of roughly 3 to 8 °C; Volkswagen calls the part regulator valve N280, a coil of around 10 ohms.
Control valve sticking or internally worn
Refrigerant charge too low, so pressures do not follow the valve command
Corroded connector or high resistance in the valve circuit
Compressor runs at fixed or minimum output
P2660: P2660 concerns V-type or boxer engines with switchable rocker arms on both cylinder banks: the controller sees the drive circuit of solenoid B on bank 2, the side without cylinder 1, as broken. An open coil, a disconnected plug after valve cover work, or a cut wire leaves the output without load, so the command and the electrical feedback disagree.
Solenoid B plug on bank 2 left unplugged or not latched after repairs
Open coil in bank 2 solenoid B
Cut or broken wire on the bank 2 harness branch
Bank 2 B stage inactive, uneven running between banks possible
P2661: "B" Rocker Arm Actuator System Performance/Stuck Off (Bank 2)

P2661 is the functional check of rocker arm stage B on bank 2: although the solenoid circuit is electrically sound, the commanded switch did not happen or the confirmation (an oil pressure switch reading or a change in cam phaser or engine response) stayed too small.
Low oil level or poor oil supply to the bank 2 head
Partly blocked oil gallery or screen on bank 2
Sticking solenoid spool or seized locking pins on bank 2
MIL after a completed drive cycle
Less power in the range where stage B should engage
P2662: "B" Rocker Arm Actuator System Stuck On (Bank 2)

With P2662 the controller concludes that stage B on bank 2 stays switched after it has requested the default mode. Detection depends on the design: a pressure switch that keeps indicating oil pressure, or engine behaviour on that bank that still matches the engaged state.
Bank 2 solenoid B seeping oil when closed
Blocked drain path keeping oil pressure on the rockers
Locking pins jammed in the coupled position by debris or wear
Uneven idle or misfire on bank 2, worse when cold
P2663: "B" Rocker Arm Actuator Control Circuit Low (Bank 2)

P2663 is stored when the control line to solenoid B on bank 2 reads too low, most often a short to ground somewhere between the module and the second cylinder head. On V engines that harness branch often runs along the back of the block or under the intake manifold, where heat and vibration wear through insulation.
Bank 2 control wire worn through and touching ground
Bank 2 solenoid B coil with collapsed resistance
Faulty output driver for bank 2 solenoid B
Stage B on bank 2 out of action, power or economy reduced
P2664: "B" Rocker Arm Actuator Control Circuit High (Bank 2)

P2664 signals excessive voltage on the control line of solenoid B, bank 2. Contact with a powered conductor, for example where several solenoid and injector feeds share a connector, or a driver that can no longer pull the line down, are the typical causes.
Short to a powered feed inside a shared engine connector
Output driver in the control module stuck off
Internally shorted solenoid B on bank 2
Misfire or rough idle on bank 2 if the stage stays engaged
P2665: Fuel Shutoff Valve B Control Circuit/Open
Engines that can burn a second fuel such as compressed natural gas use electric shut-off valves to keep that fuel locked in when it is not wanted.
Loose or corroded connector at the valve (often exposed under the vehicle)
Broken wire in the control circuit
Engine runs only on gasoline, gas mode not available
Fuel mode lamp flashes or shows an error
P2666: Fuel Shutoff Valve B Control Circuit Low

P2666 is stored when the control line of fuel shut-off valve B sits at too low a voltage, the typical sign of a short to ground between module and valve or inside the coil. Depending on how the driver is built, the valve may then open whenever the ignition is on, or the module switches the output off for protection. No manufacturer documents P2666 publicly.
Control wire chafed through and shorted to ground
Water ingress in the valve connector
Gas mode switched off, engine runs on gasoline
P2667: Fuel Shutoff Valve B Control Circuit High

With P2667 the module measures excess voltage on the wire that drives shut-off valve B, usually because the wire touches a supply circuit. Safety matters here: on a low-side driven valve a short to voltage can keep the coil energised even when the module wants the valve closed, so the gaseous fuel may not be shut off reliably.
Control wire shorted to a voltage supply
Corrosion bridging pins in the valve connector
Faulty output stage in the control module
Gas mode disabled, operation on gasoline only
Fuel mode lamp indicates an error
Possible gas smell if the valve does not close
P2668: Fuel Mode Indicator Lamp Control Circuit
Bi-fuel vehicles tell the driver which fuel is in use through a small indicator, often built into the fuel selector button.
Indicator LED or bulb in the selector switch failed
Open wire or loose connector at the switch
Lamp driver in the control module defective
Fuel mode lamp stays dark in gas mode
No flashing during fuel changeover or on errors
P2669: Many transmission controllers feed their solenoids through internal high-side switches, called actuator supply A and B. Ford's 6R140 splits its Transmission Solenoid Power Control into two wires: TSPC-A powers shift solenoids A, C and E (fault P0657), TSPC-B powers SSB, SSD, TCC and line pressure control (P2669).
Open supply wire or connector between module and transmission bulkhead
Damaged internal transmission harness or lead frame
High-side switch inside the controller failed
Transmission stuck in a fixed gear (failsafe)
Harsh engagements due to maximum line pressure
P266A: "A" Rocker Arm Actuator Position Sensor Circuit (Bank 2)

P266A is the basic circuit fault for the bank 2 position sensor of rocker arm actuator A. It only applies to engines that have a lift actuator with position feedback on each cylinder bank, which is rare; most switching rocker systems on V engines rely on oil pressure switches or none at all.
Poor contact at the bank 2 sensor connector
Damaged wiring between sensor and engine controller
Lift on bank 2 no longer adjusted
P266B: "A" Rocker Arm Actuator Position Sensor Circuit Range/Performance (Bank 2)

For bank 2, P266B means the position reported for actuator A is electrically valid but does not match what was commanded or changes too slowly. CARB expects variable lift monitors to notice when the commanded position is missed or reached too late, and a sensor whose reading drifts from the real actuator position defeats both.
Sensor reading drifting from the true position
Control software calling for an update
MIL on after a drive cycle
P266C: "A" Rocker Arm Actuator Position Sensor Circuit Low (Bank 2)

P266C reports a bank 2 position sensor signal for actuator A that has fallen under its lower plausibility limit. Grounded signal wires, a missing sensor supply or an internal sensor short pull it down; a connector left half unplugged after other work on the harder-to-reach side of the engine is another possible trigger.
Bank 2 sensor signal shorted to ground
Connector not fully seated after other repairs
P266D: "A" Rocker Arm Actuator Position Sensor Circuit High (Bank 2)

P266D is logged when the bank 2 position feedback of rocker arm actuator A climbs above its upper limit. Typical reasons are an interrupted sensor ground, a signal wire chafed through onto a supply line, or corrosion that raises resistance. Since the value no longer represents a reachable actuator position, the engine controller discards it.
Interrupted ground of the bank 2 sensor
Signal wire chafed onto a supply line
P266E: "A" Rocker Arm Actuator Position Sensor Circuit Intermittent/Erratic (Bank 2)
