P266E describes a bank 2 position signal from actuator A that flickers: brief dropouts or spikes appear while the reading is otherwise fine. Heat cycling near the exhaust side, vibration on a loose pin or a harness rubbing on a bracket can produce it, and it often comes and goes. No manufacturer documents P266E publicly.
Connector contact degraded by heat cycling near the exhaust
Loose pin vibrating in the bank 2 sensor plug
Fault often not present at the workshop
P266F: A/C Refrigerant Distribution Valve A Control Circuit Driver Current/Temperature Too High

Refrigerant distribution valve A is a solenoid that opens or closes one branch of the A/C circuit, for instance a rear evaporator or a battery chiller. Its driver stage in the control module protects itself: when the output current rises above its limit or the chip overheats, it switches off and reports P266F.
Valve coil with shorted turns drawing excessive current
Short in the valve harness or connector
Valve mechanically stuck so the coil stays loaded
Overheated or defective driver stage in the control module
One A/C zone or the battery cooling stays inactive
Fault may return after cooling down
P2670: Actuator Supply Voltage B Circuit Low

P2670 is set when the second high-side actuator supply delivers too little voltage while it is switched on, which nearly always means a short to ground somewhere on the supply line or in a load connected to it. GM documents it in several controllers.
Supply wire chafed and shorted to ground
Shorted solenoid on the supplied group pulling the line down
Faulty high-side driver in the controller
Further solenoid circuit codes stored alongside
P2671: Actuator Supply Voltage B Circuit High

P2671 points to voltage on the second actuator supply when the controller has switched it off, so the line is fed from outside or the switch inside the module no longer opens. The solenoids on that supply can then no longer be de-energised as a group, which defeats the failsafe.
Supply line shorted to another powered circuit
High-side switch in the controller stuck closed
Moisture or corrosion bridging pins in the transmission connector
Warning lamp after the next start
Failsafe may not engage correctly if another fault occurs
P2672: On diesels with an electronically controlled rotary or distributor pump, the controller needs to know how far the pump's actual delivery start sits from its nominal position relative to the crankshaft. P2672 flags that this stored or measured offset is wrong or outside the window the software accepts.
Injection pump fitted or re-timed incorrectly after repair
Faulty pump timing or crank/cam reference signal
Worn pump drive (gear, belt, coupling) shifting the timing
Engine control software fault or wrong calibration
Diesel knock, smoke or reduced power
P2673: Injection Pump Timing Calibration Not Learned

This code says the engine controller holds no valid learned value for the start of delivery of its injection pump. Such a value is usually taught after the pump or the controller is replaced, or after a software reflash, and lets the controller correct the pump's individual timing tolerance.
Timing relearn skipped after pump or controller replacement
Software update interrupted or learned values lost
Relearn aborted because enable conditions (temperature, voltage) were not met
Slightly rough running or more noise
P2674: Injection Pump Fuel Calibration Not Learned

Electronically governed diesel injection pumps meter the quantity per stroke themselves, and each unit differs slightly in how much it delivers for a given command. P2674 reports that the quantity correction for the installed pump has not been learned or stored in the controller.
Quantity learn not run after pump or controller replacement
Pump calibration data missing, wrong or not matching the installed pump
Fuel metering actuator fault preventing the learn from completing
P2675: Some engines can change where the air cleaner draws its air, for example switching between a cold inlet at the front and a second opening in the engine bay, with a flap or valve moved by a solenoid or small motor.
Connector at the inlet flap actuator loose or unplugged, often after air filter service
Broken wire in the actuator circuit
Open coil or motor winding in the flap actuator
Warning light or stored code, often without MIL
Usually no noticeable change in driving
P2676: Air Cleaner Inlet Control Circuit Low

P2676 means the control line of the air cleaner inlet flap sits at too low a voltage for the state the controller has commanded. On a low-side driven solenoid this typically appears when the line is shorted to ground and the actuator is energised permanently; on other designs a shorted coil pulls the voltage down.
Control wire chafed through and shorted to ground
Shorted coil in the inlet flap actuator
Code stored, often without warning lamp
Inlet flap stuck in one position
P2677: Air Cleaner Inlet Control Circuit High

The counterpart to P2676: the controller sees the drive line of the air cleaner inlet flap at too high a voltage, so it cannot pull the actuator in when asked. A short from the control wire to battery voltage, a failed output stage, or an open coil that leaves the line at supply level produce this pattern.
Control wire shorted to battery voltage
Open coil in the flap actuator
Failed output stage in the control module
Code stored, often without warning lamp
Inlet flap remains in its default position
P2678: In a sealed cooling system, air and vapour bubbles are carried through a thin vent line into the expansion tank, where they separate from the liquid; a bubble-free circuit avoids local hot spots, as cooling suppliers such as MAHLE point out.
Unplugged connector or broken wire to the degassing valve
Open solenoid coil in the degassing valve
Faulty driver in the control module
Check engine light or stored code
Longer warm-up or slow heater output
Gurgling or air in the cooling system
P2679: Coolant Degassing Valve Control Circuit Low

P2679 indicates that the control line of the switched valve in the coolant vent path to the expansion tank reads too low. Usually the wire is grounded somewhere, or the solenoid has shorted turns; with a low-side driver the valve may then stay energised regardless of the command. The engine controller compares the line voltage with the state it set.
Shorted turns in the degassing valve solenoid
Coolant or water leaking into the valve connector
Check engine light or stored code
Coolant level fluctuations in the expansion tank
P267A: "B" Rocker Arm Actuator Position Sensor Circuit (Bank 2)

Continuously variable lift systems turn a control or eccentric shaft with an electric motor and report the shaft angle back to the engine controller. On V engines each cylinder bank has its own mechanism; Nissan's VVEL on the VQ37VHR V6 and VK50VE V8 is an example of such a two-bank layout.
Loose, corroded or damaged plug at the bank 2 position sensor
Broken or chafed signal, reference or ground wire
Internal fault of position sensor B, bank 2
Fault in the engine or lift control module input
Variable lift on bank 2 held at a fixed default
P267B: "B" Rocker Arm Actuator Position Sensor Circuit Range/Performance (Bank 2)

P267B concerns the bank 2 feedback of lift actuator B when the signal is electrically sound but the angle it reports does not follow the commanded value, moves too slowly, or contradicts the mechanism's known travel. Faulty learning of the end stops, a slipping sensor mount, wear in the shaft drive or a sticking actuator can all produce this picture.
End-stop learn values lost or wrong after repair or battery disconnect
Worn or sticking shaft drive of actuator B on bank 2
Position sensor drifting or loose in its mount
Lift control software needing an update
Uneven idle when lift is frozen on one bank
P267C: "B" Rocker Arm Actuator Position Sensor Circuit Low (Bank 2)
With P267C the engine controller reads the bank 2 position signal of lift actuator B below its lowest valid value.
Signal wire shorted to ground through damaged insulation
5 V reference supply to the sensor missing
Internal short in position sensor B, bank 2
Lift on bank 2 fixed at a default position
P267D: "B" Rocker Arm Actuator Position Sensor Circuit High (Bank 2)

P267D is stored when the angle feedback of lift actuator B on bank 2 rises above its upper valid limit. Typical causes are an open sensor ground, which lets the signal float toward the reference, a signal conductor touching a supply line, or water bridging contacts in the connector.
Open or high-resistance ground of the position sensor
Signal wire shorted to reference or battery voltage
Moisture or corrosion bridging pins in the sensor plug
Reduced power with lift fixed on bank 2
P267E: "B" Rocker Arm Actuator Position Sensor Circuit Intermittent/Erratic (Bank 2)

Here the bank 2 angle signal of lift actuator B is mostly plausible, yet it drops out for moments or jumps by amounts the motor-driven shaft could not cover in the time between two readings. The engine controller counts such events and sets P267E once they exceed its tolerance.
Loose or fretted terminal in the sensor connector
Wire broken inside insulation, opening under heat or vibration
Interference from nearby ignition or actuator wiring
Check engine light that may come and go
Uneven running when lift control on bank 2 hunts
P267F: Control Module Internal Temperature Sensor A Circuit Intermittent/Erratic

Many control modules carry a temperature sensor on their own circuit board to protect output stages and, in transmission units, to back up fluid temperature. P267F adds an intermittent or erratic variant to the established family P0666 to P0669: the reading flickers, jumps or drops out briefly instead of being permanently too low, too high or implausible.
Internal defect of the control module or its temperature sensor
Unstable module supply or ground causing erratic readings
Module software misinterpreting the sensor signal
Check engine or transmission warning light
Harsh or delayed shifts if the module uses substitute values
P2680: Coolant Degassing Valve Control Circuit High

P2680 is the high-voltage fault of the degassing valve drive: the controller cannot pull the line down, so the valve stays in its unpowered state whatever is commanded. A wire touching a battery feed, an internally open solenoid, or a defective output transistor are the classic reasons.
Control wire shorted to a battery feed
Internally open solenoid of the degassing valve
Defective output stage in the control module
Check engine light or stored code
Air pockets, gurgling or weak cabin heat
P2681: Engine Coolant Bypass Valve A Control Circuit/Open

Bypass valve A is an electrically driven coolant valve whose role differs by maker. P2681 flags an open or otherwise faulty drive circuit. GM's 2011 Volt table checks it in the HPC2/VICM: 40 failures in 50 samples at 100 ms, Type B.
Failed bypass valve (motor, gear or electronics)
Chafed harness or open fuse in the valve supply
Engine control software causing false detection
Slow warm-up of engine or transmission
P2682: Engine Coolant Bypass Valve A Control Circuit Low

P2682 narrows the drive fault of bypass valve A to the low side: the output is pulled toward ground when it should not be. In GM's 2016 table for the second-generation Volt, the VICM sets it when motor driver 1 reports a short to low while the valve is commanded to the low position, with 4 failures in 5 samples and Type B.
Drive wire to the valve motor shorted to ground
Internal short in the valve motor or electronics
Coolant or water corrosion in the valve plug
Weak cabin heat or slow warm-up
P2683: Engine Coolant Bypass Valve A Control Circuit High

For P2683 the drive of bypass valve A is shorted toward supply voltage or draws too much current. GM's 2016 Volt table has the VICM evaluate a short-to-high report from motor driver 1 while the valve is stopped or commanded to the high position; 16 failures out of 20 samples at 100 ms give a Type B fault.
Jammed valve or shorted valve motor drawing excess current
Drive wire shorted to battery voltage
Faulty motor driver in the control module
Changed heater output or warm-up time
P2684: Some transmission controllers power groups of solenoids through several internal high-side outputs; supply C is the third of these rails, after A (P0657) and B (P2669). P2684 reports an open load on it.
Broken wire or loose terminal between the module output and the supplied solenoids
Corroded or unseated transmission connector or internal lead frame
High-side output inside the controller defective
Transmission in default gear or limp mode
Several solenoid circuit codes stored together
P2685: Actuator Supply Voltage C Circuit Low
P2685 means the third actuator supply rail sags while it is switched on, almost always because the line or one of the loads it feeds has a path to ground.
Supply wire chafed through and touching ground
Shorted solenoid coil on this rail drawing excess current
Weak battery or charging fault pulling the whole supply down
MIL on during the same trip
Blown fuse possible on the transmission supply
P2686: Actuator Supply Voltage C Circuit High

The high case of supply C concerns voltage that should not be there: the rail stays live although the controller has turned it off. Causes are an internal high-side switch that no longer opens or an outside wire touching battery positive. GM's 2023 and 2024 TCM tables run this check during shutdown.
Internal high-side switch of the controller stuck conducting
Supply wire shorted to a battery-fed circuit in the harness
Moisture in the transmission connector creating a leakage path
MIL after a second trip with the fault
Limp mode or fixed gear after restart
Code returns after clearing once the key has been off

In GM's diesel ECM tables the engine computer switches the heater relay with a low-side driver and judges the off-state voltage; more than 200 kOhm between pin and ground means open.
Heater relay coil open or relay not seated
Broken control wire or corroded terminal at the filter housing
Heater element open where it is switched directly without a relay
Hard starting or stalling in severe cold
Power loss from a waxed fuel filter
Often no warning lamp, depending on model year
P2688: Fuel Supply Heater Control Circuit Low

With P2688 the heater control line reads too low while the driver is off, which points to a grounded wire: the relay would then be energized all the time, and the filter heater runs even in summer and drains the battery after shutdown.
Control wire chafed against the engine or frame and grounded
Water or fuel in the filter-housing connector
Service message or MIL, depending on model year
Battery drained after the vehicle stands
P2689: Fuel Supply Heater Control Circuit High

P2689 is logged when the fuel heater control line stays high even though the controller has commanded it on, so the relay coil is fed from battery positive and cannot be pulled in; the heater never works.
Control wire shorted to a battery-fed wire
Heater relay sticking so feedback no longer matches the command
Low-side driver in the engine controller defective
No fuel heating, gelling risk below freezing
Hard cold starts and rough idle until warm
Warning lamp only on some model years
P268A: P268A covers injector correction that relies on a learn routine rather than a printed code. GM's diesel tables 17OBDG04 to 19OBDG04A set it, Type A in one trip, when the small quantity learning (SQL) routine was not completed and stored before the vehicle left the assembly line.
Injector quantity learn not completed after injector or controller replacement
Engine control software fault (e.g. Audi 2.0 TFSI 2025–2026)
Rail pressure deviation preventing correct learning
Injector worn beyond the correction range
Rough idle or louder combustion noise
Often no noticeable change in driving
P268B: High Pressure Fuel Pump Calibration Not Learned/Programmed

Common rail and direct-injection petrol systems use a high pressure pump whose delivery is trimmed by a metering or volume control valve. Where the pump comes with individual correction data, or the controller has to learn its behaviour, P268B reports that this data is missing or was never taught.
Pump correction data not entered after pump replacement
Controller replaced or reflashed without transferring pump data
Pump variant does not match the software
Reduced power with rail pressure deviations
P268C: Every modern diesel injector carries a correction code from the factory flow test, and the controller must hold the code of the injector in cylinder 1. P268C sets when that code is missing, outside its range or fails the checksum.
Correction code of a new cylinder 1 injector not entered
Code entered with a typing error, so the checksum fails
Controller replaced without transferring injector codes
Uneven running or knock from cylinder 1
P268D: P268D concerns the stored flow correction for the injector in cylinder 2. In GM's 2016 four-cylinder diesel table (16OBDG04) the test runs with ignition on and passes once the end-of-line injector adjustment (EIA) value has been written via DID $61; a missing value only counts as a failure when the manufacturer enable counter is zero, i.e.
Adjustment value of the cylinder 2 injector not programmed after replacement
Injectors moved between cylinders without updating codes
Programming session aborted (voltage drop, communication loss)
Slight misfire feel or noise from cylinder 2
P268E: For cylinder 3 the controller compares the injector's correction value with what its software accepts. Ford's 2023 diesel OBD summary explains the idea well: each injector's code, kept in EEPROM, describes how far that unit departs from an idealised mean part, and a DTC is logged if the value is absent, out of range or its checksum is wrong.
Cylinder 3 injector replaced, code not programmed
Code from an injector variant the software does not accept
Stored injector data corrupted in the controller
P268F: P268F flags missing or unusable correction data for the injector in cylinder 4. On four-cylinder diesels it closes the series: GM's 2014 table 14OBDG04 and 2016 table 16OBDG04 list P268C to P268F and nothing beyond.
New cylinder 4 injector fitted without code programming
Code typed incorrectly into the scan tool
Used or replacement controller carrying another engine's codes
Possible rough idle or higher combustion noise
P2690: P2690 is the first code of the series that a four-cylinder engine cannot set; it needs at least five cylinders. It reports that the flow correction for the cylinder 5 injector is absent or rejected by the controller. GM uses it in its 2025 six-cylinder diesel table 25OBDG04B as well as in its V8 diesel tables, Type A, with the value stored under DID $64.
Cylinder 5 injector replaced without entering its code
Code entered for the wrong cylinder because of the bank numbering
P2691: P2691 refers to the injector in cylinder 6. For six-cylinder diesels it is the last of the per-cylinder codes: GM's 2025 table 25OBDG04B stops at P2691, while the V8 table 25OBDG04A goes on to P2693.
Cylinder 6 injector code missing after replacement
Entered value rejected as implausible by the software
Controller memory fault losing stored injector data
Possible knock or smoke from the affected cylinder
P2692: Only engines with seven or more cylinders can log P2692, which in practice means V8 diesels. It tells that the correction code for the cylinder 7 injector has not been stored or is unusable.
Injector in cylinder 7 replaced, code not programmed
Replacement controller without the vehicle's injector codes
Software variant for the wrong engine configuration
P2693: P2693 completes the series on V8 engines and covers the injector in cylinder 8. It is set when the controller finds no valid flow correction code for that position.
Code of the new cylinder 8 injector not entered
New or reset controller lacking all injector codes
Typing error in the cylinder 8 code
P2694: P2694 would flag bad or missing correction data for the injector in cylinder 9 and therefore only fits engines with nine or more cylinders, in road vehicles essentially V10s. No manufacturer documents this code publicly.
Cylinder 9 injector code not programmed (ten-cylinder engines)
Scan tool decoding error on engines without a ninth cylinder
Controller software for a different engine
P2695: P2695 is reserved for the injector in cylinder 10, the highest cylinder number the J2012 series provides with its own data code.
Cylinder 10 injector code missing on a ten-cylinder engine
Misread code on engines with fewer cylinders
P2696: P2696 is the collective version of P268C–P2695: the controller rejects stored injector correction data without naming a cylinder. That suits systems that check the data block as a whole, or engines with more than ten cylinders. No manufacturer documents P2696 publicly; GM and Ford use the per-cylinder codes instead.
Injector codes lost during a software update or controller replacement
Injector replaced without programming its code
Corrupted injector data block in the controller
Louder engine noise or rough running
P2697: Exhaust Aftertreatment Fuel Injector A Circuit/Open

Many heavy diesels do not raise exhaust temperature for filter regeneration by late in-cylinder injection, but spray diesel straight into the exhaust ahead of the oxidation catalyst through a separate doser, often called the seventh injector. P2697 means the solenoid that meters this fuel cannot be driven because its circuit is open.
Loose, corroded or damaged connector at the dosing module
Harness to the dosing valve broken by heat or vibration
Dosing valve coil inside the module burnt open
Active particulate filter regeneration not possible
P2698: Exhaust Aftertreatment Fuel Injector A Performance

P2698 is not about wiring but about whether the exhaust fuel doser does what it is told; most often the check looks for leakage when no dosing is requested. Ford's 3.2 L Transit (2017 and 2018 summaries) compares a measured temperature downstream of the injection point with a model after at least 6 h engine-off.
Doser valve or nozzle leaking fuel into the exhaust
Coked nozzle or line causing low flow
Exhaust temperature sensor drifting and skewing the model comparison
Engine software needing the manufacturer update
MIL on, often without noticeable drivability change
Regenerations fail or take unusually long
Higher fuel use or white exhaust smoke
P2699: Exhaust Aftertreatment Fuel Injector A Circuit Low

P2699 flags the drive circuit of the exhaust fuel doser as too low, usually a grounded control wire or a shorted valve coil. The difference to P2697 matters in practice: an open circuit simply stops dosing, while a grounded line can switch the valve on without command if the short sits behind the driver, so raw fuel may reach a cold catalyst.
Doser control wire grounded against the frame or exhaust bracket
Shorted coil of the dosing valve
Fuel or water inside the module connector
Possible white smoke if the valve opens uncommanded
P269A: Exhaust Aftertreatment Fuel Injector A Circuit High

The high variant of the exhaust doser circuit means the control line shows supply voltage where the driver expects it to be pulled down, typically a short to battery positive or a driver that no longer conducts. In that state the valve cannot be opened, and a hard short can also overload the output, which the controller then switches off for protection.
Doser control wire shorted to a positive supply
Output stage in the controller not switching
Pin damage in the dosing module connector
Filter soot level climbs over time
P269B: Exhaust Aftertreatment Glow Plug Control Circuit/Open

Some diesels inject fuel into the exhaust through a small vaporizer whose glow plug turns the fuel into vapor before it reaches the oxidation catalyst. Ford calls this downstream injection (DSI) on the 3.2 L Transit, used so that filter regeneration needs fewer in-cylinder post injections and less oil is diluted.
Open wire or connector between engine computer and glow plug relay
Vaporizer glow plug relay coil open
Blown fuse in the glow plug control feed
Particulate filter regenerations fail or become rare
More frequent in-cylinder regeneration, oil level may rise
P269C: Exhaust Aftertreatment Glow Plug Control Performance

P269C is the plausibility counterpart to the electrical control codes: the wires test fine, yet the control stage of the exhaust glow plug does not behave as commanded, for example a relay or driver that does not report the expected state or reacts too slowly. No manufacturer documents this code publicly.
Glow plug relay switching late or not at all
Faulty feedback signal from the relay or driver
Low system voltage during the control check
P269D: Exhaust Aftertreatment Glow Plug Control Circuit Low
A low reading on the exhaust glow plug control line points to a path to ground before the load, so the control stage cannot set the right level and the vaporizer glow plug may be switched wrongly.
Control wire chafed on the exhaust or body and grounded
Shorted coil in the glow plug relay
Possible blown fuse in the glow plug feed
P269E: Exhaust Aftertreatment Glow Plug Control Circuit High

When the exhaust glow plug control circuit reads close to battery voltage at the wrong moment, the control side has contact with a positive feed or the switching stage hangs open, so the vaporizer glow plug may stay energized or ignore commands.
Control wire shorted to a battery-fed circuit
Relay contacts welded, glow plug permanently powered
Output stage in the engine computer defective
Glow plug failing early from constant heating
P269F: While P269B concerns the line that commands the exhaust glow plug, P269F targets the load circuit itself: the heating element or its power feed is open, so no current flows even when the control stage switches correctly. A burnt-out element is the usual reason, followed by a loose terminal at the plug in the hot exhaust area.
Loose or corroded terminal nut at the plug
Blown fuse in the glow plug power circuit
P26A0: P26A0 says the exhaust glow plug system does not perform as intended, even if no electrical fault is present.
Blown fuse or relay feedback not matching the command
Exhaust temperature control code P24A0 stored too
P26A1: Exhaust Aftertreatment Glow Plug Circuit Low
P26A1 describes a load circuit of the exhaust glow plug that reads too low: the feed or the element has found a path to ground, so the current bypasses the heater or exceeds what the circuit allows.
Glow element shorted to its housing
Feed wire melted or chafed against the exhaust
Fuse blown as a result of the short
Fuse for the glow plug circuit blows again after replacement
P26A2: Exhaust Aftertreatment Glow Plug Circuit High

The high case of the exhaust glow plug load circuit is set when the monitored point sits too close to supply voltage. Depending on how the module measures, this means the heater circuit is shorted to another positive feed or the element draws almost no current, so the voltage barely drops across it. The plug then stays cold or cannot be switched off.
Glow plug feed shorted to another battery-fed circuit
Element with greatly increased resistance near the end of its life
Glow plug relay contacts stuck closed
P26A3: Engine Coolant Bypass Valve A Range/Performance

P26A3 is a functional fault: the electrics of bypass valve A look fine, but the valve does not reach or report the position it should. GM's 2011 Volt table sets it, Type B, when the end-position learn fails with coolant above 50 °C, or when the valve has not arrived at its commanded position within 15 s.
Broken gear or jammed rotor inside the bypass valve
Contaminated coolant, e.g. stop-leak additives, blocking the valve
Engine or climate control software commanding the valve incorrectly
End-position learn not completed after replacement
P26A4: Engine Coolant Bypass Valve A Position Sensor Circuit

Many electric coolant valves carry a potentiometer or Hall element that reports the actual valve angle back to the controller. P26A4 is the general circuit code for that feedback on valve A: the signal is missing or cannot be assigned to a more specific low, high or erratic fault. No manufacturer documents P26A4 itself in public.
Moisture or corrosion inside the valve's position sensor section
Loose, corroded or damaged connector or feedback wiring
Missing 5 V reference or ground for the position sensor
Slow warm-up or weak cabin heat
Possible additional valve or coolant temperature codes
P26A5: Engine Coolant Bypass Valve A Position Sensor Circuit Range/Performance

Here the feedback signal is electrically present but sits where a healthy valve should never be. In GM's 2016 Volt table the VICM treats readings between 5 and 30 % or between 70 and 95 % of the reference as invalid; 80 failures in 100 samples at 100 ms give a Type B fault, provided the drive codes P2682/P2683/P26AD/P26AE and P26A6/P26A7 are clear.
Worn or corroded position sensor track inside the valve
Damaged gear or coupling between valve motor and sensor
High contact resistance at the valve connector
Check engine light after two drives
Engine runs too cool or warms up slowly
P26A6: Engine Coolant Bypass Valve A Position Sensor Circuit Low

P26A6 means the valve A feedback voltage has dropped below its plausible floor, typically from a short to ground, a lost reference voltage or a failed sensor. GM sets it on the Volt (2011 HPC2/VICM and 2016 VICM) once the signal falls under 5 % of reference, about 0.25 V, in 40 of 50 samples at 100 ms; it is Type B, so the lamp comes on after two trips.
Feedback wire chafed through and shorted to ground
Open 5 V reference supply to the sensor
Internal sensor failure, e.g. after coolant intrusion
Delayed warm-up or reduced heater output
Valve position shown at or near zero on the scan tool
P26A7: Engine Coolant Bypass Valve A Position Sensor Circuit High

The counterpart to P26A6: the feedback from valve A reads too high. GM's 2016 Volt table counts both a signal above its window and a broken signal circuit here, because an interrupted wire lets the input float toward the reference. The limit is 95 % of the reference (4.75 V), checked as 40 failures in 50 samples at 100 ms, Type B.
Open feedback or sensor ground wire
Feedback wire shorted to 5 V reference or battery voltage
Defective sensor in the valve housing
Scan tool shows valve position at maximum
Engine slow to reach operating temperature
P26A8: Engine Coolant Bypass Valve A Position Sensor Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P26A8 targets a feedback signal that jumps or drops out briefly instead of staying wrong. No manufacturer publishes a definition for this exact code.
Loose or spread terminal in the valve connector
Worn or contaminated sensor track giving dropouts
Harness rubbing on engine parts and shorting intermittently
Check engine light that may come and go
Erratic heater output or engine temperature
Code returns after clearing, often on rough roads
P26A9: Engine Coolant Bypass Valve A Position Sensor Stop/Minimum Stop Performance

The title refers to the learned end stop of valve A. GM's use of P26A9 shifted over time. On the 2011 Volt it covered feedback sitting in a forbidden zone (5–30 % or 70–95 %), sudden jumps above 6 % and slow drift above 3 %, all Type B.
Valve rotor sticking from deposits or contaminated coolant
End position not relearned after valve or module replacement
Open motor drive circuit preventing the learn routine
Drifting position sensor misreporting the stop
Check engine light after two drives
Engine overheats or stays too cool depending on stuck position
P26AA: Engine Coolant Bypass Valve A Position Sensor Maximum Stop Performance

P26AA is the upper-limit partner of P26A9: the controller cannot confirm or learn the maximum end stop of valve A, or the reported value at full travel lies outside the expected window. No manufacturer publishes criteria for this code.
Valve binding before reaching its maximum position
Worn or broken mechanical end stop or gear
Position sensor out of calibration near its upper end
Heater or engine temperature not as expected
P26AB: Engine Coolant Bypass Valve A Stuck/Open

P26AB is stored when valve A stays open although it was told to close. Ford's hybrid summaries (2014–2019) define the valve as the switch between a combined loop, with engine coolant through the heater core, and an isolated loop heated by a PTC heater; if the second coolant sensor reads more than 5 °F above the engine sensor within 60 s of a circuit fault, t…
Valve jammed open by deposits, wear or a broken drive part
Engine control software misjudging valve state (Ram flashes)
Drive circuit fault leaving the valve in its open default
Engine takes long to warm up, higher fuel use when cold
Heater works with engine off only poorly (hybrids)
P26AC: Engine Coolant Bypass Valve B Control Circuit/Open

Which valve carries the letter B depends on the maker. Ford names it in its gasoline OBD summaries for 2020–2023 and 2024–2025: valve B is the active transmission cooling valve, which sends engine coolant to the automatic transmission oil cooler, while valve A heats the transmission.
Broken wire or unplugged connector at valve B
Open solenoid or motor winding in the valve
Faulty output driver in the PCM
Transmission fluid temperature higher than normal when towing
Usually no change in normal driving
P26AD: Engine Coolant Bypass Valve B Control Circuit Low

P26AD indicates a drive line of valve B pulled to ground. GM uses the code differently from the title: on the second-generation Volt (2016 table, VICM) the single coolant bypass valve has an H-bridge motor with two drive lines, and P26AD stands for driver 2 reporting a short to low while the valve is commanded toward the high position.
Drive wire chafed and shorted to ground
Coolant or water in the connector creating a leak path
Check engine light after two drives (GM)
Valve no longer moves, heating or warm-up affected
P26AE: Engine Coolant Bypass Valve B Control Circuit High

With P26AE the valve B drive output sees voltage where it expects none, typically a short to battery. GM's 2016 Volt table again applies it to the second drive line of the one bypass valve: the VICM sets it when driver 2 flags a short to high while the valve is stopped or commanded low, after 16 failures in 20 samples at 100 ms, Type B.
Drive wire shorted to a battery-voltage wire
Internally shorted valve motor or solenoid drawing excess current
Damaged output stage in the control module
Valve stays in its last position
Transmission or cabin temperature control off target
P26AF: Engine Coolant Bypass Valve B Stuck/Open

P26AF is the functional fault for valve B remaining open against its command. No manufacturer documents this code publicly; Ford, for instance, monitors its valve B (transmission cooling) only electrically through P26AC/P26AE.
Valve held open by deposits or debris
Seized actuator or broken drive gear
Coolant temperature sensor bias misleading the check
Longer warm-up, higher fuel use on short trips
Lower cabin heat in cold weather
P26B0: Engine Coolant Bypass Valve B Range/Performance

P26B0 covers a valve B that is electrically sound but does not perform: it moves too slowly, stops short of its target or reports a position that does not match the command. No manufacturer publishes criteria for P26B0.
Valve moving slowly due to contaminated or wrong coolant
Worn gear train or weak valve motor
Low supply voltage or high resistance in the drive circuit
Engine or transmission temperature outside its normal band
P26B1: Engine Coolant Bypass Valve A Stuck Closed

P26B1 reports that valve A does not open when it should. The best documented user is the Volkswagen group plug-in hybrids. Porsche stores P26B100 in the thermal management unit (TME) of the 2019–2022 Cayenne E-Hybrid and the 2019–2021 Panamera E-Hybrid for the valve that admits engine coolant to the heating circuit once the engine passes 40 °C.
Thermal management software misjudging the valve (Porsche, Bentley)
Valve seized closed by deposits or a failed actuator
Swapped or kinked coolant lines after repair
Drifting coolant temperature sensor used for the check
Check engine light, sometimes only intermittent
Cabin heat relies on the electric heater longer than usual
Possible rise in engine temperature under load
P26B2: Engine Coolant Bypass Valve B Stuck Closed
P26B2 is the closed-stuck counterpart for valve B: the controller expects coolant to flow through the valve but sees no sign of it. No manufacturer documents P26B2 in public sources.
Valve seized in the closed position
Failed actuator motor or broken coupling
Blocked or kinked coolant line downstream of the valve
Rising temperature of the component served by the valve
Possible temperature warning under heavy load
P26B3: Fuel Shutoff Valve A Control Circuit Performance/Stuck Off

Fuel shut-off valves are electrically opened valves that isolate a gaseous or liquefied fuel, as on CNG or propane systems. P26B3 says valve A does not achieve its intended effect although it was commanded.
Leaking check valve or supply solenoid in the rail pressure module
Clogged bleed restrictor or kinked EVAP line
Shut-off valve A not switching as commanded
Blown fuse in the valve supply
Hard starting after the vehicle has been parked
Check engine light on some vehicles
P26B4: Fuel Shutoff Valve A Control Circuit Stuck On
P26B4 is the opposite failure to P26B3: shut-off valve A stays open or energised when the module wants it closed. No manufacturer documents P26B4 in public sources.
Control wire shorted to battery voltage
Supply relay or driver stuck on
Fuel pressure remains in the lines with the engine off
P26B5: Fuel Shutoff Valve B Control Circuit Performance/Stuck Off

With P26B5 shut-off valve B fails to open or pass fuel when commanded. Roush CleanTech documents the code for its Gen 4 propane system on 2016–2018 Ford trucks, where valve B is the supply solenoid in the module that regulates rail pressure (its circuit code there is P2665).
Supply or tank solenoid not opening
Manual valve partly closed or excess flow valve tripped
Weak fuel pumps, clogged filter or kinked lines
Blown fuse in the valve circuit
Engine cranks but does not start, or runs poorly
Long start sequence with pumps cycling repeatedly
Check engine light on some models
P26B6: Fuel Shutoff Valve B Control Circuit Stuck On
P26B6 reports that shut-off valve B cannot be switched off: the control circuit or the valve remains in the on state after the module removes the command. No manufacturer documents P26B6 publicly.
Control line shorted to battery voltage
Welded relay contact keeping the valve powered
Fuel odour near the engine or regulator after shut-off
P26B7: Engine Coolant Bypass Valve C Control Circuit/Open
P26B7 is the basic electrical test of the drive output for coolant bypass valve C, with an open load as its main case. The letter is not tied to one design.
Failed actuator motor or coil inside bypass valve C
Unplugged, corroded or broken connector or drive wire
Engine harness chafed through near the valve
Engine warms up slowly or runs warmer than usual
Valve C stays in its default position
P26B8: Engine Coolant Bypass Valve C Control Circuit Low

With P26B8 a drive line of valve C is pulled toward ground. The best public description comes from GM's 2025 ECM table 25OBDG04B for the six-cylinder diesel: valve C sits on an H-bridge, and the controller looks for a grounded line separately in the opening and the closing direction, each time only while the other direction is free of the same fault.
Drive wire chafed against the engine or body and shorted to ground

P26B9: Engine Coolant Bypass Valve C Control Circuit High

P26B9 reports supply voltage where the valve C driver should see none, in practice a short to battery positive. Two makers document it. Ford's 2024–2025 gasoline summary pairs it with the open-circuit code as P26B9/P26B7_12: the smart driver for the radiator bypass valve flags the fault and the PCM stores it after 5 s of continuous monitoring.
Drive wire shorted to a battery-voltage circuit
Engine harness damaged by chafing or heat
Internal fault in the valve C actuator

P26BA: Engine Coolant Bypass Valve C Stuck/Open
P26BA is meant for a valve C that stays open although the controller wants it shut, while its circuit tests fine. No manufacturer documents this code in public sources.
Valve C jammed in the open position by wear or deposits

P26BB: Engine Coolant Bypass Valve C Range/Performance

P26BB is GM's main functional code for its rotary coolant flow control valve. The ECM compares commanded and measured angle; a gap above 12° after the target has settled, or movement slower than calibrated, counts as a fault. In the 2019 L3B table this is Type A (4 of 5 s), in the 2025 diesel table Type B (8 of 10 s).
New valve still in its break-in phase (GM, low mileage)
ECM calibration needing an update per GM bulletin
Valve or actuator sticking or worn
Coolant temperature higher or lower than normal
Code may disappear after further driving on a new valve
P26BC: Engine Coolant Bypass Valve C Stuck Closed

P26BC covers a valve C that will not open on command even though its drive circuit is intact. Public criteria for this code are not available from any manufacturer. Valve C seized in the closed position
Actuator too weak to overcome friction or deposits
Low coolant level or trapped air distorting the temperature check
Rising engine temperature, possible overheat warning
Reduced engine power to protect the engine
P26BD: Engine Coolant Bypass Valve D Control Circuit/Open
P26BD is the open-load or general circuit fault on the output that drives coolant bypass valve D. Ford is the documented user.
Open coil or motor winding in valve D
Broken drive wire between PCM and valve
Heater output that cannot be regulated
P26BE: Engine Coolant Bypass Valve D Control Circuit Low

P26BE flags a drive circuit of valve D that reads too low, normally because the wiring or the valve itself is grounded. No manufacturer documents P26BE publicly. Ford, whose valve D is the cabin heating valve, reports only the general circuit code P26BD and, from 2024, the short-to-battery code P26BF.
Moisture or corrosion in the connector
Cabin heat stuck at full or at minimum
Valve D does not react to commands
P26BF: Engine Coolant Bypass Valve D Control Circuit High

P26BF stands for battery voltage on the valve D control line where the driver expects a switched or grounded level. Ford documents it in its 2024–2025 gasoline OBD summary: the cabin heating bypass valve is valve D, and a short to battery reported by the PCM's smart driver is stored as P26BF, internally also as P26BD_12, after continuous monitoring for 5 s.

Heater stays hot or stays cold regardless of setting
P26C0: Engine Coolant Bypass Valve D Stuck/Open

GM uses P26C0 for the block rotary valve, which controls coolant flow through the engine block between two mechanical end stops; its tables label it as the engine block coolant valve stuck open. The ECM counts a failure when requested and measured position differ by at least 10° while the raw feedback sits at 50° or more, i.e. on the open side.

Position feedback reporting a wrong angle

Higher fuel consumption on short trips
P26C1: Engine Coolant Bypass Valve D Range/Performance
P26C1 means valve D works electrically but does not deliver the expected effect. Ford is the documented user, and on its plug-in hybrids valve D governs the cabin heating loop.

Service warning without check engine lamp

Exhaust flow control valve A is the electrically driven flap that switches the sound path or back pressure of the exhaust, mostly on sporty models with selectable exhaust modes. P26C5 means the output stage driving valve A finds the circuit open or otherwise unusable.

P26C6 reports that the drive circuit of exhaust valve A sits at too low a voltage – typically because the wiring or the actuator has shorted to ground.

P26C7: Exhaust Flow Control Valve A Control Circuit High
P26C7 is the high-side counterpart: the control line of exhaust valve A carries more voltage than the driver expects, usually because the line touches battery positive or the actuator is damaged.

P26C8: Chassis Control Module 1 Requested MIL Illumination

P26C9: Chassis Control Module 2 Requested MIL Illumination

Codes stored in a chassis module in addition to the engine module

P26CC: Engine Coolant Pump Control Circuit Low
P26CC reports that the circuit controlling the engine coolant pump stays at too low a voltage while the pump should be active.

P26CD: Engine Coolant Pump Control Circuit High

P26CD is set when the control circuit of the engine coolant pump shows a higher voltage than the commanded state allows, for example while the driver is switched off. No manufacturer documents this code in public.

P26CE covers a pump that spins too fast for the current it draws – a sign that it is running dry or pumping air instead of coolant. P26CF: Engine Coolant Pump Control Module System Voltage

Smart coolant pumps carry their own electronics, which measure the supply voltage they receive. P26CF is the general code for that voltage when it is implausible but cannot be assigned to too low or too high. No manufacturer documents P26CF itself in public.

Weak battery or charging system fault
Faulty voltage measurement in the pump electronics
Other voltage-related codes stored at the same time
P26D0: Engine Coolant Pump Control Module System Voltage Low

P26D0 means the electronics in the engine coolant pump see less voltage than they should. P26D1: Engine Coolant Pump Control Module System Voltage High
P26D1 is stored when the electronics of the engine coolant pump report a supply voltage clearly above the vehicle system voltage.

Poor PCM ground making the reference voltage look low

P26D2: Engine Coolant Pump Control Module Over Temperature

The electronics of a smart coolant pump also measure their own temperature. P26D2 is set when this value climbs too high: in Ford's hybrid OBD summaries the pump module reports the temperature over LIN and the PCM stores P26D2 once it passes 130 °C for five seconds.

P26D3: Engine Coolant Pump Supply Voltage Circuit

P26D3 concerns the power feed and ground of the engine coolant pump. On Ford's 2.0 L hybrids the pump module has no way of reporting a loss of these lines, since without power it goes quiet on the LIN bus.

U019F stored at the same time
P26D4: Engine Coolant Pump Supply Voltage Circuit Low
P26D4 narrows the supply fault of the engine coolant pump down to too low a voltage on its power feed. There is no public manufacturer documentation for this code.
Corroded fuse holder or connector in the pump feed
Partial short to ground on the feed wire
Fluctuating engine temperature or heater output
P26D5: Engine Coolant Pump Supply Voltage Circuit High
P26D5 is set when the power feed of the engine coolant pump carries a higher voltage than the system allows. No manufacturer documents this code in public.
Supply relay stuck closed so the feed stays live
Feed or sensing wire shorted to another powered circuit
Overvoltage codes in other control modules
P26D6: Engine Coolant Pump Clutch Control Circuit/Open

Some engines drive their mechanical coolant pump through a switchable clutch: following a cold start the pump is left idle so the coolant stays still and the engine reaches temperature sooner, and once a target is met the clutch couples the pump to its drive again.
Broken wire or corroded, loose connector in the clutch control circuit
Open solenoid coil in the coolant pump clutch
Blown fuse or missing supply to the clutch solenoid
Faulty output stage in the engine control module
Engine and cabin heater take longer to warm up
Coolant temperature behaves differently from normal after a cold start
P26D7: Engine Coolant Pump Clutch Performance/Stuck Off

P26D7 is the serious case for a clutched coolant pump: the module has asked the clutch to couple the pump, but the cooling system shows no sign of circulation, so the pump is assumed to stay disconnected. The electrical side may be intact; worn friction faces, a seized armature or a pump that slips under load are typical mechanical reasons.
Worn or slipping clutch friction surfaces
Armature or switching mechanism seized in the disengaged position
Slipping or damaged pump drive belt
Implausible coolant temperature input or outdated engine software
Coolant temperature rises quickly, possible overheating warning
Radiator fans run at high speed
Reduced engine power to protect the engine
P26D8: Engine Coolant Pump Clutch Stuck On

With P26D8 the opposite of the warm-up strategy happens: the engine module wants the coolant pump decoupled after a cold start, but the pump keeps turning, so coolant circulates from the first second and the engine warms up as slowly as with a plain belt-driven pump.
Clutch mechanically jammed or welded in the engaged position
Weak return spring or demagnetised holding magnet
No current at the solenoid in designs that need current to disengage
Slow warm-up, heater gets warm late
Slightly higher fuel consumption on short trips
P26D9: Engine Coolant Pump Clutch Control Circuit Low
P26D9 narrows the electrical fault of the coolant pump clutch down to a control line that sits too close to ground.
Chafed control wire shorted to ground
Moisture or coolant in the connector at the pump
Changed warm-up behaviour of the engine
Possibly a blown fuse with further faults on the same circuit
P26DA: Engine Coolant Pump Clutch Control Circuit High

P26DA is the high-side counterpart of P26D9: the control line of the coolant pump clutch shows more voltage than the commanded state permits, for instance while the driver should be pulling it low or while it is switched off.
Control wire shorted to a battery-voltage circuit
Open ground or poor ground contact at the clutch solenoid
Faulty output stage in the engine control module
Pump clutch does not switch, warm-up or cooling behaves differently
P26DB: Some sporty cars shape the sound reaching the cabin or the tailpipe with an electrically driven part, such as a switchable flap in the silencer or a valve in an intake sound pipe. Circuit A is the first of up to two such actuators.
Actuator connector unplugged or not fully seated, often after exhaust or intake work
Broken wire near the hot exhaust or at a moving section of the harness
Internal open circuit in the sound valve or actuator
Sound component removed or replaced by an aftermarket part without electrical equivalent
Check engine light, depending on the manufacturer
Sport sound or valve opening no longer noticeable
P26DC: Engine Sound Control A Circuit Low

P26DC reports that the control line of sound actuator A sits at too low a voltage, which points to the wire or the actuator being grounded rather than interrupted. Depending on the design, the driver stage then cannot switch the flap or valve, or switches it permanently because the ground path bypasses it.
Control wire chafed through and touching body or exhaust metal
Moisture or corrosion in the actuator connector
Shorted winding inside the sound actuator
Faulty output stage in the controlling module
Exhaust or intake sound does not change between driving modes
Possibly a blown fuse for the actuator circuit
P26DD: Engine Sound Control A Circuit High

With P26DD the module measures a voltage on the drive line of sound actuator A that is higher than the switching state allows. The usual reason is contact with a live conductor, for instance a neighbouring supply wire in a melted harness, or an internal fault in the actuator that feeds battery voltage back.
Drive wire shorted to a supply wire, often where heat has damaged the harness
Internal fault in the actuator feeding voltage back into the drive line
Incorrect or aftermarket actuator with different electrical layout
Output stage of the controlling module defective
Valve stays in one position, sound permanently loud or quiet
P26DE: Engine Sound Control A Circuit Performance

Unlike the pure wiring codes, P26DE means the circuit of sound actuator A is electrically intact but the part does not behave as commanded, for example a flap that sticks, moves too slowly or reports an implausible position.
Exhaust sound valve sticking or worn
Engine software with too strict an evaluation, update available from the maker
Flap linkage blocked by deposits, ice or damage
Weak actuator motor or faulty position feedback
Exhaust note no longer changes, or changes late
Rattling or buzzing from the silencer area
P26DF: Sensor power supplies A to D are separate outputs of a control module that feed groups of sensors; they are a different family from the 5 V sensor reference voltages (P0641 and following). D is the fourth such output. P26DF is the general or open-circuit code for it.
Broken supply wire or splice to the sensors on output D
Loose or corroded pin at the control module or a sensor
Supply output D inside the control module failed
Reduced power or emergency mode depending on the sensors affected
P26E0: Sensor Power Supply D Circuit Low

P26E0 means the fourth sensor supply output of the control module is pulled below its normal level. Deutz documents it for the fourth ECU sensor supply, SPN 3512, in two variants: excessive current or a grounded circuit (FMI 6), and a reading below the physical limit with top severity (FMI 1).
One sensor on supply D with an internal short pulling the output down
Supply wire chafed and touching engine ground
Moisture in a sensor plug bridging supply and ground
Group of sensor faults appearing at once
P26E1: Sensor Power Supply D Circuit High

With P26E1 the fourth sensor supply of the control module reads higher than its regulated value. Deutz assigns it to SPN 3512 with FMI 0, meaning a reading beyond the upper physical limit, rated as most severe.
Supply D wire shorted to battery voltage or a higher supply
Faulty sensor feeding voltage back into the supply rail
Regulator for supply D in the control module defective
Possible derate depending on the sensors involved
P26E2: Fuel Mode Indicator Lamp Control Circuit Low

Bi-fuel vehicles show the active fuel with an indicator, often a lamp in the selector switch. GM's 2015 Impala bi-fuel lights it while running on CNG and flashes it during a fuel change; GM's 2016 CNG pickups also flash it fast to signal a gas system fault, and Ford's earlier bi-fuel trucks combined the ALT/GAS selector with its lamp in one assembly.
Lamp control wire chafed to ground
Shorted LED or bulb in the fuel selector switch
Faulty lamp output in the controlling module
Fuel mode lamp dark or permanently lit
No visible warning when the gas system has a fault
P26E3: Fuel Mode Indicator Lamp Control Circuit High
P26E3 is the opposite case of P26E2: the module that drives the fuel mode lamp sees a voltage on its control line that is higher than its commanded state allows.
Lamp control wire shorted to a battery or ignition feed
Burnt-out bulb or open LED in the selector switch
Damaged or wet connector at the selector switch
Driver cannot tell which fuel is in use
P26E4: Stop-start systems often use a second starter relay, and P26E4 is the general circuit fault of this relay B.
Open wire or loose terminal between module and relay B or pinion solenoid
Control module software misjudging the circuit, update available on some FCA models
Open coil in relay B or in the tandem starter pinion solenoid
Faulty high-side driver in the engine module
Engine does not restart from an automatic stop
P26E5: P26E5 indicates that the control circuit of starter relay B is shorted against ground.
Engine harness chafed so the relay B control wire touches ground
Shorted coil in relay B or the pinion solenoid
Damaged high-side driver in the engine module
No crank or no restart after an automatic engine stop
Blown fuses and further unrelated codes if a harness short is the cause
P26E6: P26E6 reports a short to positive on the control line of starter relay B. GM tests for it while its driver for the tandem starter pinion relay is off: if the line still shows 0.5 Ohm or less toward a power source for 40 out of 50 checks taken every 50 ms, with the engine stopped and at least 11 V available, the code is stored as type B.
Relay B control wire shorted to a battery-powered wire, e.g. under the battery tray
Relay B internally fed or contacts welded
Engine module driver output not switching off
Starter noise or grinding without a start command
P26E7: Supply D is the fourth switched rail with which a control module powers a group of solenoids or other loads, after A (P0657), B (P2669) and C (P2684). P26E7 reports an open load on it.
Broken wire or loose, corroded connector between the module output and the loads on supply D
Open coil in a solenoid powered from this rail
Internal fault in the high-side output of the transmission control module
Check engine or transmission warning light on
Transmission stays in a substitute gear or limp mode
Several solenoid or clutch codes stored at the same time
P26E8: Actuator Supply Voltage D Circuit Low
P26E8 says the voltage on supply rail D drops too far while the rail is switched on.
Supply line or a connected load shorted to ground
Loose or corroded battery, fuse or ground connections feeding the module, or weak batteries (Volvo/Mack aftertreatment module)
Faulty sensor or solenoid on the rail drawing too much current
Internal fault in the module output stage
Warning light on, often only briefly or intermittently
Transmission failsafe mode with loss of the solenoids on that rail
On trucks, lost communication with NOx, PM and DEF sensors and a derate warning
P26E9: Actuator Supply Voltage D Circuit High

The high fault of rail D is about voltage where none should be: the controller has turned supply D off, yet the line stays live. Either the high-side switch inside the module no longer opens or an outside wire touches battery positive.
High-side switch in the control module stuck closed
Supply D wire chafed against a battery or ignition feed
Water or corrosion in the module connector creating a leakage path
Warning light on after two drive cycles
Transmission in limp mode or with restricted gears
Code appears after restarting rather than while driving
P26EA: Vehicles with a second fuel pump give it its own driver module, and P26EA means that module B has reported an internal fault of its own. Ford documents the code in its gasoline OBD summary for 2020 to 2023 and again in 2024 as an internal error reported by the driver module of pump B.
Internal failure of fuel pump driver module B
Open or corroded fuel pump monitor wire between module B and the PCM or relay module
Poor power or ground at module B
Worn or seized fuel pump B overloading the module
Warning light on, depending on the vehicle calibration
Hesitation or power loss at high load
Hard starting or stalling if the second pump is needed
P26EB: Alternative Fuel Control Module System Voltage

On bi-fuel engines a separate alternative fuel control module often runs the gas side. In Ford's bi-fuel CNG documentation of 2002 it contains drivers for both injector sets, switches the fuel relays, picks the active fuel from the selector switch and shuts the tank valve when gas pressure falls below 517 kPa.
Loose, corroded or undersized power or ground connection at the gas control module
Faulty fuse, relay or feed circuit of the gas system
Weak battery or alternator voltage outside the normal range
Internal fault in the alternative fuel control module
Gas mode not available or vehicle switches back to gasoline
Fuel mode indicator flashes or shows a fault
P26EC: Where a vehicle has two sound actuators, for instance one flap per tailpipe side or a valve in addition to an intake sound tube, B designates the second one. P26EC is stored when its drive circuit is broken, so switching the output produces no current.
Connector of the second actuator loose or disconnected
Wire to actuator B broken, for example by heat or vibration
Check engine light, depending on the manufacturer
Sound changes only on one side or not at all
P26ED: Engine Sound Control B Circuit Low

P26ED concerns the second sound actuator and indicates a drive line pulled toward ground. A conductor rubbed bare on the exhaust bracket, a pinched loom or corrosion bridging the pins of a wet plug are the classic culprits, along with a shorted coil inside the actuator.
Insulation of the actuator B wire worn through against metal
Corroded or wet connector at actuator B
Second flap does not respond, sound only partly changes
P26EE: Engine Sound Control B Circuit High

For the second sound actuator, P26EE signals a drive circuit carrying more voltage than expected, i.e. a short to battery positive or a feed coming back from a damaged actuator. Because the line is then powered from elsewhere, flap B may hold its position no matter what the driver selects.
Actuator B wire in contact with a positive supply wire
Damaged actuator B feeding voltage back
Faulty output stage for circuit B in the module
Second flap stuck in one position
P26EF: Engine Sound Control B Circuit Performance
P26EF is the functional fault of the second sound actuator: wiring checks pass, yet flap or valve B does not reach or report the commanded state in time. No maker documents P26EF publicly.
Flap B binding due to soot, rust or a seized shaft
Worn gearbox or weak motor in actuator B
Evaluation in the module software too sensitive
Sound of the second branch changes late or not at all
P26F0: P26F0 says that starter relay A remains closed even though the module has withdrawn its command, so current keeps flowing to the starter or its solenoid. Unlike the circuit codes P0615 to P0617, the wiring may be intact; the problem lies in the switching itself, typically welded contacts or a sticking armature.
Welded or sticking contacts in starter relay A
Relay A control circuit fed from elsewhere so the coil stays energised
Faulty crank feedback signal suggesting a closed relay
Starter keeps running or grinding after the engine has started
Burning smell or flat battery after short trips
P26F1: P26F1 is the opposite case to P26F0: the module commands starter relay A on, but the expected reaction never arrives, so the starter receives no power. Possible reasons are burnt or contaminated contacts, a coil that no longer pulls in, or a missing feed on the load side, for example a blown fuse or a loose battery cable at the relay.
Burnt or dirty contacts in starter relay A
Blown fuse or loose power cable on the load side of the relay
Relay coil no longer pulling in
Feedback wire to the module interrupted
Engine does not crank, or only after several attempts
No restart after an automatic stop
P26F2: P26F2 concerns the second starter relay, which on stop-start vehicles may engage the pinion of a tandem starter (GM) or form the second switching path of a two-relay layout (FCA Starter Control 2). The code means relay B fails to drop out after its command ends.
Contacts of relay B welded or stuck
Control line of relay B fed from another circuit
Pinion solenoid of the tandem starter sticking mechanically
Grinding or whining from the starter after the engine runs
P26F3: P26F3 reports that starter relay B does not switch through when commanded, so the start sequence that depends on it cannot complete.
Loose power cable at the relay or power distribution unit
Burnt contacts in starter relay B
Weak battery or low system voltage so the relay does not pull in
Engine does not start or crank
Further codes for low system voltage or battery state
P26F4: Coolant pump C is a third electric pump next to pumps A and B; which circuit it serves is defined by each manufacturer. In Bentley's V8 models from the Volkswagen group it is the auxiliary pump for the heater circuit, while GM's diesel tables use the C codes for the pump of the low-temperature loop.
Broken control wire or loose connector at pump C
Corroded pins from road splash or coolant ingress
Internal electronics of the pump failed
Weak cabin heating at idle or with the engine stopped
Higher charge air or component temperatures, depending on the loop
P26F5: Coolant Pump C Control Circuit Low
P26F5 reports that the control circuit of coolant pump C is pulled too low. Bentley documents the code in the engine electronics of the Continental GT/GTC and Flying Spur.
Internal corrosion of the pump causing a short circuit
Over-sensitive internal diagnosis of the pump (known pump part number)
Control wire shorted to ground or coolant in the connector
Often no noticeable change in heating or engine behaviour
Fault may come and go (stored as intermittent)
P26F6: Coolant Pump C Control Circuit High

P26F6 is stored when the control line of coolant pump C carries a higher voltage than the commanded state allows. In practice that means the wire touches a live circuit, the pump has lost its ground so the line floats up, or the line is open between driver and pump in a way the output stage reads as high. No public service document covers P26F6 itself.
Control wire shorted to battery voltage
Missing or corroded ground at pump C
Internal electronics of the pump failed
Pump runs on after switch-off or does not run at all
Weak heater output with the engine idling
P26F7: Coolant Pump C Supply Voltage Circuit

Unlike P26F4 to P26F6, which concern the control signal, P26F7 points to the power feed of coolant pump C: the voltage arriving at the pump is missing or implausible. A blown fuse, a relay with burnt contacts, a broken feed wire or a loose ground are the usual causes; a weak battery during cranking can also trigger it.
Blown fuse or faulty relay in the pump C feed
Broken feed wire or loose, corroded ground
Low system voltage from a weak battery or charging fault
Pump C does not run at all
Further codes for the same fuse or for low voltage
P26F8: P26F8 is about mechanics rather than wiring: coolant pump C is powered and commanded but its rotor does not turn or stops under load. Smart pumps recognise this themselves from a high motor current at little or no speed, and report it to the controlling module.
Seized bearing or rotor in pump C
Debris or deposits in the pump from contaminated coolant
Frozen coolant from an incorrect mixture
Heating or component cooling of the affected loop fails
P26F9: Coolant Pump C Control Module Overtemperature

Electric coolant pumps carry their own control electronics, which are cooled by the liquid passing through the pump. P26F9 means the electronics of pump C have reported a temperature above their limit.
Low coolant level or air trapped in pump C
Partly blocked impeller causing high current
Faulty temperature sensing in the pump electronics
Pump C runs at reduced speed or switches off temporarily
Heating or cooling of the affected loop varies
P26FA: Coolant Pump C Overspeed/Air in System
P26FA flags a coolant pump C that turns far faster than it should – the classic sign of a pump moving air instead of liquid.
Low coolant level or air left in the low-temperature loop after service
Leak in the loop drawing in air
Chafed engine harness corrupting pump signals
Impeller slipping on its shaft or broken
Check engine light on after two trips
Higher charge air temperature and possibly reduced power
P26FB: EGR Cooler Bypass Control Stuck Closed (Bank 1)

A diesel engine routes recirculated exhaust around the EGR cooler while it is cold, so that the gas warms the engine and aftertreatment; later the bypass flap closes and the gas passes through the cooler. P26FB means the bypass on bank 1 does not open when commanded and stays in the closed, cooling position.
Blocked orifice or kinked vacuum line to the bypass actuator
Bypass flap sticking from soot and deposits
Faulty vacuum solenoid or weak vacuum supply
Outdated PCM calibration with too sensitive detection
Longer warm-up of engine and exhaust aftertreatment
Usually no noticeable change in driveability
P26FC: EGR Cooler Bypass Control Stuck Closed (Bank 2)
P26FC is the bank 2 version of P26FB and only exists on engines with a separate EGR cooler and bypass for each cylinder bank, typically V-configuration diesels.
Blocked, leaking or kinked vacuum line to the bank 2 actuator
Bypass flap of bank 2 sticking from soot deposits
Slower warm-up of the exhaust aftertreatment
P26FD: A/C Compressor Internal Control Module Performance

Electric A/C compressors in hybrids and electric vehicles carry their own inverter and control electronics. P26FD says this built-in module does not work as expected, as judged by the module that supervises the compressor.
Software error in the climate or compressor control
Internal electronics or inverter of the compressor failing
Fault in the high-voltage supply or fuse of the compressor
Check engine light on without a code in the engine module
Air conditioning weak or not cooling
Further A/C codes stored as sporadic
P26FE: Exhaust Flow Control Valve A Control Performance
P26FE concerns the electrically driven exhaust flap A on models with selectable exhaust sound. The circuit is fine, but the flap does not reach the commanded position.
Flap sticking from corrosion, soot or freezing moisture
Exhaust or actuator bracket not seated correctly
Actuator not aligned after replacement or outdated PCM software
Message that exhaust or drive mode is not available
No audible change in exhaust sound between modes
P26FF: Auto Configuration Throttle Input Not Present (Bank 2)

Some engine controllers set themselves up at power-on by checking which inputs are connected, so one module can serve several engine layouts. On V engines with a separate throttle body for each cylinder bank this includes a throttle position signal per bank.
Bank 2 throttle body connector unplugged or not fully seated
Open signal, reference or ground wire to the bank 2 throttle position sensor
Engine controller programmed or replaced with software for a different engine variant
Reduced engine power or limp mode
Poor throttle response or rough idle
P2700: Transmission Friction Element A Apply Time Range/Performance

Automatic transmissions shift by filling and releasing clutches or brakes, the friction elements, and the controller learns how long each one takes to apply. P2700 is set when element A engages too slowly, too quickly or not plausibly compared with the commanded shift. Which part A is depends on the gearbox.
Worn or damaged clutch A components, such as a cylinder, piston seal or one-way clutch
Sticking valve or solenoid in the main control valve body
Low, aged or incorrect transmission fluid
Adaptive shift values not relearned after repair or software update
Harsh, delayed or slipping shifts involving clutch A
Check engine or transmission warning light on
Incorrect gear ratio codes stored at the same time
P2701: Transmission Friction Element B Apply Time Range/Performance

P2701 concerns friction element B: the controller has measured an apply time for this clutch or brake that falls outside its learned window. The letter is assigned per gearbox, and bulletins show how varied the causes are.
Mechanical damage in clutch B, such as a displaced snap ring or damaged hub
Damaged one-way clutch working together with element B
Sticking valve or pressure control solenoid for clutch B
Harsh shifts or engine flare during shifts
One or more gears missing, e.g. no upshift beyond second
P2702: Transmission Friction Element C Apply Time Range/Performance

With P2702 the transmission controller reports that friction element C does not engage within the time it expects, measured from the shift command to the moment the speed ratio changes. Which clutch C stands for differs between gearbox designs. Ford names the code in several valve body bulletins.
Sticking valves in the main control valve body
Worn clutch C plates or leaking piston seals
Outdated transmission software or lost adaptive values
Harsh or delayed shifts on gears using clutch C
Vehicle may not shift out of Park on some Ford 8F35 units
Wrench or engine warning light on
P2703: Transmission Friction Element D Apply Time Range/Performance

P2703 points at friction element D: the time it needs to take up torque, as seen from turbine and output speed, no longer matches what the controller has learned. In Ford's eight-speed front-drive units the code turns up with reverse problems.
Faulty or contaminated selectable one-way clutch (Ford 8F24/8F35)
Sticking valve in the main control valve body
Worn clutch D plates or leaking seals
No reverse or harsh engagement into reverse
Harsh or delayed shifts on gears using clutch D
P2704: Transmission Friction Element E Apply Time Range/Performance

P2704 is stored when friction element E takes too long or too short a time to apply, judged against the speed change the controller expects for the shift. Ford bulletins tie the code directly to the E clutch.
Pressure loss in the E clutch circuit from worn hub or damaged O-rings
Sticking valves in the main control valve body
Transmission control software needing an update
Low fluid level from a leak
Harsh engagement into drive or poor shift quality
Wrench, engine or gearbox warning on
Limp mode in a fixed gear on some gearboxes
P2705: Transmission Friction Element F Apply Time Range/Performance

P2705 covers the sixth friction element, F, so only transmissions with at least six shift elements use it, such as Ford's ten-speed and eight-speed families. The controller has found that F applies outside the time it has learned.
Sticking valves in the main control valve body
Shift solenoid F not controlling pressure correctly
Harsh or slipping shifts in the gears using clutch F
Vehicle may fall back into Park when drive or reverse is selected (Ford 8F57)
P2706: P2706 is the general code for the sixth shift solenoid, F. Ford's 2024 OBD summary uses it as the base for all shift solenoid F faults in its 10R60/10R80, 8F35/8F40, 8F57 and 8F24 transmissions: with a fault-type byte added, P2706 marks an open, a short to ground, a short to supply, an intermittent connection, stuck off and stuck on, each also carrying its o…
Open or shorted wiring or connector to shift solenoid F, often inside the transmission
Failed shift solenoid F or main control valve body
Control module software that needs reprogramming (Ram 68RFE)
Faulty solenoid driver in the PCM or TCM
Harsh shifts, missing gears or limp mode
Vehicle may not shift out of Park on some Ford 8F35 units
P2707: P2707 is not an electrical fault: the circuit to shift solenoid F is intact, but the clutch it controls does not apply when commanded, as if the solenoid stayed off. Ford stresses that a ratio-based check cannot tell a solenoid failure apart from other faults in the clutch hydraulics.
Leaking or damaged clutch F piston or seals
Shift solenoid F or its valve sticking in the off position
Insufficient supply pressure, e.g. damaged fluid pump gasket
Gears using clutch F missing or slipping
Return to Park or no engagement in drive or reverse
P2708: P2708 means the clutch fed by shift solenoid F stays applied when the controller expects it released, although the wiring checks pass. Ford's 2024 OBD summary maps it to P2706 with the failed-on byte 7E for its 10R60/10R80, 8F35/8F40, 8F57 and 8F24 units.
Internal oil leak at a clutch cylinder or sleeve keeping the clutch applied (Ford 10R80 CDF cylinder)
Shift solenoid F mechanically sticking in the applied position (dirt, wear)
Outdated PCM/TCM calibration; Ford bulletins combine reprogramming with the repair
Debris or degraded fluid jamming valves in the valve body
Harsh or delayed engagement and shifts
MIL lit, often with other stuck-on or gear-ratio codes
Binding or shudder as two clutches work against each other
Transmission may hold a fixed gear for protection
P2709: P2709 flags an electrical fault on shift solenoid F, found by the output driver rather than by watching the gearbox shift.
Defective coil in shift solenoid F (Hyundai/Kia replace the solenoid first)
Chafed or corroded wiring or connector between PCM/TCM and transmission
Damaged internal transmission harness or lead frame
Faulty output driver in the PCM/TCM
MIL lit and transmission in a fail-safe gear
Missing gears or sudden harsh shifts
Code returns immediately after clearing if the fault is permanent
P270A: Transmission Friction Element A Temperature Too High

P270A opens a row of six codes (A to F) for an overheated clutch or brake inside the gearbox. The controller keeps track of how hot element A gets when it slips during launches and shifts and sets the code once that value passes its limit; the code is a warning of thermal overload rather than proof of a broken part.
Repeated launches, creeping or towing that load element A with long slip phases
Worn element A slipping because of low apply pressure or worn linings
Low or aged transmission fluid reducing cooling of the clutch
Restricted fluid cooler or faulty cooling valve
Reduced engine power or gearbox warning message
Harsh or slipping engagement of the affected gear
Burnt smell of transmission fluid after heavy use
P270B: Transmission Friction Element B Temperature Too High

P270B concerns the shift element lettered B. A multi-plate clutch has no sensor of its own, so the controller usually derives its heat from the energy turned into warmth while the plates slip and from the oil temperature, then compares the result with a limit.
Slow or weak apply of element B creating extra slip (pressure or seal problem)
Stop-and-go, steep grades or trailer loads
Implausible fluid temperature input distorting the calculated value
Changed shift points or skipped gears
P270C: Transmission Friction Element C Temperature Too High

With P270C the controller reports that clutch or brake C has run hotter than its permitted limit. Typical triggers are long slip phases: creeping in heavy traffic, holding the car on a slope with the throttle, or a trailer launch.
Creeping or holding on a grade with the throttle instead of the brake
Element C slipping from low apply pressure or worn plates
Faulty clutch cooling oil valve or restricted cooler (where fitted)
Warning in the cluster with reduced power
Gear using element C avoided or held only briefly
P270D: Transmission Friction Element D Temperature Too High

P270D is stored when the thermal state of shift element D rises above the controller's limit. The heat comes from friction during slip, so anything that lengthens slip on D counts: a sluggish apply, leaking seals in its hydraulic circuit, or hard use with a heavy load.
Leaking seals in the apply circuit of element D lengthening slip
Blocked or undersized fluid cooler, especially when towing
Old or wrong fluid with reduced friction and cooling properties
Limited torque or gear range for protection
Flare or slip on shifts involving element D
P270E: Transmission Friction Element E Temperature Too High

P270E reports an over-temperature of the shift element labelled E. Because the value is normally calculated rather than measured inside the clutch, a wrong input can also trigger it: an implausible fluid temperature signal or incorrect slip data from the speed sensors would distort the estimate.
Faulty fluid temperature or speed sensor signal distorting the calculated temperature
Real slip of element E under load
Poor internal contact in the transmission control electronics
Slipping or delayed shifts through element E
P270F: Transmission Friction Element F Temperature Too High

P270F closes the A-to-F series and signals that element F has exceeded its temperature limit. Only gearboxes with at least six shift elements carry a letter F, so the code belongs to modern multi-speed automatics, but no maker publishes its use or thresholds.
Element F slipping due to low pressure or wear
Severe duty such as towing, mountain driving or repeated launches
