Gears using element F temporarily unavailable
P2710: P2710 is the sporadic counterpart to P2709: the circuit of shift solenoid F drops out now and then and recovers, so a check at standstill often finds nothing.
Loose or spread terminal at the transmission or module connector
Wire rubbing through intermittently inside or outside the case
Moisture or corrosion in the connector
Heat-dependent internal break in the solenoid coil
Occasional harsh shift or brief fail-safe operation
MIL that comes and goes with the fault
No fault found during a static circuit test
P2711: P2711 is set when the transmission controller sees the drivetrain act as if a gear were no longer properly engaged although it never commanded that, for example because a clutch drags or a gear does not engage as selected.
Excessive drag torque in the dual clutch (worn or early-production plates)
Shift fork or gear actuator not holding the gear
Gear indicator flashing or lit in the cluster
Selected Drive or Reverse does not engage after start-up
P2712: P2712 targets gearboxes whose clutches or shift forks are worked by a separate hydraulic power unit, typically an electric pump that charges a pressure accumulator. Such a system loses pressure only slowly when sealed; if pressure drops faster than expected or the pump has to recharge too often, the controller concludes there is a leak.
Internal leakage at valves or seals of the hydraulic unit
External oil leak at housing, lines or connector seals
Hydraulic pump running often or for long periods
Gears not engaging or delayed engagement
P2713: P2713 is the umbrella code for pressure control solenoid D; it names the valve but not the kind of fault, so the failure type byte behind it carries the detail. Toyota works this way.
Internal transmission damage that makes the valve or its clutch stick (Toyota replaces the unit)
Pressure control solenoid D sticking from debris or wear
Wrong fluid level or degraded fluid
Wiring or connector fault on the valve circuit
MIL lit with further transmission codes
Whine noise or reduced power in some vehicles
P2714: Pressure Control Solenoid D Performance/Stuck Off

P2714 says the clutch served by solenoid D does not apply as commanded, so the gearbox slips in a gear that needs it. In GM's 2016 table 16OBDG03 valve D is clutch 4 (C2-3-4-6-8) on the eight-speed and the 2-6 brake on the T76 six-speed; slip of 400 rpm or more for 3 s, counted over three events, sets it after one trip.
Leaking clutch piston seal or damaged clutch housing (GM 10L1000 C4)
Regulator or line pressure valve stuck by debris or sediment
Internal mechanical failure such as a dislodged retainer ring (GM 10L80)
Low fluid level reducing apply pressure
Slipping or flare in gears that use the affected clutch
No reverse or no forward drive in some cases
MIL lit and transmission in a substitute mode
P2715: Pressure Control Solenoid D Stuck On

With P2715 the opposite of P2714 has happened: the clutch fed by valve D keeps holding although the controller wants it released, so it drags into the next gear. GM checks this on its eight-speed through torque-phase and inertia-phase tests on clutch 4, and its 2018 table 18OBDG04 links the code on the nine-speed to C4 exhaust delay times (Type A).
Debris holding a valve in the applied position
Solenoid D or redundant shutdown valve mechanically stuck
False detection during a stability-control fail-safe (Subaru CVT)
Faulty TCM/solenoid assembly (GM 2-mode hybrid date codes)
Harsh shift or binding as two clutches overlap
Vehicle feels braked when pulling away
MIL lit, transmission may hold a safe gear
P2716: P2716 is the general electrical code for pressure control solenoid D: the output stage sees a wrong current or voltage on the coil, without saying whether the circuit is open, grounded or shorted to supply. No manufacturer documents P2716 publicly.
Open or shorted coil in solenoid D
Loose, corroded or not fully seated connector
Faulty driver stage in the TCM
MIL lit and transmission in fail-safe mode
P2717: P2717 reports that the circuit or response of solenoid D drops out briefly and then comes back. Unlike a hard open or short, the fault is gone by the time the vehicle reaches the workshop, so a static measurement often looks fine. No manufacturer documents P2717 publicly.
Spread or loose terminal at transmission or TCM connector
Moisture or corrosion in the connector
No fault found during a workshop check
P2718: Pressure Control Solenoid D Control Circuit/Open

P2718 points to an open control circuit of solenoid D: the coil draws no current because a wire, pin or the winding itself is broken. GM's 2016 eight-speed table runs the open check on the clutch 4 valve and fails it after 0.3 s within a 0.5 s window (one trip); the 2017 and 2018 nine-speed tables use an impedance measurement.
Valve body solenoid connector not fully seated (GM 8L45/8L90)
Broken wire or pushed-out pin in the harness
Limp-home mode with limited forward gears
P2719: Pressure Control Solenoid D Control Circuit Range/Performance

P2719 means the electrical readings on the control circuit of solenoid D are implausible, although neither a clear open nor a clear short is present. In GM's 2016 table 16OBDG03 the T76 six-speed flags it when the hardware layer reports an invalid voltage in at least 4.4 of 5 seconds; valve D is the 2-6 brake there, and the code is listed without MIL.
False history code near freezing fluid temperature in Park/Neutral (GM 6T70/6T75)
High resistance at a terminal or splice
Stored history code without noticeable symptoms
No MIL on GM vehicles (Type C)
Occasional shift quality changes if the fault is real
P271A: Park Pawl Position Sensor A Circuit Low

With park-by-wire the pawl is moved by an actuator instead of a cable, and a position sensor tells the controller whether it is engaged. P271A means the signal of sensor A has dropped below its valid band.
Corrosion on the park module circuit board (Ford HF55, recall 26V688)
Sensor A signal wire shorted to ground
Missing or low reference voltage to sensor A
Vehicle cannot be shifted out of Park
Unexpected shift to Neutral while driving
Service warning such as Shifting System Error
P271B: Park Pawl Position Sensor A Circuit High

P271B is the upper-limit partner of P271A: the signal from park pawl position sensor A reads above its plausible range. Typical electrical causes are a broken ground or signal wire, which lets the input float towards the reference, or a short to a supply line. No manufacturer documents P271B publicly.
Open sensor ground or signal wire
Signal wire shorted to reference or battery voltage
Corroded or loose connector at the park actuator
Shift system warning on the display
Park cannot be selected or released
P271C: Park Pawl Position Sensor B Circuit Low

P271C covers the second park pawl position sensor, B, whose signal has fallen below the valid range. Park-by-wire designs often fit two position signals so that a single faulty reading cannot release or engage the pawl by itself; sensor B is the backup or comparison channel to sensor A.
Sensor B signal wire shorted to ground
Reference voltage to sensor B missing or low
Corrosion inside the park actuator module
Shift system warning, vehicle usually still drivable
P271D: Park Pawl Position Sensor B Circuit High

P271D is logged when the signal of park pawl position sensor B sits above its upper limit. Electrically this is the mirror image of P271C: an interrupted sensor ground, an open signal line pulled up inside the controller, or contact with a supply wire.
Open ground or signal wire of sensor B
Signal shorted to a voltage source
Moisture or corrosion in the actuator connector
Shift system warning on the display
P271E: P271E is a broad performance code for the transmission as a whole, used when the controller finds that the gearbox does not deliver what it should even though no single sensor or valve has failed. Honda applies it to the CVT of the 2016-2020 HR-V: service bulletin A21-046 adds P271E with new PCM software that detects early slip of the primary drive belt.
Slipping or deteriorating CVT drive belt (Honda HR-V)
Insufficient clamping or line pressure in the transmission
Control software without the latest calibration
Flashing D indicator and MIL on
P271F: Electronic Gear Shift - Position Not Learned
P271F tells the technician that the controller of an electronically actuated gear shift lacks valid learned positions, so it cannot place the shift elements precisely.
Learn procedure not run after replacing the control unit or transmission parts
Learn procedure aborted (conditions not met, low battery voltage)
Learned values lost after a software update or power interruption
Actuator or position sensor fault preventing a successful learn
Gearbox warning, gear selection limited or blocked
Code returns until a successful learn
P2720: Pressure Control Solenoid D Control Circuit Low

P2720 reports a low signal on the control line of solenoid D, which in practice is a short to ground. GM's 2016 eight-speed table sets it on the clutch 4 valve after a 0.3 s ground-short flag within one trip; the six-speed tables do the same for their valve D.
Control wire pinched or chafed against ground
Valve body connector not fully seated
P2721: Pressure Control Solenoid D Control Circuit High

P2721 is logged when the control line of solenoid D reads too high, typically because it touches battery positive. GM's 2016 six-speed tables describe it as circuit high covering an open or a short to power, set after 0.3 s in one trip, so on those units an open line can land here too.
Moisture in the control valve connector (Subaru TR580)
Control wire shorted to a supply circuit
Open circuit on units that report it as high (GM six-speed)
Faulty solenoid D or TCM driver
Fault may follow wet weather or washing
P2722: P2722 is the base code for pressure control solenoid E and leaves the type of fault open. No manufacturer documents P2722 publicly. The pattern can be seen on the neighbouring valve: Toyota stores P2713 for solenoid D with a failure type byte appended, so a scan tool would show the same structure for E.
Wiring or connector problem on the solenoid E circuit
MIL lit with possible further transmission codes
Engagement delay into drive or reverse
P2723: Pressure Control Solenoid E Performance/Stuck Off

P2723 means valve E fails to build the pressure its clutch needs, so that element slips or does not engage. GM's eight-speed table ties E to clutch 5 (C4-5-6-7-8-R) and sets the code after 400 rpm of slip lasting 3 s.
Blocked feed orifice in the separator plate (foreign material, GM Allison 1000)
Low fluid level or pump losing prime, especially on cold starts
Solenoid E or its regulator valve sticking
Worn clutch seals leaking apply pressure
Slip or flare in affected gears
MIL on and range inhibit or fail-safe mode
P2724: Pressure Control Solenoid E Stuck On

P2724 flags valve E as delivering pressure when it should not, so its clutch stays engaged too long. On the Allison 1000 GM watches the off-going element during shifts: an accumulated fail time of 0.3 s on upshifts, 0.5 s on closed-throttle downshifts or 3 s on direction changes counts as stuck on (Type A).
Valve or regulator held in the applied position by debris
Wheels lock or vehicle stops abruptly at low speed
MIL on, transmission may hold a safe gear
P2725: P2725 covers an unspecified electrical fault of pressure control solenoid E. The driver notices a coil current or voltage that does not fit the command but does not classify it further. No manufacturer documents P2725 publicly.
Damaged wiring between TCM and solenoid
Code returns at once if the fault is permanent
P2726: P2726 describes a fault on solenoid E that is there one moment and gone the next. The controller has seen short drop-outs in the circuit or in the valve's response, not a lasting failure, which makes the code hard to reproduce. No manufacturer documents P2726 publicly.
Harness damaged by engine movement or heat
Water or corrosion in the plug
Sporadic harsh shift or brief fail-safe
MIL that switches on and off
P2727: Pressure Control Solenoid E Control Circuit/Open

P2727 is set when the control circuit of solenoid E is open, so no current can flow through the coil. GM's eight-speed table checks the clutch 5 valve for an open-circuit flag over 0.3 s, and on the Allison 1000 the test on PCS 1 is rated Type A.
Rear wheels may lock at low speed (GM 8L90 case)
P2728: Pressure Control Solenoid E Control Circuit Range/Performance

P2728 marks the circuit of solenoid E as working but not plausible. GM uses it in two ways. On the Allison 1000 (16OBDG08, 17OBDG04) the TCM compares desired with actual current on PCS 1; a gap of at least 0.5 A in 10 of fewer than 20 samples sets a Type A fault with MIL.
Coil current deviating from command (resistance change, poor contact)
False history code near 0 °C fluid temperature (GM 6T70/6T75)
Unstable supply voltage to the TCM
History code without symptoms on GM six-speeds
Firm shifts if pressure control is degraded
P2729: Pressure Control Solenoid E Control Circuit Low

P2729 indicates the control line of solenoid E is pulled low, usually by a short to ground. On the Allison 1000 GM detects this when the output connection has almost no impedance to ground and confirms it within 75 ms (Type A). The eight-speed and six-speed tables of 2016 flag the low state for 0.3 s and set it after one trip.
Abrupt stop or wheel lock at low speed in the GM 8L90 case
P272A: Transmission Range Select Motor Control Circuit

P272A refers to the control circuit of the electric motor that moves the gearbox into the selected range in shift-by-wire designs. Mitsubishi documents it for the 2022 Outlander with CVT: the shift actuator has two three-phase windings fed through separate relays, and motor A is the one reported as range select motor.
Shift actuator relay A open or stuck off
Open U, V or W phase wire to motor A
Faulty motor coil A in the shift actuator
MIL and shift warning, often no change in driving
Gear selection refused, vehicle in neutral (second fault)
P272B: Transmission Range Select Motor Control Circuit Current Too High

P272B flags excessive current in the circuit of the range select motor, normally caused by a winding or wire shorted to supply. On the 2022 Mitsubishi Outlander with CVT, Mitsubishi checks this with ignition on: when one of the two phases that should be energised shows the non-energised voltage level (9-16 V instead of about 0 V), the code is set.
Motor coil A or B phase shorted to power
Damaged harness between shift module and actuator
Vehicle stays in neutral, no gear can be selected
P272C: P272C concerns the control circuit of the motor that engages and releases the park pawl. In the shift actuator of the 2022 Mitsubishi Outlander with CVT this is winding B, powered through its own relay B, while winding A is reported under P272A.
Shift actuator relay B open or stuck off
Open phase wire to motor coil B
Faulty motor coil B in the actuator
MIL on, Park still works normally
Shifting blocked if the other circuit also fails
P272D: Park Pawl Motor Control Circuit Current Too High

P272D reports overcurrent in the park pawl motor circuit, the counterpart of P272B for the second winding. Mitsubishi's 2022 Outlander CVT service data sets it with ignition on when one of two phases of motor B that ought to carry current sits at the idle voltage level instead of near 0 V, the pattern of a line shorted to supply.
Motor coil B or A phase shorted to power
Chafed harness at the shift actuator
Shifting locked out, vehicle held in neutral
MIL and shift warning lamp on
P2730: Pressure Control Solenoid E Control Circuit High

P2730 is stored when the control line of solenoid E sits too high, pointing to contact with a supply voltage. GM's Allison 1000 logic looks for a power short at the PCS 1 output and treats it as Type A. Its 2016 six-speed tables word the code as circuit high for an open or a power short, so there a broken wire may show up as P2730 instead of P2727.
Control wire chafed against a supply circuit
Open line on units that report it as high (GM six-speed)
MIL on and transmission in fail-safe
Code sets again immediately after clearing
P2731: P2731 is the parent code for pressure control solenoid F; the standard title names the valve without the kind of fault. GM gives it a concrete job on its nine-speed (GF9) units, where valve F feeds the C6 clutch and the selectable one-way clutch.
Selectable one-way clutch releasing too slowly
Solenoid F or its regulator valve sticking
Hesitation or weak acceleration from low speed
Tie-up feel on the 1-2 shift or stuck in first gear
P2732: Pressure Control Solenoid F Performance/Stuck Off
P2732 says that the clutch behind valve F does not take up torque although the solenoid works electrically, so the gearbox slips wherever that clutch is needed.
Mis-stamped spacer plate or worn check ball in the valve body (GM 10L80)
Worn clutch piston seal losing apply pressure (GM 10L1000)
Solenoid F or regulator valve sticking closed
Low fluid level or aerated fluid
Transmission will not shift beyond third gear
Slip or flare and MIL on
P2733: Pressure Control Solenoid F Stuck On

P2733 is the reverse case of P2732: valve F keeps pressure on its clutch after the TCM has commanded it off, so the off-going element still carries torque during the shift. GM checks this on its nine-speed units by watching C6 slip while shifting.
Solenoid F held open mechanically (solenoid body)
Debris holding the regulator valve in the apply position
Tie-up or bind-up feel during shifts
P2734: P2734 is the catch-all electrical code for solenoid F: the driver stage notices coil current or voltage at odds with the command, without saying whether the line is broken, touching ground or touching battery voltage. Public documentation of P2734 by any maker is lacking.
Corroded, loose or damaged connector at the valve body
Chafed or broken wire in the solenoid F circuit
Faulty output stage in the TCM
P2735: By its standard title P2735 reports that solenoid F or its circuit fails only now and then, so a static check in the workshop often finds nothing. GM uses the code differently on the dual-clutch gearbox of the 2023 and 2024 Corvette: there valve F is the clutch cooling valve, and P2735 stands for a stuck lube valve.
Clutch cooling/lube valve sticking (GM Corvette dual-clutch)
Loose or corroded connector causing dropouts
Harness chafing that opens under vibration
Often no noticeable symptom, code stored without MIL (GM)
Occasional harsh shift or clutch judder
Clutch overheating warning after hard driving
P2736: Pressure Control Solenoid F Control Circuit/Open

P2736 points to an open control circuit on solenoid F, meaning the coil path is interrupted. GM documents the code for several gearboxes. On the eight-speed of 2016 valve F is the line pressure solenoid, and an open-circuit flag for 0.3 s within 0.5 s sets the fault in one trip.
Valve body connector not fully seated
Firm shifts from maximum line pressure or missing gears
P2737: Pressure Control Solenoid F Control Circuit Range/Performance

The standard title describes implausible readings on the control circuit of solenoid F that are neither a clean open nor a short. GM's 2025 table 25OBDG03A fills the code with a hydraulic test on its CVT, where valve F switches the binary oil pump between half and full capacity.
Binary pump control valve sticking (GM CVT)
Primary or secondary pulley pressure sensor reading wrong
High resistance in the solenoid F circuit
Belt slip, flare or reduced power
P2738: Pressure Control Solenoid F Control Circuit Low
P2738 reports a control line on solenoid F that reads too low, which in practice means a short to ground.
Control wire chafed through to ground
Fluid or metal debris bridging connector pins
P2739: Pressure Control Solenoid F Control Circuit High

P2739 appears when solenoid F's control line sits too high, usually because it touches battery voltage. GM reacts faster here than for the low case: 25OBDG03A needs only 0.06 s within 0.13 s before the Type A fault is set.
Control wire shorted to battery voltage
Short between two solenoid lines in the harness or connector
Shifts missing or valve function lost
P273A: Transmission Friction Element G Apply Time Range/Performance

P273A carries the apply-time test of P2700 to P2705 on to a seventh shift element, G. The controller measures how long element G needs from command to full engagement and stores the code if this time is implausibly long or short. Only gearboxes with more than six clutches and brakes need a letter G, and no manufacturer documents P273A publicly.
Leaking piston seals in the apply circuit of element G
Pressure control or shift solenoid feeding element G sticking
Worn plates or wrong clearance of element G
Adaptive shift values out of range after repair or software update
Engine flare or harsh shift into gears using element G
MIL lit, possibly with ratio codes
P273B: Transmission Friction Element H Apply Time Range/Performance

P273B is the apply-time check for an eighth shift element, H, and therefore only applies to gearboxes with at least eight clutches and brakes. The test is the same as for its siblings: the time between command and full engagement is compared with a calibrated window, and a result outside it sets the code. No manufacturer documents P273B publicly.
Pressure loss in the apply circuit of element H (seals, valve body)
Worn friction plates of element H
Delayed or harsh shifts involving element H
P273C: Gear Shift Control Module A Supply Voltage Low

Gear shift control module A is the electronic selector used where the gearbox is shifted by wire – lever, rotary knob or push buttons – which turns the driver's choice into a message for the transmission control module. P273C means the supply voltage that this module sees, or reports, has fallen below its lower limit.
Weak or discharged 12 V battery, voltage dips at start
Corroded fuse contact, feed wire or ground of the selector module
Alternator or DC/DC converter not supplying enough voltage
Internal fault in the gear shift module
Selector warning, range cannot be changed
Vehicle will not shift out of Park
Gear indicator flickers or goes blank
P273D: Gear Shift Control Module A Supply Voltage High

P273D is the over-voltage counterpart of P273C: the gear shift control module A, the electronic selector of a by-wire gear selection, registers a supply above its permitted maximum. No manufacturer documents P273D publicly or names the limit.
Jump-start or charger delivering excessive voltage
Selector module misjudging its supply (software or hardware)
Selector or gearbox warning in the cluster
Other over-voltage faults in several modules
P273E: Gear Shift Control Module A Over Temperature

P273E is a condition code: the gear shift control module A – the shift-by-wire selector unit – reports that its internal temperature exceeds the safe limit. No manufacturer documents P273E or its threshold publicly.
Internal fault or overloaded output stage in the selector module
High ambient or radiant heat at the module location
Shorted lock solenoid or actuator driven by the module
Range changes refused until the module cools
P273F: Transmission Fluid Temperature Sensor B Over Temperature Condition

P273F is a condition code, not a wiring fault: sensor B delivers a valid reading, but that reading lies above the overheating limit the calibration allows. No manufacturer publishes P273F or its threshold. The analogous code for sensor A is P0218; Saab's Aisin automatic, for instance, sets it once the fluid stays above 170 °C for over 10 s.
Sustained high load – towing, track use, long climbs
Fluid cooler clogged or cooler valve not opening
Fluid level low or fluid aged
Sensor B reading too hot while still in range
Reduced torque or changed shift pattern
P2740: Transmission Fluid Temperature Sensor B Circuit

P2740 is the umbrella circuit code for a second transmission fluid temperature sensor, labelled B. The control module supplies the thermistor with a reference voltage and flags an electrical fault when the returned signal leaves its plausible window, without separating short from open.
Loose, corroded or damaged connector or lead to sensor B
Sensor B thermistor open or shorted internally
Faulty input stage in the transmission control module
Fluid temperature B shows an implausible fixed value on the scan tool
Cooler or hot-fluid protection works with a substitute value
P2741: Transmission Fluid Temperature Sensor B Circuit Range/Performance

P2741 flags a sensor B signal that is electrically intact but physically impossible or inconsistent. The clearest published test is a rate check: GM's 2023/24 dual-clutch module calls the cooler-outlet reading faulty when its filtered gradient exceeds 700 °C per second, confirmed over five samples, as a Type B code (MIL after two trips).
Contact resistance or loose pin causing signal jumps
Sensor B thermistor drifting or responding erratically
Fault in a control unit with built-in sensor (e.g. Mitsubishi TC-SST)
Fluid temperature B jumps on the scan tool
Temperature-dependent clutch or cooler control restricted
P2742: Transmission Fluid Temperature Sensor B Circuit Low

P2742 reports that the sensor B signal sits below its valid range, and how low is defined differs by maker. GM's 2023/24 dual-clutch TCM treats a cooler temperature sensor value under 200 mV, with hysteresis, for at least 500 ms as too low, Type B; for the usual NTC thermistor that equals an extremely hot reading or a signal wire shorted to ground.
Signal lead of sensor B chafed through and touching ground
Control unit with built-in sensor faulty (Mitsubishi TC-SST)
Warning lamp after two trips on GM
Scan tool shows sensor B extremely hot (GM, Ford) or extremely cold (Mitsubishi)
P2743: Transmission Fluid Temperature Sensor B Circuit High

P2743 is the counterpart of P2742: the sensor B signal is above its valid range. In GM's 2023/24 dual-clutch TCM the cooler temperature sensor must exceed 4745 mV for 500 ms, Type B; with an NTC thermistor fed from 5 V that points to a broken wire, an unplugged connector or a short to supply voltage, and the reading looks extremely cold.
Open circuit – broken lead or unplugged connector at sensor B
Signal lead shorted to a voltage source
CAN fault or control unit with built-in sensor (Mitsubishi TC-SST)
Scan tool shows sensor B extremely cold (GM, Ford) or extremely hot (Mitsubishi)
Cooler control falls back on sensor A
P2744: Transmission Fluid Temperature Sensor B Circuit Intermittent

P2744 covers brief dropouts or jumps in the sensor B signal that do not last long enough for the steady low or high codes. No manufacturer documents P2744 publicly; the makers that do use sensor B (GM and Ford dual-clutch units, Mitsubishi Twin Clutch SST) file erratic readings under P2741 instead.
Loose or spread terminal in the transmission connector
Harness to sensor B chafing on hot or moving parts
Moisture or corrosion in the connector
Warning lamp that comes and goes
Short spikes in fluid temperature B on the scan tool
P2745: Intermediate Shaft Speed Sensor B Circuit

P2745 is the general circuit code for a second intermediate shaft speed sensor, called B. Such a sensor reads a shaft that turns between input and output, on a dual-clutch box typically the second clutch shaft.
Signal or supply lead to sensor B broken or chafed to ground
Corroded or loose pins at the transmission connector
Internal fault of intermediate shaft speed sensor B
Faulty sensor input in the transmission control module
Check engine light and transmission warning
Limp-home mode with a fixed gear
P2746: Intermediate Shaft Speed Sensor B Circuit Range/Performance

P2746 means the sensor B signal exists but does not make sense. GM's 2023/24 dual-clutch TCM uses it for the clutch 2 speed sensor: with that clutch fully closed and no microslip, its speed must equal engine speed, and a gap of 150 rpm or more for 1.1 s sets the code; further tests compare it with the speed derived from the output shaft and watch synchronize…
Metal debris on the sensor tip or incorrect air gap to the reluctor
Interference or poor shielding causing signal spikes
Slipping clutch making the speed comparison fail
Damaged or loose reluctor ring on the shaft
Jerky clutch engagement or erratic shifts
Limp-home mode or one half of the gearbox disabled
P2747: Intermediate Shaft Speed Sensor B Circuit No Signal
P2747 is meant for the case where sensor B stays silent although the car is clearly moving. No manufacturer documents P2747 publicly.
Sensor B failed internally and delivers no pulses
Open supply or signal wire, unplugged connector
Reluctor ring displaced or sensor not seated in its bore
Warning lamp and transmission message while driving
Limp-home mode, often stuck in one gear
P2748: Intermediate Shaft Speed Sensor B Circuit Intermittent
P2748 records short interruptions in the sensor B circuit that heal before a permanent fault can be confirmed.
Terminal with weak contact pressure in the sensor or gearbox connector
Harness rubbing through and touching ground intermittently
Moisture or corrosion in the connector
Warning lamp that comes and goes
Occasional harsh shift or shift flare
P2749: Intermediate Shaft Speed Sensor C Circuit

P2749 covers an electrical fault in the circuit of a third intermediate shaft speed sensor, C. No manufacturer documents P2749 publicly, and it is unclear which transmission carries three such sensors: Ford's ten-speeds stop at B, and dual-clutch units have only two clutch shafts.
Open or grounded wire between module and sensor C
P274A: Transmission Fluid Temperature Sensor C Circuit

P274A is the general circuit code for a third transmission fluid temperature sensor, labelled C. Few gearboxes carry three fluid sensors, and no manufacturer publicly documents which measuring point C stands for or what limits apply to P274A. CARB obliges the module to detect broken circuits and readings outside the possible span on such inputs.
Connector or lead to sensor C damaged or corroded
Implausible value for temperature C on the scan tool
P274B: Transmission Fluid Temperature Sensor C Circuit Range/Performance

P274B means the sensor C signal is within electrical limits but does not fit the other information, for example because it barely changes while the gearbox warms or contradicts the other temperature values.
PCM software (Ford 2020 Super Duty 6.7 L, TSB 20-2044)
Sensor C drifting or slow to respond
Added resistance in connector or lead
Temperature C stays nearly constant while driving
P274C: Transmission Fluid Temperature Sensor C Circuit Low
P274C indicates that the sensor C signal has fallen below the lowest value the module accepts.
Signal lead of sensor C shorted to ground
Temperature C shows an extremely hot value
P274D: Transmission Fluid Temperature Sensor C Circuit High

P274D is set when the sensor C signal climbs above its highest permitted value. On a thermistor supplied with 5 V via a resistor, that happens when the circuit opens – a broken wire, a corroded or unplugged connector – or when the signal line touches a voltage source; the display would then show fluid colder than any real climate produces.
Open circuit in sensor C lead or connector
Temperature C shows an extremely cold value
Late converter lock-up or cautious shifting
P274E: Transmission Fluid Temperature Sensor C Circuit Intermittent

P274E stands for an unsteady sensor C signal: short interruptions or spikes that recover before a permanent low or high fault can mature. No manufacturer publishes this code or its debounce logic. Comparable intermittent coverage exists for the main sensor, where Ford's 2012 transmission strategy lists P0714 next to the open, short and in-range checks.
Harness rubbing on the transmission case
Temperature C drops out briefly on the scan tool
P274F: Transmission Fluid Temperature Sensor C Over Temperature Condition

P274F means sensor C reports a plausible value that is nevertheless above the overheat limit set in the calibration. It is a condition report rather than a circuit defect, and no manufacturer documents its threshold or the location of sensor C publicly.
High load or heavy clutch slip
Restricted oil flow or clogged cooler
Sensor C reading too hot within range
P2750: Intermediate Shaft Speed Sensor C Circuit Range/Performance

P2750 says that sensor C produces pulses whose speed is implausible – it disagrees with what the engaged gear and the other shaft speeds predict, jumps too fast or carries noise. No manufacturer documents P2750 publicly.
Metal particles on the sensor tip distorting the signal
Electrical interference on the signal lead
Internal clutch slip making the speeds disagree
Erratic shift points or flare between gears
P2751: Intermediate Shaft Speed Sensor C Circuit No Signal
P2751 is reserved for a sensor C that sends no pulses at all while the vehicle is demonstrably under way. No manufacturer documents P2751 publicly.
Reluctor missing, loose or too far from the sensor
P2752: Intermediate Shaft Speed Sensor C Circuit Intermittent
P2752 flags a sensor C circuit that cuts out now and then, briefly enough that neither the circuit code P2749 nor the no-signal code P2751 matures. No manufacturer documents P2752 publicly.
Insulation worn through at a bracket or edge
P2753: P2753 is set when the control module finds no closed circuit to the actuator that regulates transmission fluid cooling, usually an electrically switched coolant valve that opens or shuts the flow of engine coolant through the fluid heat exchanger. With the valve output open, the module cannot steer warm-up or cooling of the gearbox oil.
Open coil in the transmission fluid cooling valve
Loose or corroded connector at the valve, often after coolant contact
Broken control wire between module and valve
Faulty output stage in the control module
Transmission fluid warms up slowly or runs hot when towing
Transmission overheat warning in severe cases
P2754: Transmission Fluid Cooler Control Circuit Low

P2754 reports that the drive line to the transmission fluid cooling actuator sits at too low a voltage, which in practice means a short to ground or a heavily loaded output. The module then cannot switch the coolant valve or cooler control as intended, and depending on design the valve may remain permanently open or closed.
Control wire chafed through and shorted to ground
Water or coolant in the valve connector
Shorted turns in the valve coil
Fluid temperature higher or lower than normal for the conditions
Usually no change in shift behaviour
P2755: Transmission Fluid Cooler Control Circuit High

With P2755 the module sees a high level on the cooler actuator line at a moment when its driver should pull it down, the signature of a short to battery voltage or of a low-side driver that no longer switches. The cooling valve then either cannot be activated or stays energised all the time.
Control wire shorted to a battery-voltage line
Valve internally shorted to its supply terminal
Module output transistor no longer switching
Cooling valve permanently on or off
Slower warm-up of the transmission in cold weather
P2756: Torque Converter Clutch Pressure Control Solenoid

P2756 is the base code for the solenoid that meters apply pressure to the torque converter clutch. On its own it names only the component; in UDS-based systems a failure-type byte says what went wrong.
Internal transmission damage or debris in the valve body (Toyota 8-speed)
Lockup pressure solenoid sticking or worn
Wiring or connector fault on the solenoid circuit
Higher engine speed and fuel use at steady speed
P2757: Torque Converter Clutch Pressure Control Solenoid Control Circuit Performance/Stuck Off

P2757 means the converter clutch was commanded to apply, yet the speed difference between engine and turbine stayed too large, so the lockup never really happened. It is a functional verdict: the circuit may be electrically sound while the valve, the hydraulic feed or the clutch lining fails to deliver.
Sticking lockup solenoid or valve body (Toyota CVT solenoid SL)
Internal converter fault such as a dislodged snap ring (Ram AS69RC)
Engine speed stays high at steady cruise
P2758: Torque Converter Clutch Pressure Control Solenoid Control Circuit Stuck On

P2758 is the opposite of P2757: the converter clutch stays engaged although the module has asked it to release. Ford detects it when slip remains below 20 rpm while the release command is active and input torque is above 60 Nm, and the fault has to show up in more than one gear.
Lockup pressure valve stuck in the apply position
Debris or varnish in the valve body
Engine stalls or nearly stalls when coming to a stop
Shudder or jolt when selecting a gear
Warning lamp depends on manufacturer (Ford none, Mitsubishi MIL)
P2759: Torque Converter Clutch Pressure Control Solenoid Control Circuit Electrical

P2759 is a general electrical fault on the control circuit of the converter clutch pressure solenoid, used where a module cannot distinguish an open from a ground or supply short. No manufacturer documents P2759 publicly.
Damaged wire or connector between TCM and solenoid
P275A: Transmission Fluid Temperature Sensor D Circuit

P275A flags an electrical fault in the circuit of transmission fluid temperature sensor D, the fourth position in the SAE lettering. A gearbox with four separate fluid temperature inputs is rare, and no manufacturer publicly assigns sensor D or describes when P275A is stored.
Fault in connector or lead of sensor D
Temperature D missing or implausible on the scan tool
P275B: Transmission Fluid Temperature Sensor D Circuit Range/Performance
P275B is the rationality code for sensor D: the circuit is electrically sound, yet the value does not behave like real fluid temperature.
Sensor D thermistor aged or slow
Sludge or deposits on the sensor tip
Temperature D lags behind or deviates from the other readings
P275C: Transmission Fluid Temperature Sensor D Circuit Low

P275C reports that sensor D delivers less signal than the module considers possible. Read against an NTC thermistor this means a reading far hotter than the fluid could be, which almost always points to a pinched or melted lead touching ground, or to a short inside the sensor body. P275C is not documented by any manufacturer.
Pinched or melted lead of sensor D touching ground
Temperature D shows an impossibly hot value
P275D: Transmission Fluid Temperature Sensor D Circuit High

P275D is stored when the sensor D signal rises past the top of its window. With a thermistor on a pull-up resistor the voltage climbs towards the supply when current can no longer flow, so an interrupted lead, a pushed-back terminal or an unplugged connector is the usual explanation, followed by a short to a voltage source.
Interrupted lead or pushed-back terminal at sensor D
Signal lead shorted to a voltage source
Temperature D shows an extremely cold value
P275E: Transmission Fluid Temperature Sensor D Circuit Intermittent

P275E marks an intermittent sensor D circuit: the value drops out or spikes for moments and then returns, too briefly for P275C or P275D. Public manufacturer documentation for this code is lacking; the closest published counterpart is the main sensor's P0714, which Ford's 2012 strategy names among its fluid temperature checks.
Heat-damaged lead that fails when hot
Sensor D with an internal loose connection
Dropouts of temperature D in a data log
P275F: Transmission Fluid Temperature Sensor D Over Temperature Condition
P275F is the overheating condition for sensor D: the reading is valid and above the calibrated limit. No manufacturer documents the code, the limit or where sensor D sits.
Heavy trailer or long steep climbs
Cooler blocked or not keeping up
P2760: Torque Converter Clutch Pressure Control Solenoid Control Circuit Intermittent

P2760 records a converter clutch control circuit that drops out now and then and recovers by itself. Ford names it in its 2024 OBD summary as the circuit-intermittent result of the TCC solenoid, written as P0740 with failure byte 1F; its electrical check compares the driver feedback with the commanded state and reacts when they disagree for 1.5 seconds.
Loose or spread terminal at the case connector
Wire chafing intermittently against a bracket
Lockup drops out briefly, felt as an rpm flare
Fault not reproducible in the workshop
Warning lamp may come and go
P2761: Torque Converter Clutch Pressure Control Solenoid Control Circuit/Open

P2761 says the TCM has lost continuity to the converter clutch pressure solenoid. GM documents the check in its six-speed TCM tables (16OBDG08 for the MW7 unit in Silverado/Sierra, 18OBDG04 for the T87A): with the driver switched off, an impedance of 173 kΩ or more counts as open, while 9.6 kΩ or less does not; after three hardware counts an intrusive test o…
Broken wire or backed-out pin to the solenoid
Internal controller fault (Ram 6.7 l ECM capacitor leak)
MIL on after two trips (GM Type B)
Higher cruise rpm and fuel use
P2762: Torque Converter Clutch Pressure Control Solenoid Control Circuit Range/Performance

P2762 covers a solenoid circuit that is neither open nor shorted but does not behave as commanded. In GM's six-speed TCM tables for the MW7 (2016) and T87A (2018) the module compares desired with measured solenoid current; a gap of 0.5 A or more in at least 40 of fewer than 80 samples sets the code as Type B, with battery voltage above 10 V.
Solenoid coil resistance out of specification
Weak supply voltage or poor ground at the TCM
Current sensing fault inside the TCM
Shudder at light throttle in higher gears
Warning lamp depending on application (GM T76 none)
P2763: Torque Converter Clutch Pressure Control Solenoid Control Circuit High
P2763 means the control circuit of the lockup pressure solenoid reads high. GM's 2018 T87A table treats it as a short to power, at 1.16 Ω or less to a voltage source while the driver is on, Type B.
Moisture in the valve-body connector (Subaru TR580)
Control wire shorted to battery voltage
Open circuit where the maker includes it in this code (GM T76/T54)
No converter lockup, higher cruise rpm
Other solenoid high codes at the same time (Subaru)
P2764: Torque Converter Clutch Pressure Control Solenoid Control Circuit Low

P2764 is the low counterpart of P2763: the lockup solenoid circuit is pulled toward ground. GM's 2018 T87A table defines it as 0.01 Ω or less to vehicle ground, checked while the driver is off every 6.25 ms.
Solenoid winding shorted to its housing
Failed torque converter when the solenoid tests good (FCA 62TE)
No lockup and higher fuel consumption
MIL after one trip on some GM units
P2765: Input/Turbine Shaft Speed Sensor B Circuit

P2765 is the circuit code of a second input speed sensor, B, and what B measures varies. On Ford's DPS6 dual-clutch box (2012) it is the input shaft 2 sensor for reverse and the even gears, faulted when the TCM hardware detects a circuit failure.
Moisture or corrosion at the sensor B connector pins
Defective sensor B or integrated sensor module inside the gearbox
Open or shorted wiring between sensor and TCM
Check engine light and gearbox malfunction message
Limp-home mode, sometimes without reverse or even gears
Slow take-off and no torque converter lock-up
P2766: Input/Turbine Shaft Speed Sensor B Circuit Range/Performance
P2766 marks a sensor B signal that is present but erratic or implausible. Ford's 2012 strategy applies it to the DPS6 dual-clutch box, where sensor B reads input shaft 2.
Sensor B fouled with metal debris or not seated firmly
Interference or poor ground on the signal circuit
TCM fault keeping the code stored permanently
Check engine light after two drives
P2767: Input/Turbine Shaft Speed Sensor B Circuit No Signal

P2767 reports that pulses from sensor B are missing. Ford's DPS6 dual-clutch box of 2012 checks input shaft 2 for lack of signal under this code, alongside P2765 for circuit faults and P2766 for erratic readings.
Connector or terminal letting go, open signal wire
Sensor B failed with no output
P2768: Input/Turbine Shaft Speed Sensor B Circuit Intermittent

P2768 stands for a sensor B signal that drops out or jumps only now and then. Audi bulletin 2067653/9 (2024) covers 2020–24 A4, A5, A6, A7 and Q5 models with gearboxes built from 15 June 2020 to 30 November 2023: if P276800 is stored as passive/sporadic, alone or with P071800, control unit J217 or, where not sold separately, the mechatronic unit is replaced;…
Transmission control unit fault on affected production batches
Loose contact or damaged wire in the sensor B circuit
Electrical noise producing false speed spikes
Limp mode, loss of power or no reverse gear
P2769: P2769 reports a low level on the converter clutch circuit, in practice a short to ground. It belongs to the P0740 family for converters with a single TCC solenoid, unlike P2764, which refers to a dedicated pressure control solenoid.
TCC control wire pinched or chafed to ground
Damaged internal transmission harness or lead frame
Higher rpm and fuel use at highway speed
P276A: Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump B Motor Supply Voltage Circuit/Open

P276A means the power feed to the motor of a second electric transmission fluid pump, labelled B, is interrupted. Such pumps keep hydraulic pressure or lubrication alive when the engine-driven pump is idle, for instance during stop-start or in a dual-clutch gearbox. No manufacturer documents P276A publicly.
Blown fuse in the pump supply
Broken supply wire or relay contact
Reduced performance or limp mode in some designs
P276B: Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump B Motor Supply Voltage Circuit Low

P276B is set when the supply voltage reaching the motor of auxiliary transmission pump B sags below its lower limit. Audi names this code in bulletin 34-17-25 (revision of September 2017) covering 2017 A4/A5/A6 models and the 2018 Q5 fitted with the 0CJ, 0CK or 0CL twin-clutch gearbox.
High resistance in supply or ground of the pump
Low system voltage from a weak battery
Rattle noise from under the vehicle (Audi)
P276C: Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump B Motor Supply Voltage Circuit High

P276C flags an excessive voltage on the motor supply of auxiliary pump B. Either the circuit is shorted to another powered line, the pump module measures wrongly, or the vehicle charging system itself overshoots. No manufacturer documents P276C publicly.
Supply wire shorted to another powered circuit
Faulty measurement in the pump control electronics
Other overvoltage codes if charging is at fault
P276D: Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump B Motor Current

P276D is the general current code for the motor of auxiliary transmission pump B: the measured current does not fit the commanded speed or load, without the module saying whether it is too low or too high. The narrower siblings P276E and P276F carry that distinction, and P0C26 is the same check for pump A. No manufacturer documents P276D publicly.
Worn bearings or binding impeller in pump B
Poor ground or connector resistance at the pump
P276E: Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump B Motor Current Low

P276E tells you that the motor of a second electric transmission fluid pump, called B, takes less current than its commanded duty would require. A small draw usually means the motor is not really working: a broken winding, worn brushes, extra resistance in the feed or ground, or an impeller spinning freely because it has no fluid to move.
Worn brushes or open winding in the pump B motor
Corroded connector or high-resistance feed/ground to the pump
Low fluid level so the impeller runs without load
Faulty current measurement in the pump controller or TCM
Check engine or transmission warning lamp
Delayed or harsh drive engagement after an engine restart
P276F: Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump B Motor Current High

P276F is stored when the motor of auxiliary pump B pulls more current than the module allows. Excess draw points to a motor that is working too hard or is electrically damaged: a dragging bearing, debris or varnish in the pump, very cold thick fluid, a partially shorted winding or a chafed lead touching ground. No manufacturer documents P276F publicly.
Dragging bearing or debris inside pump B
Chafed pump lead shorting to ground
Warning lamp with transmission fault message
Possible whine or rattle from the pump area
P2770: P2770 flags a high level on the torque converter clutch circuit, meaning a short to the battery supply on the TCC solenoid or its wiring. Ford documents it in the 2024 OBD summary for the 6R80, 6R140, 10R60/10R80 and the 8F front-drive families: P2770 corresponds to UDS P0740_12, while P0740_13 covers an open line and P2769 (P0740_11) a short to ground.
TCC circuit chafed against a powered wire
Damaged or contaminated transmission case connector
Internal short in the TCC solenoid
Faulty TCC output driver in the TCM/PCM
No converter lockup, higher rpm at highway speed
Higher fuel consumption and fluid temperature
P2771: Four Wheel Drive (4WD) Low Switch Circuit

P2771 concerns the input that reports whether the transfer case sits in its low range. GM uses it on 2016 Silverado/Sierra with the MW7 gearbox as a plausibility test in the TCM: if the switch says high range while gear ratio math says low, or the reverse, for at least 0.5 s with fluid between 20 and 130 °C, the Type B code sets.
Loose tone wheel or moving output shaft in the transfer case (GM PIP4966B)
Transfer case shift actuator damaged, e.g. by water through the breather (Toyota Tacoma)
Low-range switch or position encoder defective
Damaged wiring or corroded connector between switch and control module
Check engine light, often together with a flashing 4WD indicator
Erratic speedometer or ABS warning when a speed signal is affected
Low range not engaging, or transfer case disengaging under load
P2772: Four Wheel Drive (4WD) Low Switch Circuit Range/Performance
P2772 flags a low-range switch whose signal is electrically valid but does not fit what the drivetrain is actually doing. No manufacturer documents P2772 publicly.
Low-range switch or encoder worn or out of adjustment
Range shift not completed (shift fork, actuator or linkage)
Output or turbine speed signal distorted, so the calculated range is wrong
Flashing 4WD indicator or range message on the cluster
Low range refused or engaged only after several attempts
P2773: Four Wheel Drive (4WD) Low Switch Circuit Low
P2773 is stored when the signal line of the low-range switch stays below its permitted voltage band, typically because it is pulled to ground. No manufacturer documents P2773 publicly.
Signal wire chafed through and shorted to ground
Moisture in shift actuator or connector (Toyota Tacoma breather issue)
4WD indicator flashing and warning light on
Low range cannot be selected or is reported permanently
P2774: Four Wheel Drive (4WD) Low Switch Circuit High

P2774 reports that the low-range switch input sits above its valid voltage range. With a pulled-up signal line this usually points to an open circuit, a broken ground at the switch or a short to battery voltage.
Open signal or ground wire, connector unplugged at the transfer case
Signal wire shorted to battery voltage
Low range not recognised after selection
P2775: P2775 covers an upshift paddle or tip switch whose voltage is electrically possible but belongs to neither of its two legal states. GM's twin-clutch TCM tables for 2023 and 2024 read the plus paddle as an analogue input: pressed should give 2.2–3.52 V, released 3.826–4.744 V.
Worn or dirty contacts or drifting coding resistor in the paddle
Added resistance in the clock spring or steering wheel connector
Moisture or spilled liquid in the switch
Upshift paddle has no effect, manual mode unavailable
Message on the cluster, normally no check engine light
P2776: P2776 means the upshift switch input has dropped below the lowest voltage the module accepts. In GM's 2023 twin-clutch TCM the TAPUP input is supposed to stay above 2.519 V even with the paddle pulled; a lower reading, held for at least 150 ms with battery voltage between 8.75 and 18 V and the engine not cranking, sets P2776 as Type C without MIL.
Signal wire shorted to ground, e.g. in the clock spring area
Liquid in switch or connector creating a leak path to ground
Upshift paddle or tip function inoperative
Manual mode message, no check engine light on GM
P2777: P2777 is the over-voltage counterpart for the upshift switch. GM's 2023 twin-clutch TCM watches the TAPUP input and counts up a timer once it exceeds 4.774 V; after 150 ms above that limit, with supply voltage in the 8.75–18 V band, the code is logged as Type C, so no MIL.
Open signal or ground circuit, steering wheel connector loose
Broken track in the clock spring
Signal wire shorted to a voltage source
Driver information message about manual shifting
P2778: P2778 is meant for an upshift switch signal that jumps around or drops out briefly instead of staying in one state. No manufacturer documents P2778 publicly.
Clock spring track cracked, opening at certain steering angles
Loose terminal or poor crimp in the column or wheel connector
Worn or bouncing contact in the paddle
Fault comes and goes, often depending on steering angle
P2779: P2779 is the plausibility fault of the downshift paddle or tip switch. GM's 2023 and 2024 TCM tables for the twin-clutch gearbox define two voltage windows for the minus paddle: 2.2–3.52 V when pulled and 3.826–4.744 V at rest. A reading caught between or around these windows for 120 s is treated as invalid and logged as Type C, no MIL.
Corroded contacts or drifting coding resistor in the minus paddle
Added resistance in the clock spring
Corrosion in the steering wheel connector
Manual mode refused, usually no MIL
P277A: Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump B Hydraulic Leakage
P277A is not an electrical fault. The motor of auxiliary pump B runs, yet the oil it delivers escapes before pressure can build, so the module concludes that the hydraulic path around the pump leaks.
Damaged pump seal or O-ring at the pump mounting
Low transmission fluid level letting the pump draw air
Check valve in the pump circuit not sealing
Worn valve body bores causing internal leakage
Stop-start disabled or rough engine restarts
Warning lamp, possibly fluid traces under the gearbox
P277B: Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump B Driver Circuit Performance
P277B concerns the power stage that energises the motor of auxiliary pump B, wherever it sits: inside a separate pump controller or in the transmission module.
Failing output stage in the pump controller or TCM
Poor ground or low system voltage at the driver
Pump motor loading the driver abnormally
Loose or corroded pins between driver and pump
P277C: Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump B Motor Stalled

P277C means the motor of auxiliary pump B is commanded to turn but stands still or nearly so. Volvo uses it: its technical journal 36774 covers 2024–2027 mild-hybrid S60, S90, V60/V90 Cross Country, XC40, XC60 and XC90 models with the Aisin TG-81SC eight-speed, where the TCM stores P277C07.
Jammed impeller or seized pump bearing
Known hardware issue in early gearboxes (Volvo TG-81SC before the serial break)
Pump lost prime because of low fluid
One-off detection without a real fault
Transmission warning message in the cluster
Shifts too early, too late or erratic
P277D: Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump B Motor Over Temperature

P277D reports that the motor or the integrated electronics of auxiliary pump B have become too hot. Pumps of this kind measure their own temperature and stop before damage occurs; the code records that protective shutdown.
Long high-load operation in hot conditions
Mechanical drag raising motor current and heat
Faulty temperature sensing in the pump electronics
Stop-start temporarily unavailable, especially in hot weather
P277E: Clutch A Unexpected Mechanical Gear Disengagement
P277E reports that a gear on the shaft served by clutch A dropped out of engagement by itself while that clutch was carrying the drive, without any shift being commanded.
Worn shift-fork detent or rounded engagement teeth on an odd gear
Shift rod drifting due to internal hydraulic leakage or a weak actuator
Fork end positions not relearned after repair or module replacement
Faulty shaft speed signal making a slip appear at the synchronizer
Sudden loss of drive as if the gearbox had shifted into neutral
Odd gears locked out, limp mode with reduced gear choice
Warning lamp and transmission message in the cluster
P277F: Clutch B Unexpected Mechanical Gear Disengagement
P277F is the even-gear twin of P277E: the controller has found that a gear carried by the shaft of clutch B lost its engagement on its own while the car was driving through that clutch.

Wrong or missing fork position learning after repair
Momentary loss of drive in an even gear
Even gears unavailable, gearbox skips between odd gears
Warning lamp with stored transmission fault
P2780: P2780 tells you the downshift switch voltage has fallen under its lower limit. GM's twin-clutch TCM (tables 23OBDG07 and 24OBDG07) checks the TAPDN input against 2.519 V; if the signal stays under that mark for 150 ms while the supply is inside 8.75–18 V and the starter is not engaged, P2780 is logged as Type C, no MIL.

P2781: P2781 sets when the downshift switch input climbs above its upper voltage limit. TCM software reporting a false permanent code (2021 Corvette, N212350930)

Broken track in the clock spring
Permanent code shown at an emissions inspection although the paddle works (software case)
P2782: P2782 targets a downshift switch signal that flickers, bounces or vanishes for moments. No manufacturer documents P2782 publicly.
Clock spring losing contact at certain steering angles
Loose pin in the steering column connector
Bouncing or worn contact in the minus paddle
P2783: P2783 warns that the torque converter is at risk of overheating. Ford's 2012 OBD summary shows one concrete use in its 6F front-drive six-speed. TCC control valve stuck in the apply position
Debris or varnish in the valve body
Restricted converter or cooler oil flow
P2784: P2784 belongs to transmissions with two input or turbine speed sensors whose readings can be compared. When both are healthy their values agree, or differ only by a known ratio; P2784 is set when they drift apart for longer than the module tolerates while each circuit on its own looks fine.

One sensor giving a weak or distorted signal
Damaged tone wheel or excessive air gap
Signal interference from poor shielding or connectors
P2785: P2785 indicates that the actuator which opens and closes the clutch has become hotter than the controller allows.
Long creeping, repeated hill starts or towing in slow traffic
Stiff release bearing or lever forcing high actuator current
Worn actuator motor or blocked actuator pump
Faulty temperature sensing or outdated control software
Gearbox warning and request to stop or let the system cool
Reduced engine torque or harsh, delayed take-off
Vehicle may refuse to engage a gear until cooled
P2786: Gear Shift Actuator Temperature Too High

P2786 is stored when the drive that moves the shift forks inside an automated gearbox runs too hot. Very frequent shifting, e.g. manual mode on hilly roads or in traffic
Binding shift fork, selector shaft or linkage raising actuator load
Worn shift actuator motor or low hydraulic pressure in the shift unit
Temperature model or software error in the gearbox controller
Shifts refused or delayed, gearbox stays in current gear
Transmission warning in the instrument cluster
Gearbox may select neutral and only restart after cooling
P2787: P2787 means the controller has calculated or measured a temperature for clutch A above its permitted limit. Two quite different uses are documented.
Clutch slipping because its actuator or actuator pump does not deliver full force
On all-wheel-drive couplings, damaged front differential forcing constant slip
Repeated launches, creeping or towing with high clutch slip
Worn friction lining reducing torque capacity
Overheating message, odd gears or all-wheel drive unavailable
MIL or transmission warning lamp on
Shudder or slipping when pulling away
P2788: Auto Shift Manual Adaptive Learning at Limit
P2788 is the system-level code for an automated manual gearbox whose learned correction values have reached the end of their allowed range.
Worn clutch moving the bite point beyond the learnable range
Basic setting or relearn skipped after clutch, actuator or module work
Worn or sticking shift and clutch actuators changing their travel
Outdated software or implausible engine torque signal
Jerky take-off and harsh or slow shifts
Clutch slip or engine flare during shifts
P2789: Clutch A Adaptive Learning at Limit
P2789 says the controller has pushed its learned fill or pressure corrections for a clutch to the edge of the permitted window and still cannot reach the shift quality it aims for.
Outdated transmission calibration needing a reflash
Engine reports torque inaccurately, so clutch adaptation drifts
Worn clutch plates or leaking clutch piston seals
Degraded fluid or a sluggish pressure control solenoid
Check Transmission or warning lamp on
Engine flare or slip during upshifts
Harsh or delayed engagement of the affected clutch
P278A: P278A is the general circuit fault of the kickdown switch, the contact at the end of accelerator pedal travel that asks the transmission for the lowest possible gear. No manufacturer documents P278A publicly.
Kickdown switch in or under the pedal defective
Wiring or connector of the pedal module damaged
Kickdown message missing on the data bus (networked designs)
No forced downshift at full throttle
P278B: P278B describes a kickdown switch whose state contradicts the pedal position. No manufacturer documents P278B publicly. The obvious cross-check is the accelerator pedal sensor: a switch reporting kickdown at part throttle, or staying open although the pedal is pressed to the stop, is implausible.
Kickdown switch misadjusted or detent worn
Floor mat or object preventing full pedal travel
Pedal position sensor offset so that both signals disagree
Kickdown missing at the pedal stop
P278C: P278C is recorded when the kickdown switch line reads lower than the module allows. No manufacturer documents P278C publicly, and many modern pedals have no electrical kickdown contact at all, as Mazda notes for the 2024 CX-90.
Signal wire shorted to ground at the pedal bracket
Water from the footwell in the connector
Kickdown always or never active, depending on circuit
Unexpected downshifts or lack of downshift at full throttle
P278D: P278D means the kickdown switch circuit shows a voltage above its permitted maximum. No manufacturer documents P278D publicly. With the usual pull-up input this is the reading of an interrupted line: the pedal module unplugged after a repair, a broken wire at the hinge of a floor-mounted pedal, or a missing ground at the switch.
Open signal or ground wire, pedal module unplugged
Signal wire shorted to battery voltage
P278E: P278E stands for a kickdown switch signal that drops out or toggles irregularly. No manufacturer documents P278E publicly; the monitoring idea follows CARB's call for circuit checks on inputs, and Eaton's Endurant HD diagnostics show the networked equivalent, where a kickdown message that is invalid or absent for 5 s is logged as fault 167.
Bouncing switch contact due to worn detent
Wire strands breaking where the harness flexes with the pedal
P278F: Clutch B Adaptive Learning at Limit

P278F flags that the learned values for clutch B have run out of room. In a dual-clutch gearbox this is usually the clutch for the even gears; the controller keeps adjusting its touch point and pressure or travel so that handovers between the two clutches stay seamless, and stores the code once a correction hits its end stop.
Worn clutch B lining or plates shifting the touch point
Clutch adaptation not reset or relearned after repair
Clutch B actuator or release mechanism sticking or losing pressure
Outdated software or inaccurate engine torque information
Shudder or slip when an even gear takes over
Rough or slow shifts between gears
P2790: P2790 is the basic circuit fault for the signal that tells the controller in which direction the selector mechanism is moving across the gate, that is sideways between the shift lanes of the H pattern.
Open wire or loose, corroded connector at the select sensor
Failed select direction sensor or select actuator electronics
Fault in the shift lever module where it supplies the signal
Defective input stage in the transmission controller
Gear changes refused or gearbox stuck in one gear
Vehicle may not move off from standstill
P2791: P2791 is set when the gate select direction signal sits below the lowest value the controller accepts. For a voltage-type sensor this usually points to a short to ground on the signal wire, a missing reference supply or a sensor pulling the line down internally; with switch-type inputs the contact may read as permanently closed to ground.
Signal wire chafed and shorted to ground
Sensor reference voltage missing or shorted
Select direction sensor failed with low output
No change between shift lanes, limited gear choice
Gearbox holds the current gear or selects neutral
P2792: P2792 reports a gate select direction signal stuck above its valid band. Common reasons are a short between the signal line and a supply voltage, a broken sensor ground that lets the input float up, or an open signal wire on inputs with an internal pull-up resistor; a sensor with a failed output stage can also hold the line high.
Signal wire shorted to a supply voltage
Broken sensor ground or open signal line pulled up internally
Select direction sensor failed with high output
Sideways selection blocked, shifts possible only in one lane

P2793: P2793 covers the circuit that reports the shift direction, the fore-and-aft movement along a lane that actually engages or releases a gear, as opposed to the sideways lane choice monitored by P2790.
