P282B: P282B covers electrical faults at solenoid K when the module does not break them down into open, low or high.
Broken coil winding in valve K
Damaged internal conductor in the mechatronic unit
P282C: P282C is intended for an intermittent problem at solenoid K. No manufacturer publishes a description; CARB 13 CCR 1968.2 requires monitoring of transmission actuators without prescribing a separate code for sporadic faults.
Weak pin tension or unlatched connector
Heat-related dropout of the coil or internal lead
P282D: Pressure Control Solenoid K Control Circuit/Open
P282D marks an open control circuit of solenoid K. GM's 2023 Corvette dual-clutch software applies it to the selector pilot valve.
Broken wire to the selector pilot valve
Terminal pushed back in the connector
P282E: Pressure Control Solenoid K Control Circuit Range/Performance

P282E is meant for a solenoid K control circuit whose behaviour strays from what the TCM expects although there is no clean open or short. No manufacturer documents it publicly, and CARB 13 CCR 1968.2 states the monitoring duty only in general form.
Poor ground or supply to the driver stage
Weak output stage in the TCM
P282F: Pressure Control Solenoid K Control Circuit Low

P282F reports a ground fault on the control line of solenoid K. On the 2023 Corvette, GM checks the selector pilot valve while its low-side output is switched on; the TCM compares the voltage at the sense pin with a lower limit of about 1.7 V, and a reading below it points to a ground short.
Control wire to valve K shorted to ground
Damaged insulation inside the transmission harness
Coil of valve K shorted to ground internally
Gears on one clutch shaft blocked
MIL on in the same trip
P2830: Pressure Control Solenoid K Control Circuit High

P2830 is set when the K control line carries voltage where the switched-on low-side driver should pull it down. GM applies it to the selector pilot valve of the 2023 Corvette dual-clutch box with a limit that climbs as supply voltage increases, from about 0.7 V below 11.5 V to 1.1 V above 15.5 V, confirmed after 100 ms.
Control wire shorted to a supply line
Short to an adjacent solenoid output
P2831: P2831 is the general circuit code for the position signal of shift fork A in automated manual and dual-clutch gearboxes. How makers fill it varies widely. Mercedes-Benz uses P283100 for an electrical fault of the shift fork A position sensor in the 8G-DCT (transmission 724.1) and lists it among the codes of its guided repair tool.
Shift fork A position sensor electrically defective
Fault in the module's motor current controller (Ford DPS6)
Poor contact at the sensor or module connector
Transmission warning, gear display may flash
Odd gears unavailable or limp-home mode
Delayed engagement or no drive when starting off
P2832: Shift Fork A Position Circuit Range/Performance
P2832 means the fork A position reading is electrically valid but disagrees with what the gearbox is doing.
Sensor magnet or mounting shifted on the shift rod
Learned fork positions no longer valid after repair or wear
Shift rod, fork or drum binding mechanically
Gear on the odd shaft not engaged or dropped
Clunks or long pauses during shifts
P2833: Shift Fork A Position Circuit Low

P2833 reports a fork A position signal stuck at the low end. On the Corvette dual-clutch gearbox the rod 1 sensor sends a pulse-width signal; GM's 2023 table sets the code when no pulses arrive and the pin stays under 2.0 V, or when the duty cycle drops below 8 %, each confirmed for 150 ms, with the 5 V sensor supply in range and rated Type A.
Signal wire of the fork A sensor shorted to ground
Open signal line letting the input float low
Gears of one shaft locked out
Car may only pull away in a fallback gear
P2834: Shift Fork A Position Circuit High
P2834 is the high-side counterpart: the fork A position input sits at the upper limit.
Signal wire shorted to the 5 V sensor supply or battery voltage
Sensor output transistor no longer pulling low
Shifts on the affected shaft blocked
P2835: Shift Fork A Position Circuit Intermittent

P2835 covers a fork A position signal that is present but unsteady. GM's 2023 Corvette dual-clutch table checks the carrier frequency of the rod 1 sensor and sets a Type A fault once it leaves the 1500 to 2500 Hz band for 150 ms; Ford's 2024 summary calls the same check on the TR9070 frequency out of range.
Intermittent contact at the sensor or module connector
Interference or damaged shielding on the signal line
Faulty Hall sensor in the shift drum motor (Ford DPS6)
Warning lamp that comes and goes
Hesitation or no drive when pulling away
P2836: P2836 is the umbrella circuit code for the shift fork B position input. Mercedes-Benz stores P283600 when its 8G-DCT dual-clutch transmission (724.1) detects an electrical defect at the fork B sensor and includes it in the code set evaluated by its Intelligent Predictive Repair routine in XENTRY.
Electrical defect in the fork B position sensor (Mercedes 8G-DCT)
Failed current-control chip for the second shift drum motor in the TCM (Ford DPS6)
Corroded or loose contacts between sensor and module
Gears of fork B skipped or unavailable
Delayed engagement from Park or no drive (Ford DPS6)
P2837: Shift Fork B Position Circuit Range/Performance
P2837 flags a fork B position reading that is electrically sound but contradicts the gearbox state. GM's Corvette summary from 2023 maps fork B to rod 2 on the odd-gear shaft.
Learned rod 2 positions no longer matching after repair or wear
Rod, fork or synchronizer binding so the gear does not engage or release cleanly
Sensor magnet or carrier loose on the rod
Blocked second shift drum motor (Ford DPS6)
Gear jumps out or is not engaged on fork B
Noticeable pause or clunk while the gearbox retries the shift
Warning lamp and limited gear selection
P2838: Shift Fork B Position Circuit Low

P2838 is stored when the fork B position input reads at the bottom of its range. The Corvette's rod 2 sensor, fed by GM from the same 5 V reference A as rod 1, has to send a pulse-width signal; if pulses are missing while the pin is below 2.0 V, or the duty cycle drops under 8 %, the module waits 150 ms and logs a Type A fault.
Fork B sensor signal wire chafed through to ground
Sensor output no longer producing pulses
Break in the signal or supply wire leaving the input low
Warning lamp with transmission in limp-home mode
Gears on rod 2 or fork B no longer selected
Rough or delayed shifts around the locked-out gears
P2839: Shift Fork B Position Circuit High

P2839 covers the other end of the scale: the fork B input is pinned high. GM's 2023 Corvette table for rod 2 sets it when pulses stop and the pin carries more than 3.5 V, or once the duty cycle passes 92 %.
Signal wire of the fork B sensor touching the 5 V or battery supply
Open sensor ground letting the output float high
Sensor output stage stuck in the high state
Warning lamp and fault message in the cluster
Fork B gears blocked, fewer gears available
Reduced acceleration in the substitute program
P283A: Shift Fork B Position Circuit Intermittent

P283A means the fork B signal is arriving, but not cleanly. For rod 2 of the Corvette dual-clutch gearbox GM measures the period of the sensor carrier and reacts once the equivalent frequency drops below 1500 Hz or rises above 2500 Hz for 150 ms, logging a Type A fault.
Loose or spread terminal in the fork B sensor connector
Electrical noise coupling into the signal line through damaged shielding
Faulty Hall element in the second shift drum motor (Ford DPS6)
Sporadic warning lamp that clears after a restart
Intermittent engagement problems when pulling away (Ford DPS6)
P283B: P283B is the generic circuit code for the shift fork C position sensor. The only public manufacturer listing that uses it comes from Mercedes-Benz: on the 8G-DCT dual-clutch transmission (724.1) P283B00 stands for an electrical fault of the fork C sensor and belongs to the codes covered by its XENTRY repair routine for this gearbox.
Fork C position sensor with an internal electrical fault
Poor contact or moisture at the sensor or TCM connector
Damaged sensor input in the transmission control module
Transmission warning in the instrument cluster
Gears handled by fork C no longer engaged
P283C: Shift Fork C Position Circuit Range/Performance
P283C is the plausibility code for fork C, which GM's 2023 Corvette table assigns to rod 3 on the even-gear shaft.
Rod 3 creeping out of position because of worn detent or fork
Position values not relearned after gearbox or sensor work
Synchronizer actuation on the even shaft not reaching target position
Even gears drop out or refuse to engage
Grinding or a knock during shifts on the even shaft
Warning lamp, gearbox limits gear choice
P283D: Shift Fork C Position Circuit Low

P283D reports the fork C input stuck low. In the Corvette dual-clutch gearbox GM feeds the rod 3 sensor from reference B rather than reference A, so its enable test watches that second 5 V rail and pauses while P0652 or P0653 are present.
Fork C signal line shorted to ground in the gearbox harness
Fork C sensor no longer switching its output
Damaged supply wire from reference B to the sensor
Possibly further fork D codes if the shared supply is affected
P283E: Shift Fork C Position Circuit High

P283E is the high-side fault of the fork C circuit. GM's 2023 summary checks the Corvette rod 3 sensor for two signs: no pulses at all with the pin above 3.5 V, and a duty cycle above 92 %. Either one, held for 150 ms with reference B in its 4.5 to 5.5 V window and the engine not cranking, stores a Type A code.
Pinched harness with the fork C signal touching a feed wire
Water in the connector bridging signal and supply pins
Fork C sensor without ground connection
Warning lamp and gearbox fault message
Jerky driving in the substitute program
P283F: Shift Fork C Position Circuit Intermittent

P283F stands for an unstable fork C position signal rather than a hard short or open. The rod 3 sensor in GM's Corvette dual-clutch gearbox runs at a carrier between 1500 and 2500 Hz; if the measured period puts it outside that band for 150 ms, the module records a Type A fault, as long as reference B and battery voltage are valid.
Fork C connector working loose under engine movement
Cracked insulation near hot components letting noise in
Occasional stutter or delay on even-gear shifts
Warning lamp appears only now and then
P2840: P2840 is the overall circuit code for the shift fork D position input. Mercedes-Benz is the one maker that publicly documents it: in the 8G-DCT (transmission 724.1) of its compact models, P284000 marks an electrical fault of the fork D sensor, and the gearbox has a fifth fork E with its own codes from P2863 upward.
Electrical failure of the fork D position sensor
Damaged wiring between fork D sensor and the TCM
Transmission control module input or software fault
Gears of fork D withheld, gearbox skips them
Reduced driving comfort in emergency mode
P2841: Shift Fork D Position Circuit Range/Performance

P2841 indicates that fork D reports a believable voltage but an implausible position. GM's 2023 table runs the rod 4 consistency test in the Corvette only when neither the even-clutch speed signal nor the output speed signal has shown an electrical fault for at least 100 ms, so the comparison has trustworthy speeds behind it.
Rod 4 or its synchronizer sticking so the fork lags behind the command
Outdated learned positions after a clutch or sensor replacement
Fork D sensor or magnet shifted in its mount
Hesitation or repeated attempts on even-gear shifts
Gear not held, slipping back to neutral
Warning lamp with reduced gear range
P2842: Shift Fork D Position Circuit Low

P2842 sets when the fork D sensor signal collapses toward zero. GM's 2023 Corvette table expects a pulse train from the rod 4 sensor and flags the circuit if pulses vanish with less than 2.0 V present, or if the duty cycle is lower than 8 %, both held for 150 ms; the resulting fault is Type A.
Fork D signal wire shorted to ground or housing
No 5 V feed reaching the sensor
Warning lamp, fork D gears blocked
Additional fork C code if the shared feed is at fault
P2843: Shift Fork D Position Circuit High

P2843 means the fork D position line is sitting near supply level. GM's 2023 Corvette table raises it for rod 4 when there is no pulse activity and more than 3.5 V on the pin, or when the duty cycle is above 92 %; after a 150 ms confirmation a Type A code is set.
Fork D signal wire in contact with a feed wire
Open ground circuit of the fork D sensor
Internal short in the sensor pulling its output high
Some even gears no longer selected
P2844: Shift Fork D Position Circuit Intermittent

P2844 points to a fork D signal whose timing wanders. GM's Corvette dual-clutch software derives the rod 4 sensor frequency from its period and expects 1500 to 2500 Hz; leaving that window for 150 ms stores a Type A fault, and the check is skipped while cranking or with reference B out of tolerance.
Chafed or loose harness section shared with the fork C sensor
Intermittent terminal contact at the fork D sensor
Sensor with an unstable output frequency
Warning lamp that may go out again
P2845: Shift Fork A Position Sensor Incorrect Neutral Position Indicated

P2845 means the fork A sensor reports neutral although the gearbox state says a gear is engaged, or it reports an engaged position where neutral is expected. Public manufacturer documentation for P2845 is lacking, and CARB 13 CCR 1968.2 only asks that transmission inputs be checked for plausibility.
Neutral position not learned or lost after repair or software update
Sensor magnet or target shifted on the rod
Worn fork or detent changing the neutral position
Gear display shows N while a gear is engaged, or the reverse
Shifts refused, transmission in limp-home mode
P2846: Shift Fork B Position Sensor Incorrect Neutral Position Indicated

P2846 flags a mismatch between the neutral reading of the fork B position sensor and the gear state the transmission module expects. Either the sensor claims fork B rests in neutral while the shaft speeds prove its gear carries load, or it reports an engaged fork where the module has commanded neutral. No manufacturer publicly documents P2846.
Learned neutral position of fork B missing after repair or module replacement
Magnet or target on the fork B rod loosened or shifted
Worn detent letting fork B settle off its neutral point
Gears served by fork B refused or skipped
Gear indicator disagrees with the actual gear
P2847: Shift Fork C Position Sensor Incorrect Neutral Position Indicated

With P2847 the module has decided that the neutral signal from the fork C sensor cannot be trusted. Before a dual-clutch or automated manual box preselects a gear on a shaft, it must know that the other forks on that shaft are out; a false neutral could let two ratios mesh at once, so the module normally locks the affected gears out.
Fork C sensor or magnet repositioned during transmission work without relearn
Fork C bent, so neutral lies outside the learned band
Position sensor output drifting with temperature or age
Gears of fork C locked out, jumps between remaining ratios
Warning lamp and stored transmission code
Harsh or delayed shifts on the affected shaft
P2848: Shift Fork D Position Sensor Incorrect Neutral Position Indicated

P2848 is the neutral-plausibility code for the fourth fork. It sets when the fork D sensor signal and the logical state of that fork disagree about neutral, even though the signal itself is electrically sound.
Fork D positions not relearned after software update or repair
Sensor of fork D loose in its mount
Wear on fork pads or synchronizer sleeve shifting the rest position
P2849: P2849 says that fork A did not travel when the module ordered it to, so its gear could not be put in or taken out. The reading may be valid; the fork itself is not following the command. No manufacturer publishes a strategy for P2849, and the code relies on the CARB 13 CCR 1968.2 rule that transmission components be checked for proper function.
Shift rod of fork A seized in its bore or blocked by debris
Fork A actuator or its control valve not moving the rod
Broken fork or damaged synchronizer sleeve jamming the shift
Gear of fork A will not engage or stays engaged
Clunking or grinding during shift attempts
P284A: P284A is stored when fork B stays put although the transmission module commanded a move, for instance from neutral toward an engaged gear or back. Published strategies avoid this code.
Fork B actuator, solenoid or hydraulic supply failing to apply force
Synchronizer of fork B gears jammed or damaged
Contaminated fluid restricting the fork B actuator
Gears of fork B missing or a gear stays engaged
Rough starts or lack of drive in some gears
P284B: P284B reports a third fork that refuses to travel. Two situations matter: stuck in neutral, which merely costs the gears of fork C, and stuck in an engaged gear, which is more serious because that shaft then turns with a fixed ratio and a second gear on the same shaft must never be selected.
Selector or pilot valve not routing pressure to the fork C rod
Fork C or its rod mechanically jammed
Car stays in one gear on one shaft or skips the fork C gears
P284C: P284C applies when fork D, the fourth of the generic shift forks, fails to answer an actuation request. Whether the drive is hydraulic, as in most wet dual-clutch boxes, or electric, as in automated manuals with motor-driven drums, the module sees the request but no travel at the position sensor. No manufacturer documentation for P284C is public.
Fork D actuator motor or hydraulic valve failed
Shift drum or rod binding at fork D
Module output stage not driving the fork D actuator
Gears of fork D unavailable or stuck engaged
P284D: P284D means fork A has crept away from the position of the gear it is supposed to hold, without any shift being commanded. Several makers use it.
Gear position sensors poorly calibrated (Audi DL382/DL552)
Leaking fork A actuator or weak detent letting the rod creep
Message about a drive system fault with limited performance
First or seventh gear cannot be selected (Audi report)
Gear may jump out under load
P284E: P284E reports that fork B drifted while no shift was asked for. GM's 2023 Corvette dual-clutch table describes the test on rod 2 in detail: with no actuating force applied, the measured position must stay inside wide limits around the learned point of the gear verified as engaged by clutch-shaft and output speed readings; leaving them for 500 ms is a fault.
Synchronizer pressure valve for fork B leaking and pushing the rod
Weak detent or worn gear dog teeth on fork B gears
Gear on the odd shaft pops out or is re-engaged with a jolt
P284F: P284F covers drift of fork C away from its held gear. In GM's Corvette software this is rod 3, which sits on the shaft of the even clutch; the check compares the rod position with the learned point for the gear that the even clutch speed and the output speed confirm, and sets a Type A code once the wide limit is exceeded long enough or the drift correction k…
Residual pressure on the fork C actuator from a leaking valve
Rod 3 sensor reading offset so the fork appears to move
Worn detent or synchronizer parts at fork C
Shift flare or jerk while cruising
P2850: P2850 closes the drift series for the four main forks: fork D has shifted position although the module neither commanded a change nor applied force to it. GM uses the code for rod 4 of the Corvette dual-clutch unit, again as a Type A fault that runs continuously and hands over to the even-shaft synchronizer recovery.
Leaking synchronizer or selector valve moving the fork D rod
Positions not relearned after module or sensor replacement
Weak detent or rounded dog teeth on fork D gears
Gear of fork D slips out under load
Gears of fork D blocked, emergency program
P2851: Shift Fork Position Sensor A/B Correlation

P2851 is meant for a plausibility comparison between the position sensors of forks A and B. Both readings may be in range on their own, yet together they describe an impossible state, such as both forks engaged at once, or they move in step in a way that points to a shared supply or ground fault. No maker publishes a strategy for this pair code.
Shared supply or ground of the A and B sensors disturbed
One of the two sensors drifting while still in range
Corroded contacts at the internal transmission connector
Gears of forks A and B locked out
P2852: Shift Fork Position Sensor C/D Correlation

P2852 pairs the position sensors of forks C and D and sets when their readings do not fit together. In GM's numbering these are rods 3 and 4, both on the even shaft and fed from the second sensor reference; a reference fault there would shift both signals together.
Reference voltage feeding the C and D sensors out of tolerance
Sensor C or D reporting a shifted value
Input circuit fault in the transmission module
Gears of forks C and D unavailable
P2853: P2853 is set when the pressure measured at clutch A falls short of what the control model predicts.
Clutch A pressure control valve sticking or delivering too little
Leaking seal or piston ring in the clutch A circuit
Low fluid level or clogged filter reducing supply pressure
Weak or delayed launch, engine flares
P2854: P2854 is the even-side partner of P2853: the pressure sensor of clutch B reports less than the control model expects.
Clutch B pressure control valve restricted by debris or wear
Seal leak in the clutch B feed or piston
Foamed or overheated fluid lowering effective pressure
Even gears skipped, car runs in odd gears only
Slipping or flare on shifts into even gears
P2855: P2855 points the other way from P2853: clutch A carries more pressure than the model calls for. GM's Corvette table for clutch 1 uses three paths, all Type A.
Clutch A pressure control valve sticking toward high output
Excessive line pressure feeding the clutch circuit
Clutch adaptation values out of date after repair
Harsh engagement or jerky creep from standstill
Drag felt as if the brakes were applied
P2856: P2856 flags too much pressure at clutch B, the even-gear clutch in GM's and Ford's dual-clutch layouts.
Clutch B pressure control valve hanging in a high-pressure position
Safety shutdown valve for clutch B not venting
Clutch B pressure sensor reading high within its range
P2857: Clutch A Pressure Engagement Performance/Too Low
P2857 reports that clutch A did not build up enough holding force when the control unit asked it to engage, so the expected ratio or torque transfer never appeared.
Control valve (valve body) not delivering the commanded apply pressure to clutch A
Worn clutch A linings or leaking piston seals
Low, aerated or aged transmission fluid
Engine speed flares on take-off without matching acceleration
Hesitation or reduced power, transmission emergency mode
Warning lamp with stored transmission code
P2858: Clutch B Pressure Engagement Performance/Too Low
P2858 is the clutch B counterpart of P2857: the element that should close for the second stage never reaches the pressure needed to carry torque.
Control valve unable to raise clutch B pressure
Slip damage inside the transmission (belt, clutch B linings)
Fluid level or quality outside specification
Second stage or even gears engage late or not at all
Engine revs rise at cruising speed, acceleration lags
P2859: Clutch A Pressure Disengagement Performance/Too Low

P2859 concerns the release side of clutch A: during a ratio change the control unit sees that the pressure handover is not working as planned, so the old and new power paths overlap or the wrong ratio persists. Mitsubishi's Mirage CVT shows how this is tested.
Outgoing clutch not venting in time, so both elements carry torque
Sticking pressure control solenoid or valve in the valve body
Clutch pressure switch reporting pressure that is not there
Wrong gear stage held, engine speed too low or too high
P285A: Clutch B Pressure Disengagement Performance/Too Low

With P285A the module reports a release-side pressure fault involving clutch B. Mitsubishi's Mirage CVT evaluates it while the auxiliary gearbox is commanded into its second stage: a ratio that remains within 10 % of the first stage (1.639–2.003) for 0.5 s, or that drops to 0.500 or below or climbs to 1.500 or above for 0.2 s, sets the code.
Defective control valve, especially when P0875 is stored at the same time
Leak in the clutch B circuit preventing a clean handover
Faulty clutch pressure switch or its wiring
Upper stage or even gears not available
Flare between shifts, then a hard engagement
P285B: P285B covers the electrical drive of the actuator that moves fork A, for designs where an electric motor rather than oil pressure shifts the gears. The module sets it when the output stage sees no load, typically a broken winding, a cut lead or a connector that has backed out.
Loose, corroded or backed-out connector at the fork A actuator motor
Broken lead between transmission module and actuator motor
Open phase winding inside the actuator motor
Failed motor output stage in the transmission module
Malfunction indicator lamp and transmission warning
First, third or fifth gear not available, car may only move in the even gears
Jerky starts or refusal to pull away
P285C: P285C is the functional counterpart to the electrical fork A actuator codes. The circuit may be intact, yet the actuator does not achieve what it is asked to do: it moves too slowly, draws an unexpected current or leaves the fork short of its target. No manufacturer publishes a detection strategy for P285C.
Worn or sluggish fork A actuator motor
Shift drum, rod or fork A binding mechanically
Worn reduction gearing between motor and drum
Low supply voltage to the module during shifts
Slow or harsh shifts into the gears of fork A
Wrench or transmission warning without engine lamp
Occasional gear skipping or neutral moments
P285D: Shift Fork A Actuator Circuit Low

P285D points to a fork A actuator line pulled toward ground: a chafed motor phase touching the case, water in the connector, or a short inside the motor. To protect its driver, the module normally shuts the output down at once.
Actuator motor lead chafed through against the transmission case
Water or corrosion in the actuator connector
Internal short of a motor winding to its housing
Engine lamp on, odd gears locked out
Car starts in second gear or will not move off
P285E: Shift Fork A Actuator Circuit High

P285E is logged when a line of the fork A actuator carries supply voltage where the module expects it to be switched low. Usual explanations are a harness short to a battery-fed wire or a low-side transistor in the module that no longer turns on; with some driver designs, an unloaded output can also read high.
Actuator lead shorted to a battery-fed wire in the harness
Low-side driver in the transmission module not switching
Bridged pins in the actuator or module connector
Engine lamp lit, gears 1, 3 and 5 unavailable
Gearbox stays in an even gear or neutral
P285F: With P285F the module reports that the drive circuit of the fork B actuator is open: current cannot flow when the motor or valve is energised. In Ford's DPS6 dual-clutch box, the second shift drum is turned by its own three-phase motor and places the forks for reverse plus 2nd, 4th and 6th; an open motor circuit there is P285F and requests the MIL.
Fork B actuator connector loose or with spread terminals
Open wire in the harness to the fork B actuator
Burnt or broken winding in the fork B motor
No reverse gear, even gears missing
Engine lamp and gearbox fault message
Car drives only in 1st, 3rd and 5th with large rpm steps
P2860: P2860 says the fork B actuator is electrically present but underperforms: travel takes too long, the target position is missed, or the effort needed to move it is out of line with what the module expects. No maker has published how it detects P2860.
Stiff shift drum, rod or fork B
Fork B actuator motor with worn bearings or brushes
Debris or wear in the selector track
Delayed engagement of reverse or the even gears
Wrench lamp or gearbox message, engine lamp off
Clunk or shudder during upshifts to 2nd, 4th or 6th
P2861: Shift Fork B Actuator Circuit Low

P2861 is set when a fork B actuator line reads near ground although the module has not switched it there, the classic signature of a short to ground. Ford's 2012 DPS6 summary assigns exactly this case on the motor of the drum for reverse and the even gears to P2861, and the 2014 Ford catalogue marks it as a MIL fault.
Fork B motor lead rubbed through on a bracket or the case
Corrosion bridging a terminal to ground in the connector
Fork B motor winding shorted to its housing
Engine lamp on, only odd gears in use
P2862: Shift Fork B Actuator Circuit High
P2862 indicates that a fork B actuator line sits at or near battery voltage when it should be pulled low. In practice this is a short to a powered conductor or a module transistor that stays open.
Fork B actuator wire shorted to a powered conductor
Module output transistor for fork B stuck
Insulation melted near the exhaust or a hot component
Engine lamp, no reverse or stuck in one even gear
Large rpm jumps because only odd gears are used
P2863: P2863 is the general circuit code for the position sensor of a fifth shift fork, used where the module cannot or does not distinguish between low, high and erratic signals. Only transmissions with five forks need it, such as eight-speed dual-clutch units.
Poor contact at the fork E sensor or module connector
Fork E position sensor failed internally
Sensor reference supply shared with other sensors disturbed
Gears on fork E blocked, drive continues in remaining gears
Drive system warning in the instrument cluster
Unusual shift sequence or skipped gears
P2864: Shift Fork E Position Circuit Range/Performance

P2864 sets when the fork E position signal is electrically fine but contradicts what the shaft speeds show. GM's 2023 Corvette dual-clutch table uses it as the Type A consistency check of rod 5, which belongs to the even-gear clutch shaft.
Learned positions of rod 5 missing or outdated after repair or software update
Sensor magnet on the fork E rod shifted or loose
Synchronizer actuation valve for rod 5 sticking, so the rod barely moves
Implausible even-shaft or output speed signal misleading the check
Gears on fork E locked out, warning lamp on
Harsh or aborted shifts on the even shaft
P2865: Shift Fork E Position Circuit Low

P2865 means the fork E position input is stuck low. On GM's 2023 Corvette, whose rod 5 sensor sends a pulse-width signal, the TCM runs two Type A checks under this number: no pulses at all while the pin rests below 2000 mV, or a duty cycle under 8 %, each confirmed after 150 ms.
Fork E sensor signal wire shorted to ground
Fork E sensor with internal short or failed output stage
Sensor supply missing because of an open feed
Warning lamp with fork E gears blocked
Fault returns at once after clearing
P2866: Shift Fork E Position Circuit High

P2866 is the high-level fault of the fork E sensor input. GM's Corvette TCM, reading rod 5 as a pulse-width signal, stores it as Type A in two situations: the line delivers no pulses and stays above 3500 mV, or the duty cycle climbs past 92 %.
Fork E signal wire touching a supply voltage wire
Open ground of the fork E sensor letting the signal float high
Sensor electronics holding the output permanently high
Gears of fork E withheld, warning shown
Engine lamp after a short drive
P2867: Shift Fork E Position Circuit Intermittent

P2867 reports that the fork E sensor signal is present but unsteady. GM's Corvette TCM times each cycle of the digital rod 5 signal and sets the code, Type A, when the frequency drops below 1500 Hz or rises above 2500 Hz for at least 150 ms, with the same voltage and cranking exclusions as the low and high tests.
Loose or fretted terminal in the fork E sensor circuit
Damaged shielding letting electrical noise into the signal
Sensor electronics failing intermittently when hot
Sporadic warning, sometimes without noticeable effect
Occasional lockout of fork E gears
P2868: Shift Fork E Position Sensor Incorrect Neutral Position Indicated

P2868 concerns the neutral information from the fork E sensor. The signal is electrically valid, but the module judges that the neutral it shows does not fit the real state of the fifth fork, either neutral claimed while a gear on that fork transmits drive, or a fork that seems engaged where neutral has been commanded.
Learned neutral of fork E lost after module swap or repair
Magnet or target on the fork E rod displaced
Worn detent or bent fork moving the rest position
Gears served by fork E refused
Gear display does not match the gear actually engaged
P2869: P2869 states that fork E does not follow its commands: a gear on that fork cannot be engaged or released, although the position input itself may be working. No manufacturer publishes a strategy for P2869; the basis is the CARB 13 CCR 1968.2 requirement to check transmission components for function.
Fork E rod seized in its bore or blocked by debris
Actuator or hydraulic valve of fork E not moving the rod
Synchronizer or sleeve of fork E jammed or broken
One gear stays engaged or cannot be selected
Grinding or clunking from the gearbox
P286A: P286A flags fork E creeping out of the position that belongs to its current gear, although no shift was requested and no force is being applied.
Weak detent spring or worn detent notch on the fork E rod
Leaking synchronizer actuation valve pushing the rod
Position reference of rod 5 lost after repair
Gear on fork E jumps out or shudders under load
Unexpected reshift or brief loss of drive
Warning lamp and stored transmission code
P286B: Clutch A Pressure Engagement Too High

P286B means the pressure applied to clutch A during engagement exceeded the level the control unit had planned. A clutch pressed too hard closes abruptly, which shows up as a jolt, a harsh launch or a shunt through the driveline.
Clutch A pressure control valve sticking towards high output
Clutch adaptation values missing or wrong after repair or software update
Clutch pressure sensor reading higher than actual
Harsh launch or jolt when clutch A closes
Clunk through the driveline during shifts
P286C: Clutch A Pressure Disengagement Too High

P286C sets when clutch A still holds too much pressure while it is supposed to open. The residual force keeps the clutch dragging, so in a dual-clutch or planetary layout two power paths can briefly work against each other; the result is shudder, a braking feel during shifts or creeping with neutral selected.
Valve or exhaust passage for clutch A not venting fully
Debris or clutch material in the valve body
Pressure sensor showing residual pressure that is not real
Vehicle creeps or feels braked in neutral
P286D: Clutch A Engagement Time Performance/Too Slow

P286D sets when clutch A takes longer to engage than the control unit allows. Volvo uses it in the inverter module (IEM) of the electric rear axle drive on its T8 plug-in hybrids: the rear e-motor is coupled to the wheels through a clutch, and when coupling is too slow, electric rear drive and all-wheel drive drop out and the MIL may light.
Outdated control module calibration (Volvo IEM software)
Slow clutch fill from low, aerated fluid or a restricted feed
Internal fault of the clutch or drive unit
Electric rear drive or all-wheel drive unavailable
Delayed engagement with a pause in drive
P286E: Clutch A Engagement Time Too Fast

P286E is the opposite of P286D: clutch A reaches its engaged state sooner than the control unit expects. An overly quick engagement usually means the fill phase is being skipped, because the piston was already partly applied, the pressure control overshoots or adaptation values are too aggressive; the driver feels a bang on take-off or during shifts.
Clutch adaptation values too aggressive or not matched to new parts
Pressure control overshooting due to a sticking solenoid
Clutch piston not fully retracted before the next apply
Bang or jerk when clutch A engages
P286F: Clutch A Disengagement Time Performance/Too Slow

P286F tells that clutch A needs too long to release. Torque then keeps flowing after the control unit has ordered the clutch open, which disturbs shifts and can make the vehicle creep or stall the engine at a stop. Ford lists the code as an MIL item in its 2014 diagnostic code catalogue.
Control module software needing an update (Ford PCM/TCM, Volvo IEM)
Release mechanism or return spring of clutch A sticking
Clutch wear shifting the release point beyond the learned value
Shudder or clunk on shifts out of odd gears
Creeping or engine stalling when stopping
P2870: Clutch A Disengagement Time Too Fast

P2870 flags clutch A opening faster than the control unit intended. During a shift the outgoing clutch has to pass torque smoothly to the incoming one; if it lets go too early, engine speed flares and the shift feels like a slip followed by a thump. No manufacturer publicly documents P2870.
Leaking clutch A piston seal letting pressure drop too fast
Pressure control valve venting faster than commanded
Adaptation values not suited to the current clutch condition
Engine flare during shifts, then a thump
P2871: P2871 means clutch A does not close, or slips so much that it behaves as if open. Mitsubishi documents this for the clutch in the front transaxle of the 2023 Outlander PHEV, which links the engine to the wheels in parallel mode: once parallel mode has been active for 2 s, the PHEV-ECU counts how often the speeds before and after the clutch differ by 75 rpm o…
Worn clutch A that slips under load
Low transaxle fluid or external leak
Valve body, oil pump, pressure regulator or relief valve not supplying pressure
Control unit fault or outdated software
Engine cannot drive the wheels directly, only series or electric drive
Engine speed rises without extra thrust
P2872: P2872 is set when clutch A stays closed although it should be open. Mitsubishi's 2023 Outlander PHEV uses it for the engine clutch in the front transaxle: in EV mode, or in series mode where an open clutch would leave a large speed gap, the front motor turns at 750 rpm or more, yet input and output of the clutch differ by 8 rpm or less for 3.5 s.
Clutch A plates seized or welded together
Foreign material holding the proportional valve in the apply position
Control unit commanding or reading clutch state incorrectly
Engine turns with the wheels in EV mode, unusual noise or drag
Engine stalls when the vehicle stops
P2873: Clutch B Pressure Engagement Too High

P2873 is set when clutch B is applied with more pressure than planned while it engages. In dual-clutch designs clutch B usually carries the even gears and reverse, as in Ford's DPS6 and GM's Corvette unit, so the fault tends to surface as jerky shifts into second, fourth or reverse and a hard bite when manoeuvring.
Clutch B pressure control solenoid sticking high
Drifted or reset adaptation values for clutch B
Jerky shifts into even gears or reverse
P2874: Clutch B Pressure Disengagement Too High

P2874 indicates that clutch B keeps excess pressure while it is being released or should already be open. Clutch B then goes on carrying torque alongside the engaged path, which can be felt as binding, vibration during upshifts from even gears or a car that pulls while in neutral; an overheated clutch is a typical consequence.
Clutch B valve not venting pressure on release
Contamination in the valve body from clutch wear
Seized shutdown valve or clutch B actuator
Binding or vibration on upshifts from even gears
P2875: Clutch B Engagement Time Performance/Too Slow

P2875 tells that clutch B takes too long to grip once the control unit has asked for it. Slow filling leaves a gap in drive during shifts into the gears served by clutch B, with a flare of engine speed before the clutch finally holds.
Low or aerated fluid slowing the fill of clutch B
Partly blocked filter or valve passage
Worn seals leaking while the clutch fills
Delayed shifts into even gears with engine flare
Noticeable pause in drive during shifts
P2876: Clutch B Engagement Time Too Fast

P2876 flags clutch B closing faster than its programmed fill and apply profile allows. Instead of a smooth handover the clutch grabs abruptly, which is often noticed as a knock when selecting reverse or when a dual-clutch box shifts into an even gear. No public manufacturer document describes P2876.
Adaptation values not relearned after clutch or mechatronic work
Clutch B solenoid overshooting its target pressure
Software calibration fault in the control unit
Knock when engaging reverse or even gears
P2877: Clutch B Disengagement Time Performance/Too Slow

P2877 means clutch B releases too slowly after the command to open. While it lingers, the outgoing clutch fights the incoming one, so shifts out of even gears and reverse feel heavy, the car may shudder or the engine can be pulled down at a stop. Ford includes P2877 as an MIL code in its 2014 diagnostic code list.
Clutch B actuator or return spring not opening the clutch quickly
Clutch B wear or glazing changing the release behaviour
Restricted vent path on wet-clutch systems
Heavy or shuddering shifts out of even gears and reverse
Engine pulled down or stalling at a stop
P2878: Clutch B Disengagement Time Too Fast
P2878 reports that clutch B lets go sooner or more abruptly than the release ramp held in the control unit.
Clutch B adaptation values no longer matching the linings
Actuator position count lost or misread by the hall sensors
On wet systems a clutch B valve venting pressure too quickly
Low fluid level or aerated fluid
Brief engine flare followed by a jolt when shifting
Harsh shifts out of even gears or reverse
Warning lamp, firmer substitute shift program
P2879: P2879 is set when clutch B does not reach the torque it is asked for, or stays open altogether, so a large speed difference remains across it. No manufacturer publishes a test written for P2879.
Worn or glazed clutch B slipping under load
Insufficient apply pressure from valve body, pump or regulator
Clutch B actuator motor or its drive failed
Wiring fault or control unit not commanding the clutch
P287A: P287A means clutch B stays closed, or keeps transmitting torque, at a moment when it should be open. Ford lists P287A as an MIL code in its 2014 code catalogue.
Clutch B actuator or return spring not opening the clutch
Clutch B plates seized or welded after overheating
On wet systems a valve held in the apply position by debris
Control unit or wiring commanding apply continuously
Shudder or binding, strong pull in neutral
Engine stalls when the car stops
P287B: Shift Fork A Calibration Not Learned
P287B says that the control unit has no valid learned reference positions for shift fork A and therefore cannot place it accurately in neutral or in its gears.
TCM replaced or reprogrammed without running the fork learn
Learn routine aborted by low voltage or other fault codes
Fork A position or drum fault preventing a valid learn
Worn fork, drum groove or detent
Odd gears engage late, roughly or not at all
Learn procedure with scan tool does not complete
P287C: P287C means the transmission controller finds its trim or adaptation data missing, invalid or unfinished.
Replacement TCM installed without trim or learn data
Initial start-up or learn routine not completed
Stored data rejected after a software update
Memory fault inside the control unit
Rough or inconsistent shifts after TCM work
P287D: Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump Motor Torque Out Of Range

P287D means the motor of the electric auxiliary transmission pump produces a torque outside its expected band, as estimated by the pump controller from phase current and speed. Too little torque hints at a pump that runs dry or draws air; too much hints at a dragging rotor, cold thick fluid or a blocked passage.
Low fluid or air drawn into the auxiliary pump
Dragging pump rotor or blocked suction or delivery path
Worn pump motor or faulty integrated controller
Start-stop or electric drive no longer available
P287E: In a parallel hybrid, the engine disconnect clutch (often called K0) sits between the combustion engine and the electric motor and is opened for electric driving.
Loose, corroded or water-damaged connector at the transmission or actuator
Broken wire in the actuator feed or return line
Open coil in the clutch pressure solenoid or actuator
Failed output stage in the transmission or hybrid control module
Malfunction or transmission warning in the instrument cluster
Engine does not start or cannot drive the wheels
P287F: Engine Disconnect Clutch Actuator Circuit Range/Performance

P287F concerns the actuator of the clutch that couples the engine to the electric motor of a parallel hybrid. The circuit is not broken; instead, the electrical feedback (current, voltage or duty cycle) does not match what the control module expects for its command, or the clutch reacts to the command differently than the model predicts.
Clutch solenoid or actuator with drifting resistance or sticking spool
Low, aged or contaminated transmission fluid
Lost clutch adaptation values or outdated control software
High contact resistance at connector pins
Jerky or delayed engine engagement when switching from electric to hybrid mode
Limited hybrid functions or limp-home operation
P2880: Engine Disconnect Clutch Actuator Circuit Low

P2880 is stored when the signal in the actuator circuit of the engine disconnect clutch stays below its permitted window. In practice this usually means a short to ground on the control side, or a feed that has lost supply voltage, so that the solenoid or actuator is either energised permanently or not at all, depending on which side is affected.
Chafed control wire shorted to ground or housing
Missing supply voltage (fuse, relay, feed wire)
Internal short in the clutch solenoid coil
Faulty output stage in the control module
Engine cannot be coupled, only electric driving available
Limp-home mode after the output is switched off
P2881: Engine Disconnect Clutch Actuator Circuit High
P2881 is the counterpart to P2880: the monitored signal in the circuit of the disconnect clutch actuator is above the upper limit.
Control wire shorted to battery voltage
Open return line or missing ground on the actuator
Moisture bridging pins in the transmission connector
Faulty voltage sensing in the control module
Warning lamp with hybrid system message
P2882: P2882 means the clutch between combustion engine and electric motor slips more than allowed while it is supposed to be closed: the speed on the engine side and the speed on the motor side drift apart.
Transmission or electric drive software with faulty slip evaluation
Low transmission fluid level reducing clutch pressure
Clutch touch point not or wrongly adapted
Worn clutch plates or leaking hydraulic seal
Gearbox malfunction message in the cluster
Engine revs flare while torque on the wheels lags behind
Hybrid mode limited, more electric-only operation
P2883: Engine Disconnect Clutch Temperature Too High

P2883 protects the disconnect clutch from overheating. Most systems do not measure the friction plates directly; the control module models their temperature from slip speed, transmitted torque and fluid temperature, and sets the code when the estimate passes its limit.
Heavy load such as towing, creeping or stop-and-go on grades
Clutch slipping due to low pressure or wear
Restricted transmission fluid cooling or low fluid level
Temperature model in the control software too conservative
Warning to let the transmission cool down
Reduced power or restricted starting off
Smell of hot fluid after heavy use
P2884: P2884 reports that the disconnect clutch stays open although the control module has asked it to close, so the running engine cannot pass torque to the transmission.
Faulty clutch pressure regulating valve in the mechatronic unit
Insufficient hydraulic pressure (fluid level, pump, leak)
Mechanical damage in the clutch pack or piston
Engine runs but does not drive the vehicle
P2885: P2885 is the more general engagement code: the clutch does close, but the process does not run as planned – it takes too long, synchronisation of engine and motor speed fails, or torque arrives with a jolt. It does not claim that the clutch is permanently open or closed; those cases have P2884 and P2886.
Outdated software in hybrid, transmission or engine control module
Weak hydraulic supply, e.g. auxiliary pump or low fluid
Clutch fill and touch point adaptation out of range
Faulty speed signal on engine or motor side
Jolt or hesitation when the engine is coupled in
P2886: P2886 is the opposite failure to P2884: the control module commands the disconnect clutch to open, yet engine and electric motor keep turning together. The engine is then dragged along during electric driving, which costs range and can stall it when the vehicle stops.
Clutch control valve stuck in the apply position
Residual pressure from a blocked drain or faulty pump control
Control software misjudging the clutch state
Engine turns during electric driving or stalls when stopping
Warning lamp and restricted hybrid mode
P2887: P2887 is the general circuit code for the actuator that engages and releases the park lock in park-by-wire transmissions. It covers faults that are not specifically open, low or high, and some manufacturers use it as a base code that carries a failure-type byte.
Control software misjudging the actuator circuit
Loose, corroded or damaged actuator connector or harness
Park lock actuator or hold solenoid sticking or failed
Transmission service message or warning lamp
P cannot be selected or released reliably
P2888: P2888 flags an open circuit in the park lock actuator path: the output stage switches on but finds no load. Ford's 2024-25 OBD summary maps it, alongside P2887_13, for the 8F24, 8F35/8F40 and 8F57 front-drive automatics, and in the TR9070 dual-clutch gearbox as an open load on the parking lock hold solenoid, where it can also be reported as P2887_01.
Broken wire or backed-out terminal at the actuator connector
Open coil in the park lock actuator or hold solenoid
Output stage in the control unit not switching
Vehicle stays in P or will not accept a gear
P2889: P2889 reports that the park lock actuator circuit sits lower than it should, as a rule because the line touches ground.
Harness chafed through and shorted to ground
Moisture or corrosion in the actuator connector
Actuator coil shorted to its housing
Park lock function blocked, warning shown
P288A: P288A is set when the park lock actuator circuit reads higher than allowed, typically because it has contact with battery voltage or the load itself is shorted.
Control line shorted to a battery-voltage feed
Shorted turns in the actuator or hold solenoid coil
Shift system warning, park lock function switched off
Car stays in its last position, P or drive range
P288B: P288B means the park lock actuator is electrically intact but does not do what it is told, for example the lock fails to move in time. Ford's 2024-25 summary calls it functionally stuck off on its front-drive 8-speeds and mechanically stuck off on the TR9070 dual-clutch box.
Control software needing an update (Ford, Nissan, Audi, FCA)
Sluggish or sticking park lock actuator or pawl mechanism
Low supply voltage or poor connection under load
P cannot be selected or needs several attempts to leave
Unexpected shift to P during start-stop
P288C: Engine Disconnect Clutch Actuator Control Circuit Driver Current/Temperature Too High

P288C does not look at the clutch itself but at the electronic switch inside the control module that powers its actuator. Modern driver chips measure their own current and junction temperature; if either exceeds the limit, they shut down and report this condition.
Actuator coil or motor drawing excessive current
Partial short in the actuator wiring
Control module overheating from heat or poor cooling
Defective driver chip in the control module
Clutch actuator switched off, engine cannot be coupled
Warning lamp, often after long or hot drives
P288D: Shift Fork B Calibration Not Learned

P288D is the fork B counterpart of P287B: the stored learn values that tell the control unit where fork B or its drum sits in each gear are missing or rejected. No manufacturer documents P288D publicly, and Ford's 2014 catalogue still knew only one fork calibration code, P287B, which suggests the split into A and B came later.
Fork learn not carried out after TCM or mechatronic work
Drum B position or motor fault aborting the learn
Worn or bent fork B, worn drum groove
Reverse or even gears hesitant or unavailable
P288E: Shift Fork A Actuator Control Circuit Driver Current/Temperature Too High

P288E is a self-protection code of the output stage that powers the actuator of shift fork A. The driver reports a current above its limit or an excessive chip temperature, and the module throttles or switches off that actuator. No manufacturer documents P288E publicly.
Shorted winding or lead in the fork A actuator circuit
Binding drum or fork stalling the actuator under full current
High transmission temperature adding heat to the driver
Defective driver stage in the control unit
Odd gears do not engage, car may start in 2nd
P288F: Shift Fork B Actuator Control Circuit Driver Current/Temperature Too High

P288F tells that the driver for the shift fork B actuator has crossed its current or temperature limit, after which the TCM curbs or stops the actuator to save the electronics. Public manufacturer criteria for P288F are not available.
Short in the fork B actuator motor or its lead
Seized drum B or fork worn into its groove
Driver stage in the TCM failing
Reverse not available, even gears skipped
P2890: Some engines use the spark plug as a combustion sensor: between sparks a measuring voltage is applied, and the hot, ionised gas lets a small current flow whose shape reveals misfire and knock. P2890 is the basic circuit fault for this measurement on cylinder 1 – the module receives no usable ion signal from that cylinder at all.
Ignition coil of cylinder 1 with failed ion measuring stage
Open ion signal wire or connector between coil 1 and the processing module
Faulty ion processing module or engine control module input
MIL with reduced knock and misfire monitoring on cylinder 1
Longer cranking if cylinder identification is affected
Retarded ignition and less power as a precaution
P2891: Cylinder 1 Ion Current Sense Circuit Range/Performance
Here the ion signal of cylinder 1 is present but implausible: its level or waveform does not fit engine speed and load, or it differs clearly from the other cylinders.
Sooted, oil-fouled or worn spark plug in cylinder 1
Moisture or oil in the plug well of cylinder 1
Ion measuring stage of coil 1 drifting
Real combustion fault in cylinder 1 (mixture, compression)
MIL, sometimes together with misfire codes
Reduced power due to cautious knock control
P2892: Cylinder 1 Ion Current Sense Circuit Low

P2892 says the ion measurement of cylinder 1 delivers a signal that stays below the expected range. Electrically this points to a signal line shorted to ground or a measuring stage that no longer builds up its bias voltage; Saab, for example, applies around 120 V across the plug gap between sparks to obtain the current.
Ion signal wire of cylinder 1 shorted to ground
Coil 1 no longer generates its measuring voltage
Spark plug of cylinder 1 with leakage path through deposits
MIL and stored fault for cylinder 1
Noticeably less power from retarded ignition
P2893: Cylinder 1 Ion Current Sense Circuit High

With P2893 the ion signal from cylinder 1 sits above its plausible ceiling. A signal line touching a supply voltage is the most direct explanation; crosstalk from the ignition primary circuit or a defective evaluation stage that saturates can show the same picture.
Ion signal wire of cylinder 1 shorted to a voltage source
Internal fault in coil 1 coupling ignition voltage into the signal
Saturated input in the ion processing module
Reduced power and possibly higher fuel consumption
Knock may go unnoticed on cylinder 1
P2894: P2894 covers a general fault in the ion current circuit of cylinder 2: the processing electronics get no evaluable signal from this plug. Which physical position cylinder 2 occupies depends on the maker's numbering.
Ignition coil of cylinder 2 with dead ion measurement
Interrupted ion signal path from coil 2
Defective cylinder 2 input in the processing module
MIL with a stored cylinder 2 ion fault
Hard or longer starting in some cases
Cautious ignition timing and slightly less power
P2895: Cylinder 2 Ion Current Sense Circuit Range/Performance

P2895 is set when cylinder 2 delivers an ion signal that is electrically intact but does not behave plausibly – for example, it shows almost no combustion peak at normal load, or it scatters strongly from cycle to cycle compared with the neighbouring cylinders.
Worn or fouled spark plug in cylinder 2
Combustion fault in cylinder 2 (injector, valve, compression)
Coil 2 measuring stage drifting with temperature
MIL, sometimes with misfire code P0302
Uneven running felt mainly at idle
P2896: Cylinder 2 Ion Current Sense Circuit Low

P2896 reports a cylinder 2 ion signal that remains under its lower limit. A ground short on the line from coil 2, a cracked plug insulator that drains the measuring voltage to the cylinder head, or a coil whose bias generator has failed can all produce a near-zero reading.
Chafed ion signal wire of cylinder 2 touching ground
Cracked spark plug insulator in cylinder 2
Measuring voltage generator in coil 2 failed
MIL with ion fault on cylinder 2
Engine runs on a safe ignition map with less power
Misfire on cylinder 2 may not be detected
P2897: Cylinder 2 Ion Current Sense Circuit High

P2897 applies when the ion current reading of cylinder 2 is stuck above the range the module accepts. Typical electrical reasons are a signal line that has contacted a supply or ignition feed, a damaged coil 2 that leaks primary voltage into its measuring output, or a missing ground at the coil that shifts the reference.
Ion signal wire of cylinder 2 in contact with a voltage source
Coil 2 leaking primary voltage into the measuring output
MIL and stored cylinder 2 ion fault
Less power due to retarded timing on cylinder 2
P2898: P2898 marks a basic circuit failure in the ion current measurement of cylinder 3: the engine computer receives nothing it can evaluate from that spark plug. With ion sensing, the plug doubles as a probe, because a bias voltage across the gap drives a small current through the burning, conductive gas.
Ignition coil of cylinder 3 whose ion measuring stage has failed
Loose or corroded connector at coil 3 or broken ion signal wire
Faulty cylinder 3 input in the ion processing module or engine module
MIL with ion fault stored for cylinder 3
Starting may take longer while cylinder identification is uncertain
Engine runs with cautious ignition timing and somewhat less power
P2899: Cylinder 3 Ion Current Sense Circuit Range/Performance

With P2899 an ion signal from cylinder 3 does arrive, yet it fails the plausibility check: its amplitude is too weak for the current load, it fluctuates without reason, or it no longer matches the pattern of the remaining cylinders.
Spark plug of cylinder 3 with deposits or excessive gap wear
Weak combustion in cylinder 3 (lean injector, low compression)
Damaged plug boot or moisture at the coil 3 connection
Slight roughness at idle or under light load
Knock control retards timing more than usual
P289A: Cylinder 3 Ion Current Sense Circuit Low

P289A applies when the ion reading of cylinder 3 stays below the lower plausibility limit. Usually the signal path is pulled to ground somewhere, or the coil no longer supplies the measuring voltage of roughly 80 V that Saab's T7 cassette keeps across each gap between sparks.
Ion signal wire of cylinder 3 chafed through to ground
Carbon tracking or cracked insulator on the cylinder 3 plug
Coil 3 no longer builds up its measuring voltage
MIL with low ion signal on cylinder 3
Misfire codes or no misfire detection for cylinder 3
Less power because timing is pulled back as a precaution
P289B: Cylinder 3 Ion Current Sense Circuit High

P289B signals that the ion channel of cylinder 3 sits permanently above its upper limit. A conductor touching battery voltage, a coil that couples ignition energy into its measuring output, or a lost ground reference are the usual electrical reasons.
Ion signal wire of cylinder 3 shorted to battery or supply voltage
Coil 3 coupling ignition energy into its measuring output
Missing ground reference at coil 3 or the processing module
MIL with high ion signal fault on cylinder 3
Knock on cylinder 3 may go undetected, so timing is retarded
P289C: P289C stands for a general circuit fault in the ion measurement of cylinder 4, meaning no usable signal reaches the evaluation electronics from that plug.
Ion measuring stage in the coil of cylinder 4 failed
Open circuit between coil 4 and the processing module
Cylinder 4 input of the processing module defective
MIL with ion fault stored for cylinder 4
Extended cranking because cylinder 1 and 4 cannot be told apart reliably
Conservative ignition timing with reduced power
P289D: Cylinder 4 Ion Current Sense Circuit Range/Performance

P289D is a rationality fault: cylinder 4 supplies an ion trace that is electrically present but not credible, for instance a combustion peak far smaller than the others at equal load, or erratic changes between cycles.
Worn or fouled spark plug in cylinder 4
Oil in the plug well of cylinder 4 from a leaking cover gasket
Mixture or compression problem in cylinder 4
P289E: Cylinder 4 Ion Current Sense Circuit Low

P289E means the ion signal of cylinder 4 remains below the range the module expects. A ground fault on the line from coil 4, a plug whose insulator conducts the bias voltage away, or a coil that has stopped generating that voltage are the main suspects.
Ion signal line of cylinder 4 shorted to ground
Spark plug insulator of cylinder 4 leaking the bias voltage
Bias voltage generation inside coil 4 failed
MIL with low ion signal on cylinder 4
Possible start delay or misfire codes
Power reduced by safety timing on cylinder 4
P289F: Cylinder 4 Ion Current Sense Circuit High

P289F is set when the ion measurement of cylinder 4 is held above its plausible maximum. Electrically, look for a signal conductor in contact with a supply feed, an internally leaking coil 4, or a poor ground that lifts the reference level.
Ion signal conductor of cylinder 4 touching a supply feed
Internal leakage in coil 4 raising the measuring output
Poor ground lifting the reference of the cylinder 4 channel
MIL with high ion signal on cylinder 4
P28A0: P28A0 reports that the ion current circuit of cylinder 5 delivers no evaluable signal. A cylinder 5 exists only on engines with five or more cylinders, which narrows the field considerably.
Coil of cylinder 5 with failed ion measuring circuit
Connector or wire fault between coil 5 and the evaluation electronics
MIL with ion fault stored for cylinder 5
Retarded timing and slightly reduced power
P28A1: Cylinder 5 Ion Current Sense Circuit Range/Performance

P28A1 flags a cylinder 5 ion signal that is electrically intact but implausible in size or shape compared with load, speed and the other cylinders. Ion current rises with chamber pressure and temperature, so a lean or poorly compressing cylinder 5 produces a weak trace exactly like a fouled plug does.
Fouled or eroded spark plug in cylinder 5
Lean mixture in cylinder 5 from a clogged injector or intake leak
MIL, possibly with misfire code P0305
P28A2: Cylinder 5 Ion Current Sense Circuit Low

P28A2 is stored when the cylinder 5 ion reading stays under its lower threshold. The measurement relies on a constant bias across the plug gap between sparks – about 80 V on Saab's T7 discharge modules – and anything that drains it to ground pulls the reading down: a chafed signal conductor, a cracked plug insulator, or a coil whose bias supply has failed.
Signal conductor of cylinder 5 chafed against ground
Cracked insulator on the cylinder 5 spark plug
MIL with low ion signal on cylinder 5
Misfire codes for cylinder 5 may appear
P28A3: Cylinder 5 Ion Current Sense Circuit High

P28A3 indicates a cylinder 5 ion signal locked above its permitted ceiling. Contact between the signal path and a voltage source, a coil 5 that injects ignition energy into its output, or a disturbed ground reference can cause it.
Signal path of cylinder 5 in contact with a voltage source
Coil 5 feeding ignition energy into its measuring output
Disturbed ground reference of the evaluation circuit
MIL with high ion signal on cylinder 5
Ignition retarded on cylinder 5, less power
Knock events may not be recognised
P28A4: P28A4 is the general circuit code for the ion measurement of cylinder 6: the electronics get no usable signal from that plug. Only engines with six or more cylinders are affected, and among them ion sensing is rare.
Ion measuring part of the cylinder 6 coil defective
Open ion signal circuit of cylinder 6 in the harness or connector
MIL with ion fault stored for cylinder 6
Reduced misfire and knock monitoring on cylinder 6
Moderate power loss from cautious timing
P28A5: Cylinder 6 Ion Current Sense Circuit Range/Performance

P28A5 points to a cylinder 6 ion signal that exists but makes no sense for the operating point: too little combustion response, a trace that jumps between cycles, or one that departs from the remaining cylinders. Since ionisation follows the actual burn, a misfiring or lean cylinder 6 can trigger it as readily as a worn plug or a wet plug well.
Spark plug of cylinder 6 worn or sooted
Water or oil in the plug well of cylinder 6
Poor combustion in cylinder 6 (injector, valve, compression)
Rough running at idle or light throttle
P28A6: Cylinder 6 Ion Current Sense Circuit Low
P28A6 describes an ion reading from cylinder 6 that never leaves the bottom of its range.
Damaged ion conductor of cylinder 6 leaking to ground
Cracked ceramic or heavy deposits on the cylinder 6 plug
Coil 6 no longer supplies the measuring voltage
MIL with low ion signal on cylinder 6
Engine noticeably weaker on safe timing
P28A7: Cylinder 6 Ion Current Sense Circuit High

P28A7 is logged when the ion signal of cylinder 6 is held above the upper limit the module accepts. A conductor in contact with battery voltage, crosstalk from the primary side of coil 6, or an evaluation stage driven into saturation are the typical electrical explanations.
Ion conductor of cylinder 6 touching battery voltage
Crosstalk from the primary side of coil 6
MIL with high ion signal on cylinder 6
Less power because of late ignition on cylinder 6
Knock on cylinder 6 may not be detected
P28A8: P28A8 covers a basic circuit fault in the ion current measurement of cylinder 7, so the module obtains no evaluable signal from that plug. A cylinder 7 only exists on engines with eight or more cylinders, and Saab, the best-known user of ion sensing, applied it to four-cylinder and V6 engines; no maker publicly describes an eight-cylinder version.
Coil of cylinder 7 with defective ion measuring function
Broken wire or loose connector in the cylinder 7 ion circuit
Cylinder 7 input of the evaluation electronics faulty
MIL with ion fault stored for cylinder 7

Moisture bridging contacts in the coil 7 connector

P28AD means the cylinder 8 ion signal is electrically intact but does not fit what the computer expects for the operating point, or it deviates clearly from the other cylinders. Oil deposits on the cylinder 8 plug

P28AE: Cylinder 8 Ion Current Sense Circuit Low

P28AE stands for an ion reading from cylinder 8 that stays too low or near zero. Either the measuring voltage never reaches the plug, because the coil's bias stage or its supply has failed, or it drains away to ground through a damaged signal wire, a wet plug well or a tracked boot.

P28AF: Cylinder 8 Ion Current Sense Circuit High

P28AF is logged when cylinder 8 delivers an ion signal pinned at or above the upper limit. Possible reasons include the signal conductor shorted to battery voltage or to another live circuit in the harness, internal leakage inside coil 8 that lets the high-voltage side couple into the measuring line, or a lost reference ground at the evaluation input.

Lost reference ground at the evaluation input

P28B0: P28B0 marks an electrical circuit fault, usually an interruption, in the ion current measurement of cylinder 9. A ninth cylinder appears only on engines with ten or more cylinders, such as V10, V12 or W12 designs.

P28B1: Cylinder 9 Ion Current Sense Circuit Range/Performance
P28B1 indicates that cylinder 9 produces an ion signal of believable electrical level whose shape or strength does not match engine speed, load or the neighbouring cylinders.

Weak spray from the cylinder 9 injector
Condensation in the cylinder 9 plug well

P28B2 is stored when the ion current measured at cylinder 9 remains under its lower plausibility limit. In an ion-sensing ignition each coil both fires the plug and supplies the measuring voltage, so a coil 9 with a weak bias stage, a cracked plug insulator or a signal wire grounded in the harness all reduce the current reaching the evaluator.

Cracked insulator on the cylinder 9 plug

Ten cylinders mean a V10 at minimum, where this is the last cylinder in the numbering, or a V12 or W12, where it is not.

P28B5 reports an ion signal from cylinder 10 that is electrically valid yet implausible: its amplitude or timing after the spark does not fit the load point or departs from the remaining cylinders.

P28B6: Cylinder 10 Ion Current Sense Circuit Low

P28B6 is set when the cylinder 10 ion reading is persistently too low. Cylinder 10 sense wire with damaged insulation touching ground
MIL with low ion reading on cylinder 10

P28B9 stands for an ion signal from cylinder 11 whose voltage stays inside the valid band but whose behaviour makes no sense: too weak or too strong for the current speed and load, or out of line with the other eleven cylinders. Cylinder 11 injector delivering too little or spraying poorly
Low compression on cylinder 11 (valve or ring leakage)

P28BA means the cylinder 11 ion reading has fallen below its lower limit. Between sparks a bias voltage sits across the electrodes – 80 V on Saab's T7 – and burning gas lets a current flow that pulls this voltage down in proportion to pressure and temperature.

Ion signal wire of cylinder 11 shorted to battery voltage or another ignition circuit

Poor ground of the evaluation module shifting the reference

P28BD: Cylinder 12 Ion Current Sense Circuit Range/Performance

P28BD reports that cylinder 12 delivers an ion signal of acceptable voltage whose content is not credible – its strength, timing or shape after the spark does not match the operating point or the rest of the engine.

P28BE is set when the ion reading of cylinder 12 stays below its minimum. On Saab's Trionic T8 each coil generates its own measuring voltage of about 120 V and keeps it applied to the plug; the module then reads how much current the ionised gas lets through.

P28BF: Cylinder 12 Ion Current Sense Circuit High

P28BF signals that the cylinder 12 ion input sits above its permitted window. A sense wire touching a powered conductor, moisture bridging pins in the coil 12 connector or spark energy escaping inside the coil can all push it there.
Sense wire of cylinder 12 touching a powered conductor
Moisture bridging pins in the coil 12 connector

P28C0: Ion Sense Module Supply Voltage Circuit

P28C0 points to a fault in the power feed of the module that conditions ion signals – typically an open fuse, relay contact or wire, so the module is not powered at all. On Saab's Trionic T8 that module receives battery voltage via the main relay and its ground from a body point, and on the older T7 the ignition cassette took the same route.
Blown fuse in the ion sense module feed
Main relay not switching through or burnt contact
Open supply wire or loose ground point of the module
Internal fault in the module's power stage

P28C1 means the ion sense module is powered, but its supply sits below the level it needs to work reliably. That matters because such modules turn 12 V into far higher voltages: Saab's T7 cassette converted battery voltage to 400 V DC stored in a capacitor and also kept 80 V across each plug for measuring.
Voltage drop across a corroded main relay contact or connector
High-resistance ground point of the module
Hard starting, especially when cold or with a weak battery
Misfire codes on several cylinders at once
Stored supply-voltage code, often together with system voltage codes
P28C2: Ion Sense Module Supply Voltage High

P28C2 is stored when the voltage feeding the ion sense module exceeds its upper limit. Since the module derives its measuring and, in cassette designs, its ignition voltages from this feed, an excessive input can raise the bias across the plugs, push signals toward the top of their range and stress the converter inside.
Alternator voltage regulator letting the system voltage rise too high
Jump start or charger with excessive voltage (e.g. 24 V)
Poor module ground distorting the voltage reading
Faulty voltage measurement inside the module
Stored overvoltage code, often together with P0563

Under boost the intake manifold is above ambient pressure, so turbo engines add a high-load purge path: compressed air drives an ejector (venturi) that draws canister vapour into the compressor inlet, with check valves keeping boost out of the tank side.
Check valve in high-load line B sticking, leaking or fitted the wrong way round
Line B to the compressor inlet pulled off, cracked or kinked
Ejector nozzle blocked by debris or oil residue

P28C4 means the transmission controller finds the voltage too low on a phase lead (U, V or W) of the electric motor that operates clutch A.
Phase wire to the clutch A motor chafed through and touching ground

High-side switch in the controller that no longer turns off
Warning lamp for the transmission and stored DTC

Phase wire broken at a bend or bracket

P28C7 flags that the clutch A motor's phases are electrically intact but the motor does not respond as expected, e.g. currents and rotation do not match the commanded drive.
Debris from the transmission jamming the pump in the clutch A actuator (Stellantis 7HDT300)
Worn or sluggish clutch A actuator motor

Driver overheated after repeated range changes or high ambient heat
Shift system warning in the cluster
Range change stops halfway or is refused
Problem may disappear after the system cools down
P28E5: P28E5 judges the shift motor by its result: it is driven, but the actuator does not get to the commanded range as expected. Hyundai lists it in bulletin 22-AT-001H for the shift-by-wire Palisade, Santa Fe, Sonata and Tucson (including hybrids) with two failure types: P28E577, commanded position not reached, and P28E592, SBW motor performance.
SBW actuator worn internally or mechanism stiff
Shift control unit or its harness not delivering motor current
Low 12 V supply during the shift
Shift control software needing an update
Shifter system malfunction message in the cluster
Range not engaged or engaged with delay
P28E6: P28E6 is set when the shift motor turns faster than its control allows. In a position-controlled actuator this is visible from the rotor feedback: the encoder count changes quicker than the commanded movement can explain.
Broken gear or coupling inside the actuator, motor spins without load
Faulty rotor position or encoder signal
Control software error in the shift control unit
Shift system warning in the cluster
Wrong range engaged or range change aborted
Clicking or whirring from the actuator
P28E7: The shift motor position sensor tells the controller where the selector shaft of a shift-by-wire actuator stands.
Position sensor connector loose, corroded or unplugged
Signal, supply or ground wire of the sensor broken
Shift system warning in the cluster
Vehicle refuses to shift or does not start
P28E8: Shift Motor Position Sensor Circuit High
P28E8 means the shift motor position sensor reports a value above its permitted range.
Shift control unit software on the 2024-25 Kia EV9 (service action SA594)
Sensor signal shorted to supply or battery voltage
Position sensor failed with output stuck high
Vehicle cannot be shifted out of Park
Shift system warning in the cluster
P28E9: Shift Motor Position Sensor Circuit Low

P28E9 is stored when the signal of the shift motor position sensor sits below its valid band. Typical causes are a signal line shorted to ground, a sensor supply that has collapsed, for instance because another sensor on the same feed is shorted, or a failed sensor.
Sensor signal wire shorted to ground
Sensor supply missing or pulled down
Position sensor failed with output stuck low
Shift system warning in the cluster
Range changes blocked or gear display wrong
Engine or drive system may not start
P28EA: Shift Motor Position Sensor Circuit Range/Performance

P28EA covers a position signal that is electrically valid but implausible: the two channels disagree, the value does not move although the motor runs, or the actuator ends up away from the expected detent.
SBW actuator stuck or not reaching the commanded position
Position sensor channels drifting apart (sum no longer near 100 percent)
Intermittent contact in the sensor or actuator harness
Shifter system malfunction message in the cluster
Cannot shift out of Park or into the requested range
Gear display does not match the selected range
P28EB: A shift-by-wire actuator has to learn which motor positions match P, R, N and D before it can work precisely.
Learning routine not run after replacing the control unit or actuator
Learned values cleared by a software update or memory loss
Learning aborted by low battery voltage or an active fault
Shift system warning in the cluster
Imprecise or refused range changes until learning is done
P28EC: Shift Motor Position Sensor Exceeded Learning Limit

Unlike P28EB, learning did take place here, but the result lies outside the window the controller accepts. The learned sensor values for the end stop or for the P, R, N and D detents differ too far from the nominal ones, or the measured play is too large.
Actuator or sensor mounted out of position after a repair
Worn or damaged detent plate, detent spring or linkage
Wrong or mismatched actuator or sensor fitted
Shift system warning in the cluster
P28ED: Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump B Overspeed

Pump B is a second electrically driven transmission fluid pump that works independently of the engine, for example to hold pressure during start-stop or electric driving, or to feed clutch cooling. P28ED says its motor runs faster than commanded or faster than its permitted maximum.
Low fluid level or air drawn in, so the pump runs without load
Faulty speed feedback or control in the pump controller
Transmission warning or check engine light on
P28EE: Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump B Underspeed

P28EE is the reverse of P28ED: electric transmission fluid pump B does not reach the speed its controller asks for. The motor is fed, but something holds it back, such as very cold and thick fluid, a binding or worn pump, debris in the gears or a low supply voltage. When the speed falls to zero the matching code is the stall P277C rather than this one.
Pump binding, worn or contaminated with debris
Very cold, aged or wrong transmission fluid
Low supply voltage or high resistance in the pump feed
Transmission warning or check engine light on
