P2A89: Alternative Fuel Pump C Compression Stroke Valve Control Circuit Low

P2A89 is set when the drive circuit of pump C's compression stroke valve reads low for the commanded state. Most often the control wire has found a path to ground, so the solenoid may stay on, or the coil has shorted turns and pushes the output stage into current limiting.
Control wire of valve C shorted to ground
Shorted turns in the coil of valve C
P2A8A: Alternative Fuel Pump C Compression Stroke Valve Control Circuit High

P2A8A indicates that pump C's compression stroke valve circuit sits higher than the commanded state allows, from an open coil, a broken wire or a short to the supply rail. The solenoid cannot shift the spool, which stays in the drain position, and element C never starts a compression stroke.
Open coil or broken wire at valve C
Fault in the supply or ground shared by the pump valves
Control wire shorted to the supply rail
Uneven gas pressure at high load
P2A8B: P2A8B means vaporizer A is not doing its job well enough, rather than reporting a wiring fault. On LPG engines this unit, also called reducer or converter, draws engine coolant heat to turn liquid gas into vapour at a steady pressure.
Too little coolant reaching vaporizer A (air lock, kinked hose, thermostat stuck open)
Worn diaphragm or seat in the pressure stage of vaporizer A
Oily residues from the gas clogging the vaporizer chambers
Outlet temperature sensor reading wrong but still within range
Check engine or gas warning lamp on
System stays on petrol longer after a cold start or falls back to petrol under load
Hesitation, rough running or stalling after coasting on gas
Frost or condensation on the vaporizer body
P2A8C: P2A8C flags vaporizer B as underperforming: the gas leaving it is colder, or less completely vaporized, than the module expects for the current flow. With LNG the temperature gap is extreme, and Westport's patent CA2862664C describes the typical failure.
Coolant partly frozen inside vaporizer B after cold start or long idling
Valve that switches between parallel and counter flow stuck
Low coolant level or too little antifreeze in the mixture
Deposits reducing heat transfer in vaporizer B
Reduced power or gas mode blocked, especially when cold
Ice on the vaporizer or gas lines behind it
P2A8D: P2A8D concerns a third vaporizer, found where large engines or several fuel branches need more heat exchange than one or two units provide. The code means unit C turns too little liquid into usable gas, or delivers it too cold, while its outlet sensor works.
Coolant branch to vaporizer C restricted or unbalanced against A and B
Fouled heat exchange passages in vaporizer C
Pressure stage of vaporizer C sticking or leaking internally
Outlet sensor of C drifting so that the comparison fails
Warning lamp on, often with little noticeable change in driving
Loss of power at high load when all vaporizers are needed
One vaporizer housing noticeably colder than the others
P2A8E: P2A8E reports that alternative fuel pump A no longer delivers what it should, a mechanical or hydraulic fault rather than an electrical one. Such pumps move liquid fuel, typically LNG out of a cryogenic tank.
Worn dynamic piston seals in pump A
Leaking inlet or outlet check valve of pump A
Hydraulic drive of pump A delivering too little force or speed
Impurities in the fuel passing the filter and damaging the pump
Power loss at high load, gas pressure sagging
Pump runs noticeably longer to refill the accumulator
Engine switched to reduced output or diesel-only operation
P2A8F: P2A8F applies to a second alternative fuel pump whose output has fallen short of expectations. Layouts with two pumps usually give each LNG vessel its own pump, a redundancy Westport's documents mention explicitly. In US20080302111A1, a selector valve decides which pump delivers, and once the controller judges one pump degraded it can switch to the other.
Worn seals reducing the delivery of pump B
Tank served by pump B almost empty, mimicking a weak pump
Broken drive shaft or coupling between hydraulic drive and pump B
Usable range shorter, fuel left in one tank
System changes to the other tank earlier than usual
P2A90: P2A90 marks pump C of the alternative fuel system as delivering too little. A third pump may belong to a further tank or, in Caterpillar's design US10060421B2, be one of several pumping elements driven in sequence.
Vapour at the inlet of pump C after warm soak, causing cavitation
Worn seals or valves in pump C
Clogged inlet strainer or filter ahead of pump C
Weak pull or hesitation shortly after a long stop
Gas pressure recovers slowly after heavy acceleration
P2A91: Alternative Fuel Tank Select Valve A Control Circuit/Open

A tank select valve decides which storage vessel feeds the fuel system. That sets it apart from a tank shutoff valve (P224C, P2A22 and onward), which simply opens or isolates one cylinder, and from the hydraulic fuel pump select valve (P2A70 and onward), which routes drive oil to a pump.
Loose connector or broken wire to select valve A
Burnt-out solenoid coil of valve A
Faulty output stage in the alternative fuel module
Only one tank is used, range noticeably shorter
Fuel gauge shows content left although the engine runs short of gas
P2A92: Alternative Fuel Tank Select Valve A Control Performance

P2A92 is the functional check for tank select valve A: the wiring tests pass, yet the fuel system does not behave as if the commanded vessel were connected. Software can judge this only through pressures.
Select valve A sticking from dirt, ice or wear
Valve A leaking across its seat so both vessels are drawn
Tank pressure sensor giving a misleading reading
Tanks empty unevenly or in the wrong order
Short gas supply although one vessel still holds fuel
P2A93: Alternative Fuel Tank Select Valve A Control Circuit Low

P2A93 is stored when the module measures a voltage on the control line of tank select valve A that falls short of the level expected for the commanded state. With a low-side driver this usually means the line touches ground, which can energise the solenoid permanently and keep valve A in its switched position regardless of the command.
Control wire of valve A chafed through to ground
Condensation or water in the connector of valve A
Shorted turns in the coil of valve A
Tank selection stuck, one vessel emptied completely
Fuse or output protection of the gas module trips
P2A94: Alternative Fuel Tank Select Valve A Control Circuit High

P2A94 reports a control voltage at tank select valve A above what the module expects for the commanded state. On a valve switched to ground by the module, an open coil or broken lead leaves the line floating at supply voltage; alternatively a chafed wire contacts a battery feed that the output stage cannot pull down.
Open coil or broken lead on a ground-switched valve A
Control wire of valve A touching a battery feed
Corroded pins with high resistance at valve A
No change to the next tank, gas runs out early
Engine switches to its other fuel or reduced power
P2A95: Alternative Fuel Tank Select Valve B Control Circuit/Open
P2A95 says the module finds no proper current path through tank select valve B. Where a second select valve exists, it typically serves the next vessel or supply in line.
Loose plug or broken wire to select valve B
Open solenoid coil of valve B
Output stage for valve B in the module defective
Content of one vessel cannot be used
Range well below the usual figure
P2A96: Alternative Fuel Tank Select Valve B Control Circuit Performance
P2A96 is about tank select valve B working electrically but not doing what it is told.
Valve B held by ice or cold-hardened seals
Debris preventing valve B from shifting fully
Pump defect interpreted as a select valve problem
Gas supply drops right after a tank change
One vessel stays full while the other runs dry
P2A97: Alternative Fuel Tank Select Valve B Control Circuit Low

P2A97 indicates that the drive line of tank select valve B reads too low. If the module feeds the valve from the positive side, a short to ground in the wire or a coil with shorted windings drags the output down, and the stage switches off to protect itself, so valve B falls back to its spring position.
Wire to valve B chafed against a tank strap or bracket
Shorted windings in the coil of valve B
Moisture bridging the pins of the valve B plug
Tank change does not happen or happens at the wrong time
Gas mode ends early with fuel still on board
P2A98: Alternative Fuel Tank Select Valve B Control Circuit High

P2A98 appears when the voltage on the control circuit of tank select valve B stays higher than the module allows for the commanded state. A ground-switched valve with an interrupted winding or lead shows this pattern, as does a wire that has picked up battery voltage.
Interrupted winding or lead at valve B
Control line of valve B in contact with battery voltage
Corrosion at the valve B connector raising resistance
Second vessel never used, gas runs out early
Gauge shows reserve while power drops
P2A99: Alternative Fuel Tank Select Valve C Control Circuit/Open
P2A99 belongs to installations with at least three selectable vessels or supplies and reports an open or otherwise broken control circuit at select valve C.
Disconnected plug or broken lead at select valve C
Coil of valve C burnt out
Module output for valve C failed
Third vessel stays full or is never isolated
P2A9A: Alternative Fuel Tank Select Valve C Control Circuit Performance

With P2A9A, select valve C passes its electrical tests, but the effect of switching does not show up as expected. The likely evidence is pressure: once vessel C is selected, its own tank pressure sensor should begin to fall with consumption and the pressure ahead of the regulator should match that vessel's level.
Valve C not shifting fully because of wear or contamination
Internal leakage letting vessel C feed in the wrong position
Faulty tank C pressure reading misleading the check
Tank C level hardly changes over a tank cycle
Fault appears mainly in cold weather
P2A9B: Alternative Fuel Tank Select Valve C Control Circuit Low

P2A9B is logged when the control circuit of tank select valve C reads below the expected level. Common electrical findings are a lead grounded against the frame, a pinched wire under a tank strap or a coil with internal shorts.
Lead of valve C grounded against the frame or pinched under a tank strap
Internal short in the coil of valve C
Water in the plug of valve C
Third tank used constantly or not at all
Unexpected tank changes during the drive
P2A9C: Alternative Fuel Tank Select Valve C Control Circuit High

P2A9C reports a control voltage at select valve C above the level the commanded state permits. The usual reasons are an interrupted coil or wire on a valve the module switches to ground, which leaves supply voltage on the line, or a foreign voltage fed in from a damaged neighbouring wire. Valve C then ignores commands.
Open coil or wire on ground-switched valve C
Foreign voltage from a damaged neighbouring wire
Third vessel never drawn, range reduced
Earlier change to the other fuel
P2A9D: Alternative Fuel High Pressure System Small Leak

P2A9D points to a slow loss of gas from the high-pressure side, from the cylinders up to the regulator, too small to notice while driving. A Toyota and Denso patent, US6467466B1, explains the catch: with the valves open, a modest pressure drop cannot be told apart from consumption.
Seeping high-pressure fitting or loosened connection
Tank or shutoff valve not sealing fully when closed
Aged O-rings in the filter or regulator inlet
Drifting high-pressure sensor simulating a pressure loss
Malfunction or gas warning lamp on
Tank pressure noticeably lower after parking
Faint gas smell near the tanks or lines
Gas mode blocked at the next start on some systems
P2A9E: Alternative Fuel Return Line Valve Control Circuit/Open

Liquid-phase propane and LPG systems pump more fuel to the rail than the injectors use; the surplus flows back to the tank and carries heat and vapor away with it. A return line valve opens or blocks that path.
Corroded, wet or loose connector at the tank-mounted valve
Broken wire in the frame or tank harness
Open solenoid coil in the return valve
Blown fuse or faulty relay in the valve supply
Failed output stage in the fuel control module
Hard or long cranking on a warm engine, as vapor is not flushed out of the rail
Switch to the base fuel or reduced power on bi-fuel or dedicated systems
P2A9F: Alternative Fuel Return Line Valve Control Circuit Range/Performance

P2A9F covers the grey zone between a clean open and a clean short: the control circuit of the return line valve is connected, but the current or voltage the output stage measures while driving it does not fit the command.
Solenoid coil resistance out of range or partially shorted windings
High contact resistance from corrosion or water in the connector
Low supply voltage at the valve from a weak relay contact or ground
Output stage of the fuel control module measuring incorrectly
Occasional hard starts after a hot soak
Fault comes and goes with temperature or moisture
P2AA0: Alternative Fuel Return Line Valve Control Circuit Low
P2AA0 means the module reads too low a voltage on the control line of the return line valve, which almost always points to a short to ground. What follows depends on which side the module switches.
Control wire chafed through and touching the frame or tank
Water in the valve connector bridging to ground
Internal short in the solenoid coil
Damaged output stage in the fuel control module
Return valve stays open or the valve fuse blows, depending on the circuit layout
Irregular rail pressure or switch to the base fuel
P2AA1: Alternative Fuel Return Line Valve Control Circuit High
P2AA1 is the opposite electrical case to P2AA0: the valve drive wire sits at too high a voltage, usually because it touches a battery-fed wire.
Control wire shorted to a battery-fed wire in the harness
Solenoid winding shorted to its supply terminal
Bent or bridged pins in the valve connector
Output stage in the fuel control module shorted internally
Return valve cannot be switched and stays in its rest position
Poor hot starts or switch to the base fuel
P2AA2: Alternative Fuel Return Line Insufficient Flow

P2AA2 is a hydraulic fault, not an electrical one: too little liquid fuel comes back from the rail to the tank. The return keeps the fuel in the rail cool and liquid, so a weak return lets it warm up and boil.
Return valve or return check valve sticking closed
Kinked, crushed or clogged return line or filter
In-tank pump delivering too little, leaving no surplus to return
Faulty pressure regulator in the return path
Hard starting or stalling after a hot soak from vapor in the rail
Hesitation or lean running under load
Switch to the base fuel or reduced power
P2AA3: Cold Start EGR B Flow Insufficient Detected
P2AA3 belongs to the cold-start strategy (CSERS) newer diesels run in the first minutes after a long soak.
EGR valve B sticking or slow from soot at low temperature
Faulty position sensor on EGR valve B misleading the control
Clogged EGR cooler or passage in loop B
Usually no noticeable change in driving
Higher NOx in the warm-up phase, possible inspection failure
P2AA4: Cold Start EGR B Flow Excessive Detected

P2AA4 is the mirror case of P2AA3: during the cold-start phase, EGR path B recirculates more exhaust than intended. Many calibrations deliberately keep EGR low in a cold engine, so a valve that leaks or hangs open is the classic cause.
EGR valve B leaking or stuck partly open from carbon
Position sensor offset making the valve open further than commanded
Intake or exhaust throttle fault raising the pressure difference across loop B
Rough idle and smoke after a cold start
Stalling or hesitation while the engine is cold
P2AA5: EGR Cooler Bypass Control Circuit Driver Current/Temperature Too High Bank 1

P2AA5 comes from the H-bridge that drives the DC motor of the bank 1 EGR cooler bypass flap: the driver chip itself reports that it is getting too hot. GM's diesel summary tables carry this monitor from 2017 (17OBDG04) to 2025 (25OBDG04A) as a motor overtemperature check.
Bypass flap binding on soot or corrosion, motor working against resistance
Internal fault in the bypass actuator motor
Partial short between the motor wires
Overheating or faulty H-bridge in the engine control module
Malfunction indicator lamp on after two trips
Bypass flap no longer driven, so warm-up EGR cooling stays at its last state
Possible further EGR or cooler efficiency codes
P2AA6: EGR Cooler Bypass Control Circuit Driver Current/Temperature Too High Bank 2

P2AA6 is the bank 2 version of the bypass driver protection code. It only exists on engines with a separate EGR cooler and bypass actuator for the second cylinder bank, typically V engines whose banks each have their own exhaust manifold feeding EGR.
Bank 2 bypass flap binding on soot or corrosion
Internal fault in the bank 2 actuator motor
Partial short in the bank 2 actuator wiring
Faulty driver stage in the engine control module
Bank 2 bypass flap stays in its last position
Possible NOx or EGR temperature codes for bank 2
P2AA7: Engine Coolant Bypass Valve B Position Sensor Circuit

Thermal management modules on modern engines use motor-driven rotary valves to split coolant between radiator, heater, oil or transmission cooler and engine block. A position sensor reports each valve's angle so the module can regulate it in closed loop.
Loose, corroded or coolant-wetted connector, or damaged sensor wiring
Lost 5 V supply or ground to the position sensor
Failed position sensor inside the valve module
Faulty sensor input in the engine control module
Slow warm-up or reduced cabin heating
Fluctuating or elevated coolant temperature reading
P2AA8: Engine Coolant Bypass Valve B Position Sensor Circuit Range/Performance

With P2AA8 the position sensor of coolant valve B delivers an electrically valid signal, but its content is implausible: it sticks while the motor turns the valve, jumps by more than a real valve could move, or lies outside the end stops the module learned.
Worn or contaminated position sensor in the valve module
Slipping gear or shifted magnet between valve shaft and sensor
Intermittent contact in the connector causing signal jumps
Learned end stops lost after a module or valve replacement
Engine warms up slowly or runs hotter than usual
P2AA9: Engine Coolant Bypass Valve B Position Sensor Circuit Low

P2AA9 is set once the position sensor on coolant valve B reports a value below its valid band, which nearly always means the signal wire or the sensor output is pulled toward ground. Rotary coolant valves in thermal management modules report their angle so the engine computer can steer coolant between radiator, heater and other loops.
Sensor signal wire chafed through and shorted to ground
Position sensor electronics in the valve module failed (often only as complete valve unit)
Coolant or moisture in the sensor connector creating a leakage path to ground
Engine warms up slowly or runs cooler than usual
Cabin heating or transmission warm-up weaker, depending on what valve B serves
P2AAA: Engine Coolant Bypass Valve B Position Sensor Circuit High

With P2AAA the position sensor of coolant valve B reports a value above anything a working sensor would deliver. Typical reasons are a signal line touching a supply wire, a damaged output stage inside the sensor or, depending on how the input is wired, an interrupted ground.
Signal wire in contact with a supply or reference voltage wire
Sensor ground open at the connector or splice
Position sensor in the valve module defective
Coolant temperature swings or stays off target
Possibly reduced engine power if the module protects against overheating
P2AAB: Engine Coolant Bypass Valve B Position Sensor Circuit Intermittent/Erratic

P2AAB covers a position signal from coolant valve B that is valid most of the time but drops out, jumps or flickers for short moments. Such patterns usually come from a contact that opens under vibration or heat, a lead that rubs against hot engine parts, or interference on the digital sensor line.
Widened or loose terminal in the valve connector
Harness rubbing on hot or moving engine parts
Electrical interference or poor ground on the sensor line
Check engine light that comes and goes
Occasional temperature swings without a steady pattern
Often no noticeable change in driving behaviour
P2AAC: P2AAC is the general circuit fault of a sensor meant to recognise diesel where only gasoline belongs, so the system can react to misfuelling before damage occurs. No manufacturer documents this sensor or the code publicly, and its exact design is not described in sources available.
Corroded or loose connector at the sensor near the tank or fuel line
Misfuelling warning unavailable or shown without reason
Usually no change in how the engine runs
P2AAD: Diesel Fuel Presence Sensor Circuit Range/Performance

P2AAD means the diesel presence sensor delivers an electrically valid signal whose content does not make sense: it may report diesel although no refuelling has taken place, never change at all, or contradict other information the engine computer has about the fuel. No manufacturer documents this code or its test publicly.
Sensing element coated with deposits or residues
Calibration of the plausibility check not suited to the fuel quality in use
Unjustified misfuelling message, or a real misfuelling going unnoticed
P2AAE: Diesel Fuel Presence Sensor Circuit Low
P2AAE is stored when the diesel presence sensor signal falls below the lowest value the input accepts, which points to a short to ground on the signal line or a sensor whose output has collapsed.
Signal wire shorted to ground, often chafed on the underbody
Sensor supply or reference voltage missing
P2AAF: Diesel Fuel Presence Sensor Circuit High

P2AAF reports the diesel presence sensor signal stuck above its upper limit. Common reasons are a signal wire touching a battery-fed line, an open ground or signal path that lets an internal pull-up drive the input high, or a sensor with a failed output stage.
Signal wire shorted to a voltage source
Open sensor ground or signal wire
P2AB0: P2AB0 concerns the electronics of the particulate matter sensor rather than its sensing element: the sensor control unit, which feeds the electrodes, measures their current and reports over CAN, finds an internal error in its own measuring path.
Internal fault in the PM sensor control unit (sensor and control unit usually replaced as one part)
CAN wiring fault that older sensor versions also report as P2AB0
Unstable supply or ground at the sensor control unit
P2AB1: P2AB1 reports that the control module of an electrically heated catalyst does not work as it should, for example because its self-test fails or the heating it delivers does not match the demand. Such heaters bring a catalyst to working temperature right after start or in low-load driving.
Internal fault in the heater control module (power stage or self-test)
Module software fault, update may be available
Module overheated due to poor cooling or high ambient heat at its mounting
Higher emissions after cold start; inspection may fail
P2AB2: Catalyst Heater Control Module Supply Voltage
P2AB2 points to the power feed of the catalyst heater control module: the voltage it measures at its own supply input lies outside the window in which it may switch the heater.
Blown fuse or faulty relay in the heater supply
Corroded or loose ground or high-current terminal
Weak 48-volt battery or faulty DC/DC converter in mild-hybrid systems
Catalyst heating not available, higher emissions after cold start
P2AB3: Cold Start Intake Manifold Runner Control Stuck Open Bank 1

P2AB3 is part of the cold-start component checks that CARB phases in for 20, 50 and 100 percent of new vehicles in 2026, 2027 and 2028. Right after a start that follows a long standstill, charge motion, runner and swirl valves must follow the cold-start command clearly, toward the target and further than they would at a start without that strategy.
Actuator or vacuum unit too weak to move the flaps when cold
Flap shaft stiff from carbon or oil deposits
Linkage detached or broken between actuator and shaft
Rougher idle in the first minutes after a cold start
Higher cold-start emissions, otherwise often unnoticed
P2AB4: Cold Start Intake Manifold Runner Control Stuck Open Bank 2
P2AB4 is the bank 2 version of the open-stuck check during cold start, so it only appears on engines with a separate runner control for each cylinder bank, typically V or flat engines.
Leaking vacuum line or diaphragm on the bank 2 actuator
Bank 2 flap shaft stiff from deposits
Uneven running between the banks shortly after a cold start
P2AB5: Cold Start Intake Manifold Runner Control Stuck Closed Bank 1
P2AB5 is the opposite of P2AB3: during cold start the runner control on bank 1 remains in its closed position and does not follow a command to open.
Flaps stuck closed by deposits or condensate freezing at low temperature
Actuator motor or vacuum valve does not move the shaft
Broken return spring or worn shaft bushing
Less power in the first minutes after a cold start
P2AB6: Cold Start Intake Manifold Runner Control Stuck Closed Bank 2
P2AB6 reports the runner flaps of bank 2 held in the closed position during the cold-start phase, against a command to open them.
Bank 2 flaps seized by deposits or ice
Bank 2 actuator or its control valve defective
Shared actuator supply or vacuum source weak (often with P2AB5)
Slightly uneven running and reduced pull after a cold start
P2AB7: P2AB7 is the general circuit fault for the position sensor on wastegate A, found on engines whose wastegate is moved by an electric motor rather than a vacuum can. Turbo A is the first one in the exhaust flow on series layouts or the bank 1 unit on parallel layouts.
Electric wastegate actuator failed, e-clip missing or actuator rod damaged (sensor sits in the actuator)
Chafed harness or loose connector near the hot turbocharger
PCM calibration that sets the code falsely (reflash available for some models)
Noticeable lack of power, boost limited
Often stored together with P0299 or the stuck wastegate codes P25B3/P25B4
P2AB8: Wastegate Position Sensor A Circuit Low

P2AB8 means the wastegate A position signal has fallen below its valid floor, which points to a short to ground, an open signal or reference wire, or a dead sensor. GM's 2019 tables for the 2.7L L3B read the sensor as a percentage of its reference and fail below 5 % in 30 of 38 samples taken every 100 ms; the 2025 tables use below 1 % in 10 of 12.
Sensor harness pinched or chafed between turbocharger and intake hose (short to ground)
Open reference or signal wire, or pushed-out terminal in the actuator connector
Position sensor inside the electric actuator failed
Check engine light from the first trip
Reduced power because boost control is restricted
May appear together with P0245 when a shared harness section is damaged
P2AB9: Wastegate Position Sensor A Circuit High

P2AB9 is logged when the wastegate A position signal climbs above its valid ceiling. Typical reasons are a signal wire shorted to the sensor supply or to battery voltage, an open ground return that lets the input float upward, or an internal sensor fault.
Signal wire shorted to the sensor supply or battery voltage
Open sensor ground or corroded ground terminal
PCM calibration that sets the code falsely (Ford reflash for listed models)
Position sensor inside the electric actuator failed
Check engine light from the first trip
Lower power under load, boost held back
Powertrain fault (wrench) indicator on some Ford models
P2ABA: P2ABA covers a general circuit fault of the position sensor on the wastegate of turbocharger B, so it can only occur on engines with two turbos and electric wastegates: on a parallel layout the turbo of bank 2, on a series layout the second one downstream. Ford uses it on twin-turbo EcoBoost V6 engines.
PCM calibration that sets the code falsely (Ford reflash for listed models)
Damaged harness or connector at the bank 2 turbocharger
Electric wastegate actuator B with its built-in position sensor failed
Check engine light, on Ford also the powertrain (wrench) indicator
P2ABB: Wastegate Position Sensor B Circuit Low

P2ABB reports that the position signal of the turbocharger B wastegate is too low, as a short to ground, a broken signal or supply wire or a failed sensor would cause. Ford's 2020-23 gasoline summary applies the same window as for turbo A and sets the code below 0.50 V after 4 s.
Sensor wire chafed to ground near the bank 2 turbocharger
Open reference supply or signal wire, loose connector
Position sensor in wastegate actuator B failed
Less power, especially when accelerating hard
P2ABC: Wastegate Position Sensor B Circuit High

P2ABC is the high-voltage fault on the wastegate B position sensor: according to Ford's 2020-23 gasoline summary the input sits above 4.50 V for 4 s, a picture typical of a signal line shorted to the reference supply or an open sensor ground.
PCM calibration that sets the code falsely (Ford reflash for listed models)
Open sensor ground or heat-damaged terminal at the actuator
Signal wire shorted to the reference supply or battery voltage
Check engine light, on Ford possibly the wrench indicator
P2ABD: Turbocharger/Supercharger Wastegate Actuator A Driver Current/Temperature Too High
P2ABD is raised by the output stage that powers the electric wastegate actuator of turbocharger A when it detects excessive current or overheating.
Wastegate flap or rod binding from soot, corrosion or heat so the motor stalls
Actuator supply wires chafed to ground or to each other
Driver stage in the PCM faulty
Clearly reduced power because the wastegate is no longer driven
Stuck wastegate checks P25B3/P25B4 not run while the code is stored
P2ABE: Turbocharger/Supercharger Wastegate Actuator B Driver Current/Temperature Too High

P2ABE is the turbo B counterpart of P2ABD: the output stage driving the second electric wastegate actuator signals overcurrent or thermal overload. It therefore applies only to twin-turbo engines with two electric actuators, such as Ford's EcoBoost V6.
Wastegate B rod or flap seized by corrosion or heat
Shorted winding in electric actuator B
Actuator harness pinched against the turbocharger
Reduced power, uneven boost between the two banks
P2ABF: Intake Air O2 Sensor Reference Voltage Circuit/Open Bank 1

P2ABF points to an open circuit in the reference voltage line of the intake air oxygen sensor on bank 1. This sensor is a wide-band element placed in the intake tract, usually before the intercooler, that measures how much oxygen the incoming charge still contains and therefore how much exhaust has been recirculated.
Broken reference wire or pushed-back pin between sensor and ECM
Corroded or loose sensor connector in the damp intake area
Sensing cell of the intake oxygen sensor internally open
EGR runs without sensor feedback or is reduced, higher NOx emissions
P2AC0: Intake Air O2 Sensor Reference Voltage Circuit Range/Performance Bank 1

P2AC0 is set when the reference voltage circuit of the bank 1 intake air oxygen sensor is electrically present but behaves implausibly, for example drifting or not matching what the ECM expects for the current EGR and pressure state.
Engine software that detects the fault falsely (Stellantis reflash for Giulia/Stelvio 2.0L)
Intake oxygen sensor aged or contaminated by oil mist from crankcase ventilation
High resistance in the reference wire or connector
Usually no noticeable change in driveability
P2AC1: Intake Air O2 Sensor Reference Voltage Circuit Low Bank 1

P2AC1 flags a reference voltage below the range the ECM accepts on the bank 1 intake oxygen sensor. This usually means the reference lead is shorted to ground or the sensing cell inside the sensor has broken down.
Reference wire chafed through to ground
Sensing cell of the intake oxygen sensor broken down internally
Sensor interface in the ECM faulty
EGR reduced or uncontrolled, possibly higher NOx and a failed emissions test
P2AC2: Intake Air O2 Sensor Reference Voltage Circuit High Bank 1

P2AC2 means the reference voltage at the intake oxygen sensor of bank 1 reads above its permitted range. A reference lead shorted to a supply wire or battery voltage in the harness, a lost ground on the sensor side or water in the connector are the usual triggers; a sensor with an internally damaged cell can produce the same picture.
Reference wire shorted to a supply or battery voltage wire
Moisture or corrosion bridging pins in the sensor connector
Open ground on the sensor side
EGR reduced, NOx emissions may rise
P2AC3: Intake Air O2 Sensor Reference Voltage Circuit/Open Bank 2

P2AC3 is the open circuit fault in the reference voltage lead of the intake air oxygen sensor assigned to bank 2. A second intake sensor only exists where each cylinder bank has its own intake or EGR path, for example on V engines with two separate charge air routes; engines with a single sensor use the bank 1 code P2ABF.
Broken reference wire or loose terminal at the bank 2 sensor
Harness damaged by heat near the bank 2 turbocharger or exhaust
Sensing cell of the bank 2 intake oxygen sensor internally open
EGR on bank 2 reduced or uncontrolled
P2AC4: Intake Air O2 Sensor Reference Voltage Circuit Range/Performance Bank 2

P2AC4 marks an implausible but electrically intact reference voltage on the second-bank intake oxygen sensor. It is the bank 2 twin of P2AC0, which Stellantis documents for the four-cylinder Alfa Romeo 2.0L; an inline four with one intake path has no bank 2, so P2AC4 would only appear on engines fitted with a second intake sensor.
Bank 2 intake oxygen sensor aged or contaminated by crankcase vapours
Calibration that judges the signal too strictly
High resistance in the reference wire or connector
Usually no noticeable change in driveability
P2AC5: Intake Air O2 Sensor Reference Voltage Circuit Low Bank 2

P2AC5 reports that the bank 2 intake oxygen sensor sees a reference voltage below the permitted limit, typically a short to ground in the reference lead or a breakdown of the sensing cell. No manufacturer publishes this code, and engines with a separate intake oxygen sensor for bank 2 are rare.
Reference wire of the bank 2 sensor shorted to ground
Shared sensor supply or ECM fault (if P2AC1 is present as well)
Higher NOx, possibly a failed emissions test
P2AC6: Intake Air O2 Sensor Reference Voltage Circuit High Bank 2

P2AC6 indicates an excessive reference voltage on the intake oxygen sensor serving bank 2, as happens when the reference wire touches a supply or battery feed, when the sensor ground is open or when moisture bridges the connector pins.
Reference wire of the bank 2 sensor shorted to a supply or battery feed
Moisture bridging pins in the connector
EGR on bank 2 reduced, NOx may rise
P2AC7: Charge Air Cooler Coolant Temperature Sensor B Circuit
P2AC7 is the general circuit fault of the second coolant temperature sensor in the low-temperature loop that serves a water-cooled charge air cooler.
Loose, corroded or coolant-contaminated sensor B connector
Chafed or broken wire between sensor B and the module
Faulty sensor input or reference in the engine control module
Implausible or missing value for sensor B in live data
Reduced boost or power on some engines
P2AC8: Charge Air Cooler Coolant Temperature Sensor B Circuit Range/Performance

P2AC8 sets when charge air cooler coolant temperature sensor B delivers an electrically valid value that makes no sense for the situation, for example after a long engine-off period when every temperature in the engine bay should have converged, or when it fails to change while the loop pump runs and the cooler heats up.
Low coolant level or air trapped in the low-temperature loop
Sensor B drifting out of its characteristic
Electric charge air cooler coolant pump weak or not running
Control module software needing an update
Check engine light on, often only after several drives
Sensor B reads clearly different from sensor A after a cold soak
Higher intake air temperature under load
P2AC9: Charge Air Cooler Coolant Temperature Sensor B Circuit Low

P2AC9 reports that the signal of charge air cooler coolant temperature sensor B has dropped below its permitted window. These sensors are NTC thermistors, so a low signal stands for an implausibly hot coolant and usually means the signal wire touches ground or the element is internally shorted.
Signal wire of sensor B shorted to ground
Coolant in the connector bridging the terminals
Live data shows an extremely high coolant temperature for sensor B
Coolant pump of the loop runs constantly or boost is reduced
P2ACA: Charge Air Cooler Coolant Temperature Sensor B Circuit High

P2ACA is the opposite end: the voltage from charge air cooler coolant temperature sensor B sits above anything a real temperature would produce. For a thermistor input this looks like extreme cold and is typical of an unplugged connector, a broken signal wire, a lost sensor ground or a short to a voltage source.
Disconnected plug or broken signal wire of sensor B
Open ground or return line of the sensor
Signal wire shorted to a voltage source
Live data shows an extremely low coolant temperature for sensor B
P2ACB: Charge Air Cooler Coolant Temperature Sensor B Intermittent/Erratic

P2ACB covers a sensor B signal that jumps or briefly drops out instead of following the slow temperature changes of a coolant loop. The title, without the word circuit, also includes erratic values while the wiring stays intact. No maker publishes the B-side check.
Terminal with weak contact tension in the sensor B plug
Harness rubbing through intermittently under vibration
Sensor B element with unstable output
Check engine light comes and goes
Sensor B value jumps in live data
P2ACC: P2ACC is the general circuit code for a second reductant (DEF) temperature sensor outside the tank; the tank sensors have their own series (P205A ff. and P2ADA ff.). Sensor A, coded P2042 ff., is placed by Deutz in the SCR supply path (SPN 4337) and by Volvo and Mack in the DEF pump.
Connector of sensor B corroded by DEF residue
Damaged wiring between sensor B and the controller
Check engine light and DEF/SCR warning
Countdown or speed limitation if the fault persists
P2ACD: Reductant Temperature Sensor B Circuit Range/Performance

P2ACD flags a reductant temperature sensor B reading that is electrically fine but disagrees with the other temperatures the SCR controller knows, typically checked after a cold soak, when DEF lines, tank and ambient should read about the same. No manufacturer publicly describes P2ACD.
Controller software with an overly tight plausibility check
Sensor B drifting from its characteristic
Line heater warming the sensor area during the check
Check engine light after a cold start
SCR warning with no noticeable driving change
P2ACE: Reductant Temperature Sensor B Circuit Low

P2ACE means the signal of reductant temperature sensor B lies below its valid voltage band. With the NTC elements used for DEF temperature, a low voltage translates into an extremely hot reading, so a signal line rubbing through to ground, a crushed connector or DEF that has wicked into the plug and bridges the contacts are the usual suspects.
Signal wire of sensor B shorted to ground
DEF wicked into the connector bridging the terminals
Check engine light and SCR warning
Implausibly high DEF temperature in live data
P2ACF: Reductant Temperature Sensor B Circuit High

P2ACF is set when reductant temperature sensor B reports a voltage above its valid band. For a thermistor that reads as deep cold, and it is what an open signal wire, a missing sensor ground, a disconnected plug or a short to supply voltage cause.
Open signal wire or disconnected plug at sensor B
Signal wire shorted to supply voltage
Check engine light and SCR warning
Implausibly low DEF temperature in live data
Delayed start of dosing after a cold start
P2AD0: Reductant Temperature Sensor B Circuit Intermittent
P2AD0 stands for short interruptions or jumps in the signal of reductant temperature sensor B. The current title reads circuit intermittent only, without erratic. No manufacturer publishes this test.
Moisture or DEF residue in the sensor B connector
Wire breaking intermittently inside the insulation
Check engine light that appears sporadically
Jumping DEF temperature in live data
P2AD1: Throttle/Pedal Position Sensor/Switch C/G Voltage Correlation
P2AD1 compares the voltages of position signals C and G and sets when they stop describing the same position.
Raised contact resistance in the throttle connector
Worn or drifting sensor track in the second throttle body
Fault on the shared 5 V reference or sensor ground
Reduced power or limited throttle response
P2AD2: Throttle/Pedal Position Sensor/Switch B/G Voltage Correlation

P2AD2 sets when signals B and G no longer agree in voltage. On engines with one throttle body per bank this is a cross-bank comparison: with GM's 2023 letter scheme, B is the second track of the bank 1 throttle and G the second track of the bank 2 throttle.
High resistance at the pins of the throttle actuator connectors
Drifting position track in one of the throttle bodies
Damaged wiring to one throttle actuator
Further throttle codes such as P2135 or P2136 stored
P2AD3: Throttle/Pedal Position Sensor/Switch A/G Voltage Correlation

P2AD3 compares tracks A and G. In GM's 2023 scheme A is the first sensor of the bank 1 throttle body and G the second sensor of the bank 2 unit, so the pair links both throttles of a V engine and can reveal that one plate is not where the other suggests.
Raised contact resistance in the connectors of both throttle actuators
One throttle body with a faulty position sensor
Fault on a shared sensor supply or ground
Possible loss of power or emergency throttle mode
P2AD4: P2AD4 reports that the voltage of an intermediate system, a supply level between the 12 V network and a high-voltage traction battery, has fallen below its lower limit.
Weak or deeply discharged 48 V battery
Starter-generator not charging the intermediate network
DC/DC converter drawing the network down
Warning lamp or message about the electrical system
Engine may not restart via the starter-generator
P2AD5: P2AD5 is the high counterpart: the intermediate voltage level, in current vehicles mostly a 48 V mild-hybrid network, rises above its permitted maximum.
Starter-generator regulating the voltage too high
48 V battery disconnected internally or unable to accept charge
Faulty DC/DC converter feeding back into the network
Warning message about the electrical system
Recuperation, electric boost and start-stop unavailable
P2AD6: Reductant Pump Motor Position Sensor Circuit
P2AD6 is the general circuit code of the position sensor in the motor of the reductant (DEF) pump.
Position sensor or electronics inside the pump module defective
DEF residue or corrosion in the pump connector
Missing supply or ground for the pump electronics
Check engine light and SCR warning
DEF dosing stops; countdown to speed limitation
P2AD7: Reductant Pump Motor Position Sensor Circuit Range/Performance

P2AD7 sets when the motor position signal of the reductant pump is electrically valid but does not fit what the pump should be doing, for instance a rotor position or derived speed that is out of step with the commanded drive pattern. No maker documents P2AD7 publicly.
Pump stiff or partly frozen, crystallised DEF in the pump head
Position sensor inside the pump giving a shifted signal
Check engine light and SCR warning
Pressure build-up of the DEF system fails, often after cold nights
P2AD8: Reductant Pump Motor Position Sensor Circuit Low

P2AD8 reports a reductant pump motor position signal stuck below its valid range. For Hall-type sensors this mostly means the output is pulled to ground permanently: a signal wire shorted to ground, a sensor that has lost its supply, or an internal short in the pump electronics.
Sensor supply missing, e.g. blown fuse or open feed
Internal short in the pump electronics
Check engine light and SCR warning
DEF pump does not run, no dosing
P2AD9: Reductant Pump Motor Position Sensor Circuit High

P2AD9 is the high-side fault: the pump motor position signal stays above its permitted range. An open signal line pulled up by the controller's internal resistor, a broken sensor ground or a short to the supply rail produce this picture.
Open signal line or broken sensor ground
DEF residue corroding the pump connector
Signal shorted to the supply rail
Check engine light and SCR warning
No DEF pressure build-up, dosing stops
P2ADA: Reductant Tank Temperature Sensor B Circuit Range/Performance
P2ADA checks whether the second DEF tank temperature reading is plausible. GM documents it twice.
DEF quality sensor with drifting temperature element
Chafed engine harness disturbing the signals
Check engine light after a cold start
P2ADB: Reductant Tank Temperature Sensor B Circuit Low

P2ADB flags a value from the second DEF tank temperature sensor that lies below the lowest temperature the sensor can physically report, so the controller treats it as a circuit fault and not as cold fluid. GM is the documented user.
Defective thermistor in the DEF quality or tank sensor unit
Moisture or DEF crystals in the sensor connector
Damaged signal or supply wiring to the tank sensor
Check engine light right after the fault is detected
DEF or SCR system warning in the cluster
Countdown to reduced power or restart lock if left unrepaired
P2ADC: Reductant Tank Temperature Sensor B Circuit High

P2ADC is the upper limit check on the same sensor B: the reported DEF temperature is higher than the fluid in the tank could ever get. In GM's 2017 and 2018 diesel calibrations the quality sensor thermistor has to exceed 155 °C in 40 of 50 samples, with cranking finished and more than 11 V at the powertrain relay; the outcome is a Type A code.
Internal fault in the quality sensor or smart tank sensor unit
Chafed engine harness disturbing the sensor circuit
Corroded or loose pins at the tank sensor connector
DEF system message, often together with other harness-related codes
Possible inducement countdown toward reduced power
P2ADD: Reductant Tank Temperature Sensor B Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P2ADD judges how the sensor B signal moves over time instead of how high it is. Fluid in a tank warms and cools slowly, so sudden jumps suggest a loose contact or a failing element.
Loose or corroded contact at the tank sensor connector
Degrading thermistor in the quality or tank sensor unit
Check engine light that may return after clearing
Jumping DEF temperature in live data
P2ADE: Reductant Tank Temperature Sensor B Circuit

P2ADE is the general circuit code for reductant tank temperature sensor B, intended for systems that report a fault on this input without splitting it into low, high or erratic. No manufacturer documents P2ADE publicly.
Open signal line or unplugged tank sensor connector
Input fault in the SCR or engine control module
P2ADF: P2ADF means the engine control module has concluded that air reaches the cylinders of bank 2 without passing the air measurement. Audi documents the code for the 4.0 litre TFSI V8 in the A8, S8, SQ7, SQ8, RS Q8, RS 6 Avant and RS 7 from model years 2019 to 2023.
Leaking full-load crankcase breather line on bank 2 (Audi 4.0 TFSI)
Split intake or boost hose on bank 2
Leaking intake manifold gasket on bank 2
Check engine or exhaust warning light on
Whistling noise from the engine bay
P2AE0: Intake Air O2 Sensor Pumping Current Trim Circuit Open Bank 1

P2AE0 says the calibration (trim) wire of bank 1's intake O2 sensor has lost continuity. On a Bosch-type wide-band element this is pin 5 (RT/IA), which connects a resistor in the plug that Bosch uses to set the characteristic of each individual sensor; without it the ECM scales the oxygen signal wrongly.
Trim lead (pin 5) broken in the harness
Trim contact pushed back or corroded in the sensor plug
Calibration resistor inside the sensor connector open
EGR reduced or run without oxygen feedback
P2AE1: Intake Air O2 Sensor Pumping Current Trim Circuit Low Bank 1

P2AE1 is stored when the voltage on the trim circuit of the bank 1 intake oxygen sensor falls below its window. With the ignition on, the 2010 Saab 9-5 expects roughly 2.8 V on terminal 5 of its wide-band probe, the trim connection; a value near zero suggests a lead rubbing on ground or a shorted resistor in the sensor plug.
Trim lead chafed through to ground
Calibration resistor in the sensor plug shorted
Open trim lead on sensors whose interface reports it as low
EGR cut back, possibly higher NOx
P2AE2: Intake Air O2 Sensor Pumping Current Trim Circuit High Bank 1

P2AE2 means the voltage on the trim lead of the intake air O2 sensor for bank 1 is too high. In the six-wire harness of a wide-band probe this line runs next to the heater feed, so a pinched wire or moisture bridging the pins in the connector can drag it towards battery voltage.
Trim lead touching the heater supply
Moisture bridging contacts in the sensor plug
Internal short in the sensor or its connector module
P2AE3: Intake Air O2 Sensor Pumping Current Circuit Open Bank 1
P2AE3 reports a break in the pumping current lead of the bank 1 intake oxygen sensor, pin 1 of a Bosch LSU 4.9 (APE/IP).
Sensor plug loose or not latched
Pump cell inside the sensor open
EGR runs without sensor feedback or is switched off
P2AE4: Intake Air O2 Sensor Pumping Current Circuit Low Bank 1
P2AE4 flags too low a level in the pumping current circuit belonging to the bank 1 intake sensor, usually a pump lead chafed through to ground or an internal short in the pump cell.
Pump current lead shorted to ground
Internal short in the pump cell
Sensor interface in the ECM faulty
Possibly higher NOx at an emissions test
P2AE5: Intake Air O2 Sensor Pumping Current Circuit High Bank 1

P2AE5 is the high-side fault of the pumping current lead on the bank 1 intake oxygen sensor. A short to the heater supply or another battery feed in the harness is the classic cause; because the intake sensor works in damp air close to where blow-by gas and EGR enter, water in the plug comes next.
Pump current lead shorted to the heater or another supply
Water or condensate in the sensor plug
Sensor interface in the ECM damaged by the short
P2AE6: Intake Air O2 Sensor Negative Current Control Circuit Open Bank 1

P2AE6 points to an open negative current control line on the bank 1 intake air oxygen sensor. This is the shared return of pump and Nernst cell, which Bosch names virtual ground (IPN/VM, pin 2); Saab's 2010 9-5 shows about 2.5 V on it at ignition-on, a bias that lets the pump current change direction.
Corroded or loose return contact in the plug
Internal break of the common electrode in the sensor
P2AE7: Intake Air O2 Sensor Negative Current Control Circuit Low Bank 1

P2AE7 is set when the virtual-ground return of the bank 1 intake oxygen sensor is pulled below its bias. In operation this lead sits roughly 2.5 V above chassis, as Saab's 2010 9-5 documents for its wide-band probe; a wire touching the engine block, a bracket or the intake pipe drags it towards zero.
Return lead chafed against engine or bracket
Internal short of the common electrode to ground
Bias source in the ECM faulty
EGR cut back, possibly higher NOx
P2AE8: Intake Air O2 Sensor Negative Current Control Circuit High Bank 1

P2AE8 reports that, on bank 1's intake air oxygen sensor, the negative current control line sits above its intended level. For the bias on this return to climb towards battery voltage, something must feed it: most often the heater supply sharing the six-pin plug, sometimes condensate in a connector that collects moisture from the intake air.
Return lead shorted to the heater supply
Internal short between heater and cell
P2AE9: Intake Air O2 Sensor Pumping Current Trim Circuit Open Bank 2

P2AE9 is the bank 2 version of the open trim circuit: the line from the ECM to the calibration resistor of the second intake air oxygen sensor has no continuity. A separate sensor for bank 2 only makes sense where each cylinder bank draws its charge or EGR through its own path; nobody has published a vehicle that uses P2AE9.
Trim contact pushed back in the plug
Trim lead broken, often near the hot exhaust of bank 2
Calibration resistor in the sensor connector open
EGR on bank 2 reduced or without feedback
P2AEA: Intake Air O2 Sensor Pumping Current Trim Circuit Low Bank 2

P2AEA reports a trim circuit voltage below the permitted range at the bank 2 intake O2 sensor. Likely culprits are a trim wire grounded where the harness passes the second turbocharger, or a damaged resistor inside the sensor connector.
Trim lead grounded near the second turbocharger
Calibration resistor in the plug damaged
Fault in a ground or ECM path shared with bank 1
P2AEB: Intake Air O2 Sensor Pumping Current Trim Circuit High Bank 2
P2AEB indicates excessive voltage on the trim wire serving the second bank's intake O2 sensor.
Trim lead shorted to the heater or another supply
Moisture bridging contacts in the plug
Internal short in the sensor connector module
EGR on bank 2 reduced, NOx may rise
P2AEC: Intake Air O2 Sensor Pumping Current Circuit Open Bank 2

P2AEC means the pumping current wire of the second-bank intake oxygen sensor is interrupted. On a Bosch-style element the ECM uses this lead to push oxygen into or out of the measuring gap until the Nernst cell is balanced; the current needed is the oxygen signal.
Pump current lead broken, often from heat near bank 2 exhaust
Sensor plug loose or not latched
Pump cell inside the sensor open
EGR on bank 2 without feedback or switched off
P2AED: Intake Air O2 Sensor Pumping Current Circuit Low Bank 2
P2AED stands for a pumping current circuit on the bank 2 intake oxygen sensor that reads below its limit. A pump lead grounded on the engine or a breakdown inside the pump cell are the usual reasons.
Pump current lead grounded on the engine
ECM sensor interface faulty (likely if bank 1 also reports)
EGR on bank 2 limited, possibly higher NOx
P2AEE: Intake Air O2 Sensor Pumping Current Circuit High Bank 2

P2AEE marks the pumping current lead of the bank 2 intake air oxygen sensor as too high. Contact with the heater feed in the shared plug, chafing against a live wire or water that has entered the connector can raise it.
Pump current lead touching the heater feed
Harness chafed against a live wire
EGR on bank 2 reduced, NOx may rise
P2AEF: Intake Air O2 Sensor Negative Current Control Circuit Open Bank 2

P2AEF indicates that the return line, or virtual ground, of the bank 2 intake oxygen sensor is open. Both cells of a wide-band element reference this lead, pin 2 (IPN/VM) on the Bosch LSU 4.9, which the ECM biases so current can flow both ways.
Internal break of the common electrode
Usually no noticeable change in driveability
P2AF0: Intake Air O2 Sensor Negative Current Control Circuit Low Bank 2
P2AF0 is stored when the negative current control circuit of the bank 2 intake oxygen sensor falls below its window.
Return lead worn through at a clip or bracket
Internal short of the sensor to ground
EGR on bank 2 cut back, possibly higher NOx
P2AF1: Intake Air O2 Sensor Negative Current Control Circuit High Bank 2

P2AF1 is the high-side fault of the virtual-ground return on the bank 2 intake air oxygen sensor. Lifting this biased line towards supply voltage requires contact with a feed, most often the heater circuit in the same plug, or condensed water inside a connector.
Return lead shorted to the heater circuit
Bias source in the ECM faulty
EGR on bank 2 reduced, NOx may rise
P2AF2: P2AF2 reports an open or otherwise faulty control line for a third starter relay. Such a relay appears where cranking is split across several switching stages, for instance on stop-start engines. No manufacturer documents P2AF2 publicly.
Broken control wire or unplugged relay connector
Blown fuse or missing supply to the relay coil
Faulty output driver in the control module
P2AF3: Starter Relay C Control Circuit Low

P2AF3 sets when the control line of starter relay C is pulled toward ground at a moment the module expects a different level. What that does to the relay depends on the driver type: with ground-side switching the short acts like a permanent on command, with supply-side switching the coil never gets current.
Control wire chafed through to ground
Faulty output driver in the control module
Relay energised all the time or not at all, depending on circuit design
P2AF4: Starter Relay C Control Circuit High

P2AF4 points to a control wire of starter relay C that carries battery voltage when the module has switched its driver off, typically because it touches a 12 V feed or because the driver leaks. With supply-side switching that can keep the coil energised; with ground-side switching the module can no longer pull the relay in. No manufacturer publishes P2AF4.
Control wire shorted to a 12 V circuit
Water in the relay socket or power distribution box
Relay may stay engaged with ignition off
P2AF5: P2AF5 means starter relay C remains in its energised state when it should have dropped out.
Loose or corroded B+ connection at main or auxiliary battery
Depleted auxiliary battery causing a false fail
Open or poorly seated 150 A fuse or fuse array
Stop-start inoperative, service message for the system
P2AF6: P2AF6 is the reverse fault on relay C: commanded to switch, the relay does not change state. Stellantis names it Starter Relay 3 Stuck Off, on some Wagoneers Dual Starter Relay Stuck.
Power distribution centre connector not fully seated
Depleted auxiliary battery causing a false fail
Occasional failure to restart after an auto-stop
P2AF7: P2AF7 is the open-circuit or general fault on the control line of a fourth starter relay, relay D. Four separately monitored starter relays only make sense where there is more than one cranking path, for example a pinion relay, a second starter or a battery isolation stage on a stop-start engine.
Broken control wire or corroded connector
Blown fuse feeding the relay coil
Stored code, lamp depending on manufacturer
P2AF8: Starter Relay D Control Circuit Low

P2AF8 is logged when the control line of starter relay D shows a short to ground. Depending on whether the module switches the coil on its ground side or its supply side, the relay then either sits permanently energised or can no longer be operated.
Spread or bent terminals in the power distribution centre connector
Several unrelated electrical faults at the same time
P2AF9: Starter Relay D Control Circuit High
P2AF9 indicates that the control line of starter relay D sits at supply voltage although the driver is switched off, mostly a short to a 12 V circuit or a leaking driver stage.
Control wire chafed against a live circuit
Leaking output driver in the control module
Starter may not engage, or in rare cases keep running
Stored code, lamp depending on manufacturer
P2AFA: P2AFA describes starter relay D staying engaged although the control module has commanded it to release; the module infers this from a feedback signal, a voltage or current that should have changed. No manufacturer documents P2AFA publicly.
Control wire receiving voltage from another circuit
Starter keeps turning or grinding after the engine starts
P2AFB: P2AFB is set when starter relay D ignores an on command: the module energises it, but the expected change of voltage or current in the switched circuit never appears. No manufacturer documents P2AFB publicly. Stellantis shows on relay C how such a check works.
Low supply voltage or poor ground at the relay
Loose connector at the relay or distribution box
Engine does not crank on the affected path
Stored code, lamp depending on manufacturer
P2AFC: P2AFC is the general circuit code for a fourth engine coolant temperature sensor. Engines with split cooling, electric pumps or separate head, block, radiator and heater circuits carry several such sensors, and how they are numbered is up to each maker.
Open wire or loose connector at sensor 4
Faulty input stage in the engine control module
Cooling fans running more than usual on substitute value
P2AFD: Engine Coolant Temperature Sensor 4 Circuit Range/Performance

P2AFD flags a sensor 4 coolant reading that stays inside the electrical limits but makes no sense, for instance a value that disagrees with the engine's other temperature readings once everything has cooled down for hours, or that hardly moves while the engine warms up.
Corrosion adding resistance in the connector
Air pocket at the sensor after coolant service
Check engine light, often only after a cold start
Sensor 4 value clearly differing from the others in live data
P2AFE: Engine Coolant Temperature Sensor 4 Circuit Low
Coolant sensors are NTC thermistors, so a signal from sensor 4 that is too low stands for an impossibly hot reading, usually a signal wire grounded or a shorted element.
Signal wire shorted to ground, for example by harness chafing
Faulty input in the engine control module
Check engine light after two trips
Cooling fans running at full speed
Implausibly high coolant temperature in live data
P2AFF: Engine Coolant Temperature Sensor 4 Circuit High
P2AFF reports an excessive sensor 4 signal. For an NTC thermistor that means an implausibly cold reading, mostly from an open circuit, an unplugged connector or a line shorted to voltage.
Open signal wire or unplugged connector
Check engine light after two trips
Implausibly cold coolant temperature in live data
Thermal management running on a default value
P2B00: P2B00 says the engine module could not confirm, with the engine past its cold-start phase, that injection pulses it commanded for cylinder 1 really happened. GM documents the check for its petrol direct-injection engines: the ECM digitises the voltage across both injector wires and looks for the small flux signature the armature leaves when it lifts.
Engine harness chafed through to ground (GM L3B – above the camshaft carrier or near the left shock tower)
Armature or needle of the cylinder 1 injector sticking, so no opening signature appears
Outdated ECM calibration (GM service update for the 1.2 L LIH)
High contact resistance at the cylinder 1 injector connector
Check engine light after the second faulty trip
Rough running or misfire on cylinder 1 (P0301), sometimes no noticeable symptom
With a harness short, several unrelated codes at once and possibly a no-start
P2B01: P2B01 is stored when the ECM keeps missing the opening signature of the cylinder 2 injector in normal running, i.e. it has no proof that fuel was delivered on that cylinder's commanded pulses. GM uses the code on direct-injection petrol engines.
Engine harness shorted to ground at a chafe point (GM L3B bulletin series PIT5677)
Cylinder 2 injector opening sluggishly or not at all (deposits, worn armature)
Corroded or loose injector 2 connector distorting the feedback voltage
Uneven idle, possibly misfire on cylinder 2
Together with many other codes and erratic behaviour when the harness is shorted
P2B02: P2B02 concerns cylinder 3: in warm operation the ECM did not see the voltage bump that marks the cylinder 3 injector actually opening, often enough to count pulses as not delivered. On GM's 1.2 L LIH three-cylinder, cylinder 3 is the last one, and the 2025 table for that family (cylinders 1–3 only) decides after 50 to 100 samples, Type B.
ECM calibration with false detections (GM 1.2 L LIH, service update A202310450)
Check engine light, often without any driveability complaint
On a real injector fault rough running on cylinder 3 (P0303)
P2B03: With P2B03 the engine module reports that cylinder 4 injection pulses went unconfirmed after warm-up: the coil voltage showed no proof of the armature moving.
Harness chafed near the turbo actuator or elsewhere on the engine (GM 2.7 L)
Poor contact in the fuel rail injector connector
Lamp on after the second faulty trip
Possibly misfire on cylinder 4 (P0304) or under load
Further injector codes of the same cylinder stored at the same time
P2B04: P2B04 extends the warm-running missed-pulse check to cylinder 5, so it only matters on engines with five or more cylinders. No manufacturer documents P2B04 publicly as a monitor of its own.
Cylinder 5 injector sticking or opening too slowly
Chafed or high-resistance wiring to injector 5
Calibration error in the engine software
Rough running or misfire on cylinder 5 (P0305)
P2B05: P2B05 marks missed injection pulses on cylinder 6 outside the cold-start window; on a six-cylinder engine this is the last cylinder in the order of numbers. No manufacturer documents P2B05 publicly as a stand-alone check. GM's 2025 V8 calibration (25OBDG06A/06B) lists it only in the support tables shared by the pulse family.
Deposits or wear on the cylinder 6 injector hampering small pulses
Contact problem at the injector 6 plug
Injector driver or voltage sensing in the ECM faulty
Slight shaking at idle or low speed, misfire on cylinder 6 (P0306)
P2B06: P2B06 is the warm-engine pulse check for cylinder 7 and so practically limited to V8 and larger engines. No manufacturer documents P2B06 publicly in its own entry.
Cylinder 7 injector with weak or missing armature lift
Wiring to injector 7 damaged by heat or chafing
Rail pressure outside the plausible range, distorting the opening signal
Engine light on after two trips
P2B07: P2B07 closes the warm-running row at cylinder 8, and the engine-wide check counting missed pulses over all cylinders is P2B96. No manufacturer documents P2B07 publicly as a separate monitor; GM's 2025 V8 tables mention it only in the code lists of shared calibration tables, while their cylinder 8 warm faults run as P10B1/P10B2.
Heat-damaged harness section at the rear of the engine
Misfire on cylinder 8 (P0308), especially at idle
P2B08: Cold Start Cylinder 1 Injection Pulse Performance

P2B08 is the cold-start version of the cylinder 1 pulse check. While the catalyst is being heated, many direct-injection engines split each injection into two or three small pulses, and CARB requires for 20/50/100 % of model years 2026/2027/2028 that missing split or multiple pulses be detected during the cold-start strategy.
Cold-start software anomaly (GM 1.2 L LIH, fixed by ECM reprogramming)
Cylinder 1 injector sluggish when cold, missing the short split pulses
Contact fault in injector 1 wiring that shows mainly when cold
Warning lamp, often with the engine running normally once warm
Possibly slightly rough running in the first seconds after a cold start
Code returns only after a long standstill, not on warm restarts
P2B09: Cold Start Cylinder 2 Injection Pulse Performance

P2B09 reports that while the catalyst is being warmed after a cold start the ECM missed the opening trace of injector 2 on too many commanded pulses. CARB defines the window: at least six hours engine-off, ambient at or above −6.7 °C and coolant no more than 15 °C warmer than ambient.
Cylinder 2 injector not responding to the short cold-start pulses
Wiring or connector problem on injector 2
Check engine light after cold starts on two trips
Usually no driveability issue once the engine is warm
P2B0A: Cold Start Cylinder 3 Injection Pulse Performance
P2B0A stands for missed cold-start pulses on cylinder 3. For the GM 1.2 L LIH with its three cylinders it is the highest cold-start cylinder code, since that engine's 2025 table stops at P2B0A.
ECM software anomaly on the GM 1.2 L LIH (service update A202310450)
Cylinder 3 injector reacting too slowly when cold
Lamp on, code stored only after a cold start
P2B0B: Cold Start Cylinder 4 Injection Pulse Performance

P2B0B covers cylinder 4 during the cold-start strategy and in GM's tables belongs to four-cylinder and larger engines. GM's 2025 four-cylinder table sets the window via P2B95 differently from the three-cylinder: catalyst below 400 °C, 450–2,800 rpm, pedal up to 35 % and less than 100 s run time, so the test may continue while pulling away.
ECM calibration needing an update (GM bulletin 20-NA-230)
Harness damage or poor contact at the fuel rail connector (GM 2.7 L)
Cylinder 4 injector sluggish at low temperature
Possibly slightly uneven running during the first minute
P2B0C: Cold Start Cylinder 5 Injection Pulse Performance

P2B0C flags cylinder 5 when its injector fails to show an opening signature on the split pulses used to heat the catalyst after a cold start. Publicly it is documented only by GM, in the 2025 V8 table 25OBDG06A, which lists the cold-start codes for all eight cylinders (P2B08–P2B0F): Type B, decision after 50 to 100 samples.
Cylinder 5 injector not lifting on the short cold-start pulses
Injector 5 wiring or connector with a contact fault
ECM calibration issue (check for software updates)
Check engine light after two cold-start trips
Usually unremarkable running once warm, maybe a short rough idle when cold
P2B0D: Cold Start Cylinder 6 Injection Pulse Performance

P2B0D belongs to the cold-start family and points at cylinder 6: while the engine was splitting injections to heat the catalyst, the ECM failed to register the armature-lift voltage signature on too many of that injector's pulses. GM publishes it in the 2025 V8 table 25OBDG06A as Type B with a verdict after 50 to 100 samples.
Cylinder 6 injector opening sluggishly on short pulses when cold (deposits, worn armature)
Corroded connector or chafed wire at injector 6 distorting the feedback voltage
ECM calibration detecting the opening signature unreliably in the cold-start phase
Check engine light after two cold starts with the fault
Uneven idle in the first minute after a cold start, later normal
P2B0E: Cold Start Cylinder 7 Injection Pulse Performance

P2B0E is the cylinder 7 entry of the cold-start pulse check. On engines that fire two or three short injections per cycle while heating the catalyst, the ECM expects each of them to show an opening signature on the injector feedback voltage; for cylinder 7 too many did not.
Cylinder 7 injector not lifting on the very short split pulses (deposits, armature wear)
Enable or command wire of injector 7 damaged, falsifying the measured voltage
ECM software with an overly strict opening-signature evaluation
Warning lamp after the second faulty cold start
Slight shaking right after a cold start, often nothing noticeable
P2B0F: Cold Start Cylinder 8 Injection Pulse Performance

P2B0F closes the cold-start series with cylinder 8, so it only appears on eight-cylinder engines; publicly GM documents it, in table 25OBDG06A for its 2025 V8 family (Type B, two trips, 50 to 100 samples).
Needle or armature of the cylinder 8 injector sticking on cold short pulses
Loose or corroded connector at injector 8
Chafed injector harness on the bank carrying cylinder 8
Check engine light, frequently without driveability complaints
With a real injector fault, rough cold idle and possibly misfire on cylinder 8 (P0308)
P2B10: Cylinder 1 Injection Pulse Offset Not Learned

P2B10 means the engine control holds no valid learned offset for injector 1 – the correction of the opening time used for very small injection quantities has not been established. No manufacturer documents this code publicly.
Learn values cleared – after replacing injector 1 or the control unit, or after an adaption reset with a scan tool
Too few coasting phases with fuel cut-off for the learn to run
Injector 1 opening inconsistently, so no stable value is found
Warning lamp, otherwise often no noticeable effect
Possibly harder combustion noise at idle on cylinder 1
P2B11: Cylinder 1 Injection Pulse Offset Exceeded Learning Limit
P2B11 says the learned small-quantity correction for injector 1 has drifted beyond what the engine control may apply.
Incorrectly learned injector values in the PCM (Ford TSB 18-2015, reset and reprogramming)
Injector 1 worn or coked so its opening behaviour has really shifted
Disturbed crankshaft speed signal falsifying the learn result
Diesel knock at idle, sometimes together with balance code P0263
P2B12: Cylinder 2 Injection Pulse Offset Not Learned

P2B12 is stored when injector 2's pulse offset has not been learned, so the controller still relies on a default value for the smallest injections. The public record contains no manufacturer using this exact code; the explanation here follows from the title and from the neighbouring monitors.
Driving profile without enough fuel cut-off phases (constant load, towing)
Adaption values reset after work on injector 2 or the fuel system
Crankshaft speed signal too noisy to detect the test injection
Warning lamp without a clear driveability complaint
Possibly louder combustion on cylinder 2 at low load
P2B13: Cylinder 2 Injection Pulse Offset Exceeded Learning Limit
P2B13 concerns injector 2 on Ford's Power Stroke diesels: its zero-fuel learn value has run past the permitted band.
Steering wheel oscillation disturbing the crank or cam signal (Ford SSM 48877)
Injector 2 with genuinely shifted opening time due to wear or deposits
Implausible learned values in the PCM
Often no running fault; with a worn injector, knocking or rough idle
P2B14: Cylinder 3 Injection Pulse Offset Not Learned
P2B14 tells that no offset has yet been learned for injector 3. No carmaker publishes this code for a specific engine, and the GM and Ford tables checked do not contain it.
Learn not yet completed for all rail pressure levels of injector 3
Injector 3 or control unit recently replaced without completing the learn
Rail pressure not holding steady enough during the test injection
Warning lamp, driving behaviour mostly unchanged
Slightly uneven idle in some cases
P2B15: Cylinder 3 Injection Pulse Offset Exceeded Learning Limit
P2B15 reports that the zero-fuel correction learned for injector 3 has reached Ford's limit.
Learned values unsuitable after fuel system repairs (Ford TSB 23-2076, software and adaption reset)
Injector 3 drifted mechanically (wear, coking, internal leakage)
Possibly knocking or rough running at idle
P2B16: Cylinder 4 Injection Pulse Offset Not Learned

P2B16 indicates a missing learned pulse offset for injector 4. Public manufacturer material does not tie it to any engine; Ford's published diesel monitor and its bulletins use only the exceeded-limit partner P2B17.
Injector 4 or PCM replaced, or adaptions reset, and the learn not yet completed
Learn conditions (warm engine, fuel cut-off) rarely reached
Injector 4 not opening on minimal pulses at all
Louder combustion noise, especially at idle
P2B17: Cylinder 4 Injection Pulse Offset Exceeded Learning Limit

P2B17 is set when injector 4's learned pulse offset goes past the allowed band. For the 6.7 L engine in 2020–2022 F-Super Duty trucks Ford saw this after fuel system work: stored learned values no longer matched the new parts.
Old learn values after fuel system work, cleared by a warm idle relearn (Ford SSM 50646/50816)
Rail pressure deviating from target during the test injection
Check engine light shortly after a fuel system repair
P2B18: Cylinder 5 Injection Pulse Offset Not Learned
P2B18 means injector 5 has no learned offset. No manufacturer documents this exact code.
New injector 5 or control unit without a completed learn
Enabling conditions for the learn not met often enough
Faulty injector 5 wiring preventing a valid measurement
Rarely noticeable; at most slightly uneven low-load running
P2B19: Cylinder 5 Injection Pulse Offset Exceeded Learning Limit

P2B19 flags injector 5: its learned zero-fuel offset exceeds the calibrated limit. Ford's diesel OBD summary groups the code with the other odd numbers from P2B11 to P2B1F under the Zero Fuel Calibration monitor, which it files under fuel system feedback control.
Learned values skewed by driving above about 760 m (Ford SSM 53340)
PCM software without the later calibration fix
Check engine light after mountain or high-plateau driving
P2B1A: Cylinder 6 Injection Pulse Offset Not Learned

P2B1A reports that the pulse offset for injector 6 has not been learned. Public manufacturer sources do not name this code; on the 3.0 L V6 Power Stroke built by Ford, where cylinder 6 is the last one, Ford's summary lists only the exceeded-limit code P2B1B.
Learn for injector 6 still pending after a reset or parts replacement
Mostly short trips with a cold engine, so the learn rarely starts
Injector 6 delivering so erratically that no value can be fixed
Perhaps slightly harder combustion noise at idle
P2B1B: Cylinder 6 Injection Pulse Offset Exceeded Learning Limit

P2B1B concerns injector 6. On Ford's 3.0 L V6 Power Stroke it is the last cylinder the zero-fuel monitor checks, on the 6.7 L V8 the sixth of eight. The code means the energising time at which injector 6 starts to deliver has moved too far from its stored target, beyond the learn limit.
PCM software learning wrong values at altitude (Ford TSB 25-2262)
Injector 6 drifted by wear or deposits
Adaptions not reset after an earlier repair
Slightly rough idle, driveability otherwise normal
P2B1C: Cylinder 7 Injection Pulse Offset Not Learned
P2B1C says no learned offset exists for injector 7, which only applies to engines with at least seven cylinders, in practice V8s. No manufacturer publishes a monitor for this code.
Test results for injector 7 scattering too much to be accepted
Learn restarted after injector or control unit replacement
Leak in the high-pressure system disturbing the test injection
With an erratic injector, uneven idle or knocking on one cylinder
P2B1D: Cylinder 7 Injection Pulse Offset Exceeded Learning Limit

P2B1D reports that the correction learned for injector 7 during Ford's zero-fuel calibration has gone beyond its limit; cylinder 7 exists only on the 6.7 L V8. Ford's TSB 25-2412 for 2023–2025 F-Super Duty trucks calls the warning lamp in many such cases incorrect: learned values skewed by operation above 762 m, sometimes with a slightly uneven idle.
Calibration learning wrong values at altitude (Ford TSB 25-2412)
Injector 7 worn, often with balance code P0281 as well
Interference on the crank or cam speed signal
Check engine light, sometimes without a real fault
P2B1E: Cylinder 8 Injection Pulse Offset Not Learned

P2B1E means injector 8 has not received a learned pulse offset. As the final cylinder in the group it belongs to V8 engines; Ford's 6.7 L V8 would be the obvious candidate, but Ford publishes only the exceeded-limit code P2B1F for it, so no manufacturer source for P2B1E exists.
Learn values reset or injector 8 replaced, learn not finished
Few coasting phases with fuel cut-off in everyday use
Fault in the crank speed signal or the injector 8 wiring
Mostly no noticeable change in running
P2B1F: Cylinder 8 Injection Pulse Offset Exceeded Learning Limit
P2B1F is the last code of the series: the offset learned for injector 8 has crossed the learning limit. Ford uses it on the 6.7 L V8 Power Stroke.
Adaption skewed by high-altitude driving (Ford SSM 53896, reset with FDRS)
Slightly rough idle in some cases, otherwise normal running
P2B20: Hybrid/EV Electronics Coolant Temperature Sensor B Circuit

Sensor B is a second temperature sensor in the coolant loop that serves the hybrid or EV power electronics, such as inverter, DC/DC converter or on-board charger; where it sits relative to sensor A is up to the vehicle maker. P2B20 is the undifferentiated circuit code: the controller finds the signal unusable without deciding between low and high.
Loose connector, corroded pins or broken wire in the sensor B circuit
Sensor B element open or shorted internally
Faulty input stage or reference supply in the controlling module
