Hybrid or EV system warning and stored fault code
Reduced drive or charging power as a precaution
Electronics coolant pump running more often or at higher speed
P2B21: Hybrid/EV Electronics Coolant Temperature Sensor B Circuit Range/Performance

Here sensor B delivers a voltage inside its electrical window, yet the temperature it reports does not fit the rest of the vehicle: it may stay flat while the electronics warm up, or disagree with other temperatures after the car has stood for hours. No manufacturer publishes the set condition of P2B21.
Sensor B element drifted out of its characteristic curve
Air pocket around the sensor after coolant service or a leak
Corroded or loose terminals adding resistance to the signal
Controller calibration that needs an update
Hybrid system warning, often only after a cold start
Cooling pump or fan behaviour that does not match conditions
P2B22: Hybrid/EV Electronics Coolant Temperature Sensor B Circuit Low

P2B22 says the signal voltage of electronics coolant sensor B has fallen below its valid band. Since these sensors are NTC thermistors, a low voltage would mean an absurdly hot coolant, so the usual explanation is a signal wire touching ground, moisture bridging the connector or an internally shorted element.
Sensor B signal wire chafed through and shorted to ground
Water or coolant in the sensor connector
Warning lamp or hybrid system message
Electronics coolant pump and fans running at high output
Reduced electric drive or charging power
P2B23: Hybrid/EV Electronics Coolant Temperature Sensor B Circuit High

With P2B23 the signal of electronics coolant sensor B climbs close to the reference voltage. For an NTC sensor that reads as extreme cold, which in practice nearly always points to an interruption: an unplugged or water-damaged connector, a broken signal or ground lead, an open element, or more rarely a short to a voltage source.
Open signal or ground wire, or connector not fully seated
Water intrusion and corroded pins in a connector of the sensor circuit
Signal wire shorted to a voltage source
Hybrid or EV system warning with MIL
Coolant temperature for sensor B shown at about −40 °C in live data
P2B24: Hybrid/EV Electronics Coolant Temperature Sensor C Circuit

Some electrified drivetrains measure the power electronics coolant at three points, for example ahead of the inverter, behind it and at the charger or DC/DC converter. P2B24 covers the third of these sensors, C, and reports a circuit fault the controller does not classify further. Which component sensor C watches is not standardised and varies by make.
Connector or wiring fault in the sensor C circuit
Input stage of the evaluating module faulty
Stored fault code, possibly with a hybrid system message
Lower charging or drive power in hot conditions
P2B25: Hybrid/EV Electronics Coolant Temperature Sensor C Circuit Range/Performance

P2B25 is the plausibility code for the third electronics coolant sensor. The signal is electrically sound, but its value cannot be right, for example because sensor C still reads cold while sensors A and B in the same loop have long warmed up, or because it jumps by an amount the coolant could not follow. No manufacturer publishes a set condition for P2B25.
Sensor C reading drifted away from the true temperature
Air in the loop or a weak pump leaving sensor C without flow
Corrosion in the sensor C connector
Fault code set after a cold start or a long drive
P2B26: Hybrid/EV Electronics Coolant Temperature Sensor C Circuit Low

The voltage on the signal line of sensor C, the third coolant sensor in the power electronics loop, is lower than the controller accepts. Low means voltage here, not temperature: on an NTC sensor it corresponds to an implausibly hot value.
Sensor C signal lead pinched or chafed against ground
Coolant wicking into the sensor plug
Pump and radiator fan running hard even when cool
P2B27: Hybrid/EV Electronics Coolant Temperature Sensor C Circuit High
P2B27 is logged when sensor C in the power electronics coolant loop sends a signal near the top of the reference, which the controller would have to read as deep frost.
Connector backed out, terminal pushed out or wire broken
Signal line shorted to battery voltage
Warning lamp and hybrid system message
Sensor C shown far below outside temperature in live data
P2B28: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Pump A Performance
P2B28 means battery coolant pump A is electrically reachable but does not perform as the battery controller expects.
Residual air in the battery coolant loop, often after service
Battery or hybrid controller software needing an update
Worn or failing battery coolant pump
Low coolant level from a leak
Electric drive fault message or MIL
Short or missing engine auto-stops on mild hybrids
P2B29: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Pump A Overspeed - Dry Run
A centrifugal pump that suddenly spins faster while drawing less current has lost its liquid: it is churning air. P2B29 reports exactly this for battery coolant pump A.
Air in the battery coolant loop after service or incomplete bleeding
Leak in a battery cooling line lowering the level
Battery controller software misjudging pump feedback (Ford 2020 hybrids)
P2B2A: Hybrid/EV Electronics Coolant Pump A Overspeed - Dry Run
The pump in the low-temperature loop that cools power electronics and often the drive unit reports that it is turning too fast for its load, the sign of air instead of coolant.
Air in the low-temperature circuit after filling or a leak
Damaged or leaking coolant hose (Audi e-tron)
Pumps of the wrong part number or position (Mercedes 167)
Coolant or drive system warning in the instrument cluster
Churning noise from the affected pump
Reduced drive power until the loop is bled
P2B2B: Engines with split cooling, electric pumps or separate head, block, radiator and heater branches can carry five or more coolant sensors; the numbering is the maker's choice. P2B2B is the generic circuit code for number 5, meant for controllers that do not separate low from high. No manufacturer documents a set condition for P2B2B publicly.
Loose connector or broken lead at sensor 5
Faulty sensor input in the engine control module
Cooling fans or thermal management running on default values
P2B2C: Engine Coolant Temperature Sensor 5 Circuit Range/Performance

P2B2C concerns a fifth coolant sensor whose signal is electrically valid but does not behave like coolant temperature: after a long cold soak it differs clearly from the other engine temperatures, it barely rises during warm-up although the engine heats normally, or it sits stuck at one value.
No coolant flow in the sensor's branch (stuck valve, failed pump, air)
MIL, often after a cold start
Heater or fan behaviour that does not match engine temperature
P2B2D: Engine Coolant Temperature Sensor 5 Circuit Low

A low signal from coolant sensor 5 means its NTC resistance has collapsed, which the engine computer would read as an impossibly hot engine; a grounded signal wire or a shorted element is the usual reason.
Signal wire grounded, for example by a chafed harness
Radiator fans running constantly at high speed
Other harness-related codes stored at the same time
P2B2E: Engine Coolant Temperature Sensor 5 Circuit High

P2B2E is stored when the fifth coolant sensor shows a resistance so high that only an open circuit, an unplugged connector or a line shorted to voltage can explain it; the NTC curve would put the coolant below −60 °C.
Open signal or ground wire, or unplugged connector
Chafed engine harness interrupting the circuit
Sensor 5 reads around −40 °C or lower in live data
Engine runs on a substitute temperature value
P2B2F: Unlike the circuit codes P0480, P0691 and P0692, P2B2F judges the result: radiator fan 1 is commanded on but does not deliver, up to not turning at all. Detection uses fan speed feedback from a PWM or LIN fan module, or the missing temperature drop when the fan should be cooling.
Fan 1 motor worn or seized, or blades blocked by debris
Fan control module or relay not switching the motor
Engine software judging the fan wrongly (FCA 2.0 L)
Poor power feed or ground at the fan
Rising coolant temperature in slow traffic
P2B30: P2B30 states that radiator fan 1 does not follow the command to stop or to change speed, as judged from its speed feedback or module diagnosis. The classic electrical background is a welded relay contact or a fan module that keeps driving the motor.
Road debris jamming the fan (Audi e-tron GT)
Fan control module ignoring the off command
Fan keeps running after switch-off, draining the 12 V battery
Weak cabin heating or cooling on electric vehicles
Grinding noise from the front wheel area
P2B31: P2B31 is the functional code for a second radiator fan: its circuits test fine (otherwise P0481, P0693 or P0694 would be set), yet the fan turns too slowly or not at all when commanded. Twin-fan cooling packs usually run fan 2 for high load or A/C demand, so a failure tends to show up only in heat or traffic. No manufacturer documents P2B31 publicly.
Fan 2 motor worn, seized or jammed by debris
Fan module or relay for fan 2 not switching on
Weak supply or ground to fan 2
Temperature climbing at high load or with A/C on
P2B32: With P2B32 the controller finds that the second radiator fan keeps operating, or does not change state, against its command. On conventional cars this usually traces back to a relay stuck closed, a fan 2 control line shorted to its active level or a module that has lost control of the motor.
Debris from the wheel housing jamming fan 2 (Audi e-tron GT)
Fan 2 control line shorted to its active level
Fan audible after the vehicle is switched off
Reduced heating, cooling or charging on electric vehicles
P2B33: A Camshaft Profile Actuator B Control Circuit/Open Bank 1

P2B33 concerns the second profile actuator on the intake camshaft (camshaft A) of bank 1. Such actuators are solenoids that extend a pin into a groove on a sliding cam sleeve and so move lobes of a different lift under the valves.
Connector at the actuator on the camshaft carrier loose, corroded or not latched after valve cover work
Solenoid winding of actuator B open
Control wire broken in the engine harness
Output stage in the engine control module faulty
MIL on after the first drive with the fault
No change of intake lift profile, less pull or higher fuel use depending on the stuck profile
P2B34: A Camshaft Profile Actuator B Control Circuit Low Bank 1
On bank 1 the intake camshaft (A) carries a second shifting solenoid, actuator B, which GM's L3B 2.7-litre four labels actuator 2.
Engine harness chafed through on the camshaft carrier or near the left shock tower (GM PIT5677)
Shorted turns or short to housing in actuator B
Oil or moisture in the actuator connector creating a path to ground
MIL on, often together with other codes from the same harness section
Lift switching and cylinder deactivation unavailable
With a chafed harness also rough running, reduced power or blown fuses
P2B35: A Camshaft Profile Actuator B Control Circuit High Bank 1
P2B35 is the short-to-voltage counterpart for intake-side actuator B on bank 1, the second of the sleeve-shifting solenoids on camshaft A.
Control wire chafed against a powered circuit in the engine harness
Output stage in the engine control module faulty
MIL on during the drive in which the fault appears
Intake lift profile no longer changes as commanded
Higher fuel use because cylinder deactivation is blocked
P2B36: A Camshaft Profile Actuator B Control Circuit/Open Bank 2
P2B36 describes an open control circuit at the second profile actuator of the intake camshaft (camshaft A) on bank 2. A second bank exists only on V or boxer engines.
Actuator connector on bank 2 unplugged, loose or corroded
Broken control wire between engine module and bank 2
Bank 2 intake stays on one lift profile, possibly uneven running between the banks
P2B37: A Camshaft Profile Actuator B Control Circuit Low Bank 2

Code P2B37 stands for a control line shorted to ground at intake-side actuator B of bank 2, the second lobe-switching solenoid on camshaft A of the other cylinder bank. Publicly, no maker assigns it to a vehicle.
Harness to the bank 2 actuator chafed through on the cylinder head or a bracket
Oil or water in the actuator connector
Lift switching inactive on bank 2, less power or more fuel use
P2B38: A Camshaft Profile Actuator B Control Circuit High Bank 2

P2B38 marks a short to battery voltage in the control circuit of intake camshaft actuator B on bank 2. No published manufacturer documentation uses it; only the bank 1 version P2B35 is covered, by GM's L3B summary tables, which check with the output off and react to 0.5 Ω or less towards supply.
Pinched or chafed control wire touching a powered circuit
Faulty output stage in the engine module
Bank 2 intake lift no longer changes, uneven power delivery
P2B39: B Camshaft Profile Actuator B Control Circuit/Open Bank 1

Camshaft B is the exhaust camshaft, and actuator B is the second shifting solenoid on it. On GM's 2.7-litre L3B the exhaust side has only two such actuators, so this is the last of them; GM's tables call it exhaust camshaft profile actuator 2.
Exhaust actuator connector loose or corroded on the camshaft carrier
Broken wire in the engine harness
Open solenoid coil in exhaust actuator B
MIL on in the first drive
Exhaust lift profile no longer switches, cylinder deactivation unavailable
P2B3A: B Camshaft Profile Actuator B Control Circuit Low Bank 1

P2B3A points to a short to ground in the control line of exhaust-side actuator B on bank 1, i.e. the second pin solenoid that slides the lobe sleeve along camshaft B. GM documents it for the L3B four-cylinder in its 2019 and 2025 OBD tables: driver on, a resistance to ground not above 0.5 Ω, 4 of 5 samples, supply over 11 V, Type A with immediate MIL.
Engine harness rubbed through where it crosses the camshaft carrier
Shorted turns in exhaust actuator B
Oil wicking into the actuator connector
Exhaust profile and cylinder deactivation no longer switch
With harness damage often further codes and rough running
P2B3B: B Camshaft Profile Actuator B Control Circuit High Bank 1
For the second exhaust-camshaft profile actuator on bank 1 (camshaft B, actuator B), P2B3B means its control circuit is shorted to a voltage source.
Control wire chafed against a live wire in the engine harness
Internal short in exhaust actuator B
Check engine light comes on during the drive
Exhaust lift stays in one profile, cylinder deactivation blocked
P2B3C: B Camshaft Profile Actuator B Control Circuit/Open Bank 2

This code reports an interrupted control circuit at actuator B on the exhaust camshaft (camshaft B) of bank 2. No vehicle manufacturer is known to use P2B3C in public documents. Its bank 1 twin P2B39 appears in GM's tables for the 2.7-litre L3B, an inline engine without a second bank, where an impedance of 200 kΩ or more with the output on counts as open.
Connector of the bank 2 exhaust actuator unplugged or loose
Open coil in exhaust actuator B
Exhaust lift on bank 2 no longer switches
P2B3D: B Camshaft Profile Actuator B Control Circuit Low Bank 2

P2B3D: the control wire of the second exhaust-side profile actuator on bank 2 (camshaft B, actuator B) has contact with ground. Publicly documented use by a manufacturer is not known. For comparison, GM's L3B diagnostics define the bank 1 code P2B3A as a ground short of at most 0.5 Ω with the driver on and four failed tests out of five.
Wire chafed at a bracket or valve cover edge on bank 2
Shorted coil in exhaust actuator B
Oil or water in the connector
Bank 2 exhaust stays on one lift profile
P2B3E: B Camshaft Profile Actuator B Control Circuit High Bank 2

P2B3E is set when the control circuit of exhaust camshaft profile actuator B on bank 2 is shorted to supply voltage. No manufacturer documents the code publicly, so the details come from the analogue: GM's L3B tests the bank 1 counterpart P2B3B while the output is off and treats 0.5 Ω or less towards controller power as a short.
Damaged insulation bringing the control wire against a powered line
Solenoid in exhaust actuator B shorted internally
Output stage in the engine module faulty
Exhaust lift on bank 2 fixed, slightly higher consumption
P2B3F: A Camshaft Position Actuator Position Sensor B Circuit Bank 1
P2B3F is the general circuit code for position sensor B of the intake camshaft actuator (camshaft A) on bank 1, the side with cylinder 1; the NTN-SNR sensor guide also places it on the inlet side.
Connector at the actuator loose, corroded or wire broken
Position sensor in the actuator failed (actuator replacement)
Engine harness damaged by heat or chafing
Lift switching or cylinder deactivation unavailable
Slightly higher consumption, sometimes less power
P2B40: A Camshaft Position Actuator Position Sensor B Range/Performance Bank 1
With P2B40 the wiring of the intake-side sensor B (camshaft A, bank 1) is electrically fine, but its signal does not fit what the engine module commanded.
Actuator pin sluggish or sticking (wear, oil sludge)
Engine control software outdated (Mercedes CAMTRONIC update)
Sensor signal disturbed by loose contact
Cam sleeve or shift groove damaged
Valve-lift change held in a safe position
Uneven running when the system tries to switch
P2B41: A Camshaft Position Actuator Position Sensor B Circuit Low Bank 1
P2B41 reports a voltage below the permitted window from sensor B, which watches the intake actuator of bank 1. That usually points to a grounded signal line or a sensor that has failed internally.
Signal wire shorted to ground (chafed harness)
Possibly further codes from sensors on the same supply
P2B42: A Camshaft Position Actuator Position Sensor B Circuit High Bank 1

Here sensor B of the bank 1 intake actuator reports a value stuck above its upper limit. Typical reasons are an open sensor ground, a signal line touching 5 V or battery voltage, or a defective sensor. No manufacturer explains P2B42 publicly; the supplier list from NTN-SNR only names it as the inlet-side sensor B with a signal that is too high.
Sensor ground open or connector corroded
Signal wire shorted to 5 V or battery voltage
Usually no noticeable change in driving, sometimes reduced power
P2B43: A Camshaft Position Actuator Position Sensor B Circuit Bank 2

P2B43 covers the wiring of sensor B at the bank 2 intake actuator, i.e. on the cylinder bank without cylinder 1, so it only appears on V or boxer engines. The engine module sees an open line or a signal it cannot accept at all.
Harness near the bulkhead damaged by heat
Cylinder deactivation or lift change switched off
Possibly limp-home message of the valve-lift system
P2B44: A Camshaft Position Actuator Position Sensor B Range/Performance Bank 2

P2B44 is the one code of this group with a public manufacturer use. Mercedes-Benz bulletin LI05.20-P-080192 (January 2026) lists P2B4400 on M176/M177 V8 engines – AMG 63 models, S 580, G 550, GLS 580 – and reads it as an implausible sensor signal from CAMTRONIC solenoid 2 on the intake side of bank 2.
Engine control software needs the CAMTRONIC update (Mercedes)
Actuator of an older part number (Mercedes replaces it)
CAMTRONIC limp-home mode, cylinder deactivation off
Higher fuel consumption at part load
P2B45: A Camshaft Position Actuator Position Sensor B Circuit Low Bank 2

P2B45 means the bank 2 intake actuator's position sensor B delivers an unusually low voltage – on bank 2, which a V engine places opposite cylinder 1. A grounded signal wire is the classic cause; an internally shorted sensor or a missing supply gives the same picture.
Signal wire grounded through chafing or heat damage
Lift change on bank 2 stops working
P2B46: A Camshaft Position Actuator Position Sensor B Circuit High Bank 2

P2B46 flags a signal from position sensor B on the bank 2 intake camshaft actuator that is stuck too high. Most often the sensor has lost its ground, the signal line has contact with a supply line, or the sensor element itself has failed.
Signal line in contact with a supply line
Sensor element in the actuator failed
Cam lift held in default position on bank 2
P2B47: B Camshaft Position Actuator Position Sensor B Circuit Bank 1
P2B47 moves the circuit fault to the exhaust side: it concerns position sensor B on the actuator of camshaft B, bank 1. NTN-SNR's supplier code list reads camshaft B as the outlet camshaft.
Connector unplugged or corroded, wire broken
P2B48: B Camshaft Position Actuator Position Sensor B Range/Performance Bank 1
P2B48 is the plausibility code for sensor B at the bank 1 exhaust actuator (camshaft B): the circuit works, yet the reported position contradicts the command.
Actuator pin sticking from deposits or wear
Shift groove or cam sleeve damaged
Exhaust lift switching held in one position
Possibly rough running during shift attempts
P2B49: B Camshaft Position Actuator Position Sensor B Circuit Low Bank 1

With P2B49 the module reads too low a signal from position sensor B at the exhaust camshaft actuator of bank 1. A short between signal line and ground, a sensor with an internal short or a missing feed are the usual suspects.
Exhaust cam lift change switched off
P2B4A: B Camshaft Position Actuator Position Sensor B Circuit High Bank 1

P2B4A says the position sensor B signal of the bank 1 exhaust camshaft actuator is above its limit. An interrupted sensor ground, a short to a voltage source or a failed sensor are typical. No manufacturer describes P2B4A publicly, and the Mercedes CAMTRONIC bulletin does not include any high fault of this family.
Sensor ground interrupted or connector corroded
Signal line shorted to a voltage source
Exhaust lift system kept in safe position
P2B4B: B Camshaft Position Actuator Position Sensor B Circuit Bank 2

P2B4B is set when the circuit feeding the second position sensor (B) of the exhaust actuator on bank 2 is open or otherwise unusable. Bank 2 exists only on engines with two cylinder rows, such as the Mercedes M176/M177 V8, whose CAMTRONIC bulletin lists exhaust feedback faults on bank 2 for sensor A (P34C1, P34C2) but not for sensor B.
Plug or wires at the actuator open
Heat damage to the harness above the bulkhead
Sensor in the exhaust actuator failed
Cylinder deactivation or exhaust lift change unavailable
P2B4C: B Camshaft Position Actuator Position Sensor B Range/Performance Bank 2

P2B4C stands for an implausible but electrically valid signal from the B sensor watching the exhaust actuator of bank 2. It is the exhaust-side mirror of P2B44, which Mercedes-Benz documents on CAMTRONIC V8s (M176/M177) for intake solenoid 2 of bank 2; for P2B4C itself there is no public manufacturer text.
Intermittent contact in the sensor signal
Lift system or cylinder deactivation in limp-home
P2B4D: B Camshaft Position Actuator Position Sensor B Circuit Low Bank 2
A too-low signal from position sensor B at the bank 2 exhaust camshaft actuator sets P2B4D. In practice this is a signal wire touching ground, a shorted sensor, or a sensor that gets no supply.
Signal wire touching ground (heat or chafe damage)
Exhaust lift change on bank 2 out of action
Possibly limp-home message of the lift system
P2B4E: B Camshaft Position Actuator Position Sensor B Circuit High Bank 2

P2B4E closes the group: the exhaust-side position sensor B of bank 2 sends a signal above its upper limit. Usually the sensor ground is open, the signal line is shorted to a supply, or the sensor is faulty. No manufacturer explains P2B4E publicly; the NTN-SNR code list only gives outlet sensor B, second bank, signal too high.
Signal line shorted to a supply
Bank 2 runs on the default cam profile
P2B4F: A Camshaft Profile Actuator B Control Performance/Stuck Off Bank 1
P2B4F covers the second profile actuator (B) on the intake camshaft of bank 1, a solenoid whose pin engages a groove on a sliding cam sleeve to change valve lift.
Actuator B pin extends without a command (sticking solenoid, weak return spring)
Hall feedback of the actuator delivers wrong pin states
Shift groove on the cam sleeve worn so the pin is dragged out
MIL on in the first drive with the fault
Intake lift switching locked out, less pull or higher consumption
P2B50: A Camshaft Profile Actuator B Control Performance/Stuck Off Bank 2
Bank 2 of a V-engine has its own intake camshaft (A), and P2B50 reports that the second profile actuator on it does not do its job or stays in the off position.
CAMTRONIC actuator of an older part number, superseded by Mercedes
Engine control software that needs the available update
Harness heat-damaged above the bulkhead near the windscreen
Actuator pin mechanically jammed in the retracted position
CAMTRONIC lift switching inactive on bank 2, possibly limp-home mode of the system
Slightly uneven running or higher fuel use at part load
P2B51: B Camshaft Profile Actuator B Control Performance/Stuck Off Bank 1
On the exhaust camshaft (B) of bank 1 the second sliding-cam solenoid is monitored by P2B51. GM applies it to the L3B 2.7-litre turbo four, whose exhaust side carries two such actuators.
Exhaust actuator B pin releases without command, often heat-related sticking
Faulty Hall feedback in the actuator or its signal line
Sludge or debris at the actuator bore hindering the pin
Exhaust lift profile no longer changes, turbo response may feel different
P2B52: B Camshaft Profile Actuator B Control Performance/Stuck Off Bank 2

P2B52 is the bank 2 version for actuator B on the exhaust camshaft (B): the second shifting solenoid either does not move its cam sleeve or remains in the off position. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly.
Actuator B of the bank 2 exhaust camshaft does not extend its pin
Poor contact at the actuator connector or heat-damaged harness
Engine control calibration that judges the shift too strictly
Exhaust lift switching inactive on bank 2
Possibly slightly lower power in the upper speed range
P2B53: A Camshaft Profile Actuator B Control Stuck On Bank 1
P2B53 means actuator B of the bank 1 intake camshaft is caught in the engaged position.
Actuator pin does not retract (sticking plunger, varnish, weak spring)
Engine harness chafed on the camshaft carrier (GM PIT5677 / 21-NA-149)
Hall feedback does not report the home position although the pin is back
MIL on in the first drive
Lift switching and cylinder deactivation locked out
With a damaged harness also other codes, rough running or blown fuses
Possible ticking from the valve cover if the pin rubs in the groove
P2B54: A Camshaft Profile Actuator B Control Stuck On Bank 2

With P2B54 actuator B, the second shifter on the bank 2 intake camshaft, is reported as stuck on, meaning its pin or valve stays engaged after the command to release. A public manufacturer description of this exact code was not found.
Actuator B on the bank 2 intake camshaft stays engaged (sticking plunger)
Control line shorted so the solenoid remains energised
Position feedback of the actuator stuck at the engaged value
Uneven running between the banks, especially at part load
Profile switching disabled by the engine control
P2B55: B Camshaft Profile Actuator B Control Stuck On Bank 1

P2B55 flags actuator B on the bank 1 exhaust camshaft as stuck on. Even GM, whose L3B four has a second exhaust actuator and uses P2B51 for it, lists no stuck-on code for that actuator in its 2019 and 2025 tables; no other maker documents P2B55 publicly either.
Pin of exhaust actuator B does not retract, often from heat and deposits
Solenoid stays powered because of a wiring or driver fault
Damaged shift groove holds the pin
Changed turbo response or reduced power
Possible metallic noise from the camshaft area
P2B56: B Camshaft Profile Actuator B Control Stuck On Bank 2

P2B56 completes the series: on bank 2 the second actuator of the exhaust camshaft remains engaged after it should have released. No manufacturer publishes a description of this exact code. NTN-SNR lists it as permanently active; CARB 13 CCR 1968.2 (e)(13) is the legal basis for monitoring such valve control functions.
Solenoid of exhaust actuator B on bank 2 sticking in the engaged state
Aged or wrong engine oil slowing the pin
Worn shift groove on the exhaust cam sleeve
Bank-to-bank imbalance felt as rough idle or part-load vibration
Lift switching locked by the engine control
P2B57: Low Engine Oil Pressure - Camshaft Control Disabled

P2B57 is a status code rather than a circuit fault: the engine control has measured or calculated oil pressure too low for safe camshaft adjustment and has therefore switched the cam control off. Hydraulic cam phasers and oil-operated lift switching need a minimum pressure to hold position; below it the parts would rattle or drift.
Oil level too low or oil of the wrong viscosity
Worn oil pump, faulty pump control or clogged pickup screen
Oil pressure sensor reading too low although pressure is fine
Worn bearings causing internal oil leakage at high temperature
Check engine light on, often together with an oil pressure warning
Camshaft adjustment inactive, weaker low-end torque and rough idle
Rattle from the cam phasers at start or when hot
P2B58: Engine Coolant Flow Control Valve Motor Current High

P2B58 reports that the electric motor driving the engine coolant flow control valve draws too much current. GM documents the check for its 3.0-litre inline-six Duramax diesel: in the 2025 table 25OBDG04B the driver stage flags a current above 5.5 A, and 80 failures in 100 samples taken every 12.5 ms set a Type B fault, so the MIL follows on the second trip.
Rotary valve stiff or seized from deposits or debris in the housing
Chafed engine harness on GM LM2 (bulletin 21-NA-149)
MIL on after the second drive with the fault
Slow warm-up or weak cabin heat
Fans may run more often as a precaution
P2B59: Engine Coolant Flow Control Valve Control Circuit/Open

P2B59 is the open-circuit check for the drive of the coolant flow control valve. In GM's 25OBDG04B (3.0 L Duramax) the driver reports a load resistance above 200 kΩ, meaning one of the motor wires is disconnected; 80 of 100 samples set a Type B fault.
ECU judgement logic on Hyundai/Kia 2.5 Theta III (software update 26-EM-009H / ENG 264)
Valve connector unplugged, loose or with a pushed-out terminal
Motor wire broken in the harness or valve motor winding open
MIL on, often without any noticeable driveability change
Valve stays in its default position, slower warm-up possible
P2B5A: Engine Coolant Flow Control Valve Control Circuit Low

P2B5A stands for a short to ground in the control wiring of the coolant flow control valve motor. GM's 2025 table for the 3.0-litre Duramax describes the detection: the driver sees more than 9 A flowing, which it interprets as one motor wire touching ground, and 80 out of 100 samples at 12.5 ms set a two-trip Type B fault once relay voltage exceeds 11 V.
Motor wire chafed or pinched against ground
Coolant or water in the valve connector
Internal short to housing in the valve motor
Engine temperature control fixed, slower warm-up or higher running temperature
P2B5B: Engine Coolant Flow Control Valve Control Circuit High

P2B5B covers a short to battery voltage on the motor leads of the coolant flow control valve. GM's diesel table 25OBDG04B evaluates it through the driver stage as well: a current above 9 A with a lead tied to supply counts as a failure, and the usual 80-of-100 rule with 12.5 ms sampling stores a Type B code.
Motor lead chafed against a powered circuit (GM LM2, 21-NA-149)
Corroded or wet connector bridging to supply
Driver stage in the engine control module faulty
MIL on after two drives, possibly further codes from the same harness
Blown fuses or rough running if the harness is chafed
P2B5C: Engine Coolant Flow Control Valve Supply Circuit Low

With P2B5C the supply voltage reaching the driver of the coolant flow control valve motor is too low. GM monitors this on the 3.0-litre Duramax (25OBDG04B): if the motor driver sees less than 6 V while the powertrain relay delivers more than 11 V, the difference points at the feed path, and a Type B fault follows after 80 hits in 100 samples.
Blown or loose fuse, corroded relay contact in the valve feed
Supply wire damaged or chafed in the engine harness
High resistance at a ground or splice of the feed circuit
Valve does not move, temperature control in fallback mode
P2B5D: Engine Coolant Flow Control Valve Position Sensor Circuit

P2B5D is the general circuit code for the position sensor of the coolant flow control valve, the feedback that tells the engine computer how far the rotary valve has turned. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly.
Loose or corroded terminals at the valve connector
Signal, reference or ground wire of the sensor interrupted
Position sensor inside the valve faulty
Coolant flow control in fallback, warm-up or heating behaviour changed
P2B5E: Engine Coolant Flow Control Valve Position Sensor Circuit Low

P2B5E reports a position sensor reading below its valid window. On GM's 3.0-litre Duramax the valve sends its angle as a raw SENT value in percent of 5 V; anything under 2 % counts as too low, and 80 failures in 100 samples at 6.25 ms set a Type B fault, provided there is no SENT communication fault and the relay supplies more than 11 V.
5 V reference or signal wire interrupted or shorted to ground
Chafed engine harness on GM LM2 (21-NA-149)
Position sensor in the valve faulty
Coolant flow no longer regulated, warm-up slower
P2B5F: Engine Coolant Flow Control Valve Position Sensor Circuit High

P2B5F is set when the valve position signal sits above the top of its window. The 2025 Duramax calibration (3.0 L, 25OBDG04B) treats a SENT raw value over 98 % of 5 V as implausibly high and stores a two-trip Type B code after 80 of 100 readings, sampled every 6.25 ms while the SENT link itself is healthy.
Signal wire shorted to the 5 V reference or to battery voltage
Moisture or corrosion bridging contacts in the valve connector
Position sensor in the valve faulty
Slow warm-up or weak cabin heat
P2B60: Engine Coolant Flow Control Valve Position Sensor Circuit Range/Performance

P2B60 checks whether the valve actually goes where it is told. On GM's 3.0 L Duramax the code sets when the gap between desired and measured position exceeds 12 % in 160 of 200 samples, only with a steady command, closed-loop control active and no coolant or outside temperature sensor fault (Type B).
Engine control software (GM 20-NA-039 / 22-NA-082, Hyundai/Kia ITM logic)
Corroded terminals at the valve actuator connector (GM PIP5764)
Valve sluggish or not learned, needs a relearn after test
Valve does not follow commands although wiring is fine
Engine temperature fluctuates or warms up slowly
Often no driveability complaint beyond the warning lamp
P2B61: Engine Coolant Flow Control Valve Stuck Closed
P2B61 indicates that the coolant flow control valve stays closed although the engine computer asks it to open, so coolant cannot reach the radiator path as intended.
Valve or diversion shroud mechanically stuck closed (JLR variable coolant pump)
Engine control software that needs an update
Valve drive or its wiring no longer moves the valve
Radiator fans running constantly at high speed, loud noise from the engine bay
P2B62: Coolant Pump B Supply Voltage Circuit
P2B62 flags a supply voltage problem at coolant pump B, an electrically driven auxiliary pump with its own electronics.
Pump fuse blown or supply relay not closing properly
Corroded or loose power or ground connection at the pump
Weak battery or charging system fault lowering supply voltage
Voltage detection inside the pump electronics faulty
Auxiliary pump runs slowly or not at all
Rising temperature of the component cooled by pump B
P2B63: P2B63 means coolant pump B is powered and commanded but its rotor does not turn, or stays far below target speed. Brushless auxiliary pumps notice this themselves, for example from high current without rotation, and report it to the engine computer.
Bearing seized or impeller jammed by debris or deposits
Electric motor or electronics inside the pump failed
Coolant frozen in the pump because antifreeze concentration is too low
No audible pump run after the ignition is switched on
Overheating of the component served by pump B
P2B64: Coolant Pump B Control Module Overtemperature

P2B64 reports that the electronics built into coolant pump B have become too hot and the pump has protected itself, usually by derating or shutting down. In Ford's 2024 gasoline OBD summary it is failure type 98 (system over temperature) of the pump B check under P261A, monitored continuously.
Coolant level low or air at the pump, so the electronics are not cooled
Sluggish impeller raises motor current and heat
Power stage inside the pump degraded
Damaged heat shield or high radiant heat at the mounting point
Pump stops intermittently, often after long or hot drives
Reduced cooling of the served component
P2B65: Coolant Pump B Overspeed/Air in System

When a coolant pump draws in air, its impeller loses load: speed climbs and current drops. P2B65 reports this for coolant pump B. Ford's 2024 gasoline OBD summary lists it as failure type B1 (overspeed/dry run) of pump B under P261A.
Air left in the circuit after filling or repair
Coolant loss through a leak, level too low
Restricting check valve in the vent hose (Bentley W12, 975 122 447H)
Speed or current detection inside the pump faulty
Coolant or overheating warning in the instrument cluster
Falling coolant level in the expansion tank
Gurgling noise or fluctuating temperature display
P2B66: P2B66 is the open-circuit code for the control line of coolant pump D, the pump a manufacturer labels D in its thermal management. The driver stage in the engine computer detects a broken wire, an unplugged connector or a pump input that no longer draws current. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly.
Pump connector loose, corroded or unplugged
Control wire broken between engine computer and pump
Control input inside the pump open
Pump D does not respond to commands
Higher temperature in the loop served by pump D
P2B67: Coolant Pump D Control Circuit Low

P2B67 means the control line of coolant pump D sits too low, typically because it is shorted to ground or the driver stage sees excess current. No manufacturer publishes this code. Ford's comparable entries for pumps A and B (P2602, P261C) set when the smart driver in the engine computer reports an output fault, checked continuously above 11 V.
Control wire chafed through and shorted to ground
Moisture or corrosion in the pump connector
Control input inside the pump shorted
Pump D runs constantly or not at all
P2B68: Coolant Pump D Control Circuit High
P2B68 flags a control line for coolant pump D that reads too high: it touches a voltage source or is pulled up while the driver should switch it. No manufacturer documents the code publicly.
Control wire shorted to a battery or ignition feed
Moisture bridging pins in the connector
Fault in the pump electronics pulls the line up
Pump D runs at a fixed speed or ignores commands
P2B69: Coolant Pump D Supply Voltage Circuit
P2B69 reports that coolant pump D does not receive a usable voltage on its power feed, as distinct from the control line covered by P2B66 to P2B68. No manufacturer documents this code publicly.
Fuse blown or supply relay contacts worn
High resistance at the pump ground or ground point
Code returns mainly at low battery voltage or high electrical load
P2B6A: P2B6A reports that coolant pump D is blocked or stalled: supply and command are present, yet the rotor does not come up to speed. No manufacturer documents the code publicly.
Bearing seized or impeller jammed by debris or sludge
Motor winding or pump electronics failed
Coolant frozen because antifreeze concentration is too low
Overheating of the loop served by pump D
P2B6B: Coolant Pump D Control Module Overtemperature

With P2B6B the integrated electronics of coolant pump D report excessive temperature, and the pump derates or switches itself off to survive. No manufacturer documents this code publicly; the equivalent for pump B is P2B64, which Ford lists as failure type 98 (system over temperature), and for pump A it is P2B9E.
Too little coolant or air at the pump
Power stage inside the pump degraded
Pump D cuts out after longer operation and restarts after cooling
P2B6C: Coolant Pump D Overspeed/Air in System

P2B6C means coolant pump D is spinning faster than its command would explain, the signature of an impeller moving air instead of liquid. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly. For pump B, Bentley stores the counterpart P2B6500 on W12 models and traces it to a restricting vent hose, and Ford lists P2B65 as failure type B1 (overspeed/dry run).
Circuit not fully bled after filling or repair
Vent line or bleed valve restricted, air cannot escape
Coolant warning or rising temperature display
Coolant level drops in the expansion tank
P2B6D: Engine Coolant Flow Control Valve Position Sensor Circuit Intermittent/Erratic

P2B6D covers a position signal from the engine coolant flow control valve that drops out or jumps for short moments, even though single readings may still lie inside the valid window. This exact code appears in no public manufacturer document.
Loose or widened terminal in the valve connector
Fretting corrosion on the signal or reference pins
Harness rubbing or flexing with engine movement
Position sensor inside the valve unstable
Warning lamp, code often stored as intermittent
Temperature display or warm-up behaviour fluctuates
P2B6E: P2B6E is the general circuit code for temperature sensor A on the turbocharger or supercharger. SAE J2012 names the sensor but leaves its measuring point open, so the manufacturer decides what it watches, and no manufacturer documents this exact code publicly.
Intermittent break in signal or ground wire
Implausible or jumping turbo temperature value in live data
P2B6F: Turbocharger/Supercharger A Temperature Sensor Circuit Low

P2B6F reports that the signal of turbocharger/supercharger temperature sensor A has fallen below its valid range. If the sensor is an NTC thermistor, whose resistance drops as it warms, a low voltage stands for a very high temperature, so the usual electrical causes are a signal wire shorted to ground or a sensor failed internally short.
Signal wire shorted to ground, for example chafed near the exhaust
Input circuit in the engine computer faulty
Live data shows an extreme value even with the engine cold
P2B70: Turbocharger/Supercharger A Temperature Sensor Circuit High

P2B70 is set when sensor A on the turbocharger or supercharger delivers a signal above its valid range. For an NTC thermistor this corresponds to an implausibly cold reading, the classic result of an open signal or ground wire, an unplugged connector or a short to the 5 V reference; for a PTC-type element it would indicate extreme heat.
Signal or ground wire open, connector unplugged
Signal wire shorted to the 5 V reference or another voltage
Live data shows a fixed extreme value
P2B71: Turbocharger/Supercharger A Temperature Sensor Circuit Range/Performance
P2B71 covers a reading from temperature sensor A on the turbocharger or supercharger that is electrically valid yet does not fit the operating state.
Sensor element aged by heat and reading off
Contact resistance at the connector distorting the signal
Sensor loose or not fully seated in its bore
Warning lamp, often without noticeable driving change
Turbo temperature in live data differs clearly from other temperatures after a cold start
Boost may be trimmed back as a precaution
P2B72: P2B72 says the command line to coolant heater A is open or has lost continuity. Keep it apart from the engine coolant heater family P01E8–P01EF: the other J2012 codes for this heater – internal module, supply voltage and over-temperature under P2DA4–P2DA7, lost communication under U069E – point to a unit with its own electronics, such as the electric coolant…
Command wire to the heater broken or connector not latched
Terminal pushed back or corroded in the heater connector
Input stage of the heater electronics open internally
Output stage in the commanding control module faulty
Little or no cabin heat, especially in electric driving
Engine starts more often in cold weather to provide heat (hybrids)
Warning or fault message, depending on the manufacturer
P2B73: Coolant Heater A Control Circuit Low

P2B73 is the low case on the command circuit of coolant heater A: the commanding module reads the line at or near ground when it expects a higher level. Usual reasons are a chafed wire touching body ground, coolant or water in a connector, or an input in the heater that pulls the line down.
Command wire chafed through and shorted to ground
Coolant or water in the heater connector
Input of the heater electronics shorted internally
Commanding module cannot drive the line high
Coolant heater does not switch on, weak cabin heat
Engine runs more often in the cold (hybrids)
Fuse for the request circuit may blow repeatedly
P2B74: Coolant Heater A Control Circuit High

P2B74 is the opposite of P2B73: the command circuit of coolant heater A sits at or near supply voltage while the module expects it low, or the output stage measures excess current and shuts down. A wire rubbed through onto a 12 V feed, a crushed harness next to the heater's own supply cable or a shorted input in the heater electronics are typical.
Command wire shorted to a 12 V circuit
Harness crushed or melted near the heater supply cable
Heater electronics input shorted to its supply
Output stage of the commanding module faulty
Coolant heater off, or running without request
Higher 12 V or high-voltage battery drain when parked if the heater runs on
Weak cabin heat in cold weather
P2B75: Coolant Heater A Control Circuit Performance

P2B75 is set when the command circuit of coolant heater A tests electrically sound but the heater's response does not match the request – the coolant leaving it fails to warm, for instance, or reported power or current stays off target. CARB 13 CCR 1968.2 (e)(15.2.2) asks for this kind of functional check on output components.
Air trapped in the heater loop or low coolant level
Heating element weak or partly failed
Internal fault in the heater control electronics
Coolant pump or valve in the heater loop not circulating enough
Cabin warms slowly or only with the engine running
Heater core temperature in live data stays low despite full heat request
Electric range reduced in winter because the engine starts for heat
P2B76: P2B76 reports an open command circuit for coolant heater B. Where a vehicle has two separately requested heaters or heating stages – Hyundai and Kia patent US11378000B2 describes one housing with several sheath elements that a controller switches individually – B stands for the second channel.
Request wire for heater B broken at a flex point
Terminal pushed out of the heater connector
Fuse feeding the request circuit blown
Heater B input open inside the heater electronics
Reduced heating power, cabin warms more slowly
Defrosting takes longer in cold weather
Fault entry often without other noticeable effects
P2B77: Coolant Heater B Control Circuit Low

P2B77 means the command circuit of coolant heater B reads low: the line is pulled toward ground although the module drives or expects a higher level. With a second heating stage this usually costs part of the heating power rather than all of it, because stage A can still run.
Harness branch along the coolant hoses shorted to ground
Coolant seepage corroding the heater connector
Heater B input shorted inside the heater electronics
Heating power noticeably lower than usual
Cabin and windows take longer to warm up
Possible traces of coolant at the heater connector
P2B78: Coolant Heater B Control Circuit High

P2B78 flags the command line of coolant heater B as too high: voltage is present where the commanding module expects a low level, or its driver reports overcurrent. A short to a 12 V circuit is the classic cause; with a low-side driver, a heater input that has failed short can produce it as well.
Request wire for heater B shorted to a 12 V circuit
Heater B input failed short inside the heater
Damage in a harness section shared with heater A
Heater stage B off, or running although not requested
P2B79: Coolant Heater B Control Circuit Performance
P2B79 says that coolant heater B is wired correctly but does not do what it is told: after a request the expected warming, current or status feedback fails to appear.
Low coolant or trapped air, so protection shuts the stage down
Heating element of stage B weak or open
Internal fault in the heater electronics for stage B
Heater outlet temperature rises slowly in live data
Fault may only appear at low outside temperatures
P2B7A: EVAP System Pressure Sensor/Switch C Circuit
P2B7A is the general circuit fault of a third EVAP pressure sensor or switch, C, alongside A (P0450 range) and B (P24D5 range). Each maker assigns the letters itself.
Sensor of an early design (VW G400 with narrow orifice)
Open or short in reference, ground or signal wire
Control unit logs a wrong fault entry (Audi bulletin 2069531)
Usually no change in driving behaviour
P2B7B: EVAP System Pressure Sensor/Switch C Circuit Range/Performance
P2B7B means sensor C delivers a signal that is electrically valid but implausible.
Sensor port or orifice too narrow or blocked
Fault entry assigned to the wrong sensor (Audi bulletin 2069531)
Pressure sensor C drifting or sluggish
Check engine light on, no driveability complaint
Code returns after clearing, often after a few drives
P2B7C: EVAP System Pressure Sensor/Switch C Circuit Low
P2B7C reports that the signal of EVAP pressure sensor C stays below its valid voltage window.
5 V reference to the sensor missing or shorted
EVAP leak tests not carried out, readiness incomplete
Other sensors on the same 5 V supply may report faults too
P2B7D: EVAP System Pressure Sensor/Switch C Circuit High

P2B7D is the high counterpart to P2B7C: the signal of EVAP pressure sensor C sits above its valid range. VW lists it in bulletin 01-26-01 for the 2025–2026 Jetta and Taos FWD, whose fuel tank pressure sensor G400 came with a plug-housing orifice that proved too small; the first step is to check which housing version is installed.
Sensor ground wire open or high resistance
Signal wire shorted to 5 V reference or battery voltage
EVAP readiness not set after clearing codes
P2B7E: EVAP System Pressure Sensor/Switch C Circuit Intermittent

P2B7E covers a signal from EVAP pressure sensor C that drops out or jumps for brief moments instead of failing for good. No manufacturer documents P2B7E publicly; Audi and VW use only P2B7A and P2B7B, VW also P2B7C and P2B7D, for this sensor.
Loose or corroded terminal at the sensor connector
Harness chafing near the tank or along the underbody
Electrical interference on the signal line
Pressure sensor C with an intermittent internal fault
Check engine light comes and goes
Pressure reading jumps in live data
Fault often appears only on rough roads or in wet weather
P2B7F: Turbocharger/Supercharger Boost Control Module A Calibration Not Learned/Programmed
P2B7F applies where boost control A is handled by its own electronic module, typically a smart actuator on the charger, and that module reports missing or invalid calibration data.
New or used module or charger fitted without programming or learn routine
Programming aborted, for example by low battery voltage
Module has lost its stored calibration (internal fault)
Warning lamp right after a repair on the turbo system
P2B80: Turbocharger/Supercharger Boost Control Module B Calibration Not Learned/Programmed

P2B80 is the counterpart of P2B7F for the second boost control module, which only exists where two chargers or two separately driven actuators each carry their own electronics. It is set when module B has no valid calibration or its learn step was never completed.
Module B or its charger replaced without programming or learn routine
Modules or chargers fitted on the wrong side
Warning lamp after work on the second charger
Reduced power because boost on one side is limited
P2B81: Wastegate Position Sensor A Circuit Performance
P2B81 reports that electric wastegate A does not behave as commanded although its sensor signal is electrically fine.
Wastegate valve or linkage binding (GM PIP6007A, turbo replacement)
Electric wastegate actuator worn or drawing excessive current
Linkage clip missing or rod detached
Boost too low or too high, flat or jerky acceleration
P2B82: Wastegate Position Sensor B Circuit Performance
P2B82 is the performance fault for the second electric wastegate, found only on engines with two turbochargers and position-controlled wastegates. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly.
Wastegate valve B or linkage binding from heat and deposits
Actuator B worn, gear or motor weak
Uneven or reduced boost, weaker pull
P2B83: Charge Air Cooler Coolant Pump A Overspeed/Air In System
P2B83 concerns the electric pump that keeps coolant moving through a water-cooled charge air cooler. When the impeller runs in air instead of liquid, load vanishes and the motor spins up.
Air pocket in the charge air cooler loop after service or a leak
Low coolant level in the separate low-temperature loop
Impeller loose or broken on the pump shaft
Pump electronics reporting an implausible speed
Check engine light after two drives with the fault
Reduced power under load because the intake air gets hot
Falling level in the charge air cooler coolant reservoir
P2B84: Charge Air Cooler Coolant Pump A Underspeed
P2B84 reports that the electric charge air cooler pump is turning too slowly or not at all, judged by the speed its own electronics send back.
Worn or seized pump bearing, or debris blocking the impeller
Water or corrosion in the pump connector
Low supply voltage or poor ground at the pump
Pump motor or its electronics worn out
Check engine light after the second faulty drive
Less power under heavy load or when towing
High charge air temperature shown in live data
P2B85: P2B85 applies to engines whose main water pump is electric: the pump turns clearly slower than commanded.
Failed control board inside the electric water pump
Loose or poorly latched plug at the pump
Bearing wear or deposits slowing the impeller
Low supply voltage or high resistance in power or ground
Rising coolant temperature and overheating warnings
Reduced engine power to protect the engine
Check engine light, often on the first trip
Engine may be shut down if driving continues
P2B86: Coolant Pump A Overspeed/Air in System

P2B86 says coolant pump A spins faster than it was told to – the typical sign of air at the impeller. In GM's 2025 tables (25OBDG03A, 25OBDG04B) the filtered gap between command and feedback must stay beyond a map limit, the pump running 200 to 348 rpm too fast depending on the 300–3,480 rpm request, over 8 s of a 10 s span at more than 11 V; Type B.
Air trapped in the loop after a repair or incomplete bleeding
Coolant loss through a leak, low level in the reservoir
Foreign object such as a loose O-ring at the pump ports
Restricted bleed or vent hose keeping air in the system
Check engine light after the second faulty trip
Coolant warning or gurgling noise in the heater area
P2B87: With P2B87 the reported speed of coolant pump A stays below the commanded one. GM's 2025 tables (25OBDG03A, 25OBDG04B) compare filtered command and feedback against a calibrated limit while 300–3,480 rpm is requested and more than 11 V is present; 8 s in a 10 s window, Type B.
Outdated software in the module that commands the pump
Impeller slowed by debris or a foreign O-ring
Worn bearing or motor in the auxiliary pump
Low voltage or poor contact at the pump connector
Check engine light, often without any other complaint
Reduced cabin heat at idle or with the engine stopped
P2B88: Intake Air O2 Sensor Circuit Bank 1

P2B88 is the catch-all electrical code for the oxygen sensor that some turbocharged engines mount in the intake tract, behind compressor and charge air cooler, to judge how much exhaust the recirculation system is feeding back.
Corroded or loose sensor plug, often wetted by charge air cooler condensate
Open or chafed signal wire between sensor and engine module
Intake oxygen sensor element internally failed
Fault in the sensor input stage of the engine module
EGR reduced or switched off, with slightly higher fuel use or knock-limited power
Often no noticeable change in driving behaviour
P2B89: Intake Air O2 Sensor Circuit Low Voltage Bank 1

With P2B89 the bank 1 intake oxygen sensor signal sits below the lowest voltage the engine module accepts. Typical electrical reasons are a signal lead shorted to ground, a damaged element or a corroded plug near the charge air cooler, where condensate gathers.
Engine software detecting falsely (Alfa Romeo Giulia 2.0 EC2, fixed by reflash)
Signal wire shorted to ground or pinched in the harness
Moisture or corrosion in the sensor connector
EGR flow limited or disabled by the engine module
Other stored codes such as P2AC0 or P0402 on the same vehicle
P2B8A: Intake Air O2 Sensor Circuit High Voltage Bank 1

P2B8A is the mirror image of P2B89: the bank 1 intake oxygen sensor delivers a voltage above its valid window. On a wide-band element this usually comes from a signal wire touching a supply or the heater feed, from an open ground or reference return that lets the input float upward, or from water inside the connector.
Signal wire shorted to a supply or to the heater feed
Open ground or reference return lead of the sensor
EGR switched off, possibly slightly higher fuel consumption
Intake oxygen reading on the scan tool above the fresh-air value
P2B8B: Intake Air O2 Sensor Heater Control Circuit/Open Bank 1

P2B8B is about the heater of bank 1's intake oxygen sensor: the module switches the heater on but sees no current, the classic sign of a broken heater coil, an open feed or control lead, or a blown fuse in the heater supply. A wide-band sensor only measures once its ceramic is hot.
Heater coil inside the sensor burnt through or cracked
Blown fuse or failed relay in the heater supply
Open heater feed or control wire, loose connector pin
Heater driver in the engine module failed
EGR stays inactive because the intake sensor never becomes ready
Possible companion code for the sensor signal
P2B8C: Intake Air O2 Sensor Heater Control Circuit Range/Performance Bank 1

P2B8C is not about broken wires: the heater of the bank 1 intake oxygen sensor is electrically intact, yet the element does not reach or hold its temperature as expected, or the heater needs power that does not fit the conditions. Mounted right after the intercooler, this sensor gets hit by condensate.
Water from the charge air cooler reaching the hot sensor element
Heater aged with increased resistance, sensor slow to warm up
Corroded pins or high resistance in the heater supply
Low system voltage limiting heater power
Fault often appears in humid or cold weather and with high boost
P2B8D: Intake Air O2 Sensor Heater Control Circuit Low Bank 1

P2B8D means the voltage the module sees on the heater control wire of bank 1's intake oxygen sensor is lower than the module expects for the commanded state, usually because the line is shorted to ground.
Heater control wire chafed through and shorted to ground
Heater coil with shorted turns inside the sensor
Water bridging the heater pins in the connector
Heater output stage in the engine module defective
Heater switched off by the module, EGR feedback unavailable
Repeated sensor failure if the short is not repaired
P2B8E: Intake Air O2 Sensor Heater Control Circuit High Bank 1

With P2B8E, bank 1's intake O2 heater control wire shows more voltage than expected, as when it is shorted to battery voltage or when the driver cannot pull it down. If the module switches the heater on its ground side, such a short means the heater never receives current, the element stays cold and the sensor is never released for measuring.
Heater control wire shorted to battery voltage
Heater with too low resistance tripping the driver's overcurrent protection
Damaged connector with pins touching each other
Heater output stage in the engine module defective
Intake oxygen sensor stays cold and not ready
P2B8F: P2B8F is the general circuit fault for temperature sensor B, the second sensor of this kind on a charged engine, often belonging to a second turbocharger. Which spot it watches is left to the manufacturer, and none documents this code publicly.
Loose or heat-damaged connector with intermittent contact
Wiring chafed or brittle near hot exhaust parts
Sensor B value missing or jumping in live data
P2B90: Turbocharger/Supercharger B Temperature Sensor Circuit Low
P2B90 means the signal of temperature sensor B has dropped below the lowest value the engine computer accepts.
Signal wire shorted to ground, for example melted insulation
Faulty input stage in the engine computer
Sensor B shows a fixed extreme value even on a cold engine
P2B91: Turbocharger/Supercharger B Temperature Sensor Circuit High

P2B91 is stored when temperature sensor B delivers a signal above its permitted window. By far the most frequent reason is a broken current path: an unplugged or corroded connector, a cracked wire or an element that has burned open, which pulls the input up to its reference voltage. A short to the 5 V supply or to battery voltage has the same effect.
Signal or ground wire open, connector unplugged or corroded
Sensor element or its lead wires broken by heat cycling
Signal wire shorted to the 5 V reference or battery voltage
Sensor B stuck at an end value in live data
P2B92: Turbocharger/Supercharger B Temperature Sensor Circuit Range/Performance

P2B92 says that temperature sensor B delivers a plausible voltage whose content is wrong: it may hang at one value, follow load changes too slowly or disagree with its partner sensor A on an engine with two chargers. A sensor that sits in a soot-coated or oil-wetted spot reacts sluggishly and is a classic trigger.
Sensor tip coated with soot or oil, responds sluggishly
Sensor element aged and reading off
Contact resistance in connector or wiring
Warning lamp, usually without drivability change
Sensor B lags behind or contradicts sensor A in live data
Boost may be limited as a precaution
P2B93: Wastegate Position Sensor A Exceeded Learning Limit

P2B93 concerns the learned closed position of electric wastegate A. The computer periodically drives the valve onto its seat and stores the sensor value found there; Ford's patent US9243553B2 explains why: linkage length drifts with temperature and the reference must be refreshed.
Wastegate linkage bent, stretched or wrongly adjusted
Wastegate flap or seat worn so the valve travels too far
Turbocharger or actuator replaced and relearn not completed
Boost slightly low because the valve does not fully close
P2B94: Wastegate Position Sensor B Exceeded Learning Limit

P2B94 is set when the learned end position of electric wastegate B falls outside the window the engine computer accepts. Stellantis documents it on the 2025 Ram 1500 with the 3.0L Hurricane twin-turbo: bulletin 09-008-25 (Rev.
Wastegate rod retention clips incorrectly installed (Stellantis 09-008-25)
Play or bending in the wastegate B linkage
Charger or actuator B replaced without completed relearn
MIL on, often together with P0248
Lack of acceleration from the turbo
P2B95: P2B95 belongs to the cold-start strategy of petrol direct-injection engines: while the catalyst is heated, each injection is split into two or more small pulses, and the module checks via the injector coil voltage that every pulse really opened the injector. Unlike P2B08 to P2B0F, which name a cylinder, P2B95 is the engine-wide verdict.
Engine software setting the code falsely (GM and Stellantis reflash bulletins)
Injector opening sluggishly when cold due to deposits or wear
High resistance or chafing in injector wiring
Rail pressure outside the expected range during cold start
Check engine light after two cold starts with the fault
Usually no noticeable effect on driving
Possibly rough running in the first seconds after a cold start
P2B96: P2B96 is the engine-wide check, outside the cold-start phase, that injectors on a direct-injection petrol engine really open when commanded. The module digitises the voltage across each injector and looks for the small kink the moving armature leaves; if commanded pulses repeatedly show no opening, it assumes fuel was not delivered.
Engine harness chafed against underhood parts (GM 2.7 l L3B)
Engine software detecting falsely, fixed by reprogramming
Injector armature sticking or injector worn
High resistance in an injector circuit or connector
Check engine light after two drives with the fault
Misfire or rough running if fuel is really missing
Often other codes from the same harness or injector fault
P2B97: Exhaust Pressure Control Valve A Position Exceeded Learning Limit

P2B97 concerns the electrically driven exhaust back-pressure flap of GM's 3.0-litre Duramax diesel. After key-off the module moves the flap to its fully closed and fully open stops and stores what the SENT position sensor reports there.
Flap travel blocked by welding slag, soot or corrosion
Position sensor in the actuator drifted
Actuator gear or motor worn so the stops are not reached
Weak battery during the key-off learn
Check engine light after one drive
Slower warm-up or reduced exhaust heating for aftertreatment
P2B98: Exhaust Pressure Control Valve A Supply Low
P2B98 says the motor of exhaust pressure control valve A is not getting enough supply voltage.
Blown fuse or interrupted feed to the valve actuator
Corroded connector or poor ground at the actuator
Weak battery or charging fault causing voltage dips
Check engine light after one drive
Exhaust flap without function, slower warm-up
Further codes for the same fuse or harness
P2B99: Exhaust Pressure Control Valve A Driver Current/Temperature Too High
P2B99 reports that the output stage driving exhaust pressure control valve A is running too hot or carrying too much current.
Valve motor with internal fault such as shorted windings
Flap binding from soot or corrosion so the motor stalls
Defective driver stage in the control module
Check engine light after one drive
Possibly reduced power or longer warm-up
P2B9A: P2B9A covers a DEF quality sensor whose signal drops out now and then or jumps between values, rather than sitting permanently too low or too high. The sensor in the tank module usually gauges urea concentration by timing an ultrasonic echo and passes the result on digitally.
Loose, corroded or water-damaged connector at the DEF tank module
Air bubbles or sloshing DEF disturbing the ultrasonic echo
Urea crystals or deposits on the sensor face
DEF warning message, possibly a countdown to reduced speed or no restart
Fault comes and goes, often after refilling or on rough roads
P2B9B: Vehicle Conditions Incorrect for Particulate Matter Sensor Regeneration

P2B9B is a status code of the particulate matter sensor behind the diesel particulate filter: the sensor needs to burn its electrodes clean before the next measurement, but operating conditions do not allow it. Heating the ceramic to around 780 °C is only safe once the exhaust is dry.
Short trips and long idling keeping exhaust below the dew point
Faulty exhaust temperature signal misjudging dew point conditions
Low supply voltage to the sensor control unit preventing heating
Engine software setting the enable conditions too narrowly
Particulate filter monitor shown as not complete
Code disappears after a longer drive at steady speed
P2B9C: P2B9C signals that coolant pump A is powered and commanded but its rotor does not turn, or stops. Ford uses the code in its 2024 gasoline OBD summary as fault type 71 (actuator stuck) under P2600, where pump A is the auxiliary pump in the high-temperature loop for cabin heating; the check runs continuously above 11 V battery voltage over 5 seconds.
Seized bearing or rotor in the auxiliary pump
Sludge, sealant residue or debris jamming the impeller
Coolant frozen in the pump due to weak antifreeze
Burnt motor winding or failed drive electronics
Pump silent when it should run
P2B9D: Coolant Pump A Supply Voltage Circuit

P2B9D means the power feed of coolant pump A is outside its usable range, as opposed to the command line covered by P2600 to P2603. Ford names it in the 2024 gasoline OBD summary as fault type 1C (feed voltage outside its window) of the cabin-heating auxiliary pump, monitored all the time from 11 V battery voltage with a 5-second window.
Blown fuse or faulty relay in the pump supply
Corroded connector or poor ground at the pump
Weak battery or charging system voltage too low
Fault comes and goes with battery condition or electrical load
P2B9E: Coolant Pump A Control Module Overtemperature

P2B9E is raised by the electronics built into coolant pump A when their temperature gets too high; the pump then derates or shuts down to protect itself. Ford's 2024 OBD summary for gasoline engines lists it as fault type 98 (system over temperature) of the cabin-heating auxiliary pump, monitored continuously once the battery supplies 11 V or more.
Low coolant or air at the pump, so the electronics lose cooling
Stiff bearing or impeller raising motor load
Heat from nearby exhaust parts or damaged heat shield
Ageing power stage in the pump electronics
Cabin heat drops off after some time of driving
Pump stops and restarts after cooling down
P2B9F: P2B9F means coolant pump B turns slower than requested. Ford's 2024 gasoline OBD summary places it as underspeed type B2 in the block of base code P261A, where pump B is the auxiliary pump of the high-temperature loop for component cooling no. 1; the check runs continuously from 11 V with a 5-second window.
Worn bearing or dragging impeller in pump B
Debris or sludge slowing the impeller
Low supply voltage or poor ground at the pump
Weak motor or drive electronics in the pump
Temperature warning for the cooled component under load
Possible power reduction to protect hot parts
P2BA0: P2BA0 reports that coolant pump C does not reach its speed. GM names the code Low Temperature Coolant Loop Pump Underspeed in its diesel ECM tables and treats it as a low out-of-range speed reading: in 2020 (20OBDG04) the printed limit is below -100 rpm in 5 of 8 one-second samples, in 2025 (25OBDG04A) below -50 rpm in 4 of 5; enable conditions are an active…
Engine harness chafed against brackets, shorting pump circuits
Worn or partly seized low-temperature loop pump
Air or low coolant in the low-temperature loop
Low supply voltage at the pump relay
Check engine light after the second faulty trip
Parts on the low-temperature loop cooled less, reduced power possible
Further electrical codes when the harness is damaged
P2BA1: P2BA1 is set when coolant pump D, a further electric pump in the manufacturer's thermal management, turns slower than its command. No manufacturer documents this code publicly, so which circuit pump D serves and which limits apply is unknown.
Worn bearing or dragging impeller in pump D
Debris or deposits slowing the impeller
Low supply voltage or high resistance in power or ground
Weak motor or drive electronics in the pump
Check engine light or cooling warning, depending on the vehicle
Rising temperature of the part cooled by pump D
P2BA2: P2BA2 belongs to the electric main water pump. GM uses it in a way the title does not suggest: on the 2.7-litre L3B (table 19OBDG03D) and in the 2025 table 25OBDG03B the test runs while the pump should be switched off – pump disabled or a request of 0–4 rpm for at least 3 s – and fails if the pump still reports 10 rpm or more for 8 of 10 seconds with over 11…
Pump electronics ignoring the off command
Implausible speed feedback from the pump
Impeller turned by coolant flow from another pump
Command or enable line fault keeping the pump on
Check engine light after two trips
Engine takes longer to reach operating temperature
Pump audible after the engine is switched off
P2BA3: P2BA3 concerns the belt-driven starter-generator of mild-hybrid and stop-start engines: the controller has concluded that the machine does not turn the crankshaft or take torque from it as it should, although its electrics seem healthy. The exact detection rule is not published.
Weak or defective belt tensioner or tensioner damper letting the belt slip
Worn, misaligned or thrown poly-V belt
Mechanical damage in the starter-generator (bearing, pulley)
Squealing, chirping or grinding from the belt drive, often at start
Engine fails to restart after an automatic stop
Battery runs flat because the machine no longer charges
Electrical system warning or MIL on the instrument panel
P2BA4: Many diesel SCR systems rely on the oxidation catalyst ahead of them to turn part of the NO into NO2, because a mix near half NO2 lets the SCR reaction run fast at low temperature. P2BA4 reports that this catalyst no longer delivers the needed gas mix.
Oxidation catalyst thermally aged or poisoned (sulphur, oil ash), little NO2 produced
Catalyst inlet face coated with soot or unburnt fuel after injector or EGR problems
Faulty NOx or exhaust temperature sensor distorting the evaluation
Exhaust leak upstream of the catalyst diluting the measured gas
SCR efficiency codes such as P20EE set as well
Usually no noticeable change in driving behaviour
P2BA5: Some diesel particulate filters carry a precious-metal coating that, besides helping burn soot, oxidises NO to NO2 for the SCR catalyst further down. P2BA5 says this coated filter fails to supply enough NO2.
Filter coating thermally aged, e.g. after very hot or uncontrolled regenerations
Ash or oil additives covering the catalytic layer
Weak upstream oxidation catalyst in a combined evaluation
Exhaust temperature or NOx sensor reading wrongly
P2BA6: NOx Exceedance - SCR NOx Catalyst Performance

P2BA6 opens the group of NOx exceedance codes that grew out of the European rules on reagent-based NOx control. Each code names why tailpipe NOx has climbed above the diagnostic limit; here the blame lies with the SCR catalyst itself, while dosing, reagent and EGR still look plausible.
SCR catalyst aged, overheated or chemically poisoned
Urea crystal deposits on mixer or catalyst face
Too little NO2 from upstream oxidation catalyst
MIL and emission system warning in the cluster
Countdown to speed limit or no restart after some distance
Higher DEF consumption without better NOx reduction
P2BA7: P2BA7 records that NOx control has been lost because the DEF or AdBlue tank has run dry, so no reagent can be dosed.
DEF tank simply not refilled despite level warnings
Level sensor reading empty although fluid is present (fault, ice, deposits)
Leaking DEF tank or line emptying the system
Only a small amount refilled, below the quantity the system needs to recognise a refill
DEF empty message with restart countdown
Engine will not restart once countdown expires
P2BA8: NOx Exceedence - Interruption of Reagent Dosing Activity
With P2BA8 the controller states that NOx went up because reagent dosing stopped although the engine needed it.
DEF injector clogged or stuck by crystals
Pump failure or pressure not built up
Frozen fluid because tank or line heater fails
Wiring or SCR control unit fault stopping dosing
DEF dosing malfunction message with distance countdown
MIL on, further SCR component codes stored
Reduced power or no restart if not repaired
P2BA9: P2BA9 blames high NOx on reagent that falls short of the specified quality, e.g. diluted or contaminated DEF. EU Annex XVI wants a wrong-fluid warning and inducement if not fixed within 50 km; CARB asks for improper reductant detection.
DEF diluted with water, aged or replaced by the wrong fluid
Contaminated tank or lines (also from production, FCA 25-003-15)
Air leak after the MAF sensor or at EGR cooler joints misleading the NOx model (JLR)
Outdated engine software or faulty NOx sensor
Incorrect DEF quality message with restart countdown
MIL on, often with P2BAE and P2BAF
Speed or power limit if the countdown runs out
P2BAA: P2BAA means less reagent is actually reaching the exhaust than the dosing strategy asks for, so NOx stays too high. EU Annex XVI sets the frame: actual and demanded consumption are compared, and a gap above 50 % over 30 minutes triggers the warning.
Partially blocked DEF injector delivering too little
Weak DEF pump or clogged pump filter
Calibration error setting the code without a fault (GM 25-NA-042)
Leak in the pressure line returning fluid before the injector
Service emission or exhaust fluid system message
DEF level falls more slowly than usual
P2BAB: P2BAB attributes excess NOx to exhaust gas recirculation that delivers the wrong amount of gas, so combustion temperature and raw NOx rise.
EGR valve sooted up or sticking
EGR cooler or pipe partly blocked
Faulty EGR position sensor or air mass meter distorting flow estimate
Leak in the intake or EGR path
MIL on, EGR flow codes stored
Rough running or sooting with too much EGR
Power reduction possible if not repaired
P2BAC: P2BAC is reserved for the case where exhaust gas recirculation is not just off target but shut down altogether, whether by an unplugged valve, a blocked path, an unauthorised software change or a defect that leaves the valve closed.
EGR valve unplugged, blanked off or disabled
EGR valve stuck closed or actuator failed
Modified engine software with EGR switched off
Open or short in the EGR valve circuit
MIL and NOx warning, later inducement
EGR circuit or position codes stored as well
P2BAD: P2BAD is the catch-all of the series: NOx after the SCR is measured too high, yet none of the specific causes from P2BA6 to P2BAC can be pinned down.
Poor DEF quality or partly blocked dosing without a specific code
Upstream or downstream NOx sensor drifting
Engine control software needing an update (Nissan Titan XD)
Exhaust fluid quality poor or emission warning
MIL on after the first failed run
Speed limit countdown if the condition persists
P2BAE: NOx Exceedence - NOx Control Monitoring System
P2BAE is tied to the system that watches NOx control itself, typically the NOx sensors and the logic that compares measured emissions with the permitted level.
Underlying SCR fault such as poor DEF quality or dosing pressure deviation
NOx sensor damaged, badly mounted or contaminated
Air trapped in the DEF system
MIL with DEF dosing malfunction message
Stored together with P2BAF and a root cause code
P2BAF: P2BAF does not name a faulty part; it states that the driver inducement of the NOx control system has been activated.
Active SCR fault (DEF quality, dosing, level) that started the inducement
Control module software fault, e.g. BCM on Jeep Compass (FCA 08-103-19)
Root cause fixed but the clearing monitor has not yet run
MIL and DEF system warning on
Speed or power limited, engine may not restart
P2BB0: On engines that burn compressed natural gas, LPG or another fuel besides petrol or diesel, the controller can estimate how much gas it has injected and compare that with how fast the tank actually empties, judged by tank pressure or level. P2BB0 means the tank drains noticeably more slowly than the injection quantity implies.
Alternative fuel tank pressure or temperature sensor reading wrong
Gas injectors or filter restricted, less gas delivered than commanded
Pressure regulator supplying too little pressure
Fuel mode or control software not matching actual operation
MIL on, sometimes together with lean mixture codes
Gas range or gauge reading implausible
Engine switches to petrol more often than usual
