P2BB1: P2BB1 is set when the alternative fuel store, typically a CNG cylinder, loses more gas than the injected quantity can account for. The main suspicion is a leak between tank and injectors, which is why this check doubles as a safety monitor.
Gas leak at fittings, lines, regulator or tank valve
Gas injector leaking or sticking open
Tank pressure or temperature sensor exaggerating the pressure drop
Gas range much shorter than usual
MIL on, gas mode may be locked out
P2BB2: P2BB2 reports that the tank for the second fuel, mostly CNG or LPG, has been drawn down to its usable minimum. It is a status message rather than a component fault: a bi-fuel vehicle simply goes back to petrol.
Gas tank actually used up to its reserve
Tank pressure or level sensor reading too low
Tank shutoff valve closed or not opening
Engine runs on petrol only, gas mode cannot be selected
Gas gauge shows empty or low-level warning
P2BB3: Where a separate driver module powers the fuel pump, the ECM sends a duty-cycle command and the module reports what it actually applies. P2BB3 means these two values disagree beyond a tolerance, so the pump is not running at the requested speed although no open or short has been found.
Fuel pump driver or tank zone module not delivering the commanded output
High resistance in the pump supply or ground connection
Worn or binding fuel pump drawing abnormal current
Disturbed data link between ECM and pump module
Hesitation or power loss under load
P2BB4: Engine Coolant Temperature Sensor 4 Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
This code covers jumps in the signal of the fourth coolant temperature sensor that coolant cannot physically make.
Loose or corroded terminal at the sensor 4 connector
Engine harness chafed, wire making intermittent contact
Internal intermittent break in the sensor element
Jumping temperature value in live data
Cooling fans or thermal management reacting erratically
P2BB5: Engine Coolant Temperature Sensor 5 Circuit Intermittent/Erratic

P2BB5 is the erratic-signal code for coolant sensor 5. Unlike the hard circuit faults P2B2D and P2B2E, the reading here stays within the valid range but changes faster than the sensor's thermal inertia allows, which betrays a contact that briefly opens or shorts.
Chafed engine harness with intermittent contact in the sensor 5 wires
Loose, spread or corroded connector terminal
MIL on after the second trip
Sensor 5 value spikes in live data
Often stored together with other harness-related codes
P2BB6: P2BB6 is the general circuit code for a sixth coolant temperature sensor, intended for control units that only know that the circuit is faulty and do not distinguish a grounded from an open or shorted-high line.
Sensor 6 connector unplugged, damaged or corroded
Open or shorted wire between sensor 6 and the ECM
Sensor 6 shows a fixed substitute or implausible value
Fans may run continuously as a precaution
P2BB7: Engine Coolant Temperature Sensor 6 Circuit Range/Performance

With P2BB7 the sixth coolant sensor delivers an electrically valid value that nevertheless makes no sense. Plausibility tests of this kind compare the sensor with the other engine temperatures after a long cold soak, expect a clear rise once the engine warms up, and flag a value that never moves.
Sensor 6 element drifted out of its characteristic curve
No coolant flow at sensor 6 due to failed pump, valve or air pocket
Contact resistance at connector or terminals
MIL on, usually only after a cold start and warm-up
Sensor 6 value lags or stays flat compared with the other coolant sensors
P2BB8: Engine Coolant Temperature Sensor 6 Circuit Low

Coolant sensors are NTC thermistors, so a low signal from sensor 6 means a very small resistance that the ECM would have to read as extreme heat; in practice a signal wire touching ground or a shorted element.
Sensor 6 signal wire shorted to ground, e.g. chafed harness
Moisture or coolant in the connector bridging the pins
Sensor 6 shows an implausibly high temperature
Radiator fans running at high speed
P2BB9: Engine Coolant Temperature Sensor 6 Circuit High

A high signal from coolant sensor 6 corresponds to a resistance so large that only an interrupted circuit, a disconnected plug or a wire shorted to a voltage source explains it; read as temperature it would be colder than −60 °C. GM's tables check for this once the engine has run more than 10 s or intake air is warmer than −20 °C.
Sensor 6 connector unplugged or not latched
Broken signal or ground wire, or signal shorted to voltage
MIL on after the second trip
P2BBA: Engine Coolant Temperature Sensor 6 Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P2BBA catches short dropouts or spikes in the sixth coolant sensor signal that never last long enough to count as a steady low or high fault.
Chafed engine harness with intermittent contact
Loose or corroded terminal at sensor 6 or the ECM
Sensor element with intermittent internal break
MIL on after two trips, may go out again
Sensor 6 value jumps in live data
Other harness-related codes stored at the same time
P2BBB: Turbocharger/Supercharger Bypass Valve A Position Sensor Circuit

P2BBB is the general fault of the position feedback from bypass valve A, the electrically driven valve that lets boosted air flow back from the compressor outlet to its inlet when the throttle closes or boost has to be trimmed. It is not the wastegate on the exhaust side.
Loose, corroded or unplugged connector at the bypass valve position sensor
Chafed or broken signal, reference or ground wire in the harness near the compressor
Internal fault of the position sensor in the valve actuator
Faulty sensor input or 5 V reference inside the engine control module
Reduced boost and noticeably less power
Whoosh or flutter noise when lifting off the throttle
P2BBC: Turbocharger/Supercharger Bypass Valve A Position Sensor Circuit Low
P2BBC sets when the position signal of the bypass valve A sensor sits too low – usually an open signal wire, a short to ground or a lost 5 V supply to the sensor.
Signal wire shorted to ground or chafed against the engine
Open 5 V reference wire or reference shorted by another sensor on the same supply
Pushed-out or corroded terminal in the valve connector
Defective position sensor in the valve actuator
Check engine light on in the first trip
Possibly further 5 V reference codes if the supply is shorted
P2BBD: Turbocharger/Supercharger Bypass Valve A Position Sensor Circuit High

P2BBD is the high-side counterpart: the position signal from bypass valve A rises toward the full reference voltage. That points to a short to the 5 V supply or to battery voltage, a broken sensor ground – the signal then floats upward – or a defective sensor.
Open sensor ground wire or corroded ground terminal
Signal wire shorted to the 5 V reference or to battery voltage
Defective position sensor in the valve actuator
Moisture in the valve connector creating a leakage path
Reduced power because boost is limited
Unusual noise when lifting off the throttle
P2BBE: Turbocharger/Supercharger Bypass Valve A Position Exceeded Learning Limit

P2BBE is not a wiring fault but a failed end-stop learn. GM's 2019 tables for the LT5 Corvette ZR1 describe how the electronic recirculation valve is taught after each engine shutdown: the module first drives it to the closed stop and stores the sensor value, then repeats this for the open stop.
Oil or carbon deposits keeping the valve from reaching its stops
Bent flap or shaft, or worn actuator gear
Position sensor shifted or drifted after a repair or with age
Non-matching replacement valve with a different travel range
Check engine light after the engine has been switched off and restarted
Boost limited or erratic on lift-off
P2BBF: Turbocharger/Supercharger Bypass Valve A Supply Voltage Low

P2BBF concerns the power side of bypass valve A rather than its position feedback. Electric recirculation valves are moved by a small DC motor fed through an H-bridge in the engine module, and the bridge chip itself flags when its supply drops too far.
High resistance in the engine module feed, fuse or ground connection
Weak battery or charging fault causing voltage dips
Corroded pins at the engine module or valve connector
Internal fault of the H-bridge driver in the engine module
Valve no longer moves, boost limited or surging on lift-off
Often accompanied by other low-voltage codes
P2BC0: Turbocharger/Supercharger Bypass Valve A Driver Current/Temperature Too High
P2BC0 sets when the output stage that drives bypass valve A reports too much current or overheating.
Sticking or jammed valve making the motor draw high current
Shorted winding in the valve actuator motor
Motor leads shorted to each other or to ground in the harness
Overheated or damaged H-bridge driver in the engine module
Compressor surge noise when lifting off
P2BC1: Charge Air Cooler Coolant Pump A Stuck/Stalled

P2BC1 means the electric pump that circulates coolant through the charge air cooler loop is powered, but its rotor will not turn or stops under load; the pump electronics see high current at little or no speed and report this to the engine module.
Rotor stuck after a long standstill (Audi bulletin 2080825)
Debris, deposits or a worn bearing blocking the impeller
Engine module software needing an update (FCA bulletins for Giulia/Stelvio)
Ice in the loop due to insufficient antifreeze
Check engine light, often with a reduced-power message
Hot charge air and less power under load
No running noise from the pump during an actuator test
P2BC2: Charge Air Cooler Coolant Pump A Supply Voltage Circuit

P2BC2 points to the power feed of charge air cooler pump A: the pump or its controller sees a supply that is missing or outside its working window. Typical causes are a blown fuse, a relay with burnt contacts, a broken or corroded feed or ground wire, or a water-damaged plug; a weak battery can contribute. No manufacturer documents P2BC2 publicly.
Blown fuse or faulty relay in the pump feed
Broken or corroded supply or ground wire
Water ingress or corrosion in the pump connector
Check engine light or engine warning message
Pump does not run, charge air temperature rises
Reduced power in hot conditions or under load
P2BC3: Charge Air Cooler Coolant Pump A Control Module Overtemperature

The control electronics of an electric coolant pump sit inside the pump body and are cooled by the liquid flowing through it. P2BC3 means the electronics of charge air cooler pump A report a temperature above their limit.
Low coolant level or air trapped in the low-temperature loop
Partly blocked impeller or worn bearing raising motor current
Fault in the pump's integrated electronics
Missing heat shield or pump placed close to hot engine parts
Check engine light or engine warning message
Pump runs slower or switches off, especially in hot weather
Hot charge air and reduced power
P2BC4: Battery Charging System Positive Contactor B Circuit
P2BC4 is the catch-all electrical code for positive contactor B of the charging system, the second charging switch on the plus side next to contactor A (P0D07).
Coil of positive contactor B open or shorted
Wiring or connector fault in the contactor B branch
Fault or software issue in the controlling module
DC fast charging or on-board charger charging (depending on design) refused
Charging fault message in the cluster or app
P2BC5: Battery Charging System Positive Contactor B Stuck Closed

P2BC5 reports that positive charging contactor B still conducts after the open command, normally because its contacts have fused. Mercedes-Benz stores it, often with P2BCC, in the DC charge connection unit (N116/5, on the eSprinter N24/6) of GLE, E- and S-Class plug-in hybrids, the EQB and the eSprinter; after a DC session the vehicle refuses to start.
Contacts of positive contactor B welded, e.g. after current peaks at the end of charging
Software of the charging module judges the contactor state wrongly (Mercedes update)
Ripple, overcurrent or overvoltage from the charging station
Coil driver does not switch off
Vehicle will not start after DC charging (Mercedes)
High-voltage or hybrid system warning in the cluster
P2BC6: Battery Charging System Positive Contactor B Stuck Open

P2BC6 means positive charging contactor B does not close when commanded, so the plus side of that charging branch stays dead and the session aborts or never starts. The only maker documenting it publicly is Mazda: on the 2024–2026 CX-90 and 2025–2026 CX-70 plug-in hybrids it reads OBC contactor (+) stuck off, listed with the welded cases P2BC5 and P2BCC.
Contactor B damaged inside and no longer closing (Mazda junction box)
Coil supply or drive line interrupted
Charging control software misjudging the closing check
Charging session stops or does not start
P2BC7: Battery Charging System Positive Contactor B Control Circuit/Open

P2BC7 concerns the coil drive line of positive charging contactor B, not its main contacts: the module compares its command with the voltage and current it measures on that line and sets the code when the line is broken or the driver that does not follow. No manufacturer documents P2BC7 publicly.
Control wire or connector to contactor B interrupted
Coil of positive contactor B open
Driver stage in the control module defective
Charging via the contactor B path not possible
P2BC8: Battery Charging System Positive Contactor B Control Circuit Range/Performance

P2BC8 flags a control circuit of positive charging contactor B that is connected but behaves implausibly: the coil draws a current that does not fit the command, the line voltage lies in an unexpected band, or pulling in takes too long. No manufacturer documents P2BC8 publicly.
Contact resistance at connectors of the control line
Coil resistance of contactor B outside specification
Driver stage in the module degraded
Charging works only now and then
Charging aborts with a fault message
P2BC9: Battery Charging System Positive Contactor B Control Circuit Low

P2BC9 is the low-signal fault on the coil feed of plus-side charging contactor B: the module measures less voltage on that wire than its command calls for, most often because the wire touches ground or the output stage is being dragged down.
Control wire of contactor B shorted to ground
Moisture or corrosion in a connector
Coil of contactor B internally shorted
P2BCA: Battery Charging System Positive Contactor B Control Circuit High

P2BCA means the wire energising the coil of positive charging contactor B shows too much voltage, caused by contact with battery voltage or an output stage stuck in the on state; the contactor could then pull in uncommanded.
Control wire of contactor B shorted to supply voltage
Driver stage does not switch off
Drive system cannot be activated after charging (Audi)
Drive system and electrical system fault warnings
P2BCB: Battery Charging System Negative Contactor B Circuit

P2BCB is the general electrical code for negative contactor B of the charging system, which closes the return path of the second charging branch to the traction battery. No manufacturer documents P2BCB publicly.
Coil of negative contactor B open or shorted
Wiring or connector fault on the return-side contactor
Fault in the module that drives contactor B
Charging in the affected mode refused
P2BCC: Battery Charging System Negative Contactor B Stuck Closed

P2BCC says negative charging contactor B is still closed although the module ordered it open – in practice fused contacts on the return side. Mercedes-Benz lists it in the DC charge connection unit next to P2BC5 and P0E8929 (DC input current too high); the plug-in hybrid, EQB or eSprinter then cannot be started after DC charging.
Contacts of negative contactor B welded at the end of charging
Current ripple or overvoltage from the DC station
Vehicle will not start after DC charging (Mercedes)
P2BCD: Battery Charging System Negative Contactor B Stuck Open

P2BCD is set when negative charging contactor B fails to close, so the charging branch lacks its return path and no current can flow even with the plus side connected. No manufacturer documents P2BCD publicly; Mazda lists the welded minus case P2BCC and the non-closing plus case P2BC6 for the CX-90 PHEV, but not this one.
Negative contactor B burnt or mechanically not closing
Coil supply too weak or interrupted
Charging control software misjudging the check
P2BCE: Battery Charging System Negative Contactor B Control Circuit/Open
P2BCE watches the coil drive of negative charging contactor B for an open line or a driver whose real state differs from its command. No manufacturer documents P2BCE publicly.
Control wire or terminal of negative contactor B open
Coil of negative contactor B open
Driver stage in the module defective
Charging via the contactor B path not possible
P2BCF: Battery Charging System Negative Contactor B Control Circuit Range/Performance

P2BCF points to a control circuit on negative charging contactor B that is neither open nor shorted yet still implausible: coil current, line voltage or switching time fall outside the window that belongs to the commanded state. No manufacturer documents P2BCF publicly, and no published GM table has such a check for a charging contactor coil.
Coil resistance of negative contactor B shifted
Corrosion or contact resistance in the control connector
Poor ground of the controlling module
Charging drops out or will not begin
Charging fault message from time to time
P2BD0: Battery Charging System Negative Contactor B Control Circuit Low

With P2BD0 the coil drive line of minus-side charging contactor B is too low – usually insulation damage letting the wire touch the body, or an output stage stuck low. Starved of current, the coil leaves the return path of that charging branch open. No manufacturer documents P2BD0 publicly.
Control wire of negative contactor B shorted to ground
Moisture in a connector of the control line
Coil of negative contactor B internally shorted
P2BD1: Battery Charging System Negative Contactor B Control Circuit High

P2BD1 flags excess voltage on the coil feed of minus-side charging contactor B, for instance from contact with a 12 V wire or an output stage that will not turn off. The risk is a coil that stays energised and keeps the return pole connected while the module believes it is open, so the module normally blocks charging.
Control wire of negative contactor B shorted to supply voltage
P2BD2: P2BD2 reports that the first aftertreatment line, or the only one, is not gas-tight, so exhaust escapes between engine and tailpipe or false air enters.
Loose V-band clamp or failed gasket between aftertreatment modules
Cracked exhaust pipe, flex joint or catalyst housing
Leak at a sensor, DEF injector or pressure tap mounting
Pressure sensor hose cracked, making the system look leaky
Exhaust smell, soot marks or ticking at a joint
Follow-up SCR or particulate filter codes
P2BD3: P2BD3 is the twin of P2BD2 for a second aftertreatment line, found on engines with two parallel exhaust paths, each with its own catalysts and filter. Which physical line is B is up to the maker; in practice it is usually the path of the second cylinder bank.
Loose clamp or leaking gasket in line B
Crack in pipe, flex joint or housing on side B
Leaking sensor or injector mounting on line B
Faulty pressure sensor or hose shared by both lines
Exhaust noise or smell on one side
Uneven readings between the two lines
P2BD4: Motor Electronics Coolant Pump C Control Circuit/Open

Hybrid and electric drives cool the inverter, DC/DC converter and motor with one or more electric pumps; J2012 labels them A, B and C. P2BD4 means the controlling module has found an open circuit or an unclassified fault on the control line of pump C. No manufacturer documents P2BD4, or a third pump of this kind, publicly.
Unplugged, loose or corroded connector at pump C
Broken control or signal wire between module and pump
Faulty output or input stage in the controlling module
Hybrid or drive system warning, often with the check engine light
Reduced drive power when the electronics heat up
Pump C silent during an actuator test
P2BD5: Motor Electronics Coolant Pump C Control Circuit Low

P2BD5 flags the command line of the third electric coolant pump in the inverter and motor electronics loop as sitting at too low a level. With a low-side or PWM driver this usually means the wire or the pump input is shorted to ground, so the pump either runs unchecked or not at all. No manufacturer documents P2BD5 publicly.
Pump C control wire chafed through and touching ground
Water or corrosion in the pump connector bridging the signal pin to ground
Shorted input stage inside pump C
Faulty output driver in the controlling module
Warning for the hybrid or drive system, often with the check engine light
Pump C runs constantly or stays silent regardless of command
Reduced drive power once the electronics warm up
P2BD6: Motor Electronics Coolant Pump C Control Circuit High

P2BD6 is stored when the control circuit of motor electronics coolant pump C reads higher than the commanded state allows. A short to battery voltage, or a driver stage that reports overcurrent, are the usual triggers; the pump may then keep running or ignore commands. No manufacturer documents P2BD6 publicly.
Control wire of pump C shorted to a supply wire in the harness
Pump C drawing excessive current because of an internal electrical fault
Bent or corroded pins in the pump C connector touching each other
Failed output stage in the controlling module
Hybrid system or check engine warning
Pump C keeps running after the vehicle is switched off, or does not respond at all
Power limitation during long climbs or fast driving
P2BD7: Motor Electronics Coolant Pump C Control Performance

P2BD7 means pump C in the motor electronics cooling loop is electrically reachable but does not deliver what the controller asks for: wrong speed, a fault report from the pump itself or too little cooling effect. No manufacturer documents P2BD7 publicly.
Air trapped in the electronics loop after a repair or coolant loss
Low coolant level in the electronics loop reservoir
Worn, sticking or debris-blocked pump C
Outdated software in the hybrid controller that misjudges the pump
Check engine or hybrid warning light
Cooling fan running at high speed more often than usual
Reduced electric drive or charging power when the loop gets warm
P2BD8: Motor Electronics Coolant Temperature Sensor B Circuit

Some hybrid and electric drives measure the coolant in the inverter and motor electronics loop at more than one point; J2012 names these sensors A, B and C, and which spot each letter marks is left to the manufacturer.
Loose, unplugged or corroded connector at sensor B
Damaged signal or reference wire between sensor B and the module
Faulty input circuit in the controlling module
Hybrid or drive system warning, often with the check engine light
Electronics coolant pump and fan running more than usual
Possible reduction of electric drive power
P2BD9: Motor Electronics Coolant Temperature Sensor B Circuit Range/Performance

P2BD9 means coolant temperature sensor B in the motor electronics loop delivers a voltage inside its electrical window, yet the temperature it reports does not fit the rest of the vehicle. The circuit itself is intact; a drifting thermistor, a sensor sitting in an air pocket or a value that stays frozen are typical. No manufacturer documents P2BD9 publicly.
Sensor B thermistor drifted out of its characteristic
Air pocket or low coolant leaving sensor B partly dry
Added resistance from corroded terminals shifting the reading
Wrong value from a comparison sensor such as engine coolant or intake air temperature
Check engine light, usually without a noticeable driving issue at first
Cooling fan or electronics pump running at unexpected times
Occasional power limitation on hot days
P2BDA: Motor Electronics Coolant Temperature Sensor B Circuit Low

P2BDA is set when the sensor B signal in the electronics coolant loop falls below its valid window. These sensors are normally NTC thermistors, so a low voltage translates into an impossibly hot reading; a signal wire touching ground or a shorted sensor is the classic cause. No manufacturer documents P2BDA publicly.
Signal wire of sensor B shorted to ground
Moisture in the sensor connector creating a leakage path to ground
Faulty input stage in the evaluating module
Check engine light and hybrid system warning
Scan tool shows an implausibly high electronics coolant temperature
Power reduction even with a cold vehicle
P2BDB: Motor Electronics Coolant Temperature Sensor B Circuit High

P2BDB tells that the signal of coolant temperature sensor B sits above its valid voltage range. With a thermistor fed from a 5 V reference through a pull-up resistor, a broken wire, an unplugged connector or a sensor gone open lets the voltage rise to almost the reference, which the module would read as extreme cold.
Sensor B connector unplugged, not latched or with a backed-out pin
Broken signal or ground wire of sensor B
Signal wire shorted to a voltage source
Check engine light or hybrid warning
Scan tool shows an implausibly low electronics coolant temperature
Electronics coolant pump running at a fixed high speed
P2BDC: Motor Electronics Coolant Temperature Sensor C Circuit

P2BDC reports a general fault in the circuit of coolant temperature sensor C, a third measuring point that some drives use in the loop cooling the inverter, converter and motor. The code stands for a signal the module cannot use without assigning it to the low, high or plausibility codes P2BDE, P2BDF and P2BDD.
Poor contact at the sensor C connector
Chafed or broken wiring between sensor C and the module
Fault on a 5 V reference or sensor ground shared with other sensors
Warning lamp for the hybrid or drive system
Fan and electronics pump running at high output as a precaution
P2BDD: Motor Electronics Coolant Temperature Sensor C Circuit Range/Performance

P2BDD is the plausibility check of coolant temperature sensor C: electrically the signal looks fine, but the reported value cannot be right when set against other temperatures. No manufacturer documents P2BDD publicly. Two published approaches show how such a check can run while driving instead of after a cold soak.
Sensor C reading drifted away from the true coolant temperature
Air or weak flow at the sensor C location, so it sees a local hot or cold spot
Corroded terminals adding resistance in the sensor C circuit
Faulty comparison temperature from another sensor in the system
Check engine light without an obvious drivability problem
Cooling fan behaviour that does not match the conditions
Power or charging limitation under heavy load
P2BDE: Motor Electronics Coolant Temperature Sensor C Circuit Low

P2BDE reports that the voltage from coolant temperature sensor C has dropped below its lower limit. Low describes the voltage: for the usual NTC sensor it corresponds to a reading far hotter than the coolant can be, and the cause is mostly a grounded signal wire, a crushed pigtail or a sensor that has shorted internally.
Sensor C signal wire shorted to ground or to the sensor ground
Crushed or melted sensor pigtail near hot components
Faulty analog input in the evaluating module
Hybrid warning or check engine light
Very high electronics coolant temperature shown in live data on a cold vehicle
Fan running at full speed shortly after start
P2BDF: Motor Electronics Coolant Temperature Sensor C Circuit High

P2BDF is stored when the signal of coolant temperature sensor C climbs to nearly the full reference voltage. For the module this looks like coolant colder than any climate allows; in practice a pin that has backed out of the connector, a corroded or broken signal wire, or a short to a voltage source is behind it. No manufacturer documents P2BDF publicly.
Backed-out or loose pin in the sensor C connector
Corroded or broken signal wire of sensor C
Signal wire shorted to the 5 V reference or another supply
Check engine or hybrid system warning
Live data shows the lowest possible temperature for sensor C
Pump and fan running in a fixed protective mode
P2BE0: Hybrid/EV Battery Coolant Level Sensor Circuit/Open
P2BE0 concerns the wiring of the level sensor in the coolant reservoir of the high-voltage battery loop: its signal is missing or the line is broken.
Battery coolant level actually low (leak or after service), bulletin asks to check first
Level sensor defective, e.g. internal solder joints (GM Volt)
Open signal wire or loose connector at the reservoir
Internal break in the sensor jumper harness
Service hybrid system message on the cluster
Plug-in charging disabled on some models
P2BE1: Hybrid/EV Battery Coolant Level Sensor Range/Performance

P2BE1 reports a battery coolant level signal that lies inside the electrical limits yet makes no sense, such as a value between the defined full and low states or one that flickers while the vehicle stands still. No manufacturer documents this code publicly.
Level sensor with internal fault, e.g. cracked solder joints
Intermittent contact in connector or jumper harness
Coolant level near the switching point or air in the loop
Evaluation software in the battery or hybrid controller
Coolant level looks correct at the reservoir
P2BE2: Hybrid/EV Battery Coolant Level Sensor Circuit Low

P2BE2 is stored when the voltage from the battery coolant level sensor falls below the lowest value the sensor can legitimately produce. That points to the signal touching ground or a sensor whose output collapses, not to a low coolant level, which normally reads inside the valid range. No manufacturer documents P2BE2 publicly.
Signal wire chafed through and shorted to ground
P2BE3: Hybrid/EV Battery Coolant Level Sensor Circuit High

P2BE3 means the level sensor signal of the battery coolant loop is above its valid range, typically from a short to the sensor supply or to 12 V, or from a lost sensor ground. No manufacturer documents P2BE3 publicly. GM's code P1FFD on the Chevrolet Volt shows the same test with numbers: above 4.0 V, 40 of 50 samples at 100 ms, Type A.
Signal wire shorted to sensor supply or 12 V
Open sensor ground or open signal with pull-up (read as high)
P2BE4: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Current Sensor C Circuit
P2BE4 is the general circuit code for a third current measurement in the high-voltage battery, used where sensor A (P0ABF to P0AC3) and sensor B (P0B0E to P0B13) are already taken.
Wiring or connector fault between sensor and battery controller
Input stage or software of the battery controller
P2BE5: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Current Sensor C Circuit Range/Performance
P2BE5 flags current sensor C as implausible although its signal is electrically valid, for instance an offset with no current flowing or a value at odds with the other readings.
Battery controller software (Stellantis Pacifica PHEV, reflash per bulletin)
High resistance at connector or sensor ground
Inaccurate state of charge or reduced electric range
P2BE6: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Current Sensor C Low

P2BE6 is set when the output of current sensor C drops below the lowest value it can deliver in normal service. Unlike its A and B siblings, the official title omits the word circuit, but the meaning is the same out-of-range low check. No manufacturer documents P2BE6 publicly.
MIL and hybrid or EV warning on
Reduced power, possibly no ready mode
P2BE7: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Current Sensor C High

With P2BE7 the signal of current sensor C sits above its usable range, which after conversion would be an impossibly large current. As with P2BE6, the official wording drops the word circuit. No manufacturer documents P2BE7 publicly.
Signal wire shorted to the 5 V supply or 12 V
MIL and hybrid or EV warning on
P2BE8: Hybrid/EV Battery Precharge Contactor Control Circuit B Open

P2BE8 reports an open in control circuit B of the battery precharge function, i.e. the coil drive of a second precharge contactor. Note the wording: the letter follows circuit, while the A codes P0AE4 to P0AE7 name contactor A.
Open control wire or loose connector at contactor B
Coil of precharge contactor B open internally
Driver stage in the battery controller defective
Vehicle does not become ready to drive
MIL and hybrid or EV warning on
P2BE9: Hybrid/EV Battery Precharge Contactor Control Circuit B Range/Performance

P2BE9 says control circuit B of the precharge function is connected but behaves implausibly: the coil current, the feedback voltage or the effect of switching does not match the command. No manufacturer documents P2BE9 publicly.
Coil resistance out of tolerance or sluggish armature
High-voltage load or resistor fault keeping the bus from rising during precharge
Corrosion or high resistance in the control circuit
Battery controller software or driver stage
Vehicle sometimes does not become ready
MIL and hybrid or EV warning on
P2BEA: Hybrid/EV Battery Precharge Contactor Control Circuit B Low

P2BEA is stored when control circuit B of the precharge function carries less voltage than its state requires, mostly because the coil feed touches ground or the output is pulled down. With a high-side driver the coil then gets no current and the second precharge path stays open. No manufacturer documents P2BEA publicly.
Coil feed chafed and shorted to ground
Coil of precharge contactor B shorted internally
Driver stage of the battery controller pulled low
Vehicle does not become ready to drive
MIL and hybrid or EV warning on
P2BEB: Hybrid/EV Battery Precharge Contactor Control Circuit B High

P2BEB reports too much voltage on control circuit B of the precharge function while it should be off, usually a short to 12 V or a driver that does not switch off. The risk is a second precharge path closing on its own; the resistor can overheat if it stays in circuit. No manufacturer documents P2BEB publicly.
Driver stage stuck on in the battery controller
Damaged insulation between adjacent wires in the harness
MIL and hybrid or EV warning on
High-voltage system blocked as a precaution
P2BEC: Fuel Control System A Too Lean Bank 1

Engines that combine port and direct injection keep separate fuel trim adaptations for each injection mode. Ford, which uses this code on its PFDI engines such as the 2.7 L EcoBoost and 5.0 L V8 of the F-150, assigns system A to the direct-injection mode.
PCM software fault on affected Ford models, fixed by reprogramming
High-pressure pump or its volume regulator delivering too little rail pressure
Direct injectors on bank 1 restricted or coked
Bank 1 upstream oxygen sensor reading skewed
Hesitation under acceleration, when the engine relies on direct injection
Often no noticeable change in drivability
P2BED: Fuel Control System A Too Rich Bank 1
P2BED is the rich counterpart of P2BEC: bank 1 has to remove fuel, but only while the engine is fed by direct injection, which Ford calls fuel system A on its port-plus-direct engines.
Direct injector leaking or dribbling on bank 1
PCM software fault, Ford reprogramming bulletins
Rail pressure above target because of a faulty volume regulator or pressure sensor
Long cranking or rough running right after a hot start
Fuel smell from the exhaust, higher consumption
Misfire codes on the same bank in some cases
P2BEE: Fuel Control System A Too Lean Bank 2

Here the lean correction concerns bank 2, the cylinder row without cylinder 1, and again only the direct-injection operating mode (fuel system A in Ford terms). Ford applies the same monitor as on bank 1: closed loop, warm engine, purge off, long-term trim above plus 25 percent combined with short-term trim above plus 1 percent for 2 seconds.
PCM software requiring a Ford update
Bank 2 upstream oxygen sensor reading skewed
Low rail pressure, usually with P2BEC on bank 1 too
P2BEF: Fuel Control System A Too Rich Bank 2

P2BEF says that the engine module has had to take away a lot of fuel on bank 2 while direct injection alone was supplying the cylinders. Ford sets it on port-plus-direct engines when long-term trim on that bank drops past minus 25 percent while short-term trim keeps subtracting more than 1 percent; two seconds in closed loop are enough.
Known PCM software issue on 2019-2020 F-150 2.7 L
Direct injector on bank 2 sticking open or seeping
Rail pressure sensor reading too low, pressure actually too high
Rough running after a hot restart
P2BF0: Fuel Control System B Too Lean Bank 1

Fuel system B is, in Ford's monitor documents, the port fuel injection mode of engines that also have direct injectors. P2BF0 therefore means bank 1 runs lean only when the port injectors do the work.
Low-pressure fuel pump or supply pressure too weak for the port injectors
Air leak at a port injector O-ring or intake manifold gasket
Uneven idle or surging at light load
P2BF1: Fuel Control System B Too Rich Bank 1

With P2BF1 the PCM has seen bank 1 too rich while fuel came through the port injectors, Ford's fuel system B. Ford flags it when the long-term value sits beyond minus 25 percent and the short-term value still takes away above 1 percent, for a 2 second window in closed loop.
Port injector on bank 1 leaking or dribbling
P2BF2: Fuel Control System B Too Lean Bank 2

P2BF2 combines two restrictions: the lean correction is on bank 2, and it only occurs in the port injection mode that Ford designates fuel system B. The Ford threshold is identical to the other trim codes of this family, more than 25 percent added by long-term trim plus over 1 percent by short-term trim for 2 seconds.
Air leak at the bank 2 intake gasket or injector O-ring
Weak low-pressure supply, usually with P2BF0 as well
P2BF3: Fuel Control System B Too Rich Bank 2

The last of the eight mode-specific trim codes: bank 2 is too rich while the port injectors (Ford fuel system B) are active. Ford triggers it when long-term trim has gone below minus 25 percent and short-term trim continues to subtract over 1 percent for 2 seconds, with the engine warm and purge disabled.
Port injector on bank 2 not sealing
Bank 2 upstream oxygen sensor biased lean
P2BF4: Exhaust Flow Control Valve A Position Circuit

Many electrically driven exhaust flaps report their actual angle back to the engine computer, either as an analog voltage or as a PWM duty cycle from a smart actuator. P2BF4 is the umbrella fault for that feedback path on valve A: the signal is missing, unusable or cannot be classed as clearly too low or too high.
Actuator connector loose, wet or corroded by road salt
Feedback or ground wire broken or heat-damaged near the exhaust
Position sensor inside the flap actuator failed
Exhaust flap no longer switched, sound stays in one mode
P2BF5: Exhaust Flow Control Valve A Position Circuit Range/Performance

Here the position signal of exhaust valve A is electrically fine, yet its value does not fit: the reported angle disagrees with the command, the end stops are not where the learned values say, or the signal jumps.
Muffler or tailpipe not fully seated in its clamps, straining the actuator
Actuator bracket bent or not welded flush to the tailpipe
Pinched actuator harness giving an unstable signal
Flap shaft binding from corrosion or soot
Exhaust mode or drive mode not available message
Exhaust tone does not change between modes
P2BF6: Exhaust Flow Control Valve A Position Circuit Low
P2BF6 means the position feedback of exhaust valve A sits below its valid range, as with a signal shorted to ground or a lost sensor supply.
PCM software misjudging the sensor (Mazda bulletin 01-004/20)
Position signal wire shorted to ground
Sensor supply open or connector not latched
Position sensor in the shutter valve failed
Master warning or check engine light on
P2BF7: Exhaust Flow Control Valve A Position Circuit High

P2BF7 is set when the position feedback of exhaust valve A rises above its plausible maximum. Electrically that points to the signal line touching the sensor reference or battery voltage, or to a lost sensor ground, which lets the input float up to its pull-up level.
Open sensor ground letting the signal float high
Signal wire shorted to reference or battery voltage
Position sensor in the valve assembly failed
Exhaust flap held in its default position
Exhaust sound no longer changes as expected
P2BF8: Exhaust Flow Control Valve B Control Circuit/Open

Valve B is the second exhaust flap; Ford's gasoline OBD summaries 2020-2024 put it on bank 2, while valve A (P26C5) serves bank 1. P2BF8 reports that the drive circuit for flap B is open or unusable. On Ford a smart driver checks the output continuously and flags it within about 5 seconds; the 2024 summary files the open circuit as subtype 13.
Broken or unplugged harness to the bank 2 flap actuator
Open circuit inside the flap actuator
Actuator not aligned after replacement or outdated PCM software (subtype 78)
One tailpipe flap no longer moves
P2BF9: Exhaust Flow Control Valve B Control Circuit Low

With P2BF9 the control line of exhaust flap B is pulled toward ground. A bare spot rubbing on the body or exhaust, or a shorted actuator, is the classic cause, which is why the code tends to appear after exhaust work or with a sagging harness.
Control wire chafed through and touching ground
Harness pinched at the actuator bracket
Internal short in the flap B actuator
Bank 2 flap stuck, uneven sound left and right
P2BFA: Exhaust Flow Control Valve B Control Circuit High

P2BFA reports too high a level on the control line of exhaust flap B. Either the wire has contact with a powered circuit, or the actuator electronics feed voltage back, so the driver cannot pull the line down when it should. Ford's 2024 OBD summary lists it as subtype 12 of the bank 2 check, monitored continuously with a 5 second window.
Control wire shorted to a powered circuit
Flap B actuator electronics feeding voltage back
Damaged tailpipe actuator harness, Ford service part 14A411
Exhaust mode warning in the cluster
Bank 2 flap in wrong position for the selected mode
P2BFB: Exhaust Flow Control Valve B Control Performance

P2BFB is the functional fault of flap B: wiring checks pass, but the flap does not reach or hold the commanded angle. Ford runs two tests on its bank 2 flap. The smart driver reports a stuck valve over its PWM feedback line, and a rationality check compares measured with commanded position, its duration depending on ambient conditions.
Flap B binding from corrosion, soot or ice
Exhaust or actuator bracket not seated correctly
Actuator not aligned or outdated PCM calibration
No audible difference between exhaust modes
P2BFC: Exhaust Flow Control Valve B Position Circuit

P2BFC covers a general fault in the feedback path that tells the engine computer where exhaust flap B is. It applies only to systems with a second position-monitored flap, such as one per tailpipe, so on single-flap vehicles it cannot occur. No manufacturer documents P2BFC in public material.
Flap B connector loose, wet or corroded
Feedback wire to flap B broken or heat-damaged
Position sensing in actuator B failed
Exhaust mode selection limited or unavailable
P2BFD: Exhaust Flow Control Valve B Position Circuit Range/Performance

P2BFD flags a position signal from exhaust flap B that is electrically valid but implausible, for instance an angle that lags the command, end points that drifted from the learned values, or a reading that wanders while the flap should rest. Ford is the public user.
Muffler and tailpipe not fully engaged in the clamps
Actuator bracket not welded flush to the tailpipe
Drive mode or exhaust mode not available message
Exhaust tone stays the same in every mode
P2BFE: Exhaust Flow Control Valve B Position Circuit Low

The position feedback of exhaust flap B reads below its lowest valid value. For an analog sensor that means a signal at or near 0 V, typically a short to ground or a missing 5 V supply; for a PWM feedback it means a duty cycle stuck near zero. No manufacturer publishes P2BFE.
Flap B signal wire shorted to ground
Sensor reference supply open or shorted
Position sensor in actuator B failed
Flap B no longer adjusted, exhaust sound unchanged
P2BFF: Exhaust Flow Control Valve B Position Circuit High

P2BFF is the upper limit fault for the position feedback of exhaust flap B. An analog signal pinned near supply voltage, or a PWM feedback stuck near 100 percent, usually comes from a lost sensor ground, a signal wire touching voltage, or water bridging the connector pins. No manufacturer documents P2BFF publicly.
Open ground at the flap B position sensor
Water or salt bridging the actuator B connector pins
Signal wire shorted to a voltage source
Exhaust mode warning, flap B held in default position
P2C00: P2C00 reports that a third fuel pressure regulator, labelled C, cannot hold the pressure the engine module asks for, although its circuit tests fine. Letters beyond A and B are only needed on fuel systems with several pressure control elements, for example engines with two high-pressure pumps or separate control of low and high pressure.
Regulator C or the pump it controls worn or sticking
Insufficient feed pressure to the controlled pump
Fuel pressure sensor drifting, so the regulator appears off target
P2C01: GM uses P2C01 in its 2023 and 2024 summary tables 23OBDG07 and 24OBDG07 for an engine control module that drives two fuel quantity control valves on the high-pressure side: P0089 covers the first, P2C01 the second, labelled regulator D. The ECM compares the filtered output of the high-pressure controller with fixed bounds.
Second high-pressure pump or its quantity control valve worn or sticking
Low tank level or weak low-pressure supply
Check engine light on after two trips
Reduced power or stumbling at full load
P2C02: Fuel Pressure Regulator D Control Circuit/Open

P2C02 is the open-circuit check on the control line of fuel pressure regulator D. In GM's tables 23OBDG07 and 24OBDG07 this is the second fuel quantity control valve of the high-pressure system, the twin of the valve watched by P0090.
Broken wire or loose terminal in the valve circuit
Corroded or unplugged connector at the high-pressure pump
Open coil in the quantity control valve
Power reduction because one pump is no longer controlled
Possible rail pressure fault codes alongside
P2C03: Fuel Pressure Regulator D Control Circuit Low

P2C03 is set when the switched low side of the regulator D control circuit has contact with ground. GM documents it in 23OBDG07 and 24OBDG07 for the second fuel quantity control valve, where it mirrors P0091 of the first valve.
Low-side wire chafed through to ground
Internal short in the quantity control valve
P2C04: Fuel Pressure Regulator D Control Circuit High

P2C04 covers the opposite electrical fault to P2C03: the switched ground end of the regulator D circuit is connected to battery voltage. In GM's 23OBDG07 and 24OBDG07 tables the circuit belongs to the second fuel quantity control valve, counterpart of P0092 on the first.
Low-side wire shorted to a supply voltage
Moisture or corrosion bridging pins in the valve connector
Faulty output stage in the engine control module
P2C05: A Camshaft Profile Actuator Position Sensor A Circuit Bank 1

Engines with switchable cam lobes use small solenoid actuators that push a pin into a groove of a sliding cam sleeve; a feedback signal confirms that the pin has moved. P2C05 is the general circuit fault for feedback A on the intake camshaft (camshaft A) of bank 1.
Engine harness chafed, sometimes with blown fuses (GM L3B bulletins)
Loose or corroded connector at the profile actuator
Open circuit inside the actuator or its feedback element
Cam lift switching and cylinder deactivation unavailable, slightly reduced power or economy
With harness damage, many other codes and possibly no start
P2C06: A Camshaft Profile Actuator Position Sensor A Range/Performance Bank 1

P2C06 deals with a feedback signal that is electrically intact but makes no sense. On GM's 2.7 L L3B, the ECM follows each shift of the intake profile actuator A on bank 1 through three Hall feedback states: extending once the reading falls below 55, extended below 45 and retracted, back at home, above 68.
Actuator pin sticking or slow because of wear or dirty oil
Worn groove or sliding sleeve on the intake camshaft
Hall feedback element in the actuator giving wrong values
Lift switching disabled, engine stays on one cam profile
Possible ticking noise from the cylinder head
P2C07: A Camshaft Profile Actuator Position Sensor A Circuit Low Bank 1

On GM's 2.7 L turbo four L3B (Silverado and Sierra 1500 from 2019) each of the four intake sliding-cam actuators reports its pin travel through a Hall element; GM calls the first one intake Hall sensor 1, which is position sensor A in J2012 terms. P2C07 means this circuit is pulled to ground.
Engine harness chafed through to ground, e.g. over the camshaft carrier cover
Internal short to ground in the profile actuator or its Hall element
Oil or water in the actuator connector bridging to ground
Check engine light on from the first drive
Engine stays on one lift profile, no cylinder deactivation, slightly higher consumption
With harness damage, possibly blown fuses and many further codes
P2C08: A Camshaft Profile Actuator Position Sensor A Circuit High Bank 1
P2C08 flags a short to voltage on position sensor A, the Hall feedback of the first intake profile actuator on bank 1.
Chafed engine harness touching a live circuit (GM bulletins PIT5677, 21-NA-149)
Internal short to supply inside the actuator or its feedback element
Faulty output stage in the ECM
No valve lift change and no cylinder deactivation
After harness damage also rough running, reduced power or no start
P2C09: A Camshaft Profile Actuator Position Sensor B Circuit Bank 1

Position sensor B belongs to the second of the four intake actuators that slide the cam sleeves on GM's L3B; GM's tables call it intake Hall sensor 2. The sensors are thus one per actuator, not one per lift step: sensors A to C get J2012 codes, while GM puts the fourth (sensor D) under its own codes P30B0 to P30B3.
Loose, unplugged or corroded connector on actuator 2
Wire broken by harness chafing on the camshaft carrier (GM L3B bulletins)
Open circuit inside the actuator or its Hall element
Check engine light on in the first trip
Lift switching and cylinder deactivation locked out
Usually no noticeable change in driving apart from fuel use
P2C0A: A Camshaft Profile Actuator Position Sensor B Range/Performance Bank 1

Here the wiring of position sensor B is intact, but its report does not match what the second intake actuator on bank 1 was told to do. On the L3B, GM follows every shift through three Hall readings: below 55 while the pin is moving out, below 45 once fully out, and above 68 when it is back home.
Pin of actuator 2 sticking or slow (wear, sludge, wrong oil)
Worn shift groove or detent on the intake cam sleeve
Hall element in the actuator reporting implausible levels
Engine kept on a fixed cam profile, no cylinder deactivation
Possible ticking from the camshaft carrier or slightly uneven idle
P2C0B: A Camshaft Profile Actuator Position Sensor B Circuit Low Bank 1
P2C0B reports that the circuit of position sensor B, the Hall feedback of the second intake actuator on bank 1, is shorted to ground.
Insulation of the sensor B line worn through against engine metal
Shorted actuator 2 or its integrated Hall element
Moisture or oil in the connector
Check engine light on straight away
Valve lift no longer changes, fuel use may rise
P2C0C: A Camshaft Profile Actuator Position Sensor B Circuit High Bank 1
A short from the sensor B line to a voltage source triggers P2C0C. The sensor is the Hall feedback built into the second intake profile actuator on bank 1.
Chafed harness bringing the line against a powered wire (GM PIT5677, 21-NA-149)
Internal short to supply in actuator 2
MIL on in the first trip
Cam profile switching and cylinder deactivation unavailable
With harness damage, further codes, rough running or no start
P2C0D: A Camshaft Profile Actuator Position Sensor C Circuit Bank 1

Position sensor C is the third of the Hall feedback elements on the intake side of bank 1; on GM's L3B it sits in intake actuator 3 and is named intake Hall sensor 3. That engine has four intake and two exhaust profile actuators, so a fourth intake feedback exists beyond the J2012 letters and GM handles it with P30B0 to P30B3.
Harness rubbed through over the camshaft carrier, wire broken (GM L3B bulletins)
Connector on actuator 3 loose, damaged or corroded
Open circuit inside actuator 3 or its Hall element
Check engine light on in the first trip
No lift switching, no cylinder deactivation
Further codes, reduced power or no start if the harness is damaged
P2C0E: A Camshaft Profile Actuator Position Sensor C Range/Performance Bank 1

P2C0E is the plausibility test for the feedback of the third intake actuator on bank 1. On the L3B, the ECM classifies each shift by the Hall signal of that actuator: extending when it drops below 55, fully extended under 45, retracted when it rises above 68 again.
Pin of actuator 3 sticking or responding late
Damaged groove or detent on the cam sleeve served by actuator 3
Old or wrong-grade oil slowing the pin
Lift switching suspended, engine runs on one profile
Occasional ticking or uneven running if a sleeve sits halfway
P2C0F: A Camshaft Profile Actuator Position Sensor C Circuit Low Bank 1
With P2C0F the ECM sees the position sensor C circuit of bank 1, the Hall feedback in the third intake actuator, connected to ground.
Sensor C line pinched or chafed against ground
Check engine light comes on during the first drive
Engine no longer switches cam profile or deactivates cylinders
P2C10: A Camshaft Profile Actuator Position Sensor C Circuit High Bank 1

P2C10 completes the sensor C group for the bank 1 intake camshaft: the feedback line of the third profile actuator is shorted to voltage. GM's L3B logic switches the output off and checks the line against controller power; 0.5 ohm or less in 4 of 5 samples, with supply above 11 V, sets a Type A code and the MIL straight away (19OBDG03D, 25OBDG03B).
Harness wear at the camshaft carrier cover shorting to a live wire (GM bulletins)
No lift change and no cylinder deactivation
With harness damage, possibly stalling or no start
P2C11: Reductant Pump A Current Too Low

P2C11 watches the electric motor of the DEF (AdBlue) pump from the other side than P214E: its driver output carries less current than a working motor should draw, which points to an open winding, a poor plug contact or a motor spinning freely or not at all.
DEF pump motor with open winding or worn brushes/electronics (pump module in the tank)
Loose, corroded or spread terminals at the pump connector
Open or high-resistance control or low-reference wire between control module and pump
Faulty output stage in the DEF control module
MIL and exhaust fluid system warning in the instrument cluster
No DEF consumption, higher NOx emissions
Speed or restart limitation if the fault persists (inducement)
P2C12: B Camshaft Profile Actuator Position Sensor A Circuit Bank 1

Camshaft B is the exhaust camshaft in J2012 terms, and P2C12 reports an open circuit in the feedback of its first profile actuator on bank 1. GM's 2.7 L turbo L3B (Silverado and Sierra 1500 from model year 2019) is the documented user: its tables call this element exhaust Hall sensor 1.
Engine harness worn through where it crosses the camshaft carrier cover (GM PIT5677, 21-NA-149)
Connector on exhaust actuator 1 not latched or corroded
Open Hall element inside the exhaust actuator
Check engine light from the first trip
Exhaust cam profile no longer switched, fuel economy mode unavailable
With harness damage, several other engine codes at the same time
P2C13: B Camshaft Profile Actuator Position Sensor A Range/Performance Bank 1

P2C13 is the rationality test for the first exhaust profile actuator's feedback on bank 1, so the wiring is not in question. GM's L3B tracks every exhaust shift through exhaust Hall sensor 1: the reading must drop below 55 as the pin starts to fire, below 45 when it is fully out and climb above 68 once the pin is home again.
Pin of exhaust actuator 1 slow or sticking (sludge, overdue oil change, wrong oil grade)
Worn shift groove or weak detent on the exhaust cam sleeve
Hall element in actuator 1 delivering drifting levels
Exhaust lift locked on one profile, cylinder deactivation inactive
Occasional clicking from the top of the engine
P2C14: B Camshaft Profile Actuator Position Sensor A Circuit Low Bank 1
With P2C14 the ECM reports that the line of exhaust position sensor A on bank 1 is grounded.
Signal wire of exhaust sensor A rubbed bare against the head or a bracket
Internal short to ground in exhaust actuator 1
Engine oil wicked into the actuator plug
No exhaust lift change, slightly higher consumption under light load
P2C15: B Camshaft Profile Actuator Position Sensor A Circuit High Bank 1
P2C15 stands for a short to voltage on the exhaust position sensor A circuit, bank 1, i.e. the Hall feedback of GM's first exhaust actuator on the L3B four.
Chafed harness letting the sensor line touch a supply wire (GM PIT5677, 21-NA-149)
Short to supply inside exhaust actuator 1
Defective output stage in the ECM
Together with harness damage, blown fuses, no start or reduced power possible
P2C16: B Camshaft Profile Actuator Position Sensor B Circuit Bank 1
P2C16 is the open-circuit fault of position sensor B on the bank 1 exhaust camshaft.
Plug on exhaust actuator 2 pulled off or not locked after engine work
Wire broken where the harness rubs at the camshaft carrier (GM L3B bulletins)
Open circuit in the Hall element of actuator 2
Check engine light in the first trip
Exhaust lift switching and economy modes blocked
P2C17: B Camshaft Profile Actuator Position Sensor B Range/Performance Bank 1

P2C17 flags implausible feedback from exhaust Hall sensor 2, the position sensor of the second exhaust profile actuator on bank 1 of GM's L3B. The electrical circuit tests pass, yet the shift pattern is wrong: after a command GM expects the reading to pass below 55 (pin extending), below 45 (pin fully out) and back above 68 (pin retracted).
Pin of exhaust actuator 2 binding because of deposits or degraded oil
Exhaust cam sleeve not snapping into its detent, worn groove
Low or aerated engine oil slowing the shift
Engine runs on a fixed exhaust profile, no cylinder deactivation
Possibly a light tapping noise from the valve train
P2C18: B Camshaft Profile Actuator Position Sensor B Circuit Low Bank 1
A ground short in the position sensor B line on the bank 1 exhaust side sets P2C18. On GM's L3B this is the feedback wire of exhaust actuator 2.
Harness insulation damaged at the camshaft carrier cover or under the air cleaner housing
Exhaust actuator 2 shorted internally to ground
Water or oil bridging contacts in the plug
MIL comes on in the first trip
Exhaust profile no longer changes, small rise in fuel use
P2C19: B Camshaft Profile Actuator Position Sensor B Circuit High Bank 1
P2C19 closes the sensor B group on the exhaust camshaft of bank 1: the feedback circuit of GM's exhaust Hall sensor 2 is shorted to a voltage source.
Harness chafed at generator bracket or coil spring stud, line touching a live wire (GM 21-NA-149)
Exhaust actuator 2 shorted internally to supply
MIL on in the first drive
With extensive harness damage, stalling, no crank or blown fuses
P2C1A: B Camshaft Profile Actuator Position Sensor C Circuit Bank 1
P2C1A would report an open circuit in a third position feedback on the bank 1 exhaust camshaft. No manufacturer documents this code publicly.
Disconnected or corroded plug at the third exhaust actuator
Broken feedback wire in the engine harness
Internal open in the position sensor
Exhaust cam profile switching locked out
P2C1B: B Camshaft Profile Actuator Position Sensor C Range/Performance Bank 1

Range/Performance for exhaust position sensor C, bank 1: the signal is electrically fine but does not match the commanded pin movement of a third exhaust profile actuator. There is no public manufacturer documentation for P2C1B.
Actuator pin sticking or reacting too slowly
Sludge or wrong oil viscosity in the valve train
Exhaust lift held on one profile, possibly ticking from the head
P2C1C: B Camshaft Profile Actuator Position Sensor C Circuit Low Bank 1

P2C1C is reserved for a circuit-low fault, typically a short to ground, in the feedback of exhaust position sensor C on bank 1. It is not used in any public manufacturer documentation. GM's L3B tables show how its siblings work: P2C14 and P2C18 compare the line against ground with the driver on and declare a short at 0.5 ohm or less in four of five samples.
Sensor C wire chafed through to ground
No change of exhaust cam profile
P2C1D: B Camshaft Profile Actuator Position Sensor C Circuit High Bank 1
P2C1D, the circuit-high code for exhaust position sensor C on bank 1, covers a feedback line pulled towards supply voltage, usually by a short to power. No carmaker publishes a use for it.
Sensor C line rubbing against a powered wire
Internal short to supply in the actuator
Faulty driver stage in the ECM
P2C1E: Cold Start Fuel Pressure Regulator A Performance

Direct-injection petrol engines often run a catalyst-heating mode after a cold start, with split injections that need tightly held rail pressure. P2C1E says regulator A, which meters the high-pressure pump, ran out of authority in that phase.
Worn high-pressure pump that needs full stroke to reach the target
Insufficient feed pressure from the in-tank pump or a clogged filter
Sticking quantity control valve on the high-pressure pump
Worn pump drive cam or follower reducing effective stroke
MIL after two cold starts with the fault
Rough idle or hesitation in the first minute after a cold start
Often no noticeable symptom once warm
P2C1F: Cold Start Fuel Pressure Regulator A Exceeded Control Limits - Pressure Too Low

P2C1F is the underpressure half of GM's cold-start fuel pressure check on direct-injection petrol engines: while the catalyst is being heated, measured rail pressure lags the target by more than a calibrated margin.
High-pressure pump with worn plunger or sticking control valve delivering too little
Low feed pressure from in-tank pump, filter or pressure regulator
Leaking or sticking injector bleeding off rail pressure
Rail pressure sensor reading too low
MIL after a single faulty cold start
Long cranking, rough running or stalling when cold
Reduced power possible if pressure stays low
P2C20: Cold Start Fuel Pressure Regulator A Exceeded Control Limits - Pressure Too High
P2C20 mirrors P2C1F: during catalyst heating after a cold start the rail pressure overshoots its setpoint because the high-pressure pump supplies more fuel than requested or cannot be throttled back.
Quantity control valve on the high-pressure pump stuck in the delivering position
Wiring or connector fault in the control valve drive circuit
Rail pressure sensor drifting so the controller overshoots
Engine control software that needs an update
MIL after one faulty cold start
Harsh, loud cold idle or ticking injectors
Possible reduced power or rich running smell
P2C21: Engine Oil Temperature Sensor A/B Correlation
Engines with two oil temperature sensors can check them against each other; P2C21 means sensors A and B disagree although each signal is electrically valid.
One oil temperature sensor drifting or stuck within its range
Corroded or loose contacts adding resistance on one sensor
Low oil level leaving one sensor partly uncovered
Block or oil heater use skewing the cold-start comparison
Oil life or oil temperature display may be wrong
P2C22: Exhaust Heat Exchanger Exhaust Bypass Valve A Position Sensor Circuit

Full hybrids with exhaust heat recovery pass hot exhaust through a coolant heat exchanger after a cold start and divert it around the exchanger with flap A once enough heat has been gathered. A sensor in the flap actuator reports the flap angle to the engine module.
Water intrusion into the heat exchanger or its actuator (Ford Maverick hybrid)
Failed bypass valve actuator with integrated position sensor
Corroded or loose connector at the actuator under the vehicle
Harness near the exhaust chafed or heat-damaged
Slower engine warm-up and weaker cabin heating in cold weather
Engine of the hybrid runs longer before it may shut off
P2C23: Exhaust Heat Exchanger Exhaust Bypass Valve A Position Sensor Performance

P2C23 means the flap position reported for exhaust heat exchanger bypass valve A is electrically valid but does not make sense – for example it disagrees with the command or with how the coolant behind the exchanger warms up. A Ford patent shows that such plausibility can be judged from temperatures.
Water or corrosion in the connectors of exhaust coolant temperature sensors 3/4 (Ford)
Worn, sticking or frozen bypass actuator
Flap or linkage in the heat exchanger binding
Check engine light, often after frost
P2C24: Exhaust Heat Exchanger Exhaust Bypass Valve A Position Sensor Circuit Low

P2C24 is stored when the position signal of exhaust heat exchanger bypass flap A drops below its permitted band. Typical reasons are a signal wire shorted to ground, an open sensor supply or an actuator whose sensor has failed low.
Position signal wire shorted to ground near the exhaust
Open or missing 5 V supply to the position sensor
Position sensor inside the actuator failed low
Heat recovery switched off, slower warm-up
P2C25: Exhaust Heat Exchanger Exhaust Bypass Valve A Position Sensor Circuit High

P2C25 is the counterpart of P2C24: the feedback from the position sensor of exhaust heat exchanger bypass flap A sits above the highest value a working sensor can deliver. This usually points to a signal line touching a voltage source, an interrupted sensor ground or an internal sensor fault that pulls the output toward the reference.
Position signal wire shorted to a voltage source
Open ground circuit of the position sensor
Position sensor in the actuator failed high
Cabin heater slow to warm up in winter
P2C26: Fuel Injector Group B Supply Sense Circuit

Many engines feed their injectors in groups from a switched supply, for example through an injector relay or a high-side driver. A separate sense line lets the engine module read back whether voltage really arrives at group B.
Open or high-resistance sense wire between injector supply and module
Injector relay or its socket making poor contact
Corroded connector in the injector supply harness
Faulty sense input inside the engine control module
Possible misfire or rough running on the cylinders of group B
Hard starting if the group is switched off
P2C27: Fuel Injector Group B Supply Sense Circuit Low

P2C27 reports that the voltage read back on the supply sense line of injector group B is too low while the module expects the group to be powered. In practice the feed never reaches the injectors – a blown fuse, a relay that does not close, a broken supply wire or a grounded feed – or only the sense wire itself is grounded.
Blown fuse in the injector group B supply
Injector relay not closing or burnt contacts
Supply or sense wire shorted to ground
Internally shorted injector pulling the group supply down
Misfire on several cylinders, rough idle
Clearly reduced power or engine will not start
P2C28: Fuel Injector Group B Supply Sense Circuit High

P2C28 is set when the sense line of the injector group B supply shows more voltage than allowed – either above the upper limit while the group is switched on, or voltage present while the module has switched the group off.
Sense or supply wire shorted to battery voltage
Excessive system voltage from the charging system
Internal fault of the supply switch in the engine control module
Often no noticeable change in running
Battery drain if the relay stays closed after switch-off
P2C29: Bypass valve B is the compressor recirculation valve of the second charger – the later one in series layouts, the bank 2 unit on parallel twin-turbo engines. It is not the wastegate. P2C29 means a position-controlled valve no longer follows its target and stays where it is. No manufacturer documents P2C29 publicly.
Oil or carbon deposits binding the valve flap or piston
Worn gears or motor in the electric actuator
Bent shaft or damaged housing of the valve
Fluttering compressor noise when lifting off
P2C2A: Turbocharger/Supercharger Bypass Valve B Position Sensor Circuit/Open

P2C2A covers an open or otherwise unreadable position feedback from compressor bypass valve B, the electrically positioned recirculation valve of the second charger. Without a valid feedback the engine module cannot confirm how far the valve has opened, which an Achates Power patent names as the reason such sensors are monitored.
Unplugged, loose or corroded connector at valve B
Broken signal, reference or ground wire of the sensor
Internal open in the position sensor of the actuator
P2C2B: Turbocharger/Supercharger Bypass Valve B Position Sensor Circuit Low

With P2C2B the position signal of compressor bypass valve B lies below the lowest value a healthy sensor delivers. Likely reasons are a signal wire grounded against the engine, an open 5 V reference or a sensor that has failed low. For valve B no public manufacturer data exist.
Signal wire of the position sensor shorted to ground
Missing 5 V reference at the sensor
Position sensor in the valve actuator failed low
P2C2C: Turbocharger/Supercharger Bypass Valve B Position Sensor Circuit High

P2C2C flags a position signal from compressor bypass valve B that rises above the plausible top of its range, close to the sensor reference. A signal line touching 5 V or battery voltage, a broken ground wire or a defect inside the sensor are the typical findings. No manufacturer publishes P2C2C.
Signal wire shorted to reference or battery voltage
Open ground of the position sensor
Boost limited by the engine module
P2C2D: Turbocharger/Supercharger Bypass Valve B Position Exceeded Learning Limit

Electrically positioned compressor bypass valves have their end stops relearned regularly so that the sensor reading can be converted into a true opening. P2C2D means that for valve B, belonging to the second charger, a learned stop came out beyond the allowed window. No manufacturer documents the B-side code.
Carbon or oil deposits preventing the valve from reaching its stop
Worn actuator gear or loose sensor magnet
Valve replaced without relearn or with incorrect part
Check engine light after a key-off
Boost control less precise, possible surge noise
P2C2E: Turbocharger/Supercharger Bypass Valve B Supply Voltage Low

P2C2E concerns the power stage of compressor bypass valve B, not its position signal. Such valves are moved by a small DC motor driven through an H-bridge, and the bridge reports when its own supply sags below a safe level. No manufacturer documents the B-side code publicly.
Weak battery or voltage drop on the module feed
Poor ground or corroded relay contacts in the supply
Internal fault of the H-bridge driver
Valve no longer responds, boost reduced
Often accompanied by other low-voltage codes
P2C2F: Turbocharger/Supercharger Bypass Valve B Driver Current/Temperature Too High

P2C2F is stored when the output stage driving compressor bypass valve B signals excessive current or overheating. The motor driver protects itself by limiting current and finally switching off, and reports this to the engine module.
Jammed valve forcing the motor to stall against its stop
Shorted winding in the valve actuator motor
Motor leads shorted to each other or to ground
Overheated or faulty driver inside the engine module
P2C30: Ignition Coil Primary Circuit Fuse A
On engines whose ignition coils are fed through more than one fuse, the module checks each fuse so that it notices when a whole group of coils loses power. P2C30 points to fuse A.
Ignition system control module software (Stellantis 3.0L Hurricane)
Fuse A blown by a shorted ignition coil or supply wire
Reduced power while cylinders are shut off
P2C31: Ignition Coil Primary Circuit Fuse B
P2C31 is the second of two fuse checks in the coil primary supply: the fuse B group of coils has lost voltage, or the module believes so.
Ignition system control module calibration (Stellantis 3.0L Hurricane)
Shorted ignition coil in group B blowing the fuse
Chafed coil feed wire shorting to ground
P2C32: A crankcase pressure sensor tells the engine module how the pressure in the crankcase ventilation compares with ambient, mainly so it can detect a disconnected or leaking breather line. P2C32 is the general circuit fault of sensor B: its signal is missing or cannot be decoded at all, without saying high or low.
Unplugged, loose or corroded sensor connector
Open or chafed wire between sensor and engine module
Engine module input or software fault
Crankcase ventilation leak check not available
P2C33: Crankcase Pressure Sensor B Circuit Range/Performance

P2C33 means crankcase pressure sensor B delivers a signal inside its electrical limits that the engine module finds implausible, such as an offset from ambient pressure with the engine stopped or values a running engine cannot produce. Two bulletin families name it.
Engine control software needing an update (Alfa Romeo and Maserati V6/V8)
Sensor offset or drift, partly due to moisture or ice in the port
Faulty blow-by (PCV) valve producing abnormal crankcase pressure
Harness or pin resistance shifting the signal
MIL on, often together with other PCM codes
Limp-in mode possible on affected Alfa Romeo models
P2C34: Crankcase Pressure Sensor B Circuit Low

Circuit Low means the voltage from crankcase pressure sensor B stays under the lowest value the sensor can deliver, typically because the 5 V reference is missing, the signal wire is shorted to ground or the sensor itself has failed.
5 V reference open or shorted to ground
Signal wire shorted to ground or chafed insulation
Crankcase pressure sensor B internally failed
Bent or corroded pins at sensor or ECM
Other sensors on the same 5 V supply may report faults too
P2C35: Crankcase Pressure Sensor B Circuit High

P2C35 is set when the signal of crankcase pressure sensor B sits above the highest voltage the sensor can legitimately produce. That usually means an interrupted signal wire pulled up inside the module, a broken sensor ground, or a short from the signal to the 5 V supply or to battery voltage.
Open signal wire or unplugged connector
Signal shorted to 5 V reference or battery voltage
Faulty sensor or outdated engine control software
P2C36: Crankcase Pressure Sensor B Circuit Intermittent/Erratic

P2C36 covers a crankcase pressure sensor B signal that drops out briefly or jumps faster than real crankcase pressure can change, while staying mostly inside its electrical range. That pattern points to a contact that opens for moments, a wire chafing on the engine, moisture in the plug or a sensor failing internally.
Loose or fretting contacts at the sensor or an intermediate connector
Wire rubbing on engine parts and shorting briefly
Moisture or oil in the connector
MIL that may come and go
Erratic crankcase pressure value in live data
P2C37: Cold Start Engine Coolant Pump Performance

Engines with a switchable or electric main coolant pump often keep the coolant still, or nearly so, right after a cold start so the cylinder head and catalyst warm up sooner. P2C37 reports that the pump did not behave as commanded during this cold-start phase, for example running when it should rest or failing to start when flow is requested.
Switchable pump stuck engaged or disengaged (clutch, shroud or valve actuator)
Electric coolant pump with failing motor or electronics
Air in the system or low coolant level
Coolant or head temperature sensor reading wrong and misleading the check
Slow warm-up and weak cabin heat, or rising temperature when the pump stays off
Overheating warning possible in severe cases
P2C38: Cylinder Head Temperature Sensor B Circuit

A cylinder head temperature sensor is an NTC thermistor seated in the head metal that tells the module how hot the engine really is, even without coolant. P2C38 is the general circuit fault of a second such sensor, B: the signal is open, shorted or otherwise unusable, without separating low from high (P2C3A/P2C3B do that, P2C39 judges plausibility).
PCM software causing false faults (Ford 2025 Explorer/Aviator, TSB 24-2393)
Loose or corroded connector at the head sensor
Heat-damaged or chafed wiring near the cylinder head
Fail-safe cooling mode with reduced power possible
Temperature warning even though coolant level and fan are fine
P2C39: Cylinder Head Temperature Sensor B Range/Performance

P2C39 flags a second cylinder head temperature sensor, B, whose voltage is electrically valid but whose reading does not fit the engine's state, for instance a value that jumps, lags or disagrees with other temperature inputs.
PCM calibration misjudging sensor B (Ford EcoBoost bulletins, cured by reprogramming)
Sensor B drifted or responding slowly
Sensor not seated properly in the head or corroded terminals
Genuine local overheating from low coolant or trapped air
Engine over-temperature warning although the gauge and coolant level look normal
Check engine light, often together with P1299 or P1285
Reduced power while the fail-safe cooling strategy is active
P2C3A: Cylinder Head Temperature Sensor B Circuit Low

P2C3A reports that the signal of cylinder head temperature sensor B sits below the lowest voltage the module accepts. Because these sensors are NTC thermistors, a very low voltage would stand for an impossibly hot head, so the usual reasons are a signal wire shorted to ground, water inside the plug or a sensor with an internal short.
Signal wire of sensor B chafed through to ground
Moisture or coolant in the sensor connector
Internal short in the thermistor of sensor B
Overheat warning or very high head temperature in live data on a cold engine
Cooling fans running at full speed without reason
Check engine light, possibly reduced engine power
P2C3B: Cylinder Head Temperature Sensor B Circuit High

With P2C3B the voltage from cylinder head temperature sensor B stays above the valid ceiling, which the module would have to read as a head far colder than any real engine. An interrupted signal wire, a lost sensor ground, a terminal that has backed out of the plug or a thermistor cracked by heat cycling are the typical finds.
Open signal wire or terminal pushed out of the connector
Sensor return (ground) circuit open or high resistance
Thermistor of sensor B broken internally
Live data shows head temperature B at the lowest possible value
Fans run more often, idle and warm-up behaviour unusual
P2C3C: Cylinder Head Temperature Sensor B Circuit Intermittent/Erratic

P2C3C is stored when the head temperature signal of sensor B drops out briefly or jumps in steps that no mass of hot metal could follow, while the samples on their own may still lie within the valid window.
Loose or spread terminal in the sensor B connector
Harness rubbing on engine parts and shorting only at times
Check engine light that comes and goes
Jumping head temperature B in live data
Occasional fan runs or brief warnings without real overheating
P2C3D: Cylinder Head Temperature Sensor A/B Correlation

An engine with two head temperature sensors can check one against the other: after a long soak both should read close to each other and to coolant temperature, and while running their gap should stay inside an expected band. P2C3D means sensors A and B disagree beyond that limit although neither circuit shows a fault.
One of the two sensors has drifted out of tolerance
Contact resistance in one sensor circuit shifting its reading
Engine control software judging the pair too tightly
