Real temperature difference from air pocket or poor flow in one head area
Check engine light without driveability complaints
Clearly different values for head temperature A and B after a cold start
P2C3E: P2C3E reports a fault on the control circuit of a fourth fan output: the driver in the engine or fan control module sees an open line, a missing load or an error it cannot sort into low or high. What counts as fan 4 is up to the maker.
Broken wire or loose connector in the fan 4 control line
Fan 4 relay coil open or relay missing
Blown fuse feeding the relay or fan module
Output driver in the control module defective
One fan or fan stage does not run when commanded
Rising temperature at idle or in traffic, weaker A/C at standstill
P2C3F: With P2C3F the module senses the control line of fan output 4 at too low a level, which in practice means a short to ground or, with a driver that switches to ground, a line held there by a fault downstream.
Fan 4 control wire chafed through to body or engine ground
Shorted relay coil or fan module input
Water in the fan connector near the radiator
Fan 4 runs constantly or not at all
P2C40: P2C40 states that fan control output 4 is held at too high a level: the line has contact with battery voltage, or the driver cannot pull it down when it should.
Fan 4 control wire in contact with a battery-voltage circuit
Relay or fan module input failed internally
Moisture bridging pins in the connector
Fan 4 runs constantly, sometimes after switch-off
P2C41: P2C41 judges the outcome rather than the wiring: fan 3 is commanded on and its circuit checks out (otherwise P0482, P0695 or P0696 would appear), yet the controller sees little or no response, usually through speed feedback from a fan module or a missing current draw. No manufacturer publicly documents this code.
Fan blades blocked by dirt, stones or leaves
Worn or seized fan motor, corrosion from moisture
Fan control module does not drive the motor
Weak power or ground supply to the fan
Engine temperature climbs in traffic or under heavy load
Warning lamp or fan failure message
P2C42: P2C42 reports that the fourth fan output does not deliver what is asked of it: the fan stays still or reaches far too little speed while its control line shows no electrical fault (those would be P2C3E to P2C40). No manufacturer publicly documents P2C42.
Fan jammed by debris or a damaged shroud
Integrated fan electronics or fan module failed
Temperature warning or reduced power under high load
Fan 4 does not turn when activated with a scan tool
Grinding noise before the fan stops
P2C43: Some vehicles split their 12 V system with a switch so that a heavy starter load, typically an automatic restart, cannot pull the supply of control units and displays down. A Ford patent on start-stop cars puts that dip at roughly 5 to 7 V without such separation.
Open control wire or loose connector at the isolator
Isolator relay coil or electronic switch failed
Poor ground connection of the isolator circuit
Output driver in the control module defective
Warning lamp or powertrain fault indicator on
Automatic stop-start no longer stops the engine
Radio or displays may reboot during engine starts
P2C44: Battery Isolation/Voltage Stabilization Control Circuit Performance

P2C44 means the isolation or voltage stabilization stage is wired and commanded, yet its behaviour does not match what the module expects. Ford is the one maker with published cases: 2021–2022 F-150 trucks with the 3.5 L PowerBoost hybrid and 10R80 MHT gearbox carry a second 12 V battery that an auxiliary battery isolator separates from the main battery.
Auxiliary battery isolator faulty (Ford replaces it per bulletin 23-2031)
Poor ground in the isolator circuit (Ford GD132, G102, C146, C1989C)
Weak or failing auxiliary 12 V battery
P2C45: Battery Isolation/Voltage Stabilization Control Circuit Low

P2C45 is stored when the line that commands the battery isolation or voltage stabilization switch reads lower than its commanded state allows, the classic picture of a short to ground or, with a high-side driver, an open coil pulling the sense voltage down.
Control wire chafed through and shorted to ground
Corroded or water-damaged connector near the battery
Possible blown fuse in the control circuit
P2C46: Battery Isolation/Voltage Stabilization Control Circuit High

P2C46 is the opposite of P2C45: the control line of the battery isolation or voltage stabilization switch sits higher than expected, which points to a short to battery voltage, or, on a low-side driven relay, to an open circuit that leaves the sense input floating high.
Control wire shorted to battery positive
Open circuit with low-side driver (input pulled high)
Control module input or driver fault
Screens or radio may reset when the engine restarts
P2C47: Battery Isolation/Voltage Stabilization Control Circuit Intermittent
With P2C47 the module saw the command line of the isolation or stabilization stage drop out and come back, rather than stay permanently open or shorted.
Loose or spread terminal in the isolator connector
Ground strap or ground point with intermittent contact
Cracked solder joint inside the isolator
P2C48: Coolant Pump C Control Circuit Performance/Stuck Off
P2C48 is a performance check on coolant pump C: the pump is driven, but what it draws or delivers does not match the request.
Low coolant or air in the low-temperature loop, e.g. from a chafed hose (GM 21-NA-265)
Worn, sluggish or partly blocked pump
Fault in the pump's integrated motor electronics
Weak supply from the powertrain relay or poor ground
Check engine light after two trips
Higher intake air or fuel temperature, possibly reduced power
P2C49: Coolant Pump D Control Circuit Performance/Stuck Off

P2C49 is the functional check of coolant pump D: the command arrives and the control line is intact, but the pump does not run or does not reach the effect the module expects. No manufacturer publicly documents P2C49.
Air in the loop or low coolant after a leak or repair
High resistance in supply, ground or control wiring
Control module software judging the pump wrongly
Higher temperature in the circuit served by pump D
Possible power reduction to protect components
P2C4A: The clutch actuator position sensor reports how far the release mechanism of an automated or partly automated clutch has travelled, taken at the slave cylinder or inside the actuator rather than at the pedal. Typical designs are Hall sensors reading a magnet on the clutch piston. P2C4A is the general circuit fault of this sensor.
Damaged or corroded sensor connector near the gearbox
Open supply, signal or ground wire
Position sensor on slave cylinder or actuator failed
Control module fault (Ford internal check P166F)
Automated clutch may refuse to engage or drive off
P2C4B: Clutch Actuator Position Sensor Circuit Range/Performance

P2C4B flags a clutch actuator position signal that is electrically valid but does not fit the situation, for example a reading that does not move when the actuator is commanded, or end stops that lie outside the learned window.

Sensor drift or loose sensor mounting

P2C4C means the signal of the clutch actuator position sensor has fallen below its valid band.

P2C4D: Clutch Actuator Position Sensor Circuit High

P2C4D is set when the clutch actuator position signal rises above its upper limit. Ford lists it beside P2C4C in its 2020–2023 and 2024 gasoline OBD summaries: continuous monitoring, under one second to detect, and in 2024 reported as P2C4A with failure type 12. Ford does not state whether the MIL comes on.
Signal wire shorted to a supply voltage
P2C4E: Clutch Actuator Position Sensor Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P2C4E covers a clutch actuator position signal that jumps, drops out briefly or changes faster than the mechanism could physically move.

Wiring chafed against the gearbox housing
Sensor or magnet loose, changing the air gap
P2C4F: P2C4F concerns the actuator itself, the electric motor or electro-hydraulic unit that opens and closes an automated clutch, rather than its position sensor. The code means the actuator does not reach or hold the commanded position within the expected time or effort.

Air or leak in the clutch hydraulics

P2C50: Clutch Pedal Position Sensor A/Clutch Actuator Position Sensor Correlation

P2C50 compares two views of the same clutch: what the pedal sensor A says the driver is doing and what the sensor at the release side says the clutch is actually doing. In a hydraulic system both move together, so a lasting gap points to a fault in one sensor or in the hydraulics between them.

P2C51: Saddle tanks have two chambers and therefore two level senders, A and B; the engine module combines both resistances into one fuel level. GM's bulletin PI0926 for the 2011–2013 Equinox and Terrain shows this layout, with each sender reading about 40 Ω when full. P2C51 means the two senders disagree more than the tank design allows.

Jet pump not transferring fuel between the tank halves
Corroded connector adding resistance on one sender
Wrong or misassembled sender after tank work

P2C52: Cylinder 1 Fuel Injector B Offset Learning At Min Limit

Engines with two injectors per cylinder call the second one injector B; with port plus direct injection that is usually one of the two sets, but which one is the maker's choice. For every B injector the engine control learns an offset, a correction for the dead time between the electrical command and the start of real fuel flow.

Possibly fuel smell or higher consumption

P2C53 is the opposite end of the injector B offset learn on cylinder 1: the engine control has lengthened the command as far as it may, and the cylinder still gets less fuel than requested. Ford patents describe the offset as the time the pintle and the driver circuit need before fuel moves, so a sticky or varnished valve or a weak supply raises it.
Engine software (Volvo TJ 36016: update, then reset injector adaptations in VIDA)

P2C62: O2 Sensor Pumping Current Trim Circuit/Open Bank 1 Sensor 3

P2C62 points to an open trim circuit at the third oxygen probe of bank 1. Wide-band probes such as Bosch's LSU 4.9 carry a trimming resistor in the connector on a pin of its own (RT/IA) that sets each probe's characteristic; the engine module reads it to scale the pump current, so with the lead broken the signal still moves but with the wrong gain.

Moisture or corrosion in the connector of the rear probe

Check engine light, possibly limp mode
Fault may disappear after the engine has cooled down
P2C7F: Turbocharger Turbine Inlet Valve Position Sensor Exceeded Learning Limit
P2C7F means the turbine inlet valve's position sensor has delivered an end-stop value outside the window the module accepts during its learning routine.
Carbon deposits preventing the valve from reaching its end stop
Replaced actuator or turbocharger without a completed learn procedure
Bent or worn linkage shifting the end positions
Position sensor or its magnet shifted on the shaft
Inconsistent boost during changeover between turbine paths
P2C80: P2C80 says the secondary air pump on bank 1 is turning faster than it should. Newer designs use a brushless motor whose speed is measured: an FCA patent describes a pump with a Hall sensor and target wheel so the controller can infer the air mass delivered from the revolutions and adjust pump speed.
Outlet hose detached or split so the pump runs without back-pressure
Damaged impeller or loose coupling between motor and impeller
Faulty speed signal (Hall sensor) or its wiring
Defective control electronics inside the pump
Louder or higher-pitched pump noise after a cold start
Secondary air readiness not completed, emissions test may fail
P2C81: P2C81 reports that the secondary air pump on bank 1 has become too hot. The pump is only meant to run for a short time after a cold start, until the catalyst lights off, as Hella describes; a pump with integrated electronics can sense its own temperature and protect its motor.
Pump running too long (many short cold starts, relay stuck on)
Clogged intake filter or blocked outlet path
Worn bearings or debris increasing friction
Moisture or condensate inside the pump
Pump stops early or does not run on the next cold start
Hot smell or grinding noise from the pump
P2C82: AIR System Pump Supply Voltage Circuit Bank 1

P2C82 points to a fault in the supply voltage circuit of the bank 1 secondary air pump. Conventional pumps are switched on by a relay; pumps with their own electronics, like the brushless design in an FCA patent, receive a feed and can judge whether the voltage arriving there is plausible.
Blown high-current fuse for the pump
Relay with burnt or sticking contacts
Damaged feed or ground wire to the pump
No pump noise for the first minute after a cold start
P2C83: Cold Start Shift Time Too Short

California requires every part of an emission-reducing cold-start routine to be checked while it is active and its faults to be stored apart from ordinary ones. Many automatics take part in that strategy: a warm-up gearshift mode lets the engine rev further before each upshift so engine and catalyst heat faster, as a ZF patent describes.
Clutch apply pressure too high while the fluid is cold
Fill or pressure adaptation for cold fluid outside its target, e.g. after a reset or software fault
Transmission fluid temperature signal implausible, so the wrong cold-start values are used
Pressure control solenoid sticking or overshooting
Harsh or jerky first upshifts after a cold start
Shifting returns to normal once the gearbox is warm
P2C84: Cold Start Shift Time Too Long

P2C84 is the opposite verdict to P2C83: a shift observed during the active cold-start phase took longer than its calibrated limit. Cold transmission fluid is thick, so clutches fill slowly and the engine can rev up between gears; a gearbox module normally compensates with temperature-dependent pressure and fill adaptation.
Transmission fluid level low or wrong fluid specification
Shift valve or solenoid sticking when cold
Worn clutch plates needing more fill volume
Fluid temperature signal faulty, so cold-start shift values are misapplied
Slow, slipping upshifts with engine flare after a cold start
Possible emergency program with a fixed gear
P2C85: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage External Isolation Fault

P2C85 means the isolation monitor has found a fault-level loss of insulation on the vehicle side of the battery, in cables or components connected through the contactors. Mercedes-Benz uses the code in the battery management system with the text vehicle-side insulation fault.
Insulation breakdown in the high-voltage A/C compressor
Moisture in the high-voltage PTC heater or its connector
Chafed or crushed high-voltage cable touching the body
Coolant or water inside inverter, motor or charger
Red high-voltage or battery warning, do not restart message
Vehicle cannot be restarted after switching off
Electric heater or A/C not working
P2C86: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Internal Isolation Warning

P2C86 is an early warning that the insulation inside the traction battery, between cells, busbars or module electronics and the pack housing, is dropping but has not yet reached the fault limit. The full internal fault is P0E74. No manufacturer documents P2C86 publicly.
Coolant leaking inside the battery pack
Condensation or water ingress through a failed pack seal or vent
Damaged cell sensing or busbar insulation inside the pack
Isolation measurement in the battery controller drifting
Battery or high-voltage service message, often without immediate limits
Charging may be refused if the value keeps falling
P2C87: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage External Isolation Warning

P2C87 is the warning stage for weakening insulation outside the battery, on the vehicle-side high-voltage network. Many systems use two limits; Volkswagen's ID.4, for example, shows a yellow lamp below 510 kOhm and a red one below 90 kOhm.
Moisture or corrosion in an external HV component (compressor, heater, charger)
Insulation fault inside the on-board charger or DC/DC converter
Reduced power or no gear engagement on some models
Intermittent, often after rain or washing
P2C88: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage System Isolation Warning

P2C88 is the warning counterpart to P0AA6: the isolation resistance of the high-voltage system as a whole has fallen below a first limit without the monitor yet being able to say whether the battery or the vehicle side is to blame.
Moisture in a high-voltage component that is only switched in at times (heater, compressor)
Gradual insulation aging in cables or connectors
Beginning insulation loss inside the battery pack
High-voltage warning message, sometimes towing not allowed notice
Electric heater stays cold if it is the leaking part
P2C89: Hybrid/EV Battery System Precharge Current Too High

Before the main contactors close, the DC link capacitors are charged through a current-limiting path. P2C89 is stored when the current in that phase exceeds its limit, which points to a short or an unexpected load on the high-voltage bus, a precharge resistor that is bypassed, or a measurement error.
Battery management or DC/DC converter software misjudging the precharge
Short or active load on the high-voltage bus during precharge
Precharge resistor shorted or main contactor closing early
Pack current sensor reading too high
MIL and high-voltage system warning at start-up
Electric drive or charging unavailable, engine-only on plug-in hybrids
P2C8A: Hybrid/EV Battery Interface Control Module A Performance

Battery interface control modules are the satellite boards in the traction battery that measure cell voltages and temperatures and report them to the battery energy control module. P2C8A says module A is reachable but not working properly.
Battery energy control module software or calibration error
Supply dip at the cell monitoring module (12 V battery weak, wake-up issue)
Damaged communication or supply harness inside the battery pack
MIL or Service High Voltage message
Many battery communication codes stored at the same time
P2C8B: Hybrid/EV Battery Interface Control Module B Performance

P2C8B is the performance fault for the second battery interface control module, B. In GM's Ultium bulletins it never appears alone: PIP6021 applies only if P2C8B is stored together with P2C8A and the module communication codes U3577 to U35AF, and the 2025-26 versions of PIP6081 extend it through U3584 and add U2BAA-U2BB1.
BECM software anomaly affecting several monitoring modules at once
Weak 12 V battery causing a brownout of the monitoring modules
Connector or harness fault at interface module B
P2C8C: DC/DC Converter Temperature Sensor D Circuit

P2C8C reports a general fault in the circuit of the fourth temperature sensor of a DC/DC converter, after sensors A, B and C (P0C38, P0C3D, P0E58). Where sensor D sits inside the converter is up to each maker.
Sensor connector or wiring damaged or corroded
Temperature sensor D in the converter defective
Sensor reference or evaluation circuit inside the converter faulty
Converter output limited, 12 V charging voltage may drop
P2C8D: DC/DC Converter Temperature Sensor D Circuit Range/Performance

P2C8D is the plausibility test of DC/DC converter temperature sensor D: the voltage is electrically valid, but the temperature it implies does not match what the controller expects. Typical cross-checks compare the sensor with its neighbours after a long rest or look for a value that hardly changes while the converter works hard.
Hybrid control software level (FCA HCP update per 08-037-21)
Sensor D drifting and disagreeing with the other converter sensors
Uneven cooling of the converter, e.g. low coolant or air in the circuit
MIL on, with newer FCA software after one faulty drive
Reduced eTorque assist or start-stop availability
P2C8E: DC/DC Converter Temperature Sensor D Circuit Low

P2C8E is logged when the voltage from DC/DC converter temperature sensor D drops under the lower limit of its window. Power electronics mostly use NTC thermistors, where a falling voltage means rising temperature; an implausibly low value therefore reads as a converter far hotter than it can be.
Sensor D signal wire shorted to ground
Converter genuinely overheating because of a cooling fault
Converter derated right away, less electrical power available
P2C8F: DC/DC Converter Temperature Sensor D Circuit High

P2C8F stands for a sensor D signal stuck above the upper edge of its permitted range. With a thermistor fed through a pull-up resistor, the voltage climbs towards the reference as soon as the loop is broken, so an unplugged connector, a cracked wire or a corroded pin is the classic finding; a short to a supply voltage gives the same picture.
Connector unplugged or sensor wire broken
Corroded or pushed-back pin at the converter connector
Signal shorted to a supply voltage
Electrical power limited as a precaution
P2C90: Crankcase Ventilation System - Hose A Disconnected

Under California's phase-in (20 % of 2023, 50 % of 2024, all 2025 models) every PCV hose carrying crankcase vapour must be watched for a break as large as its smallest bore, so makers moved from the general P04DB to per-hose codes. P2C90 covers hose A.
PCV hose A pulled off, cracked or with a broken fitting
Detection software too sensitive (Ford, Toyota/Lexus and Stellantis updates)
PCV valve or make-up-air check valve not sealing
Crankcase pressure sensor or its signal faulty
Engine warning lamp, often without any other complaint
Oil mist or oily residue near the disconnected hose
Possibly unstable idle or lean mixture codes
P2C91: Crankcase Ventilation System - Hose B Disconnected

P2C91 is the second hose-specific PCV disconnection code: crankcase vapour line B is detected as open or broken, separately from line A (P2C90). Which physical hose carries the letter is the maker's choice; the code slot exists so that systems with two monitored lines can name the faulty one.
Engine control software reporting a disconnection that is not there (Alfa Romeo 2.9 V6)
PCV hose B loose, split or with a broken connector
Crankcase pressure sensor B or its wiring faulty
Oil residue or hissing at a crankcase ventilation hose
P2C92: Hybrid/EV Battery Contactor Control Supply Circuit/Open

The main contactors of a traction battery are relays whose coils are energised by driver stages in the battery controller, and those drivers take their energy from a dedicated supply feed. P2C92 means this feed is missing or interrupted, for example because of a blown fuse, a broken wire or a feed relay that does not pull in.
Fuse in the contactor supply feed blown
Supply wire or connector at the battery pack interrupted
Relay or switch feeding the contactor drivers not closing
Battery controller input or driver stage defective
Vehicle does not become ready to drive
P2C93: Hybrid/EV Battery Contactor Control Supply Circuit Range/Performance

With P2C93 the supply for the contactor drivers is present but does not behave as it should: it sags when a coil is switched on, ripples, or recovers too slowly before the next contactor in the closing sequence. A high-resistance contact or a weak feed therefore shows up here rather than as an open circuit.
Corroded or loose contact in the supply feed causing voltage drop
Weak 12 V battery or ground connection sagging under coil load
Contactor coil drawing excessive current or driver stage faulty
Several attempts needed before the vehicle is ready
P2C94: Hybrid/EV Battery Contactor Control Supply Circuit Low

P2C94 says the supply feeding the contactor drivers lies below its lower limit. Ford is the maker that documents it: special service messages 51513 and 51783 (2023) describe 2021–2023 Escape, Corsair, Aviator, Mustang Mach-E, F-150 and Transit plug-in models whose AC charging at level 1 or 2 stops with the MIL on and P2C94 logged in the SOBDM, the on-board c…
Supply feed pulled down by a weak 12 V battery or poor ground
Partial short or high resistance in the supply wiring
AC charging stops while plugged in, MIL on
Charging resumes after unplugging and reconnecting
Vehicle may not become ready to drive
P2C95: Hybrid/EV Battery Contactor Control Supply Circuit High
P2C95 is the upper-limit counterpart of P2C94: the voltage on the feed for the contactor coil drivers exceeds what the battery controller accepts.
Supply or sense line shorted to a higher voltage
Supply regulator or measurement in the battery controller faulty
12 V system overvoltage from a faulty DC/DC converter or jump start
Vehicle may not become ready or may shut down HV
P2C96: Besides commands over the vehicle network, many high-voltage batteries have a separate wired input through which another controller can force the contactors open.
Disable line or its connector at the battery pack interrupted
Sending controller (e.g. crash or airbag module) not driving the line
Connector left unplugged after body or battery repair
Input stage in the battery controller defective
Vehicle does not become ready to drive
P2C97: P2C97 is set when the high-voltage battery's wired disable input sits below its valid range, typically because the line is chafed through to body ground or the sending module pulls it low permanently. Whether low means shut down depends on the design.
Disable line chafed and shorted to ground
Sending module holding the line low permanently
Water in the connector creating a leakage path to ground
High-voltage battery stays switched off, no ready mode
P2C98: P2C98 flags a battery disable line whose level is above the permitted range, usually through a short to 12 V or a sender that drives the line too high. Unlike the low case, the risk here can be hidden: if a high level means all clear, a stuck-high line would no longer pass on a real shutdown request.
Disable line shorted to 12 V supply
Sending module driving the line above the valid level
Input stage in the battery controller misreading the level
High-voltage system warning, often without noticeable driving fault
Ready mode may be blocked after the next restart, depending on maker
P2C99: Throttle Actuator A Control Exceeded Learning Limit

An electronic throttle relies on learned values: the closed-stop position of its sensors and, in many systems, a correction that widens the commanded opening as carbon narrows the bore. P2C99 says a learned value for throttle A has run into its permitted limit, so the module can no longer compensate. No manufacturer publishes P2C99.
Heavy carbon deposits in the throttle bore needing more correction than allowed
Throttle body cleaned or replaced without resetting and relearning the adaptation
Worn throttle shaft, plate or end stop shifting the closed position
Engine warning lamp, possibly an electronic throttle warning
Idle speed too high, too low or hunting
Reduced power in a throttle emergency mode
P2C9A: Throttle Actuator B Control Exceeded Learning Limit

Throttle B exists only on engines with two electronically driven throttle bodies, usually one per cylinder bank on large V engines. P2C9A means a learned value of that second throttle – its closed-stop reference or the airflow correction stored for it – has reached the edge of the allowed range.
Carbon deposits in throttle body B only
Throttle body B replaced or cleaned without relearn
Throttle plate B sticking or its return spring weak
Position sensor of throttle B drifting
Reduced power if the throttle is restricted
P2C9B: Cold Start Turbocharger/Supercharger Wastegate Actuator A Range/Performance
P2C9B checks wastegate A while the engine runs its catalyst warm-up strategy after a cold start, when the wastegate is commanded open so hot exhaust reaches the catalyst rather than the turbine.
Wastegate flap or linkage stiff from corrosion or deposits, worst when cold
Electric wastegate actuator with worn motor or gears
Poor contact at the actuator connector or wiring
Check engine light shortly after a cold start
Rattle or noise from the wastegate area when cold
Often no noticeable change in performance
P2C9C: Cold Start Turbocharger/Supercharger Wastegate Actuator B Range/Performance

P2C9C is the counterpart of P2C9B for wastegate B and only exists on engines with two turbochargers: GM's tables define turbo A as the first in a series layout or the bank 1 unit in a parallel one, so B is the second or the bank 2 charger.
Bank 2 wastegate flap or linkage stiff from corrosion or deposits
Worn or weak wastegate actuator B
Wiring or connector fault at actuator B
Check engine light shortly after a cold start
Uneven boost between banks later in the drive
Often no noticeable change during the cold start
P2C9D: Fuel Pressure Regulator C Exceeded Control Limits - Pressure Too High

P2C9D reports that the fuel pressure in the section governed by regulator C stays above its target although that regulator is already reducing delivery as far as it can. A third regulator letter is only needed where an engine has several pressure control elements, for instance two high-pressure pumps or separate rail circuits.
Quantity control valve of circuit C sticking in the delivery position
Rail pressure sensor of that circuit reading too high
Wiring or connector fault keeping the valve from being switched
MIL on, often after a single trip
Harsh or noisy idle, especially when cold
P2C9E: Fuel Pressure Regulator C Exceeded Control Limits - Pressure Too Low

P2C9E is the underpressure counterpart of P2C9D: the circuit run by regulator C cannot reach its pressure target even with the regulator already asking for full delivery. No manufacturer publishes a definition of P2C9E, so the detail comes from analogous codes.
Worn high-pressure pump of circuit C
Low feed pressure from the tank pump or a clogged fuel filter
Quantity control valve stuck closed or open circuit to it
Extended cranking before the engine starts
P2C9F: Fuel Pressure Regulator D Exceeded Control Limits - Pressure Too High

P2C9F concerns regulator D, which GM uses for the second quantity control valve of a twin high-pressure system. GM's 2023 and 2024 tables 23OBDG07 and 24OBDG07 carry it in an ECM section that also lists the bank 2 rail sensor codes of bulletin 24-NA-106 for the 5.5 L LT6 Corvette.
Second quantity control valve (bank 2) not regulating correctly
Water intrusion or fault in the bank 2 fuel harness connector (GM LT6)
Bank 2 rail pressure sensor reading implausibly
Very low tank level causing pressure dropouts
Further fuel pressure or bank 2 injector codes stored
P2CA0: Fuel Pressure Regulator D Exceeded Control Limits - Pressure Too Low

P2CA0 is the low-pressure verdict for regulator D. GM bulletin 24-NA-106 names it as a bank 2 low-pressure fault on the 2023–24 Corvette with the 5.5 L LT6 and links it, together with P228C, P01BF, P312B and several injector high-side codes, to an incorrect twelve-pin inline plug with an unsealed cavity that admits water to the bank 2 injector wiring; the fi…
Incorrect 12-way in-line connector admitting water to the bank 2 harness (GM 24-NA-106)
Weak bank 2 high-pressure pump or its quantity valve stuck
Insufficient feed pressure from the tank pump
Several bank 2 injector or rail sensor codes at the same time
P2CA1: Charge Air Cooler Coolant Pump Sense Circuit High

Some electric pumps in a water-cooled charge air cooler loop report back to the engine computer on a dedicated sense or feedback wire, kept apart from the line commanding them. P2CA1 means the level on that return wire stays above its plausible band.
Feedback wire chafed through and touching a battery or ignition feed
Broken feedback wire or backed-out pin, input floats to its high level
Pump electronics no longer pulling the feedback line down
Damaged input stage in the engine control module
Reduced power or boost under load, especially in hot weather
Pump fault messages from the pump no longer reach the controller
P2CA2: Charge Air Cooler Coolant Pump Sense Circuit Low

P2CA2 is set when the return wire from the intercooler pump sits below its valid range for longer than allowed. Insulation worn through against the body, water in the plug, or pump electronics that keep pulling the line down are the usual suspects.
Feedback wire chafed against body or engine ground
Pump electronics holding the line low because of an internal fault
Moisture or corrosion bridging pins in the pump connector
Engine power limited when charge air temperature rises
Code may appear together with pump speed or performance codes
P2CA3: Charge Air Cooler Coolant Pump Sense Circuit Performance

With P2CA3 the feedback signal from the intercooler pump is electrically inside its limits but does not fit what the controller expects: a reported speed or status that contradicts the command, a pulse pattern it cannot decode, or a reply that changes although the request stayed constant.
Loose or corroded terminal distorting the feedback signal
Pump circuit board sending erratic or implausible feedback
Interference from ignition or alternator on a poorly routed wire
Pump or engine module software not matching each other
Power reduction on long climbs or in hot weather
P2CA4: Particulate Filter Pressure Sensor Signals Swapped A/B

P2CA4 means the engine module believes the readings of particulate filter pressure sensors A and B arrive on each other's inputs, typically because connectors, sensors or sensing hoses were interchanged during service. Such a mix-up yields values that look electrically sound but invert the pressure picture across the filter.
Sensing hoses of sensors A and B fitted to the wrong ports
Electrical connectors of the two sensors interchanged after service
Replacement sensor with different pin assignment or range
Crossed wires after a harness repair
MIL on, usually right after work on the exhaust or sensors
Regeneration too frequent or not taking place
Implausible filter pressure values in live data
P2CA5: DC/DC Converter Temperature Sensor E Circuit
P2CA5 is the general circuit fault of the fifth temperature sensor in a DC/DC converter, the one carrying letter E.
Loose, corroded or pushed-out terminal at the converter connector
Temperature sensor E inside the converter failed
Evaluation circuit of the converter control board faulty
Hybrid or electrical system warning and MIL on
DC/DC converter output limited, 12 V battery discharges
P2CA6: DC/DC Converter Temperature Sensor E Circuit Low

P2CA6 is logged when the voltage of DC/DC converter temperature sensor E sits below the lower edge of its window. Converter sensors are usually thermistors whose resistance falls as they warm, so a signal that collapses towards zero would mean a converter hotter than physically plausible.
Signal wire of sensor E chafed through and shorted to ground
Thermistor of sensor E shorted internally
Actual severe overheating of the converter, e.g. coolant loss
MIL and hybrid or charging warning on
Converter switched off or strongly limited immediately after start
Low 12 V voltage message on longer drives
P2CA7: DC/DC Converter Temperature Sensor E Circuit High

P2CA7 means the signal of DC/DC converter temperature sensor E is stuck above its upper limit. In a thermistor input fed through a pull-up resistor, an interrupted loop lets the voltage rise to the reference, so a pin pushed out of the connector, a broken conductor or a short to a supply line gives this result.
Open circuit in the sensor E signal or return line, e.g. pushed-out pin
Signal line shorted to a supply voltage
MIL and hybrid or charging warning on
Implausibly cold converter temperature in live data
Reduced converter output, 12 V battery charge drops
P2CA8: DC/DC Converter Temperature Sensor E Circuit Range/Performance

P2CA8 covers sensor E of the DC/DC converter when its voltage is electrically fine but the temperature it reports does not make sense. Typical plausibility tests compare all converter sensors after a long soak, when they should agree, or check whether a reading moves at all while the converter is under heavy load.
Sensor E drifting away from the other converter sensors
Sensor E has lost thermal contact with the part it measures
Outdated converter or hybrid control software with too tight limits
Contact resistance in the connector shifting the signal
MIL on, possibly after a single drive
Converter temperature in live data not following load or ambient
P2CA9: DC/DC Converter Temperature Sensor F Circuit

P2CA9 is the general fault code for the circuit of the sixth DC/DC converter temperature sensor, letter F. Which component this sensor watches is left to the manufacturer. No manufacturer documents P2CA9 publicly; the converter sensors visible in bulletins end at D (Ram 1500 eTorque, FCA 08-037-21).
Damaged harness or poor contact in the sensor F circuit
Temperature sensor F inside the converter failed
Input stage on the converter control board faulty
MIL and hybrid system warning on
Converter output limited, 12 V voltage may sag
P2CAA: DC/DC Converter Temperature Sensor F Circuit Low

P2CAA reports that the input for DC/DC converter temperature sensor F reads too low. With the usual thermistor circuit this corresponds to an impossibly hot reading, so the controller suspects the signal path before the hardware: a ground short in the harness, moisture in the connector or a thermistor that failed short.
Sensor F signal shorted to ground in the harness
Moisture or contamination in the converter connector
Thermistor of sensor F failed short
MIL and hybrid or charging warning on
Very high converter temperature shown even with a cold vehicle
P2CAB: DC/DC Converter Temperature Sensor F Circuit High

P2CAB is set when DC/DC converter temperature sensor F delivers a voltage above the top of its valid band. For a thermistor input this is the typical signature of an open circuit, since the pull-up drags the line to reference voltage, or of a short to a higher voltage.
Converter connector not latched or terminals spread
Broken signal or return wire of sensor F
Signal line shorted to a higher voltage
MIL and hybrid system warning on
Converter temperature shown far below ambient
Reduced 12 V supply from the converter
P2CAC: DC/DC Converter Temperature Sensor F Circuit Range/Performance

P2CAC flags DC/DC converter temperature sensor F as implausible although its signal is electrically valid. With six sensors in one converter the controller has plenty of reference values: after a cold soak all should read close to ambient, and during operation sensor F should rise and fall in step with the load on the part it watches.
Sensor F detached from its heat sink or measuring point
Sensor F drifting against the other converter sensors
Outdated converter or hybrid control software
Uneven cooling of the converter, e.g. air in the coolant circuit
MIL on, sometimes after a single drive
Sensor F reading out of line with the other converter temperatures
P2CAD: Charge Air Cooler Coolant Pump B Control Circuit/Open

Where a charge air cooling loop has a second electric pump, it carries the letter B. P2CAD reports that the control line to that pump is open, so the driver stage in the engine computer sees no load. No manufacturer documents a pump B or this code publicly.
Pump B connector loose, unplugged or corroded
Broken control wire between engine module and pump B
Open motor winding or internal board fault in pump B
MIL on, often after the first trip
Pump B silent; charge air temperature rises under load
P2CAE: Charge Air Cooler Coolant Pump B Control Circuit Low
P2CAE concerns the second electric pump of a charge air cooling loop: its control line is held at ground potential where the driver expects a higher level. No manufacturer documents pump B publicly.
Control wire of pump B rubbed through to ground
Water or corrosion in the pump B connector
Internal short in the electronics of pump B
Pump B runs continuously or stays in a fallback mode
Possible power reduction when the charge air gets hot
P2CAF: Charge Air Cooler Coolant Pump B Control Circuit High

P2CAF says the control line of charge air cooler pump B is tied to supply voltage, so the engine computer cannot pull it down when it switches the pump on. As with the rest of the pump B series, no manufacturer documents the code publicly.
Control wire of pump B pinched against a 12 V feed
Moisture bridging supply and control pins at the pump
MIL on after the first faulty trip
Pump B does not start when commanded
P2CB0: Charge Air Cooler Coolant Pump B Performance
P2CB0 flags that charge air cooler pump B is electrically in order but does not work the way its operating data say it should. No manufacturer documents the code publicly.
Low coolant level or air pockets in the charge air cooler loop
Worn bearing or damaged impeller in pump B
Kinked hose, clogged cooler or debris restricting flow
Charge air temperature higher than normal, power reduced
Unusual whining or rattling from the pump
P2CB1: Charge Air Cooler Coolant Pump B Overspeed/Air In System

P2CB1 means pump B in the charge air cooling loop turns faster than it should. An electric pump loses its hydraulic load when the impeller churns air instead of coolant, so overspeed is mostly a symptom of a low level or poor bleeding. No manufacturer documents P2CB1 publicly.
Air trapped in the loop after service or incomplete bleeding
Low coolant from a leak in the charge air cooler circuit
Impeller loose or broken on the shaft of pump B
Gurgling or a high-pitched pump noise
Low coolant warning or falling expansion tank level
P2CB2: Charge Air Cooler Coolant Pump B Underspeed

With P2CB2 the speed reported by charge air cooler pump B stays below what it should reach. The motor is braked mechanically or gets too little power: a dragging bearing, debris or sludge at the impeller, a weak supply or a high-resistance connector. No manufacturer documents P2CB2 publicly.
Dragging bearing or sludge slowing the rotor of pump B
Water or corrosion in the pump connector raising resistance
Low supply voltage from a poor ground or weak battery
Charge air runs hot, engine power reduced under load
P2CB3: Charge Air Cooler Coolant Pump B Stuck/Stalled

P2CB3 is reported when charge air cooler pump B receives power and a command but its rotor does not turn. The pump's own electronics usually detect this from current flowing without rotation and pass the result to the engine module. No manufacturer documents P2CB3 publicly.
Rotor stuck after a long period without use
Debris or deposits jamming the impeller of pump B
Coolant frozen because of insufficient antifreeze
Burnt winding or failed drive electronics in the pump
MIL on, often with a reduced-power message
No flow in the second branch of the charge air cooling loop
P2CB4: Charge Air Cooler Coolant Pump B Supply Voltage Circuit

P2CB4 concerns the power feed of charge air cooler pump B rather than its command line: the pump finds its supply missing or outside the window in which it can run. No manufacturer documents P2CB4 publicly.
Blown fuse or faulty relay in the pump B feed
Corroded or loose ground connection of the pump
Moisture or corrosion at the supply pins of the connector
Weak battery or charging fault pulling the voltage down
Pump B silent, charge air temperature climbs
Other supply-related codes may be stored at the same time
P2CB5: Charge Air Cooler Coolant Pump B Control Module Overtemperature

P2CB5 is raised by the electronics inside charge air cooler pump B when their temperature exceeds the limit; the pump then throttles back or stops to protect itself. No manufacturer documents P2CB5 publicly.
Pump running dry or partly in air because of low coolant
Stiff impeller making the motor draw more current
Pump mounted close to hot exhaust or turbo parts
Ageing power stage in the pump electronics
Pump B slows down or switches off, charge air gets warmer
Reduced power in hot weather or on long climbs
P2CB6: P2CB6 rates the boost control loop of charger B as a whole: the pressure produced by the second turbocharger or supercharger strays too far, upward or downward, from what the engine module requests in steady closed-loop operation. It is the B counterpart of P2263 and only applies to engines with two separately controlled chargers.
Leak in the charge air path of charger B
Sticking wastegate or variable vanes of charger B
Restriction in the exhaust upstream or downstream of turbine B
Boost pressure sensor B reading inaccurately
Uneven or reduced power under load
Hissing or whistling from the charge air system
P2CB7: Turbocharger/Supercharger Boost Pressure B Not Detected - Mechanical

P2CB7 states that charger B delivers practically no boost although the operating point calls for it, and that the reason is likely mechanical rather than electrical: the pressure measured after the second compressor hardly rises above ambient. It mirrors P2262 for charger A and is relevant only to engines with two separately monitored boost paths.
Intake or charge air hose of charger B detached or split
Wastegate or bypass of charger B stuck open
Actuator linkage or vacuum supply to charger B failed
Unusual hissing or no turbo sound
P2CB8: Turbocharger/Supercharger Boost Pressure B Too High - Mechanical

P2CB8 reports that the second charger, B, produces more boost than the engine module allows, and attributes this to a mechanical cause such as a wastegate or bypass of charger B that no longer opens, a seized actuator rod or sooted variable vanes stuck in the closed position. It is the B twin of P226B. No manufacturer documents P2CB8 publicly.
Wastegate of charger B stuck closed
Variable turbine vanes of charger B sooted and sticking
Seized actuator rod or linkage on charger B
Boost pressure sensor B reading too high
Sudden power cut under full load
P2CB9: P2CB9 means the second electric cooling fan reports a lower speed than its command calls for, while communication and wiring are judged sound. GM uses it in two ways. In tables 23OBDG07 and 24OBDG07 the fan must stay below a speed-dependent floor of up to 3550 rpm for 20 s once it has been commanded above 7.65 % for more than 5 s.
Fan blades slowed by debris, leaves, snow or ice
Fan 2 motor or its integrated electronics worn or faulty
Blown fuse, weak supply or poor ground at the fan
Sporadic entry without fault found (GM investigated without a fix)
Check engine light after two trips
Coolant temperature rises at idle or when towing
P2CBA: With P2CBA the controller finds fan 2 spinning clearly faster than its own estimate of what the current command should produce.
Fan blade broken or partly missing, less load on the motor
Fan electronics drive the motor harder than commanded
Implausible speed feedback from the fan module
Shroud damaged or detached so the rotor runs free
Check engine light after two trips
Unusually loud or vibrating fan noise
Fan runs at high speed even with a cool engine
P2CBB: P2CBB concerns vehicles with three electric radiator fans: the third one turns slower than modelled for its command. GM's 2025 diesel table 25OBDG04B describes the check for a LIN-controlled fan 3.
Fan 3 slowed by debris, ice or a distorted shroud
Fan 3 motor bearings or integrated controller worn
Voltage drop on the fan 3 power feed or ground
Check engine light after two trips
Engine runs warmer under high load or in heat
Reduced A/C cooling at low speed
P2CBC: P2CBC is the counterpart to P2CBB: the third cooling fan turns noticeably faster than the controller expects for the present request. No manufacturer publicly documents this code.
Fan 3 blade broken or rotor unbalanced
Fan 3 electronics ignore the speed command
Wrong speed value reported by the fan module
Check engine light, depending on the maker
P2CBD: Some engines heat the crankcase ventilation path so that moisture and oil carried by blow-by gas cannot freeze and block it; engines with two such paths, for example a PCV line and a separate make-up air line feeding the turbo intake, may carry a second heater, B.
Corroded or loose connector at heater B
Faulty output stage in the engine control module
MIL on (depending on manufacturer) or code stored only
No noticeable effect in mild weather
In hard frost, iced ventilation path with oil leaks or rough idle
P2CBE: PCV Heater B Control Circuit High

P2CBE says the switched control line of PCV heater B carries too high a voltage, usually because it touches battery positive. Since the module normally completes the heater circuit by pulling this line to ground, a short to supply means the output can no longer switch the element on, or the driver shuts down to protect itself, so heater B stays cold.
Control wire chafed through and touching battery voltage
Moisture bridging pins in the heater B connector
Internal short in heating element B
Damaged output stage in the engine control module
Code stored, MIL depending on manufacturer
Heater B inactive, risk of an iced ventilation path in frost
P2CBF: PCV Heater B Control Circuit Low

P2CBF is set when the control line of PCV heater B sits at ground potential at a moment the module expects a voltage on it. On the usual low-side layout, with supply fed directly to the heater and the module providing the ground, a short to ground on that line turns heater B on permanently regardless of command.
Control wire pinched or chafed to engine ground
Output stage in the engine module shorted internally
Code stored, MIL depending on manufacturer
Heater B constantly on, slightly higher electrical load
P2CC0: P2CC0 covers PCV heater B when its wiring passes the electrical tests but the heater does not behave as expected: current outside the plausible window, an overheated output stage, or no sign of the commanded warming. It complements the circuit codes P2CBD to P2CBF, which only detect opens and shorts.
Heating element B with drifted resistance
High-resistance contact in connector or supply
Output stage overheating in the engine control module
Code stored, MIL depending on manufacturer
Possible icing of the ventilation line in frost
P2CC1: P2CC1 is the general fault of a second sense line through which the engine controller reads the actual charging voltage. In the charging system, generator means the alternator; a sense input taps the voltage at the rectifier or battery without load current, so wiring losses do not distort it.
Sense wire B, its fuse or connector open or corroded
Second alternator or its regulator faulty
Sense input in the engine control module faulty
Battery or charging warning lamp on
Charging voltage regulated to a fixed or unsuitable value
P2CC2: Generator Voltage Sense Circuit B Range/Performance

P2CC2 means the voltage arriving on generator sense circuit B is within electrical limits but does not agree with what the controller expects, such as the battery voltage measured elsewhere, the commanded set point or the reading of sense circuit A.
Voltage drop from corroded terminals, loose ground strap or damaged fusible link
Alternator B delivering too little or unstable output
Battery with high internal resistance distorting the comparison
Charging warning lamp on or flickering
Battery not fully charged or charging voltage fluctuating
P2CC3: Generator Voltage Sense Circuit B Low

P2CC3 is stored when generator sense circuit B reports a voltage below its lower limit, in practice often close to zero. Typical causes are an open sense lead, a blown fuse in it or a short to ground; on Chrysler alternators, according to Remy, an internal 2.4 kΩ resistor shields the sense terminal against such a ground fault.
Sense wire B broken or its fuse blown
Sense wire B chafed and shorted to ground
Corroded sense terminal at the alternator or module
Charging voltage too high or held at a fixed value
P2CC4: Generator Voltage Sense Circuit B High

P2CC4 indicates that generator sense circuit B reads above its upper limit. Either the line is shorted to a higher voltage, or the voltage at the measuring point really is excessive, for example because the regulator keeps the field fully energised; Remy warns that a full-field alternator can quickly push the system above 16 V.
Regulator of alternator B stuck in full field, real overvoltage
Sense wire B shorted to a higher-voltage line
Sense input of the engine control module faulty
Very high system voltage, bulbs failing early
P2CC5: Generator Inverter Power Supply B Circuit/Open

P2CC5 concerns supply B inside the inverter that drives a hybrid's generator (motor-generator), typically a low-voltage rail feeding the gate drivers of the power transistors. Which supply gets the letter B is defined by the manufacturer; a second inverter channel or second generator would also fit. The code covers a missing supply or an interrupted feed.
Supply B for the gate drivers failed inside the inverter
12 V feed, fuse or connector of the inverter interrupted
Poor ground connection of the inverter control electronics
Hybrid system warning light and MIL on
Generator out of operation, vehicle may not become ready to drive
P2CC6: Generator Inverter Power Supply B Circuit Low

P2CC6 means supply B of the generator inverter is present but below its permitted level. A weak gate driver feed is dangerous for the power stage: transistors that are not driven fully on run in a lossy partial state and heat up quickly, so the inverter typically blocks the generator. No manufacturer documents P2CC6 publicly.
Internal regulator of supply B delivering too little voltage
Low 12 V input to the inverter, e.g. weak auxiliary battery
Corroded ground or connector of the inverter
Hybrid system warning light and MIL on
Generator limited or switched off, reduced hybrid performance
P2CC7: Generator Inverter Power Supply B Circuit High

P2CC7 is set when supply B of the generator inverter exceeds its upper limit. Gate inputs of IGBTs tolerate only a limited voltage, so overvoltage on the driver rail puts the switches at risk and the inverter is normally shut down.
Regulator of supply B inside the inverter faulty
Short between two internal supply rails
Overvoltage in the 12 V system from a DC/DC converter fault
Hybrid system warning light and MIL on
Generator blocked, battery no longer charged while driving
P2CC8: Some engines measure how fast a coolant pump turns with a dedicated speed sensor, for instance on a pump that can be engaged and released or on an electric pump read back by the controller. P2CC8 is the general fault of that sensor's circuit: the signal is absent or cannot be used, without the controller deciding whether it is too low or too high.
Failed speed sensor delivering no usable signal
Damaged wiring or loose connector at the sensor
Missing reference voltage or ground for the sensor
Coolant pump held in a default state, warm-up may change
P2CC9: P2CC9 means the coolant pump speed sensor delivers a clean electrical signal whose value does not make sense. The controller compares it with what the pump should be doing: a belt-driven pump has to follow engine speed in a fixed ratio once engaged, an electric pump should match its commanded speed.
Slipping belt or clutch, so the pump turns slower than expected
Sensor loose, wrong air gap or damaged trigger wheel
Sensor electronics drifting or dropping pulses
Engine may run warmer than usual or take longer to warm up
P2CCA: Coolant Pump Speed Sensor Circuit Low

P2CCA is stored when the signal line of the coolant pump speed sensor remains below its lower limit, so no pulses or levels above the threshold arrive. Most often the signal wire is shorted to ground, the sensor has lost its supply voltage and therefore cannot switch, or its output stage has failed in the off state. No manufacturer documents P2CCA publicly.
Sensor supply voltage missing because of an open feed
Sensor output stage failed in the low state
Pump speed reads zero in live data although the engine runs
P2CCB: Coolant Pump Speed Sensor Circuit High

P2CCB covers the upper end of the coolant pump speed sensor signal: the input stays above its permitted maximum. On sensors with an open-collector output and a pull-up resistor in the controller, an interrupted signal wire or a sensor that has lost its ground leaves the line resting high, so the open case often lands here rather than under P2CCA.
Open signal wire, input pulled up by the controller
Lost ground connection at the sensor
Signal wire shorted to a voltage feed
Pump speed missing or stuck at an implausible value in live data
P2CCC: P2CCC continues the state-of-health series for sectioned traction batteries in the P2 block: after A (P0A7F) and B to F (P0EDD to P0EE1), section G is the seventh. The controller has concluded that this part of the pack has lost too much usable capacity or power.
Battery module of group 7 lost capacity or power
Single weak cell block dragging the section down
State-of-health estimate of the battery controller wrong
Electric driving mode unavailable or ends early
P2CCD: P2CCD reports that section H, the eighth subdivision of a traction battery, has aged past the limit its controller accepts. In practice this code only exists on large packs that the battery management splits into at least eight separately judged groups.
Battery module of group 8 worn out
Module aged faster due to heat or uneven cooling
Faulty state-of-health judgement by the battery controller
P2CCE: P2CCE is reserved for the ninth section, I, of a traction battery whose controller rates the health of each section on its own. The fault is a capacity or power verdict, not an electrical one: section I no longer delivers what a healthy unit should. No manufacturer publicly documents P2CCE.
Module or cell group of section I aged beyond its limit
Uneven pack temperature stressing this section
Misjudged state of health in the battery controller
MIL or hybrid system warning on
P2CCF: P2CCF belongs to the deterioration series that rates each section of a divided traction battery on its own; J is the tenth section after A (P0A7F), B to F (P0EDD–P0EE1) and G to I (P2CCC–P2CCE). It is not an electrical fault: the controller has decided that the modules of section J have given up more usable capacity or power than allowed.
Modules of section J worn beyond the accepted capacity or power limit
Section J repeatedly ran hotter than the rest of the pack
Health estimate of the battery controller wrong after software or sensor issue
MIL or hybrid system warning on
Less power available in electric driving
P2CD0: With P2CD0 the battery controller reports that section K, the eleventh separately judged part of the high-voltage battery, has exceeded its ageing limit. Such a verdict normally rests on comparing what this section stores and delivers with its neighbours over many charge cycles, so it rarely appears suddenly after one event.
Cells of section K lost capacity faster than the other sections
Internal resistance of section K increased, limiting power
Uneven coolant flow leaving section K warmer over years
Warning lamp for engine or hybrid system
Shorter range on a full charge
P2CD1: P2CD1 marks section L, the twelfth subdivision of the high-voltage pack, as worn: its usable capacity or power capability has fallen below what the controller accepts.
Section L has reached the end of its usable life
One weak cell block pulling the whole section down
Faulty voltage sensing making section L look weaker than it is
Battery charge falls faster than usual
P2CD2: P2CD2 flags section M, the thirteenth part of a sectioned high-voltage battery, as degraded in capacity or power. Unlike sections J to L, M has no matching over-temperature code in the available code lists, so the thermal history of this section has to be read from general pack temperature data.
Section M degraded by age and charge cycles
Long standstill at low charge damaged cells of section M
Cell balancing of section M no longer working
Hybrid or engine warning lamp on
P2CD3: P2CD3 closes the lettered deterioration series: N is the fourteenth section of a drive battery whose management assesses each section's condition separately. When it sets, section N can no longer hold or release the energy expected of it, even though wiring and sensors may be intact.
Cells in section N aged beyond the acceptance limit
Earlier replaced neighbour modules leave section N as the weak link
Battery controller misjudges section N after a reset or update
P2CD4: A/C Refrigerant Pressure Sensor A/B Correlation

P2CD4 is a plausibility check between two refrigerant pressure sensors that serve one A/C or heat pump circuit: the module flags it when the pair disagrees beyond what the system allows, even though each sensor is electrically fine.
Thermal management software misjudging the sensor comparison (Bentley 2025 campaign)
One pressure sensor drifting or failing internally while still in range
Contact resistance at one sensor connector shifting its signal
A/C cools weakly or the compressor is limited
Code stored in the thermal management or climate module
P2CD5: Bypass valve C is a third compressor recirculation valve, which only exists on layouts with three charging paths or stages; on lift-off it routes boosted air back to the compressor inlet so the compressor does not surge. It is not the wastegate. P2CD5 says the valve no longer moves when commanded and stays in one position.
Valve or piston seized by oil and soot deposits from the crankcase breather
Electric actuator or diaphragm of the valve worn or failed
Missing vacuum or control signal on a pneumatically operated valve
Position feedback reports movement wrongly although the valve works
Fluttering or surging noise from the intake when lifting off the throttle
Boost builds slowly or stays low when the valve is stuck open
Warning lamp on and engine power limited
P2CD6: A fourth boost pressure sensor, D, is only needed where charge pressure is read at four points, for example on twin-turbo engines with two stages per bank or on combinations of supercharger, turbocharger and electric compressor. Which tap gets the letter is up to the manufacturer.
Corroded or loose connector, chafed wire at sensor D
5 V reference or sensor ground interrupted
Input stage of the engine control module faulty
Reduced boost and noticeably less power
Other sensor codes at the same time if a shared 5 V supply is affected
P2CD7: Turbocharger/Supercharger Boost Sensor D Circuit Range/Performance

With P2CD7 the boost sensor D signal is electrically valid but does not fit the other pressure readings or the engine's air model. No manufacturer documents this code publicly; the checks used for sensor A show what it would cover.
Sensor D drifted or contaminated with oil
Leaking seal or blocked port at the sensor's measuring point
Charge air leak in the section monitored by sensor D
Sensor with the wrong pressure range fitted
Scan tool shows sensor D value differing from barometric pressure with the engine off
P2CD8: Turbocharger/Supercharger Boost Sensor D Circuit Low

P2CD8 is stored when the voltage from boost sensor D falls below the lowest value a healthy sensor can output. Since these sensors rise in voltage as pressure rises, a reading near zero almost always points to the electrics: signal shorted to ground, an interrupted 5 V supply, or a broken signal wire that the module pulls low.
Signal wire of sensor D shorted to ground
5 V reference to the sensor open or shorted
Sensor D internally failed with output stuck low
Only base boost available, clear loss of power
Live data shows sensor D at or near minimum pressure even under load
P2CD9: Turbocharger/Supercharger Boost Sensor D Circuit High

P2CD9 reports a boost sensor D voltage above the highest valid level. A signal pinned near the reference rarely reflects real overboost; more often the signal wire touches 5 V or battery voltage, the sensor ground is open, or a broken signal line floats up through a pull-up inside the module. No carmaker publishes a sensor D limit.
Sensor ground open or high resistance at the connector
Signal wire shorted to 5 V reference or battery voltage
Sensor D internally failed with output stuck high
Engine runs on base boost only with reduced power
Live data shows sensor D at maximum even at idle
P2CDA: Alternative Fuel Tank A Vacuum Insulation Deteriorated

P2CDA concerns cryogenic fuel storage, in practice liquefied natural gas (LNG) and possibly liquid hydrogen, kept in a double-walled tank whose gap is evacuated. Once that vacuum softens, heat leaks in, the liquid boils faster and pressure climbs until the relief valve vents gas.
Vacuum between inner and outer tank wall lost through a leaking weld, fitting or seal
Gradual vacuum decay from outgassing over years of service, tank due for pump-down
Dent or impact damage to the outer shell breaching the insulation space
Pressure rise from another cause (economizer, pressure regulator, sensor) misread as insulation loss
Tank pressure rises quickly while the vehicle stands, relief valve vents gas
Frost or condensation on the outer tank shell
Fuel loss and shorter standing time after refuelling
P2CDB: Cold Start Cylinder 1 Deactivation/Intake Valve Control Performance

P2CDB is part of the monitoring of cold start emission strategies: some engines shut off cylinders or hold intake valves closed right after a cold start to heat the catalyst faster, and CARB requires the commanded elements of such a strategy to be checked while it is active.
Latch pin of the switchable rocker or lifter on cylinder 1 sticking, often from contaminated oil
Wrong oil grade or low oil level slowing the switching while the oil is still cold
Cylinder 1 control solenoid responding sluggishly at low temperature
Engine control software misjudging the cold start test, cured by an update
Check engine lamp after a cold start
Rough running in the first minutes after starting a cold engine
Misfire code for cylinder 1 stored alongside
P2CDC: Cold Start Cylinder 2 Deactivation/Intake Valve Control Performance

With P2CDC the control unit reports that cylinder 2 did not take the valve state that the cold start routine asked for. Timing matters here: in a Ford patent on electrically latched rockers, intake deactivation is wanted at engine start, yet the cam of cylinder 2 sits on its lobe, so its latch pin cannot move at first.
Latch pin on cylinder 2 seized by dirt or varnish in the oil
Hydraulic lash adjuster pumped up so the rocker stays loaded on base circle
Weak cylinder 2 solenoid or high resistance in its connector
Worn cam lobe or collapsed lifter on cylinder 2
Uneven idle while the engine warms up
Warning lamp, sometimes with a cylinder 2 misfire code
Engine control may suspend the cold start strategy
P2CDD: Cold Start Cylinder 3 Deactivation/Intake Valve Control Performance

P2CDD flags cylinder 3 when its deactivation or intake valve control misbehaves during the cold start phase. No maker documents this code publicly, so the closest evidence comes from neighbouring checks.
Cylinder 3 valves keep opening because the switching element does not unlock
Insufficient oil pressure or flow to the switching gallery right after a cold start
Cylinder 3 control solenoid sticking or leaking internally
Manifold pressure signal biased, so a sealed cylinder looks like it still breathes
Malfunction lamp, typically after repeated cold starts
Vibration or rough idle shortly after a cold start
Engine takes longer to settle into normal running
P2CDE: Cold Start Cylinder 4 Deactivation/Intake Valve Control Performance
On a four-cylinder engine cylinder 4 is the last one in the count; P2CDE reports that cylinder 4 did not follow the cold start valve command. Engines may do two different things during a cold start.
Switchable rocker or lifter on cylinder 4 not changing state
Cylinder 4 solenoid drawing too little current due to corroded terminals
Aged or overdue engine oil impairing the hydraulic switching when cold
Implausible coolant or oil temperature signal triggering the cold start strategy wrongly
Rough first minute after a cold start
P2CDF: Cold Start Cylinder 5 Deactivation/Intake Valve Control Performance
P2CDF only occurs on engines with at least five cylinders, mostly V6 and V8 units, and says cylinder 5 did not respond correctly to the cold start deactivation or intake valve command.
Deactivation lifter or rocker on cylinder 5 failing to lock or unlock
Restricted oil gallery or screen feeding the switching elements of that bank
Faulty cylinder 5 control valve in the valve lifter oil manifold
Calibration issue in the engine control module
Lamp on after cold starts, sometimes with a cylinder 5 misfire code
Ticking or tapping valve noise when cold
Rough idle until the engine is warm
P2CE0: Cold Start Cylinder 6 Deactivation/Intake Valve Control Performance

P2CE0 closes this series of cold start codes; numbering ends at cylinder 6 although many deactivation engines have eight cylinders. It indicates that cylinder 6 did not reach the valve state demanded during the cold start routine. No manufacturer documents P2CE0 publicly.
Engine control software that misjudges or mis-times the cold start switching, fixed by reprogramming
Deactivating lifter or rocker on cylinder 6 not switching
Low or delayed oil pressure after a cold start
Cylinder 6 control solenoid or its wiring degraded
Rough idle or misfire while warming up
Check engine lamp, often with a cylinder 6 misfire code
Cylinder deactivation may stay disabled afterwards
P2CE1: P2CE1 reports an interrupted circuit at intake air heater C, part of the grid-type pre-heat system a diesel uses to warm the incoming air for cold starts.
Damaged supply power cable between relay and heater, not always visible on an ohmmeter
Pre-heat relay contacts or output burnt open
Poor terminal tension at the heating element or relay plug
Heating element C itself burnt through
Hard starting and long cranking in cold weather
White smoke after a cold start
P2CE2: Intake Air Heater C Circuit Range/Performance

P2CE2 is the plausibility test for intake air heater C: the circuit is neither open nor shorted, but current draw, voltage drop or heating effect do not fit the command. Under the heavy-duty OBD rules a glow plug or intake air heater must react properly to commands and its circuit must show plausible current and voltage drop.
Extra resistance from corroded terminals or a worn supply cable lowering heater current
Pre-heat relay switching with excessive voltage drop
Heating element C aged, drawing current outside the expected window
Weak batteries or poor main ground distorting the current and voltage reading
White smoke and rough running until warm
Warning lamp without an open or short code for heater C
P2CE3: Intake Air Heater C Circuit Low

P2CE3 means the signal in the circuit of intake air heater C reads too low, as with the control or feedback line shorted to ground or a relay output pulled down. Volvo uses it with the suffix -11, which in the failure type scheme denotes a ground short.
Control or feedback wire of heater C chafed through to ground
Pre-heat relay with an internal fault pulling its output low
Outdated engine management software, addressed by a Volvo update
Moisture or corrosion in the relay connector creating a path to ground
Pre-heat not working, hard cold starts
White smoke after starting in cold weather
P2CE4: Intake Air Heater C Circuit High

P2CE4 is stored when heater C's circuit shows an excessive signal, typically a short to battery voltage on the control line or a relay that remains switched on. Volvo and Mack document it as P2CE4-12, the suffix standing for a short to battery.
Pre-heat relay contacts welded or stuck closed
Control line of heater C shorted to a battery-voltage wire
Faulty supply power cable or loose bracket mounting affecting the circuit
Engine control module output stage for the relay faulty
Batteries drained after the truck has been parked
Hot or discoloured cable near the heater
Warning lamp and possibly hard starting if the heater no longer switches
P2CE5: Particulate Filter Pressure Sensor C Circuit

Two manufacturers use P2CE5, with different meanings. In GM's 2025 diesel tables 25OBDG04A and 25OBDG04B, sensor C is the downstream relative pressure sensor that reads gauge pressure behind the particulate filter.
Sensor C zero point drifted (offset at standstill too large)
Condensate or soot in the sensing hose holding pressure
Damaged connector or wiring of a digital sensor C
Warning lamp on, usually after two trips on GM diesels
Particulate filter regeneration may run less accurately or more often
Usually no noticeable change in driving
P2CE6: Particulate Filter Pressure Sensor C Circuit Range/Performance

P2CE6 marks a sensor C reading that is electrically valid but physically wrong. GM's 2025 diesel tables use it for a frozen downstream relative pressure signal: during transients, with engine speed changing faster than 150 rpm/s and fuel and airflow also changing quickly, the signal must move; too little variation (25OBDG04B: 0.14 % or less in 40 of 50 sampl…
Sensing hose to sensor C kinked, blocked or disconnected
Condensate or frozen water in the sensing line
Exhaust leak near the measuring point
Particulate filter regenerations triggered too early or too late
Filter monitoring (missing substrate test) cannot complete
P2CE7: Particulate Filter Pressure Sensor C Circuit Low
P2CE7 means the raw signal of filter pressure sensor C has dropped below its electrical floor, the typical picture of a signal wire shorted to ground or a lost 5 V supply.
Signal wire of sensor C shorted to ground, often from heat damage near the exhaust
5 V supply to the sensor interrupted
Sensor C internally failed with output stuck low
Live data shows sensor C at minimum regardless of engine load
Regeneration planning relies on a soot model only
P2CE8: Particulate Filter Pressure Sensor C Circuit High
P2CE8 is the high-side electrical fault of filter pressure sensor C: its output sits above the range a working sensor can produce.
Sensor ground or signal wire open
Signal wire shorted to 5 V reference or battery voltage
Sensor C internally failed with output stuck high
Live data shows sensor C at maximum even at idle
Regeneration requests may become more frequent
P2CE9: Particulate Filter Pressure Sensor C Circuit Intermittent/Erratic

P2CE9 catches a sensor C signal that jumps rather than drifts. GM's 2025 diesel tables call this a quick change check: when two consecutive raw samples of the downstream relative pressure sensor differ by more than 20 %, the sample counts as failed, and 99 failures in 200 samples set a Type B code.
Loose or corroded terminal in the sensor C connector
Harness rubbing through on a bracket or exhaust part
Intermittent internal fault of the sensor
Warning lamp on, sometimes after rough roads or rain
Pressure value jumps in live data
P2CEA: Particulate Filter Pressure Sensor D Circuit

Sensor D is the fourth slot for particulate filter pressure and only appears in Ford's 2024–25 petrol OBD summary, which watches a filter on each bank (missing substrate codes P226D and P226E); Ford does not say publicly which letter belongs to which filter or tap.
Damaged or corroded connector at sensor D
Harness to sensor D damaged by exhaust heat
Particulate filter monitoring for one bank incomplete
P2CEB: Particulate Filter Pressure Sensor D Circuit Range/Performance

P2CEB says sensor D reports a pressure that is electrically fine but does not match what the exhaust flow should produce. Ford is the only maker found using it, in its 2024–25 petrol summary for engines with a gasoline particulate filter per bank.
Sensing hose to sensor D cracked, kinked or disconnected
Condensate in the sensing line after short trips
Sensor D drifted or responding slowly
Missing substrate test for that bank cannot be completed
Usually no noticeable change while driving
P2CEC: Particulate Filter Pressure Sensor D Circuit Low

P2CEC is set when an analog filter pressure sensor D delivers less voltage than it can in normal service. In Ford's 2024–25 petrol summary, the only public source using sensor D, the limit is 0.3 V for 5 s, checked continuously alongside the A, B and C sensors of the gasoline particulate filters.
Signal wire of sensor D shorted to ground
5 V reference to sensor D open or pulled down
Sensor D failed with output stuck low
Live data shows sensor D at minimum
Further 5 V sensor codes if the shared supply is affected
P2CED: Particulate Filter Pressure Sensor D Circuit High

With P2CED the analog output of filter pressure sensor D lies above its usable top end. Ford's gasoline OBD document for 2024–25, with filters on both banks and up to four pressure sensors, sets the code above 4.73 V lasting 5 s.
Sensor ground open or high resistance
Signal wire shorted to 5 V reference or battery voltage
Sensor D failed with output stuck high
Live data shows sensor D at maximum with the engine at idle
Filter monitoring for that bank incomplete
P2CEE: Particulate Filter Pressure Sensor D Circuit Intermittent/Erratic

P2CEE stands for brief dropouts or jumps in the sensor D signal that do not last long enough for the low or high codes. Ford's 2024–25 petrol summary includes it in the continuous analog check of its gasoline particulate filter sensors, about 5 s to register, with no separate threshold given.
PCM software setting the code falsely (Ford bulletin 20-2257, F-150 2.7L)
Loose or corroded terminal in the sensor D connector
Harness to sensor D chafed or intermittently shorted
Intermittent internal fault of sensor D
Warning lamp on, sometimes only now and then
Pressure value of sensor D jumps in live data
Possibly stored together with other, unrelated codes after a software issue
P2CEF: P2CEF concerns a second thermostat that regulates its own part of the cooling system; stuck open means coolant passes through it before the intended temperature, so that circuit warms too slowly or stays too cool.
Debris in the coolant holding the thermostat valve off its seat
Worn or leaking wax element, piston no longer returns
Earlier thermostat version superseded by the maker (Mercedes M139)
Low coolant temperature warning or slow warm-up
Weaker cabin heating in cold weather
P2CF0: P2CF0 is the closed-side counterpart of P2CEF: auxiliary thermostat A fails to open, so the circuit it governs gets too little flow and its temperature climbs past the regulating point while other parts of the engine may look normal. No manufacturer documents P2CF0 publicly.
Wax element lost its charge, thermostat no longer opens
Piston jammed by deposits or debris
Air pocket around the element after a coolant service, so it never sees hot coolant
High temperature in one cooling circuit or an overheating warning
Possible power reduction to protect the engine
P2CF1: P2CF1 covers a further auxiliary thermostat, labelled B, that stays open, so its loop loses its warm-up phase and runs below the intended temperature. Which loop B controls is the maker's choice: engines with split cooling may regulate head, block, oil or heater flow with separate thermostats, each needing its own temperature sensor for diagnosis.
Valve held open by debris or a weak return spring
Worn wax element that no longer retracts fully
Temperature sensor of that loop reading too low and faking the fault
Slow warm-up and higher fuel use in cold weather
P2CF2: P2CF2 is logged when auxiliary thermostat B does not open: the temperature in its loop keeps rising beyond the opening point while the controller expects it to level off.
Leaking wax charge, thermostat stays shut
Piston seized by corrosion or deposits
Temperature sensor of that loop reading too high
Overheating warning or high oil temperature
Reduced power to protect the engine
P2CF3: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Pump A Underspeed

P2CF3 is set when battery coolant pump A turns more slowly than the controller commands, although it is powered and not fully blocked.
