Typical reasons are a sluggish bearing, deposits on the impeller, low supply voltage or a pump motor that has lost strength; a faulty speed signal can produce the same picture.
Battery controller software misreading pump speed (Ford 2020 hybrids)
Worn bearing or deposits slowing the pump
Voltage drop on the pump feed or ground under load
Implausible speed feedback from the pump electronics
P2CF4: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Pump B Supply Voltage Circuit

P2CF4 is about the power feed of the second battery coolant pump, B: the pump or its control unit sees a supply voltage outside the permitted window, or none at all. Unlike the control-circuit codes P0E1A to P0E1C, which watch the command line, this code looks at the line that actually powers the motor, typically a fused 12 V feed plus ground.
Blown fuse or faulty relay in the pump B feed
Corroded connector or poor ground on the pump B supply
Weak 12 V battery or DC/DC output dragging the supply down
Internal fault in the pump electronics misreading the supply
Charging or drive power limited when the battery warms up
P2CF5: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Pump B Stuck/Stalled

P2CF5 means battery coolant pump B does not turn at all although it is commanded and powered: the rotor is blocked, or the pump electronics has given up after failed start attempts. A seized bearing, debris or deposits after coolant work, a failed motor winding or frozen coolant in a weak mixture are the usual suspects.
Pump B rotor or bearing seized
Debris or deposits jamming the impeller after coolant work
Pump motor or its electronics failed
Coolant frozen due to insufficient antifreeze
Warning lamp for hybrid system or engine
Power reduced as battery temperature rises
P2CF6: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Pump B Overspeed/Air in System

P2CF6 reports that battery coolant pump B spins above its commanded speed. Once a centrifugal pump loses its load it accelerates, so the most common explanation is air or a low level in the loop, which the title names directly.
Air left in the battery loop after service or poor bleeding
Leak at a battery coolant tube or joint lowering the level
Impeller slipping on the shaft or broken
False speed feedback from the pump electronics
Gurgling or whining from the pump area
Coolant level in the battery reservoir drops
MIL or hybrid warning, sometimes without other effect
P2CF7: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Pump B Underspeed

P2CF7 is the underspeed fault of battery coolant pump B: the pump turns, but clearly below the commanded speed for longer than the controller tolerates. Compared with the stall code P2CF5 the rotor is still moving, so friction, a partly obstructed impeller, coolant that is too viscous in the cold or a sagging supply are likelier than a dead motor.
Worn bearing or deposits slowing pump B
Supply voltage of pump B dropping under load
Wrong or aged coolant too viscous at low temperature
Battery controller software misjudging pump speed
P2CF8: Engine Coolant Bypass Valve D Control Circuit Driver Current/Temperature Too High
P2CF8 is raised by the driver of coolant bypass valve D when it measures excessive current or overheats and protects itself.
Valve stiff or seized, so the motor or solenoid draws excess current
Shorted winding in the valve actuator
Valve wires partly shorted to ground or to each other
Overheated or faulty output stage in the control module
Cabin heat weak or not adjustable (heater valve)
Engine warms up abnormally if the valve sits in the engine loop
P2CF9: Belt Integrated Starter Generator Belt Tensioner Control Circuit/Open
P2CF9 applies to belt starter-generator systems whose belt tensioner is moved by an actuator rather than by a spring alone.
Broken wire or loose connector in the tensioner drive circuit
Open coil or motor winding in the tensioner actuator
Output stage in the controlling module failed
Belt squeal or slip during automatic restarts
P2CFA: Belt Integrated Starter Generator Belt Tensioner Control Circuit Low
P2CFA is logged when the control line of an electrically adjusted BISG belt tensioner reads too low, typically a ground short or a driver that holds the line down permanently.
Tensioner control wire chafed through to ground
Internal short in the tensioner actuator
Water or corrosion bridging pins at the actuator plug
Belt noise at start or under load
P2CFB: Belt Integrated Starter Generator Belt Tensioner Control Circuit High

P2CFB mirrors P2CFA on the high side: the tensioner control circuit of a belt integrated starter generator shows a voltage above the expected range, usually from a wire touching a battery-voltage feed or a driver stage that cannot switch off. The actuator may then be held in one position permanently.
Control wire shorted to a supply voltage
Output stage in the module unable to switch off
Actuator electronics reporting an implausibly high level
Belt slip or squeal at engine start
Faster belt wear or bearing noise
MIL on, stop-start or assist unavailable
P2CFC: P2CFC is the general fault of the output that powers the compressor clutch coil directly, unlike P0645, which covers a clutch relay. Ford is the documented user and runs it in a body module, not the PCM.
Spread or pushed-out terminals at the body control module connector
Open or burnt clutch field coil
Damaged wire or connector between module and compressor
Faulty clutch output in the controlling module
Code stored in the HVAC or body control module, usually without engine lamp
P2CFD: P2CFD means the voltage on the clutch coil output reads lower than the module expects for the commanded state, most often because the line or the coil is grounded. With a high-side driver that short pulls the feed down, so the clutch cannot engage and the driver may protect itself; on a low-side design a grounded line would hold the clutch in instead.
Clutch feed wire chafed through and touching ground
Damaged terminals at the body control module (Ford SSM 50811/51380)
Clutch coil shorted internally to its housing
No cooling, compressor clutch stays disengaged
Possibly blown fuse in the clutch feed
P2CFE: P2CFE reports a clutch coil output that sits higher than it should, typically because the line touches a battery feed. Then the clutch may stay energized after the module switches off, so the compressor keeps running and can ice the evaporator; a low-side driver instead shuts down and the clutch never engages. No manufacturer documents P2CFE publicly.
Clutch control wire shorted to a battery-powered circuit
Output stage in the module stuck switched on
Moisture bridging pins in the compressor or module connector
Compressor runs even with A/C switched off
Iced evaporator, weak airflow after a while
Alternatively no cooling at all if the driver shuts down
P2CFF: A/C Clutch Control Circuit Driver Current/Temperature Too High
P2CFF does not come from a voltage comparison but from the protective logic of the clutch output itself.
Clutch field coil with shorted turns drawing too much current
Feed wire partly shorted to ground
Output stage overheating from poor module cooling or an internal fault
Compressor clutch disengages under load or after warm-up
P2D00: Motor Electronics Coolant Pump A Stuck/Stalled
P2D00 reports that coolant pump A of the motor electronics loop, which cools the inverter and drive-motor electronics, does not rotate although commanded.
Battery or powertrain controller software misreading the pump (Ford 2020 hybrids)
Debris jamming the impeller after coolant work
Pump motor or integrated electronics failed
Reduced drive power when the inverter gets hot
P2D01: Motor Electronics Coolant Pump A Overspeed/Air in System

P2D01 is logged when the first electric pump of the motor electronics loop, which carries heat away from the inverter and drive-motor electronics, spins faster than commanded. A centrifugal pump that suddenly has nothing to push races, so the title points straight at air or a low coolant level.
Low coolant level or trapped air in the motor electronics loop, for example after service work
Monitoring strategy in the control software (Ford 2020 hybrids, cured by reprogramming)
External leak at hoses, connectors or the pump housing that keeps drawing in air
Loose impeller or false speed feedback from the pump electronics
Coolant level in the degas bottle at or below minimum
Gurgling or whining from the electric pump
Reduced drive power when the inverter runs hot
P2D02: Motor Electronics Coolant Pump A Underspeed

With P2D02 the controller sees pump A of the motor electronics cooling loop turning, but clearly below its target speed for longer than allowed. The rotor is not locked, which separates it from P2D00; a stiff bearing, deposits on the impeller, cold and thick coolant or a supply that sags under load are therefore more likely than a dead motor.
Stiff bearing or deposits on the impeller of pump A
Control software strategy (Ford 2020 hybrids, fixed by reprogramming)
Voltage drop on the pump feed or ground under load
Wrong, contaminated or aged coolant raising viscosity at low temperature
Higher inverter or motor electronics temperatures in live data
P2D03: Motor Electronics Coolant Pump A Supply Voltage Circuit

P2D03 concerns the power feed of motor electronics coolant pump A rather than its command line: the pump, or the module reading its status, finds the supply outside its allowed window or missing. That points to a blown fuse, a corroded connector, a weak ground or a 12 V system that drops too low.
Blown fuse or faulty relay in the pump feed
Corroded connector, loose terminal or poor ground at pump A
Weak 12 V battery or DC/DC converter output too low
Software strategy on 2020 Ford hybrids, cured by reprogramming
Pump A runs intermittently or not at all
Further low-voltage codes in other modules
P2D04: Motor Electronics Coolant Pump A Control Module Overtemperature

P2D04 refers to the small electronics built into coolant pump A of the motor electronics loop: its own temperature has exceeded the limit, and the pump usually reports this before cutting back or switching off to protect itself.
Pump running dry or with too little coolant, so it loses its own cooling
Blocked or kinked line forcing the pump to work at high load
Internal fault in the pump control electronics
Software strategy on 2020 Ford hybrids, cured by reprogramming
Malfunction indicator lamp on, sometimes only after longer drives or in hot weather
Pump stops temporarily and restarts after cooling down
Inverter overtemperature warning or reduced power
P2D05: Motor Electronics Coolant Pump B Stuck/Stalled

P2D05 opens the pump B block of the motor electronics series: the second electric pump in the loop that cools inverters and drive-motor electronics is commanded and supplied, yet its rotor does not move. Where a vehicle has two electric drive units, B may be the pump serving the second inverter.
Seized bearing or blocked rotor in pump B
Debris or deposits in the loop after repairs or coolant change
Failed motor winding or pump electronics unable to start the motor
Coolant frozen because the antifreeze ratio is too low
Malfunction or hybrid system warning lamp on
No pump noise or vibration when the pump should run
Rising temperature of the second inverter, power limited
P2D06: Motor Electronics Coolant Pump B Overspeed/Air in System
P2D06 says pump B of the motor electronics loop turns above its commanded speed, the classic sign of a pump that has lost its coolant column to air or a falling level.
Coolant leak anywhere in the shared loop, such as faulty battery coolant tubes (Ford 23B09)
Air left in the loop after filling without the prescribed bleeding procedure
Impeller slipping on the shaft or implausible speed feedback
Often none apart from the stored code
Falling level in the degas bottle or traces of coolant
Inverter overtemperature warning and reduced acceleration if the loss continues
P2D07: Motor Electronics Coolant Pump B Underspeed
P2D07 is the underspeed report for the second motor electronics pump: B is moving, so it is not stalled as in P2D05, yet its actual speed stays well short of the request for too long.
Worn bearing or friction inside pump B
Impeller partly obstructed by deposits or debris
High resistance in feed or ground causing the voltage to sag under load
Pump motor or its electronics losing performance with age
Pump B speed in live data clearly below the target value
Power limitation during long climbs or towing
P2D08: Motor Electronics Coolant Pump B Supply Voltage Circuit

P2D08 watches the line that actually powers motor electronics coolant pump B, typically a fused 12 V feed plus ground: the voltage there is too low, too high or absent. The control-line faults of the same pump have their own codes, P0B38 to P0B3A, so P2D08 sends the search to fuses, relays, splices and the ground point rather than to the signal wire.
Corroded connector, loose terminal or poor ground at pump B
Blown fuse or faulty relay in the pump B feed
Weak 12 V battery or DC/DC converter delivering too little voltage
Chafed supply wire with intermittent contact
Additional voltage codes in neighbouring modules
P2D09: Motor Electronics Coolant Pump B Control Module Overtemperature
P2D09 is raised when the controller inside motor electronics coolant pump B reports that it has become too hot.
Low coolant or air, so pump B electronics lose their cooling
Restricted line or clogged component raising pump load and current
Internal defect of the pump B control board
Code appears mainly in hot weather or under sustained load
P2D0A: Motor Electronics Coolant Pump C Stuck/Stalled

P2D0A starts the five codes for pump C, a third electric pump that some layouts add to the motor electronics loop, for example for a further drive unit or a separate charger and DC/DC branch. The code means pump C is driven and powered but its rotor stays still.
Seized bearing or blocked rotor in pump C
Foreign bodies or deposits jamming the impeller
Burnt motor winding or failed start electronics in the pump
Pump C silent while commanded on
Rising temperature in the branch cooled by pump C and reduced power
P2D0B: Motor Electronics Coolant Pump C Overspeed/Air in System

P2D0B is stored when pump C of the motor electronics loop reaches a speed above the commanded value. Since a pump with air around its impeller loses load and accelerates, the code is first of all a hint at a low level, a leak or incomplete bleeding; a third pump in a branch that sits high in the vehicle is especially prone to trapping air.
Air trapped in the pump C branch after incomplete bleeding
Coolant loss through a leak in the loop
Loose impeller or false speed signal from the pump
Warning lamp on, sometimes without other effects
Coolant level below minimum or visible leak traces
Gurgling noise from the pump area
P2D0C: Motor Electronics Coolant Pump C Underspeed
P2D0C tells you that pump C, the third pump of the motor electronics loop, is turning too slowly for longer than its controller accepts.
Dragging bearing or internal friction in pump C
Partly clogged impeller or screen in the pump C branch
Voltage drop on feed or ground of pump C under load
Pump C speed below target in live data
Higher component temperatures and power limits under load
P2D0D: Motor Electronics Coolant Pump C Supply Voltage Circuit

P2D0D flags the supply side of motor electronics coolant pump C: the voltage on its power feed is outside the permitted window or missing. Its counterparts on the command line are P2BD4 (open), P2BD5 (low) and P2BD6 (high), so a technician who sees P2D0D alone should check the fuse, relay, power splice and ground of pump C before touching the signal wire.
Poor ground or corroded supply terminal at pump C
Blown fuse or faulty relay in the pump C feed
Weak 12 V battery or low DC/DC converter output
Pump C runs intermittently or not at all
Other voltage-related codes stored at the same time
P2D0E: Motor Electronics Coolant Pump C Control Module Overtemperature

P2D0E closes the motor electronics pump series: the control electronics integrated in pump C have reported an internal temperature above their limit. Smart pumps protect themselves by derating or switching off, and the module storing the code learns of it through the pump's status feedback.
Pump C running with too little coolant or air
Blocked branch raising pump load and electronics temperature
Defective control board inside pump C
Code sets mainly in heat or after long high-load operation
Pump C switches off and restarts after cooling
P2D0F: Pre-ignition means the charge ignites by itself ahead of the spark, mostly at low engine speed and high load in small turbocharged direct-injection engines.
Fuel with too low an octane rating or poor quality
Oil droplets in the chamber, unsuitable oil or oil diluted by fuel
Glowing carbon deposits on pistons or valves
Spark plugs with too hot a heat range or worn electrodes
Engine control calibration that needs a manufacturer update
Check engine light, often after hard acceleration from low speed
Sharp knocking or a single loud bang under load
Rough running or misfire if a piston has already been damaged
Rising oil consumption after repeated events
P2D10: Engine Pre-Ignition Above Threshold - Forced Limited Power

P2D10 is the escalated form of P2D0F: pre-ignition events have exceeded the threshold, and the engine computer now restricts power to protect pistons and rings. A Ford patent gives an idea of the scale, cutting engine load by about 10 percent after three detected events while also capping boost and enriching the mixture.
Engine software fault, known on VW 1.5 L turbo together with P0196
Repeated pre-ignition from low-octane or contaminated fuel
Oil droplets, wrong oil grade or fuel-diluted oil in the cylinder
Piston or ring damage that already keeps causing hot spots
Noticeably reduced power, often with a warning message
Check engine or EPC light on
Knocking noises under load before the limit kicks in
P2D11: Exhaust Flow Control Valve A Position Not Learned

Electrically driven exhaust flaps need their end stops taught to the control unit, so that commanded and actual angles line up. P2D11 says this adaptation is missing or invalid for valve A, as after a new actuator, a new muffler, a reflashed ECM or a flat battery.
Learn procedure not run after actuator, silencer or ECM work
Learned values lost after a flat or disconnected battery
Corroded or binding flap that cannot reach its end stops
Control software that rejects the learn result
Unusual exhaust noise, rattling or a flap hunting for position
Exhaust sound modes no longer change
P2D12: Exhaust Flow Control Valve B Position Not Learned
P2D12 is the counterpart of P2D11 for the second flap or bank 2: the stored end positions of exhaust valve B are missing or were rejected. No manufacturer documents P2D12 publicly.
Alignment or learn run for valve B skipped after repair
Adaptation erased by a discharged or disconnected battery
Actuator mounted out of position or flap shaft binding
Outdated engine software that makes the learn fail
MIL on, sometimes with an exhaust mode not available message
Flap B noisy or searching for position
No audible change between sound modes on one side
P2D13: Exhaust Flow Control Valve C Control Circuit/Open

P2D13 tells that the drive circuit of a third exhaust flap, valve C, is open or cannot be evaluated. Such a valve only exists on layouts with more than two controlled flaps, for instance a separate bypass in the rear silencer next to one flap per bank. No manufacturer publishes P2D13 or any other valve C code.
Actuator connector unplugged or loose after exhaust work
Broken control wire near the hot exhaust or at a bracket
Internal open in the valve C actuator
Failed output stage in the control module
Flap C stays in its rest position, exhaust sound does not change
Message that an exhaust or drive mode is unavailable
P2D14: Exhaust Flow Control Valve C Control Circuit Low

With P2D14 the drive wire of flap C is dragged toward ground when the driver expects a higher level. Chafed insulation touching the body or the exhaust, a crushed harness after the car was jacked up, or a shorted actuator winding are the classic reasons. No manufacturer documents P2D14.
Control wire chafed through and touching ground
Shorted winding or electronics in the valve C actuator
Water or salt bridging pins in the connector
Flap C does not move or stays at its default angle
Exhaust louder or quieter than the selected mode
P2D15: Exhaust Flow Control Valve C Control Circuit High

P2D15 is set when the drive wire of flap C carries too high a level, so the output stage cannot pull it down as commanded. Either the wire touches something live, or the electronics inside the actuator push voltage back onto it. No manufacturer publishes P2D15.
Control wire shorted to a voltage-carrying circuit
Defective electronics in the valve C actuator feeding voltage back
Output stage in the control module stuck high
Flap C open or moving without being commanded
P2D16: Exhaust Flow Control Valve C Control Performance

P2D16 covers the case where flap C passes every wiring test but still fails to follow its command: it moves too slowly, stops short of the target or drifts away from it. No manufacturer documents valve C codes publicly. Ford's handling of its A and B flaps shows the idea.
Flap shaft seized by soot or corrosion
Worn or overheated actuator motor or gearbox
Silencer or actuator bracket misaligned after exhaust work
MIL on, possibly with an exhaust mode warning
Rattle or buzzing from the flap area
Exhaust sound no longer matches the selected mode
P2D17: Exhaust Flow Control Valve C Position Circuit

P2D17 is the catch-all fault for the return signal by which actuator C reports its angle to the engine computer. The signal is missing or unusable, yet it does not fit the clear low or high pattern of P2D19 and P2D1A. The code can only appear where a third flap with its own position output exists. No manufacturer documents P2D17.
Corroded or loose connector on actuator C
Damaged feedback or ground wire near the exhaust
Failed position sensor inside the actuator
Flap C held in a default position by the control unit
P2D18: Exhaust Flow Control Valve C Position Circuit Range/Performance

With P2D18 the position signal of flap C is electrically sound, but its value makes no sense: the reported angle lags or contradicts the command, the end points have wandered off the stored values, or the reading creeps while the flap is idle. No manufacturer publishes P2D18.
Actuator or silencer shifted so the end points no longer match
Worn or drifting position sensor in the actuator
Pinched or chafed wiring causing an unsteady signal
Learned values no longer valid after parts were replaced
MIL on after a drive cycle
Exhaust note changes at the wrong moment or flap C hunts
Drive or exhaust mode reported unavailable
P2D19: Exhaust Flow Control Valve C Position Circuit Low

P2D19 is stored when the angle feedback from actuator C drops beneath the bottom of its permitted band. With an analog sensor the line then reads close to zero volts, mostly through a ground short or a lost 5 V supply; with a PWM return the duty cycle hangs close to zero. No manufacturer documents P2D19.
Missing sensor supply voltage or open supply wire
Position sensor in actuator C failed low
Faulty evaluation logic in the engine software
Flap C no longer adjusted, default position held
Possible power reduction on engines that tie the flap to cylinder deactivation
P2D1A: Exhaust Flow Control Valve C Position Circuit High

P2D1A flags an angle feedback from actuator C that sits above the top of its permitted band: an analog line close to the supply level, or a PWM return hanging near full duty. Typical reasons are a broken sensor ground, a feedback wire chafed against a live conductor, or water creeping between the connector contacts.
Feedback wire touching a voltage-carrying wire
Moisture or road salt in the actuator connector
Position sensor in actuator C failed high
Control unit ignores flap C feedback and stops adjusting it
Exhaust sound stuck in one mode
P2D1B: Exhaust Flow Control Valve C Position Not Learned

P2D1B closes the valve C series: the control unit holds no valid end stop values for the third exhaust flap, so it cannot translate its position feedback into a reliable angle. No manufacturer documents P2D1B publicly, and so far even the A and B versions P2D11 and P2D12 are rare in published material.
Learn run for flap C not completed after installation or repair
Learned end stops lost after battery disconnection
Flap blocked or binding so the learn run aborts
Engine software that needs an update before the learn succeeds
Check engine light shortly after exhaust or battery work
Flap C hunting, buzzing or rattling
Sound modes do not switch as expected
P2D1C: Cold Start EGR A/B Ratio Performance

P2D1C belongs to engines with two exhaust gas recirculation paths, A and B, whose share of the total recirculated flow is scheduled differently right after a cold start. The code says that during the cold start strategy the split between both paths did not follow its target.
EGR valve A or B sooted or sluggish, so it cannot reach its cold start position
Restricted EGR cooler or leaking pipe in one of the two loops
Faulty pressure, temperature or position signal used to estimate the flows
Engine control software that misjudges the split in cold weather
Check engine light after cold starts, often without noticeable driveability change
Rough or smoky running in the first minutes after starting
Further EGR flow codes such as P0401 or P049B stored alongside
P2D1D: Reductant System Leak Detected - Small Leak

P2D1D reports that the pressurised DEF (AdBlue) circuit between pump, line and dosing valve loses fluid slowly, too little to collapse pressure but enough to be measurable. No manufacturer documents this code publicly.
Seeping quick connector or damaged O-ring on the DEF pressure line
Worn seal or gasket at the DEF dosing valve on the exhaust pipe
Hairline crack in the DEF line, often after freezing or chafing
Pump module leaking internally or at its housing seal
Check engine light, usually with an exhaust service message
White crystalline deposits at line fittings or the dosing valve
DEF consumption noticeably higher than usual
P2D1E: Reductant System Leak Detected - Large Leak

P2D1E is the severe form of the DEF leak verdict: the pump cannot build or hold working pressure because fluid escapes freely, for example from a split or disconnected line. No manufacturer documents this code publicly.
DEF line pulled off or connector not latched after service
DEF line split by ice expansion or road debris
Cracked dosing valve body or blown seal at the exhaust
Cracked pump module housing in the tank unit
Check engine light and DEF system warning soon after start
Puddle or wet trail of DEF under the vehicle
Countdown to restricted speed or no restart
P2D1F: P2D1F means DEF still moves, but less than the dosing command implies, typically because a filter, line or dosing valve tip is partly clogged.
Urea crystals partly blocking the dosing valve nozzle
Clogged DEF pump filter or suction strainer
Kinked or pinched DEF line after body or exhaust work
Contaminated or aged DEF leaving deposits
Check engine light with exhaust fluid service message
Code returns intermittently, often without a lasting fault
Possible NOx efficiency code if dosing stays low

Dosing valve stuck closed or nozzle fully crystallised
Frozen DEF in line or valve due to a failed line heater

Pump filter completely blocked by deposits
Check engine light and DEF warning, often in frost
Countdown to speed limitation or start inhibit
P2D21: Turbocharger Interstage Pressure Sensor A Circuit

Engines with two turbochargers in series can measure the pressure between the low-pressure and the high-pressure compressor. GM's patent on two-stage boost control uses this mid-stage value to split the pressure ratio between both stages and to steer the low-pressure wastegate; Cummins describes the same sensor between the stages and the intercooler.

Chafed or heat-damaged harness near the turbochargers
Reduced power, boost held to a safe value
P2D22: Turbocharger Interstage Pressure Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance
P2D22 flags an interstage pressure reading that is electrically valid but implausible, for instance offset, stuck or out of step with the other pressures. No manufacturer documents a detection rule.
Sensor port clogged with oil or soot deposits
Leak in the duct or intercooler between the stages

Uneven boost build-up or reduced power
P2D23: Turbocharger Interstage Pressure Sensor A Circuit Low

P2D23 says the interstage pressure signal sits below the lowest voltage a working sensor can produce. Further codes if the shared sensor supply is affected
P2D24: Turbocharger Interstage Pressure Sensor A Circuit High

P2D24 is the opposite case to P2D23: the interstage pressure signal is pinned near or above the top of its range. On a three-wire sensor this usually points to an open ground, a signal wire touching the 5 V reference or battery voltage, or an open signal line pulled up inside the controller.

Open signal wire pulled up by the controller
Signal wire shorted to 5 V reference or battery voltage

P2D25: Turbocharger Interstage Pressure Sensor A Circuit Intermittent/Erratic

P2D25 is set when the interstage pressure signal jumps or drops out faster than any real pressure between two turbo stages could change, typically through brief interruptions in the circuit. No manufacturer documents the code or its rate limit publicly.
Loose or spread terminal in the sensor plug
Moisture or oil in the connector
Check engine light that comes and goes
P2D26: Coolant Pump E Control Circuit Performance/Stuck Off

P2D26 belongs to the general auxiliary coolant pumps, not to the motor electronics family above: pump E is the fifth electric pump of a vehicle, and its assignment (low-temperature loop, charge air cooler, turbo or component cooling) depends entirely on the manufacturer.
Pump E seized or mechanically worn so it does not reach its target
Air or low coolant in the loop served by pump E
High resistance in connector, feed or ground of pump E
Control module software requiring an update
Higher temperature in the circuit cooled by pump E
Possible reduced power, depending on what pump E cools
P2D27: Coolant Pump F Control Circuit Performance/Stuck Off

P2D27 is the functional check for coolant pump F, the sixth auxiliary pump in the lettering scheme and thus only relevant on vehicles with very many electric pumps, typically plug-in hybrids, electric vehicles or heavy diesels with several separate loops.
Pump F blocked or worn so it runs too weakly
Air pocket or low coolant in the circuit of pump F
Corroded connector or high resistance in the pump F supply
Overtemperature in the component or loop served by pump F
Power limitation if the cooled component protects itself

Throttle, intake leak or airflow error, so retarded spark cannot be balanced by more air
Misfires or weak ignition while spark is heavily retarded

Check engine light shortly after a cold start
Hesitant or uneven pull while the engine is still cold
Often no noticeable symptom when the cause is software
P2D29: Hybrids and electric vehicles drive the A/C compressor with its own high-voltage motor and inverter. P2D29 reports that this motor is commanded to turn but does not rotate. No manufacturer documents P2D29 publicly.
Mechanically seized compressor, often after oil loss or refrigerant leak
Fault in the compressor's integrated inverter or phase output
Restart against high head pressure or overcharged system
High-voltage supply to the compressor interrupted or weak
Warning about reduced battery cooling or charging power
Compressor phase current or overload codes stored alongside
P2D2A: Hybrid/EV Electronics Coolant Temperature Sensor A/B Correlation

Some drives measure the coolant of the inverter and power electronics loop at two points. After a long rest both should read nearly the same, so P2D2A records that sensors A and B disagree by more than the allowed margin; the code does not say which one is wrong. No manufacturer documents P2D2A publicly.
One of the two sensors has drifted
Added resistance in a connector or wire shifting one reading
Air pocket at one sensor after coolant service
Replacement sensor with a different characteristic
Electronics coolant pump runs more often or at full speed
Possible power reduction to protect the inverter
P2D2B: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Temperature Sensor A/B Correlation

Liquid-cooled traction batteries often have coolant sensors at pack inlet and outlet. When the pack has rested long enough, sensors A and B should agree; P2D2B records a gap beyond the limit without naming the faulty one. No manufacturer documents P2D2B publicly.
One pack coolant sensor has drifted
Corroded or loose connector at a sensor
Air trapped in the battery coolant loop after service
Faulty measuring input in the battery control module
Battery heater or chiller running unexpectedly
P2D2C: Engine Coolant Temperature Measurement System - Multiple Sensor Correlation

Engines with split or map-controlled cooling carry several coolant sensors, for example at head, block, inlet, outlet, radiator and heater core. After a cold soak all should read alike; P2D2C reports that the set as a whole disagrees and the module cannot single out one sensor. No manufacturer documents P2D2C publicly.
One coolant sensor in the set has drifted
Uneven soak, e.g. block heater or short stop, misread as a fault
Low coolant or air leaving one sensor dry
Temperature gauge or fan behaviour unusual
Rough cold running or higher fuel use when warming up
P2D2D: Cold Start Intake Manifold Runner Performance Bank 1

P2D2D reports that the intake manifold runner or swirl flaps of bank 1 did not reach the position the cold start strategy asked for. Many engines hold these flaps in a special setting after a cold start to stir the charge and stabilise combustion while the catalyst warms up.
Engine control software that judges the cold start flap check too strictly
Flap shaft or runner coated with soot and oil deposits, stiff when cold
Worn actuator or loose linkage on bank 1
Position sensor signal or wiring fault
Check engine light, usually without a noticeable driving change
Slightly rougher idle in the first minutes after a cold start
P2D2E or P200A may be stored too
P2D2E: Cold Start Intake Manifold Runner Performance Bank 2

P2D2E is the bank 2 version of the cold start runner check, so it only appears on V or boxer engines whose second cylinder row has its own flaps or actuator. The module compares the position commanded for the cold start phase with the feedback from that bank and flags a flap that stays short of target.
Engine control software, especially when P2D2D is stored at the same time
Deposits making the bank 2 flap shaft stiff in the cold
Bank 2 actuator, linkage or connector worn or corroded
Check engine light, often with no other complaint
Uneven idle shortly after a cold start
P2D2D or P200B may appear alongside
P2D2F: P2D2F means boost from turbocharger or supercharger A stayed below its target during the cold start strategy; P0299 is the same complaint in normal operation. CARB counts electronic wastegate position on petrol engines and variable turbine geometry on diesels among the features that must follow their cold start command.
Leak in charge air pipes, intercooler or intake manifold
Intake manifold damaged by combustion after an internal EGR cooler crack (FCA EcoDiesel recalls)
Variable turbine vanes or wastegate sticking in the cold
Engine control software that needs an update
Weak pulling power shortly after a cold start
Check engine light, sometimes together with P0299
Hissing noise under load if the charge air path leaks
P2D30: P2D30 is the opposite of P2D2F: during the cold start strategy, boost from turbocharger or supercharger A rose above the permitted value. Outside that phase P0234 covers it. CARB lists electronic wastegate position as a cold start feature that has to follow its command, so a gate that stays shut when the strategy wants it open is the classic trigger.
Wastegate flap or linkage stuck closed or stiff in the cold
Wastegate regulator solenoid blocked by frozen moisture or oil deposits
Electric wastegate actuator or its position feedback faulty
Boost pressure sensor reading too high
Sudden power reduction shortly after starting in the cold
Check engine light, sometimes with P0234 or a wastegate code
Unusually strong surge of power while the engine is cold
P2D31: Intake Manifold Tuning Valve Exceeded Learning Limit Bank 1

An intake manifold tuning valve switches the effective volume or length of the intake to use pressure waves for more cylinder filling. Electrically positioned versions learn the feedback value at their end stop, and P2D31 says that learned value lies outside its tolerance band.
Worn end stop or deposits changing the closed position of the valve
Bent valve plate or shaft after mechanical stress
Position sensor inside the actuator drifting
Actuator replaced without completing the relearn
Less torque in some engine speed ranges
P2D32: Intake Manifold Tuning Valve Control Circuit Driver Current/Temperature Too High Bank 1

P2D32 is an electrical self-protection code: the power stage that drives the motor of intake manifold tuning valve 1 has reported excessive current or overheating. Smart drivers watch both values internally and switch off before damage.
Valve jammed or stiff, so the motor draws excessive current
Internal short in the actuator motor
Chafed control wiring touching ground or another circuit
Faulty driver stage in the engine control module
Tuning valve stays in one position, with less torque in some rev ranges
Code may return soon after clearing if the valve stays jammed
P2D33: Hybrid/EV Battery Inductive Charger Control Module Processor Performance

P2D33 concerns the electronics on the vehicle side of a contactless charging system and states that the processor of the inductive charger module has failed one of its own self-tests, for example a memory checksum, a RAM test or a watchdog.
Internal fault of the inductive charger control module (memory, processor, watchdog)
Corrupted or outdated module software, for example after an interrupted update
Unstable 12 V supply or poor ground at the charger module causing resets
Wireless charging does not start or stops shortly after starting
Charging fault message in the instrument cluster or app
Code returns after clearing even though the vehicle is correctly positioned
P2D34: Hybrid/EV Battery Inductive Charger Control Circuit Range/Performance

P2D34 points at the control line of the inductive charger, the wired path over which a vehicle controller wakes, enables or commands the charger module. The circuit is not open or shorted, but its level or duty cycle lies outside the expected window or does not follow the command.
Corroded or loose connector raising the resistance of the control line
Software levels of charger module and commanding controller that do not match
Faulty output or input stage in one of the two modules
Inductive charging is not offered or ends without a clear reason
Charging works intermittently depending on vibration or temperature
P2D35: Hybrid/EV Battery Inductive Charging System High Voltage Interlock Circuit Performance

The inductive charger feeds its rectified DC power into the high-voltage system, so its connectors are usually part of a high voltage interlock loop (HVIL), a low-voltage circuit that breaks as soon as a plug or cover is opened.
Interlock or high-voltage connector at the inductive charger not fully latched
Oxidised or spread interlock terminals with high contact resistance
Chafed interlock wire near the underbody pad, which is exposed to water and stone impact
Faulty interlock source or sense stage in the monitoring module
Fault appears after work on the underbody or after driving through deep water
P2D36: Hybrid/EV Battery Inductive Charger Output Voltage Performance

P2D36 judges the DC side of the inductive charger: the voltage it hands to the traction battery is outside what the controller expects for the current state, too low to push charge current or above what the battery may accept. No manufacturer documents P2D36 publicly.
Faulty rectifier, switching stage or output filter in the vehicle assembly
Output voltage sensor drifting against the battery voltage measurement
Vehicle parked off-centre over the ground pad, so the output cannot be held
Regulation software of the charger module
Inductive charging stops shortly after it begins
Charging power far below the expected value
P2D37: Hybrid/EV Battery Inductive Charger Input Circuit Range/Performance

P2D37 looks at the input of the inductive charger, the high-frequency AC that arrives from the vehicle pickup coil before rectification. The measured input is present but implausible: it fits neither the power being transferred nor the other readings, or it does not react when the transfer ramps up.
Damaged or loose connection between pickup coil and charger module
Large coil offset, excessive ground clearance or metal object on the pad
Faulty input voltage or current sensing inside the charger module
Inductive charging starts with low power or not at all
Positioning aid reports the car as aligned, but charging still fails
P2D38: P2D38 is the functional check of the traction battery heater: it was switched on, yet the pack or its coolant did not warm as expected, or the heater ran too hot. CARB asks for such a heating check wherever feasible.
Heater element or its power switch delivering no or too little heat
Air, low coolant or a weak pump so that heat does not reach the pack sensors
Pack inlet or cell temperature sensor reading wrong, faking a missing rise or overheating
Control software that judges the heating too strictly (Toyota bZ4X case under investigation)
Malfunction indicator lamp or hybrid/EV system warning on
Slow charging or reduced power in cold weather
Battery stays cold although preconditioning was requested
P2D39: P2D39 is an event record: the traction battery opened its contactors because another system demanded it, not because the battery found a fault of its own. The classic trigger is a crash.
Collision or crash signal from the airbag control module
Shutdown request from another controller after a safety fault (isolation, interlock)
Spurious signal on the hard-wired disable line or network message error
Vehicle cannot be switched to ready or drive mode
High-voltage system warning in the instrument cluster
Code persists until it is erased with a scan tool
P2D3A: P2D3A records that the high-voltage system as a whole was shut down by force rather than in the normal power-down sequence. Stellantis uses it in the battery pack control module (BPCM) of its 400 V STLA Large electric cars, the 2025 Dodge Charger Daytona (bulletin 08-025-25) and the 2024–2025 Jeep Wagoneer S (08-011-25, 08-128-25).
Battery control module reset or reprogramming leaving the shutdown latched (Stellantis BPCM)
Software fault in the battery or vehicle control module
Safety reaction to another high-voltage fault, which is stored alongside
Vehicle does not enter drive-ready mode
Wrench or service warning in the instrument cluster
P2D3B: After the contactors open, the capacitors of inverter and DC link still hold high voltage, so a discharge system, either a resistor or an active circuit in the power electronics, drains them within seconds. P2D3B is the general fault code for this system; the narrower ones are P0C75 and P0C76 for discharge time and P0EED for the discharge circuit.
Faulty active discharge switch or driver in the inverter
Open or degraded passive discharge resistor
Wrong high-voltage reading in the inverter or battery module
Contactor that does not open, so the bus stays fed from the battery
Vehicle does not become ready on the next start
P2D3C: Cold Start Hybrid/EV Drive Motor Performance
In a hybrid the electric drive motor can be part of the strategy that cuts emissions after a cold start, and P2D3C says it did not perform as that strategy required.
Motor output derated by temperature or another motor fault
Cold or weak traction battery limiting the power available to the motor
Calibration of the cold start strategy in the hybrid controller (software update)
Resolver or motor position sensor fault affecting torque delivery
Engine starts earlier or runs rougher after a cold start than usual
Often no noticeable change in driving
P2D3D: Cold Start Hybrid/EV Drive Motor Inverter Torque Performance

P2D3D narrows the cold start check to the inverter: during the cold start strategy, the torque it produced through the drive motor did not match the torque the hybrid controller commanded. Precise torque matters in this phase because motor and engine share the work.
Phase current sensing error in the inverter distorting the delivered torque
Torque derating because of very low or high power electronics temperature
Torque coordination of the cold start strategy in software
Slight jerk when the engine fires after a cold start
P2D3E: P2D3E states that the traction battery could not support the cold start emission strategy as planned, typically because it could not deliver the power the strategy relied on. While the engine heats the catalyst at low output, the battery has to carry most of the driving load.
Aged traction battery with raised internal resistance and voltage sag
Very cold pack after a long rest, limiting discharge power
State of charge too low to carry the load during warm-up
Weak module or cell imbalance pulling a single cell to its limit early
Engine has to work harder right after a cold start, electric assist feels weak
Other battery capacity or temperature codes stored
P2D3F: Hybrid/EV Battery Cooling System B Performance

P2D3F is the functional check of a second cooling path of the traction battery, alongside A (P0C32) and C (P2D40). Which path carries which letter is the manufacturer's choice; packs may be cooled by air, by a coolant radiator or by a refrigerant chiller, and some switch between them. No manufacturer documents P2D3F publicly.
Low coolant or trapped air in the battery loop
Blocked radiator, cooler or air duct of this cooling path
Diverter valve or pump that does not route enough flow through path B
Coolant or cell temperature sensor reading wrong
Malfunction indicator lamp or hybrid system warning on
Reduced electric power or slower fast charging in hot weather
P2D40: Hybrid/EV Battery Cooling System C Performance

P2D40 is the functional check of the third cooling path of the traction battery. Ford uses it for the refrigerant chiller on the 2020–2023 Explorer, Aviator and Police Interceptor Utility hybrids (FHEV and PHEV); the code is stored in the secondary OBD module SOBDMC and lights the MIL.
Low refrigerant charge in the A/C circuit feeding the battery chiller
Air in the coolant or pinched, kinked battery coolant hoses
Partly blocked battery chiller (high voltage battery cooler)
Coolant diverter valve or battery coolant pump not delivering flow through the chiller
Battery temperature rises during hard driving or towing, power may be reduced
Weak cabin air conditioning if the refrigerant charge is low
P2D41: A/C Compressor Motor Voltage B Performance

P2D41 is a plausibility check on the second voltage value that an electric A/C compressor reports for its motor drive: the reading is electrically valid but disagrees with a reference, for example the traction battery voltage or the first compressor voltage value.
Faulty voltage measurement inside the compressor control module
Contact resistance at the high-voltage connector of the compressor
Implausible reference value from the battery or hybrid control module
Hybrid or EV warning message, warning lamp depending on the manufacturer
A/C cooling reduced or switched off
P2D42: A/C Compressor Motor Voltage B Low

P2D42 is stored when voltage B at the electric A/C compressor motor stays below the lower limit of its working range, so the inverter cannot drive the motor properly and usually switches it off. Unlike a sensor circuit code, it refers to the voltage that is actually present. No manufacturer documents P2D42 on an official public source.
Blown A/C high-voltage fuse, often after an internal compressor short
Loose or corroded high-voltage connector at the compressor
Internal fault in the compressor inverter or measurement
Hybrid system warning, possibly reduced battery cooling or charging power
P2D43: A/C Compressor Motor Voltage B High

With P2D43 the controller reports that compressor motor voltage B has climbed above the level its power stage can withstand; the compressor controller normally stops the motor to protect its transistors. No manufacturer documents P2D43 on an official public source.
Faulty voltage measurement in the compressor control module
Voltage spikes on the high-voltage bus during charging or regeneration
Faulty DC/DC converter or on-board charger
A/C switches off, sometimes only for a while
P2D44: P2D44 is the overall function check of the electric A/C compressor motor: it is commanded to run but does not deliver what is expected, typically a speed feedback that does not follow the request, while no single voltage or current fault is flagged. No manufacturer documents P2D44 on an official public source.
Internal mechanical wear or lack of oil in the compressor
Wrong refrigerant charge or excessive high-side pressure
Fault in the compressor inverter or its speed evaluation
A/C cools poorly or not at all
Battery cooling restricted on plug-in hybrids and EVs
P2D45: P2D45 means the diesel exhaust fluid in the tank does not warm up as it should while the tank heater is working, so frozen or very cold fluid cannot be dosed. GM uses the code in its diesel OBD tables from 2021 to 2025 in two variants.
Tank heater element degraded or partly failed
Low supply voltage to the heater, e.g. weak battery or poor ground
Tank temperature sensor reading too low
MIL after two trips in cold weather
DEF or SCR warning message, dosing delayed
Possible countdown to speed limitation if the fault persists
P2D46: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack B Over Temperature

P2D46 extends the pack over-temperature check to a battery that is split into several separately watched sections: section B has run hotter than its protection limit, while section A, on undivided batteries the whole pack, uses P0A7E. No manufacturer documents P2D46 publicly.
Restricted coolant or air flow through section B (blocked channel, kinked hose, clogged intake)
Sustained high load or repeated fast charging in hot weather
Temperature sensor in section B reading too high without a circuit fault
Aged modules in section B with raised internal resistance
Hybrid or EV system warning and check engine light
Reduced electric drive power and regeneration
P2D47: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack C Over Temperature
With P2D47 the battery controller reports that the third section of a divided traction battery, C, has exceeded its temperature limit.
Blocked cooling channel or air duct serving section C
Poor thermal contact between section C modules and the cooling plate (missing or displaced thermal paste/pad)
Temperature sensor in section C reading high
Check engine or hybrid system warning light
Less electric power, especially after longer drives
Battery cooling fan or pump running at high speed
P2D48: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack D Over Temperature

P2D48 is the over-temperature code for the fourth section, D, of a sectioned high-voltage battery. Before treating it as real heat, a technician should ask whether the temperature value itself can be trusted.
Implausible temperature data from the battery electronics (internal communication or software fault)
Insufficient cooling of section D (coolant flow, pump, chiller, air path)
Genuine cell overheating in section D due to an internal cell defect
Hybrid system or battery warning, possibly a fire hazard message
Vehicle may refuse to start or enter drive-ready mode
P2D49: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack E Over Temperature

P2D49 says that section E, the fifth separately monitored part of a traction battery, is hotter than permitted. One trap with every pack over-temperature code is heat produced after the car has been switched off.
Battery controller logic or threshold too strict for normal post-shutdown warming (software update)
Reduced cooling of section E (coolant flow, fan, duct)
Parking in strong sun or heat after hard use
Hybrid warning light, sometimes only after the car has stood
P2D4A: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack F Over Temperature
P2D4A covers section F, the sixth part of a battery whose controller watches temperature section by section.
Aged modules in section F producing extra heat (often with P0EE1)
Insufficient cooling flow to section F
Sensor in section F reading too high
Warning light; timing depends on manufacturer (first or second trip)
Shorter electric range and weaker electric drive
Battery fan or coolant pump louder than usual
P2D4B: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack G Over Temperature
P2D4B reports overheating in section G, the seventh separately supervised part of the traction battery. Such a letter only makes sense for big packs with many groups.
Insufficient cooling of section G (coolant distribution, trapped air, pump)
Worn module in section G (compare with P2CCC)
Temperature sensor of section G reading too high
Displayed electric range shorter than usual
P2D4C: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack H Over Temperature

P2D4C stands for overheating of section H, the eighth monitored portion of a traction battery. Eight sections is also the largest split found in public service information, the Audi Q5 PHEV with groups 1 to 8, so H marks the edge of documented practice; Audi publishes only the ageing code P2CCD00 for its group 8, and no manufacturer documents P2D4C.
Battery cooling loop fault (low coolant, pump, chiller, valve) affecting section H
Local flow restriction or poor cold-plate contact at section H
Worn module in section H (see P2CCD)
Warning lamp and possibly further battery cooling codes
P2D4D: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack I Over Temperature

P2D4D is meant for section I, the ninth subdivision of a battery that is supervised section by section; no published battery has that many monitored groups, and no manufacturer documents the code. Where it is used, the reaction depends on how much margin the controller keeps.
Heavy charging or discharging current (fast charging, towing, climbs) beyond cooling capacity
Temperature sensor of section I reading high
Charging power drops sharply during fast charging
Reduced drive power with warning message
Check engine or EV system light
P2D4E: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack J Over Temperature

P2D4E marks overheating of section J, the tenth separately judged part of a sectioned pack; its ageing counterpart is P2CCF. No manufacturer documents P2D4E publicly. The useful first step is to compare the temperatures of section J with those of its neighbours in live data.
One temperature sensor in section J drifting high while neighbours read normal
Worn modules in section J (check P2CCF)
Warning light with reduced electric power
Section J temperature clearly above its neighbours in live data
P2D4F: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack K Over Temperature

P2D4F reports that section K, the eleventh supervised section of a high-voltage battery, has gone over its temperature limit; overheating and ageing of the same section are kept apart, the latter being P2CD0. No manufacturer documents P2D4F publicly.
Low coolant level or air trapped in the battery loop, often after service
Weak or intermittently failing battery coolant pump
Worn modules in section K (compare with P2CD0)
Warning light, often under load or in summer
Reduced electric drive and charging power
Coolant pump or fan audible for a long time after driving
P2D50: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack L Over Temperature

P2D50 is the last code in the lettered over-temperature series: after P0A7E for section A, or the whole pack if it is undivided, and sections B to K (P2D46 to P2D4F), L is the twelfth section. The deterioration series runs further to N (P2CD3), but sections M and N have no matching heat code in the current lists. No manufacturer documents P2D50 publicly.
Worn or imbalanced modules in section L (see P2CD1, P0BBD)
Temperature sensor of section L reading high
P2D51: P2D51 is the general electrical code for the control circuit of an air-assist injection system, the circuit counterpart to P0065 to P0067. Assist air flowing around the injector tip breaks the fuel spray into finer droplets.
Open or shorted coil in the air-assist solenoid valve
Damaged wiring or corroded connector at the valve
Faulty output stage in the engine control module
Unsteady idle or harder cold starts
P2D52: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Temperature Sensor C Circuit

P2D52 is the general circuit code for a third coolant temperature sensor, C, in the liquid loop of a hybrid or EV battery. Sensors A and B are commonly the pack inlet and outlet; where C sits is not published and depends on the design. The code says only that the signal is unusable, without saying whether it lies under or over its limits.
Loose connector, damaged wire or corroded pin in the sensor C circuit
Battery controller software flagging the circuit wrongly (update)
Check engine or hybrid system light
Battery heating or cooling not working as expected
Charging or electric power may be limited
P2D53: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Temperature Sensor C Circuit Range/Performance

P2D53 means coolant temperature sensor C of the battery loop delivers an electrically valid value that does not fit its surroundings. Unlike P2D2B, which only sees that sensors A and B disagree, this code blames sensor C itself. No manufacturer documents P2D53 publicly.
Sensor C drifting or reacting slowly
Plausibility limits in the controller software too tight (update)
Contact resistance in the connector or air pocket at the sensor
Warning light, often after the car has stood for hours
No obvious driveability change at first
P2D54: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Temperature Sensor C Circuit Low

P2D54 flags the signal voltage of battery coolant temperature sensor C as too low. These sensors are NTC thermistors pulled up to a reference, so a falling voltage reads as rising temperature; a short to ground or an internally shorted sensor therefore looks like boiling coolant, while the loop itself may be cold. No manufacturer documents P2D54 publicly.
Signal wire of sensor C shorted to ground (chafed harness)
Moisture or coolant in the connector bridging the pins
Live data shows an implausibly hot coolant reading for sensor C
Warning light and possibly reduced power
P2D55: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Temperature Sensor C Circuit High

P2D55 is the counterpart to P2D54: the signal of battery coolant temperature sensor C sits at or near the reference voltage. On an NTC circuit with pull-up that is what an open circuit produces, so the controller sees an impossibly cold coolant value.
Open circuit: connector unplugged, broken wire or spread terminal
Signal wire shorted to a supply voltage
Live data shows about -40 °C for sensor C
Battery heating or cooling uses substitute values
Warning light; reduced power in cold weather possible
P2D56: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Temperature Sensor C Circuit Intermittent/Erratic

P2D56 points to a coolant temperature signal from sensor C that jumps around faster than liquid in the battery loop can really change temperature, while mostly staying inside the electrical limits. No manufacturer documents P2D56 publicly.
Loose or corroded terminal in the sensor C connector
Harness rubbing or moving with the battery, causing brief interruptions
Detection logic reacting to normal conditions (software update)
Warning light that comes and goes
Sensor C value jumps in live data, especially when wiggling the harness
P2D57: P2D57 belongs to a second alternator, called generator B, as fitted to some heavy trucks; GM, for instance, offered a secondary generator (option KHB) on 2019 Silverado medium-duty trucks with the 6.6 L diesel.
Damaged control line (LIN or command wire) or corroded connector
Faulty voltage regulator of the second alternator
Replacement alternator with an incompatible regulator
Second alternator charges at a fixed default voltage or not at all
P2D58: P2D58 reports that generator B, the second alternator of a dual charging system, does not deliver as commanded for mechanical reasons, most often because its drive slips. Such machines often sit on their own belt and idler.
Worn, glazed or oil-soaked drive belt slipping
Weak tensioner or loose idler pulley mounting
Stiff alternator bearing or faulty overrunning pulley
Charge warning lamp, low charging voltage
Belt squeal or noise from the second alternator
P2D59: P2D59 indicates that generator B has become too hot. Which machine B means is up to the manufacturer: a second alternator in a dual charging system or a second motor-generator in a hybrid. No manufacturer documents P2D59 publicly.
Obstructed cooling air path or reduced oil/coolant flow to the generator
Sustained high electrical load at low engine speed
Temperature sensor or regulator measuring wrongly
Reduced charging output or charge warning
On hybrids, limited electric or series-mode power
P2D5A: P2D5A compares two level sensors of the diesel exhaust fluid system: each delivers a valid signal, yet together they describe a fill level that cannot be true. Tanks with several level contacts, or vehicles with a main and an auxiliary tank, can cross-check their sensors this way. No manufacturer documents P2D5A on an official public source.
One level sensor failed or contaminated
Urea crystals or deposits on the sensing elements
Corrosion or poor contact at the tank sensor connector
Implausible or jumping DEF level display
Possible inducement countdown despite sufficient fluid
P2D5B: Battery Charging System Positive Contactor C Circuit
P2D5B is the umbrella electrical fault for charging-system contactor C on the plus pole, a third plus-side switch next to contactors A (P0D07) and B (P2BC4).
Coil of contactor C open or shorted internally
Damaged wiring or loose plug at the contactor or its module
Output stage or software of the controlling module
One charging mode refused or aborted
Charging or high-voltage warning in the cluster
P2D5C: Battery Charging System Positive Contactor C Stuck Closed
P2D5C is set when positive charging contactor C still conducts after the module commanded it to open; fused contacts are the usual reason. No manufacturer documents P2D5C publicly.
Main contacts of contactor C welded, e.g. after switching under load
Coil output stage does not switch off
Faulty voltage measurement on the charger side simulating a weld
Charging blocked after the previous session
High-voltage warning, possibly no ready mode
Code appears at the end of a charging session or at start-up
P2D5D: Battery Charging System Positive Contactor C Stuck Open

P2D5D means positive charging contactor C stays open although it was commanded closed, so the plus pole of that charging path never connects and the session fails right at the start. No manufacturer documents P2D5D publicly; Mazda, which lists the non-closing case for contactor B (P2BC6), says nothing about a C contactor.
Contactor C does not pull in (burnt contacts, jammed armature)
Insufficient coil supply due to wiring or connector resistance
Control software misjudges the precharge voltage
Charging in the affected mode does not start
Charging station reports an aborted session
P2D5E: Battery Charging System Positive Contactor C Control Circuit/Open

P2D5E concerns the wire that energises the coil of plus-side contactor C, not its power contacts: the module finds that the state of its output driver and that of the line disagree, typically because a wire or the coil winding is broken. No manufacturer documents P2D5E publicly.
Broken coil feed wire or pushed-back terminal
Coil winding of contactor C open
Output stage in the module defective
Charging in the affected mode not possible
Fault present continuously, not only while charging
P2D5F: Battery Charging System Positive Contactor C Control Circuit Range/Performance

P2D5F reports that the coil circuit of plus-side charging contactor C is intact yet behaves in a way that does not match the command: the coil current, the voltage on the line or the pull-in delay drift out of their expected band without amounting to a clear open, low or high condition.
Corroded or loose pins raising resistance in the coil circuit
Coil resistance of contactor C out of tolerance
Ageing output stage in the module
Contactor clicks late or audibly chatters
P2D60: Battery Charging System Positive Contactor C Control Circuit Low

P2D60 is logged when the coil feed of positive charging contactor C reads lower than commanded – usually the wire has found ground or the driver output is dragged low. Where the driver switches the supply side, the coil then gets too little current and the contactor stays open, or the driver shuts itself off for protection.
Coil feed wire shorted to ground
Moisture or corrosion in the contactor plug
Shorted turns in the coil of contactor C
Fault may appear only in wet weather
P2D61: Battery Charging System Positive Contactor C Control Circuit High

P2D61 points to excess voltage on the wire feeding the coil of plus-side contactor C, caused by touching a 12 V feed or by an output stage that no longer switches off. The real danger is a coil energised without command, closing the plus pole of the charging path while the module assumes it is open; charging is therefore normally inhibited.
Coil feed wire shorted to a 12 V supply
Output stage does not switch off
Wires swapped at a connector after repair work
Contactor may click without a charging request
P2D62: Battery Charging System Negative Contactor C Circuit

P2D62 is the collective electrical code covering minus contactor C, which connects the return conductor of the third charging path to the traction battery. Neither the code nor the meaning of C is documented by any manufacturer.
Coil of minus contactor C open or shorted
Wiring or plug fault on the minus contactor
P2D63: Battery Charging System Negative Contactor C Stuck Closed

P2D63 says negative charging contactor C has not opened on command; the return-side contacts are almost certainly fused. No manufacturer documents P2D63 publicly, and the Mercedes and Mazda bulletins that report a welded minus contactor B (P2BCC) do not mention C.
Fused main contacts of minus contactor C
Charger still supplying voltage during the check (false detection)
Vehicle may not become ready if the plus side is welded too
P2D64: Battery Charging System Negative Contactor C Stuck Open

P2D64 appears when minus charging contactor C does not close; the third charging path then lacks its return conductor and no current flows even with the plus contactor in. No manufacturer documents P2D64 publicly.
Minus contactor C does not pull in or contacts burnt
Weak coil supply from wiring or connector faults
Charging in the affected mode never starts
P2D65: Battery Charging System Negative Contactor C Control Circuit/Open

P2D65 concerns the line that drives the coil of minus-side charging contactor C: the module notices that what it commands and what the line actually shows do not match, which usually means a broken wire, a loose terminal or an open coil. No manufacturer documents P2D65 publicly.
Broken coil-drive wire or terminal pushed out of the connector
Open winding in the coil of minus contactor C
Faulty output stage in the controlling module
The charging mode routed through contactor C does not start
Code is stored even without a charging request
Charging fault message in the cluster
P2D66: Battery Charging System Negative Contactor C Control Circuit Range/Performance

P2D66 flags a coil circuit of minus charging contactor C that is connected but responds outside its expected band while showing neither a break nor a short. P2D66 is not described by any manufacturer, and GM's public tables list no range test for charge contactor coils.
Corroded or loose terminals raising circuit resistance
Coil resistance drifted through ageing or overheating
Module software with an unsuitable reference or calibration
Charging via contactor C drops out now and then
Fault occurs mainly in very cold or very hot conditions
P2D67: Battery Charging System Negative Contactor C Control Circuit Low

P2D67 is stored when the drive line of minus charging contactor C sits lower than the module expects, typically because the wire touches ground or the connector has taken in water. No manufacturer documents P2D67 publicly.
Drive wire chafed against the battery housing or body
Moisture or corrosion in the contactor connector
Shorted turns in the coil of minus contactor C
Charging mode via contactor C refused
Fault more frequent after rain or washing
P2D68: Battery Charging System Negative Contactor C Control Circuit High

P2D68 means the wire energising minus charging contactor C carries more voltage than commanded, for instance where it rubs on a 12 V line or the output stage keeps conducting. No manufacturer documents P2D68 publicly.
Drive wire chafed against a 12 V supply line
Output stage in the module no longer switches off
Wires swapped or pinched after repair work
Contactor may click without a charging request
P2D69: Battery Charging System Positive Contactor D Circuit

P2D69 collects electrical faults of positive charging contactor D, a fourth plus-side switch after A (P0D07), B (P2BC4) and C (P2D5B). What D connects is not public: none of the makers documents P2D69, and the NHTSA bulletin index since 2015 names neither P2D69 nor any contactor D.
Defective coil or contacts of plus contactor D
Wiring or connector fault between module and contactor D
Fault in the module that switches contactor D
Fault may only show when that charging mode is used
P2D6A: Battery Charging System Positive Contactor D Stuck Closed
P2D6A reports that positive charging contactor D still conducts after being told to open, nearly always because its contacts have welded. No manufacturer documents P2D6A publicly.
Contacts of plus contactor D welded by arcing
Coil kept energised by a faulty output stage
Faulty charger-side voltage measurement simulating a weld
Charging locked after the previous session
Vehicle may not become ready if the other pole is welded too
Fault appears at the end of a charging session
P2D6B: Battery Charging System Positive Contactor D Stuck Open
P2D6B is logged when positive charging contactor D fails to close on command, leaving the plus pole of its charging path disconnected. No manufacturer documents P2D6B publicly.
Burnt contacts or jammed armature in plus contactor D
Insufficient coil supply voltage or poor ground
Module software misjudging the voltage rise
Charging in the affected mode never starts
Charging station reports an immediate abort
P2D6C: Battery Charging System Positive Contactor D Control Circuit/Open

P2D6C covers the coil supply of positive charging contactor D rather than its main contacts. The module finds the line in a state that contradicts the command to its driver, mostly due to an interrupted wire or coil. No manufacturer documents P2D6C publicly.
Interrupted coil supply wire or backed-out terminal
Open coil in plus contactor D
Output stage of the module defective
Fault present permanently, not only while charging
P2D6D: Battery Charging System Positive Contactor D Control Circuit Range/Performance

P2D6D points to a coil circuit of positive charging contactor D that works but behaves implausibly: current or voltage on the line drifts out of its normal window although no open or short is present. No manufacturer documents P2D6D publicly, and GM's published tables contain no such range test for charge contactors.
Raised contact resistance in the coil circuit
Sluggish or partly jammed armature in contactor D
Ageing output stage delivering too little current
Charging via contactor D interrupted sporadically
Contactor pulls in late or chatters
P2D6E: Battery Charging System Positive Contactor D Control Circuit Low
P2D6E is set when the voltage on the coil supply of plus contactor D reads too low, usually a wire touching ground. No manufacturer documents P2D6E publicly.
Coil feed wire shorted to ground
Water or corrosion in the connector of contactor D
Shorted coil in plus contactor D
Charging mode via contactor D refused
Fault set as soon as the contactor is commanded
P2D6F: Battery Charging System Positive Contactor D Control Circuit High

P2D6F says the supply wire to the coil of plus contactor D sits above its commanded level. No manufacturer documents P2D6F publicly. GM's 2016 drive test for plus contactor A (P0D0A) treats an idle output within 0.4 V of the supply voltage as shorted to power.
Coil feed shorted to a 12 V supply
Contactor clicks unexpectedly with ignition on
P2D70: Battery Charging System Negative Contactor D Circuit

P2D70 groups electrical faults of negative charging contactor D, the return-side partner of plus contactor D (P2D69). What D switches and when P2D70 is set remain undocumented. Separate contactors in both poles of a charging path exist so that the inlet can be fully cut off; for diagnosis that means each pole must be tested alone.
Defective coil or contacts of minus contactor D
Wiring or connector fault on the contactor D circuit
Charging connector may stay locked after a session
P2D71: Battery Charging System Negative Contactor D Stuck Closed
P2D71 indicates that negative charging contactor D has stayed closed after an open command, as happens when the contacts fuse. No manufacturer documents P2D71 publicly.
Fused contacts in minus contactor D
Station kept supplying voltage during the check
Coil held on by a faulty output stage
Charging locked after a DC session
Vehicle may refuse to become ready if the plus side is welded as well
P2D72: Battery Charging System Negative Contactor D Stuck Open

P2D72 appears when negative charging contactor D will not close, leaving its path without a return lead; even with plus contactor D pulled in, nothing can be charged. No manufacturer documents P2D72 publicly.
Minus contactor D does not close mechanically
Weak coil supply or poor ground at contactor D
Module software misattributing a station fault
Charging in the affected mode never begins
Station aborts right after plugging in
P2D73: Battery Charging System Negative Contactor D Control Circuit/Open

P2D73 concerns the coil drive of negative charging contactor D: commanded and measured state of the line differ, pointing to an open wire, terminal or winding. No manufacturer documents P2D73 publicly. GM's test for the minus charge contactor (P0D11) is the direct analogue.
Open coil drive wire or loose terminal
Broken winding in minus contactor D
Defective driver or current sensing in the module
Charging mode via contactor D not available
P2D74: Battery Charging System Negative Contactor D Control Circuit Range/Performance

P2D74 says the coil circuit of minus charging contactor D answers commands in an unexpected way, although it is neither open nor shorted. No manufacturer documents P2D74 publicly, and no published GM table has a range test for charge contactor coils.
Aged connector adding resistance to the coil circuit
Coil of minus contactor D with changed resistance or inductance
Output stage no longer delivering full current
Charging via contactor D stops intermittently
Delayed contactor click when charging starts
P2D75: Battery Charging System Negative Contactor D Control Circuit Low

P2D75 is stored when the drive line of negative charging contactor D reads low. No manufacturer documents P2D75 publicly. How serious this is depends on wiring: a GM patent shows the coil switch either on the supply side or on the ground side.
Drive wire of contactor D shorted to ground
Moisture in the contactor D connector
Output stage shorted inside the module
Contactor may click without a command
P2D76: Battery Charging System Negative Contactor D Control Circuit High

P2D76 means the control wire of minus contactor D shows more voltage than the module asked for. No manufacturer documents P2D76 publicly. GM's 2016 test for the minus charge contactor (P0D11) flags a power short when the idle output gets within 0.4 V of the supply.
Drive wire of contactor D touching a 12 V feed
Output stage that no longer switches off
Crossed wires after work on the battery
Charging mode via contactor D blocked
Fault appears as soon as ignition is on
P2D77: Battery Charger Control Module B Performance

P2D77 says the control electronics of charger B, a second on-board charger or charger stage, do not work as intended; faults of its processor are filed separately under P2D78. No manufacturer documents P2D77 publicly.
Internal power or control stage of charger B failed (unit replacement)
Internal low-voltage supply rail of charger B out of tolerance
Weak 12 V supply or poor ground at the charger
Charger software fault, cured by an update where one exists
AC charging does not start or stops after a short time
Charging fault message or warning in the instrument cluster
Charging possible only at reduced power, if the other charger path still works
P2D78: Battery Charger Control Module B Processor Performance

P2D78 points at the processor inside the control module of charger B: its self-tests of program or working memory have failed, so the module no longer trusts its own computations. All other functional faults of that module belong to P2D77. No manufacturer documents P2D78 publicly.
Memory or processor hardware in the charger B control unit defective
Corrupted charger software, e.g. after an interrupted update
12 V supply dip while the charger boots
Plug-in charging is refused right after connecting
Charging system warning in the cluster
P2D79: P2D79 covers the circuit of a charging stop switch as a whole, a button the driver presses to end external charging before the battery is full. The code is set when the switch line carries no valid signal at all; high, low, performance and intermittent faults of the same line have their own codes P2D7A to P2D7D. No manufacturer documents P2D79 publicly.
Loose, corroded or unplugged connector at the stop switch
Broken wire between stop switch and charging control unit
Charging cannot be ended with the stop button
Charging may be refused as a precaution
P2D7A: P2D7A means the voltage on the charging stop switch line stays above the band the control unit accepts. This refers to the signal, not to the button position: typical causes are a broken wire or switch contact on a line held up by a pull-up resistor, or a short to a supply voltage. No manufacturer documents P2D7A publicly.
Stop switch signal wire chafed through and touching a supply voltage
Open circuit in the stop switch line or connector (pull-up design)
Burnt or broken contact inside the stop switch
Charging does not start although the plug is connected
Pressing the stop button has no effect during charging
P2D7B: P2D7B is stored when the charging stop switch line is pulled below its permitted voltage, most often by a short to ground in the wiring, water in the switch or a contact that no longer opens on a switch that grounds the line when pressed. No manufacturer documents P2D7B publicly.
Stop switch signal wire shorted to body ground
Moisture or corrosion bridging the stop switch contacts
Stop switch contact stuck closed (ground-switching design)
Charging does not begin or ends immediately after plugging in
Charging indicator shows no active session
