P2D7C: P2D7C covers a stop switch signal that is electrically valid but does not make sense. A typical rationality test asks whether the reported state fits the situation, for instance a stop request that never ends although no one can hold a button that long, or a switch that reports pressed before any charging session has begun.
Stop button mechanically sticking in the pressed position
Internal leakage in the switch giving an in-between signal
Trim panel or object pressing on the button
Charging blocked although the plug is seated correctly
Stop button feels stiff or does not spring back
P2D7D: P2D7D flags a stop switch signal that jumps between states without a matching button press, or drops out briefly and returns. Since the charging control treats a stop signal as an order to end charging, as both the Toyota and the Honda patents describe, a flickering line can end a session without anyone touching the button.
Loose or fretting terminal at the stop switch connector
Cracked solder joint or worn contact inside the switch
Wire chafing that shorts only intermittently
Battery not full in the morning despite being plugged in
P2D7E: P2D7E is the umbrella circuit code for a charging start switch, the control with which a person begins a charging session by hand, for example to override a charging timer. It is set when the start switch line delivers no usable signal; the split into high, low, performance and intermittent follows in P2D7F to P2D82.
Loose, corroded or unplugged connector at the start switch
Broken wire between start switch and charging control unit
Pressing the start button does not begin charging
Charging only begins at the programmed timer time
P2D7F: P2D7F reports a start switch line sitting above its allowed voltage, caused by an open wire or contact on a pulled-up input or by contact with a supply voltage. No manufacturer documents P2D7F publicly. With a start button the consequences run the other way than with the stop switch P2D7A.
Open circuit in the start switch line or connector (pull-up design)
Start switch signal wire shorted to a supply voltage
Start switch contact no longer closes
Charging begins only by timer or after re-plugging
P2D80: P2D80 is set when the start switch line is dragged below its valid voltage, typically through a short to ground or a contact that stays closed on a button that grounds the input when pressed. No manufacturer documents P2D80 publicly. In that common layout a grounded line reads as a start button held down forever.
Start switch signal wire shorted to ground
Start switch contact stuck closed or bridged by moisture
Corrosion in the connector creating a path to ground
Charging ignores the timer or starts unexpectedly before the code is set
Start button no longer works after the fault is detected
P2D81: P2D81 is the plausibility code of the charging start switch: the wiring reads as healthy, yet the reported switch behaviour cannot be right.
Start button sticking or not returning
Worn switch contacts giving an unclear signal
Connector detection signal wrong, so a valid press seems implausible
Start button works only sometimes or not at all
Charging message about a switch fault
P2D82: P2D82 describes a start switch signal that toggles on its own or vanishes for moments. Because a start command is a trigger rather than a stop order, the visible effect is different from P2D7D: a flickering contact may start a charging session nobody asked for, for example ahead of a cheaper overnight tariff set in the timer, or swallow a deliberate press.
Loose or fretting terminal at the start switch connector
Worn contacts bouncing inside the start switch
Wire damage that makes contact only at times
Charging starts at unexpected times despite a timer
P2D83: Battery Charger B Input Current Sensor Circuit Low

P2D83 says the current sensor at the input of charger B outputs a signal under its valid range. No manufacturer documents P2D83 publicly. For charger A the same fault is P0D3A, which Mitsubishi interprets on the 2022 Outlander PHEV as a ground short.
Current sensor of charger B or its signal path shorted to ground inside the unit
Sensor supply inside the charger missing
Damaged internal connection or external harness where the sensor is separate
AC charging aborts shortly after starting
Reduced charging power if only charger A is still used
P2D84: Battery Charger B Input Current Sensor Circuit High

P2D84 is the high-side fault of charger B's input current sensor: its signal climbs above what the measuring range allows. No manufacturer documents P2D84 publicly, so the A-side code P0D3B serves as reference.
Charger B current sensor output shorted toward its supply inside the unit
Current sensor of charger B failed (charger repair or replacement)
Reference or ground of the sensor lost, pushing the signal up
AC charging does not start or stops within seconds
Charging fault warning in the cluster
P2D85: Battery Charger B Input Current Sensor Circuit Range/Performance
P2D85 is for an input current reading of charger B that lies within the electrical limits yet cannot be true. No manufacturer documents P2D85 publicly.
Zero-point drift of the charger B current sensor
Real residual current through a defective input stage while charging is not released
Calibration or software fault of the charger
Charging refused or stopped soon after plugging in
P2D86: P2D86 checks two fuel temperature sensors against each other. Where both ought to show nearly the same value, because they measure the same fuel or after a long engine-off soak, a gap larger than a calibrated margin makes the pair implausible, without telling which sensor lies. No manufacturer documents P2D86 publicly.
One of the two fuel temperature sensors has drifted and reads too warm or too cold
Corroded or loose connector adding resistance to one sensor signal
Replacement sensor of the wrong type or fitted in the wrong position
Engine control software with too tight a comparison limit
Malfunction indicator lamp, usually after two drives
Often no noticeable change in how the engine runs
Occasionally rougher hot restarts if fuel quantity correction is off
P2D87: Current electric radiator fans carry their own electronics, which turn the PWM or LIN request of the engine controller into motor current. P2D87 means this control module of fan 1 reports that it has become too hot.
Worn bearings or debris make the fan motor stiff, so the module overheats from excess current
Clogged radiator or condenser fins, missing air guides, heat build-up at standstill
Ageing power stage or thermal contact inside the fan control module
Fan runs slower or switches off temporarily
Rising coolant temperature in slow traffic
P2D88: P2D88 means the electronics of fan 1 do not behave as expected although supply and communication are present: the module reports an internal fault, or the speed it sends back does not fit the request. Audi documents the code for 2025 Q5, Q5 Sportback, SQ5 and SQ5 Sportback in TSB 2081184/1.
Poor or wrongly fitted ground connection of the fan
Internal fault of the fan control electronics
Fan blocked or slowed by debris or bearing wear
Moisture or corrosion in the fan connector or LIN line
Fan does not run or runs irregularly
P2D89: Fan 1 Control Module Supply Voltage Circuit

P2D89 concerns the power feed of the fan 1 control module: the voltage at its supply terminal, or the value the module reports back, is missing or outside the permitted window. Porsche uses the code in the DME of the 2021–2023 718 Cayman GTS 4.0, Boxster GTS 4.0, Cayman GT4 and Spyder and names it radiator fan 1 (left), power supply.
Engine control software that misjudges the fan supply during start-up (Porsche 198/22)
Blown fuse, loose terminal or high-resistance supply cable to the fan module
Corroded or loose ground of the fan module
Weak battery or charging system dropping the supply during high fan load
Engine control warning in the instrument cluster
P2D8A: P2D8A is the second-fan twin of P2D87: the electronics that power fan 2 signal that they have reached their temperature limit. On cars with two radiator fans the second one usually sits on the other side of the shroud; Porsche, for instance, calls its right-hand fan number 2. No manufacturer publicly documents P2D8A.
Stiff or partly blocked fan 2 motor overloading its electronics
Heat build-up around the module, e.g. clogged fins or damaged air guides
Defective temperature sensing or power stage in the fan 2 module
Second fan slows down or cuts out after long idling
P2D8B: With P2D8B the module that drives fan 2 fails a plausibility or self-test: it has supply and receives a request, yet the status or speed it reports does not fit. Audi's TSB 2081184/1 for the 2025 Q5 family lists P2D8B next to P2D88 and the local LIN bus error U366500, all stored in the thermal management control unit (address 00C5).
Damaged or incorrectly fitted ground point of fan 2
Foreign objects or worn bearings slowing fan 2
Internal electronics fault of the fan 2 module
Water ingress or corrosion at connector or LIN line
P2D8C: Fan 2 Control Module Supply Voltage Circuit

P2D8C concerns the supply circuit of the fan 2 control module. The engine controller registers that the module does not get proper operating voltage, whether through an open or high-resistance feed, a blown fuse, a poor ground or a reported voltage outside its window.
Blown fuse or high-resistance supply line to the fan 2 module
Engine control software error at start-up (Porsche 198/22)
Second radiator fan fails now and then
P2D8D: In a P2 hybrid a disconnect clutch between combustion engine and electric machine lets the car drive on electric power alone and couples the engine in when needed. P2D8D aims at the clutch hardware itself, not at its actuator, pressure sensor or wiring, which have their own codes: the clutch does not take up or release torque the way the control expects.
Worn or glazed clutch plates that slip or no longer hold torque
Mechanically binding piston or plates so the clutch does not release fully
Pressure regulating valve of the clutch mechanically faulty
Wrong, aged or contaminated transmission fluid changing friction behaviour
Engine does not couple in or starts with a jerk
Transmission or hybrid warning in the cluster
Limp mode with reduced power or electric-only driving
P2D8E: Engine Oil Pressure Sensor/Switch C Circuit

Some engines have more than one oil pressure sensor or switch; which one is labelled A, B or C is up to the manufacturer. P2D8E is the general circuit code for sensor or switch C: the controller sees an electrical fault, or with a digital SENT sensor a message or internal error, that it cannot classify as too low or too high.
Oil-soaked, corroded or loose connector at sensor C
Internal electronics fault of the sensor or switch
Chafed or broken wire between sensor and engine control unit
Malfunction indicator lamp, depending on make
Oil pressure warning may come on without real pressure loss
Switchable oil pump may stay in its safe high-pressure stage
P2D8F: Engine Oil Pressure Sensor/Switch C Circuit Low
P2D8F means the signal of oil pressure sensor C lies below its valid electrical range, which usually points to a short to ground, a lost supply or a defective sensor.
Voltage spike from a workshop charger switched on with the ignition (Audi EA888 evo5)
Signal or supply wire of sensor C shorted to ground
Sensor C defective with output stuck near zero
Engine control calibration that sets the fault too readily
Oil pressure warning without real pressure loss
Warning message in the instrument cluster
P2D90: Engine Oil Pressure Sensor/Switch C Circuit High

P2D90 is set when sensor C delivers a voltage above its valid range. Typical reasons are a broken ground or signal wire that lets the input float up, a short to battery voltage or a sensor with a failed output stage. No manufacturer publicly describes P2D90; for the EA888 evo5 Audi documents only the low counterpart P2D8F.
Open ground or signal wire of sensor C
Signal wire shorted to battery or reference voltage
Malfunction indicator lamp, depending on make
Oil pressure gauge or warning shows implausible values
Variable oil pump may stay in its safe stage
P2D91: Engine Oil Pressure Sensor/Switch C Circuit Range/Performance

P2D91 says sensor C is electrically in range, but its reading does not fit the engine's state: pressure while the engine stands still, too little at speed, or a value that stays frozen while conditions change.
Sensor C drifted or stuck at one value
Real oil pressure deviation from worn pump, wrong oil or low oil level
Sticking oil pressure control valve of a variable pump
Sludge or debris in the sensor bore
Malfunction indicator lamp after two drives on some makes
Oil pressure warning flickers or appears without reason
Possible engine noise if pressure is really low
P2D92: Starter/Generator Phase X Current Sensor Circuit High
P2D92 is set when the signal from the phase X current sensor of a belt or crankshaft starter/generator rises above the range the control electronics treat as valid.
Phase X sensor signal wire shorted to a supply or reference voltage
Current sensor output failed at the upper end of its range
Damaged, corroded or water-contaminated connector at the starter/generator
Fault in the evaluation circuit of the starter/generator control module
Warning lamp or MIL, often only after the fault has been seen on two trips
Reduced electric assist and weaker restarts after automatic engine stop
P2D93: Starter/Generator Phase Y Current Sensor Circuit High

P2D93 reports that the current reading for phase Y of the starter/generator has climbed past its upper validity limit. Y is the middle letter of the X/Y/Z set this code series uses; the same list also has U/V/W variants (P2D9B to P2D9D), and no maker explains publicly how it assigns them. Not every design measures every phase.
Phase Y sensor signal lead chafed and touching a voltage-carrying wire
Internal fault of the phase Y current sensor in the machine electronics
Defective input stage in the starter/generator control module
Hybrid or charging system warning on the instrument cluster
Boost function during acceleration missing or reduced
Engine restarts by the conventional starter or not at all after auto stop
P2D94: Starter/Generator Phase Z Current Sensor Circuit High

P2D94 completes the high-side series: the phase Z current sensor of the starter/generator outputs a value above its valid window. Inverters for 48 V starter/generators are built for three- or six-phase machines, and the controller relies on measured phase currents to set torque for engine restarts, boost and energy recovery.
Pinched sensor lead or loose plug at the starter/generator
Water ingress into the machine-mounted electronics
Phase Z current sensor defective, output reads too high
Battery warning because the machine charges less or not at all
P2D95: Starter/Generator Phase X Current Sensor Circuit Low

P2D95 means the phase X current sensor of the starter/generator delivers a signal below the lowest value the controller accepts. The machine works as motor and as generator, so its phase currents change direction and the sensor reports signed values; GM's eAssist table, for example, uses limits of minus and plus 440 A.
Phase X sensor signal wire shorted to ground or housing
Sensor supply voltage missing because of an open wire or terminal
Current sensor output failed at the lower end of its range
Starter/generator runs in a restricted mode with less torque
P2D96: Starter/Generator Phase Y Current Sensor Circuit Low
P2D96 covers the phase Y current sensor of the starter/generator when its signal drops below the valid range, for instance through a short to ground or a missing sensor supply.
Phase Y sensor signal pulled to ground by damaged insulation
Open circuit in the sensor supply or a backed-out terminal
Electric assist reduced or switched off
Battery or system warning, charging may be reduced
P2D97: Starter/Generator Phase Z Current Sensor Circuit Low

P2D97 is the last of the three low codes: the Z-phase current sensor of the starter/generator reports a value under the bottom of its valid window. Because the machine both drives the engine and charges, its phase current is signed, so a low fault stands for an impossible negative reading or a collapsed output, not for a weak current.
Phase Z sensor signal lead shorted to ground or to the machine housing
Sensor supply interrupted by an open wire or a pushed-back terminal
Phase Z current sensor output stuck at the bottom of its range
Warning lamp or MIL, typically after the fault has repeated on a second trip
Electric boost and recuperation reduced or switched off
No automatic engine stop, or restarts via the conventional starter
P2D98: Starter/Generator Phase X Current Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P2D98 points to a phase X current signal of the starter/generator that briefly drops out, jumps or flickers, even though most individual samples may still sit inside the accepted range.
Connector contact at the starter/generator opening under engine vibration
Phase X sensor lead chafed against the belt drive or a bracket
Ageing current sensor with unstable output at high temperature
Warning that appears and disappears between trips
Electric assist briefly cut during acceleration
P2D99: Starter/Generator Phase Y Current Circuit Intermittent/Erratic

P2D99 is stored when the phase Y current value of the starter/generator behaves in a way a real winding current cannot: sudden steps, dropouts to zero or noise between consecutive samples. The winding inductance smooths the true current, so such jumps implicate the measuring path.
Corrosion or weak pin tension in the phase Y sensor connector
Harness damaged by heat from the exhaust side or by contact with moving parts
Phase Y current sensor producing a noisy or unstable signal
Sporadic hybrid or charging system warning
P2D9A: Starter/Generator Phase Z Current Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P2D9A marks an unsteady current signal on phase Z of the starter/generator. Before replacing hardware it is worth asking whether the detection itself is too sharp.
Starter/generator software with overly sensitive detection, update available
Loose or spread terminal in the phase Z sensor plug
Water in the connector after washing or driving through deep water
Battery and engine warning lamps that come on now and then
P2D9B: Starter/Generator Phase U Current Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P2D9B concerns phase U, the first phase of the starter/generator's main U-V-W group, when its current signal is unsteady rather than permanently out of range.
Marginal contact in the phase U sensor connector
Phase U sensor lead with damaged insulation or a partly broken strand
Phase U current sensor beginning to fail
Intermittent warning lamp, sometimes only after several trips
Sudden loss of electric assist, returning after a restart
P2D9C: Starter/Generator Phase V Current Circuit Intermittent/Erratic

P2D9C reports an erratic current signal on phase V of the starter/generator. V is the phase that some designs never measure: in a star-connected three-phase winding the three currents add up to zero, so GM's eAssist table runs sensor checks only on U and W.
Phase V sensor plug not fully latched or with fretting corrosion
Intermittent break in the phase V sensor wiring
Phase V current sensor with unstable output
Sporadic system warning on the instrument cluster
Short interruptions of stop-start or boost
P2D9D: Starter/Generator Phase W Current Circuit Intermittent/Erratic

P2D9D covers phase W of the starter/generator when its current signal flickers or drops out for moments. The W sensor is one of the two that GM's eAssist belt machine monitors. GM's checks there look at solid failures: below -440 A or above 440 A for 41.6 ms, Type B, and a learned zero offset beyond 30 A while the inverter is off.
Cracked solder joint in the sensor path after many heat cycles
Poor contact in the phase W sensor connector
Warning lamp that shows up mostly when the engine is hot or the weather is wet
Charging through the starter/generator briefly interrupted
P2D9E: P2D9E reports that the voltage of the high-voltage system – the DC network joining traction battery, inverters, DC/DC converter and other HV consumers – has dropped below its lower limit while the system is switched on. P0AFA judges the battery pack itself; P2D9E looks at the network side. No manufacturer documents P2D9E publicly or names its threshold.
Traction battery deeply discharged or cell groups weak
Main contactor dropping out or precharge circuit faulty
Loose or corroded HV connector or busbar under load
Voltage sensing in the inverter or controller reads too low
Hybrid or EV system warning and check engine light
Noticeably reduced drive power or limp mode
Vehicle does not reach ready mode or engine does not start
P2D9F: P2D9F is the over-voltage case: the DC voltage on the high-voltage network rises above the permitted maximum. Too much voltage stresses capacitors, power semiconductors and cells, so controllers react within milliseconds by cutting regeneration or charging. No manufacturer documents P2D9F publicly.
Regenerative braking or charging while the battery is already full or cold
Contactor or HV connection opening while the motor generates
Voltage measurement in the inverter or controller reads too high
Voltage limits in control software too tight, update available
Hybrid or EV system warning and check engine light
Little or no regenerative braking, more wear on the friction brakes
Power limited or HV system shut down
P2DA0: P2DA0 is the plausibility code of this group: the high-voltage system is neither clearly too low nor too high, but its readings or behaviour do not fit together. CARB 13 CCR 1968.2 asks for such rationality checks on inputs, stored separately from circuit and range faults. No manufacturer documents P2DA0 publicly.
Voltage sensors in battery and inverter disagree
High resistance in an HV connector, busbar or fuse
Main contactor contacts burnt or welded
Calibration or software of a controller, update available
Hybrid or EV system warning, check engine light
Reduced drive power or no electric drive
Fault appears under heavy load or after a long stop
P2DA1: Gear Shift Control Module B Supply Voltage Low

With shift-by-wire, the selector the driver touches is an electronic module; module B is a second one, such as a further selector station or a redundant unit. Allison's 6th-generation controls show such a pair: for module 2 they list performance, lost communication, incompatibility and invalid data (P085E, U0291, U0333, U0592), but no supply codes.
Weak 12 V battery or voltage dip during cranking
Corroded ground, loose connector or high-resistance feed to module B
Fuse for module B blown or with poor contact
Voltage evaluation in module software too strict
Shifter warning in the instrument cluster
Range selection at the second selector ignored, vehicle stays in P
Fault appears together with other low-voltage codes
P2DA2: Gear Shift Control Module B Supply Voltage High

P2DA2 is the over-voltage counterpart of P2DA1: gear shift control module B, the second selector unit of a shift-by-wire system, sees a supply above its permitted maximum. No manufacturer documents P2DA2 publicly or names the limit.
Alternator regulator or DC/DC converter delivering too much voltage
Jump start with 24 V or charger connected during operation
Module feed shorted to a circuit with higher voltage
Voltage measurement inside module B faulty
Shifter warning in the instrument cluster
Second selector does not respond, main selector may still work
Further overvoltage codes in other modules, flickering lights
P2DA3: Gear Shift Control Module B Overtemperature

P2DA3 is a condition code: gear shift control module B reports that its internal temperature exceeds the safe limit. The circuit is fine, the module simply runs too hot. No manufacturer documents P2DA3 or a threshold publicly; Allison's 6th-generation controls, which give module 2 its own performance and communication codes, do not list it.
Strong sun load or nearby heat source at the mounting location
Output stage for lock solenoid, display or lighting drawing excess current
Internal defect or faulty temperature sensing in module B
Shifter warning, mainly in hot weather or after long operation
Second selector temporarily ignores range requests
Fault disappears after the module has cooled down
P2DA4: Coolant Heater A Internal Control Module Performance

Coolant heater A here is an electric heater with built-in electronics, usually a high-voltage PTC or wire-element unit that warms coolant for cabin and battery in hybrids and EVs; it is separate from the engine block heater codes P01E8 ff.
Power switch inside the heater shorted or failed
Internal temperature or current measurement faulty
Coolant or moisture inside the electronics housing
Software fault in heater or commanding module, update available
Little or no cabin heat in electric mode
Engine of a hybrid runs more often just to supply heat
Climate system message, usually without check engine light
P2DA5: Coolant Heater A Supply Voltage Circuit

P2DA5 concerns the feed that powers coolant heater A, the electric coolant heater with its own electronics found in hybrids and EVs. The heater's controller finds its supply input missing or outside the expected window and reports it as a circuit fault, unlike P2DA7, which rates the voltage level of the module. Which feed is meant is up to the maker.
12 V or HV fuse for the heater open
Corroded or loose pin in the heater supply connector
Poor ground connection of the heater electronics
Supply input inside the heater electronics faulty
No heat from the electric coolant heater
Cabin heat only when the engine of a hybrid runs
Possibly lost communication with the heater stored at the same time
P2DA6: P2DA6 says coolant heater A, the electric coolant heater of a hybrid or EV, has become too hot. Such heaters measure outlet coolant or housing temperature and switch off above a limit; a Hyundai/Kia patent (US11378000B2) does exactly that, mainly to protect the elements when coolant is missing.
Software of the controlling module (Ford Lightning SOBDMC), reprogramming
Low coolant level or air trapped in the heater loop
Heater loop coolant pump not running or valve blocking flow
Temperature sensor in heater or loop reading too high
Often no noticeable symptom, code found during service
Heater switches off, cabin warms only weakly
Climate system message, no check engine light
P2DA7: Coolant Heater A Control Module System Voltage

P2DA7 is logged when the electronics built into coolant heater A – the HV heater of a hybrid or EV – see a system voltage outside the window in which it may work. While P2DA5 points to the feed circuit, this code judges the level.
Traction battery voltage at the edge of the heater's range (very low or very high charge)
Weak 12 V battery or poor ground of the heater electronics
Voltage measurement inside the heater faulty
Fault occurs with very low or very high battery charge
Cabin heat only from the engine of a hybrid
P2DA8: DC/AC Converter Control Module A Switch A Circuit

DC/AC converter control module A is the inverter that turns direct current from the vehicle battery into household AC for sockets in the vehicle; Ford calls it DCACA and uses it for Pro Power Onboard on the F-150, where TSB 21-2127 handles a related fault, P0364 in the PCM.
Open or shorted wire or corroded connector between switch A and the module
Switch A or its relay failed
Water ingress at an outlet panel in the bed or cargo area
Internal fault of the DC/AC converter module
AC outlets of group A without power
Message that onboard power is unavailable
P2DA9: DC/AC Converter Control Module A Switch A Circuit Range/Performance

P2DA9 belongs to switch A of the DC/AC converter control module A, the inverter that supplies AC sockets in the vehicle. Unlike P2DA8 the circuit is intact, but the switch does not behave as expected: its signal sits between valid states, or the commanded state does not show up at the output.
Worn, sticking or burnt contacts of switch A or its relay
High contact resistance in connector or outlet wiring
Outlet button jammed by dirt or damage
Voltage sensing in the converter module implausible
Outlets of group A work only intermittently
Outlet power switches off unexpectedly under load
Switch position in the display does not match the outlet state
P2DAA: DC/AC Converter Control Module A Switch B Circuit

P2DAA flags an electrical fault in the line of switch B belonging to DC/AC converter control module A, the vehicle's inverter for 120/230 V sockets. The module finds the switch B line open, shorted to ground or to supply, or without a usable signal.
Open or shorted wire or corroded connector in the switch B circuit
Switch B or its relay failed
Shared feed, ground or converter module faulty (when group A also fails)
AC outlets of group B without power, other outlets work
Message that onboard power is limited or unavailable
P2DAB: DC/AC Converter Control Module A Switch B Circuit Range/Performance

With P2DAB, switch B of converter module A – the unit feeding the vehicle's AC sockets – fails a plausibility test. Wiring tests pass, yet switch B does not deliver what was asked of it: it stays closed after an off command, opens under load, or reports a position that disagrees with the measured output.
Contacts of switch B or its relay welded, sticking or worn
Moisture or dirt at the outlet panel of group B
Load management or software in the converter module, update available
Outlets of group B switch off unexpectedly or cannot be switched off
Warning about onboard power in the display
Fault appears mainly with high loads connected
P2DAC: Drive Motor A Temperature Sensor B Circuit

P2DAC is the general circuit fault of a second temperature sensor (B) in drive motor A; sensor A has its own series from P0A2A. A motor carries a second probe either as a backup element beside the first – Sensata's hairpin sensor patent allows two NTCs, or an NTC plus a PTC, in one housing – or as a probe on another phase winding.
Broken or shorted sensor B lead between motor and inverter
Loose, corroded or pushed-out terminal at the motor connector
Sensor B thermistor failed inside the stator
Faulty sensor input in the inverter or motor control unit
Hybrid system warning or check engine light
Sensor B shows a fixed or missing value in live data while sensor A looks normal
P2DAD: Drive Motor A Temperature Sensor B Circuit Range/Performance

P2DAD covers a sensor B signal that stays inside the electrical window yet does not fit the situation. CARB asks for rationality checks on hybrid input components where feasible, logged under a code of their own apart from circuit and range faults.
Sensor B thermistor drifted from its resistance curve
Added resistance at a worn or corroded terminal
Probe no longer seated firmly against the winding
Fault in the reference value, e.g. sensor A or coolant temperature
Hybrid system warning or check engine light
Sensor B differs clearly from sensor A after the car has stood overnight
Electric drive power limited in some situations
P2DAE: Drive Motor A Temperature Sensor B Circuit Low

P2DAE means the sensor B voltage has fallen below the lowest value a healthy sensor can deliver. Winding probes are mostly NTC thermistors whose resistance collapses as they heat – Thinking Electronic quotes roughly 0.46 kOhm at 180 °C for its stator probes – so with the usual pull-up circuit a near-zero voltage would read as an impossibly hot winding.
Sensor B signal lead shorted to ground or motor housing
Thermistor shorted internally (often replaceable only with the motor)
Lead pinched or chafed after work on the drive unit
Hybrid system warning or check engine light
Sensor B shows an extremely high fixed temperature in live data
P2DAF: Drive Motor A Temperature Sensor B Circuit High

P2DAF is the high-side counterpart: the sensor B voltage rises close to the reference. For an NTC probe that would be an impossibly cold winding, so the controller treats it as an interrupted circuit – broken lead, unplugged or corroded connector, cracked thermistor – or, less often, a short to a supply voltage.
Open signal or ground lead of sensor B
Connector unplugged or terminal backed out, often after drive unit work
Thermistor open or cracked inside the stator
Signal lead shorted to a supply voltage
Hybrid system warning or check engine light
Sensor B shows an implausibly low temperature in live data
P2DB0: Drive Motor A Temperature Sensor B Circuit Intermittent

P2DB0 logs short dropouts or jumps in the sensor B signal that come and go too fast for the steady low and high checks. Because CARB requires circuit monitoring of input components to run continuously, such glitches are caught while driving.
Resistance jumps in the sensor crimp at high temperature
Worn or loose terminals in a connector of the sensor B line
Chafed lead with intermittent contact under vibration
Warning light that comes and goes, often after hard driving
Sensor B value spikes briefly in live data
Electric drive power briefly limited on some models
P2DB1: Drive Motor A Temperature Sensor C Circuit

P2DB1 reports a circuit fault on a third temperature sensor (C) in drive motor A. Three probes in one motor make most sense when each phase winding of the three-phase machine gets its own: Mitsubishi equips the front motor of the 2023 Outlander PHEV with U-, V- and W-phase coil sensors, and a fault on any of them lights both the hybrid warning and the MIL.
Broken or shorted sensor C lead between motor and inverter
Loose or corroded terminal at the motor connector
Sensor C thermistor failed in its phase winding
Faulty sensor input in the inverter or motor control unit
Hybrid system warning and check engine light
Sensor C missing or frozen in live data while the other motor sensors read normally
P2DB2: Drive Motor A Temperature Sensor C Circuit Range/Performance
P2DB2 flags a sensor C reading that is electrically valid but disagrees with what the motor should show.
Sensor C thermistor drifted from its resistance curve
Extra resistance at a corroded or worn terminal
Probe loose on its phase winding
Hybrid system warning or check engine light
Sensor C stands well apart from the other motor sensors after a cold start
No noticeable driving change in many cases
P2DB3: Drive Motor A Temperature Sensor C Circuit Low

P2DB3 sets when the sensor C voltage drops below its valid floor. For an NTC probe this would stand for a temperature far beyond any real winding heat, so a short is much more likely than a genuine hot spot: signal lead to ground or motor housing, insulation damaged inside the stator, or a thermistor shorted internally.
Sensor C signal lead shorted to ground or motor housing
Probe insulation damaged inside the stator
Hybrid system warning and check engine light
Sensor C reads extremely hot while the other sensors look normal
P2DB4: Drive Motor A Temperature Sensor C Circuit High

P2DB4 is the open-circuit side of sensor C: the voltage climbs toward the reference because hardly any current still flows through the thermistor. A broken wire, a terminal backed out of the motor connector, corrosion or a cracked thermistor are the likely finds; a short to a supply voltage is rarer.
Open signal or ground lead of sensor C
Terminal backed out or corroded in the motor connector
Signal lead shorted to a supply voltage
Hybrid system warning and check engine light
Sensor C reads far below ambient temperature in live data
P2DB5: Drive Motor A Temperature Sensor C Circuit Intermittent
P2DB5 is set when the sensor C signal drops out or jumps briefly and then recovers – a flickering contact rather than a lasting open or short. No manufacturer documents P2DB5.
Crimp of sensor C changing resistance when hot
Loose or fretted terminals in the sensor C connector
Lead rubbing through and touching intermittently
Warning light that disappears and returns
Brief spikes or gaps in the sensor C value in live data
Fault mainly after long or hard drives
P2DB6: Battery Charger B Cooling System Performance

P2DB6 is set when the cooling of a second on-board charger, charger B, cannot hold the unit inside its permitted temperature window, so the charger has to cut its power or stop. No manufacturer documents P2DB6 publicly.
Low coolant level or trapped air in the charger cooling circuit
Electric coolant pump of the low-temperature circuit weak or failed
Coolant hoses connected to the wrong circuit after assembly or repair
Low-temperature radiator clogged or its airflow obstructed
Charging power reduced at the charge station
Plug-in charging stops after some minutes
Charging fault message in the instrument cluster
P2DB7: Battery Charging System B High Voltage Interlock Circuit/Open

P2DB7 reports that the high voltage interlock loop of charging system B is broken. Such a loop is a low-current wire run in series through the HV plugs and covers of a charging path; once it opens, the control unit treats the path as unsafe and keeps it switched off. B denotes a second charging path, for example a further on-board charger.
HV connector in the charging path not fully seated or its catch not closed
Broken interlock wire or pushed-out terminal
Service cover or HV cover of the charger not closed properly
Fault in the interlock evaluation of the control module
No charging through charging path B
Charging system warning in the instrument cluster
P2DB8: Battery Charging System B High Voltage Interlock Circuit Performance
P2DB8 means the interlock loop of charging system B carries a signal, but one that does not behave as the control unit expects.
Raised contact resistance in an interlock terminal
Plug in the charging path inserted only partway
Corrosion or moisture in an interlock connector
Test source or measuring stage of the module not working correctly
Charging via path B refused or interrupted
P2DB9: Battery Charging System B High Voltage Interlock Circuit Low

P2DB9 is stored when the sensed voltage of the charging system B interlock loop stays too low. Since the module feeds a test voltage into the loop, a low reading usually means current is escaping to ground: a chafed wire touching the body, moisture in a connector, or a failing measuring stage inside the module. No manufacturer documents P2DB9 publicly.
Interlock wire chafed through and touching ground
Water or dirt in an interlock connector causing leakage to ground
Defective interlock source or measuring stage in the control module
Charging through path B not possible
P2DBA: Battery Charging System B High Voltage Interlock Circuit High

P2DBA flags an interlock signal of charging system B that reads too high. A loop fed from a test source and measured at its far end shows a raised level when it is shorted to a supply voltage, or, depending on the circuit, when added resistance or a break lets the measuring input float upward. No manufacturer documents P2DBA publicly.
Interlock wire shorted to a supply voltage
Added resistance or partial break in the interlock loop
Faulty measuring input in the control module
P2DBB: Battery Charging System B High Voltage Interlock Circuit Intermittent/Erratic

P2DBB covers an interlock loop of charging system B that keeps dropping out and recovering, so its state flips between valid and invalid. The trigger is usually mechanical: a terminal with low contact pressure, a plug that is not fully latched, or a wire that only loses contact when the body flexes or the parts heat up.
Loose or widened terminal in an interlock connector
Connector in the charging path not fully latched
Chafed interlock wire that loses contact only with movement or heat
Charging via path B stops without warning
Fault comes and goes, often depending on temperature
P2DBC: Battery Charger B Coupler Lock Position Sensor Circuit

P2DBC is the general circuit fault of the lock position sensor at charger B's coupler, the feedback telling the vehicle whether the pin that holds the charging plug in the inlet has moved out or back in. B marks a second inlet or charging path. No manufacturer documents P2DBC publicly.
Open or shorted wire between lock actuator and control module
Lock pin broken after the plug was pulled while still latched
Corroded or loose connector at the lock actuator
Faulty sensor input in the control module
DC fast charging not possible at inlet B
Charger service warning in the instrument cluster
P2DBD: Battery Charger B Coupler Lock Position Sensor Circuit Range/Performance

P2DBD is the plausibility fault of the coupler lock feedback on charger B: the signal is electrically valid yet does not fit what the lock is doing, for example a travel that is too short after a lock command, or longer than the pin could ever move with a plug inserted. No manufacturer documents P2DBD publicly.
Lock pin broken off or missing, so the measured travel is implausible
Lock mechanism sticking or jammed by dirt or ice
Loose low-voltage contacts at the charger or actuator
Plug cannot be locked or released normally
P2DBE: Battery Charger B Coupler Lock Position Sensor Circuit Low

P2DBE means the coupler lock sensor of charger B delivers a voltage below its valid band. No manufacturer documents P2DBE publicly. The A-side code P0DA0 is documented by Mitsubishi for the 2023 Outlander PHEV: with the ignition-controlled supply on, the PHEV-ECU sets it on a low input from the inlet's lock sensor.
Sensor signal line shorted to ground
Lock position sensor with internal short or wrong resistance
Damaged lock actuator after the plug was pulled while latched
Faulty sensor input in the control module
Charging system warning lamp or message
P2DBF: Battery Charger B Coupler Lock Position Sensor Circuit High
P2DBF is set when the lock position signal of charger B's coupler stays above its permitted range. No manufacturer documents P2DBF publicly.
Open ground connection of the lock position sensor
Open signal line between sensor and control module
Signal line shorted to a supply voltage
Faulty inlet assembly with integrated lock actuator
Fast charging at inlet B not possible
P2DC0: Battery Charger B Coupler Lock Position Sensor Circuit Intermittent/Erratic

P2DC0 describes lock feedback at the charger B inlet that jumps or drops out for short moments instead of failing steadily. Because the lock state is a release condition for charging, a flickering signal can end a session or stop it from starting even though the plug is held properly. No manufacturer documents P2DC0 publicly.
Loose low-voltage plug at the lock actuator or charger
Sensor wire chafed near the charging inlet
Water ingress into the inlet or actuator connector
Charging at inlet B stops or fails to start sporadically
Fault appears only at certain temperatures
P2DC1: Starter/Generator Phase X Current Sensor Circuit

P2DC1 is the general circuit code for the phase X current sensor of the starter/generator: the controller sees an electrical fault in the sensor path without, or in place of, a separate high or low verdict.
Phase X current sensor on the integrated electronics board defective
Open or shorted lead between an external phase X sensor and the controller
Unstable 12 V supply or ground of the starter/generator electronics
Starter/generator in a reduced mode or switched off
P2DC2: Starter/Generator Phase X Current Sensor Circuit Range/Performance

P2DC2 means the starter/generator's phase X current sensor delivers values that are electrically valid but do not make sense. CARB requires such rationality faults to be detected where feasible and kept in a code of their own, separate from wiring and out-of-limit faults.
Zero point of the phase X sensor drifted, for example through ageing or heat
Sensor reference voltage out of tolerance
Phase X current sensor with gain error or slowly failing
Warning lamp after the plausibility check has failed on two trips
Less electric torque because current control runs in a substitute mode
P2DC3: Starter/Generator Phase Y Current Sensor Circuit

P2DC3 flags an electrical fault in the circuit of the phase Y current sensor of the starter/generator. Such a sensor needs a supply, a ground and a signal line, and a break or short in any of the three can end up here when the controller cannot or does not tell high from low.
Missing supply or ground at the phase Y sensor
Open phase Y signal line between sensor and controller
Phase Y current sensor without output
Battery charged less by the starter/generator
P2DC4: Starter/Generator Phase Y Current Sensor Circuit Range/Performance

P2DC4 says the phase Y current reading of the starter/generator is inside its electrical limits but fails a plausibility test. One way to test it is an energy balance: the power drawn or delivered on the phase side must match the current on the DC side.
Phase Y current sensor reading consistently too high or too low
Zero offset of the phase Y sensor drifted
Comparison value wrong because the DC-side current measurement is faulty
Warning lamp after two trips with the fault
Noticeably weaker boost and smoother but slower restarts
P2DC5: Starter/Generator Phase Z Current Sensor Circuit

P2DC5 records a circuit fault of the phase Z current sensor in the starter/generator. A Z phase only exists on machines with more than one phase group. Mazda, for one, gives an integrated machine a second set of stator drivers labelled X, Y and Z, and CARB asks for circuit checks on such hybrid inputs.
Phase Z sensor inside the starter/generator electronics failed
Low-voltage connector of the starter/generator damaged or not latched
Supply or ground fault of the machine electronics
No recuperation and no electric boost
P2DC6: Starter/Generator Phase Z Current Sensor Circuit Range/Performance

P2DC6 is the plausibility code for the starter/generator's phase Z current sensor. The reading stays within its electrical window but does not match what the controller expects from commanded current and machine state.
Phase Z sensor has lost sensitivity or drifted
Real current deviation from a poor phase Z connection or winding fault
Controller software or calibration judging the signal wrongly
Warning lamp, usually after two trips
Reduced starter/generator output or rough automatic restarts
P2DC7: P2DC7 is the general fault for the excitation current of a starter/generator, meaning the DC current in the rotor field winding does not behave as commanded. Only wound-field machines have one.
Worn brushes or contaminated slip rings on the rotor
Fault in the excitation H-bridge of the starter/generator electronics
Rotor field winding with interrupted turns or a short
P2DC8: P2DC8 reports that too little excitation current reaches the rotor field winding of a wound-field starter/generator. With a weak field the claw-pole machine produces little torque and little voltage, so both charging and electric assist fade.
Brushes worn down so they no longer contact the slip rings reliably
Open circuit in the rotor field coil or its connections
Excitation driver stage in the electronics unable to deliver current
Charging warning and falling battery voltage
No electric boost and weak or no belt-driven restarts
P2DC9: P2DC9 means a starter/generator with an electrically excited rotor draws more field current than its controller expects or allows. In such machines, for example Valeo's 48 V claw-pole belt starter generator, the stator windings get their three-phase supply from an inverter, and an extra full bridge sets the rotor's DC field via brushes on slip rings.
Excitation driver stage in the controller shorted or no longer regulating
Shorted turns in the rotor field coil lowering its resistance
Faulty field current measurement inside the controller
Field lead chafed and shorted to a supply voltage
Check engine light and 48 V or charging system warning
Start-stop and electric boost switched off
Overvoltage protection cuts in, electrical consumers may flicker
P2DCA: P2DCA is set when the field current of a starter/generator with electrically excited rotor does not stay steady but drops out or jumps for short moments, without staying beyond the low or high limit long enough for P2DC8 or P2DC9.
Worn or sticking brushes, dirty or worn slip rings
Loose connector or terminal on the field leads
Cracked solder joint in the excitation bridge of the controller
Charge warning that comes and goes
Jerky or delayed restarts after start-stop
Electric boost and recuperation work only at times
P2DCB: Starter/Generator Phase X-Y-Z Current Sensor Correlation

P2DCB compares the three current sensors of the starter/generator's X-Y-Z phase group with one another or with the DC side. In a star-connected winding the instantaneous phase currents must add up to roughly zero; if they do not, at least one sensor is wrong, even though each may sit inside its own limits.
Gain or zero drift of one phase current sensor
Disturbed supply or reference voltage shared by the sensors
Calibration or software fault in the starter/generator controller
Check engine light with hybrid or 48 V system warning
Reduced electric boost and recuperation in substitute mode
P2DCC: P2DCC reports that the rotor position or speed the starter/generator derives from its own sensor disagrees with an independent reference. For a belt-driven machine the natural reference is the crankshaft: engine speed times the pulley ratio has to match machine speed.
Slipping drive belt or weak belt tensioner
Rotor position sensor degraded or shifted
Faulty engine speed reference from the crankshaft sensor or its CAN signal
Belt squeal or engine restart via 12 V starter instead
P2DCD: P2DCD is meant for a second particulate filter, labelled B, that the engine control unit finds to be absent or not the specified part, for instance after the filter has been cut out, replaced by an empty housing or swapped for an unsuitable aftermarket unit. No manufacturer documents P2DCD publicly, and makers catch such tampering with other codes.
Filter B removed or replaced by an empty housing or pipe
Filter substrate cracked, melted or blown out
Leaking or blocked pressure lines misleading the detection
Louder exhaust or visible soot at the tailpipe
P2DCE: Control Pilot Charging Switch B Circuit/Open
P2DCE reports an open or otherwise faulty control circuit of charging switch B, a vehicle-side switch on the control pilot line.
Broken wire or pushed-back pin in the switch B circuit
Switch or its driver inside the charging module open
Corroded contacts at the charge inlet or module connector
Station detects the car but charging never starts
Charging fault message in the instrument cluster
P2DCF: Control Pilot Charging Switch B Range/Performance
P2DCF means charging switch B responds electrically, but the pilot level it creates is not plausible.
Resistor in the switch B branch drifted out of tolerance
High contact resistance in switch, inlet or connector
Fault in the pilot voltage measuring path of the charging module
Charging refused or stopping after a short time
P2DD0: Control Pilot Charging Switch B Circuit Low
P2DD0 says the drive or sense wire of switch B reads below its valid range. The usual reasons are a wire chafed through to body ground or a shorted transistor stage in the charging electronics.
Switch B wire chafed and shorted to ground
Output stage in the charging module failed shorted
Moisture in the charge inlet creating a leakage path
Charging starts immediately on plug-in or not at all
P2DD1: Control Pilot Charging Switch B Circuit High

P2DD1 reports a voltage on the drive or feedback wire of switch B that is higher than it should be. Likely culprits are a wire touching battery voltage or another feed somewhere between inlet and module, or a transistor stage that has lost the ability to pull its output low. Whether the switch then stays open or closed depends on the design.
Switch B line shorted to a supply voltage
Driver stage in the charging module no longer pulling low
Moisture or pushed-back pins at inlet or module connector
Car stays in plugged-in state, station supplies no power
Charging session cannot be ended cleanly
P2DD2: Control Pilot Charging Switch B Intermittent/Erratic

P2DD2 is stored when the signal of charging switch B changes state erratically: it drops out or toggles for brief moments, while lasting faults would end up as P2DCE, P2DD0 or P2DD1. Loose terminals, green corrosion at inlet pins or the module plug, and conductors that break contact only when the car moves or temperatures change are the usual suspects.
Loose terminal in the charge inlet or module connector
Corrosion from water ingress at the charge inlet
Chafed wire losing contact with movement or temperature
Battery not fully charged after a charging session
P2DD3: Control Pilot Charging Switch B Stuck Off

Stuck Off: although the module orders charging switch B to close, nothing changes on the pilot; the voltage sits near 9 V, the plugged-in level, rather than dropping to about 6 V. Through this switch the station thus never sees a request for energy.
Switch or relay B no longer closing
Open resistor in the charge-request branch
Pilot voltage measurement in the module faulty
Car recognised at the station but no charging
P2DD4: Control Pilot Charging Switch B Stuck On

P2DD4 describes the reverse case: switch B remains closed against the module's command to open, and the pilot goes on asking for energy at about 6 V although charging should have ended or paused. Welded or sticking contacts, a driver stage shorted on, or software that does not release the switch are all possible.
Charger software not releasing the switch
Charging does not end or pause as planned
Charging error message after the session
P2DD5: Fuel Injection Quantity B Lower Than Expected

P2DD5 reports that the injection path the manufacturer calls B delivers less fuel than the engine control commanded. SAE leaves open what B is: a second injector set, an injector group or a separate operating mode. No manufacturer documents this code publicly.
Injectors of group B coked or partly blocked
Supply or rail pressure for this path too low (filter, pump)
Airflow or lambda measurement off, so the computed fuel looks too small
Engine control software or injector calibration data
Less power, sluggish response under load
P2DD6: Fuel Injection Quantity B Higher Than Expected

With P2DD6 the engine control has found that path B injects more fuel than requested, so the mixture ends up richer than planned. Typical reasons are an injector that drips after closing, a worn nozzle passing extra fuel, or rail pressure above target; a sensor that under-reads airflow can fake the same result.
Injector in group B dripping or nozzle worn
Rail pressure above target (regulator, pressure sensor)
Airflow sensor reading low or intake leak after the sensor
Black smoke, more frequent particulate filter regeneration
P2DD7: Cold Start Fuel Injection Quantity B Lower Than Expected
P2DD7 limits the shortfall of P2DD5 to the cold-start phase. Many engines inject differently just after a cold start, with extra or shifted injections that heat the catalyst or SCR system.
Fuel filter restricted, fuel waxing in cold weather
Rail pressure builds too slowly after start
Injectors of group B sluggish or partly blocked
Coolant or fuel temperature signal implausible
Check engine light on after a cold start
Hard cold start, rough running while cold
P2DD8: Cold Start Fuel Injection Quantity B Higher Than Expected

P2DD8 means path B delivered more fuel than requested while the cold-start routine ran. A cold engine burns surplus fuel poorly, so it leaves as white or blue smoke and raw hydrocarbons before the catalyst is warm, and some of it can reach the oil. No manufacturer uses P2DD8 in public documents.
Injector of group B leaking or sticking slightly open
Coolant temperature signal reads colder than real, too much start fuel
Cold-start calibration in engine control software
Check engine light on after a cold start
White or blue smoke and fuel smell after a cold start
Rising oil level from fuel dilution
P2DD9: EVAP System Leak Detection Pump Control Circuit Performance

P2DD9 means the drive circuit of the evaporative leak detection pump is electrically intact, yet the pump does not react the way the command implies: the feedback the engine computer reads back, usually motor current or driver state, does not match the on or off request.
Pump motor worn or sluggish, current draw off target
Corroded connector or chafed wire adding resistance in the pump feed
Water or ice in the pump module (mounted near the wheel arch)
Faulty output stage or current sensing in the engine control module
P2DDA: EVAP System Leak Detection Pump Performance/Stuck Off
P2DDA is stored when the leak detection pump fails to create the pressure change the leak test expects, as if it never started or moves too little air.
Pump motor or vane inside the leak check module seized or worn out
Fresh-air filter or vent line of the module blocked by dirt or water
Switching valve in the module not moving, so the pump works against the wrong path
Hose between module and canister split or off
Evaporative leak test never completes, readiness stays open
Possible refuelling message or locked filler flap on some hybrids
P2DDB: EVAP System Leak Detection Pump Stuck On
P2DDB reports a leak detection pump that keeps running, or keeps moving air, after the engine computer has turned it off.
Pump supply permanently live, e.g. stuck relay or shorted output stage
Internal fault of the leak check module (pump or its electronics)
Control wire chafed against a powered line
Humming from the tank area after the car is switched off
Leak test results unusable, EVAP readiness incomplete
P2DDC: Fuel Injection Quantity C Lower Than Expected

P2DDC is the shortfall code for a third injection path, C. Engines that need it split their injection into more parts than A and B, for example by injector group or by operating mode; the split is defined by the maker, and none documents P2DDC openly.
Injectors of group C coked or partly blocked
Low-pressure supply weak (lift pump, filter, air in fuel)
High resistance in injector wiring of group C
P2DDD: Fuel Injection Quantity C Higher Than Expected

P2DDD flags excess fuel from injection path C: the quantity really burned, as estimated from airflow and lambda, sits above the request. Besides the classic leaking injector, a possible trigger after repairs is a replacement injector whose individual flow code was not programmed into the engine control, so the module calculates with the wrong flow curve.
Injector of group C leaking or nozzle worn
Injector correction code not programmed after replacement
EGR valve not closing fully, too little fresh air
P2DDE: Fuel Injection Quantity D Lower Than Expected
P2DDE covers a fourth injection path, D, delivering too little fuel. The letter is assigned by the manufacturer; no one documents this code openly.
Injectors of group D blocked or worn
Fuel supply weak (pump, filter, rail pressure)
Air mass or lambda signal inaccurate
P2DDF: Fuel Injection Quantity D Higher Than Expected

P2DDF says injection path D sends more fuel than the engine control asked for. The estimate behind it depends heavily on the air side: if the airflow meter reports too little air, or the NOx or oxygen sensor shows a richer lambda than real, the module sees a surplus that the injectors never delivered, so sensors deserve a check before injectors are replaced.…
Airflow, NOx or oxygen sensor reading wrong
Injector of group D leaking or nozzle eroded
Boost or intake leak after the airflow meter
Black smoke, particulate filter loading faster
P2DE0: Cold Start Fuel Injection Quantity C Lower Than Expected

P2DE0 is the cold-start shortfall for path C. Its partner P2DE1 is used by Honda, which treats it as a rich fault of its cold-start mixture control: that check compares the ratio the PCM commands just after a cold start with what the wide-band sensor measures.
Fuel pressure too low at start (pump, regulator, check valve)
Unmetered air entering behind the airflow meter
Injectors of group C dirty, poor spray when cold
Cold-start calibration in engine control software
Check engine light on after a cold start
Stalling or stumbling shortly after a cold start
P2DE1: Cold Start Fuel Injection Quantity C Higher Than Expected

P2DE1 is the only code of this family with public manufacturer use. Honda names it Cold Start Air Fuel Ratio Control System Rich: during the cold-start emission strategy the PCM checks whether the mixture measured by the LAF (wide-band) sensor is richer than commanded.
Injector leaking, extra fuel during cold start
Coolant temperature or airflow signal wrong
Check engine light on after a cold start
Oil level above the upper mark possible
P2DE2: Cold Start Fuel Injection Quantity D Lower Than Expected
P2DE2 reports that path D fell short of its fuel request during the cold-start strategy.
Deposits on injector tips of group D
High-pressure pump slow to build pressure after start
Check engine light on after a cold start
Rough idle in the first seconds after a cold start
P2DE3: Cold Start Fuel Injection Quantity D Higher Than Expected
P2DE3 is the excess counterpart of P2DE2: during the cold-start strategy path D injected more than commanded.
Pressure regulator sticking, rail pressure too high when cold
Coolant temperature sensor reading too cold
Check engine light on after a cold start
White smoke and fuel smell when cold
P2DE4: Drive Motor A Clutch Stuck Engaged

Some hybrids and electric drive units can uncouple electric drive motor A from its axle through a clutch, so the motor stops turning when its torque is not needed. P2DE4 means the clutch stays closed although the control module has asked it to open; position feedback or speeds still show a coupled motor. No manufacturer documents P2DE4 publicly.
Disconnect clutch actuator does not move to the open position (motor, solenoid or linkage)
Clutch position switch reports engaged although the clutch has opened
Shift sleeve, pawl or teeth jammed or loaded with torque in the engaged state
Control module software or calibration error in the disconnect strategy
Warning lamp or hybrid/drive system message
Higher energy consumption, electric range reduced
Drive unit noise at speed, possible speed or mode limitation
P2DE5: Drive Motor A Clutch Stuck Disengaged

P2DE5 is the reverse of P2DE4: the module commands the clutch of drive motor A to close, yet the motor stays uncoupled from the wheels. The motor may spin up without the axle following, or the position signal never reaches the engaged state. No manufacturer documents P2DE5 publicly.
Actuator motor or solenoid fails to push the clutch into engagement
Clutch teeth blocking on each other, speed synchronisation not reached
Position switch or sensor stuck at disengaged
Worn or broken internal parts of the clutch or fork
Warning lamp, hybrid or all-wheel-drive fault message
No electric drive or reduced traction from the affected axle
Combustion engine starts more often, reduced recuperation
P2DE6: Drive Motor A Clutch Actuator Performance

Whereas P2DE4 and P2DE5 describe the clutch end state, P2DE6 judges the actuator that moves the clutch of drive motor A: its circuit is intact, but it acts too slowly, draws implausible current or does not reach the commanded position within the expected time. No manufacturer documents P2DE6 publicly.
Actuator motor or gearing worn, sluggish movement
Increased friction at fork, sleeve or pawl, e.g. from contaminated fluid
Low supply voltage or resistance in the actuator feed
Position switch or sensor reporting late or erratically
Warning lamp or drive system message
Delayed or jerky coupling of the electric axle
Electric drive of that axle temporarily disabled
P2DE7: Cold Start Engine Coolant Bypass Valve C Range/Performance
California requires a fault found while the cold-start warm-up strategy runs to be stored apart from the same fault found later. P2DE7 is that cold-start counterpart of P26BB for coolant valve C.
Rotary valve sluggish from deposits or worn seals
Valve actuator motor or gearing weak
Position sensor reading drifting without a circuit fault
Engine control software needing an update
Check engine light on (after two trips)
Engine and cabin heater warm up more slowly
P2DE8: Cold Start Engine Coolant Bypass Valve D Stuck Open

P2DE8 is GM's cold-start variant of P26C0 for valve D, the block rotary valve that sits between two mechanical end stops and meters coolant through the engine block. In the 2025 ECM tables (25OBDG03B) a failure counts when requested and measured position differ by more than 5° while the raw feedback is above 50°, i.e.
Block rotary valve sticking in an open position (deposits, wear)
Valve actuator unable to drive the valve to the closed side
Chafed or corroded engine harness to the valve
End-stop learn values implausible after repair or power loss
Check engine light on after two trips
Slow warm-up, weak cabin heating in cold weather
Possibly higher fuel consumption on short trips
P2DE9: Cold Start Engine Coolant Pump Underspeed
Engines with an electric main water pump run it at a tightly metered speed after a cold start so the block heats quickly. P2DE9 flags that during this phase the pump turns too slowly.
Worn pump bearing or debris at the impeller slowing the rotor
Low supply voltage at the pump (battery, ground, connector)
Faulty pump electronics or speed feedback
Wrong or aged coolant, very thick when cold
Check engine light on after two trips
Uneven warm-up, local hot spots possible
P2DEA: P2DEA says the intake valves of cylinder 1 do not reach the lift the engine computer asks for, or get there too slowly. It is the first of a row of per-cylinder lift checks.
Switching element or hydraulic link of cylinder 1 sticking (sludge, wear)
Low oil level, wrong oil or restricted oil feed to the lift actuator
Cylinder 1 lift solenoid sluggish though electrically intact
Damaged cam follower, valve spring or lifter on cylinder 1
Rough idle or shaking at low load
Misfire code for cylinder 1 at the same time
P2DEB: P2DEB singles out cylinder 2: its intake valve lift misses the target or follows a command too late.
Cylinder 2 solenoid in the lift actuator responding slowly or leaking internally
Aged, contaminated or wrong-grade engine oil in the hydraulic chamber
Air in the high-pressure chamber after oil starvation or service
Damaged driver stage in the engine control module
Misfire felt at idle, cylinder 2 misfire count rising
P2DEC: P2DEC applies only to cylinder 3: the lift its intake valves actually achieve is outside the commanded window or arrives too late.
Lock pin or switching follower of cylinder 3 not latching
Partly blocked oil passage to the cylinder 3 element
Broken return spring in the lift mechanism
Uneven idle, often with a cylinder 3 misfire entry
P2DED: P2DED is the cylinder 4 member of the per-cylinder lift checks: the engine computer finds this cylinder's lift off target or slow to follow. On four-cylinder engines with hydraulic lift control the oil comes first.
Low, aged, diluted or wrong-viscosity oil
Clogged oil screen in the gallery feeding the lift unit
Oil filter not meeting the maker's specification
Worn cylinder 4 section of the lift actuator
P2DEE: P2DEE can only occur on engines with five or more cylinders and means the intake valve lift of cylinder 5 is outside the commanded range or late. Two-step lift reached V6 engines such as the 3.6 L Pentastar, which FCA updated for 2016.
Switching roller finger follower of cylinder 5 stuck in one mode
Oil control valve for the lift switching sticking or contaminated
Oil pressure too low to move the lock pins
Ticking from the valvetrain on one bank
P2DEF: P2DEF covers cylinder 6, typically on a V6 or straight six: its intake valves do not reach the commanded lift or take too long to switch. Detection follows the same idea as for the other cylinders; for the driver the reaction matters more.
Lift mechanism of cylinder 6 stuck in high or low lift
Restricted oil feed to the cylinder 6 element
Actuator for cylinder 6 slow despite correct wiring
Engine speed limited or lift switching disabled (substitute mode)
P2DF0: P2DF0 means that intake valve lift on bank 1 as a whole does not follow the command, rather than one cylinder.
Eccentric or control shaft on bank 1 stiff from wear or sludge
Lift adjusting motor of bank 1 worn or weak
Shaft position sensor reading offset or loosened
Air mass meter error or intake leak making the lift appear wrong
Reduced power, engine may fall back to throttle control
P2DF1: P2DF1 is the bank 2 counterpart of P2DF0 and therefore only appears on V engines or boxers, on the side without cylinder 1. Nissan's VVEL, used on the VQ37VHR V6 and on V8 engines, is a good example: on the 2014 QX80 V8 both banks carry a separate VVEL ladder assembly with an actuator and a control shaft position sensor.
Control shaft or ladder assembly on bank 2 binding
Control shaft position sensor on bank 2 moved or faulty
Lift actuator motor of bank 2 weak
Oil sludge in the bank 2 lift mechanism
Uneven running between the banks, possible fuel trim difference
P2DF2: P2DF2 points to the intake valve lift system as a whole rather than to one cylinder or bank, typical for inline engines where one actuator sets lift for every cylinder, as on four-cylinder Valvetronic engines; Toyota's Valvematic also varies lift continuously.
Lift actuator motor or its gear worn
Engine control software needing an update (known on some models)
Eccentric or control shaft stiff from wear or sludge
Faulty air mass reading or intake leak falsifying the plausibility check
Noticeably reduced power, engine in substitute mode
Rough idle and higher fuel consumption
P2DF3: Engine Disconnect Clutch Actuator Position Not Learned

The clutch between combustion engine and electric machine in a P2 hybrid is only usable when the controller knows where its actuator begins to transmit torque. P2DF3 is a status code: that learned position is missing or invalid, often after a battery disconnect, module replacement, software update or clutch repair, before the learn routine has completed.
Learn routine not yet completed after battery disconnect, repair or module replacement
Learn repeatedly aborted because enable conditions were not met
Actuator position sensor delivering implausible values during the learn
Clutch wear or actuator fault pushing the learned value out of its window
Warning lamp or hybrid system message
Jerky engine start or clutch engagement
P2DF4: Electric coolant pumps are usually commanded through a PWM wire or a LIN bus, and pump E is the fifth such pump in a vehicle's lettering; what it cools depends on the manufacturer. P2DF4 reports an open or otherwise faulty command line to pump E. No manufacturer documents P2DF4 publicly.
Pump connector loose, corroded or with pushed-back pin
Broken command wire in the harness
Pump electronics with failed control input
Faulty output driver in the commanding module
Pump runs at fixed speed or not at all
Temperature warning or power reduction of the cooled component
P2DF5: Coolant Pump E Control Circuit Low

P2DF5 means the command line of coolant pump E sits too low, typically shorted to ground, so the module's driver cannot pull it up to the commanded level. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. In Ford's 2024 gasoline OBD summary the matching fault type is 11 (circuit low), again flagged by the smart driver for pumps A and B, continuously above 11 V.
Command wire chafed through and shorted to ground
Moisture or corrosion bridging the command pin to ground
Internal short in the pump's control input
Output stage of the commanding module defective
Pump stopped or stuck at one speed
Rising temperature of the component served by pump E
P2DF6: Coolant Pump E Control Circuit High

P2DF6 is set when the command line of coolant pump E stays high although the module wants it low, most often because it touches a battery-voltage wire. No manufacturer documents P2DF6 publicly. For pumps A and B, Ford's 2024 gasoline document assigns fault type 12 (circuit high), raised by the smart driver once battery voltage reaches 11 V.
Command wire shorted to a battery-voltage wire
Internal fault in the pump electronics pulling the line high
Corrosion bridging adjacent pins in the connector
Commanding module's output stage stuck high
Pump audible at full speed all the time
Slower warm-up of the affected loop
P2DF7: Coolant Pump E Overspeed/Air in System

When an electric pump draws air instead of liquid, its impeller loses load and the rotor races above the commanded speed. P2DF7 reports this for coolant pump E; the title already names trapped air as the usual cause. No manufacturer documents P2DF7 publicly.
Air pocket left after coolant service or component replacement
Low coolant level from a leak in the loop
Damaged or loose impeller, rotor spins freely
Implausible speed feedback from the pump electronics
Warning lamp or coolant level message
Gurgling or whining from the pump area
Overheating or derating of the cooled component
P2DF8: P2DF8 means coolant pump E keeps turning, but slower than the module asked for. No manufacturer documents P2DF8 publicly. Ford's 2024 gasoline summary treats underspeed as fault type B2 of its pumps A and B, monitored continuously from 11 V over 5 seconds.
Bearing wear or debris dragging on the rotor
Air pocket causing the pump to slow or pause for self-protection
Voltage drop in the pump feed or ground
Insufficient cooling or heating of the served circuit
Power reduction possible at high load
P2DF9: P2DF9 covers the hard case: coolant pump E is powered and commanded, but its rotor does not start or comes to a standstill. Brushless pumps sense this internally, for instance from current flowing without commutation feedback, and pass the result to the commanding module. No manufacturer documents P2DF9 publicly.
Seized bearing or impeller jammed by debris
Frozen, gelled or sludged coolant (wrong mixture)
Burnt winding or failed pump electronics
Rotor stuck after long standstill, deposits on the bearing
No coolant flow in the affected circuit
P2DFA: Coolant Pump E Supply Voltage Circuit

Unlike P2DF4 to P2DF6, which concern the command line, P2DFA concerns the power feed of coolant pump E. Smart pumps measure the voltage at their own supply pin and report when it leaves the window they need to run reliably. No manufacturer documents P2DFA publicly.
Blown fuse or relay with burnt contacts in the pump feed
Loose or corroded ground of the pump
Weak 12 V battery or charging fault
Resistance in feed wire or connector
Pump stops intermittently, often with other low-voltage faults
Reduced cooling of the served component
P2DFB: Coolant Pump E Control Module Overtemperature
Electric coolant pumps carry their own driver electronics, and P2DFB reports that those of coolant pump E have run too hot. Which loop pump E serves differs between makers.
Coolant level too low or air trapped in the pump, so the electronics lose their cooling
Impeller or bearing running stiff, motor draws high current and heats up
Driver electronics inside pump E faulty or reporting temperature wrongly
Heat shield missing or pump too close to hot exhaust or turbo parts
Warning lamp or message about the cooling system
Reduced cabin heating or cooling of the component served by pump E
Pump runs at reduced speed or stops for a while, often together with air or stall codes
P2DFC: P2DFC states that the liquid loop cooling the high-voltage battery is losing coolant. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly.
Leaking hose, clamp or quick connector in the battery coolant loop
Leak at the battery chiller, heat exchanger or cooling plates inside the pack
Loop not filled or bled correctly after a repair
Level sensor reporting low although the level is correct
Hybrid or EV system service message and MIL
Charging blocked or drive power reduced
Coolant level in the battery reservoir visibly low, possibly traces of coolant under the car
P2DFD: Some turbocharged and hybrid engines cannot count on intake vacuum to empty the charcoal canister, so an electric purge pump moves the fuel vapour into the intake. P2DFD means this pump does not achieve the expected effect, for instance the pressure or speed it should reach.
Pump connector not fully latched (Nissan Rogue 2022)
Purge pump motor or impeller worn, pump no longer reaches its speed or pressure
Purge hose cracked, disconnected or blocked between canister, pump and intake
Condensation or ice in the intake path, needs ECM update (Hyundai hybrids)
MIL on, usually without noticeable change in driving
EVAP readiness not complete, emissions inspection may fail
Occasional fuel smell when the canister is not purged
P2E00: Gear Lever Position Sensor A Circuit

Gear lever position sensor A is the first of up to four sensors through which an electronic selector tells its control module where the lever sits. In the designs GM and Toyota document, A and B form a redundant pair that each report the full lever position; GM's patent US9249877 has each of its two sensors deliver an x and a y value.
Loose connector or chafed wire at the selector assembly
Supply or ground of sensor A interrupted
Sensor A inside the selector assembly failed
Input stage of the evaluating module faulty
Gear selection still possible through sensor B, sometimes delayed
With a second fault, the vehicle may stay in P or N
P2E01: Gear Lever Position Sensor A Range/Performance
Here sensor A of the gear lever delivers values that are electrically valid but not believable. Two makers document the code.
Selector logic needs a software update (Lexus NX 2022–24)
Sensor A reports an internal error
Magnet or lever mechanism shifted, so sensor A reads off the gate
Shift-system message, selector still works through sensor B
P2E02: Gear Lever Position Sensor A Circuit Low

P2E02 says the signal of gear lever position sensor A is stuck below the lowest value a healthy sensor can output. Typical reasons: the signal wire touches ground, the reference voltage is missing, or the sensor output has collapsed. No manufacturer publishes P2E02.
Signal wire of sensor A shorted to ground
Sensor reference voltage missing or pulled down
Lever position shown on the display jumps or is missing
If sensor B also fails, no range can be selected
P2E03: Gear Lever Position Sensor A Circuit High

With P2E03 the module sees the signal of sensor A above the highest value the sensor can legitimately send. On a pulled-up input this happens when the signal wire is open; it also follows a short to the supply or a lost sensor ground. No manufacturer publishes P2E03.
Signal wire of sensor A open at a connector
Signal wire shorted to supply voltage
Shift-system message, ranges still selectable via sensor B
Start or range change refused if both sensors are affected
P2E04: Gear Lever Position Sensor B Circuit
Sensor B is the second, redundant gear lever position sensor; it measures the same lever travel as sensor A so that a single failure does not leave the driver without range selection.
Connector or wire of sensor B at the selector loose or damaged
Sensor B in the selector assembly failed
Separate supply branch of sensor B interrupted
Selector works normally on sensor A alone
Any further sensor fault can block range changes
P2E05: Gear Lever Position Sensor B Range/Performance
P2E05 flags implausible data from sensor B, the backup gear lever sensor. It is one of the few codes of this family with public manufacturer use.
Floor shift assembly logic outdated (Lexus NX bulletin L-SB-0050-22)
Sensor B signals an internal error
Sensor B or its magnet misaligned after a repair in the console
