MIL on, usually without a driveability change
Shift-system warning may appear and disappear
P2E06: Gear Lever Position Sensor B Circuit Low

The signal of sensor B, the redundant gear lever sensor, has dropped under its permitted minimum. Electrically that points to a short to ground in its signal line, a dead sensor or a missing feed on its own supply branch. P2E06 is not published by any manufacturer.
Signal line of sensor B shorted to ground
Supply branch of sensor B dead
Selector keeps working on sensor A
Range selection lost if sensor A fails as well
P2E07: Gear Lever Position Sensor B Circuit High

P2E07 is the high-side circuit fault of gear lever position sensor B: its signal reads above anything the sensor may legitimately produce. An interrupted signal line on an input with pull-up, a short to battery or reference voltage, or a broken sensor ground are the classic causes. No maker publishes P2E07.
Signal line of sensor B open
Signal line shorted to battery or reference voltage
With P2E03 present as well, range selection may be blocked
P2E08: Gear Lever Position Sensor C Circuit

A third gear lever position sensor, C, only exists on selectors with more than the usual redundant pair. Toyota's patent US10180184 shows such a design: four Hall sensors in a row face a magnet in the shift lever, the voltages they produce encode the position, and if any one of them is faulty the other three still allow limp-home driving.
Connector or wiring at the selector assembly faulty
Sensor C inside the selector failed
Shifting continues on the remaining sensors
A further sensor fault may force neutral
P2E09: Gear Lever Position Sensor C Range/Performance

P2E09 means sensor C produces an electrically valid signal that contradicts the lever position given by the other sensors. No manufacturer documents this code or names the role of a sensor C, so the logic can only be inferred from the component.
Sensor C output frozen at an intermediate value
Magnet or lever mechanism worn or displaced
Plausibility logic of the selector software too strict
Warning appears only after certain lever movements
Range display briefly disagrees with lever position
P2E0A: Gear Lever Position Sensor C Circuit Low

For P2E0A the module reads the signal of gear lever sensor C below the window a working sensor can occupy. On a voltage-output Hall sensor like those in Toyota's four-sensor selector patent (US10180184), this means a signal line pulled to ground, a missing feed or a sensor that has stopped driving its output.
Signal wire of sensor C shorted to ground
No noticeable change while other sensors are valid
P2E0B: Gear Lever Position Sensor C Circuit High

P2E0B: sensor C of the gear lever reports more than its maximum valid signal. That is the typical picture of a broken signal wire on a pulled-up input, contact with the feed line or a lost sensor ground. No manufacturer documents P2E0B, and the function of a third lever sensor is nowhere specified publicly.
Signal wire of sensor C open
Signal wire shorted to supply voltage
Selector keeps working with the other sensors
Neutral forced if another sensor also fails
P2E0C: Gear Lever Position Sensor D Circuit

Sensor D is the fourth and last letter in this family of gear lever position sensors. A layout that needs four is described in Toyota's patent US10180184: four Hall sensors lined up along the shift direction under one magnet, whose voltage pattern flips when the lever moves sideways, so both shift and select movement can be read.
Selector connector or wiring of sensor D faulty
Module input for sensor D faulty
Neutral fail-safe possible after a second sensor fault
P2E0D: Gear Lever Position Sensor D Range/Performance
With P2E0D the fourth lever sensor, D, stays within its electrical limits but its reading does not fit the lever position. No manufacturer documents P2E0D.
Sensor D frozen at a middle value
Magnet position in the lever changed by wear or impact
Selector software tolerance needs an update
Code appears only after selecting a certain position
P2E0E: Gear Lever Position Sensor D Circuit Low

P2E0E is set when the output of gear lever position sensor D drops beneath its lowest plausible level, usually near 0 V or 0 % duty cycle. Likely reasons are a ground short in the D signal path, a sensor without feed or a Hall element whose output died. No maker publishes P2E0E or a meaning for sensor D.
Signal path of sensor D shorted to ground
Hall element of sensor D failed low
Selector still usable on the other sensors
Shift to neutral if another sensor fails
P2E0F: Gear Lever Position Sensor D Circuit High

P2E0F closes the series: sensor D, the fourth gear lever position sensor, reads above the top of its valid range. An open signal wire where the module input pulls up, contact with a voltage-carrying wire or a lost sensor ground produce this picture. No manufacturer documents P2E0F, nor the role of sensor D in a real selector.
Signal wire of sensor D open
Signal wire touching a voltage-carrying wire
Normal shifting on the remaining sensors
Neutral fail-safe after a further fault
P2E10: Gear Selection Actuator Position Sensor Circuit

P2E10 is the general circuit code for the sensor reporting where the gear selection actuator stands, the motor-driven unit that moves the shift mechanism of an automated manual or dual-clutch gearbox to the wanted gear or gate.
Corroded or loose connector, damaged harness at the actuator
Position sensor in the actuator failed (often only replaceable with the actuator)
Sensor reference voltage missing or loaded down by another fault
Input stage in the transmission control module faulty
Gearbox holds one gear or goes to neutral (limp mode)
Shifts refused or engaging drive or reverse not possible
P2E11: Gear Selection Actuator Position Sensor Performance

With P2E11 the position sensor of the gear selection actuator delivers values that are electrically fine but do not fit the situation: the reading stays put although the actuator was driven, or it contradicts the gear that shaft speeds prove to be engaged. No manufacturer documents P2E11 publicly.
Learned end positions lost or outdated, e.g. after battery disconnect or part replacement
Sensor magnet or sensor mounting shifted, reading offset
Wear or binding in the selection mechanism, actuator does not reach its target
Delayed or harsh shifts, gear sometimes not engaged
Transmission warning, possibly limp mode with fixed gear
Fault may clear after a relearn procedure
P2E12: Gear Selection Actuator Position Sensor Circuit Low

P2E12 sets when the signal of the gear selection actuator's position sensor stays below the lowest valid level. Usual reasons are a short to ground on the signal line, a missing 5 V reference or a defect inside the sensor; with many designs an interrupted signal wire also reads low. No manufacturer documents P2E12 publicly.
Signal wire chafed through and shorted to ground
5 V reference missing or pulled down by another sensor on the same supply
Internal short in the position sensor
Limp mode, no gear changes or only one gear
Further sensor codes if the shared 5 V supply is affected
P2E13: Gear Selection Actuator Position Sensor Circuit High

P2E13 is the opposite case to P2E12: the position signal of the gear selection actuator sits above its highest plausible value. A short between the signal line and a supply wire is the classic cause; an open ground or, on pull-up inputs, a broken signal wire produce the same picture. No manufacturer documents P2E13 publicly.
Signal wire shorted to a supply or 5 V reference line
Sensor ground open or high resistance
Position sensor faulty, output stuck high
Moisture in the actuator connector bridging pins
Gearbox stays in one gear or in neutral
P2E14: Gear Selection Actuator Position Sensor Circuit Intermittent/Erratic

P2E14 covers a position signal from the gear selection actuator that is present but unsteady: it drops out for moments, jumps or carries an implausible frequency or pattern, without staying low or high long enough for P2E12 or P2E13. No manufacturer documents P2E14 publicly. Two related checks show what erratic means in practice.
Loose or fretted terminal in the actuator connector
Harness chafing that only shorts or opens under vibration or heat
Interference from damaged shielding or nearby motor wiring
Sensor with an internal intermittent fault
Short drops to neutral while driving
Warning lamp that comes and goes
P2E15: Intermediate Shaft Selection Actuator Position Sensor Circuit

P2E15 is the basic circuit code for the position sensor of a second selection actuator, one assigned to the intermediate shaft (layshaft) of the gearbox rather than to the main gear selection, which has P2E10 to P2E14. Which gearboxes use such an actuator, and what exactly it engages there, no manufacturer documents publicly for this code.
Connector or harness to the intermediate shaft actuator damaged or corroded
Position sensor of the actuator failed
Faulty input stage in the transmission control module
Some gears unavailable or gearbox in limp mode
Vehicle may only drive in a restricted range of gears
P2E16: Intermediate Shaft Selection Actuator Position Sensor Range/Performance

P2E16 flags a position reading from the intermediate shaft selection actuator that is electrically valid but not credible, for example a travel that does not match the commanded movement or the learned end stops. No manufacturer documents P2E16 publicly.
End stops not learned or lost after battery disconnect or repair
Actuator or selection linkage binding, target position not reached
Sensor or its magnet shifted, reading offset
Harsh, slow or failed shifts involving the intermediate shaft
Fault returns until a relearn has been done
P2E17: Intermediate Shaft Selection Actuator Position Sensor Circuit Low

P2E17 tells you the position signal of the intermediate shaft selection actuator is stuck at the bottom of its range or below it. On the bench this usually turns out to be a signal line touching ground, a dead reference supply, or a sensor whose output stage has failed. No manufacturer documents P2E17 publicly.
Output stage of the position sensor failed
Signal wire interrupted (on sensors that then read low)
Code returns at once after clearing
P2E18: Intermediate Shaft Selection Actuator Position Sensor Circuit High

Here the position sensor of the intermediate shaft selection actuator reports a value above its upper limit. Most often the signal line has contact with battery voltage or the 5 V feed, or the sensor has lost its ground so the output floats upward. No manufacturer documents P2E18 publicly.
Signal line shorted to battery voltage or the 5 V feed
Faulty input stage in the transmission control module
Poor acceleration because the gearbox holds an unsuitable gear
P2E19: Intermediate Shaft Selection Actuator Position Sensor Circuit Intermittent/Erratic

P2E19 is stored when the intermediate shaft selection actuator's position sensor delivers a signal that flickers, drops out briefly or changes faster than the mechanism could physically move. Because the fault comes and goes, the code often shows as pending or with only a few occurrences. No manufacturer documents P2E19 publicly.
Loose or corroded terminal at the actuator or gearbox connector
Harness rubbing on the housing, contact only under vibration
Sensor with an internal intermittent fault
Sporadic shift faults that disappear again
Warning lamp only now and then
P2E1A: Drive Motor A Inverter Voltage Sensor A/B Correlation

P2E1A sets when the two DC voltage readings inside the drive motor A inverter, sensor A and sensor B, stop agreeing although they should describe the same high-voltage potential. Each value may pass its own range test; the fault lies in the mismatch. No manufacturer documents P2E1A publicly.
One of the two voltage measuring channels in the inverter has drifted
Fault in the inverter or power drive unit electronics
Poor high-voltage connection between the two measuring points
Control software with an unsuitable comparison window
Hybrid system or drive warning lamp, MIL possible
Reduced or no electric drive power
Further inverter voltage codes stored at the same time
P2E1B: Drive Motor A Phase X Current Sensor Circuit

P2E1B reports an electrical fault in the circuit of the phase X current sensor of drive motor A, without a separate low or high verdict. X, Y and Z name a second three-phase winding group: a Mitsubishi Electric patent on two-group motors for hybrid drives couples one current sensor to the conductor of each of the six phases.
Phase X current sensor in the inverter failed
Reference supply or ground of the current sensors faulty
Loose or corroded low-voltage connector at the inverter
Defect on the motor control board that evaluates the sensor
Hybrid system warning lamp and MIL
Reduced electric drive or no electric drive
Rough or noisy motor operation under load
P2E1C: Drive Motor A Phase X Current Sensor Circuit Range/Performance

P2E1C means the phase X current sensor of drive motor A delivers a value that is electrically valid but implausible. No manufacturer documents P2E1C publicly; GM's U/V/W counterparts show the usual test, a zero check.
Zero offset of the phase X sensor has drifted
Sensor gain error after ageing or overheating
Unstable reference voltage for the current sensors
Fault in the measuring stage of the inverter control board
Electric drive limited, uneven torque at low speed
Code returns after clearing at the next start
P2E1D: Drive Motor A Phase X Current Sensor Circuit Low

P2E1D says the phase X current sensor signal of drive motor A lies below its lowest valid value. Phase current flows in both directions, so the sensor reports a signed quantity; low therefore means a reading more negative than any real current, not a weak current. That other case, too little current in an energised phase, is P2C6A.
Sensor signal shorted to ground inside the inverter
Supply voltage of the phase X sensor missing
Sharp loss of electric drive power
Vehicle may only drive in a reduced mode
P2E1E: Drive Motor A Phase X Current Sensor Circuit High

P2E1E flags a phase X current sensor signal of drive motor A above the top of its valid range. No manufacturer documents P2E1E publicly. GM's U-phase counterpart on the 2016 Volt trips above 700 A for 0.05 s within 0.1 s, Type A.
Sensor signal shorted to the sensor supply
Open ground of the phase X current sensor
Phase X current sensor failed high
Electric drive cut off or strongly limited
Possible jolt when the inverter shuts down
P2E1F: Drive Motor A Phase Y Current Sensor Circuit
P2E1F stands for a circuit fault of the phase Y current sensor of drive motor A that is not sorted into a low or high case.
Phase Y current sensor in the inverter failed
Poor contact at the inverter's low-voltage connector
Electric drive limited or switched off
Other phase current codes may be stored as well
P2E20: Drive Motor A Phase Y Current Sensor Circuit Range/Performance

P2E20 is set when the phase Y current sensor of drive motor A reads within its electrical limits but not believably. No manufacturer documents P2E20 publicly. Besides the zero check, a current balance can expose a sensor with a wrong gain.
Gain error of the phase Y sensor
Zero offset of the phase Y sensor shifted
Disturbed reference voltage of the current sensors
Motor control software needing an update
Less electric assist, torque not as requested
P2E21: Drive Motor A Phase Y Current Sensor Circuit Low

P2E21 records that the phase Y current sensor of drive motor A reports a value under the bottom of its scale. No manufacturer documents P2E21 publicly. GM's eAssist logic shows a clean way to test for this: the low and high checks of its U and W sensors run while PWM output is disabled, so the inverter is not switching and no phase current can flow.
Phase Y sensor signal shorted to ground
Engine runs more often than usual on hybrids
P2E22: Drive Motor A Phase Y Current Sensor Circuit High

P2E22 is stored when the phase Y current sensor signal of drive motor A sticks above its upper limit. No manufacturer documents P2E22 publicly. On GM's 2016 Cadillac ELR the U/V/W counterparts fail above 800 A, judged as 4 bad samples out of 6 at 10.4 ms intervals, Type A.
Phase Y signal shorted to the sensor supply
Open ground of the phase Y sensor
Shared sensor reference faulty, other phases affected too
Electric drive switched off or strongly limited
High codes of other phases stored at the same time
P2E23: Drive Motor A Phase Z Current Sensor Circuit
P2E23 points to a wiring or circuit defect around the phase Z current sensor of drive motor A that is not classed as low or high. Whether a Z sensor exists at all depends on the design.
Loose or corroded low-voltage connector at the inverter
Phase Z current sensor in the inverter failed
Supply or ground of the Z sensor interrupted
Electric drive limited or switched off
Fault may come and go with vibration or temperature
P2E24: Drive Motor A Phase Z Current Sensor Circuit Range/Performance
P2E24 concerns a phase Z current reading of drive motor A that passes the electrical checks yet fails a plausibility test. No manufacturer documents P2E24 publicly.
Zero offset of the phase Z sensor drifted
Gain error of the phase Z sensor
Faulty measuring stage on the inverter control board
P2E25: Drive Motor A Phase Z Current Sensor Circuit Low

P2E25 means the phase Z current sensor of drive motor A reports below its valid minimum. No manufacturer documents P2E25 publicly. A zero reading is not the same thing: if phase Z carries no current because a lead is open, the sensor correctly reads about zero and the open phase is judged by P2C70.
Phase Z sensor signal shorted to ground
Shared sensor reference or ground faulty
Low codes of other phases possibly stored too
P2E26: Drive Motor A Phase Z Current Sensor Circuit High
P2E26 reports a phase Z current sensor signal of drive motor A that sits above its permitted range. No manufacturer documents P2E26 publicly.
Phase Z signal shorted to the sensor supply
Open ground of the phase Z sensor
Phase Z current sensor failed high
Vehicle continues only in a reduced-power mode
P2E27: Drive Motor A Phase X-Y-Z Current Sensor Correlation

P2E27 compares the three current sensors of phases X, Y and Z of drive motor A with each other. Mitsubishi Electric's patent joins the X, Y and Z windings in a star, so their currents must add up to almost zero at every instant; a clear residual means at least one sensor is wrong, even if every reading passes its own checks.
One of the three X/Y/Z sensors drifted in offset or gain
Disturbed common reference of the current sensors
Leakage current from the X/Y/Z winding group to the housing
Electric drive limited or temporarily switched off
No single sensor code stored alongside
P2E28: Drive Motor A Excitation Current Sensor Performance

P2E28 concerns a drive motor with an electrically excited rotor, the type Nissan uses in the Ariya and BMW in its fifth-generation eDrive. Such a rotor carries a field coil that receives direct current through brushes and slip rings; a sensor measures that current for the closed field-control loop.
Excitation current sensor drifted (offset or gain no longer correct)
Faulty excitation power stage, so actual and expected current differ
Worn brushes or dirty slip rings changing the field circuit resistance
Inverter or motor control software fault
Electric drive warning or service message
Vehicle may refuse to drive or stop driving
P2E29: Drive Motor A Excitation Current Sensor Circuit Low Voltage

P2E29 reports that the signal voltage of the excitation current sensor of drive motor A has dropped below the band the controller accepts. The sensor sits in the excitation stage that feeds direct current to the rotor field coil of an electrically excited motor; TI names shunts with isolated amplifiers or isolated Hall-effect sensors for this job.
Sensor signal line shorted to ground
Sensor supply or reference voltage missing
Excitation current sensor or its isolated amplifier failed
Loss of drive power from motor A
Vehicle may not become ready to drive
P2E2A: Drive Motor A Excitation Current Sensor Circuit High Voltage

P2E2A is the counterpart to P2E29: the signal from the sensor that measures the rotor field current of drive motor A sits above the highest voltage a working sensor can deliver. Typical reasons are a signal line touching a supply rail, an open ground or reference connection that lets the input float up, or a failed sensor output stage.
Sensor signal line shorted to a supply voltage
Open sensor ground or reference connection
P2E2B: Drive Motor A Excitation Current Too High

P2E2B does not blame the sensor: the measured field current of drive motor A itself exceeds what the controller allows. In TI's example of an excitation stage, two switches and two diodes sit between the high-voltage rails; with both switches on, the rotor coil sees the entire DC-link voltage, and switches of this kind are rarely sized above about 50 A.
Excitation power switch shorted or stuck on
Field current control or gate driver fault in the inverter
Shorted turns in the rotor field winding
Sudden loss of drive power from motor A
Vehicle may not restart the drive system
P2E2C: Battery Charger A Module Supply Voltage Performance

P2E2C covers the low-voltage supply that powers the control electronics of on-board charger A, not the AC input. The code means this supply voltage is present but behaves implausibly, for example it fluctuates or disagrees with what other modules see on the same 12 V network.
Loose or corroded supply or ground connection at the charger
Ground offset between charger and other modules
Unstable 12 V supply from weak battery or DC/DC converter
Faulty voltage measurement inside the charger module
Plug-in charging does not start or stops early
Fault comes and goes with electrical load or vibration
P2E2D: Battery Charger A Module Supply Voltage Low

P2E2D is set when the 12 V feed of the control board in on-board charger A stays below its lower limit. The usual suspects sit outside the charger: a discharged or failing 12 V battery, a DC/DC converter that is not keeping the network up, a blown fuse in the feed, or resistance in supply or ground wiring that eats voltage under load.
Blown fuse or failed relay in the charger supply
High resistance in supply or ground wiring
DC/DC converter not maintaining the 12 V network
Further low-voltage faults in other modules
P2E2E: Battery Charger A Module Supply Voltage High
P2E2E reports the opposite of P2E2D: the low-voltage feed of on-board charger A rises above its upper limit.
DC/DC converter regulating the 12 V network too high
External battery charger or jump starter with excessive voltage
Faulty voltage measurement inside the charger module
Plug-in charging stops or will not start
Overvoltage faults stored in other modules as well
Lamps unusually bright or 12 V battery overcharged
P2E2F: Battery Charger B Module Supply Voltage Performance

P2E2F concerns the 12 V feed of the control electronics in a second on-board charger, charger B, not its grid input. The voltage is within limits but behaves implausibly, for example it jumps around or disagrees with the system voltage that other modules report. No manufacturer documents P2E2F publicly.
Loose or corroded supply or ground terminal at charger B
Ground offset between charger B and the reference module
Fluctuating 12 V network from weak battery or DC/DC converter
Faulty supply voltage measurement inside charger B
Plug-in charging starts late, pauses or stops
Fault appears with electrical load changes or vibration
Charging system warning in the instrument cluster
P2E30: Battery Charger B Module Supply Voltage Low

P2E30 is stored when the 12 V feed reaching the control board of charger B stays under its lower limit. Most causes lie upstream: a flat or aged 12 V battery, a blown fuse or failed relay in the charger feed, or corroded supply and ground contacts that lose voltage under load. No manufacturer documents P2E30 publicly, and no threshold is published.
Blown fuse or failed relay in the charger B feed
Voltage drop across corroded supply or ground contacts
DC/DC converter not holding up the 12 V network
Charging through charger B does not start
Low-voltage or communication faults in other modules too
Reduced charging power if only one charger works
P2E31: Battery Charger B Module Supply Voltage High

P2E31 is the high-side counterpart of P2E30: the low-voltage feed of charger B climbs above what its control electronics accept. On plug-in cars the DC/DC converter holds the 12 V network, so a converter regulating too high is the main suspect; a workshop charger or jump pack set too high, or a faulty measurement inside charger B, can give the same reading.
DC/DC converter regulating the 12 V network too high
Workshop charger or jump starter with excessive voltage
Faulty supply voltage measurement inside charger B
Charging via charger B stops or will not start
Overvoltage codes stored in several modules
12 V battery gassing or lamps unusually bright
P2E32: Battery Charger A Module Forced Shutdown Voltage Performance
P2E32 belongs to the forced shutdown input of on-board charger A, a hardwired signal with which another module can switch the charger off regardless of bus messages.
Contact resistance or partly corroded terminal in the shutdown line
Shutdown input stage inside charger A not responding correctly
Fault or software issue in the module driving the shutdown signal
Plug-in charging refused or ended unexpectedly
P2E33: Battery Charger A Module Forced Shutdown Voltage Low

P2E33 reports that the voltage on the forced shutdown line of charger A sits below its valid band. What that means in practice depends on the logic, which no manufacturer publishes for this code. Shutdown lines are often built fail-safe, as in Watt & Well's EVCC charging controller, where a missing loop current counts as an emergency stop.
Shutdown line chafed through and shorted to ground
Broken wire or backed-out pin in the shutdown circuit
Moisture or corrosion in the charger signal connector
Output stage of the commanding module stuck low
Charging aborts when the car or harness is moved
P2E34: Battery Charger A Module Forced Shutdown Voltage High

P2E34 is set when the forced shutdown line of charger A reads above its permitted voltage. The usual cause is contact with a battery-fed or switched 12 V wire in the same harness, or an internal leak inside the charger or the commanding module. No manufacturer documents P2E34 publicly.
Shutdown line shorted to a 12 V feed in the harness
Internal leakage in charger A or the commanding module
Incorrect wiring after a previous harness repair
Charger A disabled, plug-in charging not possible or slower
P2E35: P2E35 covers the enable line of charger B, the hardwired 12 V signal that wakes the charger or allows it to work, and reports a general circuit fault, usually an open. No manufacturer documents P2E35 publicly.
Broken enable wire or backed-out terminal
Signal connector at charger B not fully latched
Failed enable driver in the commanding module
Charger B does not wake when the cable is plugged in
Charging slower than usual or not at all
P2E36: Battery Charger B Enable Circuit Low

P2E36 means the enable signal to charger B is pulled under the level its commanded state allows, most often by a short to ground or by a driver stage that cannot pull the line up. No manufacturer documents P2E36 publicly.
Enable wire chafed and shorted to ground
Water or corrosion in the charger B signal connector
Damaged high-side driver in the commanding module
Charger B stays off whenever charging is requested
Lower charging power or no charging
P2E37: Battery Charger B Enable Circuit High

P2E37 is stored when the enable line of charger B carries more voltage than its commanded state allows, typically because it touches a powered wire or the driver in the commanding module is stuck on. No manufacturer documents P2E37 publicly.
Enable wire shorted to a 12 V feed
Enable driver in the commanding module stuck on
Internal leakage in the charger B input circuit
Charger B fan or pump runs with nothing plugged in
P2E38: Battery Charger B Enable Circuit Range/Performance
P2E38 flags an enable circuit of charger B that is electrically sound, while the charger or its partner modules do not react to it as expected. No manufacturer documents P2E38 publicly.
Software mismatch between charger B and battery control module
Battery control module not waking or starting too slowly
Enable level marginal due to contact resistance
Charging begins only after a long delay or not at all
Fault appears only on some charging sessions
P2E39: P2E39 concerns the high-voltage fuse in the branch between the traction battery and charger B. Battery management units usually judge such fuses by comparing the voltage behind the fuse with the pack voltage; Volvo's technical journal TJ 37376 on BECM codes P0A9500 and P0E2F00 has technicians read exactly those values at the fuse outputs.
Fuse opened by an internal short in charger B
Spurious entry from battery management software
Faulty voltage sensing behind the fuse
Charging through charger B no longer possible
P2E3A: Battery Charger B Output Voltage Performance

P2E3A says the high-voltage output of charger B does not follow its target, typically in the constant-voltage phase near the end of a charge, without being clearly too low. No manufacturer documents P2E3A publicly. The A-side code P0D20 shows two readings of the same check.
Degraded power stage or regulation inside charger B
Charger or battery module software needing an update
Battery does not reach full charge
Charging stops early or takes longer
P2E3B: Battery Charger B Output Voltage Too Low
P2E3B is set when the high-voltage output of charger B stays below what the control unit expects while charging. No manufacturer documents P2E3B publicly.
Charger module software fault fixed by reprogramming
Failed power stage inside charger B
High resistance in the HV output connection
MIL on and vehicle will not charge
Level 2 charging fails, wall box breaker may trip
P2E3C: Battery Charger B Output Current Performance

P2E3C means charger B does not deliver the high-voltage current it has been asked for. No manufacturer documents P2E3C publicly. Its A-side model P0D22 is well covered: the 2011 Volt compares actual and desired current in constant-current mode against a table and sets the code after 150 bad samples in 300, One Trip Type A.
Control software or calibration of charger or hybrid module
Weak power stage inside charger B
Charging takes noticeably longer or aborts
Problem more frequent in cold weather
P2E3D: P2E3D points to a short on the high-voltage output side of charger B. No manufacturer documents P2E3D publicly.
Internal short in the charger B output stage
Damaged high-voltage cable between charger B and battery
Leaking or stuck contactor path in the charging circuit
Charging blocked as soon as the cable is plugged in
P2E3E: Battery Charger B Module Forced Shutdown Voltage Performance

P2E3E is the charger B version of P2E32: the forced shutdown signal of the second charger is electrically in range but its behaviour is implausible. Examples are a shutdown request that the charger ignores, or a level that changes state without a matching command, so the control unit can no longer trust its hardwired off-switch for path B.
Shutdown input stage inside charger B not responding correctly
Intermittent contact in the charger B shutdown line
Software issue in the module issuing the shutdown
Charging slower than usual because charger B is locked out
P2E3F: Battery Charger B Module Forced Shutdown Voltage Low
P2E3F reports a forced shutdown signal at charger B that stays below its permitted voltage. No manufacturer documents P2E3F or the shutdown logic behind it publicly.
Shutdown line of charger B shorted to ground
Broken wire or loose pin in the signal plug
Output stage of the commanding module stuck low
Charger B never takes part in charging
Reduced charging power or no charging
P2E40: Battery Charger B Module Forced Shutdown Voltage High

P2E40 means the forced shutdown signal of charger B reads above its valid band, typically from a short to a 12 V wire or a leak inside the charger or the module that drives it. No manufacturer documents P2E40 publicly.
Shutdown line of charger B shorted to a 12 V wire
Internal leakage in charger B or the commanding module
Miswiring after a harness or charger repair
Charging slower or impossible with charger B locked out
P2E41: Hybrid/EV Electronics Coolant Pump B Control Circuit/Open

P2E41 flags an electrical fault on the line over which the controller commands electronics coolant pump B, the second pump serving inverter, DC/DC converter and frequently the charger; the maker decides which pump is B. No manufacturer publicly documents P2E41.
Broken or disconnected control wire between module and pump B
Corroded or pushed-back pins at the pump connector
Pump B electronics no longer load the command line
Faulty output stage in the controlling module
Hybrid or electric drive warning and MIL
Pump B does not run, electronics loop warms up faster
Reduced drive power or interrupted charging under high load
P2E42: Hybrid/EV Electronics Coolant Pump B Performance

P2E42 is the functional verdict on electronics coolant pump B: the circuits test fine, yet the controller concludes the pump is not doing its job. Two ways of reaching that verdict are documented for pump A.
Air pocket after service or slow coolant loss
Worn pump B delivering too little flow
Debris, kinked hose or clogged cold plate in the loop
Higher inverter or charger temperatures than usual
Power reduction or slower charging in hot conditions
P2E43: Hybrid/EV Electronics Coolant Pump B Control Circuit Low

P2E43 means the command signal of electronics coolant pump B sits too low, typically because the line has contact with ground or the output stage cannot drive it up. On PWM-controlled pumps this usually stops the pump outright.
Control wire chafed through and shorted to ground
Moisture or corrosion bridging pins in the pump connector
Shorted input stage inside pump B
Output stage of the module stuck low
Pump B stops, electronics coolant heats up
MIL with hybrid or drive system message
Limited power or charging rate under load
P2E44: Hybrid/EV Electronics Coolant Pump B Control Circuit High

P2E44 is the opposite fault: the command line of electronics coolant pump B reads higher than its commanded state allows, mostly because it touches a battery-fed wire or the driver can no longer pull it down.
Control wire shorted to a battery-voltage circuit
Module output stage unable to pull the line low
Moisture linking supply and signal pins in the connector
Pump B runs continuously at high speed, audible hum
Pump does not respond to commanded speed changes
P2E45: Hybrid/EV Electronics Coolant Pump B Enable Circuit
Some designs switch electronics coolant pump B on through a separate enable line or a relay, independent of the speed command; P2E45 reports a fault in that path.
Enable wire open or shorted between module and pump
Pump relay or its fuse failed, where the design uses one
Faulty enable output in the controlling module
Pump B never starts although commanded
MIL and hybrid or charging warning
Power or charging limited as electronics heat up
P2E46: Hybrid/EV Electronics Coolant Pump B Overspeed - Dry Run

P2E46 is the dry-run report of electronics coolant pump B: faster than commanded at lower current, the signature of air at the impeller. Porsche describes such self-monitoring on the traction-battery pump of the 2018 Panamera plug-in hybrid (code P0C4A00 there).
Low coolant level from a leaking hose, joint or component
Air left in the loop after service without vacuum fill
Pump B damaged by earlier dry running
Pump starts briefly, then stops again
Gurgling noise or falling level in the electronics reservoir
P2E47: Hybrid/EV Electronics Coolant Pump B Underspeed

P2E47 is set when electronics coolant pump B keeps turning but clearly slower than requested. GM's 2018 hybrid tables describe the check for pump A (P19FC): the filtered difference between commanded and reported speed must stay within a calibrated band once the pump has run for 5 s at 11 to 90 % duty, otherwise a Type B fault results.
Stiff bearing or worn pump B
Deposits or debris slowing the impeller
Voltage drop on pump supply or ground under load
Incorrect or aged coolant, too viscous when cold
Electronics temperatures rise during long drives or fast charging
P2E48: Hybrid/EV Electronics Coolant Pump B Overspeed

With P2E48 the controller sees electronics coolant pump B turning faster than commanded, without the separate dry-run test (P2E46) having fired. The usual reason is lost load, since a centrifugal pump accelerates when its impeller gets less liquid, whether from a low level, a collapsed suction hose, partial air or an impeller slipping on its shaft.
Low level or residual air in the electronics loop
Collapsed or kinked hose on the pump inlet side
Impeller slipping on the pump shaft
Implausible speed feedback from the pump electronics
MIL, sometimes with a coolant level warning
Rising electronics temperatures and power limits
P2E49: Hybrid/EV Electronics Coolant Pump B Stuck/Stalled

P2E49 reports that electronics coolant pump B is powered and commanded, but its rotor does not turn or comes to a standstill. Mitsubishi's 2022 Outlander PHEV shows such a test for its electric water pump: with more than 9 V supply the PHEV-ECU sets P10D9 once the reported speed stays under 100 rpm for 0.5 s, against about 500 rpm when healthy.
Seized bearing or failed pump B motor
Debris or sealant residue jamming the impeller
Frozen coolant due to insufficient antifreeze
Supply or ground lost under load
MIL and hybrid or drive system warning
Rapid temperature rise in inverter or charger
Strong power reduction or charging stops
P2E4A: Battery Charger Coupler Temperature Sensor C Circuit

P2E4A is the general electrical fault of a third temperature measuring point in the charging inlet, logged when the module sees a defective circuit but does not sort it into low, high or implausible. Unlike sensors A and B, the C row has no intermittent code of its own.
Sensor lead or crimp between inlet and evaluating module broken
Low-voltage connector of the inlet harness loose or corroded
Temperature element C (or one element of a PTC chain) failed inside the inlet
Measuring input in the charger or charge control module defective
Charging refused or only possible at reduced power
Charging system warning in the cluster or the app
Charge indicator at the inlet signals a fault
P2E4B: Battery Charger Coupler Temperature Sensor C Circuit Range/Performance

P2E4B concerns a sensor C value that is electrically valid yet does not fit the situation, for instance a reading that ignores a heavy charge current, departs from the other inlet sensors or jumps without cause. CARB wants such rationality faults kept under their own code, apart from codes for wiring faults and values beyond the limits.
Worn or widened terminals in the charging station plug heating the contact unevenly
Sensor no longer in good thermal contact with its pin
Plausibility logic in the charging software too strict, update available
Temperature element drifted from its characteristic curve
Charging stops or starts at reduced power, often at busy public stations
Fault does not reappear until the car has been driven for a while
P2E4C: Battery Charger Coupler Temperature Sensor C Circuit Low

P2E4C says the voltage on the sensor C input has fallen under its lower limit. Low is about the signal; the temperature it implies depends on the element. Volex fits its NACS inlet with NTC thermistors of 100 kΩ at 25 °C and a B value of 4150 K, whose resistance shrinks as they warm, so with a pull-up a very low voltage stands for an absurdly hot contact.
Sensor C signal wire shorted to ground
Water or corrosion bridging the sensor terminals in the inlet or its connector
Measuring input of the evaluating module defective
Charging blocked at once or ended shortly after start
Fault may follow rain or a car wash
P2E4D: Battery Charger Coupler Temperature Sensor C Circuit High

P2E4D is stored when the sensor C input rises above its upper limit. In a pull-up circuit that is the signature of an open loop, an unplugged connector or a short to a supply voltage. Read as temperature, it means very cold for an NTC, but very hot for a PT1000 or a PTC element.
Sensor C loop open, for example a broken wire or unplugged connector
Signal wire shorted to a supply voltage
Temperature element C or one link of a PTC chain open inside the inlet
Measuring input of the evaluating module defective
Charging does not start or stops immediately
Displayed inlet temperature stuck at an extreme value
P2E4E: Battery Charger Coupler Temperature C Too High

P2E4E is no sensor fault: measuring point C works, but the contact it watches has become too hot, so charging is cut back or ended. For orientation, a DOE laboratory report from August 2025 compares the IEC 62196-1 ceiling, 90 °C when the air is at 40 °C, with the fixed 100 °C of SAE J3400. No manufacturer documents P2E4E publicly.
Worn, widened or dirty pins in the station plug or the vehicle inlet
Charging cable with thin conductors heating up at high current (Porsche)
Long high-current session in strong heat or direct sun
Temperature logic in the charging software, update available
Charging slows down or stops partway through
Charge indicator at the inlet flashes a fault or reduced-power state
Discoloured or heat-marked pins at the plug or inlet
P2E4F: Battery Charger Coupler Temperature Sensor D Circuit

P2E4F is the general circuit fault of the fourth inlet temperature sensor, used when the wiring is clearly wrong but not classed as low, high or implausible; the D row has no intermittent code either.
Low-voltage connector between inlet harness and evaluating module loose (smart for sensor A)
Sensor D wiring chafed or broken
Temperature element D failed (normally replaced with the inlet)
Measuring input in the SOBDM or charger defective
DC fast charging refused or limited
Fault may only show with a warm or cold inlet
P2E50: Battery Charger Coupler Temperature Sensor D Circuit Range/Performance

P2E50 flags sensor D for delivering a believable voltage that the logic still rejects. A module can test this in several ways: compare D with a sensor on a contact that carries the same current, check whether it warms as expected under load, or look for steps no metal pin could make.
Sensor D has lost good thermal contact with its pin
One contact heating far more than its partner due to wear or dirt
Plausibility thresholds in the module software, update available
DC fast charging limited or ended early
P2E51: Battery Charger Coupler Temperature Sensor D Circuit Low

P2E51 reports a sensor D voltage below the valid band. TE Connectivity lists thermistors, thermocouples and resistance temperature detectors as candidate elements for inlet sensing (US10960781), and the patent also explains the stakes: contact resistance heats the inlet at high current and could melt parts or start a fire if nobody watches.
Sensor D signal wire shorted to ground
Moisture or corrosion in the inlet harness connector
Measuring input of the evaluating module defective
Inlet temperature reading implausible in live data
P2E52: Battery Charger Coupler Temperature Sensor D Circuit High
P2E52 is the mirror case of P2E51: the sensor D input sits above its valid band, usually because of an interrupted sensor lead, a connector that has backed out, or a short to a supply line.
Sensor D lead broken or connector backed out
Signal wire shorted to a supply line
Temperature element D open inside the inlet
Measuring input of the evaluating module defective
DC fast charging does not start or stops at once
Inlet temperature reading fixed at an extreme value
P2E53: Battery Charger Coupler Temperature D Too High

P2E53 means measuring point D in the charging inlet reports a contact that is too hot, and charging is throttled or halted. Ford documents this exact code in SSM 55080: on Mustang Mach-E built up to 25 June 2023, E-Transit 2022-2025 and F-150 Lightning 2022-2023, DC fast charging can stop with P2E53:27 and/or P0EEE:27 in the SOBDM.
SOBDM software misjudging DC fast-charge heating (Ford SSM 55080)
Worn or contaminated DC pins in the station plug or the inlet
Very high charging current in hot weather
Heat-damaged inlet contacts needing a new charge port
DC fast charging stops at level 3 stations
AC charging at home or level 2 still works
Charging power reduced during fast charging
P2E54: P2E54 is the general circuit fault of a third exhaust pressure sensor, C. Its position is set by the manufacturer; engines can carry several such sensors, as in a GE patent with one pressure sensor in each of two exhaust manifolds. No manufacturer publicly documents P2E54; Ford's 2023 diesels and its EcoBoost petrol engines use sensor A only.
Exhaust pressure sensor C failed internally
Wiring near the exhaust damaged by heat or chafing
Corroded or loose connector at sensor C
Reduced power if boost or EGR control falls back to substitute values
Other exhaust or EGR monitors may not run
P2E55: Exhaust Pressure Sensor C Circuit Range/Performance

P2E55 is the plausibility test of exhaust pressure sensor C: the voltage is in range, but the pressure does not suit the operating state. CARB wants such rationality faults stored apart from circuit faults. No maker documents P2E55; Ford's 2023 diesel summary shows the pattern for sensor A.
Real back pressure from a clogged particulate filter or catalyst
Sooted or cracked sensing tube to sensor C
Sensor C offset drifted or stuck mid-range
Exhaust leak near the measuring point
MIL, often without noticeable driveability change
Particulate filter or EGR codes alongside
Reduced power if the pressure is really too high
P2E56: Exhaust Pressure Sensor C Circuit Low

P2E56 means the signal of exhaust pressure sensor C stays under the lowest voltage a working sensor can produce. Analogue exhaust pressure sensors return a share of their 5 V reference; Ford's petrol transfer function for sensor A puts 49 kPa at 0.3 V and flags anything under 0.21 V for 5 s, while its 2023 diesels use 0.1 V for 2 s.
Signal wire of sensor C shorted to ground
5 V reference open or pulled down by another sensor
Possible loss of power from substitute values
Further low codes of sensors sharing the reference
P2E57: Exhaust Pressure Sensor C Circuit High

P2E57 reports a signal from exhaust pressure sensor C above the plausible ceiling. For sensor A Ford sets that ceiling at 4.80 V, on petrol engines checked while the EGR monitor runs and with 5 s to fail, on 2023 diesels with 2 s; in Ford's petrol transfer function 4.7 V already equals about 378 kPa.
Open ground circuit of sensor C
Signal wire shorted to the 5 V reference or battery voltage
Open signal wire pulled high by the module input
Boost or EGR control in substitute mode, possibly less power
P2E58: Alternative Fuel Random/Multiple Cylinder Misfire Detected

P2E58 is the collective misfire code for running on the second fuel, mostly CNG or LPG: misfires are counted while gas is burned, but no single cylinder can be blamed, or several each carry a large share.
Gas pressure regulator or LPG vaporiser iced up or not heated enough (low coolant flow, moisture in the gas)
Too little gas pressure at the rail – clogged gas filter, nearly empty tank or weak regulator
Worn plugs or weak coils on several cylinders that cope with petrol but not with the harder-to-ignite gas mixture
Lean gas mixture from an intake air leak or wrong gas-system calibration
Rough running or jerking only while the engine runs on gas
Bi-fuel vehicle switches back to petrol on its own
Check engine light on or flashing, gas-mode indicator may flash
P2E59: P2E59 means that, while the engine is burning its gaseous fuel, the misfire monitor puts the dropouts on cylinder 1; CARB allows a single-cylinder code once more than 90 % of counted misfires fall on one cylinder. In most numbering schemes cylinder 1 is the frontmost. No manufacturer publishes P2E59.
Sticking or leaking gas injector on cylinder 1
Cracked injector hose or loose nozzle in the intake port of cylinder 1
Weak coil or worn plug on cylinder 1 that fails only under gas
Fault in the fuel changeover module or its programming (misfire only at the switch from petrol to gas)
Rough idle on gas that disappears in petrol mode
Stumble at the moment the system changes over to gas
Check engine light, possibly flashing under load
P2E5A: P2E5A says cylinder 2 is the one losing combustion while the engine is supplied with alternative fuel; P0302 is its petrol twin. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. On inline engines cylinder 2 follows cylinder 1; on V engines it is either the foremost cylinder on the other bank (GM, Chrysler) or the second one of the first bank (Ford, Audi).
Gas injector on cylinder 2 gummed or sluggish from compressor oil in the gas
Injector harness of the conversion routed crosswise, so cylinder 2 receives another cylinder's pulse
Injection nozzle of cylinder 2 not properly seated in the manifold port
Coil or plug on cylinder 2 too weak for gas operation
Uneven running on gas, normal on petrol
Higher gas consumption and loss of power
P2E5B: P2E5B flags misfire on cylinder 3 during operation on CNG or LPG; on petrol the matching code is P0303. No manufacturer publishes P2E5B.
Valve seat recession on cylinder 3 from dry gas operation, valve no longer seals
Worn plug or failing coil on cylinder 3
Retrofit gas conversion on an engine without hardened valves and seats
Misfire on gas that slowly gets worse, later also on petrol
Low compression on cylinder 3, sometimes a ticking valve noise
P2E5C: P2E5C is stored when the misfire counter blames cylinder 4 while gas is being burned; in petrol mode the code would be P0304. No manufacturer documents P2E5C publicly, and Deutz's fault list for its eControls LPG, CNG and bi-fuel engines reports such events with the ordinary P0301 to P0304. On four-cylinder engines cylinder 4 is the last one in the block.
Spark plug on cylinder 4 worn or unsuited for gas (gap too wide, wrong heat range)
Coil or plug boot on cylinder 4 breaking down under the higher firing voltage
Gas injector on cylinder 4 sticking or delivering too little
Misfire mainly under load or acceleration on gas
Engine runs cleanly after switching to petrol
Check engine light, flashing during heavy misfire
P2E5D: P2E5D assigns gas-mode misfire to cylinder 5, which exists only on engines with five or more cylinders, such as the 3.6-litre V6 in GM's 2015 Impala bi-fuel, V8 trucks or inline-six gas engines in buses. P0305 is the petrol equivalent. No manufacturer publishes P2E5D.
Spark plug on cylinder 5 past its change interval or damaged when handled
Low-pressure oil separator/filter not serviced, oil reaches the gas injector of cylinder 5
Cracked coil extension or boot on cylinder 5 (heavy-duty gas engines)
Vibration and power loss on gas
Bi-fuel vehicle drops back to petrol
P2E5E: P2E5E names cylinder 6 as the misfiring one while the engine runs on alternative fuel; P0306 is its petrol twin. No manufacturer documents the code openly. On inline sixes cylinder 6 is the rearmost.
Gas or liquid-propane injector on cylinder 6 sticking or leaking
Propane vapour in the liquid-injection rail (hot restart, low rail or tank pressure)
Plug or coil on cylinder 6 failing under gas
Low tank pressure in cold weather or nearly empty tank
Misfire or rough running shortly after a hot restart
Long cranking time when the engine is warm
P2E5F: P2E5F puts alternative-fuel misfire on cylinder 7, so it concerns eight-cylinder engines, for instance GM's Vortec 6.0 V8 in the bi-fuel Silverado/Sierra or the dedicated CNG and LPG Express/Savana vans that GM lists in its gaseous-fuel overview bulletin. P0307 is the petrol counterpart. No maker documents P2E5F publicly.
Gas injector on cylinder 7 faulty or sticking
Leaking injector sleeve or loose nozzle at cylinder 7's intake runner
Conversion injector harness damaged or misrouted near the rear of the engine
Coil or plug on cylinder 7 too weak for gas
Rough running on gas, smooth on petrol
Gas-mode indicator flashing or automatic return to petrol
P2E60: P2E60 is the last cylinder-specific code of the alternative-fuel misfire group and points to cylinder 8; the next code, P2E61, covers misfire with low fuel. Petrol twin: P0308. No manufacturer documents P2E60 openly. On GM V8s cylinder 8 is the rear cylinder of the even-numbered bank, on Ford V8s the rear of the second bank.
Deposits from compressor oil in the gas injector serving cylinder 8
Coil or plug on cylinder 8, often hard to reach at the rear of the engine
Uneven gas split between the two rails starving the bank with cylinder 8 (older bi-fuel systems)
Valve seat wear on cylinder 8 after long gas operation
Misfire on gas, possibly with lean codes on one bank
Engine shakes at idle on gas
P2E61: Alternative Fuel Misfire Detected With Low Fuel
P2E61 records misfire that occurs while the engine burns its gaseous fuel and that fuel is almost used up. No manufacturer documents the code publicly.
Gas tank close to empty, so the regulator can no longer hold rail pressure
Tank pressure or level signal reads too high, so the system stays on gas too long
Restriction in the gas line (clogged filter, ice) that only shows when tank pressure is low
Worn plugs or coils that cannot ignite the leaner gas mixture near empty
Stumbling or power loss on gas when the gas gauge is near empty
Vehicle changes over to petrol on its own
P2E62: Engine Coolant Bypass Valve E Control Circuit/Open

Coolant bypass valve E is the fifth electrically driven coolant valve in the SAE lettering; which coolant path it controls (heater, radiator, transmission, block) is up to the carmaker. P2E62 says the engine computer sees an open or otherwise faulty drive circuit. No manufacturer documents valve E publicly.
Loose, corroded or unplugged connector at the valve
Broken wire in the drive or supply line
Open winding in the valve actuator motor or solenoid
ECM software fault or defective output stage
Check engine light or service message
Heating, warm-up or cooling behaves differently, depending on what valve E controls
Valve stays in its de-energised default position
P2E63: Engine Coolant Bypass Valve E Control Circuit Low

P2E63 flags a drive line for coolant bypass valve E whose voltage is lower than the commanded state allows, typically a grounded wire or a heavy leakage path to ground in the harness or the actuator. No carmaker documents valve E publicly. CARB does not even force separate codes for open and shorted outputs, so many systems use only one code.
Chafed drive wire touching engine ground
Internal short in the valve actuator, often after coolant got into it
Corrosion bridging pins in the connector
Faulty output stage in the engine control module
Check engine light, sometimes a maintenance message
Valve does not move or stays in its default position
Slower warm-up or changed heater output
P2E64: Engine Coolant Bypass Valve E Control Circuit High

P2E64 is the high-side counterpart: the control line of coolant bypass valve E carries more voltage than expected, usually because it touches a supply wire, or the load has gone open in a way the output stage reads as high. Valve E itself appears in no public manufacturer document.
Drive wire chafed through and touching a battery-voltage wire
Moisture or coolant in the connector creating a path to supply voltage
Open actuator winding that the output stage reads as high voltage
Defective output stage in the engine control module
Valve is not driven and stays in its de-energised position
Possible change in heater output or warm-up time
P2E65: Engine Coolant Bypass Valve E Stuck/Open

P2E65 is a functional fault: the electrics of valve E are fine, but the valve remains open although it was told to close. The official title is written Stuck/Open, though it means stuck open, the partner of P2E67. No carmaker documents valve E publicly.
Valve body jammed open by deposits or worn seals
Broken gear or weak actuator that cannot drive the valve closed
Position sensor or its wiring reporting an open valve that is actually closed
Chafed engine harness disturbing drive or feedback signals
Engine and cabin heat take longer to come up
Slightly higher fuel use on short trips
P2E66: Engine Coolant Bypass Valve E Range/Performance

P2E66 is the broad plausibility code for valve E: the valve moves, but not to the right place, not fast enough, or its feedback does not match the command, without a clear stuck-open or stuck-closed verdict. No manufacturer documents valve E publicly.
Cracked or worn gear inside the valve actuator
Valve sluggish from deposits, degraded coolant or worn seals
Position sensor drifting or lost end-stop learn values
Low supply voltage slowing the actuator
Check engine light, sometimes a coolant or maintenance message
Possible fallback to a fixed valve position
P2E67: Engine Coolant Bypass Valve E Stuck Closed
P2E67 means valve E stays shut although the control asked it to open. No manufacturer documents valve E publicly.
Valve jammed closed by deposits, debris or swollen seals
Actuator motor or gearing unable to open the valve
Position feedback stuck at the closed value
Wrong coolant or trapped air after service upsetting the temperature-based check
Little or no heat from the heater, or rising engine temperature, depending on the circuit
Possible reduced engine power to protect the engine
P2E68: System Too Lean During Cylinder Deactivation Bank 1
P2E68 is a fuel trim fault that is judged only while cylinders are shut off: in that mode bank 1 needs more fuel correction than allowed.
Restricted injector on one of the cylinders that keep firing on bank 1
Unmetered air entering bank 1 (intake leak, seal, PCV)
Deactivating rocker or lifter on bank 1 not holding the valves shut, pumping air into the exhaust
Bank 1 oxygen sensor reading biased rich
Check engine light after two trips
Slight shake or surge at light cruise when cylinders are shut off
Cylinder deactivation may be used less often
P2E69: System Too Rich During Cylinder Deactivation Bank 1

P2E69 is the rich mirror of P2E68: with cylinders deactivated, bank 1 has to pull fuel out beyond the permitted range. In GM's 19OBDG07 tables for the 4.2-litre twin-turbo V8 the separate long-term trim factor learned for deactivation mode must drop below 0.77 and stay steady; it shares the enable logic of P2E68 and is Type B, MIL on the second trip.
A cylinder that should be off still breathing, so measured airflow and fuel delivery are too high
Leaking or dribbling direct injector on bank 1
Fuel vapour from diluted oil or a stuck-open purge valve
Bank 1 oxygen sensor reading biased lean
Check engine light after two trips
Higher fuel use, possible fuel smell
P2E6A: System Too Lean During Cylinder Deactivation Bank 2

P2E6A applies the lean test to bank 2, the cylinder row without cylinder 1. GM sets it on the 4.2-litre twin-turbo V8 of the 2019 table 19OBDG07 when the trim factor learned for deactivation mode on bank 2 exceeds 1.23 while stable; Type B.
Weak injector on cylinder 4 or 6, which carry bank 2 in deactivation mode
Bank 2 high-pressure fuel pump delivering too little
Deactivating rocker on bank 2 letting air pass into the exhaust
Exhaust leak ahead of the bank 2 oxygen sensor
Check engine light after two trips
Hesitation at light load in deactivation mode
Often no noticeable change in normal driving
P2E6B: System Too Rich During Cylinder Deactivation Bank 2

P2E6B closes the set: bank 2 runs rich while cylinders are switched off. GM's 19OBDG07 tables (4.2-litre twin-turbo V8, LTA) fail the test when bank 2's deactivation-mode trim factor falls below 0.77 and has settled; Type B, two trips, same enable conditions as the other three codes.
Leaking injector on bank 2, including one on a cylinder that should be shut off
Deactivation rocker or its oil-control solenoid not switching on one cylinder
Excess purge vapour or fuel-diluted engine oil
Bank 2 oxygen sensor reading biased lean
Check engine light after two trips
Higher fuel consumption on the highway
Possible sooty tailpipe on bank 2 side
P2E6C: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack A Cell Thickness

P2E6C means the cells of high-voltage pack A have become thicker than the battery controller tolerates: the cells are swelling. A healthy cell only breathes a little while charging; GE and University of Michigan measured about 0.1 mm, 1 % of its thickness, on the Sanyo cell of Ford's Fusion HEV pack.
Aged cells in pack A that have grown permanently thicker
Gas build-up in cells after overcharging or overheating
Module clamping or end plates loosened, so cells can expand further
Hybrid or EV system warning, often with reduced power
Vehicle may not switch to READY because the main contactors stay open
P2E6D: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack A Cell Thickness Sensor Circuit High
P2E6D says the signal from the cell thickness sensor of pack A sits above the range the controller accepts as a real reading. The code describes the voltage, not swollen cells.
Open signal or ground wire, unplugged or corroded connector inside pack A
Signal wire chafed against a supply or reference line
Thickness or pressure sensing element itself failed open
Power or charging limited as a precaution
In some designs the vehicle will not go to READY
P2E6E: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack A Cell Thickness Sensor Circuit Low

P2E6E is the low-side counterpart to P2E6D: the thickness or swelling sensor of pack A delivers less signal than any intact circuit should, typically from a short to ground, a missing supply or a dead sensor amplifier. No manufacturer documents P2E6E publicly. Two patents show why a low reading can hide a real problem.
Signal wire shorted to ground or to the module housing
Sensor supply or amplifier supply missing
Sensing element or its amplifier failed
Moisture or coolant in a connector inside the pack creating a leakage path
P2E6F: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack A Cell Thickness Sensor Circuit Performance
P2E6F covers a thickness sensor in pack A whose reading is electrically valid but does not behave as the controller expects.
Sensor loosened, shifted or no longer bonded to the cell or end plate
Sensor drifting with age or temperature
Contact resistance in connectors distorting the reading
Missing calibration or relearn after module replacement
Warning light without noticeable driving change at first
Charging or power may be restricted later
P2E70: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack B Cell Thickness

P2E70 is the swelling code for a second high-voltage pack, B, in vehicles that carry two; which pack is A and which B is set by the maker. The controller judges that cells in pack B have grown too thick. No manufacturer documents P2E70 publicly. Research explains why thickness is watched at all.
Cells in pack B aged and permanently thicker
Gas generation after overcharge, deep discharge or heat
Poor cooling of pack B accelerating cell degradation
Hybrid or EV warning with power reduction
P2E71: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack B Cell Thickness Sensor Circuit High

P2E71 flags the thickness sensor circuit of pack B as reading too high. Not every swelling detector is analog: LG's module patent uses a panel that slides along a ramp until it touches a contact sensor, and a Lithium Energy and Power patent fits cells with insulated contact elements that close under pressure.
Sensor connector in pack B not fully seated after battery work
Broken signal or ground wire to the sensor
Signal line shorted to a supply voltage
P2E72: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack B Cell Thickness Sensor Circuit Low

P2E72 means the pack B thickness sensor reports a signal below its valid floor. On a bridge-type strain gauge, the output is a small fraction of the excitation voltage that grows with strain, so losing that excitation or shorting a bridge leg to ground pulls the reading towards zero.
Signal line or sensor shorted to ground inside pack B
Sensor excitation or reference supply lost
Fault in the measuring circuit of the battery monitoring module
Power or charging may be reduced as a precaution
P2E73: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack B Cell Thickness Sensor Circuit Performance
P2E73 indicates that the thickness sensor of pack B delivers values within range that the controller cannot reconcile with what it otherwise knows about the pack.
Sensor mounting or gap changed, for example after module work
Sensor drift or degraded sensing element
Plausibility limits in the battery controller software too tight
Warning light, often with no other complaint
Battery controller may limit power or charging rate
P2E74: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Temperature Sensor D Circuit

P2E74 covers any circuit fault of coolant temperature sensor D, the fourth such sensor a maker can fit to the battery's liquid cooling. Battery controllers typically watch coolant at the pack inlet and outlet; GM's Volt and ELR tables use sensor A for the inlet and B for the outlet. Where a sensor D sits is not public.
Damaged wire, loose connector or corroded terminal at sensor D
Fault on the shared 5 V reference circuit of the battery controller
Hybrid system or check engine light
Battery cooling or heating not working as intended
Reduced electric power or charging rate
P2E75: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Temperature Sensor D Circuit Range/Performance

P2E75 means battery coolant sensor D gives a reading that is electrically fine yet does not match the other temperatures in the loop. No manufacturer documents P2E75 publicly. GM's sensor B (outlet) shows how such a check works: with the pump above 20 % the outlet value is compared with inlet and average cell temperature.
Sensor D drifting or responding slowly
Plausibility logic in controller software too strict (update available)
Air pocket or poor coolant flow around the sensor
Warning light, frequently with no other symptom
Less effective battery cooling or heating
P2E76: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Temperature Sensor D Circuit Low

P2E76 reports that the voltage on battery coolant sensor D has dropped below its lower limit. Because these sensors are NTC thermistors whose resistance falls as they warm, a low voltage stands for very hot coolant, and a grounded signal wire or a sensor with an internal short produces exactly that picture. No manufacturer documents P2E76 publicly.
Signal wire of sensor D shorted to ground
Sensor D shorted internally, for example after coolant entered it
Actual overheating of the battery coolant loop
Cooling may run at full effort or power may be cut back
P2E77: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Temperature Sensor D Circuit High

P2E77 is set when the signal of battery coolant sensor D rises to or near the reference voltage. In a pull-up NTC circuit that is the signature of an open: a disconnected plug, a broken wire, a spread pin or a sensor element that has gone open, and the controller then sees a coolant temperature colder than physically plausible.
Sensor D connector unplugged or not latched after cooling system work
Broken wire or spread terminal in the sensor D circuit
Battery heating may switch on needlessly or behave oddly in winter
P2E78: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Temperature Sensor D Circuit Intermittent/Erratic

P2E78 stands for a coolant temperature from sensor D that jumps around, mostly without leaving the electrical limits. A liquid loop changes temperature slowly, so fast swings point to a loose contact rather than to the coolant. No manufacturer documents P2E78 publicly.
Loose or fretting terminal in the sensor D connector
Harness rubbing through near moving or vibrating parts
Warning light that comes and goes
Coolant temperature in live data jumping
P2E79: Hybrid/EV Electronics Coolant Pump C Performance

P2E79 is the functional verdict on a third pump in the coolant loop of the traction electronics: command and wiring look healthy, yet the pump does not move coolant the way the controller expects. No manufacturer documents P2E79 or says which pump it calls C.
Air trapped in the electronics coolant loop after service or a leak
Pump C worn or impeller fouled, delivering too little flow
Kinked hose or clogged cooler passages in the loop
Control software misjudging pump function (update available)
Hybrid or EV system warning lamp, possibly MIL
Drive power or charging rate limited because electronics run warm
Gurgling or whirring noise from the electronics coolant loop
P2E7A: Hybrid/EV Electronics Coolant Pump C Overspeed

P2E7A means the third electronics coolant pump spins faster than the speed it was given. A centrifugal pump that draws air instead of liquid loses its load and races, so a low coolant level, a leak or a poorly bled loop come first, a slipping impeller or false speed feedback later. No manufacturer documents P2E7A.
Coolant level low or air pocket at the pump inlet
Leak or defective seal in the electronics coolant loop
Impeller loose on its shaft or broken
Faulty speed feedback from the pump electronics
Coolant or hybrid system warning, possibly MIL
Coolant reservoir level dropping, traces of leakage
Pump runs loud or churns; power or charging may be reduced
P2E7B: Drive Motor A Excitation Current Sensor Circuit

P2E7B is the general circuit fault of the measuring element for the DC field current in the rotor of drive motor A. It exists only in electrically excited synchronous motors, whose rotor field comes from a winding, as in Renault's Megane E-Tech, Nissan's Ariya and BMW's fifth-generation eDrive.
Supply or reference of the excitation current sensor lost
Open or corroded connection between sensor and motor controller
Excitation current sensor or its isolated amplifier failed
Measuring input inside the inverter or motor controller defective
Electric drive warning lamp and MIL
Noticeably reduced power or no drive from motor A
Vehicle may refuse to enter ready mode
P2E7C: A/C Compressor Control Module Internal Temperature Sensor B Circuit
P2E7C covers the second internal temperature sensor in the control electronics of an electric A/C compressor.
Sensor B or its circuit on the compressor control board defective
Compressor controller fails to evaluate or transmit the value
Unstable 12 V supply, ground or data link to the compressor
A/C cools weakly or switches off
On plug-in hybrids and EVs, battery cooling and fast charging may be limited
Warning message on the climate display; MIL depends on the manufacturer
P2E7D: A/C Compressor Control Module Internal Temperature Sensor B Performance

P2E7D is the plausibility check for internal temperature sensor B of the electric A/C compressor controller: the reading is electrically in range yet conflicts with other temperatures. The test runs after a long rest, when all sensors should read alike. No manufacturer documents P2E7D.
Sensor B drifted or poorly coupled to its measuring point
Comparison value wrong, e.g. outside air or second internal sensor faulty
Compressor still warm from recent use or preconditioning when the test ran
Usually no noticeable effect at first; fault stored after a cold start
Compressor may derate early or shut off on a wrong temperature
MIL on some vehicles after two drive cycles
P2E7E: A/C Compressor Control Module Internal Temperature Sensor B Circuit High

P2E7E reports that internal temperature sensor B of the A/C compressor controller delivers a signal above its valid range. Most sensors of this kind produce a voltage that falls as temperature rises; TI's compressor inverter reference uses such an analog part, so a high signal stands for an impossibly cold reading.
Sensor B path open, e.g. cracked solder joint on the board
Reference or ground of the measuring circuit lost inside the module
Analog input of the compressor controller defective
Compressor runs restricted or not at all
Cabin and, where present, battery cooling weaker
MIL possible after two drive cycles depending on manufacturer
P2E7F: A/C Compressor Control Module Internal Temperature Sensor B Circuit Low
P2E7F is the low-signal counterpart: sensor B inside the compressor control module reports a value below its valid band, which for a sensor with falling output means an impossibly hot reading.
Short circuit in the sensor B path on the control board
Power stage genuinely overheating, e.g. low refrigerant charge
Measuring circuit of the compressor controller defective
Compressor derates or shuts down for overheat protection
Air conditioning blows warm, battery cooling may be limited

P2E80: A/C Compressor Control Module Internal Temperature Sensor B Circuit Intermittent/Erratic

With P2E80 the controller sees the reading of sensor B, a second internal thermometer in the compressor electronics, flicker: values leap or vanish for an instant and then look normal again. Set criteria for P2E80 are not published by any manufacturer.
Loose contact or cold solder joint in the sensor B circuit
Electrical interference from the inverter switching on the measuring line
Fluctuating 12 V supply or ground of the compressor controller
A/C cuts out and recovers sporadically

P2E81: Cold Start Engine Coolant Bypass Valve D Stuck Closed

P2E81 is the cold-start version of P26C2 for valve D, which GM uses as the block rotary valve between two mechanical end stops. Its 2025 ECM tables (25OBDG03B) count a failure when commanded and measured position differ by more than 5° while raw feedback stays below 50°, i.e. on the closed side, in 4 of 5 seconds; Type B, MIL after two trips.
Block rotary valve stuck on the closed side (deposits, wear)
Valve actuator too weak to turn the valve when coolant is cold and thick
Chafed or corroded harness to the valve actuator
Invalid end-stop learn values after repair or battery disconnect
Check engine light after two trips
Engine temperature rising faster or unevenly after a cold start
P2E82: Cold Start Engine Coolant Pump Overspeed

P2E82 flags an electric main coolant pump that spins faster than requested while the cold-start warm-up strategy runs. GM's 2025 ECM tables (25OBDG03B) subtract reported from requested speed, filter the result and fail the test when it falls below −200 rpm in 8 of 10 seconds; Type B, MIL after two trips.
Low coolant level or air trapped after service, so the impeller runs dry
Impeller loose or damaged, so the motor turns without load
Faulty pump electronics or speed feedback signal
Flow path blocked by a stuck valve, changing the pump load
Check engine light after two trips
Gurgling noises or weak heater output
Rising engine temperature if coolant is missing
P2E83: Fuel Rail Pressure Performance - Engine Off

P2E83 covers a fuel rail pressure check that runs once the engine is shut down: the residual pressure in the rail falls too fast, stays too high or behaves implausibly. No manufacturer documents the code publicly. For monitors active at standstill, CARB extends the driving cycle through the shutdown period until the next start.
Injector leaking into the cylinder, so rail pressure decays too quickly
Leaking pump check valve or pressure relief valve
Rail pressure sensor with offset or drift, implausible at rest
Pressure rising after shutdown from heat soak with no way to relieve it
Long cranking or rough start after the car has stood
Possible fuel smell or smoke right after starting
P2E84: Battery Charger B Input Voltage Sensor Circuit Range/Performance

P2E84 questions the plausibility of the grid voltage that charger B reads at its input: the sensor answers within its electrical limits, yet the figure does not suit the moment, such as a voltage with no supply connected or a value that contradicts other readings. No manufacturer documents P2E84 publicly.
Voltage sensing inside charger B drifting or faulty
Corroded or loose AC contacts between charge inlet and charger B
Unstable or unusual supply from the charging station or house circuit
AC charging does not start or stops after a short time

Charging fault message in the instrument cluster or app
P2E85: Battery Charger B Input Voltage Sensor Circuit Low

P2E85 means the input voltage signal of charger B sits too low, so the car sees little or no grid voltage while it expects AC. GM uses the code on its battery-electric models, from the 2017 Bolt EV to the Lyriq, Hummer EV, Blazer, Equinox and Silverado EV and BrightDrop vans, under the wording input voltage sensor circuit low voltage.
DC-only NACS adapter used on an AC charger
Charging station or house circuit not delivering AC voltage
Open or high-resistance AC path between inlet and charger B
Sensing circuit inside charger B shorted to ground
Vehicle does not charge on a Level 1 or Level 2 AC charger

P2E86: Battery Charger B Input Voltage Sensor Circuit High

P2E86 flags an input voltage signal of charger B above the highest value the measurement can plausibly produce. Home sockets and AC stations stay far below that, so the fault normally lies in the sensing path or its signal line, rarely in the grid. No manufacturer documents P2E86 publicly.
Voltage sensing circuit inside charger B faulty
Sensor signal line shorted to a supply voltage
Lost reference ground of the measurement
AC charging refused or ended immediately
Charging system warning in the cluster

P2E87: P2E87 is the general fault of a second plug-detection circuit, B, whose job is to tell the vehicle that a connector is seated in an inlet.
Damaged or corroded proximity contact in inlet B
Open or poorly seated connector between inlet B and the controller
Faulty charging cable or plug resistor
Evaluation circuit in the charger or control unit faulty
No charging through the affected inlet
Plug not recognised or vehicle reports a cable while none is fitted
Vehicle may refuse to enter drive readiness
P2E88: P2E88 flags plug sensing on circuit B whose value is electrically valid but makes no sense, typically a voltage that falls between the defined steps for no plug, plug latched and release button pressed.
Worn or dirty proximity contact raising the resistance
Charging cable or adapter with off-standard coding resistor
Moisture in inlet B creating leakage paths
Control software judging the signal wrongly
Charging aborts or the current is limited unexpectedly
Plug status changes without anyone touching the connector
Fault appears only with certain cables
P2E89: P2E89 stands for a voltage on proximity circuit B below the band the controller accepts in a state where no plug can be present.
Proximity line of circuit B chafed and shorted to ground
Water or dirt in inlet B bridging the contact to earth
Defective charging cable left in the inlet
Input stage in the evaluating control unit damaged

Warning lamp, depending on manufacturer the MIL
P2E8A: P2E8A is the opposite of P2E89: the proximity line of circuit B sits above the accepted band. Because the evaluating controller usually pulls the pin up to a reference such as 5 V, as described for Watt & Well's EVCC, an open wire or a missing earth path reads high just like a short to a supply.
Broken proximity wire or unplugged connector at inlet B
Missing protective-earth path in inlet or cable
Proximity line shorted to a supply voltage
