Warning lamp, depending on manufacturer the MIL
P2E8B: P2E8B describes a plug-detection signal on circuit B that drops out or jumps for moments, so the car sees a connector appear and vanish although nobody touched it.
Loose low-voltage connector on the proximity line
Worn proximity contact in inlet B or on the cable plug
Chafed wire with intermittent contact to ground
Moisture in the inlet after rain or washing
Charging stops and restarts at random

P2E8C: Battery Charger B Charge Sequence Signal 1 Circuit High

Charge sequence signals 1 and 2 belong to DC fast charging to CHAdeMO, used for example on the Nissan Leaf, the Mitsubishi i-MiEV and the Outlander PHEV. Signal 1 runs over connector pin 2: the station closes its switch d1 and applies 12 V to the line, which tells the car it is ready and starts the CAN dialogue.
Sequence signal 1 line shorted to a 12 V source
Moisture or debris in the DC inlet bridging pins
Faulty input stage in the evaluating control unit
Station switch d1 not opening at the end of a session
DC fast charging refused or ending with an error
Charging fault message in the cluster
P2E8D: Battery Charger B Charge Sequence Signal 1 Circuit Low

P2E8D means the vehicle finds the first CHAdeMO sequence line low while the fast charger should be driving it. Signal 1 is the opening move of a session: once the plug is detected the station closes d1 and applies 12 V, and only after that does the CAN exchange of battery limits begin.
Sequence signal 1 line shorted to ground
Open wire or damaged pin 2 in the DC inlet
Fast charger not closing its switch d1
Faulty input stage in the evaluating control unit
DC fast charging does not start
Station reports a communication or vehicle error
P2E8E: Battery Charger B Charge Sequence Signal 2 Circuit High

P2E8E concerns the second CHAdeMO sequence line, which works differently from the first: the station closes switch d2 to tie the line to ground, completing the circuit that sequence signal 1 feeds, and only then may the vehicle close its high-voltage contactors. Before that the connector has been latched and the vehicle has given charge permission.
Open wire or damaged pin 10 in the DC inlet
Fast charger switch d2 not closing
Sequence signal 2 line shorted to a supply voltage
Faulty input stage in the evaluating control unit
DC session stops after insulation test without current flowing
P2E8F: Battery Charger B Charge Sequence Signal 2 Circuit Low

P2E8F reports the second CHAdeMO sequence line pulled low at a time it should be released. Because the station uses d2 to connect this line to ground as the very last step before the vehicle closes its contactors, and opens d2 first when the session ends, a line already at ground early, or still at ground once d2 is open, contradicts the sequence.
Sequence signal 2 line shorted to ground
Fast charger switch d2 stuck closed
Water or dirt in the DC inlet
Faulty input stage in the evaluating control unit
DC fast charging refused right after plugging in
Session ends with an error instead of a normal stop
P2E90: Battery Charger A Internal Power Supply Performance
P2E90 says the internal power supply of charger A, the rails that feed its control and gate-driver electronics, does not behave as intended.
Internal supply stage of charger A or the ICCU failed
Weak 12 V feed or loose low-voltage connector at the charger
No AC charging at home or on Level 2 stations
DC fast charging may still work
Charging system warning in the cluster
P2E91: Battery Charger B Internal Power Supply Performance

P2E91 is the same verdict for charger B: one of its internally generated supply voltages is wrong, so the charger cannot run its power stages safely. Polestar uses the code on the Polestar 3, whose grid-to-high-voltage converter GHCA reports as charger B.
Internal supply stage of charger B failed
Loose low-voltage connector or weak 12 V feed at charger B
AC charging fails while DC fast charging still works
Charging time much longer or charging stops early
Charging socket light signals a fault
P2E92: Charge Port Door B Open Request Switch Wake-Up Circuit

P2E92 concerns cars with a second electrically opened charge door. Its open-request switch or sensor must be able to rouse sleeping control units, so besides its normal signal it drives a wake-up line, and P2E92 records that the two disagree.
Open or shorted wake-up wire between switch and control unit
Worn switch or sensor at door B giving mismatched signals
Water ingress or corrosion at the door B connector
Wake-up input of the control unit faulty
Charge door B does not open on request every time
Door opens only from the screen or the other side works normally
Increased standby drain if the line keeps waking modules
P2E93: Charge Port Door B Open Request Switch Circuit
P2E93 is the basic circuit fault of the input with which the driver asks the second charge flap to open.
Touch or wipe sensor of flap B with a wrong internal resistance
Partly broken or corroded signal wire to the flap B sensor
Moisture in the connector at the flap module
Faulty input stage in the control unit reading the sensor
Charge flap B does not react to touch or hand gesture
Flap B still opens via the central display or app
Charging flap warning in the instrument cluster
P2E94: Charge Port Door B Open Request Switch Circuit Performance
With P2E94 the open request input of charge flap B is electrically sound, yet its behaviour cannot be right, for example a request that stays active for far too long.
Deformed or recessed flap B keeping the request button pressed
Sensor of flap B shifted or not seated correctly
Ice or dirt acting on the sensor area

Opening via the display or charging menu still works
Flap B sits deeper than the surrounding body panel
P2E95: Charge Port Door B Open Request Switch Circuit Low

P2E95 says the request signal from charge flap B has dropped under the bottom of its permitted range. Usual reasons are a signal wire touching ground, water bridging the connector pins or an internally shorted sensor. Depending on the wiring, the control unit may take this as a button held down all the time. No manufacturer documents P2E95 publicly.
Signal wire of the flap B sensor shorted to ground
Water in the flap B connector bridging the contacts
Request sensor of flap B failed short internally
Flap B does not open on touch, or only with the manual release
Control unit may stay awake longer, raising standby drain
P2E96: Charge Port Door B Open Request Switch Circuit High

P2E96 is stored when the request signal of charge flap B climbs past the top of its permitted range. Contact with a 12 V supply raises it, and so does a broken sensor ground or switch path that lets a pulled-up input float. The control unit then usually sees a request that never arrives. No manufacturer documents P2E96 publicly.
Sensor signal wire shorted to a 12 V supply
Interrupted ground or switch path at the flap B sensor
Pushed-back or loose pin in the flap module connector
Flap B never reacts to the hand or touch
Opening from the centre console or display still works
Warning that the charging flap is impaired
P2E97: Charge Port Door B Open Request Switch Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P2E97 points to a request signal from charge flap B that briefly vanishes or jumps, while no permanent fault can be found.
Sensor on flap B not held firmly, adhesive strip loosened
Loose terminal in the flap B connector
Harness to flap B damaged by repeated movement
Flap B opens only on some attempts
Code stored without a lasting fault in the workshop
P2E98: Charge Port Door B Position Sensor Circuit
P2E98 is the general circuit code for the sensor that reports whether charge flap B is open or shut.
Software fault in the DC charging unit reporting a false sensor fault (Mercedes)
Position sensor of flap B with a wrong internal resistance
Damaged wire or connector between sensor and control unit
Malfunction indicator lamp on, charging and starting normal (Mercedes)
Flap B may stay shut or show a wrong status
P2E99: Charge Port Door B Position Sensor Circuit Performance
P2E99 means the position signal of charge flap B is within its electrical limits yet contradicts what the flap is doing, for instance closed although the flap was just opened.
Position sensor or its harness giving a wrong end-position signal
Oxidation or particles in the flap actuator that houses the detection
Software misreading the flap state at start-up
Message asking to close a charging flap although both are closed
Opposite flap A locked and not operable
P2E9A: Charge Port Door B Position Sensor Circuit Low

P2E9A reports that the flap B position signal has fallen under its lowest valid value. A signal wire chafed against ground, water in the connector or an internally shorted sensor are the usual reasons.
Position signal wire of flap B shorted to ground
Water in the sensor connector at flap B
Flap B status in the display does not change
Charging blocked or charging flap warning
P2E9B: Charge Port Door B Position Sensor Circuit High

P2E9B is the high-side position fault of charge flap B: the reading lies above anything a working sensor can deliver. A signal wire touching 12 V, or a missing sensor ground, letting the input drift upwards, are typical explanations. No manufacturer documents P2E9B publicly.
Position signal wire shorted to a 12 V feed
Broken ground wire of the flap B position sensor
Corroded or loose connector at the flap module
Permanent message that a charging flap is open
Charging not possible on either side
P2E9C: Charge Port Door B Position Sensor Circuit Intermittent/Erratic

P2E9C covers a flap B position signal that flickers or drops out briefly instead of failing for good. Common sources are loose terminals, a harness bent at every flap movement, or a sensor sitting loose in its holder. No manufacturer documents P2E9C publicly. Two official cases show how fragile this signal path can be on two-flap cars.
Loose terminal in the position sensor connector
Harness to flap B strained or chafed by flap movement
Oxidation or particles in the flap actuator with integrated detection
Flap status in the display switches without reason
Sporadic charging flap warnings or interrupted charging

P2E9D concerns the output that releases or drives charge flap B, not its sensors. Depending on the design this is a latch actuator or a small motor: Audi's e-tron family uses lock actuators F496 and F497 for its high-voltage charging flaps on the two sides, and Porsche's Taycan a servo motor per charge port door. Faulty output stage in the control unit

P2E9E is a function check: the control unit commands flap B to unlock and then expects the position sensor to confirm an open flap. GM's tables for the A flap of the Volt set P0CD2 when that report is missing after 5 seconds (2011) or 13 seconds (2013, only above minus 12 °C), skip the test while position or output codes are active, and use Type B.

P2E9F is the low-voltage form of the flap B release output fault: the driver stage measures its control line close to 0 V where a higher level is expected. A control wire chafed to body ground or an actuator winding that has shorted are the usual culprits, and a protective fuse or driver shutdown can follow. No manufacturer documents P2E9F publicly.

P2EA0 marks the opposite case at the flap B release output: the line sits at a high voltage while the driver stage should be pulling it down or keeping it off. Contact with a 12 V circuit does this, and on low-side switched outputs an interrupted actuator or wire gives the same reading. No manufacturer documents P2EA0 publicly.

P2EA1 is the general electrical fault of a sixth exhaust temperature probe on bank 1, counting from the engine towards the tailpipe. P2EA2 says the signal of the sixth bank 1 exhaust probe sits above its upper electrical limit. Which temperature that implies depends on the element. Most probes form a voltage divider with a pull-up resistor in the module; an open lead then drives the input to the reference, which an NTC part reads as extreme cold and a platinum (PTC) part as extreme heat.

With P2EA3 the input of the sixth bank 1 exhaust probe drops below the lowest value a healthy circuit can deliver. Electrically this is nearly always a short: the signal wire touching ground or the exhaust, or an element whose insulation has broken down.
Signal wire chafed through to ground or to the exhaust pipe

Water or road salt bridging the connector pins

P2EA5: Exhaust Gas Temperature Sensor Circuit Range/Performance Bank 1 Sensor 6
P2EA5 is the plausibility fault of the sixth bank 1 exhaust probe: the voltage is electrically valid, yet the temperature does not match what the exhaust is doing.

P2EA6 is the general circuit fault of the temperature sensor in the charge pipe between the turbo compressor and the charge air cooler.

P2EA8 is the reverse of P2EA7: the DC input of converter A lies above its permitted window. P2EAA: Active Radiator Air Flow Control Module A Control Circuit Performance

The active radiator air flow system meters cooling air with motor-driven flaps between bumper opening and radiator; J2012 keeps its control module apart from the grille shutter modules (P05C0, U0284).

P2EB2: Throttle Valve Intake Air Pressure Sensor Circuit High

P2EB3 covers a throttle inlet pressure that is electrically fine but wrong. With the engine stopped, the pressure ahead of the throttle must equal manifold and barometric pressure; Ford checks this at key-up after at least 10 s off, allowing about 2.7 inHg between boost and manifold sensor.

Object or ice between ground pad and vehicle coil

No noticeable change in how the engine runs
P2EBC: P2EBC means the crankcase temperature sensor delivers an electrically valid value that does not suit the engine state: it may stick, react too slowly or sit far from the coolant and oil temperatures after a long stop. The CARB rule 13 CCR 1968.2 calls in (e)(15.2.1) for rationality checks that catch readings that are wrongly high as well as wrongly low.
Sensor drifted or slow because of sludge or oil coking on the tip
Contact resistance in the connector shifting the value
Replacement sensor with a different characteristic fitted
Check engine lamp after the fault is confirmed
Crankcase reading disagrees with oil and coolant temperature on a cold start
Crankcase ventilation checks may not complete
P2EBD: P2EBD is set when the crankcase temperature signal rises above its highest valid voltage. With the usual pull-up arrangement this happens when the current path through the sensor is interrupted, for example by an unplugged or oil-soaked connector, a broken wire or an open element, or when the signal touches the 5 V reference or battery voltage.
Connector unplugged, oil-soaked or with spread terminals
Signal shorted to 5 V reference or battery voltage
Crankcase temperature fixed at an extreme value
P2EBE: P2EBE reports a crankcase temperature signal below the lowest voltage the circuit can produce when intact. In practice a short is behind it: either the signal lead has rubbed through to ground on the engine block, or the insulation inside the sensor has given way, for instance after oil has crept into the housing.
Signal wire chafed through to ground on the engine
Sensor shorted internally after oil ingress
Faulty input stage in the engine control module
Live data shows an implausible crankcase temperature
Crankcase heating or ventilation checks suspended
P2EBF: P2EBF reports that the control used to select a battery charging mode stays in one state, most likely a button that reads as permanently pressed.
Button mechanically jammed or contact welded in the pressed state
Spilled liquid or dirt in the console switch panel
Short in the switch signal wire imitating a held button
Engine keeps running to charge the traction battery
Charging mode cannot be switched on or off
Higher fuel use and less electric driving
P2EC0: Turbocharger Compressor Outlet Temperature Sensor Circuit Low

P2EC0 reports that the compressor outlet temperature signal has fallen under the lowest valid voltage. Air temperature sensors on the intake side are usually NTC thermistors, as Bosch states for its combined boost pressure and temperature sensor; their resistance shrinks as they warm, so a signal pulled towards ground is read as extreme heat.
Signal wire shorted to ground, e.g. chafed on the charge pipe
Oil or moisture bridging the connector pins
Live data shows an implausibly hot charge air temperature
Possible loss of power if a substitute value limits boost
P2EC1: Turbocharger Compressor Outlet Temperature Sensor Circuit High

P2EC1 is set when the compressor outlet temperature sensor delivers a voltage above its permitted window. Because the module feeds the sensor through a pull-up resistor, any break in the current path lifts the input to the reference: an unplugged or corroded connector, a cracked wire or a burnt-out element.
Connector unplugged, corroded or with spread terminals
Signal shorted to 5 V reference or battery voltage
Live data shows a fixed extreme value
Usually no noticeable change in driving
P2EC2: Turbocharger Compressor Outlet Temperature Sensor Circuit Range/Performance

P2EC2 flags a compressor outlet temperature that is electrically valid but does not fit the operating point. A reference is easy to build: Cummins (US6401457) derives the outlet temperature from inlet temperature and pressure, turbo speed, air mass and pressure ratio, and after a long soak the sensor should also agree with intake and ambient readings.
Sensor drifted or reacting too slowly
Tip coated with oil from crankcase or turbo seals
Sensor loose or not reaching into the air stream
Check engine lamp after the fault is confirmed
Reading disagrees with intake and ambient temperature after a cold soak
Charge air cooler diagnosis may be suspended
